about: THE WIKI, baked from the game's own data by Bake/content/make_wiki.py with the hand-written rules of Bake/content/wiki_rules.json (Design/wiki.md; DECISIONS.md, 7 October 2026, rulings 3 and 6). Do not edit: change the data or wiki_rules.json and bake again. pages: id, kind, title, hint (what it is called before it is known), brief (the box under the pointer), game (what it is and does for the player), known (what the record says, from the data's own notes; game and known may hold line breaks between paragraphs), source (as the data gives it), links (the pages its text names, and for a port its sites and people), opens, first_release. later: text that names a day after the first morning (21 June 793), each piece with the date after which it may be shown and the part (game or known) it belongs to: show a piece only when that day has passed in the game. opens: always | port_heard:<port> (heard of, or seen) | port_seen:<port> | good_seen:<good> | person_met:<person> | word_heard:<tongue.word> | text_held:<text> | date:<yyyy-mm-dd> (the day has passed); two rules joined by & must both hold. A How to play page also has built (false: ruled but not in the game, hold the page back), built_note and holds, which are for the builders, not the player. names: every word or phrase that links, the longest first; a note says who else wanted the word and why this page won, and 'also' lists the others, so that the frame may choose by where it stands (on a port's own pages, that port's Gerbrand). A name is matched exactly as written, capitals and all, where the letters before and after it are not letters; the longest wins; the first use in a box becomes the link. shields: phrases that hold a name and must not link (New York is not York): match a shield like a name and make no link of it. The baker read each page's links from its brief and game text, and from its known text too for ports, goods, peoples, faiths, days and rules; the known text of the other kinds and every source line are citations, and are better left unlinked. left_out: words that would have linked and were kept back, with the reason. (?) in a text marks what the record leaves in doubt or what was not checked; LATER marks a source written long after.

pages.title: This book
pages.hint: This book
pages.brief: What you know, and how you came to know it. The rules are here from the first day; the world comes in as you learn it.
pages.game: This book holds what you know and how you came to know it. The rules are all here from the first day. A port comes in when you see it or hear it named, a good when you see it traded, a person when you meet them, a word when someone says it to you. The true account of a dated event shows only when that day has passed in your game. Each page keeps two things apart: what a thing is in the game, and what the record says of it, with its source. A word in the link colour, anywhere on the screen, has a page: rest the pointer on it for a brief word, and click it to open the page. A (?) marks what the record leaves in doubt or what was not checked, and LATER marks a source written long after.
pages.built_note: On 7 Oct, 10:40, no Wiki panel stood in Assets/Kapman/Code/Game/UI/Frame/Panels, and wiring_plan.md 8.8 says the panel and the links are not built. If the panel builder has reached it since, set this to true.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, rulings 3 and 6; Design/wiki.md.

pages.title: Days and the clock
pages.hint: Days and the clock
pages.brief: Days are what everything costs. The clock has a pause and five speeds, and only a card or a talk that needs an answer holds it.
pages.game: Days are what everything costs: bread is eaten by the day, pay is owed by the day, and the debt falls due on a day. The clock has a pause and five speeds. At speed 1 a minute of the game passes in each second of yours, and a day in 24 minutes. At speed 2 a day passes in 6 minutes, at speed 3 in a minute, at speed 4 in fifteen seconds, at speed 5 in four seconds. No time is skipped at any speed: the same things happen, only sooner, and resting and waiting for a tide run at the speed you have chosen. Windows never hold the clock, at sea or in port, so you read, plan, trade and look things up while she sails. Only a card or a talk that needs an answer holds it, and your own pause. When a card holds the clock you may set it running again at once, with Space or a clock button: the card stays open and waits. The clock slows by itself when something needs you: nearing the port you are bound for, made fast, raiders made out, little bread, the debt's day. The plus key then goes back to the speed you had. Each of these has a switch under Menu, The clock. Space pauses and goes on; the plus and minus keys change the speed.
pages.built_note: PanelClock.OnlyCards and PanelClock.GoOn; GameSpeed (pause and five speeds; Space; + and -); the game steps its own clock a game minute at a time (ClockStepper, KapmanGame.RunClock), so a wait runs at the chosen speed; ClockDrops and ClockSettings are the clock's own drops and their switches.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October: the picker's ruling 1 (no time is skipped) and rulings 5 and 6 of later the same day ('It stops the clock but you can override it immediately if you want'), and ruling 26 (five speeds, like CK3).

pages.title: A card left unanswered
pages.hint: A card left unanswered
pages.brief: A card you leave open while the clock runs answers itself: an ordinary one after seven days, a pressing one sooner.
pages.game: A card opens and holds the clock. If you set the clock running without answering, an ordinary card stays open for seven days of the game and then takes one of its choices by itself. The card names which choice; if it names none, it takes the one that changes least. It says so in the log. A pressing card, such as a raider, a squall or a man overboard, holds the ship where she is until it is answered, and takes its choice after a shorter time of its own, set by the card. The seven days count only while the clock runs.
pages.built_note: Not in the game. A card whose hold was let go is marked (Float.released in FrameRoot.Floats.cs), but nothing counts its days, and the cards' files have no urgency and name no choice to take (wiring_plan.md 8.9).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, rulings 10 and 12. Ruling 12 corrects 10: an ordinary card waits a week, not for ever.

pages.title: Who you are
pages.hint: Who you are
pages.brief: Three picks before the first morning: your people, your faith and your past.
pages.game: Before the first morning you make three picks: your people, your faith and your past. Your people sets where you begin, your first tongue, the tongues you half know, and the colours of the chart. Your faith sets what you may do on which day, what you may carry and how you swear. Your past tilts your stats and puts one thing in your chest. The pasts are: the steersman's child; schooled at the minster, and left; a freed thrall; the toll-keeper's clerk; a younger child of a hall; the widow who kept the boat; a captive come home; a foundling of the house of God.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Self.cs asks the three picks on a new game; Self.Begin makes the self; ChartWorld.StartAt lays her at her people's port; a click on a people shows the chart in its colours. Of what a faith asks, nothing bites yet (see Faith and days).
pages.holds: Design/fate_faith_and_self.md sections 1 and 6a; story/self_793.json.

pages.title: The five stats
pages.hint: The five stats
pages.brief: Tongue, Name, Nerve, Lore and Troth, each from one pip to five. They rise by use, never by spending points.
pages.game: You have five stats. Tongue is talking a thing through; Name is how you look and who stands behind you; Nerve is holding firm; Lore is what you have read, heard and can quote; Troth is how well you keep the way of your own faith. Each runs from one pip to five. All begin at one, and Troth at three; your past adds its tilt. A stat rises by use and never by spending points: each check you win by it adds a share of a pip, and a larger share against someone who resisted you. Troth is not raised that way: it follows how you keep the days and duties of your own faith.
pages.built_note: Self.cs: five stats of 1 to 5, the start from self_793.json, Self.Used (a third of a pip against one who resisted, a tenth otherwise, less the higher the stat). The cards read me.tongue and the rest. Nothing moves Troth yet, and the other ways a stat rises or falls in self_793.json are not wired.
pages.holds: Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 2; story/self_793.json.

pages.title: Talk and the odds
pages.hint: Talk and the odds
pages.brief: A choice that rests on a stat wears its name, like [Nerve]. Its odds are a word: sure, likely or doubtful.
pages.game: In a talk or on a card each choice says what it is. A choice that rests on one of your five stats wears the stat's name before it, like [Nerve]. Where there is a chance in it, the odds are given as a word: sure, likely or doubtful. Each pip of the stat above three makes the chance a little better, and each pip below three a little worse. What came of your choice is written out before you go on.
pages.built_note: FloatOption has a tag and odds as a word; the engine's rule is the written chance plus 0.05 for each pip over three (EncounterGameVars.cs, Effects). Quote, As kin, the gift and how you look (fate_faith_and_self.md section 2) are not built and are not described here.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 4 October, no. 18 (odds as a word); Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 2.

pages.title: Cards and talks
pages.hint: Cards and talks
pages.brief: A card or a talk opens as a window floating over the chart. One that needs an answer holds the clock.
pages.game: A card or a talk opens as a window floating over the middle of the chart, and whoever speaks stands in the portrait's place while he speaks. Several may be up at once; a click brings one forward. Keys 1 to 9 take a choice of the one in front, Enter takes its marked choice, and Esc shuts it if it may be shut. One that needs an answer holds the clock until you answer, or until you set the clock running yourself.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Floats.cs (FloatSpec, CardFloat, TalkFloat, AlertFloats). A speaker's face is an empty shape until the cards' people are joined to the places files' people (wiring_plan.md 8.8).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 2 (pop-ups over the middle of the chart) and the picker's ruling 3 (whoever is speaking, while they speak).

pages.title: Setting a course
pages.hint: Setting a course
pages.brief: Pick a port in the Voyage window and set its course. She sails it by herself: you do not steer.
pages.game: The Voyage window lists the ports you know, seen or only heard of, each with the days to it for your boat as a low and a high figure. Pick one and its course is drawn on the chart; a click on a port's mark picks it too. Set this course charts it. In port she stays moored until you cast off; at sea she takes the new course up at once. You do not steer her: she sails her course by herself.
pages.built_note: VoyagePanel.cs, Course, VoyagePlanner (VoyagePlanner.Moored holds a course set in port until Cast off), ChartBody.cs (no steering on the chart).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 4 October night (the chart is the game: set a course, her mark moves on the clock); 7 October, ruling 1 (a window sets, a button does).

pages.title: The measure
pages.hint: The measure
pages.brief: Click two places on the chart: the measure draws the way by water and says the days, low and high.
pages.game: The measure tells you a way in days before you spend them. Take it up with its button, or with D, and click two places on the chart. It draws the way between them by water and says how many days it would take your boat: a low figure for a fair wind and a high one for a light wind dead ahead. A third click begins again, a click on a port's mark takes that port, and Esc puts the measure down.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Measure.cs and FramePassage.cs. Its button is still one of the eight (FrameRoot.Rack.cs); ruling 8 moves it to the right with the chart tools, which is not done.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October (a measure in days) and ruling 8 of later the same day.

pages.title: The chart tools
pages.hint: The chart tools
pages.brief: Everything that belongs to the chart stands on the right; everything else on the left.
pages.game: Everything that belongs to the chart stands on the right of the screen, with the portrait and the view of the ship. The chart tools are the measure in days, nearer, farther, find her, names, winds, sails and pins. Everything else stands on the left.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: no chart tools stand on the right, and the measure is still among the eight buttons (wiring_plan.md 8.9).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 8.

pages.title: The view of the ship
pages.hint: The view of the ship
pages.brief: A window on your own ship: water only, with the sea, the weather and the wind as they are.
pages.game: The window at the bottom right is a view of your own ship. It shows water only, with a simple dock when she is moored. The sea, the weather and the wind are shown as they are, and the crew row when she is under oars.
pages.built_note: Today the window is a drawn stand-in (FrameShipView), with where she is and the wind under it. The 3D view is the lead's to build after the builders and the reviewer (ruling 11).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 11.

pages.title: The ship and the chart change places
pages.hint: The ship and the chart change places
pages.brief: A button on the top left corner of the view of the ship: she fills the screen and the chart goes small.
pages.game: The view of the ship has a button on its top left corner. Press it and she fills the screen behind the frame, and the chart goes small in her window. Press it again and they change back.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: the ship window has no button and there is no small chart (wiring_plan.md 8.9).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 7.

pages.title: Windows and workspaces
pages.hint: Windows and workspaces
pages.brief: The left side is tiled with windows. Any window holds any panel; keys 1 to 4 change workspace.
pages.game: The left side of the frame is tiled with windows, and any window can hold any panel. There are four workspaces, on keys 1 to 4, and each keeps its own windows. R, C and T lay the windows as rows, columns or tabs. N opens a new window and X shuts the one you are in; the arrow keys or a click move from one to the next, and the one you are in is edged in gold. A window's title steps to the next panel, or picks any from the list.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.cs and FrameWindows.cs: four workspaces (the mock-up has a fifth for the Wiki). Panels built on 7 Oct, 10:40: Voyage, Trade, Port, Hold, Tasks, The word, Chronicle, Event.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 2 (a window system like i3 or sway).

pages.title: Brief panels and full windows
pages.hint: Brief panels and full windows
pages.brief: Every panel has a brief face of one to four lines. Press it for its full window.
pages.game: Every panel has two faces. In the left column it is brief: one to four lines, the first the one that matters now, in a small, medium or large size. Press it and its full window opens over the chart, with all its controls.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: FramePanel.Fill is the full face and is all there is (wiring_plan.md 8.9).
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 9.

pages.title: The eight buttons
pages.hint: The eight buttons
pages.brief: Eight buttons under the top bar. Each does one thing; they are apart from the windows.
pages.game: Under the top bar stand eight buttons, four by two. Each does one thing when pressed. They are apart from the windows below them: a button does, a window shows and sets. A press acts at once and writes a line in the log, or opens a small window with the choices. A button that cannot be used now is greyed, and says why when the pointer rests on it and when it is pressed.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Rack.cs. As built the eight are Cast off, Wait, Measure, Look out, Sound, Hail, Rest, Offer: Measure stands where ruling 8 puts Oars.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, rulings 1 and 8.

pages.title: Cast off, Lie to, Sail on
pages.hint: Cast off, Lie to, Sail on
pages.brief: In port it lets her go on the course you set. At sea it stops her, and then sends her on.
pages.game: In port, with a course set in the Voyage window, Cast off lets her go. At sea the same button is Lie to: she stops where she is, and the clock runs on. When she lies to by that button it becomes Sail on, and she takes her course up again. With no course set it is greyed and says so.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Rack.cs, case CastOff. This Sail on is the course taken up again, at the clock's own speed: it is not the struck 'Sail on' of the book, which skipped time.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1.

pages.title: Wait
pages.hint: Wait
pages.brief: Wait till first light, or till the wind is fair for your course. The clock runs, and bread is eaten.
pages.game: Wait asks for what: till first light, or till the wind is fair for your course. The clock runs while you wait, and bread is eaten. At sea she lies to meanwhile, and takes her course up again by herself when the wait is over. Press the button again to stop waiting. A tide she must have before the flats on her course is waited for without your asking.
pages.built_note: FrameWait in FrameRoot.Rack.cs. The mock-up's third choice, till the flood at the bar, is not a choice here: TideWait does it by itself.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1; 4 October, no. 8 (waiting in port costs days).

pages.title: Oars
pages.hint: Oars
pages.brief: Out oars, or back to the sail.
pages.game: Oars puts the oars out, or brings them in and sets the sail again. It has the place among the eight that the measure had.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: the rack has Measure in this place. She rows by herself in a calm, or when rowing beats tacking (Travel.Speed). The ruling says only: 'Oars (out oars, or sail) has its place for now'.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 8.

pages.title: Look out
pages.hint: Look out
pages.brief: What can be seen from the masthead now: the wind and the sky, the sails in sight, the nearest port you know.
pages.game: Look out says what can be seen from the masthead now. First come the wind and the sky. Then the sails in sight, the nearest first: what she is if she is near enough to make out, and otherwise only that a sail is there, and where. Last comes the nearest port you know, if one lies near. What the lookout sees between times he says in the log by himself.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Rack.cs, LookOutFloat and LookoutLog; SeaWatch.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1.

pages.title: Sound
pages.hint: Sound
pages.brief: Heave the lead: how much water there is on this stretch of her course.
pages.game: Sound heaves the lead. It says how much water there is at the shallowest of the stretch of her course she is on, in fathoms. It warns when a stretch dries at low water: she must cross that on the flood. It needs a course to sound along.
pages.built_note: FrameRoot.Rack.cs, Sounding: the lanes' own depths along the leg she is on. It does not say what the bottom is.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1.

pages.title: Hail
pages.hint: Hail
pages.brief: Hail a sail in sight, the shore, or your own crew.
pages.game: Hail calls to a sail in sight, to the shore, or to your own crew.
pages.built_note: The button writes 'not yet' in the log (FrameRoot.Rack.cs). Meetings at sea do not happen on the chart yet (wiring_plan.md 8.8). The ruling names the button; what a hail does is not ruled beyond these words, so the page says no more.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1.

pages.title: Rest
pages.hint: Rest
pages.brief: All hands rest for a watch. No time is skipped for it.
pages.game: Rest gives all hands a watch of rest. No time is skipped for it: the clock keeps the speed you have chosen while they sleep.
pages.built_note: The button writes 'not yet' in the log. The old Rest.cs ([Z] at night, till dawn) is still in the code and is capped to the clock's own speed under the frame; whether [Z] still answers on the chart was not checked.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, rulings 1 and 5.

pages.title: Offer
pages.hint: Offer
pages.brief: An offering, or a vow, by your own faith.
pages.game: Offer makes an offering or a vow, by your own faith.
pages.built_note: The button writes 'not yet' in the log: 'Offerings and vows come with the faiths.' What an offering costs and does is not ruled, so the page says no more.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 1.

pages.title: In port
pages.hint: In port
pages.brief: The Port window says where she lies, how you stand there, and what can be done.
pages.game: When she moors, the Port window says where she lies, how you stand there, and what can be done: the talk of the waterfront and the errands of the place. What a line leads to opens as a window over the chart. The market is the Trade window, and casting off is the button above the windows.
pages.built_note: PortPanel.cs shows the port's own menu, which the ports' graph still makes. The sites, people and acts of the places files are not read by the game yet.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 7 October, rulings 1 and 2.

pages.title: Buying and selling
pages.hint: Buying and selling
pages.brief: The Trade window shows the market where she lies. A good is cheap where it is made and dear where it is wanted.
pages.game: The Trade window shows the market where she lies: what they ask for each good, what they pay, how many lie there and how many you have aboard. Buy and Sell deal one at a time. A market asks a little over its price and pays a little under. A good is cheap where it is made and dear where it is wanted, and a market that is sold more than it wants pays less for the next. Looking at a market is seeing its prices: they go into what you know. At sea there is no market.
pages.built_note: TradePanel.cs, Trade.cs, Deal.cs, Market.cs, trade_rules.json (spread 0.20: a tenth over, a tenth under). The seasons and the chronicle's shocks move prices too (Seasons.cs, Shocks.cs).
pages.holds: GAME_MAKER.md 4.1; DECISIONS.md, 4 October, no. 16 (the seasons are trade strategy).

pages.title: Silver and the penny
pages.hint: Silver and the penny
pages.brief: All prices, tolls and the debt are reckoned in silver pennies, written d.
pages.game: All prices, tolls and the debt are reckoned in silver pennies, written d. Each realm takes its own coin at its full worth: the Frankish penny among the Franks, the English penny among the English. In the north there is no coin of their own and all silver goes by weight on the scales. Coin and silver that are not the place's own are taken for less than their weight.
pages.known: Deniers: The Frankish penny. Charlemagne's reform of 793/4 made it heavier (about 1.7 g); struck at Dorestad, Quentovic and every royal mint. Pennies: Offa's broad pennies and the older sceattas of England and Frisia (about 1-1.3 g). Dirhams: Silver of the Caliphate, come north by the Volga and the Baltic; in the north it goes by weight, often cut. Hacksilver: Silver by weight: cut rings, ingots and broken jewellery, weighed on folding scales (counted in grams).
pages.source: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/trade_rules.json (the notes on the coins); Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md
pages.built_note: Purse.cs and the zones of trade_rules.json (foreign_loss a tenth among Franks and English, less where silver is weighed).
pages.holds: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/trade_rules.json; GAME_MAKER.md 4.1 would fold the four coins into one purse until 865, which is not ruled by the user and is not done.

pages.title: The toll
pages.hint: The toll
pages.brief: Taken from what you sell: a tenth among the Franks, a twentieth among the English, none where silver goes by weight.
pages.game: The toll is taken from what you sell, not from what you buy. In the Frankish realm it is a tenth, among the English a twentieth, and where silver goes by weight there is none. The Trade window says the toll before you sell, and each sale says what was taken. A card may ease the toll at a port for a time.
pages.known: The Frankish king's toll, the tenth, was taken at Dorestad, at Quentovic and at the river tolls. Among the English, toll was taken at London and at the wics.
pages.source: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/trade_rules.json (the notes on the money zones); Design/content/lore/law_tolls.md
pages.built_note: Deal.cs: the zone's toll comes off what the market pays; EncounterRunner.TollFactor eases it; Chest.TollFreeAt frees a port where a riddle won that.
pages.holds: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/trade_rules.json; GAME_MAKER.md 4.1.

pages.title: The word, and how old it is
pages.hint: The word, and how old it is
pages.brief: You know a price only where you have seen it or been told it. Every word says how it came and how old it is.
pages.game: You know a price only where you have seen it or been told it. Every word says how it came to you: seen with your own eyes, told by one who saw it, talk, a written word, a rumour, or what every merchant knows. It also says how old it is, and a price goes half stale in a month. Under each good in the Trade window stands one line: the freshest thing you know of it elsewhere, or else what the season or the law means for it. A price you were told is given as a word and not a number: it pays well, poorly, or the usual. The Word window lists every market you have word of, the freshest first.
pages.built_note: Known.cs, Word.cs, PriceNotes.cs, WordLine, WordPanel; the numbers are knowing_793.json.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 4 October night (next build: the word on the item); GAME_MAKER.md 4.1.

pages.title: News
pages.hint: News
pages.brief: News is as old as the ship that brought it. The Chronicle window keeps what you have heard.
pages.game: News is as old as the ship that brought it. The Chronicle window holds what you have heard, the newest first: when a thing happened, and when word of it reached you. What happened before your first morning every merchant knows already. Other talk heard on the water, such as a raid told of by a passing ship, stands below it.
pages.built_note: ChroniclePanel.cs, Known.EntryFact, Known.News.
pages.holds: GAME_MAKER.md 4.1 (a price is a word: a teller, a place, an age).

pages.title: Standing
pages.hint: Standing
pages.brief: Each port and each region keeps its own opinion of you, from very bad to very good.
pages.game: Each port and each region keeps its own standing with you. A deed counts in full where it was done, in part across its region, and a little among the same people elsewhere; each people weighs a deed by its own values. Word of a deed travels with the ships, as news does. Standing moves your prices there, how hard the king's men search you, and whether a place will deal with you at all. The Port window says how you stand where she lies.
pages.built_note: Reputation.cs and reputation_793.json; PortPanel prints Reputation.Line.
pages.holds: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/reputation_793.json; GAME_MAKER.md 4.4; DECISIONS.md, 7 October, the picker's ruling 4 (word of the slave trade travels as news does).

pages.title: The debt
pages.hint: The debt
pages.brief: You begin owing the count 1,920 pennies, eight pounds of silver: a fixed sum, due on a day.
pages.game: You begin owing the count 1,920 pennies: eight pounds of silver. It is a fixed sum, due on a day. The top bar says what you owe, the day it falls due and how many days are left, and it turns to a warning in the last fourteen. You pay toward it at any market, from the Tasks window: twenty pennies at a time, or all of it. The four casks of wine aboard at the start are the count's own: what they fetch is his stake, not your gain.
pages.built_note: Trade.Debt, Trade.DebtDue, Trade.DebtDaysLeft, Trade.PayDebt; the top bar (FrameGame.DebtLine) and TasksPanel. The count's casks: Lot.whose in the hold, Trade.SaleReckoned. Nothing happens yet when the day passes unpaid: the bar counts the days overdue. The count's own chain of cards still names the old sum of 480 pennies: Bake/economy/apply_debt_sum_cards.py changes it once the content pass is merged.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 4 October, no. 10 (the debt is a fixed sum due on a day); 7 October, ruling 30 (eight pounds, with the traders' margin of a quarter).

pages.title: The day of the debt
pages.hint: The day of the debt
pages.brief: The debt falls due at Michaelmas, the twenty-ninth of September: a hundred and fifty-one days after a first morning on the first of May.
pages.game: The debt falls due at Michaelmas, the twenty-ninth of September: a hundred and fifty-one days after a first morning on the first of May. In 793 that day is a Sunday. On the Lord's day no market is held and no court sits, so have the silver in hand by the Saturday. The sum is 1,920 pennies.
pages.built_note: Trade.Begin with the calendar sets the day (trade_rules.json: due_month, due_day, due_name); FrameGame.DebtDay says it and FrameGame.DebtDayWarning warns of the Sunday in the Tasks and House windows. One sum, 1,920 d, with no choice of terms (the hard terms of no. 10 are not built). self_793.json gives each people its own creditor and its own day; ChartWorld.cs says the debt is the same at every home for now. The game does not yet shut a market on a Sunday: the warning is the period's rule, not the engine's.

pages.title: Orders and tasks
pages.hint: Orders and tasks
pages.brief: The Tasks window holds what you have taken on: the debt first, then the orders.
pages.game: The Tasks window holds what you have taken on: the debt and its day first, then the orders you have taken, each with the days it has left. Orders are posted in the ports. When she lies in one, the window lists those posted there, and Take takes one. When you carry what was ordered to its port, Deliver hands it over.
pages.built_note: TasksPanel.cs and Commissions.cs. The game carries no passengers, and the window says so.

pages.title: The hold
pages.hint: The hold
pages.brief: What she carries, the room taken and the room left. Light, bulky goods take more room than they weigh.
pages.game: The Hold window lists what she carries: each good, what it weighs and what it cost you, the room taken and the room left. Room is counted in kilograms, but light and bulky goods take more room than they weigh, so wool fills her before stone does. The water casks take their room too. Below the goods stand the crew's stores, as days of food and days of drink.
pages.built_note: Hold.cs (a good's room is its weight times its bulk) and HoldPanel.cs.
pages.holds: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/goods_793.json (bulk); GAME_MAKER.md section 3 (stage 1 shows lots and 'full').

pages.title: How deep she sits
pages.hint: How deep she sits
pages.brief: The more she carries, the deeper she sits: light, fair or deep.
pages.game: The more she carries, the deeper she sits in the water. The Hold window says it in one of three words: light, fair or deep.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: the hold counts room only. GAME_MAKER.md section 3 gives the load line (light, fair, deep) and three places to stow (low, high, dry) for stage 2. What a deep load costs her in speed or at a bar is not ruled anywhere, so this page does not say.

pages.title: Food and drink
pages.hint: Food and drink
pages.brief: Each man eats and drinks every day aboard. The top bar says how many days of bread are left.
pages.game: Each man eats and drinks every day aboard. Food is bought at a market and carried in the hold: ship's bread, cheese, dried fish, stockfish, salt pork and bacon, salt herring, butter, flour, wheat, rye, barley, hazelnuts and dates, figs and raisins. Drink is ale or mead, and water when those are gone. Water is put aboard free in any port, in four casks. The top bar says how many days of bread are left. Men with no food or nothing to drink lose health and heart, and thirst is the quicker of the two.
pages.built_note: Voyage.cs and voyage_rules.json: 0.7 kg of food and 3 litres of drink a man a day; four casks of 60 litres.
pages.holds: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/voyage_rules.json.

pages.title: The crew's pay
pages.hint: The crew's pay
pages.brief: A quarter of a penny a man for every day aboard, paid in port.
pages.game: Each man is owed a quarter of a penny for every day aboard. He is paid in port, out of your silver. When pay has been owed more than a week the crew lose heart. A man owed fourteen days may go ashore for good at the next port.
pages.built_note: Voyage.cs and voyage_rules.json (pay_per_man_day 0.25, leave_if_owed_days 14).
pages.holds: GAME_MAKER.md 4.4 (wages, one rule: 0.25 d a man a day aboard, paid in port).

pages.title: The crew
pages.hint: The crew
pages.brief: Four men work the boat. Two words say how they are: their health and their heart.
pages.game: Four men work the boat. The frame says how they are in two words: their health (sound, worn, ailing or sick) and their heart (in good heart, steady, low or close to leaving). Hunger, thirst and pay long owed bring both down, and days in port bring them back. In rough water the men are seasick until they find their sea legs, after about six days at sea.
pages.built_note: Voyage.cs (men, health, heart, seasickness); the words are FrameGame.HealthWord and HeartWord, shown in the portrait block. There is no Crew window yet.

pages.title: The four men
pages.hint: The four men
pages.brief: Each of the four has a name, a seat and one want of his own.
pages.game: Each of the four men has a name, a seat and one want of his own. The seats are the helm, the lookout, the lead and the weather. The man in a seat is the one who speaks when his matter comes up.
pages.built_note: Not in the game: the crew is a number of men with one health and one heart (Voyage.cs).
pages.holds: GAME_MAKER.md 4.4 (four men with names, each in a seat).

pages.title: Wind, sail and oar
pages.hint: Wind, sail and oar
pages.brief: She sails her course by herself and makes what speed the wind allows. In a calm the crew row.
pages.game: She sails her course by herself and makes what speed the wind allows. She is fastest with the wind on her quarter, and slower with it dead astern. She cannot sail straight into the wind: she works to and fro across it and makes poor way. In a calm, or when rowing makes better way than tacking, the crew row. In a gale she lies to until it has blown over.
pages.built_note: Travel.Speed and ChartBody.cs: her class's own speeds from ship_classes_793.json, a gale over 17 metres a second, the oars as a day's mean.
pages.holds: DECISIONS.md, 4 October night (her mark moves on the clock at a real ship's speed); ship_classes_793.json.

pages.title: Tides and the bar
pages.hint: Tides and the bar
pages.brief: Where the way in lies over flats, she waits for the tide by herself. Aground, you choose how to get her off.
pages.game: A bar is a shoal across a river mouth, and flats are ground that dries at low water. Her course keeps off the flats where there is another way, but some ports have no way in but over them. Before such a stretch, if there is not water enough for her, she lies to at its edge and waits for the tide by herself, at the speed of the clock. If no tide soon to come gives enough, she goes over on the best high water there is, and may stick. Aground, you choose how to get her off: wait for the tide, row her off, or over the side and push.
pages.built_note: TideWait.cs and Aground.cs, with their pace capped to the clock's by FrameRoot. Whether the chart scene carries a tide (LevelWater) could not be checked without running Unity: on a level with no tide there is no waiting.
pages.holds: The user's rule of 3 October in TideWait.cs ('the crew will stop completely and just wait ... until the tide is back up'); DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 5.

pages.title: Faith and days
pages.hint: Faith and days
pages.brief: Your faith has a calendar. Its days are yours to keep or to break, and they move prices.
pages.game: Your faith is a way of living with a calendar. The days it keeps are yours to keep or to break: a Christian who sells on a Sunday makes silver and loses Troth. Feasts and fasts move prices too: fish is dear in Lent. The page of each day says what it asks, and what it makes dear or cheap.
pages.built_note: The engine knows the main feasts (Runtime/Levels/Feasts.cs) and a card can ask whether today is one, but calendar_793.json is not read by the game: no day shuts a market, moves a price or moves Troth yet.
pages.holds: Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 3 ('the calendar bites'); story/calendar_793.json.

pages.title: Tongues and the turning line
pages.hint: Tongues and the turning line
pages.brief: People speak plain English with words of their own tongue set in. At a moment that matters a line turns from their tongue into English as you watch.
pages.game: People speak plain English in the game, with words of their own tongue set in where a stranger would hear them first: greetings, oaths, kin words, trade words and curses. A word in another tongue has a page here once you have heard it. At a moment that matters a line comes up whole in the speaker's own tongue and turns into English word by word. How fast it turns, and how much of it, is how well you know that tongue: one you know turns at once, one you half know turns slowly and keeps its hard words, and one you do not know does not turn unless a man aboard speaks it. A word you have seen turn ten times stays English from the start.
pages.built_note: Self.cs keeps how well each tongue is known and how often a piece has been seen (StaysAfter = 10), but the game does not read tongues_793.json and the turning itself is not in the frame (FloatSpec.content is where it would go).
pages.holds: Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 6c; story/tongues_793.json.

pages.title: Bonds
pages.hint: Bonds
pages.brief: You may bind yourself to anyone you meet, by four steps: known, trusted, bound, sworn or beloved.
pages.game: You may bind yourself to anyone you meet. A bond grows by four steps: known, by meeting and talk; trusted, by a favour done and a thing kept quiet; bound, by an oath, a shared danger or a gift that cost you; and sworn or beloved, as in marriage, sworn brotherhood, fostering or godparenthood. Each step is a talk with your stats in it, and each takes seasons. What a bond gives is what that person is. What it costs is that it can be used against you, and that people die.
pages.built_note: Not in the game. The game does keep who has been met (Self.MarkMet), and the frame has the dots a bond would be drawn with.

pages.title: Saving
pages.hint: Saving
pages.brief: F5 saves the game and F9 loads it again.
pages.game: F5 saves the game and F9 loads it again; the menu saves and loads too. A save holds the whole game: the day, where she lies and where she is bound, the crew and their stores, your silver, the hold and the debt, every market, the other ships, and all you have seen and heard. You cannot save while something is going on, such as a meeting or an open card: the game says so.

pages.title: Dorestat
pages.hint: A market among the Frisians
pages.brief: The greatest emporium of the north, where the Kromme Rijn leaves the Lek; a kilometre of jetties; the king's toll and mint.
pages.game:
Dorestad is the Frankish king's toll port and mint in the north: three kilometres of timber houses and earth dams along the west bank of the Crooked Rhine, just below the fork where the Lek leaves it, with no wall round any of it. Frisian shippers bring Rhine wine, Mayen quernstones, Badorf pots and glass down the river and carry cloth, combs, salt and fish back up, and the king's men take a tenth of every sale.
No fair has a day here: ships lie between the dams and wait for a cargo, a wind or company. The winter and spring floods drown the low ground and in a hard winter the river carries ice; in high summer half the comb of dams stands dry and the big ships lie off the heads on the sand. The new wine comes down after the vintage, about Martinmas, and the reckoning with the count is at Michaelmas.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine and bar iron; wanted here, and so dearer: oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the hungry year. Bread is dear, the poor crowd the church door, and grain is the cargo everyone asks for. The mint still strikes the light penny. English ports are shut to Frankish ships and finished quernstones pile up unsold.
pages.known:
The greatest emporium of the north, where the Kromme Rijn leaves the Lek; a kilometre of jetties; the king's toll and mint. The place is now Wijk bij Duurstede. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 695 Pippin the mayor beat Radbod, king of the Frisians, at the fort of Dorestad, and the Franks kept the fork of the river. (The year is not exact.) In 716 Winfrid, who was afterwards called Boniface, crossed from London to Dorestad with a fair wind and found Radbod at war with the Franks. In 777, on the eighth of June King Charles gave to Saint Martin's of Utrecht the church called Upkirika above Dorestad, with a hundred perches of land, the bank due on the Lek, and the island eastward between Rhine and Lek. In 779 the king freed an abbey's ships of the toll at Dorestad, as at Quentovic, Rouen, Amiens and Maastricht. About 780 Alcuin sent a letter in verse down the Rhine: at Utrecht honey, porridge and butter, since Frisia pours neither oil nor wine; then hoist sail and flee Dorestad, for Hrotberct the black, the greedy merchant, will give no lodging. In 793 there was great hunger in Francia. At Dorestad the mint still struck the light penny with CARO/LVS on one face and DOR/STAT with an axe on the other.

Everything dated here rests on it.; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); Fredegar's continuator, by L. van der Tuuk, http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html (the year (?)); Willibald, Life of Boniface c. 4, by Design/content/ships.md; Oorkondenboek Sticht Utrecht I no. 48, by http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html; Charter for Saint-Germain-des-Pres, 779, by http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html and story/unlocks_793.json; Alcuin, carmen 4, MGH Poetae I 220-223 (our rendering): https://sourcebook.stanford.edu/text/alcuin_song_4_go_quickly/; chronicle_793.json 793-great-famine; the mint: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/B5.html

later.text: From midsummer 794 only the heavy one passes, the king's price for grain is cried on the dams, and the count's steward checks every measure against the new one.
In 794 the king's new heavy penny with his monogram was ordered taken in every place, and the old light pennies had to be brought to the mint.

From 795 to 813: the king's port at its work. The quarrel with the English ends in 796 and the stones move again. The count is away with the host most summers; in 797 boats and men are pressed to haul the king's ships into Saxony, and in 810 every boat is called out against Godfred's two hundred sails. Dirhams begin to turn up in the purses of men from the north.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.

From 814 to 833: the good years, as rich as the place will ever be. Great storehouses stand on the newest ground of the dams, which are built further out every few years after the river. The penny shows a ship with the town's name (812 to 818). In 826 a baptised Danish king goes by with a monk called Ansgar. The children of the people you knew hold the dam heads.

In 815, on the eighteenth of March the emperor Louis confirmed to Saint Martin's its tenth of the king's income and its banks in Dorestad: its men there owed no bank due and no 'giscot', no one might lodge in their houses, and no one might seize their goods at death.
In 825 Martinmas was the last day on which the old pennies could be paid.
In 826 Harald the Dane, baptised at Mainz, went home down the Rhine by Dorestad with the monk Ansgar, in a ship with two cabins that the bishop of Cologne had lent them.
In 828 the emperor's own merchants, free of toll everywhere else, were told they still owed the tenth at Quentovic, at Dorestad and at the passes.

From 834 to 849: the raid years. A fleet comes up from Utrecht in 834, in 835 and in 836; in 837 it takes tribute; about 847 the place burns in sight of the emperor at Nijmegen. Between raids loot is sold cheap and houses are mended. People put their silver in the ground and go armed to the boats. From Pentecost to Lammas nobody sleeps well.
In 834 the Danes came by Utrecht to Dorestad and plundered it. They killed some, carried others off captive, and burned a part.
In 835 the heathen men came to Dorestad again and wasted it.
In 836 they came a third time. Antwerp and Witla at the mouth of the Maas were burned.
837: This year, after they had taken Walcheren on the seventeenth of June, the Danes came to Dorestad and took tribute. The emperor hurried to Nijmegen, blamed disobedience and ordered a fleet.
About 847 Dorestad was burned with two other villages while the emperor Lothar looked on from Nijmegen, and the Danes held Dorestad and the Betuwe.

From 850 to 863: Rorik's town. A Dane holds Dorestad for the king and his man takes the tenth on the dam; the fleets pass by while he is at home. The churches are full again and the poor are many: Catla of Birka brings her mother's silver for them. The pennies are poor ones in Lothar's name. The river is leaving: the heads stand in mud. In 857 other Danes storm the town; in January 863 the last sack comes with the flood.

In 850 Rorik the Dane came by the mouths of the Rhine with a fleet, and Lothar, who could not drive him out, granted him Dorestad and other counties, on terms: to pay in the king's dues and keep the pirates off.

About 852 Catla of Birka came to Dorestad with the silver of her dead mother Frideburg and gave it to the poor and the holy places. In the same years Swedes said the way to Dorestad was beset by pirates.
In 857 Rorik sailed to the Eider with his fleet, and while he was gone other Danes stormed Dorestad.
As a trading place it ends about 863.

863: This year, in January, in a winter of floods, the Danes came up the Rhine to Dorestad. Frisian merchants who had fled to a large estate were killed there. The Danes left on Rorik's advice and went on up the river.

From 864 to 875: the leaving. The houses that are left sell their timber. The merchants go to Tiel, Deventer and Utrecht and take the name of Dorestad's freedom with them. Rorik is driven out in 867, comes back, and is last heard of in 873. A few boats still lie where the dams reach water.
In 867 the people the annals call Cokingi drove Rorik out of Frisia.
In 873 Rorik swore faith to King Louis. He is not heard of again.
About 875 the harbour was given up: the river had left the dams, and flood clay lay over the old plots.

From 876 to 947: clay over the plots. The harbour is given up. Cattle graze the dams; posts stand out of the grass in rows. Men of Tiel and Deventer say 'as we had it at Dorestad' when they argue a toll.
In 896, on Saint John's day King Zwentibold gave Saint Martin's men at Deventer and Tiel the freedom they had had 'in Dorestadio'.

From 948 to 1066: Wik: a village with a church and a lord's estate on the bank of a small river. From 1016 it is the abbey of Deutz's. Children find green pennies with a ship on them after the plough.
In 948, on the first of April King Otto named it in a charter: 'the estate once called Dorsteti, but now Wik'.
About 1016 the church and estate of Wijk passed from Adela of Hamaland to Archbishop Heribert of Cologne and his abbey of Deutz.
In 1057 King Henry confirmed to the bishop of Utrecht the banks of Dorestad, nearly two hundred years after the last ship lay at them.

pages.title: Traiectum
pages.hint: A town among the Frisians
pages.brief: Willibrord's see and the church of Saint Martin, on the Rhine where the Vecht leaves it north.
pages.game:
A Roman stone fort on the south bank of the Rhine, given to Willibrord's church: two small churches, a school, a bishop's household and a bank where boats are drawn up. In 793 there is no market, no toll and no mint here: the church buys wax, wine, oil, incense and books, and pays in silver, in letters and in its good word. A merchant comes for the bishop's custom, for the road north by the Vecht to the Almere, and because the men who can read live here.
The year runs by the church: fish and fasting through Lent, the river high with meltwater at Easter, letters and ships moving from Pentecost. Saint Willibrord's day and Martinmas close it with goose and the new wine from up the Rhine, then forty days of fast to Christmas while the boats lie on the bank.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine and bar iron; wanted here, and so dearer: oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a church stronghold and nothing else. Patched Roman walls, two small stone churches, a timber school, the bishop's hall, and a sloping bank west of the fort where a dozen boats lie. The trade passes by to Dorestad; the church buys what an altar and a scriptorium eat.
pages.known:
Willibrord's see and the church of Saint Martin, on the Rhine where the Vecht leaves it north. The place is now Utrecht. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 630 King Dagobert has a chapel built in the old Roman fort. The Frisians pull it down. 695: Willibrord is made archbishop of the Frisians. Pippin gives him the fort, which the people there call Wiltaburg and the Franks Traiectum. He builds Saint Salvator's and raises Saint Martin's again. 723: Charles Martel gives the fort and its land, with Vechten up the river, to the church of Utrecht. 739: Willibrord dies on 7 November. He is buried at Echternach, not here. About 750 Saint Martin's becomes the bishop's church, and Gregory, never a bishop, rules the house and its school as abbot until about 775. 754: The body of Boniface, killed at Doccinga, comes by boat over the Aelmere. The count reads King Pippin's ban on moving it. The church bell rings with no hand on it, and the body goes on to Mainz. 772: Liudger, schooled here and then at York under Alcuin, comes home with books when the Angles and the Frisians fall out at York. 777: The king gives the church Leusden, four woods in Eemland and the Upkirika at Dorestad. About 780 Alcuin sends a poem down the Rhine. It greets Bishop Alberic as 'vaccipotens praesul', mighty in cows, and Prior Hadda, who will serve honey, porridge and butter, for Frisia yields no oil or wine. About 790 Hamacar is bishop. Nothing but his name and his years is known.

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
806: Ricfried is bishop after Hamacar, until 815 or 816.

From 834 to 856: the same place with its ears up. The fleet of 834 went by on its way to Dorestad and comes back most summers. The bishop keeps a boat ready, the school buries its ink horns, and after 850 the toll down the river is taken in Rorik's name.
In 834 a Danish fleet came by Utrecht to Dorestad and plundered it.
836: Between 835 and 838 Bishop Frederik is stabbed by two men after Mass. Later writers blame the Empress Judith, or men of Walcheren.
850: Rorik the Dane takes Dorestad and is granted it. One account gives him Utrecht too.

From 857 to 919: wasted. The churches are roofless, the bishop lives at Deventer, and yellow flood clay lies over the strand where the houses stood. A few boatmen and fishers keep the crossing. A priest comes from inland to say Mass on Martin's day.
857: While Rorik is away in Denmark other Danes sack Utrecht. The churches are destroyed and Bishop Hunger flees.
858: King Lothar II gives the clergy of Utrecht Saint Peter's at Sint-Odilienberg to live in. Later the bishops sit at Deventer.
863: Northmen take Utrecht and Nijmegen and winter there.

From 920 to 952: Balderik is home. Scaffolds stand on the walls, there are new gates and a bridge on the west side, the school has boys again and a king's son among them. Merchants who lost Dorestad build on the strand, which they now call the Stathe.
About 920 Bishop Balderik brings the see home. He rebuilds the churches, the school and the walls, with gates, bastions and a bridge on the west side.

From 953 to 1006: a bishop's town with a mint and a toll. Timber houses and revetments run along the Vecht side; grain, wine, stone, glass and pots come in, herring goes out, and goods that pass must be offered for sale here.
953: King Otto gives the bishop the mint, and Muiden with its toll on the Vecht. (One source puts the mint in 936.)

From 1007 to 1026: the merchants burned their own quarter when the Northmen came and have built it again, closer under the wall. The cathedral burns in 1017 and stands new in 1023. The bishop is a count now and rides with the emperor's army.
1007: The Northmen come, a year after they burned Tiel. The merchants set fire to their own harbour quarter and go into the fort. No attack follows.

1010: Bishop Ansfried, once the emperor's sword-bearer and blind for five years, dies on 3 May. Utrecht men carry off his body while the people of the Heiligenberg fight a fire that did not start by chance.
1017: Fire takes the cathedral and the bishop's house.
1018: Bishop Adelbold is with the emperor's army that Count Dirk beats at Vlaardingen.
1023: Adelbold's new cathedral is consecrated before the Emperor Henry and twelve bishops.

From 1027 to 1066: stone everywhere. Bernold raises Saint Peter's, Saint John's and Saint Paul's around the cathedral, the emperor has a palace in the fort, and an emperor dies in it. The merchants have a church of their own on the Stathe and long barges on the Vecht.
1039: The Emperor Conrad dies here at Pentecost, 4 June. His body goes up the Rhine to Speyer; his entrails stay in the cathedral.
1040: King Henry III gives Groningen to Saint Martin's. About now the emperor's palace of Lofen stands in the fort, of tuff, with a row of sandstone columns.
1054: Bishop Bernold dies on 19 July and is buried in Saint Peter's, one of the three churches he built.
1064: The king gives Bishop Willem the county of West Frisia, on parchment.

pages.title: Walichrum
pages.hint: A market among the Frisians
pages.brief: An emporium on the dunes of Walcheren at the Scheldt mouth, later lost to the sea.
pages.game:
Walichrum is a long strip of oak houses behind the dunes of Walcheren, the king's ground, where Dorestad's trade meets the sea. In 793 its best coin years are behind it, but the marsh still gives salt, cheese, wool and hides, and ships for England wait here for a wind. A merchant comes for cheap salt in autumn, for news of the crossing, and to sell Rhine pots and oak to people who have neither clay nor trees.
The sheep go out on the salt marsh after Easter and are shorn about Saint John's (a guess); cheese comes from the hay month on. The salt is boiled from Lammas, and by Michaelmas it is cheap, in time for the Martinmas slaughter. From Martinmas to Easter gales stand on the shoals, little moves, and the sea is looked at every morning from the high dune.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cheese; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish pottery and oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the long street behind the dunes, a little past its best. No wall, no church, no tower: houses, pens, pits and four grave fields. Ships for England and for the Rhine lie on the creek mud together. The king's steward is the only officer, and he is mostly counting sheep.
pages.known:
An emporium on the dunes of Walcheren at the Scheldt mouth, later lost to the sea. The place is now Domburg, Walcheren. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 690 Willibrord breaks an idol of the old belief at the villa Walichrum. Its keeper strikes him on the head with a sword and does not wound him, and dies three days later. 715: The years of the small thick silver pennies: about a thousand of them will be picked off this beach a thousand years on. Whether any were struck here is not known. 753: About now the small thick pennies go out of use. The coin of the strand is the Frankish king's denier. 769: An oak is felled near Hamwic for an English clinker ship. Her planks end their days on this island.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md (6 Oct 2026 reading): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what is not known and is kept to here.; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi (about 796), not quoted; the year is local tradition (zeeuwseankers.nl, Willibrord op Walcheren) (?); Metcalf and Op den Velde 2009-10; a mint here for the first 'porcupine' pennies is a hypothesis only; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sceat; the dossier reckons them forty years out of use by 793; Ufkes 2012, Paleo-aktueel 23 (tree-ring date of ship timber found in the ring fort)

later.text: About 796 Alcuin writes the Life of Willibrord for Beornrad of Echternach, and names the villa Walichrum.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.

From 815 to 836: quieter and warier. Bishop Frederick's priests come out from Traiectum and scold. Guard ships are talked of more than seen. From 834 every summer brings word of fleets on the Rhine, and the count sets a watch on the high dune.
816: Frederick becomes bishop of Utrecht (815 or 816). He is said to have preached on the island and to have charged its people with marrying close kin.

From 837 to 840: after the raid. The count and the emperor's Dane are dead, many women are gone north, and tribute has been taken. Sods are being cut for a ring wall. On Saint Stephen's day 838 the sea comes almost over the dunes. Fewer ships; salt and wool still.

837: This year, a week before Saint John's, Northmen fell on our people unprepared on the island called Walacria, killed many and plundered more. They stayed some while, took what tribute they liked, and went on to Dorestad and did the same.

837: Eggihard, count of that place, and Hemming, Halfdan's son, a Dane in the emperor's service, are killed here on the same day. The heathen lead many women away captive. A star with a tail is seen that year.

837: The emperor gives up his journey to Rome and comes to Noviomagus. The inquiry lays the loss partly to impossibility and partly to the disobedience of some. Abbots and counts are sent to curb the Frisians, and a fleet is ordered.
In 838, on Saint Stephen's day the sea covers nearly all Frisia, almost to the tops of the dunes. Two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven are counted drowned.
838: About these years a ring fort of sods with a moat is begun by the dunes, the largest of five on the islands. Others date it after 851, or about 890. Who built it is not known.

From 841 to 850: Harald's years. A heathen lord's hall on a Christian shore: no toll, but a gift in kind, and his men take what they like from those who bring none. The fleets that pass leave the strand alone. Priests stay away.
841: Lothar gives Walcheren and the places round it to the Dane Harald. The annalist calls it a deed to be detested, that Christians should serve men who worship demons.
As a trading place it ends about 850.
850: Harald is dead by this year. His brother Rorik takes Dorestad and is given it by the same king.

From 851 to 875: the last traders. Harald is dead and Rorik holds Dorestad. One house in three stands empty; the timbers of the rest are taken down and carried inland one by one. The ring fort has byres in it.
875: About now the traders are gone from the strand. Inside the fort five byre-houses are farmed until about 950.
From 876 to 950: farms inside the wall and a few on the old strand. Great fleets pass and nobody goes down to the water to look. Sand lies against the west doors.
879: Between this year and 892 great fleets pass the island eight times. The army winters at Ganda in 879.
From 951 to 1013: the fort's farms are given up. The old street is posts in the sand, and after a gale the dead show in the dune foot. The people live inland, and churches are rising on the island.
1000: About now blown sand drives the last people inland from the old strand.
1012: Count Baldwin of Flanders is said to receive Walcheren in fief from the emperor.

From 1014 to 1066: after the flood of 1014 the island is the count of Flanders's and the churches of Saint Willibrord's. Where the trading place stood there is beach. Fishermen find pennies there and do not know whose face is on them.
In 1014, on Michaelmas eve a sea flood wrecks the island.

pages.title: Witla
pages.hint: A market among the Frisians
pages.brief: A lost trading place at the mouth of the Maas.
pages.game:
Witla is a strand market in a tidal creek on the south shore of the Maas mouth: perhaps forty houses on the marsh ridge, boats on the mud, the king's toll post where the Maas and Waal roads reach the sea without passing Dorestad. A merchant comes for the pilot who knows the bar, for Frisian cloth, dried fish and peat salt at the price of the place that makes them, and for the wine, pots and quernstones that come down river and wait here for a wind to England. It is the last dry ground before the crossing and the first news after it.
The sea is open from about Easter to Martinmas, and the strand is busy only in those months; after the winter floods the pilot sounds the bar again, because the channel never comes back where it was. Sheep are shorn before Saint John's day and the cloth comes to the strand at Lammas; fish is dried in the spring winds; in winter the place is cattle, looms and peat smoke, and the marsh goes under at every storm tide, for there are no dykes.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine and bar iron; wanted here, and so dearer: oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: king Charles's years. A working strand: the toll post at the creek mouth, cloth and fish going out, wine and stone coming down, old Gerlef sounding the bar with a pole taller than himself. The first two summers are hungry.
pages.known:
A lost trading place at the mouth of the Maas. The place today: lost, the Maas mouth (?). In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
690: One Rathadus gives the abbey of Saint Peter at Ghent a farm at Witle, a small place in the Frisian district: a house, grazing for five cows, and four serfs. Witle is probably Witla. The gift is of the late 7th century; the note of it may be of the early 9th. 726: Willibrord gives the church 'in the district Marsum, where the Maas goes into the sea', with a sheep pasture, to his abbey of Echternach. He had it from the cleric Heribald. It stands on the north bank, across the water from Witla.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/witla.md (researched 4 Oct 2026): the base of everything here; where this file says more than the dossier, it says 'invented' or '(?)'.; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); Dijkstra 2011, pp. 175, 324; Gysseling 1960, p. 1084 (?); Dijkstra 2011, p. 282 (Oorkondenboek van Holland en Zeeland I, not opened)

later.text: 794: At Frankfurt the king names the most that may be asked for a measure of grain and orders his new heavy pennies taken in every market.
Until 796 the stones for England lie unsold above the tide line.

796: King Charles writes to Offa about pilgrims, tolls, black stones and the length of cloaks; the merchants of each realm have the other king's protection again. The quernstones that go to England pass this river mouth.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.

802: The law of the Frisians is written down at Aachen. It counts the coast from the Sincfal to the Vlie as its western part, where the blood-price of noble, free and half-free runs as four, two and one.

From 814 to 833: the emperor Louis's years. Gerlef is dead and whoever has his marks takes ships over the bar. New pennies with the emperor's name pass on the strand. There is a beacon watch kept by turns, and each year fewer men turn out for it.

From 834 to 836: the last seasons. Fleets pass the mouth to Dorestad in 834 and 835; boats lie ready to run, stores go inland by the creeks, and the count of Walcheren comes over to count spears. In the summer of 836 Witla burns.
834: A fleet of the Danes wastes part of Frisia and comes by Utrecht to Dorestad.
835: The Northmen come to Dorestad a second time.
A lost trading place at the mouth of the Maas, burned in 836 (?).
As a trading place it ends about 836.

In 836 the Northmen burned the town of Antwerp, and likewise Witla, the trading place near the mouth of the river Maas, and took tribute from the Frisians. It is the only time Witla is named as a market.

From 837 to 840: no market. Black posts on the ridge, tribute paid to the Northmen, the count dead on Walcheren. On Saint Stephen's day 838 the sea goes over everything. A ship crossing the bar finds nobody to ask the way.

In 837, on 17 June the Northmen take Walcheren and kill its count, Eggihard, and Hemming son of Halfdan. The emperor hurries to Nijmegen, holds an inquiry into the lords charged with the coast watch, and orders ships built.
In 838, on Saint Stephen's day the sea covers nearly all Frisia; 2,437 are counted dead. If anything of Witla still stood, this is thought to have ended it.

From 841 to 984: a river mouth without a market. The Danes hold Walcheren and Dorestad in their years; a few farms stand on the creeks of the south bank with Rhenish pots on their shelves; ships for England pass without stopping.
841: Lothar gives Walcheren and the places near it to the Dane Harald. Whether the Maas mouth was among them is not said.
885: Godfrid the Northman is killed; Gerulf is count on this coast. A ring fort is built for the Rhine mouth. None is known on the Maas.
The note of it may be of the early 9th, in a copy of 941.

From 985 to 1066: the land is Masaland and the count's. From about 1018 a fort and a toll stand at Vlaardingen on the north bank, and the ships of Tiel pay there on their way to England. Of Witla there is a name, and a bank where the nets catch.
In 985, on 25 August at Nijmegen King Otto III makes Count Dirk II's fiefs his own, Masaland between Lier and IJssel among them.

In 1018, on 29 July Count Dirk III beats the emperor's army at Vlaardingen, on the north bank, where he has built a fort and takes a toll the merchants of Tiel call robbery. The ships had stood off into deep water for the ebb, and men drowned trying to reach them.
1047: The emperor Henry III takes Rijnsburg and Vlaardingen from Count Dirk IV.

pages.title: Medemelacha
pages.hint: A market among the Frisians
pages.brief: West Frisian trading place on the Almere shore, on the inland route north from Dorestad.
pages.game:
One row of some twenty thatched houses on the south bank of a peat stream, at the end of a sandy ridge in wide wet moss, a long day north of the Vecht mouth across the Almere. It is the king's ground: every hull that passes pays him a tenth, and a tenth of that tenth is Saint Martin's at Traiectum. A merchant comes to break the run between the Rhine and the terps, to sell Rhenish pots, querns, wine, iron and timber to people who have none, and to load cloth, hides, salt beef and cheese.
The water opens at Easter and the Rhine boats come north with it; the cattle are driven in from the lake hamlets and killed and salted at Martinmas, when hides are cheap and salt is dear. In a hard frost the stream and the lake bear a man, and the boys go out on bone runners with pricker poles; at the thaw the bank is mended, each household its own length.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cheese, Frisian cloth, eels, butter and cattle; wanted here, and so dearer: wheat, Mayen quernstones, oak timber, rye and barley. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the king's toll in its quiet years. One row of houses ten paces back from a soft bank, Rhine boats nosed into the reeds, a king's man with a tally and a small wooden church of Saint Martin (?). The first two summers are hungry: the moss grows cattle, not bread.
pages.known:
West Frisian trading place on the Almere shore, on the inland route north from Dorestad. The place is now Medemblik. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 675 the place begins, probably as a seasonal bank market for skippers between the Rhine and the terps; people soon stay the year round. 719: About this year, on Radbod's death, the country comes under the Franks. The place is the king's own, and he takes toll from every trader who sails past. 753: Pippin grants Saint Martin's at Traiectum a tenth of the king's income from his lands and tolls; the tenth here most likely goes back to this grant, which does not name the place (?).

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
About 802 the law of the Frisians is written down: between the Vlie and the Sincfal a noble's life is 100 solidi, a free man's 50, a half-free man's 25, and Sunday work costs 4 solidi.

From 810 to 837: the first fleets are on the islands. Nothing is written of a raid here, but silver goes under hearth stones and the cattle are kept further from the water. Trade goes on; the pots in the houses are still Badorf ware.
810: The first raids on this coast are written down: a Danish fleet of two hundred ships on the Frisian islands, and a hundred pounds of silver paid. What it did here is not recorded.
From 838 to 840: after the flood of Saint Stephen's day: the lake hamlets drowned, the cattle dead, salt in the wells, the bank torn out. Everything is wanted and there is no silver to pay with.
In 838, on the day after Christmas a storm flood goes over Frisia and 2,437 people are counted drowned. Its effect here is unknown.

From 841 to 885: Danish lords over western Frisia. The toll is taken as before, by a Dane, for a Dane, in a Frankish king's name; silver is weighed as often as counted. Dorestad's boats come less each year, and after 863 not at all.

850: Rorik the Dane is granted Dorestad 'and other counties'. That he held this toll is likely, not stated. About now 1,662 g of silver goes into the ground in a Badorf pot at Westerklief on Wieringen, nearly a day's walk north.
About 863 Dorestad ends. The house row here lives on, perhaps because of its toll.
882: Godfrid the Dane is given Rorik's lands; he is killed in 885, and the Danish lords of western Frisia end with him.

From 886 to 984: the counts' time. Dorestad is gone and the row has grown: more houses, thin turf walls, a byre at one end. The peat behind is being ditched and ploughed, and the boats from the south now come from Tiel and Daventre with Pingsdorf pots.
In 889, on 4 August King Arnulf grants lands to Count Gerulf; the place probably stands under him and his heirs from now on.
About 900 the place is first written down: 'In Medemolaca regalis decima', the king's tenth, in the goods register of Saint Martin's, drawn together about 918 under Bishop Balderik.

From 985 to 1066: the bishop's toll. Count Ansfried has the king's share from 985 and takes it with him to Saint Martin's in 995. West of here the Frisians kill a count and owe nobody anything; a potter works on the row, combs are cut from antler, and the dead begin to be laid by the church.

In 985, on 26 June King Otto, a child of five, gives Count Ansfried the king's share of toll, mint and rent at 'villa Medemelacha'. On 25 August at Nijmegen he gives Count Dirk his fief between the rivers Medemelacha and Chinnelosa as his own.
In 993, on 18 September Count Arnulf is killed at Winkel, half a day's walk west, fighting the West Frisians.
995: Ansfried becomes bishop of Traiectum, and Saint Martin's now holds all the king's income here.
1064: King Henry gives Bishop William of Traiectum the count's rights in Westflinge, the first time the district is named.

pages.title: Winaldum
pages.hint: A king's seat among the Frisians
pages.brief: A great terp in Westergo, seat of Frisian lords (?).
pages.game:
Seven house mounds in a row on a salt-marsh ridge in Westergo, two days north of Dorestad by the Almere and the Vlie. The gold of its old lords is a hundred and fifty years in the ground; in 793 it is a rich farm terp under the Frankish king, with a smith, weavers, a bead bench and more sheep than people. A merchant comes for Frisian cloth, cheese, hides and stock, and brings grain, Rhenish pots and glass, iron and antler, because the terp country grows no bread of its own.
Shearing after Easter, cloth off the looms from midsummer to Martinmas, and the cattle killed and salted at Martinmas. From the first autumn gales the marsh floods between the mounds and a boat can lie against the terp itself; in a hard winter the creek freezes and the children go out on skates of bone.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cheese, Frisian cloth, eels, butter and cattle; wanted here, and so dearer: wheat, Mayen quernstones, oak timber, rye and barley. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a rich farm terp two generations after the Franks came. One leading house with its dependants, weaving huts full of looms, a smith, a bead bench when the bead man is in. No church: a priest comes when he comes. The old who saw the shrines burn are still alive, and in a hungry year the terp buys bread with cloth.
pages.known:
A great terp in Westergo, seat of Frisian lords (?). The place is now Wijnaldum. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 630 a great gold brooch set with more than three hundred garnets is worn on the terp, and a goldsmith works there with touchstones and a die for patterned foil. About 700 small silver pennies of the kind called series D are struck in Frisia, possibly on this terp (?). In 734 Charles, the Franks' leader, beat the Frisians on the Boorne, took the land between Vlie and Lauwers and burned the shrines. About 780 Liudger was sent to break the shrines of the Frisians and brought back the treasure found in them; the king took two thirds. No shrine is named: that one stood at Winaldum is the game's (?).
