Diekamp 1881), by way of spine.json

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
About 802 the Frisians' law was written down for the king. Between Lauwers and Vlie three new pennies make a solidus; a noble's life is eighty solidi, a free man's fifty-three and a penny.

From 810 to 837: after the two hundred ships. The terp has paid its share once and knows it can be asked again. The law is written now and is quoted at the hearth. Landric the island priest says Mass at the cross by the old mound. Cloth goes south to the abbeys' collectors every autumn.
In 810 two hundred Danish ships lay on the Frisian islands. Three fights were lost and a hundred pounds of silver paid.

From 838 to 849: the flood years and the tribute years. Salt in the pits, fewer cattle, the mound raised by a layer of sods. In 846 the Northmen go through Westergo: on this terp silver is in the ground, not on the table, and strangers are watched from the top of the mound before they are greeted.
838: This year, on the day after Christmas, the sea came over Frisia and 2,437 people were counted drowned.
In 845 the Frisians are said to have killed more than twelve thousand heathen men.
In 846 the Northmen laid waste Ostracia and Westracia: the one annal that names Westergo. The Danes took tribute and held nearly the whole province.

From 850 to 873: the Danes' years. Whoever holds Dorestad sends for his due, and pennies with a dead emperor's name are copied on this coast because everyone trusts them. Wells are dug on the terp. The pendants and knucklebones are no longer worn. In 867 the Frisians drive Rorik out; in 873 Rodulf dies in Oostergo.
In a hard winter the creek freezes and the children go out on skates of bone (after 850).
As a trading place it ends about 850.
In 850 Rorik the Dane was given Dorestad and other counties. No text gives him Westergo.
In 852 252 ships took payment in Frisia and went away.
In 867 the people newly called Cokingi drove Rorik out of Frisia.
In 873 in June Rodulf the Northman asked tribute of Count Albdag's Oostergo and fell there with five or eight hundred men; the Frisians were led by a Northman turned Christian.

From 874 to 950: quieter. The sunken huts are gone and weaving is done in the houses. The children skate on bone. The old middle of the mound is given up for building, and the houses move outward as the terp grows.
880: In the later part of this century (?) more than 2,600 pennies, copies of the emperor Lothar's Dorestad coin, were buried at Tzummarum, a short walk north-east along the ridge.
950: By about this year the dug part of the terp Tjitsma is no longer lived on, but the mound itself goes on growing to its greatest size in the next century.

From 951 to 1005: a big terp village among dikes that are just beginning: a ring dike stands round Pingjum to the south. The creek is narrower every year. Cloth and stock still go out, by the Vlie and Stavoren.

From 1006 to 1066: the count is a Saxon lord from Brunswick whom nobody here has seen. His pennies come from Bolsward and Stavoren, and the terp's trade goes to those markets. The mound is at its greatest; what was a lords' seat is a village of free farmers who say so.
1006: From this year Liudolf of Brunswick is count in Westergo; under his son Bruno (1038-1057) pennies are struck at Bolsward, Dokkum, Leeuwarden and Stavoren.

pages.title: Doccinga
pages.hint: A village among the Frisians
pages.brief: Terp village in Oostergo, where Boniface was killed in 754.
pages.game:
A wooden church on a raised mound in the salt marsh, kept as the place where Boniface and his companions were killed in 754, with a clergy house, a graveyard and a spring. South of it a long dwelling mound of stock farmers lies above a tidal creek. A merchant comes for Frisian cloth, cheese, butter and hides straight from the farms, and brings what the marsh lacks: grain, timber, iron, querns, pots, and wine and wax for the altar.
The year turns on the fifth of June, Boniface's day, when the marsh fills with pilgrims and Liudger rides through; he comes again in autumn on his way to teach at Traiectum. Shearing and the new cheese come before midsummer, slaughter and hides at Martinmas, and from then until Easter the storm tides run over the unembanked marsh and the creeks are no place for a stranger.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cheese, Frisian cloth, eels, butter and cattle; wanted here, and so dearer: wheat, Mayen quernstones, oak timber, rye and barley. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the mission church of the bishop of Traiectum, two generations old, with its priests back after the rising of 784. No market, no toll, no mint: a church, a spring, farms and a muddy landing. East of the Lauwers the churches burn in 793 and priests come here on foot. Liudger passes each spring and autumn. Bread is dear in the hungry years and the farms pay for grain in cloth and cheese.
pages.known:
Terp village in Oostergo, where Boniface was killed in 754. The place is now Dokkum. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
734: Charles Martel beat the Frisians on the Boorne. The land west of the Lauwers has been the Franks' since. In 754, on the fifth of June Boniface was killed with Bishop Eoba and about fifty companions. Willibald names only the river Bordne; the people here hold that it was on this ground. Fulda and Mainz count the year as 755. 754: The killers broke open the mission's chests looking for gold, found books, and strewed them over the meadow and into the reeds, where some were found long after, unharmed. 768: By this year, on King Pippin's order, Count Abba and a great part of the Frisian folk had raised a mound against the spring tides. A church and a house for the clergy were built on it, and a spring of sweet water broke out where a horse sank. 770: Willehad, a Northumbrian priest, began his mission here some time between 765 and 774, then crossed the Lauwers, where heathens cast lots on whether he should die. He left alive. 777: Liudger, a Frisian taught at Traiectum and York, was set over Oostergo from this church. He taught here seven years and went to Traiectum each autumn to teach there. 784: In Widukind's rising the Frisians drove out the priests, burned churches and went back to the old gods. Whether this church burned is written nowhere (?). 793: Saxons and Frisians east of the Lauwers, the next river east, rose again. Churches were burned and priests driven out. Doccinga stayed quiet and took in those who fled.

Robinson 1916, paraphrased); dossier section 8; Willibald ch. 8 (paraphrased); Willibald ch. 9 (paraphrased); the mound is 3 to 4 m of salt-marsh sods, built in one go: Cultuurhistorische verkenning binnenstad Dokkum, 2008; Catholic Encyclopedia, Willehad; Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, Willehad; the year is the middle of the range (?); Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.17-21, as in the spine and the Catholic Encyclopedia, Ludger; Catholic Encyclopedia, Ludger; dossier section 8; chronicle_793.json 793-autumn-saxon-revolt; the fugitives here are the game's reading (?)

later.text: 794: The king's new heavy penny was ordered to be taken in every place. The Frisian law counts its fines in old money and new.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
809: Liudger died on the twenty-sixth of March, bishop at Mimigernaford.

From 810 to 838: Liudger is dead and his feast is kept on the twenty-sixth of March beside Boniface's. In 810 the Danish fleet lies on the islands and every mound is told its share of the hundred pounds. Afterwards the church is fuller than before, the old people who saw 754 are dying, and clerks from Traiectum begin to write down what they say.
810: In summer two hundred Danish ships ravaged the Frisian islands. Three fights were lost and a hundred pounds of silver was paid.
In 838, on the day after Christmas a storm flood went over Frisia. 2,437 were counted drowned.

From 839 to 873: after the great flood of Christmas 838 the mounds stand in a marsh of dead cattle and new creeks, and the graveyard is larger. Danish lords hold the Rhine mouths to the south. Baptised Northmen live among the Frisians here; one of them has a farm and grandchildren. In June 873 Rodulf comes for tribute and is killed.

About 840 Altfrid wrote his Life of Liudger, the first sure text to name this place. In the same half-century a cleric of Utrecht asked here about Boniface, and a very old woman swore she had seen the killing.

873: In June Rodulf, a baptised Dane of royal kin, demanded tribute of Oostergo. The Frisians answered that they owed it to none but King Louis and his sons. He fell with five or eight hundred men; the rest, shut in a building, bought their lives with their treasure and an oath never to return. No annal says where.

From 874 to 999: a quiet century by the record. The church keeps its day, Fulda holds land at Aalsum, and the clergy house is where church law is spoken for the district. Frisians of this coast carry cloth and take silver in every sea, and bring some of it home.
945: Aalsum, the mound just north, is in Fulda's list of its lands as Atlesheim.

From 1000 to 1037: the name is written Doccinga. A church of grey tuff stone from the Rhine is going up for canons and pilgrims, and a small one of Saint Martin south of it for the parish. The first low sea dikes run along the creek. There is a market on the long mound and a man who takes the count's toll.
About 1000 the name is written Doccinga. In this century come churches of tuff stone, the first sea dikes along the creek, a market, a toll and a mint.
1024: The counts of Brunswick hold Oostergo, from this year or from 1006. None of them is known to have come here.

From 1038 to 1066: count Bruno of Brunswick, who has never been seen here, has pennies struck in his name: small, thin, with the king's crowned head. Skippers take them north and east by the bagful. In 1057 Bruno is killed and Egbert follows. The place is a market town in all but name.
1038: Count Bruno's silver pennies are struck here, reading DOCC and BRVN, with the king's crowned head on the other face. They are found as far off as the Baltic lands and Russia.
1057: Count Bruno was killed on the twenty-sixth of June. Egbert followed him.

pages.title: Emuthon
pages.hint: A market among the Frisians
pages.brief: A trading terp at the mouth of the Ems.
pages.game:
In 793 Emuthon is hardly a place yet: a low rise of clay sods where a creek meets a loop of the Ems, a few plank houses of Frisian traders, sheep to the edge of the sky. It is the last landing under the Frankish king before the Saxons and the Danes, and this summer it is in revolt. A merchant comes for wool, grey cloth, cheese and hides, and brings what the marsh has none of: grain, timber, iron, querns and wine.
New cloth comes off the looms before Easter, the wool at midsummer after the shearing, butter and cheese all summer, and cattle are sold on the hoof before Martinmas. From Martinmas to Easter the boats are drawn up, the marsh floods at every spring tide, and the people sit on their mound among the stalled beasts and weave.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cheese, Frisian cloth, eels, butter and cattle; wanted here, and so dearer: wheat, Mayen quernstones, oak timber, rye and barley. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a summer landing more than a village: a sod rise above the spring tides, plank houses of a few trading households, sheep-houses on the marsh. In 793 the district is in revolt, the chapel up the river is burned and no priest shows his face.
pages.known:
A trading terp at the mouth of the Ems. The place is now Emden. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
785: King Charles takes Frisia as far as the Weser. The district of the Ems mouth, Emisga, is the king's from now on. 787: Liudger, a Frisian taught at Utrecht and York, is set over five districts east of the Lauwers, Emisga among them, and the island Bant. 791: Liudger builds the first chapel in these parts, of timber, at Leer up the Ems. In 793 the East Frisians rose with the Saxons under Unno and Eilrat, burned the churches and drove out the priests. Liudger fled, and was back within the year.
pages.source: J. M. Grimm, Animal keeping and the use of animal products in medieval Emden (Lower Saxony, Germany), thesis, Groningen 2010, chapters 1 and 7 (summarising Haarnagel 1955, Brandt 1994, van Lengen 1994, Stilke 1995): https://pure.rug.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/2611577/01c1.pdf ; https://pure.rug.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/2611583/07c7.pdf; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); de.wikipedia 'Geschichte Ostfrieslands'; dossier section 1; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22 (ed. Diekamp 1881), through de.wikipedia 'Liudger'; de.wikipedia 'Leer (Ostfriesland)'; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22; chronicle_793.json

later.text: In 794 Liudger is back and nobody is punished who comes to be shriven.
Bread is dear in 793 and 794.

From 800 to 838: the first mound with its ditch: forty metres of crowded ground, small houses, looms, a rain pond. Liudger's priests come and go by boat. In 810 the Danes are on the islands and the mound pays its share of the hundred pounds. The flood of Christmas 838 drowns the low marsh and leaves the mound an island for a week.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.

About 800 a ditch less than a pace wide is dug round the first mound, some forty metres across. It is the oldest thing at Emden that can be dated; the place was most likely founded near this year, by traders.
802: The law of the Frisians is written down, with its own fines for the land between Lauwers and Weser.
805: Liudger is made bishop at Mimigernaford and keeps his five Frisian districts. The Ems mouth belongs to that see from now on.
In 809, on the twenty-sixth of March Liudger dies.
In 810 two hundred ships of the Danes came to the Frisian islands, beat the Frisians in three fights and took a hundred pounds of silver as tribute.
814: The emperor Louis gives back to the Frisians who had risen their right to inherit.
In 838, on the day after Christmas a great flood goes over Frisia; two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven are counted drowned.

From 839 to 899: the mound grows northward, a palisade marks its edge, and a street runs along its crown with narrow houses of traders and craftsmen fronting it. After 870 the Ems mouth is East Frankish and a count's man takes the king's toll (?). The Danes leave the place more or less alone; in 884 they are beaten at Norditi.
870: At Meerssen the Ems mouth falls to the East Frankish kingdom. From about now the mound is enlarged northward with clay sods, a street is laid on it, and Emden is a market for its district.
884: In the autumn the Frisians under Archbishop Rimbert beat the Danes at Norditi, a day's walk to the north. Many of the Danes are drowned by the tide.

From 900 to 1019: a second mound with a farmer's long house and byre, the counts of Werl far away in Westphalia, and from the 940s a timber church on its own mound to the west with the dead laid east and west about it. Emuthon has outgrown Groothusen and Hatzum. The first sea banks are thrown up along the coast about 1000.
About 900 the counts of Werl, a Westphalian house, hold the county of the Ems, and the mound is enlarged again.
941: Not before this year a timber church is built on a mound of its own to the west, with a graveyard.
966: A second timber church is built on the place of the first, of oak felled this year.

From 1020 to 1066: a count's market with a mint: light pennies with HERIMAN on one side and AMVTHON on the other go out to the Danes and the east. Plots are ditched and fenced, a fire takes part of the street, and from 1062 the count and the archbishop of Bremen both claim the toll.
1020: From about this year until about 1051 pennies are struck here with the names HERIMAN and AMVTHON: the first writing of the name. They are light, three quarters of a gram.
1050: In this age, the year not known, a fire burns houses on the mound.
1062: The king orders the county of the Ems handed to Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg and Bremen. Count Bernhard of Werl does not give it up, and about 1063 the archbishop's man Gottschalk is killed.
1066: Archbishop Adalbert falls from power at the king's court.

pages.title: Daventre
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: Lebuinus's church on the IJssel, the road east to the Saxons.
pages.game:
A wooden church on a river dune, a row of houses on a sand ridge and a bank where boats lie, on the east side of the IJssel where the king's land ends and the Saxons' begins. The road from the Rhine to the Weser crosses the river here, so every May the host and its carts cross too. A merchant comes to sell to the army and the church, to buy heath iron, eels, horses and Saxon honey, and to hear what is happening in the east before anyone downriver knows.
After Easter the count's men buy up grain, horses and salt meat for the host, and prices on the bank go up until the army has marched. At summer's end the river is low enough to wade; after Martinmas it rises, a second channel runs round the north-east and the place is an island until spring, with ice in a hard winter. Lebuin's feast is the morrow of Martinmas.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine and bar iron; wanted here, and so dearer: oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the border in wartime. A wooden church, fishers, a few traders and a smith; every spring the count's men, carts and horse lines for the host that goes into Saxony, and every autumn hostages coming back west over the ferry. Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers stand at the same Mass.
pages.known:
Lebuinus's church on the IJssel, the road east to the Saxons. The place is now Deventer. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
754: Lebuin (Liafwin), an English priest, came to Utrecht, and was sent from there to the IJssel. About 768 Lebuin's wooden church was built on the river dune; Saxons burned it and it was built again. 773: About 773 to 775 Lebuin died here. The church was burned again after his death, and the Saxons looked three days for his body and did not find it. 776: About 775 to 777 Liudger, sent by Alberic of Utrecht, built the church a third time, found the grave under the south wall he had just raised, and moved the foundations so that the grave lay inside. 793: The Saxons and the East Frisians rose again and burned churches; the road east from the IJssel was not safe.

Diekamp 1881); dossier 2 and 7; chronicle_793.json 793-autumn-saxon-revolt (Annales regni Francorum 793)

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.

802: About 802 to 803 the law of the Franks of 'Amor' was written down in 48 chapters: a Frankish man's wergild 600 solidi, a freeman's 200. 'Amor' is usually read as Hamaland, the land about this river.

From 806 to 856: the war is over and the place is quiet: a church town on a minor river, under the law of the Franks of 'Amor'. The Saxons across the border have bishops of their own now, and the road east carries wine, quernstones and pots instead of spears.

From 857 to 881: the bishop of Utrecht's people are here in exile and Dorestad's merchants follow as their river fails. New plots are pegged out along the bank; a timber revetment holds it; an abbey in the far west holds seven manses 'in the port'.
About 857 the clergy of Utrecht fled the Northmen; for some sixty-five years the bishops of Utrecht kept a house here.
In 877, on 20 June Charles the Bald confirmed to the abbey of Saint-Bertin seven manses 'in Daventre portu'.
From 882 to 889: burned by the Northmen late in 882. For some years the bank is charcoal and new timber, and everyone who has stayed carries sods for a wall nearly two kilometres round.
882: Late in the year the Northmen burned the port 'called Taventeri in the Frisian tongue, where Saint Liobomus rests', and killed many.
889: Before 890 an earth wall was finished round the place, over a layer of burning 20 cm thick: sods, probably a palisade, 1.9 km long.

From 890 to 920: a walled port and a bishop's seat. The king's toll is taken on the bank, the church's men go free of it as they did at Dorestad, and Bishop Radboud writes verses in a house by Lebuin's church.
896: King Zwentibold ruled on the king's toll at Deventer and Tiel in favour of the church of Utrecht, whose men were to have the freedom they had had at Dorestad.
In 917, on 29 November Bishop Radboud died at Ootmarsum and was buried here, in the north part of the church.
About 920 Bishop Balderic took the see back to Utrecht.

From 921 to 989: the bishop has gone home to Utrecht. What is left is the king's: a court, two farmsteads, some thirty dwellings inside the wall, given piece by piece to Magdeburg. A stone church stands where the wooden one was. Barges of Ardennes oak work the river.
952: In 952, 956 and 960 Otto I gave the king's property here to Saint Maurice's at Magdeburg: a court, two farmsteads and some thirty dwellings. The charters call the place urbs or civitas.

From 990 to 1045: a mint town. Deventer and Tiel strike the pennies of these lands, and most of them go north and east to pay for furs and wax. Old barges are broken up to face the quay. About 1040 Bishop Bernold's basilica rises over the saint.

About 990 the first pennies were struck here, reading ODDO REX and DAVNER/A in three lines after the pennies of Cologne. In the spring of 990 the oak was felled for a flat river barge that later went into the quay.
1014: After this year the king's mint struck the Hand type, which Countess Adela of Hamaland had struck first, with the English king's Hand on one side and Deventer's cross on the other.
About 1040 Bishop Bernold built the stone basilica: three aisles, columns, transepts, a westwork and a crypt.
From 1046 to 1066: the bishop's town: toll, mint and court are his by the emperor's gift, twenty canons and a provost sing in the basilica, and a bishop's palace stands against its north side.
1046: Henry III gave Deventer, with toll, mint and justice, and the county in Hamaland to the bishop of Utrecht.

pages.title: Noviomagus
pages.hint: A king's seat among the Franks
pages.brief: The king's palace above the Waal.
pages.game:
Noviomagus is a king's house, not a town: a palace being built inside the walls of an old Roman fort, on a hill above the south bank of the Waal, with a small settlement of boatmen, craftsmen and farmers on the bank below. In 793 the king is elsewhere and the place is half a building yard and half a farm that feeds a court which has not come. A merchant comes for what a court eats and wears when it does come, for the ear of the men who serve it, and because every count on the lower Rhine must one day stand in that hall.
The year here is the court's: when the king keeps Lent and Easter at the palace, a few hundred mouths arrive by ship and everything is wanted at once; in spring and autumn he hunts the Ketil wood, and the assemblies fall in May, June and October. Between courts the bank is quiet, the river runs high after the thaw and low at harvest, and the cellarer buys ahead.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine and bar iron; wanted here, and so dearer: oak timber. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a building yard on a hill. Masons and carpenters work inside the old fort; the king has not been seen here since 777. The cellarer buys little and slowly, the bank settlement lives off the works, and news from court comes by letter.
pages.known:
The king's palace above the Waal. The place is now Nijmegen. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 320 the Romans built the ditched fort on the hilltop whose walls still partly stand in 793, and the thick, high wall of tuff along the river bank. 595: Gold tremisses reading Niomago, found in the Escharen hoard of 590-600, were very likely struck here. No mint is known in the game's years. About 700 burial with weapons and pots ended and the old grave fields were closed: over 2,000 graves, the largest early medieval grave field found in the Netherlands. 777: Charles kept Easter here. A charter of 8 June, dated 'in Niumago palacio publico', gave Leusden and four forests to Saint Martin's of Utrecht. 793: The palace that Charles 'began at Nimeguen, on the Waal, the stream that washes the south side of the island of the Batavians' is perhaps still unfinished.

S. E. Turner 1880; nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts (dossier Ein 17, VP)

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
Historians date its completion about 804 or later.

From 806 to 814: the old king's Lents. In 806 and 808 Charles comes by ship with his whole house, laws are written in the palace, and for forty days every boat on the Waal has a buyer. An exiled English king passes through in 808.

806: Charles came by ship down the Moselle and the Rhine and kept Lent and Easter here. The capitulary made here capped famine prices by the modius (oats 2 d, barley 3, spelt 3, rye 4, cleaned wheat 6), called buying at harvest to sell dear 'shameful gain', forbade new tolls and ordered church treasure guarded.

808: Charles kept Lent and Easter here after a mild, sickly winter. Eardwulf, the exiled king of Northumbria, came to him and went on to Rome. The capitulary of April capped a best double cloak at 20 solidi, a single at 10, a marten or otter coat at 30.

From 815 to 840: Louis's house: hunts in the Ketil wood, oaths sworn in May, an assembly that waits for a Dane who does not come. From 834 the emperor arrives after each raid downriver, too late, and holds inquiries. A merchant with a count or a bishop to speak for him can win the emperor's own letter here.
817: Louis the emperor hunted here twenty days, after the wooden portico fell on him at Aachen.
821: In May the division of the realm among the emperor's sons was read again here and sworn. Louis came down the Maas by ship.
825: Louis hunted here in spring, and again in autumn with his son Lothar.
827: An assembly waited here for Horik, son of King Godfrid of the Danes, who had promised to come and did not.

About 828 Gerward, the palace librarian, who had charge of the palace works and buildings, was here; on the road to Aachen he heard of a healing from his host, questioned the woman and told the emperor next day.
830: About the first of October the assembly was held here so that Saxons and East Franks could come, and Louis recovered his power from his sons.
837: Northmen took tribute on Walcheren and at Dorestad. Louis hurried here and they left at once.
838: In May and June the coast defences were shared out here; a Danish fleet drowned in a storm; Louis the German was stripped of lands.

From 841 to 879: a fort more than a palace. Lothar's men watch the river; in 846 Dorestad burns and nothing is done. Courts are few. In 870 a western king and a Danish count make their bargain in the hall. Burned people come up the river and stay.
846: Lothar, in the fort at Noviomagus, saw Dorestad burned by the Northmen and could not avenge it.
870: Charles the Bald met Rorik the Northman, lord of Dorestad, in the palace and bound him by treaty.

From 880 to 881: the Northmen's winter. Their ships lie under the hill, a rampart of earth and timber rings the palace, and a king's army sits outside in the frost and cannot get in. At the thaw they burn it all and go.

880: A fleet of Northmen entered the Waal, put 'a very strong rampart and walls' round the palace and wintered in it. Eberhard the Saxon, son of Count Meginhard, was taken captive; his mother Evesa ransomed him 'at a great price'.
881: Louis the Younger besieged the palace in a hard winter, failed, and left on the Northmen's promise to go. They burned the palace and their works and made for the mouths of the Rhine.

From 882 to 924: a burned shell slowly mended. Black beams, a few roofs made good, the bank settlement back west of the hill. Kings pass and seldom stay. What Dorestad used to do is now done at Tiel, lower down the Waal.
898: Charles the Simple was here.

From 925 to 1029: the Saxon kings' house. Tiel leads the river trade and Noviomagus follows it. Otto holds an assembly here; the child Otto III is here often with his mother, and in 991 the empress Theophanu dies in the palace. Counts and abbesses bring their quarrels. In 1006 and 1007 fleets are on the Waal again and Tiel burns (as places/traiectum.json has it (?)); burned-out Tiel men set up sheds against the old wall here.
949: Otto the king held an assembly here.
980: Otto III was born in the Ketil wood, on the road between Noviomagus and Xanten.
In 991, on 15 June the empress Theophanu died here. She was buried at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne.
996: In 996 and 997 Count Balderik and Adela of Hamaland were heard here before Otto III over the abbey of Elten.

In 1018, on 16 March a great synod here excommunicated Count Otto of Hammerstein and his wife Irmingard, and ruled from an old book that the chalice stands to the right of the host. On 6 April, at the Easter court, Bishop Adalbold and the merchants of Tiel complained of Count Dirk's toll. The army sent against him was beaten at Vlaardingen on 29 July.

From 1030 to 1046: the Salian courts. An eight-sided chapel of tuff stands in the palace yard; the emperor comes most years; in 1036 a daughter of King Cnut is married here at Pentecost. English and Rhineland silver pass on the bank.
1030: About 1030-1040 the eight-sided chapel was built in the palace after the pattern of Aachen: tuff, and reused Roman tiles stamped by the Tenth Legion. Some date it 996, some after 1047.
1036: At Pentecost Henry, the emperor's son, wedded Gunhild, daughter of King Cnut, here. She took the name Kunigunde and was crowned on 29 June.
From 1047 to 1066: burned again in the duke's rising of 1047. The chapel stands among scorched walls. The settlement by the river trades on, with one eye on the counts at the river mouths.
1047: The palace was burned in Duke Godfrey the Bearded's rising against Henry III. Who set the fire is not certain.

pages.title: Quentovic
pages.hint: A market among the Franks
pages.brief: The Franks' Channel emporium on the Canche; the king's toll, the crossing to the English.
pages.game:
The king's wic on the Canche: with Dorestad one of the two sea gates of the Frankish realm, and the usual landing for the English bound for Francia and Rome. In 793 there is no wall and no count, only a long busy bank, a mint, abbey storehouses and the toll of the king's procurator, Abbot Gervold. A merchant comes for wine, quernstones and glass to sell over the water, for English wool, tin and lead coming back, and for news, because every letter between the two kingdoms passes this bank.
The short crossing runs most of the year: bishops cross at Easter, pilgrims from Pentecost to Michaelmas, and a king's envoy has sailed home in December with a fair wind. New wine comes down after the vintage and the men of the wic go up to the fair of Saint Denis in October (?); in Lent the cell of Saint Josse feeds whoever is waiting on the wind, and on the saint's day in the dark of December his keepers show the shrine.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, Frankish wine, flour, horses and linen; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and ermine. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the quarrel of the two kings. English hulls are few and nervous, one lies under arrest with her wool going sour, and Frisians carry what the English may not. Every letter between Charles and Offa passes the toll house.
pages.known:
The Franks' Channel emporium on the Canche; the king's toll, the crossing to the English. The place is now Visemarest, La Calotterie. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
668: Theodore of Tarsus, on his way to be archbishop at Canterbury, falls sick at Quentovic and sails when he mends (668-669). About this year Judoc, a Breton king's son, dies a hermit near the river mouth. 718: Boniface crosses from Lundenwic in a small swift ship with great sails and lands at the mouth of the river called Cuent. 754: King Pippin's new deniers are struck here; coins had been struck at the wic since the sixth century. 779: King Charles frees the ships and carts of Saint-Germain-des-Pres from his toll at Wicus, Rouen, Amiens, Maastricht and Dorestad. 787: Gervold becomes abbot of Saint-Wandrille on the Seine. For many years he is procurator over the kingdom's trade, taking tributes and tolls in divers ports and cities, chiefly at Quentawich. 790: King Charles, angered over a marriage refused, orders that no Englishman land in Gaul to trade. The abbey's history says Gervold's plea stopped the order; Alcuin writes that sailing is forbidden to merchants on both sides. 792: About now the king entrusts the cell of Saint Josse to Alcuin, to give alms to pilgrims.

The sources disagree on whether the ban bit; Lupus of Ferrieres, letter 11, with the editor's date (Desdevises du Dezert 1888) (?)

later.text: The toll is still a tenth, the mint is busy with the king's new heavy penny from 794, and it is a hungry year: the cell feeds a crowd at its gate.
794: In the autumn Alcuin's priest Martin lies sick at Wicus, at Saint Josse. The same year the king's heavier penny is ordered to be taken in every place and market.
796: King Charles writes to King Offa: true pilgrims pass free, traders among them pay the toll; each king's merchants have the other's protection.

From 797 to 814: the peace. English wool, tin and cloaks come over again and pilgrims crowd the bank from Pentecost; the toll men open bundles looking for traders dressed as pilgrims. From 800 the king's guards watch the coast, in 806 the old abbot dies, and from 811 a light burns at Boulogne that a steersman can find the coast by.
In 799, on the tenth of July a letter reaches Alcuin at Wicus.
King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
800: In spring King Charles inspects the Channel coast, sets a fleet and posts guards against pirates, and keeps Easter at Saint-Riquier.
801: Archbishop Aethelheard of Canterbury, bound for Rome, is met at Saint Josse by Alcuin's man with a horse and Alcuin's own saddle.
In 806, on the fourteenth of June Abbot Gervold dies.
811: The emperor comes to Boulogne, inspects the new fleet and has the old lighthouse relit.
812: Deniers with a ship on them are struck at Quentovic and at Dorestad, and at no other mint (812-814).

From 815 to 841: the wic at its fullest: abbey houses along the street, ship pennies in every purse, the emperor's merchants paying the tenth here and nowhere else. From 834 the talk is of fleets on the Rhine. Nobody builds a wall.
828: The emperor's own merchants go free of toll everywhere but Quentovic, Dorestad and the Alpine passes, where the tenth is taken.

From 842 to 863: after the dawn. Burnt plots between the houses that paid, fewer English names, a watch kept at the river mouth. The trade goes on: a prefect rules the port, the cell has monks again from about 849, and lead for a church roof is landed at Stapulas. In 858 the saints of the Seine come here as fugitives.
842: A fleet of Northmen comes on the emporium suddenly at first light and so rages with plunder, captivity and killing that nothing is left in it but the buildings ransomed for a price.
849: Lupus, abbot of Ferrieres, wins back the cell of Saint Josse and asks King Aethelwulf of the West Saxons for lead for his church roof, to be landed at the vill of Stapulas.

In 858, on the eleventh of May the bodies of Saint Wandrille and Saint Ansbert, carried from the Seine for fear of the Danes, reach Saint Peter's near the emporium and lie on its altar five days. That December or soon after, Grippo the prefect is caught by a storm on his way home from the kings of the English.

From 864 to 898: one of the king's ten mints, and striking more pennies than ever, while the port itself thins. Raiders come again and again (864, 881, 890, 894 (?)). People who can do so move up the river to the hill of Montreuil; about 898 Danes are said to hold the bank.
864: The edict of Pitres: new pennies from ten mints only, Quentovic among them, and the mint of Rouen belongs to Quentovic by ancient custom. Death for selling arms or horses to Northmen.
866: The saints' bodies lie at Saint Peter's again. A blind and lame boy and his fevered mother are healed.
898: Montreuil, on its hill a short way up the river, is first named. Danes are said to hold the port about now.

From 899 to 980: a landing below a castle. The counts of Montreuil hold the river and fight Flanders for it; the monks of Saint Josse are gone to England; the channel is harder each year. A few potters and one moneyer keep the old name, and pennies of Quentovic are still struck.
903: The monks of Saint Josse flee to England; the saint's relics go to Winchester.
939: Count Arnulf of Flanders takes Montreuil through a traitor and sends Herluin's wife and sons over the sea to King Athelstan; Herluin retakes it with Northmen.
980: Hugh Capet takes Montreuil, soon called his only sea port. About now the last known penny of Quentovic is struck.

From 981 to 1066: grass over the street. Ships for the king of the Franks lie under Montreuil, and Wissant and Boulogne have the crossing. An old man will show you where the mint stood, for a cup of ale, and be wrong.
1064: Harold Godwinson, wrecked on the coast of Ponthieu, is held by Count Guy at Beaurain on the Canche.

pages.title: Rotomagus
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: Archbishop's city on the Seine, the tide's reach.
pages.game:
Rotomagus is an old Roman city in a square wall of robbed stone on the north bank of the Seine, an archbishop's seat, and the place where the tide stops being of use. Sea ships come up to the wall on the flood; above it the barges take over, so the wine of the Paris country changes hulls here and the king's toll is taken as it does. A merchant comes for wine going out, for English lead, wool and tin coming in, for the fair of Saint-Denis upriver, and for news, which reaches this gate from both ends of the river.
Salmon run in Lent and a small silver fish that smells of cucumber is netted under the wall before Easter. The wheat is cut after Saint Ouen's (24 August); the wine boats go up for the fair of Saint Denis (9 October) and come down full before Martinmas, and wine is dear over the sea until Christmas. The big tides come with the new and the full moon; in a hard winter the river can freeze from bank to bank and a white goose with red feet comes down from the north.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, Frankish wine, flour, horses and linen; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and ermine. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: archbishop Mainard's city, old and quiet inside a wall too big for it: gardens and ruins between the houses, two churches joined by galleries, canons who sing in the Roman way. The toll is the king's and Abbot Gervold's men take it. These are hungry years: the poor sit at the gate of Saint Peter's, and men tell of grain that stood in the field and came to dust in the hand.
pages.known:
Archbishop's city on the Seine, the tide's reach. The place is now Rouen. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
About 395 Bishop Victricius builds a basilica inside the wall for relics of Gervase, Protase and others, sent to him by Ambrose of Milan. 684: Bishop Ouen is buried in Saint Peter's church outside the wall, which will one day take his name. 760: About these years Bishop Remigius, the king's brother, brings singers from Rome to teach the Roman chant and sets canons in the cathedral. 779: The king frees the boats of Saint-Germain-des-Pres of toll at Rotomagus, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht and Dorestad. So a toll is taken here; its rate is not written. 787: Gervold, bishop of Evreux, becomes abbot of Saint-Wandrille, a tide below the city. For many years he takes the king's tolls in the ports of this coast, chiefly at Quentovic.

later.text: English ships are few until the kings make peace in 796.
King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
800: After Easter King Charles crosses the Seine at Rotomagus on his way to Saint Martin's at Tours. He has been along the coast setting ships and guards against pirates.

From 801 to 840: the emperors' peace. Guard ships are ordered for the coast and seldom seen. The wine fleet goes up every October and the court comes by now and then: Charles in 800, Louis in 818 and 824, when Greeks in silk are seen in the street. From 804 Saxon families are set down on abbey land near the city (?). The river freezes in the winter of 821. Nobody mends the wall.
818: The emperor Louis passes through the city.
820: Bera, count of Barcelona, charged with bad faith and beaten in a duel on horseback, is spared his life and sent to live at Rotomagus.
822: In the winter of this year the Seine is frozen for thirty days and loaded carts cross on the ice.

In 824, on 17 November the emperor Louis comes back from Brittany to Rotomagus, where he had told his wife to wait for him. The envoys of the emperor of the Greeks are heard here on the matter of images, with Fortunatus, patriarch of Grado.

From 841 to 857: after the fire. On 14 May 841 the heathen men burned the city; the cathedral is patched with what did not burn, Saint Peter's stands roofless and its monks are gone with their saint. Fleets pass under the wall as they please. Trade goes on between the fleets, quickly, and every house has someone missing.
841: In spring a seething tide carries merchant ships up from the river mouth and leaves them by the city. King Charles fills twenty-eight of them with armed men and crosses.

841: This year, on the fourteenth of May, Danish pirates came up from the sea and fell on Rotomagus. They raged with plunder, sword and fire, and gave the city, the monks and the rest of the people over to killing and captivity.
841: Jumieges is burned ten days after. Saint-Wandrille buys itself off for six pounds of silver.
845: In March a hundred and twenty ships pass under the wall on their way to Paris. The king pays seven thousand pounds for them to go.
846: About these years King Charles has the head of Saint Romanus and the bodies of Remigius and Godard carried to Soissons for safety.
851: Northmen leave their ships at Rotomagus and go on foot as far as Beauvais.

From 858 to 884: the Northmen sit on the island at Oissel, a short pull upriver, and the king's works at Pitres rise and are never finished. From 864 the mint strikes the king's new penny by law, and it is death to sell a Northman a horse. The city buys back its people when it can and sells wine to whoever holds the river.
858: From July to the twenty-third of September the king besieges the Northmen on their island at Oissel, above the city, and fails.
864: The king's edict at Pitres, 25 June: new pennies from ten mints only, Rotomagus one of them; death for any man who sells a mail coat, arms or a horse to the Northmen.
In 876, on 16 September about a hundred ships of Northmen enter the Seine.

From 885 to 910: the Northmen's harbour. The army came in with all its ships in 885 and some never left. An archbishop still sits in the cathedral; outside it the strand is a market for what was taken elsewhere, silver by weight and people by the head. Honest cargoes come with a safe-conduct or not at all.
In 885, on 25 July the Northmen enter Rotomagus with their whole army. They find ships on the river and cross in them.

From 911 to 942: Rollo's city, then his son William's. One lord, one toll, thieves hanged. Land is measured out by the rope, the monks come home in 918, and wine goes out to England again. Norse is spoken on the strand and Romance in the market. Other Northmen are not let up the river.
911: King Charles grants Rotomagus and the land about the lower Seine to Rollo and his Northmen, to hold against other Northmen. Archbishop Franco baptises him, by Dudo's telling in 912.
918: The monks of Saint Peter's come back, and Saint Ouen's body with them.
925: The Northmen of Rotomagus break the peace. The Franks burn their land on this side of the Seine.
About 934 Riulf and his men rise against William, Rollo's son, and are beaten in the meadow between the west wall and the river.
942: William receives King Louis royally in the city. There is famine and a plague of cattle. On 17 December William is murdered at a parley on the Somme.

From 943 to 996: count Richard's long years. A stone tower stands at the south-east corner where the red brook meets the river, with his hall beside it. The mint strikes pennies in his name and the archbishop's. The town fills; a traveller from Spain finds it built of old stone, with no vines, and remembers a beard.
943: King Louis kills the Northman Turmod, who had gone back to idols and pressed the boy Richard to do the same, and the heathen king Setric with him. He gives Rotomagus to Herluin of Montreuil.
945: King Louis is seized by the men of Rotomagus and held in the city.
946: King Otto and King Louis waste the Northmen's land as far as the city. The Norman writers make it a siege, with Otto's nephew killed at the north gate.
965: About these years Ibrahim son of Jacob, a Jew of Tortosa, visits the city: a town of old stone, wheat and rye but no vines, salmon, and a young man whose beard reaches his knees.
996: Count Richard dies after fifty-four years. The country people hold assemblies to use wood and water by their own law, and are put down.

From 997 to 1035: the second Richard and his brother the archbishop. Danish fleets sell here what they take in England, and English exiles lodge in the same streets. Men of the city carry wine and whale to London in their own ships. Clerks at the count's court write Latin verse and mock each other in it.
About 1000 the king's toll at London names the men of Rouen, who come with wine or great fish: six shillings for a large ship and a twentieth of the fish.
1013: After Christmas, which he keeps on Wight, King Aethelred crosses to his wife's brother, Count Richard, at Rotomagus. Queen Emma and the boys Edward and Alfred are there before him.
1014: Archbishop Robert baptises Olaf, a Northman chief who will be king of the Norwegians.

From 1036 to 1066: the young duke's town, uneasy until he is grown and then very busy. A new church of Saint Mary rises over a crypt and is dedicated in 1063. In the last summer every wright on the coast is building ships, and nobody is told for where, and everybody knows.
1036: Archbishop Robert opens the shrine of Saint Romanus.
1055: Archbishop Mauger, the duke's uncle, is put out of his see at a council at Lisieux. Maurilius, a monk, follows him.
In 1063, on the first of October the new church of Saint Mary is dedicated before Duke William. The bodies of Rollo and William his son are moved into it.
About 1064 Earl Harold of the English is the duke's guest in the Tower.

pages.title: Parisius
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: The Seine city; the great autumn fair of Saint-Denis draws English and Frisian merchants.
pages.game:
Parisius is two places two hours' walk apart: an old Roman city on an island in the Seine, the seat of a bishop and a count, and the abbey of Saint Denis to the north, which a boat from the sea reaches first because the river loops. In 793 no king lives here; the abbey is the great house, and its fair, which opens on Saint Denis's day, is where the men from over the sea sell wool and cloth and buy wine. A merchant comes for the wine, the honey and the dyers' roots, for the orders of two rich abbeys, and for the weeks of the fair, when every toll in the district is the saint's and not the count's.
The year hangs on two days: Saint Denis's, the ninth of October, when the fair opens for a month (some say until Saint Andrew's) with the new wine still working in the cask, and the day the church was hallowed, late in February, when there is a smaller fair. The grapes are cut about Michaelmas; the hungry time is from Easter to the first sheaves.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, Frankish wine, flour, horses and linen; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and ermine. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the old king's years. A Lombard abbot at Saint-Denis and an old count on the island share the district and watch each other. No king lives here. The fair is full of Frisians. The new heavy penny comes in the first winter.
pages.known:
The Seine city; the great autumn fair of Saint-Denis draws English and Frisian merchants. The place is now Paris (Saint-Denis fair). In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
About 508 King Clovis began the church of the Holy Apostles on the hill of the left bank. He lies in it, with Queen Clotilde and the holy woman Genevieve. About 558 Saint Vincent's in the left-bank meadows was hallowed: a roof of gilded copper, a floor of mosaic, columns of marble. Bishop Germain's body has lain behind its high altar since 25 July 754 (or 756). 710: The count of Paris claimed half the toll of the fair and lost before the king. The judgment says the fair had been moved 'because of a disaster' from Saint-Denis to Paris, between Saint Martin's and Saint Laurence's. 753: The monks told King Pippin that merchants were staying away: since Charles Martel's day the count had taken four pennies a head from every free merchant, and five from a slave, who first had to swear he was one. Pippin struck the tax down and confirmed that every toll of the fair is the abbey's. Saxons (English) and Frisians are named among those who come 'to buy wine in the ports and on the rivers'. In 775, on 24 February Abbot Fulrad's new church at Saint-Denis was hallowed before King Charles: three aisles, a ring crypt, King Pippin's grave before the west door. About this year Charles confirmed the fair's tolls to the abbey from Saint Denis's Mass until the market ends: on ships, harbours, carts and pack beasts, and the wheel, bridge and gate tolls. In 779, on 27 March the king freed the traders of Saint-Germain from toll at Rouen, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht, Dorestad and Paris. 793: Fardulf, a Lombard priest, was given the abbey of Saint-Denis for uncovering the plot of the king's son Pippin the Hunchback the year before. Stephen has been count since 779; Erchanrad is bishop.

later.text: In 793 and 794 the abbeys feed hundreds at their gates.
The English stay away until the kings make peace in 796, and wool is dear.
799: A description of the church of Saint-Denis gives it 245 feet, 101 windows, and doors of gold, silver and ivory. It is copied from one of Saint Martin's at Tours, with the numbers made bigger.
King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
800: In summer King Charles passed through Paris. It is the only time he is recorded here in the game's years.
802: Abbot Fardulf and Count Stephen were named the king's envoys for Paris, Meaux, Melun, Provins, Étampes, Chartres and Poissy.
803: Count Stephen had the new chapters of the Salic law read in the public court at Paris before the law-finders. All agreed and set their hands to them.
From 804 Saxon families are said to be set down on church land up the river (?).

From 815 to 844: the abbeys' great years. Hilduin, the emperor's own chaplain, rules Saint-Denis like a lord: a Greek book, a chapel where the Mass never stops, parchment bought by the bundle. At Saint-Germain Abbot Irminon has every farm and tenant written down. The river freezes in 821-822 and floods in 834. Nobody has yet seen a Northman's ship above Rotomagus.
821: In the winter of 821-822 the Seine froze so hard that carts crossed on the ice.
827: Greek envoys brought the emperor a book of Dionysius the Areopagite. Abbot Hilduin, who held that his own saint was that Dionysius, had it put into Latin.

832: Hilduin built a chapel behind the church of Saint-Denis, where eight monks sang Mass day and night. In this year the Croult, a canal over six kilometres long that feeds the abbey, is first named.
834: The Seine was in flood. On 1 March, in the church of Saint-Denis, the bishops gave the emperor Louis back his arms.

From 845 to 869: the fleets. In 845 the fair's silver goes into the Northmen's scales; in 856-857 and again in 861 the city burns. The saints' bones are carried away and brought back. Northmen sit on the island beside the abbey for most of a year. The fair is thin, the king takes a tenth of what merchants are seen to have, and men of the city keep a boat ready and the wine hidden.

845: After a hard winter 120 ships came up the Seine in March and reached Paris at Easter with no one resisting. The king paid 7,000 pounds of silver for them to go. The annal names no leader. The monks had carried Germain and Genevieve away.
In 856, on 28 December Danes took Paris and burned every church but Saint Stephen's, Saint Vincent's and Saint Denis's, which paid a great sum. The Holy Apostles on the hill burned.

858: Abbot Louis of Saint-Denis and his brother Gozlin were seized by Northmen. Saint-Denis alone gave 685 pounds of gold and 3,250 of silver toward the ransom. On 21 September of the next year the martyrs' bones were carried to Nogent.
861: In January Paris and Saint-Germain were burned. Merchants fleeing up the river by boat were chased and caught.

864: The edict of Pîtres: a new penny with the king's monogram on one side and the city's name and a cross on the other, struck at ten mints only, Paris among them; and no mail coat, weapon or horse to a Northman, on pain of death.

865: Two hundred Northmen came to Paris for wine, found none, and went back unharmed. On 20 October Northmen entered Saint-Denis and stayed about twenty days, carrying plunder to their ships. They left their island by the abbey in June 866.
866: To pay the Northmen 4,000 pounds of silver the king took a levy on every farm and a tenth of all that merchants were seen to have. Part was paid in wine.

869: King Charles, who had kept the abbey for himself since Abbot Louis died on 9 January 867, had a stronghold of wood and stone built round Saint-Denis: about eight hectares, with a double ditch fed by the Croult.

From 870 to 888: walls and bridges. Saint-Denis stands inside a stronghold of wood and stone with a double ditch, and the fair is held behind it. On the island the old wall is mended and the king's new Great Bridge shuts the river. In the winter of 885-886 the city holds against the great fleet for a year, and its count is made king.

877: King Charles died in the Alps on 6 October, asking to lie at Saint-Denis. His men gutted him, filled him with wine and spices, and at last put him in a pitched barrel wrapped in hides. The smell beat them; they buried him, barrel and all, at Nantua.

In 885, on 24 November the great fleet came to Paris. Count Odo, Bishop Gozlin and Abbot Ebles held the island. On 6 February 886 a flood broke the Little Bridge and its tower was burned with the twelve men in it. Gozlin died on 16 April. In November the emperor promised 700 pounds and let the fleet winter in Burgundy.
The river has no tide here and no bar: it runs high and brown after the thaw and low at harvest, froze hard enough for carts in the winter of 821-822, and came over its banks in 834 and 886.
888: Count Odo was made king. Saint Germain's bones were carried home to the meadows.

From 889 to 986: the counts' city. The counts of Paris are abbots of Saint-Denis too, and greater than the king. The abbey has mills on its canal and shoemakers inside its wall. From 911 a baptised Northman holds Rotomagus and takes the toll of the lower river, which is quiet again. In 978 an emperor from the east camps on Montmartre and goes home.
898: A shoemakers' shop inside the stronghold of Saint-Denis is named. Its offcuts were found in the ditch. The abbey's first mill is named in 894.
978: In autumn the emperor Otto II camped on Montmartre, burned a suburb, and left on 30 November.

From 987 to 1066: the king's island. The count is king from 987 and there are no more counts. King Robert rebuilds the palace with a King's Hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas; Abbot Morard builds Saint-Germain a tower. The suburb on the right bank gets a bank and ditch. From 1053 there is a second great fair in June. Every keel from the sea passes the duke of the Normans' toll at Rotomagus.
987: Hugh Capet, count of Paris, was made king. Bouchard of Vendôme held the county after him and died a monk in 1007: there were no more counts.
In 1053, on 9 June the fair called the Lendit was first held at Saint-Denis. In 1059-1060 King Henry refounded Saint Martin's on the road north.

pages.title: Ganda
pages.hint: A monastery among the Franks
pages.brief: The abbeys of Saint Bavo and Saint Peter where the Lys meets the Scheldt.
pages.game:
Ganda in 793 is not a town: two of the king's abbeys and a village on the river bank, where the Leie runs into the Scheldt in several arms. Saint Bavo's stands at the meeting of the waters and Saint Peter's on the sand hill of Blandinium upstream; canons serve both, serfs and tenants work their land, and boats lie on the Scheldt's left bank between the abbey and the village. A merchant comes because the abbeys gather wool, cheese, cloth and dues from estates as far as the sea and must send them on, because wax and good silver are always wanted here, and because the bank has wrights who can mend a hull.
The Leie meadows lie under water for part of every winter and are sheep ground when they dry; shearing is before Saint John's day. The year's great day is Saint Bavo's Mass on the first of October, when the dues come in, the abbot's men ride home and every bench on the bank is taken. Saint Veerle is kept on the fourth day after the new year and Saint Amand in the first week of February, when the river is often too high to bring a boat up against it.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, Frisian cloth, woollen cloth and linen; wanted here, and so dearer: wool, woad, madder and alum. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: king Charles's years. Two half-kept royal abbeys served by canons, a village on the Scheldt bank, sheep on the flood meadows. No market, no toll, no mint: the abbeys gather what their land yields and pass it on. Saint Peter's on the hill has few clerics and a bad roof.
pages.known:
The abbeys of Saint Bavo and Saint Peter where the Lys meets the Scheldt. The place is now Ghent. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
639: Before this year the missionary Amand founds a church of Saint Peter at the meeting of the Leie and the Scheldt; it is an abbey before 700 and holds the grave of Bavo by the 8th century. The people threw Amand into the river more than once before they listened. About 754 the bones of Pharaildis (Veerle) are brought to Ganda. Her feast is the fourth of January.
