Verhulst, 'Ontstaan en vroegste geschiedenis van Gent' (dossier 7); nl.wikipedia Sint-Baafsabdij; en.wikipedia Saint_Amand; en.wikipedia Pharaildis (dossier 18) (?)

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
In 810 and 811 the bank is full of oak and the noise of adzes, and in November 811 the emperor comes to look at the ships.
811: In November the emperor Charles comes to the river Scheldt, to the place called Gand, and looks at the ships built there for his fleet.

From 815 to 840: Einhard's years. He is abbot of both houses from Aachen and comes seldom; his steward Erembert runs them and his letters ask for the dues in full and in good silver. Twenty-four clerics on the hill, probably the first stone church at Saint Bavo's, and from 819 a charter that keeps the count off abbey land. In the summer of 828 the sick come by boat and on crutches to the new relics.

In 815, on 2 June the emperor Louis takes Blandinium under his protection at the asking of its abbot, Einhard, who sets twenty-four clerics there. A later list says the house had come almost to nothing before him.

In 819, on 13 April Louis does the same for Saint Bavo's: the count has no power on abbey land, the abbey fines and punishes there, and owes the emperor prayers, gifts and army service. The charter survives whole, with the emperor's head in white wax; the scribe signs as Faramund.

In 828, on 3 July relics of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter reach Saint Bavo's. Until the end of September the sick are healed there: the blind girl Hartlinda of Furnes, the serfs Eberald and Gundrada, Liodold of Alphen on two crutches, and blind Germar from the sea-coast of the Frisians near the mouth of the Scheldt.

830: Einhard is at Blandinium on 21 January and, sick, at Saint Bavo's in the spring. He came by boat from Valenciennes, and reckons fifteen days by boat from here to his house at Seligenstadt on the Main.
In 840, on 14 March Einhard dies, abbot of both houses for twenty years and more. He ruled them from Aachen.

From 841 to 850: three kings share the realm and Ganda falls to Charles the Bald, with the Scheldt as his border. Danes hold Walcheren at the river mouth for the emperor Lothar, and the abbey's wool land there pays them. Boats still come up; fewer go down with anything worth taking.

From 851 to 878: saint Bavo's is burned in 851 and its canons are at Laon with the saint. The village on the bank goes on without them and is called a port; for eleven years the king's pennies are struck in it. A ditch in a half circle is dug round the houses, some time in these years or after (?).
851: Danes rage as far as the monastery of Saint Bavo which they call Gant, and burn it. The canons flee to Laon with Bavo's bones.
860: Between 858 and 865 Usuard of Paris writes 'in portu Ganda' of Saint Bavo: the first time the village on the Scheldt bank is called a port.
864: From about this year to 875 pennies of King Charles the Bald are struck here, reading GANDAVVM. Sixteen are known.

From 879 to 881: the great army from England sits in the monastery. Its ships lie along the bank, its horses on the meadows; it sells what it took in England and takes what there is in Flanders. Saint Peter's is plundered. A merchant who comes up the river comes by the army's leave.
879: In November the army that had sat at Fulham on the Thames crosses the sea and takes its winter seat in the monastery of Ganda. It went 'to Ghent in Frankland, and sat there a year'.
880: The army wastes Tournai and the monasteries on the Scheldt, beats Abbot Gauzlin and moves to Courtrai in November. Saint Peter's on the hill is plundered that winter.
881: After its defeat at Saucourt the army comes back to Ganda, refits its ships and goes on to the Meuse.

From 882 to 936: saint Bavo's stands roofless and empty. The counts of Flanders, Baldwin II and then Arnulf, hold the abbeys' lands and make Saint Peter's their burial church; the countess is an English king's daughter. The port inside its ditch grows slowly. Wool comes up from the sheep marshes of the coast.

918: Count Baldwin II dies on 10 September and is laid at last in Saint Peter's, so that his widow may one day lie by him. A charter dated the next day has her, Aelfthryth, King Alfred's daughter, give the abbey Lewisham, Greenwich and Woolwich on the Thames.
In 929, on 7 June Aelfthryth dies and is buried by her husband at Saint Peter's.

From 937 to 964: count Arnulf's years. The canons of Saint Bavo's are back; Gerard of Brogne makes monks of both houses; Saint John's is consecrated in the port, and the abbeys own every house plot in it for a yearly rent. About 950 a timber castle of the count's rises on the Leie, with a hall and grain stores. An English archbishop to be spends a winter on the hill.
937: By about this year the community of Saint Bavo's has come back to its burned house. Count Arnulf holds its lands.

941: Gerard of Brogne turns Saint Peter's from canons into monks under Benedict's Rule and is its abbot for three years; he does the same at Saint Bavo's in 946. House plots between the Scheldt and the Leie are named for the first time.
942: Bishop Transmar of Tournai consecrates Saint John's church inside the ditch of the port.
956: Dunstan, driven out of England, finds shelter at Saint Peter's for a year or more.
964: King Edgar confirms Lewisham to Saint Peter's. Count Arnulf I dies on 27 March of this year or the next.

From 965 to 1006: a wool and cloth place now. The Scheldt is the border of the empire, and each abbey looks to a different lord across it. The two houses quarrel over which is older and write old charters to prove it. Odwin builds a great stone church at Saint Bavo's. Men of Flanders pay toll at London.
974: The emperor Otto II takes Saint Bavo's under his protection: the Scheldt is his empire's border, and the abbey stands on the far side of it from the count.
981: The same year died Womare, Abbot of Ghent. Odwin becomes abbot of Saint Bavo's and begins a great stone church.

From 1007 to 1066: the eastern king takes the castle in 1007 and gives it back. Saints arrive: Livinus in 1007, the stranger Macarius dying in the plague of 1012. From 1038 rich families begin to buy their plots free of the abbeys' rent. English wool goes to Flemish looms (?). Saint Bavo's new church is not finished when the game ends: it is dedicated in May 1067.
1007: King Henry II, emperor from 1014, takes the count's castle on the Leie. In the same year the bones of a saint called Livinus are brought from Houtem to Saint Bavo's.
In 1012, on 10 April the eastern pilgrim Macarius dies of the plague at Saint Bavo's. He had knocked first at Saint Peter's and been sent away.
1044: A charter in King Edward's name confirms the Thames manors to Saint Peter's.

pages.title: Andoverpis
pages.hint: A fort among the Franks
pages.brief: A fort and landing on the Scheldt.
pages.game:
Andoverpis in 793 is a church, a toll and a landing on a sand rise where the Schijn runs into the Scheldt: a few timber houses among fields, a point of firm ground called the werf where boats lie, and a river that turns twice a day. A merchant comes for pork, hides and antler combs at the maker's price, for the ferry north, and for a quiet tide on the way between the sea and the abbeys at Ganda. It is small, and it is the only place on this reach where somebody takes the toll by an old right and can show the leaf that says so.
The river is tidal and grey-brown, and the flats flood from midwinter to Lent, so boats come between Easter and Martinmas. The comb-maker comes with the swallows and leaves at Martinmas; pigs are driven in from the mast woods and killed before Advent; salt comes up from the islands in autumn. The feast of the church is Peter and Paul, in the week after Saint John's day, and Saint Amand is kept in the dead of winter.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, Frisian cloth, woollen cloth and linen; wanted here, and so dearer: wool, woad, madder and alum. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: king Charles's years and his son's. A hamlet on a sand rise: the church of Peter and Paul, a toll taken at the werf, one big house on posts where ale is brewed, a round pen, pigs. The first two summers are hungry. A Frisian comb-maker works under a lean-to from spring to Martinmas, and Rhenish pots come down in every boat.
pages.known:
A fort and landing on the Scheldt. The place is now Antwerp. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 645 Eligius, bishop of Noyon, preaches at Andoverpis and turns the Suevi there from their errors. It is the oldest writing of the name. About 650 the moneyer Chrodigisilus strikes small gold pieces with the name ANDERPVS. No coin is known from the place in the game's years. In 726, on the twentieth day of October Rauchingus and his wife Bebelina give Willibrord the church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, built by Amandus within the castrum Antwerpis, with a third of the toll, for incense and lights and for the priests' prayers. Rauchingus had the church by exchange from Abbot Firminus for his hamlet Tumme. In 793 there is famine across the Frankish lands. The digs show Andoverpis as ploughland on a sand rise with the first timber buildings going up: a house on deep posts, stake fences, a round pen. No rampart and no wall.
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); Life of Eligius, as printed in Mertens and Torfs, Geschiedenis van Antwerpen I (1845): 'jugi instantia Andoverpis decertavit, et multis erroribus implicatos Suevos convertit'; nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen (dossier 3, 6); Bellens 2021; nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen (dossier 4); The charter of 20 October 726, in Dutch in Mertens and Torfs I (1845), pp. 74-75 (the Latin not read: Wampach, Echternach no. 34 (?)); nl.wikipedia Rauchingus; chronicle_793.json 793-great-famine; Bellens 2021, chapters 2.2-2.8 (dossier 1, 2)

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
805: At Thionville the emperor rules that only old and just tolls may be taken. The toll here was already taken in 726.
In 809, on the twenty-eighth day of December (or in 808) a great flood is written down at Saint-Amand, up the Scheldt.

From 836 to 849: the year it burned, and after. Black posts and a toll nobody takes for a season; then new sills laid on the old ground, with timber from a boat nobody came back for. Danes hold Walcheren at the river's mouth from 841 and every ship from the sea has passed them.

In 836 the Northmen burned the town of Andwerpa, and likewise Witla, the trading place by the mouth of the Maas, and took tribute from the Frisians. No leader is named, and no burnt layer has been tied to it.
837: The Northmen take Walcheren at the river's mouth and kill its count. In 841 the emperor Lothar gives the island to the Dane Harald.
843: At Verdun the brothers share the kingdom. The Scheldt becomes a border: the right bank, and Andoverpis with it, is Lothar's.

From 850 to 899: houses stand close, side by side, short end to the path. The river is the border between two kings. In 879 and 880 the great army sits at Ghent, a tide and a half upstream, and the stock is kept inland again. Graves are dug on the rise east of the houses.
850: From about this year the first close-set houses stand side by side on sill beams, five to six metres wide, some built of timber used before. The oldest had ship's timber in them.
879: In November the great army crosses from England, winters at Ghent and raids the Scheldt for a year.

From 900 to 973: a bank of turves in a half ring, open to the water, with a palisade under it and log paths along its foot. Inside: long narrow plots, wattle houses with ash on the floors, stables, a smith, leather on every fence. White pots from the Maas outnumber the red-painted ones from the Rhine. From about 925 the lord is the eastern king's.

About 900 a palisade, and then a bank of turves and spoil thirteen and a half metres wide, is thrown up in a half ring open to the river. Leather is worked inside it; paths of split logs run along its foot.
925: Between 923 and 927 Andoverpis, chief place of the land of Rien, passes to the eastern kingdom. The river is the border with the count of Flanders.

From 974 to 1007: a march of the empire against Flanders: a margrave's timber hall, a toll house, armed men at the bank. Dwellings stand where the stables were, and houses have spilled outside the bank. Sea fish begins to be eaten.
977: Between about 974 and 980 the emperor makes a march of the place against Flanders. The date is not settled. Godfrey of Verdun is listed, with reserve, as its first margrave.

From 1008 to 1046: count Gothelo's years. Oak piles are driven along the castle's edge and stone from Tournai comes down the river by the bargeload; a chapel of Saint Walburga stands in the middle. The name is said Antwerf.
1008: A charter names 'the county of Count Gozilo, which is called Antwerf'. Gothelo is margrave from 1005 or 1008. Between 1007 and 1015 oak piles are driven along the castle's edge.

From 1047 to 1066: Flanders wants the march. Baldwin holds it for two years and gives it back; in 1055 his men come again, cannot take the castle and burn every house outside it. Those are built again within the year. Saint Michael's, south of the castle, is the mother church, with twelve canons.
1047: Baldwin, count of Flanders, takes the march in his war with the emperor, and in 1049 gives it up.
In 1055 the Flemings besiege Duke Frederick in the castle, fail to take it, and burn the houses that stand round it.

pages.title: Colonia
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: The old Roman city on the Rhine, an archbishop's see; wine and Rhenish pottery.
pages.game:
The old Roman city on the left bank of the Rhine, three to five days above Dorestad with the stream and ten to fifteen back against it. In 793 it is a bishop's seat inside a Roman wall of nineteen towers, with a strip of low ground between wall and river where boats lie and things are made. A merchant comes for Rhenish wine, the grey-yellow pots of the Vorgebirge villages, querns of black Mayen stone, glass and iron, and brings Frisian cloth, salt, fish and whatever the north sells.
The vintage is in the weeks before Saint Gereon's day and the new wine is ready by Martinmas, when every hull on the river is wanted at once. The river is low in late summer and high with the snow water in spring; there is no tide and no bar, but in a hard winter the Rhine freezes and nothing moves for a month.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine, Mayen quernstones, millstones, Rhenish pottery and glass vessels; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and walrus ivory. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Hildebold's years. The bishop is the king's archchaplain and seldom at home; his clerks run the church's business and hold the king's lists. Inside the wall are gardens, ruins and churches; the trade is outside it, on the low ground by the river, among pit houses, smiths, glass workers and bone workers. Pennies of King Charles are struck. In the hungry years the king's grain comes down the river.
pages.known:
The old Roman city on the Rhine, an archbishop's see; wine and Rhenish pottery. The place is now Cologne. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 310 the emperor Constantine joined the city to the fort of Deutz on the far bank by a bridge on stone piers with a timber deck, nearly three hundred paces long. Whether any of it stood in 793 is not known (?). 717: After this year Plectrude, Pippin's widow, died here and was buried in the church she had built on the mound of the old temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva. In 787 Hildebold became bishop of Colonia. From 791 he was also the king's archchaplain, and was more often at court than in his city.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.; ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); de.wikipedia Römerbrücke (Köln); Kastell Deutz (dossier); de.wikipedia St. Maria im Kapitol (dossier); de.wikipedia Hildebold von Köln (dossier)

later.text: 794: In this year or the next Colonia was made an archbishop's seat, set in time over Utrecht, Liège, Bremen, Minden, Münster and Osnabrück.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
In the hungry years the king's grain comes down the river, and in 799 and 804 Saxon families wait on the bank to be sent into Francia.
In 814 Archbishop Hildebold gave the dying emperor Charles the last rites at Aachen.
818: This year, on the third day of September, Hildebold died. He was buried at Saint Gereon's outside the wall.

From 819 to 842: Hadebald's years. A church of Saint Peter has burned and is building again. The river is busy and safe as far as anyone here knows. In 826 a Danish king goes down it in the bishop's boat. The books of Saint Peter's are counted and lent.
822: In the winter before this year the Rhine was frozen for thirty days, and carts crossed where boats had.
In 826 Harald, king of the Danes, newly baptised, and the monk Anskar took boat here for Dorestad. Bishop Hadebald gave them a good boat with two cabins.
In 833 the books of Saint Peter's were listed: one hundred and seventy-five.

From 843 to 880: the middle kingdom's years. Whose town this is changes four times in a lifetime, and the archbishop's chair is quarrelled over by kings and the pope. Dorestad is raided year after year and its merchants come upriver to ask about plots. The great church with a choir at each end is dedicated in 870.
In 843 the kingdom was parted in three and Colonia fell to Lothar's middle share; in 855 to the second Lothar; in 870 to the eastern king.
In 852 King Louis came to Colonia by boat.

857: This year, on the fifteenth day of September, in a great storm the people ran into Saint Peter's and rang the bells. Lightning like a fiery dragon split the church and killed a priest, a deacon and a layman at three altars.
In 863 in October the pope put Archbishop Gunthar out of his office over King Lothar's divorce. He went on acting as archbishop regardless.

In 870 Willibert was ordained archbishop on the seventh of January at King Louis's order, and on the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh of September Saint Peter's was dedicated. The night before, evil spirits were heard grieving that they must leave seats they had held so long.

In 876 Charles, the western king and since Christmas emperor, sat at Colonia with his army. Archbishop Willibert sent the priest Hartwig to warn the younger Louis, who beat Charles at Andernach on the eighth of October.

From 881 to 883: the burning. The Northmen winter on the lower river, take a ransom and burn the town anyway. The clergy are at Mainz with the saints. People live in what is left against the wall, the strand is bare of boats, and nothing is sold that cannot be carried off in a hurry.

881: In the winter of this year the Northmen burned Colonia and Bonn with their churches and buildings. The clergy fled to Mainz with the treasures and the bodies of the saints. A ransom paid in January did not save the town.
In 883 Colonia was rebuilt, without its churches and monasteries, and its walls restored with gates, bars and locks. The Northmen went by.

From 884 to 952: rebuilt behind mended walls with gates, bars and locks. The river suburb grows again; by 922 its market has a name in writing, and the pennies read S COLONIA A. Nuns from Gerresheim keep the church of the Holy Virgins. The fine painted pots now come from Pingsdorf.
In 891 Archbishop Hermann asked the pope for relics to replace those that had burned.
In 922 a market of Colonia is first named in writing, and in the same year nuns from Gerresheim, fleeing the Hungarians, came to the church of the Holy Virgins.

From 953 to 999: Bruno's town and his successors': the archbishop is lord of court, market, mint and toll. The river suburb is taken inside the walls. There is a chapter at Saint Martin's on the old island, with Irish monks before the century is out, and an abbey at Saint Pantaleon. Gero's great oak cross hangs in Saint Peter's.
In 953 Bruno, King Otto's brother, became archbishop and duke of Lotharingia; from his day the archbishop held court, market, mint and toll. He died on the eleventh of October 965.
About 957 the hay market by the river was first laid, by the date of its timbers; about 960 Bruno set a chapter at Saint Martin's on the old island.
In 999 at Christmas Heribert entered the town barefoot as archbishop. In 1003 he founded an abbey in the old fort of Deutz across the river.

From 1000 to 1066: the largest town on the Rhine, of some ten thousand people. Its merchants own sea-going ships and are known in London as the emperor's men. Heribert's abbey stands in the fort at Deutz. Under Anno the archbishop's hand is heavy, and the merchants have begun to say so to each other.

About 1000 the men of the emperor who came to London in their own ships paid toll there, and at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five men's gloves and two casks of vinegar. The men of Colonia are usually counted among them (?).
In 1049 Pope Leo consecrated an altar at Saint Mary's on the temple mound.
In 1062 in April Archbishop Anno took the boy king at Kaiserswerth. The boy jumped from the ship into the Rhine, was pulled out by Count Ekbert, and was brought to Colonia.

pages.title: Mogontia
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: Archbishop's city at the Main's mouth; Frisian merchants have their own quarter.
pages.game:
Mogontia is the old Roman city on the west bank of the Rhine where the Main comes in: a wall far too long for the people inside it, an archbishop, a mint, and a shore of long plots and jetties where Frisian shippers live. A merchant comes for wine from the hills all round and for the grain the Main boats bring down, and brings cloaks, pots and whatever the sea sells. It is the top of the river for a small boat: every mile here was hauled on a rope, and everything bought here rides home on the stream.
The year turns on the vine: pruning in the cold, the vintage in the weeks after Michaelmas, new wine in the cask by Martinmas and the Frisians gone downriver with it before the ice. Saint Alban's day at midsummer fills the hill with pilgrims, mid-Lent brings the bishop's business, and the Rhine runs high from the Alps' snow in early summer, when the haul up is slowest.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine, Mayen quernstones, millstones, Rhenish pottery and glass vessels; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and walrus ivory. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Riculf's city. A Roman wall round more gardens than houses, the Frisians' plots and jetties on the shore, stone going up the hill for Saint Alban's, the king at Ingelheim or Frankfurt and never far.
pages.known:
Archbishop's city at the Main's mouth; Frisian merchants have their own quarter. The place is now Mainz. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
About 780 the bishop of Mainz becomes an archbishop: his province grows into the largest north of the Alps. 787: Riculf, a Frank of the Wetterau and a pupil of Alcuin, becomes archbishop. He begins a great church for Saint Alban on the hill south of the wall. In 793 there was famine. In autumn the king's ditch between the Main's waters and the Danube's was given up, and at Christmas his boats came down the Main.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/mogontia.md (the research this file is built on; its section 9 has every reference in full); ARF 785, 814; Einhard VK 30; dossier dorestad (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.json); de.wikipedia 'Erzbistum Mainz' (780/82); dossier 1; de.wikipedia 'Richulf'; 'Stift St. Alban vor Mainz'; chronicle_793.json: 793-great-famine, 793-autumn-fossa-carolina, 793-12-25-wurzburg-christmas

later.text: In 794, on 10 August Queen Fastrada died at Frankfurt and was buried at Saint Alban's. The same summer the king's council at Frankfurt made the penny heavier and set a top price on grain and bread.
About 796 Riculf sent his old master Alcuin an ivory comb, and Alcuin thanked him with a riddle: a beast with two heads and sixty teeth, and not as big as an elephant.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
800: The king held his assembly at Mainz before he went to Rome.
803: The king held his assembly at Mainz. About this year his timber bridge on the old Roman piers was begun: five hundred paces long, and ten years in the building.
About 805 thirty-seven Saxon hostages, kept by bishops and counts among the Alemans, were ordered brought to Mainz at mid-Lent. On 1 December Saint Alban's basilica was consecrated.
810: The relics of Saint Caesarius were brought to Saint Alban's. From 9 to 11 December a fast was kept against the plague on men and cattle.
From about 803 the king's carpenters are laying a timber bridge on the old piers; in May 813, hardly finished, it burns.
813: In May the king's bridge, hardly finished, burned in three hours. On 9 June a council for the mending of the church sat at Saint Alban's. On 9 August Riculf died.

From 814 to 843: the emperor Louis's years. The piers stand bare again and the ferry keeps its trade. Otgar is archbishop from 826, the year a Danish king is baptised; grain men boat pilgrims down the Main to Einhard's new saints. In 840 two armies face each other outside the wall.
In 826, on Saint John's day Harald, a king of the Danes, was baptised with his wife and many of his people: at Saint Alban's, the annals of Fulda say; at the palace of Ingelheim, others say.
In 840, on 20 June the emperor Louis died on an island in the Rhine by Ingelheim. In August two kings' armies lay facing each other outside Mainz.
843: At the sharing of the kingdom Mainz went to Louis, king of the eastern Franks.

From 844 to 881: the eastern kingdom's first city. Hrabanus, born here, feeds the hungry in 850; councils sit at Saint Alban's; the earth shakes again and again and the old wall splits. Dorestad dies downriver and the Frisians who come up are fewer and richer.

847: Hrabanus, born in this city, was made archbishop and held a council at Saint Alban's. A woman called Thiota, who had foretold the end of the world for that year, was flogged; she said a priest had taught her the words for gain.
In 850 there was famine: a measure of wheat cost ten pieces of silver at Mainz, and Hrabanus fed more than three hundred poor every day at Winkel.
In 858, on 1 January the earth shook: the old walls split, and Saint Michael's oratory at the west end of Saint Alban's fell.
In 873 there was famine, and then locusts a thumb long that lay like snow and stripped a hundred iugera near Mainz in an hour.

In 881, on 30 December, before cockcrow, the earth shook: pots knocked together and broke, as the potters said. That winter the Northmen burned Colonia and Bonn, and their clergy fled to Mainz with treasures and the bodies of saints.

From 882 to 913: the frightened years. Colonia's clergy and their saints lodge here; the wall is mended and a ditch dug; in 886 the Frisians' shore burns and the Rhine floods. Under Hatto the river wall moves forward to the water and the bishop becomes lord of the city.
882: The Northmen having burned as far as Koblenz, the wall of Mainz began to be mended and a ditch was dug outside it.
883: The Northmen came up the Rhine; Archbishop Liutbert met them with a few men, killed many and took back the plunder. They never reached Mainz.
886: In March, after mid-Lent, the best part of the city burned, where the Frisians lived. From May to July the Rhine flooded from its source to the sea.
In 891, on 26 June Archbishop Sunderold was killed fighting the Northmen on the Geul. Hatto followed him, and in his time the river wall was rebuilt nearer the water.

From 914 to 974: the Ottonian kings' city. Rich merchants of the town go as far as the Greek emperor; Jewish traders from Italy and the south settle; a king besieges his own son here in 953; by 965 Samarkand silver and Indian spice lie on a stall.
949: Liutefred, a rich merchant of Mainz, went as King Otto's envoy to the Greek emperor: he left Venice on 25 August and reached Constantinople on 17 September.
953: From July to September King Otto besieged his son Liudolf and Conrad the Red in Mainz.
965: A traveller from Tortosa, Ibrahim son of Yaqub, saw at Mainz silver struck at Samarkand fifty years before, and pepper, ginger, cloves, spikenard, costus and galangal, so far in the west.

From 975 to 1011: Willigis's city, now called golden. He is the king's chancellor, strikes coin with his own head, and builds a cathedral east of Saint Martin's with bronze doors. It burns on its consecration day in 1009 and he begins again.
975: Willigis, of free but not noble birth, became archbishop: chancellor and later regent of the kingdom, and the first archbishop in it to put his own head on a coin.
In 1002, on 7 June Willigis crowned Henry king at Mainz.
In 1009, on the day it was to be consecrated, 29 or 30 August, Willigis's new cathedral burned.

From 1012 to 1066: the crowning city. Kings are made here in 1002 and 1024; the cathedral is consecrated at last in 1036; a pope sits in synod in 1049. The Jews have a school known as far as Spain and a graveyard outside the wall.
1012: King Henry drove the Jews out of Mainz; they were back within a few years (?).
In 1036, on 10 November the rebuilt cathedral was consecrated.
1049: In October Pope Leo and the emperor Henry held a synod of forty bishops at Mainz against the buying of church offices and the marriage of priests.

pages.title: Diusburg
pages.hint: A market among the Franks
pages.brief: A trading place on the Rhine at the Ruhr's mouth.
pages.game:
A king's estate on a dry hill above a bend of the Rhine, where the Ruhr comes in and the road east into Saxony, the Hellweg, begins. In 793 it is a landing and not yet a town: barges going down to Dorestad with wine, pots and querns lie a night under the hill, and the king's war with the Saxons comes down the road on foot. A merchant comes for the crossing, for the road and the news it carries, and for whatever the army or the monks up the Ruhr are short of.
The year runs by the river and the dues: high brown water at Easter, the host on the road east from May, the new wine coming down from Martinmas, and the boats drawn up through the dark weeks to Christmas. The Rhine has no tide here and no bar; the flood silts the foot of the hill each spring.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Rhenish wine, Mayen quernstones, millstones, Rhenish pottery and glass vessels; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, squirrel pelts, marten, sable and walrus ivory. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a king's estate and a landing. Timber halls and barns on the hill with no wall round them, a row of boats on the mud below, an ale-house, a smith and a ferry. The war is a day's walk east: the host goes up the Hellweg in May and comes down it in autumn with hostages and cattle. Nobody here is a count; a steward answers for everything.
pages.known:
A trading place on the Rhine at the Ruhr's mouth. The place is now Duisburg. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768.
450: From about this year Franks bury their dead in a field south of the hill, and go on doing so into the eighth century. 740: About this year, some say, a court of the Frankish rulers stands on the hill, a base for the wars against the Saxons. The digs do not prove it so early. In 793 the Saxons beyond the Rhine rise again and drive out the priests, and there is hunger in Francia.

later.text: From 799 to 809: the same place with a new neighbour. Liudger has a house of monks at Werden up the Ruhr and passes through with books, masons and questions. The king's assemblies at Lippeham in 799 and 810 fill the river with boats. After 804 the Saxon war is over and the last deported families go by; the steward's men turn to searching eastbound packs for blades.
About 799 Liudger founds his house of monks at Werden, a few hours up the Ruhr. This year too the king holds his assembly at Lippeham, where the Lippe meets the Rhine.
King of the Franks from 768, emperor from 25 December 800.
809: Liudger dies on 26 March and is buried at Werden.

From 810 to 862: quiet. The road east is a road for salt, cattle and monks now, not for the host. Werden grows and sends down for wine, wax and calfskin. The estate pays its dues at Christmas and Easter and the barges go by in the stream without stopping unless the wind makes them.
810: The emperor musters his host at Lippeham against Godfred of the Danes. His elephant, Abul Abaz, dies there.

From 863 to 882: the Danes have been up the Rhine and everybody has seen the smoke of Xanten. All the same there is more trade than before: a market at the foot of the hill beside the landing, a timber well dug in 872, boats lying round to the Ruhr mouth, and the first Frisians who stay. When Cologne burns in the winter of 881 people begin to bury things.
863: Danes go up the Rhine. The church at Xanten is burned.
872: A timber well is sunk at the foot of the hill, where a market and a harbour are beginning.
881: In the winter of this year the Northmen burn Cologne and Bonn.

From 883 to 884: the Northmen's winter. They come up in autumn, take the place and wall themselves in. The houses burn; the dead are buried in haste. Duke Henry lies in camp at the Ruhr crossing and lets nothing in or out. In spring they fire their own camp and row away downstream.

883: Northmen who had come from Denmark to Kennemerland sail up the Rhine with Godfrid's consent, take the stronghold of Diusburh, fortify it in their usual way and stay there all winter. Duke Henry camps against them and lets them take no plunder.
884: When spring comes the Northmen burn their camp and go back to the coast. About now the Emperor Charles gives the royal estate to the abbey of Herrieden.

From 885 to 928: building. The court on the hill is laid out new as a palace, with a ditch on the east side, a hall, the Saviour's church and stone houses with cellars. The abbey of Prüm holds the church and nineteen holdings; its Frisians pay it silver at Martinmas and Easter and trade under its freedom from toll. A causeway is laid from the river to the gate.
888: King Arnulf takes the estate back for the crown.
893: The abbey of Prüm writes down what it has at Dusburhc: the church, nineteen holdings and two more, and the Frisians who stay there and pay in silver at Martinmas and at Easter.
In 904, on 3 August a king's charter names the district of Diuspurch, in the counties of Otto and Eberhard.

925: By about this year the court on the hill has been rebuilt as a palace: a hall, a church, and a closed ring of stone houses with cellars. In these years, or about the year 1000, the Rhine breaks through its bend and leaves the place on a side arm.

From 929 to 1016: a king's house. Henry, the three Ottos and the second Henry hold court here sixteen times and more, with bishops, dukes and their horses, and the market eats well in those weeks and waits in the others. A rampart and ditch go round the settlement. Some time in these years the Rhine breaks through its bend and the landing is on a quiet side arm.
929: A synod here puts out of the Church the men who blinded Bishop Benno of Metz.

In 945, on the Rogation days, 12 to 14 May, King Otto holds an assembly of Lotharingians and Franks here. Two bishops accused of disloyalty are cleared, and the clergy of Maastricht carry the body of Saint Servatius before the king to complain of Count Immo.
In 966, on 1 March the Emperor Otto gives an estate to the nuns of Essen. His clerk dates it 'at Diuspargum, which we commonly call Diusburg'.
1002: King Henry waits here for the slow Lotharingians. The bishops of Liège and Cambrai come first; the archbishop of Cologne comes late.
In 1016, on 6 December the Emperor Henry, here, gives two estates to the abbey of Burtscheid. After this year, or about 1011, he gives Duisburg and Kaiserswerth to the Count Palatine Ezzo.

From 1017 to 1066: the Count Palatine's, and then the king's again. Ezzo's house holds the place until 1045. Pennies are struck here with the king's name, and they travel: Duisburg men are known by their tariff at Koblenz, a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine. In 1065 the boy king gives court, mint, toll and forest to the archbishop of Bremen, who falls from the king's side within the year.
1024: From about this year pennies are struck here in the king's name, on the Cologne pattern: Conrad's, then Henry's, then the young Henry's.
1045: Otto, Ezzo's son, gives Duisburg and Kaiserswerth back to the king and is made duke of Swabia.

1050: About now the toll list of Koblenz is set: a ship of Duisburg gives a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine, a ship of Cologne four pennies and wine; a bought slave pays four pennies, and a seller of swords gives every tenth sword.

In 1065, on 16 October King Henry gives 'our court called Tusburch' in the Ruhrgau, with its mints, its tolls and the forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel, to Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg and Bremen.
1066: Adalbert falls from the king's side. What becomes of his gift is not known.

pages.title: Lundenwic
pages.hint: A market among the Mercians
pages.brief: Bede's 'mart of many peoples': the wic on the Strand, ships beached on the Thames foreshore.
pages.game:
An open trading town on the gravel bank north of the Thames, a short walk upstream of the empty Roman city, held by King Offa of the Mercians. In 793 it has no wall, no bridge and no quay: ships are run onto the hard at high water and sold from where they sit, with the king's wic-reeve as witness. A merchant comes with wine, quernstones, pots and glass from the Rhine and goes home with cloaks, combs, hides and wool, and with whatever the reeve chose to tell him.
The tide is the calendar: a ship waits at the Nore for the flood and rides it up, and the springs after each new and full moon are the days to beach and to float off. Wine comes in the dark of the year after the vintage, wool after the shearing near midsummer, stock is driven in and killed at Martinmas; no fair is recorded, the beach is the market every day but Sunday.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, woollen cloth, wool and parchment; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, silk, marten, walrus ivory and Rhenish wine. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Offa's wic. Past its best: the busiest years were before 750, and some plots are rubbish dumps now, but there is a loom in almost every house and the beach is full on a spring tide. The ports of the Franks are shut to English ships, so Frankish hulls are turned away here and a Frisian is asked whose man he is. The new heavy penny is the only coin the reeve will count.
pages.known:
Bede's 'mart of many peoples': the wic on the Strand, ships beached on the Thames foreshore. The place is now London (the Strand). In 793 it is under Offa, king of the Mercians.
604: Saint Paul's is founded inside the old walls for Mellitus, the first bishop of the East Saxons. 679: Imma, a Northumbrian thegn taken in battle whom no fetter would hold, is sold at London to a Frisian, who lets him ransom himself. 685: By the law of the Kentish kings a man of Kent who buys in the wic of London has two or three honest men or the king's wic-reeve as witness, and vouches his warranty at the king's hall in the wic (673-685). 716: Boniface comes to London, pays his fare to a shipmaster and sails to Dorestad. 731: Bede calls London the chief town of the East Saxons and a mart of many peoples coming to it by land and sea. 733: King Aethelbald of the Mercians frees one ship of the bishop of Rochester from the toll at the port of London. 764: King Offa confirms the freedom from toll at London of a ship of the minster in Thanet (761-764). About 789 King Charles closes his ports to English ships after a quarrel over a marriage offer; Gervold, abbot of Saint-Wandrille and keeper of the tolls from Rouen to Quentovic, helps to mend it. 793: King Offa's moneyers leave off the light penny for a heavier, broader one (792 or 793).

later.text: The dates are loose: about 789 to before 796.

796: King Charles writes to King Offa of the black stones the English want and the cloaks the Franks want at the old length. Offa dies on 29 July; his son Ecgfrith reigns 141 days; Coenwulf is king by December.

From 797 to 841: Coenwulf's royal town, and then his heirs'. The ban is over and the wine comes freely. The town burns in 798 and again in 801 (?) and is built back thinner each time. Kent rises and is harried; kings meet in council here; for one year (829-830) a West Saxon's name is on the pennies. Nothing is forbidden but what always is.
798: London burns with great loss of life. Pope Leo refuses to move the southern archbishopric here from Canterbury.
801: Bishop Heathoberht of London dies, and soon after a great part of London burns.
811: King Coenwulf's council sits 'in the famous place and royal town, the wic of London'.
829: King Ecgberht of the West Saxons holds Mercia for a year and strikes pennies at London (829-830).

From 842 to 870: an open beach in the years of the fleets. After the slaughter of 842 and the storm of 851 ditches two metres deep are dug across the roads at the north and the back of the town. Fewer houses, more fences. The penny is worse each year, and weighing is the king's and is paid for.
In 842 there was great slaughter at London, at Quentovic and at Rochester.
851: Three hundred and fifty ships come into the mouth of the Thames; the crews storm Canterbury and London and put King Beorhtwulf of the Mercians to flight.
857: King Burgred grants Bishop Alhhun of Worcester the plot called Ceolmundingchaga, not far from the west gate, with measure and weights 'as is the custom in the port'.

From 871 to 885: the army winters here in 871-872 and the Mercians pay it to go. The king of the Mercians is driven over sea in 874. What is left of the wic trades with whoever holds the river; honest people have begun to carry their goods inside the old walls at night.
871: The army goes from Reading to London and takes its winter quarters there (871-872). The bishop of Worcester sells land to pay his share of the tribute, in 'the year the pagans sat in London'.

From 886 to 960: Lundenburh. King Alfred has given the town to Ealdorman Aethelred, and it lives inside the Roman walls, two kilometres east of the old beach, which is going back to fields and is called the old wic. Bishops hold plots at Aethelred's hithe with ship stations in front; trade on the street or the shore pays the king. By the 930s there are eight moneyers and a peace-guild that rides after thieves.
886: King Alfred occupies London and gives it to Ealdorman Aethelred of the Mercians. The town moves inside the old walls; the wic becomes the old wic, Ealdwic.

889: Bishop Waerferth of Worcester is given 'Hwaetmund's stone', an old stone building by the trading shore. Trade on the public street or the shore pays the king; the bishop keeps the urn and scales in his own court.
896: The men of London help to storm the Danish fort at Benfleet (893) and to take the Danish ships on the Lea (896).
898: Plots at Aethelred's hithe are given to Bishop Waerferth and Archbishop Plegmund, each with ship stations before the wall (898 or 899).

935: The bishops and reeves of London set down the rules of their peace-guild: the brothers, in tens and hundreds, pay fourpence a year, ride out together after stolen stock, and pay a man for what he lost (about 930-939).

From 961 to 1015: a rich walled town with a bridge, a toll read out at Billingsgate and the men of Rouen, Flanders and the Emperor on the bank. It burns in 982 and beats off ninety-four ships in 994. From 1009 the army is in the river most years; the town holds, pays, buries an archbishop and at last gives in to Swein.
961: Saint Paul's burns and is restored the same year.
982: London burns.
In 994, on the Nativity of Saint Mary Olaf and Swein come to London with ninety-four ships and are driven off.

About 1000 the toll at Billingsgate is set down: a small boat a halfpenny, a sailing ship a penny, a keel or hulk four; the Emperor's men give at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar.
1009: Thorkell's army lies in the Thames. 'Oft they fought against the city of London; but glory be to God, that it yet standeth firm.'
1012: Archbishop Aelfheah, killed by the army at Greenwich on 19 April, is carried to London and buried at Saint Paul's. In 1023 King Cnut has him taken to Canterbury.
In 1014, on Michaelmas eve the great sea-flood comes far up over the land and drowns many towns and people. The year before, London had submitted to Swein.

From 1016 to 1042: Cnut's London. The siege, the ditch round the bridge, then 10,500 pounds and peace. Danes live in the town and lie in Saint Paul's churchyard under stones cut in their own letters; the shipmen of the fleet have a voice in choosing kings. The best years of all for a ship between Frisia, London and Denmark.
1016: King Aethelred dies at London on Saint George's day and Edmund is chosen king there. Cnut's ships dig a ditch on the south side, drag their ships round the bridge and besiege the town.
1018: England pays King Cnut 72,000 pounds, and London 10,500 pounds besides.
1042: King Harthacnut dies at Lambeth on 8 June, as he stood drinking, at the wedding feast of Tovi the Proud and Gytha, Osgod Clapa's daughter.

From 1043 to 1066: king Edward's town. A port-reeve and a staller answer for it; upriver on Thorney the king builds a great stone church in the Norman manner. Godwin's fleet passes the bridge in 1052. In the last year a king is buried and two are crowned at Westminster.
1051: Spearhafoc, goldsmith, abbot and bishop-elect of London, vanishes with the gold and gems given him for the king's crown.
1052: Earl Godwin's fleet waits at Southwark for the flood and passes the bridge close by the south bank.
1066: King Edward dies on 5 January, eight days after his church at Westminster was hallowed. Harold is king, and at Christmas William is crowned there.

pages.title: Hamwic
pages.hint: A market among the West Saxons
pages.brief: Wessex's emporium on the Itchen, trading with Quentovic and the Seine.
pages.game:
Hamwic is the West Saxons' one great trading town: an open, timber-built place of gravel streets on the west bank of the Itchen, with no wall, no tower and no quay, where ships are drawn up on a shelving beach. In 793 King Beorhtric's reeve keeps it, and the coin in hand is King Offa's. A merchant comes for wool and English cloth, and brings wine, black Seine pots, glass and quernstones; Rouen is a day and a night away with the wind on the beam.
The wool comes in after the June shearing (?) and the Frankish ships come for it through the summer; pilgrims take ship at summer's end, and the wool men cross for the fair of Saint-Denis in October. The tide here comes twice: high water stands for hours and the ebb is short and hard, so a boat can beach or float off at almost any hour but must not be caught on the mud flats when the water goes.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, woollen cloth, wool and parchment; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, silk, marten, walrus ivory and Rhenish wine. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: king Beorhtric's town, and King Offa's coin. The two great kings have shut their shores to each other's merchants; whether the order binds here nobody has said aloud (?), and the reeve has not asked. English cloth goes over to the Franks as pilgrims' bundles. Two thousand people, perhaps three: smiths, weavers, comb-makers, no farmers.
pages.known:
Wessex's emporium on the Itchen, trading with Quentovic and the Seine. The place is now Southampton. In 793 it is under Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, Offa's son-in-law.
686: Abbot Cyneberht, whose minster lay near this water, baptised two princes of Wight before King Caedwalla had them killed. Bede calls this shore Jutish. 704: Oak was felled soon after this year for the first works of the town, probably under King Ine. Its straight gravel streets were laid before the houses. About 721 Willibald and his father and brother took ship for the Seine near 'the mart called Hamwic', paid their fares to the master, and pitched their tents by the river at Rouen. 764: 'Homwic' is listed among the towns burnt this year. No burnt layer has been found in the ground. 769: An oak was felled near Hamwic and went into an English clinker ship. Her planks ended their days on Walcheren. 786: Beorhtric took the kingdom of the West Saxons. In 789 he took to wife Eadburh, King Offa's daughter; and in his days three ships of Northmen came to Portland, and the reeve Beaduheard, who took them for traders, was killed.

later.text: From 797 to 839: the ports are open again. Under King Ecgberht (from 802) the town is at its fullest: pennies with a West Saxon king's name are struck here or at Winchester, the pits behind the houses fill with Frankish pots, and wool men cross to the fair of Saint-Denis every October.
802: King Beorhtric died and Ecgberht came home from the land of the Franks and took the kingdom.
In 825, on the day after Christmas King Ecgberht was at 'Omtune' and gave land by his charter.

From 840 to 850: the fleets have found the water. Thirty-three crews are beaten on the shore in 840 and the ealdorman dies of it; two years on the place is plundered, or people say it was. Houses stand empty between lived-in ones. Nobody builds a wall. People with silver bury it.

840: Ealdorman Wulfheard fought at Hamtun against thirty-three ship-crews, made great slaughter and had the victory; and he died the same year. King Aethelwulf gave land to his thegn Duda 'in the royal vill called Hamtun'. About now the West Saxon mint stopped.
842: Northmen sacked Quentovic, crossed the sea and plundered 'Hamwig and Nordhunnwig'. The Chronicle says nothing of it, and it may be the fight of 840 told twice (?).
About 850 the town on the Itchen stood largely empty. Silver was put in the ground about 850 and again about 870, and not fetched.

From 851 to 899: a near-empty shore. St Mary's graveyard, the king's enclosure at the north end and a few fishers' houses remain; the streets go to grass. Hamtun is still the king's vill and the head of the shire, and its men fight for Winchester in 860. A ship that calls is noticed.
860: A great fleet came up and stormed Winchester. Ealdorman Osric with the men of Hamtunscir, and Ealdorman Aethelwulf with the men of Berkshire, fought it and put it to flight.

From 900 to 979: a new town with a ditch and a bank stands on the Test shore, a short walk south-west of the old hythe, and takes its trade. From about 928 two moneyers sit there by the king's law, and nothing above twenty pence may be bought outside a port. After 950 it thrives.
900: From about this year a new ditched town of some six hectares rose to the south-west, on the Test shore; the Burghal Hidage rates Hamtun at 150 hides. It throve after 950.
About 928 King Aethelstan's law allowed two moneyers at Hamtun, and forbade any man to buy goods worth more than twenty pence outside a port.

From 980 to 1015: plundered in 980, and most of its people killed or carried off. Rebuilt. In the winter of 994 Olaf's and Swein's fleet lies here, fed by all Wessex, waiting for sixteen thousand pounds: the worst guests and the best market the town has had. The pennies say HAMTUN or HAMWIC as the die-cutter pleases.
980: 'Southampton was plundered by a pirate-army, and most of the population slain or imprisoned.'

994: Olaf and Swein came to London with ninety-four ships and were beaten off. They took winter quarters at Southampton and were fed from all the West Saxon land, and were paid sixteen thousand pounds. Bishop Aelfheah and Ealdorman Aethelweard fetched Olaf to the king at Andover, where he promised never to come back in enmity.

From 1016 to 1066: the great men swear to Cnut here in 1016, and there is one peace on both shores. The mint closes about 1023. The old town is 'Wic', a minster and a hythe named in King Edward's charters; the new one is Hamtun, with the king's seventy-six men, wine from Rouen, and French voices on the strand before 1066 is out.
1016: The bishops, abbots and ealdormen came to Cnut at Southampton, forswore the line of Aethelred and swore to him. London chose Edmund.
About 1023 the mint at Hamtun closed for good. Its pennies from about 973 had been signed both HAMTUN and HAMWIC.
1045: King Edward's charters named the minster at Wic, the wic-hythe and a haw in Hamtun.
1066: King Edward had seventy-six men (or seventy-nine) in the town. Twenty years on, sixty-five Frenchmen and thirty-one Englishmen had been settled beside them.

pages.title: Gipeswic
pages.hint: A market among the East Angles
pages.brief: The East Angles' wic on the Orwell, its potters' Ipswich ware sold up the coast.
pages.game:
The East Angles' one trading town, at the head of a long tidal estuary, half a tide's run from the sea, where the Gipping meets the salt water: a grid of gravelled streets, no wall, craftsmen's yards and a smoking potters' quarter, with boats aground on a bank faced with posts and hurdles. In 793 its king is Æthelberht, under Offa of Mercia, and its trade is mainly with Dorestad. A merchant comes for the hard grey pots that every house in East Anglia cooks in, for wool, cloth and honey, and brings wine in casks, Rhineland quernstones, hones from the north and fine pots for lords' tables.
The kilns are fired from the first dry weeks after Easter until the autumn rains; shearing is done by Saint Botolph's day (17 June) and the wool comes down the Gipping after it. The herring are in from Lammas to past Michaelmas, and in winter the estuary belongs to the swans, the geese and the fowlers; the mud dries twice a day in every season, and a deep boat waits on the flood.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: eels, wool, Ipswich ware, barley and malt; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Frankish wine, Mayen quernstones and whetstones. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the last year of the East Angles' own king. An open town on a street grid, the potters' smoke over the north-east corner, Frisian keels on the hurdle bank. Æthelberht's pennies pass beside Offa's new heavy ones, and the reeve answers to a king he has seen.
pages.known:
The East Angles' wic on the Orwell, its potters' Ipswich ware sold up the coast. The place is now Ipswich. In 793 it is under Æthelberht, king of the East Angles.
About 630 Felix comes to the East Angles and sets his bishop's seat at Dommoc; the kingdom has been Christian since. 654: Botolph begins his minster at Icanho, taken to be Iken on the Alde, a day's sail up the coast. 680: By about this year the dead of the first settlement have been laid on the heath north of the crossing for two generations: 71 graves, some under small barrows, two in coffins like small boats, three men with belt sets from northern Francia. About 720 the town is laid out anew on a grid of metalled streets over the old graveyard and across the river into Stoke: some 50 hectares, no wall. The potters begin to make the grey ware, on Frisian models.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/gipeswic.md (the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed); ASC (A) 792 (=794); his pennies (moneyer Lul) (Design/content/realms/england_south.json); Bede II.15; en.wikipedia Dommoc (dossier [Dm]); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 654; en.wikipedia Botolph of Thorney (dossier [Bo]); Buttermarket cemetery, c. 610/635-680/690: Suffolk Heritage Explorer, Saxon Ipswich; Ipswich 1974-1990 Excavation Archive (dossier [SH], [A]); Suffolk Heritage Explorer, Saxon Ipswich; en.wikipedia Ipswich ware (dossier [SH], [Iw]). The start of the ware is put at c. 720 or the late 7th century.

later.text: From 794 to 825: a Mercian town. The king is dead at Offa's word and a chapel to him is talked of; the reeve answers to a king he has never seen, for two years to Eadwald, then to Coenwulf. The kilns do not notice. Wine, querns and fine pots come from Dorestad as before.
794: King Æthelberht of the East Angles is beheaded by order of Offa of Mercia, who takes the kingdom.
796: Offa dies. For two years or so a king Eadwald, known only from his coins, rules the East Angles; by about 805 Coenwulf of Mercia is coining there.
About 825 the East Angles kill Beornwulf of Mercia, and in 827 his successor Ludeca; Æthelstan is their king and strikes his own penny, some with a ship on it.

From 826 to 864: the East Angles have a king again, Æthelstan and then Æthelweard and Edmund, and a penny with a ship on it. Dorestad is burned year after year from 834 and fewer Frisians come. About 850 the potters change to the fast wheel and the old grey ware stops.
About 850 the grey hand-built ware gives way to Thetford ware, thrown on a fast wheel, from new kilns at Carr Street, St Helen's Street and Turret Lane.

From 865 to 879: the army's years. In 865 it winters in the kingdom and is given horses; in 869 it kills the king. Nobody trades far. Silver is hidden, the minsters are empty, and a stranger is asked whose man he is before he is asked what he sells.
In 865 a great heathen army took winter quarters among the East Angles, and there they were horsed; and the East Angles made peace with them. Gipeswic is not named.
In 869, on 20 November King Edmund is killed and the army takes the kingdom; they destroy the monasteries they come to.

From 880 to 917: a Danish town in a Danish land. Sunken-floored houses, an iron smelter, comb makers from over the sea; silver goes on the scale as well as by the tale, and the pennies carry the name of the king the Danes killed. Toward the end a bank and ditch go up, and the streets that crossed their line are closed.
880: Guthrum's army settles East Anglia and shares out the land. In the town the sunken-floored house comes back, iron is smelted, and combs are cut in the Danish fashion.
885: King Alfred's fleet takes sixteen ships of the Danes at the mouth of the Stour, and is beaten the same day on its way home by a large fleet. The Stour and the Orwell share one mouth.
917: By this year a bank and ditch stand round the town for the first time, with gates west, north and east; the army of East Anglia swears to King Edward.

From 918 to 990: the English king's borough, with a market inside the bank and a reeve to witness every sale. Trade turns inland to the east Midlands; few keels come from over the sea. From 970 Ely holds Stoke across the bridge, and from about 973 the pennies say GIPES.
950: By about this year Theodred, bishop of London, has bought a town plot inside Gipeswic and leaves it in his will to his sister's son Osgot.
970: King Edgar gives ten hides at Stoke, across the bridge, to Ely, at Queen Ælfthryth's asking. The bounds begin at the hythe and name the bridge, a marsh mill and a holy well.
973: From about this year pennies are struck that name the town: GIPES. Where the moneyers worked is not known.

From 991 to 1016: the worst years. Ninety-three ships in 991; Thorkell's army up the river in 1010; the sea-flood in 1014; Cnut's ships in the Orwell in 1016. Between fleets the moneyers strike the tribute and the potters go on firing. Houses stand on cellars now, two floors high.
991: Olaf comes with ninety-three ships. This year was Ipswich plundered; and very soon afterwards the ealdorman Byrhtnoth was slain at Maldon, and tribute was first paid: ten thousand pounds.
1010: After Easter Thorkell's army goes up at Ipswich and straight to where Ulfcytel is with his levy. On 5 May the East Angles are beaten at Ringmere; three months of burning follow.
In 1014, on Michaelmas eve the great sea-flood comes widely over this land, further than it ever did before.
1016: Cnut's ships go into the Orwell; his army goes up there and on into Mercia.

From 1017 to 1042: Cnut's peace, under Earl Thorkell until he is outlawed in 1021. Trade over the sea picks up again: wine, querns, and Danes who come to buy and not to burn. One king's writ runs on both shores.

From 1043 to 1066: a full town: 538 burgesses, ten churches, a mint, the queen's grange. The herring is now a trade for the whole coast. Earl Gyrth takes the third penny, and in the autumn of 1066 he takes the borough's men south and does not come back.
1066: The town has 538 burgesses, read as over three thousand people, and some ten churches. It pays fifteen pounds and six sesters of honey; Queen Edith has two parts and Earl Gyrth the third penny.

pages.title: Eoforwic
pages.hint: A market among the Northumbrians
pages.brief: Northumbria's city: the minster, Alcuin's school, and the wic where the Foss meets the Ouse.
pages.game:
The chief city of the Northumbrians: an old stone fortress of the Romans on the Ouse with the archbishop's minster and the best book room north of the Alps inside it, and a trading strand downstream where the Foss runs in. A merchant comes for wool, hides, cloth and jet, and sells wine, quern-stones, pots and, in a hungry year, grain. A Frisian comes carefully: one of his people killed a nobleman's son here twenty years ago, and the dead youth's brother is still counting.
The way in is the Humber and then the tide up the Ouse, two days of flat banks; the river floods after the winter rains and on the great tides a wave the river men call the Aegir runs up it. Wool comes at midsummer, about Saint Peter's feast (?), hides and salt meat after Martinmas, and from the leaves' fall to Easter the minster and the halls want wine. No fair is recorded: the city buys all year.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley, oats, wool, jet and books; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, Rhenish wine, Droitwich salt, olive oil and pepper. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a hungry city with bad omens. Blood ran from the minster roof in Lent, the harvest failed, and on the eighth of June the heathen sacked Lindisfarne; the minster reads Alcuin's letters aloud and collects for the boys carried off. Grain sells for whatever is asked and a Frankish cargo is looked at twice, because King Charles and the English kings have quarrelled over ships. King Æthelred is blamed for all of it.
pages.known:
Northumbria's city: the minster, Alcuin's school, and the wic where the Foss meets the Ouse. The place is now York. In 793 it is under Æthelred I, king of the Northumbrians.
627: King Edwin was baptised at York at Easter, the twelfth of April, in a wooden church of Saint Peter built for the day. A stone church round it was finished about 637. About 670 Bishop Wilfrid mended Saint Peter's: lead on the roof and glass in the windows. 741: The minster burned in April. It burned again in 764. 773: About this year, as the citizens were going out to war, a Frisian merchant killed the son of a count of the province in a brawl, and all the Frisians made haste to leave for fear of the dead youth's kin. Alcuin sent his Frisian pupil Liudger home with them, after three years and six months at the school, with a store of books. 780: The church of Holy Wisdom, lofty, with thirty altars, many columns and arches and glazed windows, built for Archbishop Æthelbert by Eanbald and Alcuin, was consecrated ten days before the old man died on the eighth of November. Where it stood is not known. 793: In Lent a rain of blood fell from a clear sky on the north side of the roof of Saint Peter's, as Alcuin wrote to the king. There was famine in the land, and on the eighth of June heathen men sacked Lindisfarne.

later.text: King Æthelred is blamed for all of it, and at Easter 796 his own men kill him.

796: King Æthelred was killed by his own people on the eighteenth of April. Osbald was king twenty-seven days. Eardwulf was consecrated at York on the twenty-sixth of May, at the altar of Saint Paul in the minster. Archbishop Eanbald died on the tenth of August and was buried at York; a second Eanbald, Alcuin's pupil, was consecrated four days later.

From 797 to 810: king Eardwulf and Archbishop Eanbald, Alcuin's pupil, watch each other across the city; the archbishop rides with more spears than a churchman should and shelters the king's enemies. Boys from Tours copy in the book room. The strand by the Foss is busy and the Frisians are still missing from it, unless someone has paid what is owed.
797: Eanbald II received the pallium. About this year Alcuin, now abbot at Tours, asked leave to send boys to York to fetch the books he lacked: 'the flowers of Britain'.
798: Archbishop Eanbald II held a synod at Finchale.
808: King Eardwulf, driven out about 806, was brought home by the emperor's and the pope's men. Archbishop Eanbald is not heard of afterwards.

From 811 to 866: thirty quiet years under Eanred and then two bad kings at once. No raid, no famine, and the money goes to brass: the moneyers strike small dark coins by the bucket that no stranger will carry home. Bring your own silver and take goods away. The wic by the Foss thins year by year, and by the 850s the mint has stopped.

837: From about this year to about 855 the small coin of the Northumbrians, struck at York for kings and archbishops alike, sank from poor silver to plain copper. A bucket buried at Hexham held some eight thousand of them.
852: Abbot Lupus of Ferrières wrote to Abbot Altsig at York asking for the loan of books: Quintilian, Jerome and Bede.
In 866, on the first of November, All Saints' Day, the great army crossed the Humber and took York.

From 867 to 875: the army's camp. Both kings are dead inside the wall, the strand is given up, and the archbishop comes and goes as the army allows. Ships in the Ouse belong to the host or pay it. A merchant sells ale, horses and iron to men who weigh their silver, or he stays away.
In 867, on the twenty-first of March the Northumbrians broke into the city: 'both the kings were slain on the spot. The survivors made peace with the army.' The kings were Osberht and Ælla.
869: 'The army went back to York, and sat there a year.'
872: The Northumbrians rose against the king the army had set over them; Archbishop Wulfhere fled with him, and came back the next year.

From 876 to 926: the army has shared out the land and begun to plough. Danish kings sit at York beside an English archbishop; from about 895 the mint strikes good pennies with Saint Peter's name, and later a sword and a hammer beside it. About 900 the ground between the fortress and the Foss is cut into long plots, and combs, shoes, cups and amber beads are made there. Ships come from the Danes' own country and from Dublin.
876: 'Healfden divided the land of the Northumbrians; so that they became afterwards their harrowers and plowers.'
895: King Guthred, a baptised Dane, died on the twenty-fourth of August and was buried in the minster. About this year the mint, silent for forty years, began to strike good silver pennies.
900: From about this year the empty ground between the fortress and the Foss was laid out in long narrow plots with wattle houses, workshops, pits and wells.
919: Ragnall, of the kin that held Dublin, took York.

From 927 to 954: kings by the season. Athelstan pulls down the Danes' stronghold; after him come Olaf, another Olaf, Ragnall, Edmund, Eadred, Eric, Olaf again, Eric again. A safe-conduct dies with the king who gave it, so ask on the Humber who rules before coming up. The town itself grows richer through all of it: silk, amber, soapstone and silver from the far end of the world lie on the benches.
927: King Athelstan took York and levelled the Danes' stronghold. About then someone buried a gilt Frankish cup with 617 coins in it near Harrogate, and never came back.
939: King Athelstan died, and the men of York chose Olaf of Dublin. King Edmund took the city back in 944.

948: King Eadred burned the minster at Ripon because the Northumbrians had taken Eric for their king. Eric was king twice, and in 954 was driven out and killed on Stainmore. After him earls ruled, and the archbishop Wulfstan, held by the king since 952, was let go.

From 955 to 1015: no more kings: an earl for the king of the English, a lawmen's court, and Danish speech in every street. King Edgar lets the Danes keep their own law but every sale needs sworn witnesses, and from 973 the pennies are called in and struck again every few years. York is the second town of England and full of merchants. The raids come back to the south in the 980s and reach the Humber in 993.
About 1000 a monk wrote that York was filled beyond telling with the goods of merchants, who came above all from the Danish people, and that thirty thousand grown people lived there.
1014: Archbishop Wulfstan, who signed himself 'the Wolf', preached his sermon to the English: the world is in haste and nears its end.

From 1016 to 1066: Cnut's peace, then Siward's and Tostig's hard hands. Nothing is sold on a Sunday, nothing over four pence without four witnesses, and no Christian is sold out of the land. The earl's house stands at Galmanho outside the west wall beside Saint Olaf's church. In October 1065 the thegns break Tostig's treasury; in September 1066 three hundred Norwegian ships lie in the Ouse, and two battles are fought within a week.
1055: Earl Siward died at York and was buried in the church he had built to Saint Olaf at Galmanho, outside the west wall. Tostig, Godwin's son, was made earl.
In 1065, on the third of October the thegns of the north rose at York, killed Tostig's men, broke open his treasury and chose Morcar for their earl.

In 1066, on the twentieth of September the earls were beaten at Fulford by Harald of Norway and Tostig, and York yielded. On the twenty-fifth King Harold came through the city and killed both at Stamford Bridge. Tostig was buried at York. Twenty-four ships were enough to take the Norwegians home.

pages.title: Serræ
pages.hint: A market in Kent
pages.brief: A toll place on the Wantsum channel, where ships cut inside Thanet.
pages.game:
Serræ is a landing under a chalk bank on the Thanet shore of the Wantsum, where the strait is narrowest and the two tides meet. The king's toll men take toll on ships here, the road from Canterbury crosses the water, and every hull that goes inside Thanet between the Channel and the Thames lies here a tide. A merchant comes for the man who knows the fords, for the abbess's ships and her freedom from toll, for Thanet corn, salt and oysters, and for news that is half a day younger than anywhere else in Kent.
Ships pass from about Easter to Martinmas, and lie here to change one tide for the other. Thanet's corn is cut from Lammas; Saint Mildrith's day falls in high summer, thirteen days into July, and the island walks to Minster for it; oysters are gathered in the cold months and salt is boiled in the dry ones. In winter the saltings flood and the road to the crossing is a line of stakes in grey water.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, woollen cloth, wool and parchment; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, silk, marten, walrus ivory and Rhenish wine. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Offa's last years. The toll men are a Mercian king's, the pennies are his new heavy ones, and Frankish hulls are turned away from English shores. The abbess's three ships pass free and everyone else counts them. The wic-reeve of Lundenwic comes down the strait now and then on the king's business.
pages.known:
A toll place on the Wantsum channel, where ships cut inside Thanet. The place is now Sarre, Thanet. In 793 it is under Offa, king of the Mercians, ruling Kent without a king.
597: Augustine lands on Thanet with about forty companions. The island is reckoned at six hundred hides, and the Wantsum that parts it from Kent is about three furlongs over and can be crossed in two places only. 650: The dead of Sarre are laid on the down above the landing with swords, amber, scales and gaming pieces, until about this time. More than 270 graves have been found; there were more swords here, one to every ten graves, than in any grave field its digger knew. 695: King Wihtred's law fines gifts to idols and meat eaten in a fast. A stranger who leaves the track and neither shouts nor blows his horn may be killed or taken as a thief. 748: King Æthelbald of Mercia lets Abbess Eadburh of Minster off half the toll on a ship at London. She had bought the ship from a man named Leubucus, and had built the church of Peter and Paul for Saint Mildrith's body. 763: King Eadberht of Kent gives Abbess Sigeburh of Minster the toll on the carriage of two ships that was his by right 'in the place called ad Serrae', and all tribute and toll on a third, lately built in the minster, at the public places Fordwic and Seorre. If that ship is broken, worn out with age or wrecked, another may take her place; and what the nuns gain by her trading they must offer to the king at Fordwic. It is the only time Sarre is named before the Conquest. 785: Offa of Mercia rules Kent himself; Kent has no king of its own until he dies.
