later.text: From 796 to 798: Eadberht Præn's rising. Nobody at the toll place is sure whose toll it is; the archbishop has fled; in 798 the Mercian army burns its way across Kent. Ships go through without stopping, and the ale-house bars its door at dusk.
796: Offa dies on 29 July. Eadberht Præn takes Kent, and Archbishop Æthelheard flees Canterbury.
In 798 Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, laid waste Kent as far as the Marsh, took Eadberht Præn and led him bound into Mercia. Cuthred, the king's brother, is set over Kent.

From 799 to 824: Mercian Kent, quiet for a merchant. King and archbishop quarrel over who owns the minsters of Thanet and Reculver, and from about 811 the abbess is the king's own daughter. Letters go up and down the strait and it is wise to carry none.

811: Cwenthryth, King Coenwulf's daughter, is named as abbess: she holds Minster in Thanet and Reculver with Winchcombe. Archbishop Wulfred claims both Kentish houses, and the quarrel runs past her father's death.

From 825 to 850: west Saxon Kent. The toll man answers to a new king's reeve; the minsters are the archbishop's. Sheppey is harried in 835 and a watch is kept on the down. More ships use the south mouth, where a landing at Sandwich is growing.
825: Kent passes from Mercia to Ecgberht of Wessex. King Baldred is driven north over the Thames.
827: By about this year Cwenthryth has given up Minster and Reculver to Archbishop Wulfred.

From 851 to 865: the heathen men winter on Thanet. Some summers the strait is theirs and the landing is empty; the ealdorman's levy fights on the island in 853 and both ealdormen die. The toll man asks whom you mean to sell to.
851: King Æthelstan and Ealdorman Ealhhere fight in ships at Sandwich and take nine of the enemy's. This year the heathen men for the first time stay the winter on Thanet.
853: Ealhhere with the men of Kent and Huda with the men of Surrey fight the heathen army on Thanet. Many are slain and drowned on either hand, and both ealdormen are killed.
865: The heathen army sits on Thanet and makes peace with the men of Kent for a promise of money. Under cover of the peace it steals inland by night and overruns all east Kent.

From 866 to 979: a long quiet. The great army goes north; burhs are built elsewhere; one king takes the toll from Chester round to Gipeswic. Reculver and its Thanet land go to Christ Church. In 969 King Edgar has the whole island plundered for robbing merchants, and for a while after a stranger's goods are very safe here.
949: King Eadred gives Reculver, with its land in Thanet, to Christ Church at Canterbury. Some doubt the charter.
In 969 King Edgar ordered all Thanet-land to be plundered. A later writer gives the reason: the islanders had robbed merchants come from York.

From 980 to 1016: the ship-armies come back. Thanet is overrun in 980, the fleets lie at Sandwich in 991, 1006, 1009 and 1013, and the island pays its part of three thousand pounds. The saltings silt a little more each year and the big ships no longer come through loaded.
980: Thanet is overrun by a ship-army, the same year that Hamwic is sacked.
1009: Soon after Lammas Thorkell's army comes to Sandwich. East Kent buys peace for three thousand pounds.
1011: Canterbury falls between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas. Abbess Leofrun is among those taken; she is counted the last abbess of Minster.

From 1017 to 1066: Cnut's peace and after. Sandwich is the port of the strait and Sarre is its back door: a ferry, a few boats, salt and corn. Saint Mildrith is carried off to Canterbury in 1030. In 1048 the islanders keep twenty-five ships from landing or watering, and in 1052 Godwine's fleet goes through to London.
1030: Saint Mildrith's body is carried from Minster to Saint Augustine's at Canterbury, by King Cnut's gift, against fierce opposition on the island. Her lands go with her.

1048: Lothen and Yrling come to Sandwich with twenty-five ships and take men, gold and silver beyond counting. Then they go about Thanet, but the land's folk withstand them and deny them both landing and water.
1052: Earl Godwine and Harold go with their ships from Sandwich to the North-mouth and so toward London: through the Wantsum and past Sarre, as it is read.

pages.title: Fordwic
pages.hint: A market in Kent
pages.brief: Canterbury's landing on the Stour.
pages.game:
Fordwic is a row of fenced plots on the low south bank of the Stour, at the last place the tide reaches, where the king's toll men take toll by the ship. It is the landing for Canterbury: the archbishop, his scribes, the moneyers and the abbey of the kings' graves are two miles up the track, behind a Roman wall. A merchant comes to sell to the two churches, to change silver into the king's new pennies, to buy a leaf of riddles or carry a book, and to hear what the archbishop's household knows before the rest of Kent does.
Ships come up on the flood from Easter to Martinmas and go down on the ebb; in a dry summer the last reach is shallow and a laden boat waits for a spring tide. Hay is cut on the marsh after midsummer and the mares are driven off it before the winter floods. The city fills for the feasts of its saints, Augustine in the last week of May and, in later ages, Dunstan a week before him and Ælfheah after Easter.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, woollen cloth, wool and parchment; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, silk, marten, walrus ivory and Rhenish wine. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Offa's last years. The toll men are a Mercian king's and the pennies are his new heavy ones. The archbishop is his man, newly enthroned, and Kent does not love either of them. Frankish hulls are turned away; pilgrims still go out with letters from Christ Church.
pages.known:
Canterbury's landing on the Stour. The place is now Fordwich. In 793 it is under Offa, king of the Mercians, ruling Kent without a king.
675: A marsh 'called Stodmerch beside Fordeuuicum' is granted away: the first time the place is named. 679: King Hlothhere grants land at Sturry, over the ford. It is the oldest English charter that survives as it was first written. 695: King Wihtred's law punishes gifts to idols, meat in a fast and a slave's work on Sunday. A stranger who leaves the track and does not blow his horn may be killed or taken. It is dated the sixth day of Rugern, the rye harvest. 734: Archbishop Tatwine dies, leaving forty riddles in Latin verse. A man called Eusebius adds sixty to make the hundred. 763: King Eadberht of Kent frees a ship newly built at Minster in Thanet of all tribute and toll that his toll-gatherers take in the public places called Fordwic and Seorre. If she is wrecked, broken or worn out another may take her place, and what her people gain by trading they must faithfully offer to the king, with the ship, at Fordwic. 785: Offa of Mercia rules Kent himself. Kent has no king of its own until he dies. 792: Offa frees the churches of Kent of their burdens, except service in Kent against pagan seamen with roving fleets. 793: Æthelheard, Offa's man, is enthroned as archbishop on 21 July by Hygberht, Offa's own archbishop of Lichfield. Offa's new heavy penny is being struck in the city.

later.text: From 796 to 798: Eadberht Præn's rising. The archbishop is gone, the moneyers cut dies for a king who was a priest, and the toll man is not sure whose toll he takes. In 798 the Mercian army wastes Kent; the track to the city is full of people going the other way.
796: Offa dies. Eadberht Præn, who had once been a priest, takes Kent, and the archbishop flees.
In 798 Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, wasted Kent and led Eadberht bound into Mercia. His brother Cuthred is made king of Kent.

From 799 to 825: Mercian Kent, ruined and then quiet. The archbishop comes home, goes to Rome and wins back his rank at Clofesho; after him Wulfred quarrels with the king over the minsters. Nuns from Lyminge keep a refuge inside the wall. The scribes are busy.
In 803, on 12 October the council of Clofesho ends the archbishopric of Lichfield. Canterbury has its old rank again.
804: The nuns of Lyminge are given, as a refuge in need, six acres by Saint Mary's church in the west of the city, between the Stour and the city wall.
825: King Baldred is driven north over the Thames, and Kent turns to Ecgberht of Wessex.

From 826 to 850: west Saxon Kent. A new king's name on the penny, the same moneyers at the benches. The books are still being written, in a worse hand each year, and there is talk at every landing of ships on Sheppey.

From 851 to 892: the heathen years. Canterbury is stormed in 851 and east Kent overrun in 865. Books are carried off for their covers and bought back with gold. The churches are short of men who can write Latin, and the landing sees more armed men than merchants.
In 851 the heathen men for the first time stay the winter on Thanet. Three hundred and fifty ships come into the mouth of the Thames, and the crews storm Canterbury and London.
858: A charter of the city is witnessed by Æthelstan 'and the inner townsmen' and by Æthelhelm 'and the cnihts' guild': the first guild named in England. Rats have since cut a hole in the leaf.
865: The heathen army sits on Thanet and takes Kent's promise of money. Under cover of the promise it steals inland by night and overruns all east Kent.

870: About these years a gospel book written in gold letters, probably made in Canterbury, is in a heathen army's hands. Ealdorman Alfred and his wife Wærburh buy it back with pure gold and give it to Christ Church.

From 893 to 978: the slow mending. The city is walled and watched, seven moneyers strike there by King Æthelstan's law, and under Dunstan the monks come back to their books. Fordwic is a row of plots where foreign merchants land for the two churches.
930: King Æthelstan's law gives Canterbury seven moneyers: four the king's, two the bishop's, one the abbot's.
In 969 King Edgar ordered all Thanet-land to be plundered.
978: The abbey of Saint Peter and Saint Paul outside the wall is dedicated anew, to Augustine as well, by Archbishop Dunstan.

From 979 to 1016: the raids again. Thanet is overrun, east Kent pays three thousand pounds, and in 1011 the city is taken by treachery and its archbishop led away. Every keel on the river is counted twice: once for the toll and once for the tribute.
991: Bruman the port-reeve is said to have given Abbot Sigeric two fenced plots and a meadow at Fordwic for his life, and then to the abbey. The year fits neither the abbot nor the reeve.
1009: Soon after Lammas Thorkell's army comes to Sandwich and turns at once on Canterbury. East Kent buys peace for three thousand pounds.

1011: Between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas the army besets Canterbury and takes it by treachery: Ælfmær betrayed it, whose life Archbishop Ælfheah had saved. The archbishop, Bishop Godwine, Abbess Leofrun and the king's reeve Ælfweard are taken.
In 1012, on 19 April the army, drunk on wine brought from the south, kills Archbishop Ælfheah at Greenwich with the bones and horns of oxen.

From 1017 to 1041: Cnut's peace. The murdered archbishop comes home a saint, Saint Mildred is carried in from Thanet, Sandwich haven is given to Christ Church. Pilgrims come up the Stour with silver, and the toll man smiles.
1023: In June King Cnut has Saint Ælfheah's body carried from London to Canterbury and laid on the north side of Christ's altar.
In 1030, on 18 May Saint Mildred's body is brought from Thanet to Saint Augustine's, against fierce opposition on the island.
1031: Cnut gives Christ Church the haven of Sandwich, as far inland as a man can throw a taper-axe from a ship afloat at the highest tide.

From 1042 to 1066: king Edward's day. Fordwic is a small borough of ninety-six plots. The king gives his two thirds of it to Saint Augustine's, and from then the toll is the abbot's. Bruman the reeve takes the customs of foreign merchants, some of them unjustly.
1055: King Edward's writ gives Saint Augustine's as much land within Fordwic as he had: his two thirds of the borough. Earl Godwin had held the third.
1066: Fordwic is a small borough of ninety-six house plots, paying thirteen shillings and worth a hundred.

pages.title: Dofras
pages.hint: A market in Kent
pages.brief: The short crossing to the Franks.
pages.game:
A minster town in a gap of the white cliffs, where a short chalk stream called the Dour runs out over shingle: timber houses and Saint Martin's wooden church stand inside the walls of a Roman fort, and on each height above them is an old Roman light tower with no fire in it. In 793 it answers to King Offa of Mercia through a reeve, and half the toll of the landing belongs to the clerks of Saint Martin. A merchant comes for the crossing, the shortest there is to the Franks, for Kentish cloth and wool, and for news, because whoever is going over the water or coming back has to wait here for the wind.
The crossing runs most of the year, and the other shore shows as a pale line on a clear day. Wool comes down at midsummer, pilgrims wait on the shingle from Pentecost to Michaelmas, the herring boats go out from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew, and the town keeps its own feast at Martinmas in slaughter month, when the beasts that cannot be wintered are killed and salted. A winter gale from the south-west shuts the strand for days and heaps the shingle across the stream mouth.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wheat, woollen cloth, wool and parchment; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, silk, marten, walrus ivory and Rhenish wine. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Offa's Kent. A reeve who is the Mercian king's man takes the king's half of the toll and a clerk of Saint Martin takes the other. The Frankish shore is shut to English merchants by King Charles's order, so the shingle is full of people who say they are pilgrims, and the boatmen of the strand have never been busier. It is a hungry year and the minster feeds a line at its door.
pages.known:
The short crossing to the Franks. The place is now Dover. In 793 it is under Offa, king of the Mercians, ruling Kent without a king.
270: The Romans build a shore fort at Dubris, 'the waters', beside the older harbour and its two light towers on the heights. The English houses of the game's years stand inside its walls. 640: By the tradition of the house, King Eadbald of Kent, who died this year, set twenty-two canons in Saint Mary's chapel on the hill. 695: King Wihtred's law for the men of Kent: the church pays no tax and prays for the king; there are penalties for gifts to idols and for meat in a fast; a stranger who leaves the track and neither shouts nor blows his horn may be taken for a thief. 696: By the same tradition King Wihtred moves the canons down from the hill to a new church of Saint Martin in the town, built to keep a vow to the saint, and gives them half the toll of the port. Hasted gives the year as 691.

later.text: 796: King Offa dies on 29 July. Eadberht Praen takes the kingdom of Kent, and Archbishop Æthelheard, Offa's man, leaves Canterbury. Where he took ship is not recorded.

From 797 to 825: Kent rises under Eadberht Praen and is beaten flat in 798; the reeve changes, and changes again. The peace of the two kings holds over the water, pilgrims cross free and traders pay, and after 811 a fire can be seen at night on the far shore where the emperor has lit the tower of Boulogne. Dofras stays dark.
798: Cenwulf of Mercia lays Kent waste, takes Eadberht Praen and maims him, and sets his own brother Cuthred over the Kentish.
807: King Cuthred dies and Cenwulf rules Kent himself.
811: The emperor Charles has the old light tower at Boulogne repaired and a fire lit on it at night. From the heights of Dofras it can be seen. The towers here stay dark.
825: After the fight at Ellendun the men of Kent turn to Ecgberht of Wessex, and the reeve at Dofras is a West Saxon king's man.

From 826 to 850: west Saxon Kent. The same houses, the same clerks, a king's reeve with a different accent. Quentovic over the water is at its fullest and the crossing is steady work: wool and cloth out, wine, querns and pots back.

From 851 to 899: the heathen years. Fleets winter on Thanet and Sheppey and pass through the strait in hundreds; a watch is kept on the east height and people drive their beasts inland when the word comes. Saint Martin's burns and is built again. The landing over the water thins, and fewer cross.
851: The heathen men winter on Thanet for the first time, and three hundred and fifty ships come into the Thames mouth and storm Canterbury. Nothing is recorded of Dofras.
860: At some time in this century Saint Martin's church burns and is built again in timber on the same lines. No cause is recorded, and no year: the game sets it here.
865: The heathen army sits on Thanet and takes the Kentish men's promise of silver, then steals away by night and overruns all east Kent.
892: The great army crosses from Boulogne in two hundred and fifty ships, horses and all, and goes up the Limen to Appledore. The whole fleet passes through the strait.

From 900 to 990: the kings of Wessex hold all England. Pennies are struck here with the town's name, the canons' church is in its fourth timber building, and the men of the strand go north each autumn after the herring. Quentovic is a name on old coin; boats cross to Boulogne and to the bank under Montreuil.
950: By about this time pennies are struck at Dofras with the town's name on them.

From 991 to 1041: the fleets come back. Folkestone is harried in 991, Thorkell lands at Sandwich in 1009 and east Kent pays three thousand pounds for a peace that lasts a season. A stone church of Saint Mary goes up on the height and bells hang in the old light tower. Under Cnut there is one king on both shores of the sea, and nobody is afraid of a sail.
991: Olaf comes with ninety-three ships to Folkestone and harries it, and goes on to Sandwich. Dofras is not named.

1000: About now a church of Saint Mary is built on the east height of flint and Roman tile, cross-shaped with a tower in the middle, and the Roman light tower beside it is given a fifth stage and bells.
1009: Thorkell's army lands at Sandwich after Lammas, and the people of east Kent buy peace of it for three thousand pounds.

From 1042 to 1066: king Edward's time: a town of burgesses with a hall of their own, who owe the king twenty ships for fifteen days in the year and carry his messengers over to Wissant, and are quit of toll through all England for it. The king's peace lies on the town from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew. In 1051 they fight Count Eustace's men in their own doorways. In October 1066 the town burns.

1051: Count Eustace of Boulogne's men put on their mail short of the town and demand lodging where they please. A householder is wounded, kills his man and is killed at his own hearth; more than twenty townsmen die and nineteen of the Frenchmen. The king orders Earl Godwine to harry Dofras. He will not, and is driven out of England.
1052: Godwine and Harold come back by sea, and at Dofras and the other harbours take as many ships and hostages as they choose before sailing on to London.

1066: In October Duke William comes from Hastings. While the people are yielding his men set fire to the stronghold, and the town burns with it, Saint Martin's among the rest. He stays eight days adding to the defences.

pages.title: Lindisfarena
pages.hint: A monastery among the Northumbrians
pages.brief: Cuthbert's holy island; the northmen fall on it on 8 June 793.
pages.game:
A bishop's monastery on a low island that the sea cuts off twice a day, the shrine of Saint Cuthbert, with the kings' rock of Bebbanburg in plain sight to the south. On 21 June 793 it is thirteen days since heathen men came from the north: the doors are off the church, some brethren are dead, some drowned, and boys of the house are gone in the ships. Nothing is sold here by custom. This is a house that receives: a merchant comes with wine, wax, oil, lead and grain, and leaves with thanks, letters, a little silver and the bishop's list.
The tide is the clock: the sand to the mainland is dry twice a day and drowned twice. Saint Cuthbert's day is the twentieth of March and falls in Lent, when a brother keeps the fast alone on the rock offshore; the gathering is at Saint Aidan's mass at the end of August. Seals pup on the sands at the back end of the year, geese come with the first frosts, and from the first of May to the end of September every brother looks north before he looks anywhere else.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley, oats, wool, jet and books; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, Rhenish wine, Droitwich salt, olive oil and pepper. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the wound. Bishop Higbald counts what is gone and will not leave. The church has no doors and half its lamps; the cross in the graveyard has lost its head; the writing house has been turned out on its floor. Famine is in the land in 793, so grain is worth more here than silver. The house takes wine, wax, oil, lead and bread corn, and pays in what it has: a little old silver, wool, a letter, a prayer by name.
pages.known:
Cuthbert's holy island; the northmen fall on it on 8 June 793. The place is now Lindisfarne. In 793 it is under Æthelred I, king of the Northumbrians.
About 634 Aidan comes from Hi at King Oswald's asking and is given the island for his bishop's seat. 651: Bishop Finan (651 to 661) builds a church not of stone but of hewn oak, thatched with reeds. Bishop Eadberht (688 to 698) takes off the thatch and covers roof and walls with plates of lead. 687: Cuthbert dies on Farne on the twentieth of March. A brother on a height on the island waits for two candles shown from the rock; the body comes over by ship and is buried in a stone coffin at the right side of the altar. 698: The grave is opened after eleven years and the body found whole. It is laid in a new coffin of carved oak above the floor of the sanctuary; Bishop Eadberht dies soon after and is laid in the grave beneath. 715: Between about this year and 720 a great gospel book is written on the island on some hundred and fifty calfskins. The house that made it has not been found by the diggers. 737: King Ceolwulf gives up his kingdom and enters the house as a monk. From then the brethren may drink wine or ale, who before had only milk or water. About 750 Offa, son of King Aldfrith, flees to Saint Cuthbert's body and is dragged away from it almost dead of hunger. King Eadberht shuts Bishop Cynewulf up at Bebbanburg. 780: Higbald takes the bishop's seat. In 793, on 23 April the body of Sicga, the ealdorman who killed King Ælfwald and died by his own hand, is carried to the island. The same year: lights and whirlwinds, fiery dragons in the sky, and a great famine. In 793, on 8 June heathen men come from the north in ships. Some of the brethren they kill, some they carry off in chains, most they strip and drive out of doors, and some they drown in the sea. The bishop's seat stays where it is. 793: Later in the year Alcuin writes from Francia to Higbald and the brethren. He promises that when King Charles comes home he will go to him and do what he can for the youths led away captive.

later.text: 794: Heathen men plunder the monastery at the mouth of the Tyne. Their leader is killed and a storm breaks their ships.
In 796 a king of twenty-seven days comes over the sand in a hurry.
796: In May Osbald, king for twenty-seven days, flees to the island and goes from it by ship with some of the brethren to the king of the Picts. He dies an abbot in 799.
In 800, on Christmas eve a great wind; the sea comes over its bounds and floods the land.
He holds it until his death on 25 May 803.
803: Higbald dies on 25 May. Ecgberht is hallowed bishop at Bywell on 11 June.

From 804 to 829: mended. Bishop Ecgberht, then Heathwred. The doors hang, the head of the cross is run on again with lead, new boys are in the school. The sea broke over the low ground at Christmas 800 and the brethren still talk of it. The scribes work again and want calfskin and colours. Styca coins of the Northumbrian kings pass at the cellarer's door, small and getting baser.

From 830 to 874: half a house. Bishop Ecgred builds at Norham on the Tweed, and the bishops are as often there as here; the island keeps the shrine, the graveyard, the school and a farm on the north shore that turns calves into pages. About 840 the book of names is begun. Pennies of Wessex turn up beside the brass stycas. After 867 York is the army's, and the talk at the guest fire is of how far the Tyne is.

830: Ecgred is bishop (830 to 845), a man of noble birth and energetic. He builds a church at Norham on the Tweed and moves King Ceolwulf's body there; one later book says Saint Cuthbert's body went with it for a time.
About 840 a book of the names of the house's friends, living and dead, is begun in gold and silver letters, probably here.
867: The heathen army holds York. On 21 March both Northumbrian kings, Osberht and Ælle, are killed there. The army comes no further north than the Tyne.

From 875 to 883: the leaving. In 875 the bishop and the saint's people go over the sand with the coffin on a cart and do not come back for a lifetime. A few stay: a priest, the farm, the fishers. The church is locked and the shrine is an empty place on the floor that people still kneel beside.

875: Halfdan winters on the Tyne. Bishop Eardulf and Abbot Eadred leave the island with Saint Cuthbert's body, Saint Oswald's head, some of Aidan's bones and the bones of three bishops, two hundred and forty-one years after the founding.
883: After seven years on the road the body rests at Chester-le-Street. King Guthred's law gives thirty-seven days' peace to anyone who flees to it.

From 884 to 994: a cell and a farm under the bishop at Chester-le-Street. Graves are still dug and stones still carved. No one guards it: Scots plunder it in the time of King Guthred, and in 941 the men of York come and kill many. A merchant finds a priest, a few households, sheep, seals and a very good anchorage with nobody to take a toll.
890: Between 883 and 895 Scots cross the Tweed and plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne.
941: The men of York ravage the island of Lindisfarne and kill many.

From 995 to 1066: Durham's island. The body lies at Durham from 995 and the island is where it began: pilgrims cross the sand barefoot at the ebb, a priest keeps the old church, and a penny of King Edward is lost in the grass. In 1061 the king of Scots breaks the saint's peace here. The land is the earls' of Bebbanburg in all but name.
995: Bishop Aldhun carries the body from Chester-le-Street to Durham. The island is from now a holy place of Durham's saint and not his house.
1061: Malcolm, king of Scots, harries Northumbria and breaks the peace of Saint Cuthbert on the island.

pages.title: Bebbanburg
pages.hint: A king's seat among the Northumbrians
pages.brief: The Northumbrian kings' rock fortress on the coast.
pages.game:
A black rock on the shore with a wall round its top, a hall, a church that keeps a dead king's hand, and a well cut down through the stone. It is a king's house and not a market: nobody here lives by buying and selling, and a merchant deals with the steward of the household or with nobody. He comes for wool, hides and herring, for a sword-smith who welds better than any on this coast, and for the word of the men who hold the gate.
Sea fog lies on the islands from Easter to midsummer and the herring come from Oswald's feast to the leaves' fall; the seals pup on the Farnes when the nights are long. The household eats its food-rents in winter, so wine and grain are wanted most between Martinmas and Easter, and after Michaelmas no sensible skipper lies on this open strand a night longer than he must.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley, oats, wool, jet and books; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, Rhenish wine, Droitwich salt, olive oil and pepper. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a king's rock in a hungry year, with the smoke of Lindisfarne hardly blown away. The wardens are short with strangers and shorter with each other, the steward buys any grain that lands, and the priests of the shrine pray for the brethren across the flats. King Æthelred is blamed in his own halls.
pages.known:
The Northumbrian kings' rock fortress on the coast. The place is now Bamburgh. In 793 it is under Æthelred I, king of the Northumbrians.
547: Ida began to reign and built Bebbanburg, 'which was first surrounded with a hedge, and afterwards with a wall'. 642: King Oswald was killed in battle on the fifth of August. His head went to Lindisfarne; his hands and arms were brought to his royal city and kept in Saint Peter's church on the rock, the right hand undecayed in a silver case. 651: Penda of the Mercians heaped the beams, wattles and thatch of the villages round about against the rock and lit them. Bishop Aidan saw the smoke from Farne and prayed, and the wind turned. On the thirty-first of August that year Aidan died leaning on a post of the wooden church in the king's vill near by; fire could not burn the post afterwards. 687: Cuthbert died in his cell on Inner Farne, in sight of the rock. 750: King Eadberht held Bishop Cynewulf of Lindisfarne captive at Bebbanburg, after a king's kinsman who had fled to Cuthbert's relics was dragged out, starving, and killed. 774: King Alhred was driven from York, fled here with a few companions and went on to the king of the Picts. The annal describes the place: 'exceedingly well fortified, but by no means large, containing about the space of two or three fields, having one hollowed entrance ascending in a wonderful manner by steps', with a church 'of very beautiful architecture, in which is a fair and costly shrine', and on the west and highest point 'a well, excavated with extraordinary labour, sweet to drink, and very pure to the sight'. In 793, on the eighth of June heathen men sacked Lindisfarne, in plain sight of the rock across the flats. What the fortress did that day is not recorded.

The line of sight is real; that the king's men watched and did not come is the game's invention (spine, thread holy_island)

later.text: In April 796 he is killed, and for a month nobody at the gate knows whose men they are.
796: King Æthelred was killed on the eighteenth of April. Osbald was king for twenty-seven days and then took ship from Lindisfarne to the Picts. Eardwulf was made king on the fourteenth of May.

From 797 to 866: the kings change and the rock does not. Food-rents come up the steps, the smiths weld, and the small coin of the country turns from poor silver to plain copper that no stranger will take. The gale of 800 throws sand into the inlet. Bishops of Lindisfarne come over the flats for Oswald's feast, and each summer the watch looks north a little longer than it used to.
In 800, on the day before Christmas a great gale blew and the sea came over the land.
About 855 the styca, the small base coin of the Northumbrians, ceased to be struck. In the later ninth century a small building in the workshops burned with a purse of stycas in it.

From 867 to 926: the kings are dead at York and the Danes share out the land to the south. Beyond the Tyne the English keep their own lords, and the lord of the rock is one of them: no coin is struck in the north, silver is weighed, and from 875 Lindisfarne stands empty. A hull from the south is asked which army she has leave from. Eadwulf, who dies in 913, is called a king by the Irish and a reeve by the West Saxons.
867: Both kings of the Northumbrians, Osberht and Ælla, were killed at York on the twenty-first of March. After that one Ecgberht reigned under the Danes 'over the Northumbrians beyond the Tyne'.
875: Halfdan wintered on the Tyne and wasted the minsters. Bishop Eardwulf and Cuthbert's people left Lindisfarne with the body. No source says the rock was taken.
913: Eadwulf died: 'king of the northern English' to the Irish annals, the reeve of the town called Bebbanburg to Æthelweard, and a friend of King Alfred.

From 927 to 992: the lords of the rock bow to the southern kings and keep everything north of the Tyne all the same. From 954 they are earls. The hall is rebuilt, a gleeman has a place at the board, and merchants out of Danish York come up the coast with pots, querns and combs, and are let ashore under the wardens' eyes.
In 927, on the twelfth of July Ealdred son of Eadwulf, of Bebbanburg, bowed to King Æthelstan at Eamont with the kings of the Scots and the Welsh.
954: King Eric was killed, betrayed by Oswulf of Bebbanburg and one Maccus; 'the province was committed to earl Osulf'.

From 993 to 1040: in 993 a fleet takes the rock and carries off all that is in it. The house builds again in timber and stone and holds on: Waltheof grows old behind the wall, Uhtred breaks the Scots and is murdered in 1016, and after Carham the border comes down to the Tweed. Some time in these years the saint's arm leaves the shrine for the south and does not come back.
993: 'This year was Bamborough destroyed, and much spoil was there taken.'

1006: The Scots besieged Durham. Old Waltheof shut himself up in Bebbanburg; his son Uhtred raised the men of the north, broke the Scots, and was made earl. He set the best-looking heads on stakes round Durham and gave four women a cow each for washing them.
1016: Uhtred went to submit to Cnut and was killed with forty of his men by Thurbrand Hold.
1018: The men between Tees and Tweed were beaten by the Scots at Carham. Eadwulf Cudel held Bebbanburg.

From 1041 to 1066: Siward the Dane and then Tostig Godwinson are earls at York, and the old house holds the rock under them, sourly. The shrine is empty. In 1061 the Scots come over the flats; in 1065 the north throws Tostig out and one of the old blood has the land beyond the Tyne again, for as long as it lasts.
1041: King Harthacnut 'betrayed Eadulf, under the mask of friendship'. Siward, who had married a daughter of the house, held all Northumbria after him.
1061: Malcolm of the Scots ravaged the earldom while Earl Tostig was at Rome, and broke Cuthbert's peace on Lindisfarne.
1065: The Northumbrians drove out Tostig. Morcar gave the land beyond the Tyne to Oswulf son of Eadwulf, of the old house.

pages.title: Gyrwe
pages.hint: A monastery among the Northumbrians
pages.brief: Bede's monastery on the Tyne (with Wearmouth).
pages.game:
The monastery of Saint Paul stands on a low rise where the little river Don runs into the Tyne, an hour's row inside the bar, with a wide tidal mudflat below it where a boat can take the ground. It is Bede's house, fifty-eight years after his death: stone churches with coloured glass, a boys' school, and scribes who cannot copy his books as fast as the Continent asks for them. Nothing is sold here by custom and no toll is asked. A merchant comes with calfskin, colours, wax, wine, oil and incense, and in 793 with bread corn; he leaves with barley, wool, hides, salmon, a letter, and now and then a book worth more than his boat.
The year is the church's: the hallowing day of Saint Paul's on the twenty-third of April, the master's day on the twenty-sixth of May, the apostles Peter and Paul at midsummer's end, Abbot Ceolfrith at the back of harvest, Father Benedict in the dead of winter. Salmon run in the Tyne from spring and the eels go down on the first dark flood nights after Michaelmas. In winter the ink thickens and the scribes' hands stop; in summer every brother looks down the river toward the bar.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley, oats, wool, jet and books; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, Rhenish wine, Droitwich salt, olive oil and pepper. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the full house, afraid. The glass is in the windows, the book chests are full, the boys sing in two choirs. There is famine in the land, so the cellarer wants bread corn more than wine. Alcuin's letter has been read aloud in chapter and nobody has forgotten the line about the sea. The brothers ask every skipper what lies off the bar.
pages.known:
Bede's monastery on the Tyne (with Wearmouth). The place is now Jarrow. In 793 it is under Æthelred I, king of the Northumbrians.
About 681 King Ecgfrith gives forty hides by the Tyne, and Benedict Biscop sends Ceolfrith with a company of brethren to build a second house, Saint Paul's, one monastery with Saint Peter's at the Wear mouth. 685: The church of Saint Paul is hallowed on the twenty-third of April, in the fifteenth year of King Ecgfrith and the fourth of Abbot Ceolfrith. The stone that says so is set in the wall. 686: A plague takes every brother here who can read or sing the office, except Abbot Ceolfrith and one little boy. The two of them keep the psalms going until others are taught. 690: Benedict Biscop, the founder, dies on the twelfth of January, having ordered that the library he brought from Rome be kept whole and not scattered. 716: Abbot Ceolfrith leaves for Rome with one of the three great Bibles the house has made, and dies on the road at Langres on the twenty-fifth of September. The two houses then hold about six hundred brethren. Hwaetberht is chosen abbot. 735: Bede, priest and master of this house, dies on the twenty-sixth of May. Among the things in his box are pepper, napkins and incense, which he shares out among the priests. About 746 Boniface writes from Germany to Abbot Hwaetberht asking for the works of Bede, and sends a coverlet of goat hair. 764: Abbot Cuthbert writes to Bishop Lul of Mainz: the winter has numbed his scribes' hands. He sends Bede's lives of Saint Cuthbert and asks for a man who can make glass and a man who can play the harp. In 792, on the fourteenth of September Osred, who had been king, is killed, and his body is laid at Tynemouth, on the north headland of the river mouth. 793: Signs in the sky, a great famine, and on the eighth of June the heathen men at Lindisfarne. Alcuin writes from Francia to the brothers of Wearmouth and Jarrow: you live by the sea, from which the plague first came.

later.text: 794: The heathen men ravage the harbour of King Ecgfrith and plunder the monastery at the mouth of the Don. Their chief is put to death by the English; a storm breaks some of their ships.

From 795 to 830: after the heathen. The house was plundered, not burned: the altar plate is gone, some windows are boarded, and broken ship timber lies on the south sand for years. The scribes still work and letters still come asking for Bede's books, but the house is poor and counts everything. Kings change at York faster than the abbot can write to them. The sea flood of Christmas 800 and the cattle plague of 810 are both long remembered at the cellarer's door, where copper stycas pass.
796: King Aethelred is killed at Corbridge, up this same river, on the eighteenth of April. Osbald is king for twenty-seven days; Eardwulf is hallowed in May.
800: One late book has the heathen plunder Hartness and Tynemouth this year. On Christmas eve a great wind, and the sea comes over the land.
810: A plague of cattle through all Britain.
821: Tidfrith, the last bishop of Hexham, is dead by about this year, and no one is hallowed after him. The house has no bishop of its own country.

From 831 to 866: thinning. No bishop sits at Hexham. Fewer boys are given to the house and the old hands are not replaced; the writing house copies for itself and sells little. The coin is base copper and the cellarer would rather have goods. The glass workers by the river are a memory and one furnace floor (?).
About 850 some eight thousand copper stycas are buried in a bucket at Hexham, a day up the Tyne.

From 867 to 882: the army on the Tyne. York has fallen, and in 875 Halfdan's fleet winters in the river. The brothers go, by ones and by companies, with what books they can carry; no one writes down the day. Fishers still work the Slake and bury their dead by the church. A merchant here trades with Danes or with nobody.
867: The heathen army holds York and both Northumbrian kings are killed there. The army comes no further north than the mouth of the Tyne.

875: Halfdan, king of the Danes, enters the Tyne with a great fleet, lands at Tynemouth and winters by the river. By now, or soon after, there are no monks at Saint Paul's. No year for their going is safe.

From 883 to 1021: saint Cuthbert's land. The churches stand, one with half a roof; the long halls are cattle sheds and quarries. A priest of the saint's people comes from Chester-le-Street, and after 995 from Durham, to say mass at Bede's grave, and country people come on the master's day. The Slake has a few boats, salmon and eels. Who serves the church from year to year is not recorded (?).
About 883 King Guthred gives Saint Cuthbert all the land between the Wear and the Tyne. The churches of Bede's house are now the saint's.

From 1022 to 1066: the empty grave. Bede's bones are at Durham and the visitors fewer. The church is still used and the fishers still land; brambles are in the refectory. In 1066 a Norwegian fleet lies at the river mouth for some days in early autumn and nobody on the Slake lights a fire. (After the game: King William's army burns the church in 1069, and in 1074 Aldwin finds the buildings half ruined and begins again.)

About 1022 Elfred son of Westou, priest and sacrist of Durham, who has come here every year on Bede's day, leaves early and alone and does not come again. Bede's bones are afterwards at Durham with Saint Cuthbert's.
1065: The bones of Saint Oswine are raised at Tynemouth, across the river mouth.
1066: Harald, king of the Norwegians, comes unlooked for to the mouth of the Tyne with a very great fleet, where Earl Tostig joins him.

pages.title: Streonæshalch
pages.hint: A monastery among the Northumbrians
pages.brief: Hild's abbey on the cliff above the Esk.
pages.game:
A house of monks and nuns on a high headland above the mouth of the Esk, founded by King Oswiu and ruled first by Hild, with a king's grave in its church and lay families at hearths along the cliff edge. There is no quay, no toll and no market place: a ship takes the ground on the sand inside the river mouth and deals at the cellar door. A merchant comes for jet picked up under the cliffs, for the house's cloth, wool and hides, and to sell it wine, wax, glass and colours for its books.
Jet is gathered after the winter gales have brought the cliff down, so the best of it is on offer between Easter and midsummer. Salmon run the brown river in summer and autumn; wool comes after the shearing. The house keeps Saint Hild's day eight days before the end of November, after sailing has stopped, so only a ship that winters on this coast sees it. The harbour dries at every ebb and the river comes down fast and peat-brown after rain on the moors.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley, oats, wool, jet and books; wanted here, and so dearer: silk, Rhenish wine, Droitwich salt, olive oil and pepper. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the watching years. The house is whole: the church with the kings in it, the writing house, the looms, the guest fire, hearths along the cliff edge. But news of Lindisfarne came down the coast in June 793 and of the Tyne a year after, and the abbess asks every shipman what he saw to the north. The house wants wine, wax and colours, and pays in cloth, jet, hides and a little silver.
pages.known:
Hild's abbey on the cliff above the Esk. The place is now Whitby. In 793 it is under Æthelred I, king of the Northumbrians.
657: King Oswiu founds the monastery in thanks for his victory over Penda, with Hild as its first abbess, for men and women both. The year is 'about 657'. 664: King Oswiu hears Colman for the custom of Iona and Wilfrid for the custom of Rome on the keeping of Easter, here, with Cedd interpreting, and chooses for Peter, who holds the keys. 670: King Oswiu dies on 15 February and is buried in the church of Saint Peter here. King Edwin's body lies here too; his head is at York. 680: Hild dies on 17 November, aged 66. In her last year she founded the daughter house at Hackness, where the nun Begu saw her soul carried up by angels that night. 685: Bishop Trumwine flees here from Abercorn after the Picts' victory, lives out his days in the house and is buried in Saint Peter's. 713: A Life of Pope Gregory is written here, 'by a monk or, possibly, a nun': the oldest telling of the Angles and the angels. The year is 'about 713'. 714: Abbess Aelfflaed, Oswiu's daughter, dies. She is the last head of the house whose name is known. In 793, on 8 June heathen men plunder Lindisfarne, up this same coast. Nothing is recorded of Streonaeshalch in this year.

later.text: 794: Heathen men raid the mouth of the Tyne; their leader is killed and a storm wrecks their ships.
From 799 a sea chest lies above the tide line.

From 811 to 843: forty quiet years. King Eanred reigns long and no sails come. The talk of moving the books has gone stale; new hands are at the desk and the door. The small coins of York pass at the cellar, baser each year, and are worth nothing south of the Humber: a merchant takes his price in goods.

From 844 to 866: thinning. A king is killed by heathen men in 844 and the old fear comes back. Fewer brothers and sisters sing the hours; some cells stand shut; the brass coins stop coming about the middle of these years. The cliff-edge families still gather jet and still want salt, iron and news.
844: King Raedwulf is killed fighting heathen raiders, the first on this coast for forty years.
855: About now the run of small Northumbrian coins lost on the headland stops. The year is a guess from the finds.

From 867 to 875: empty. The great army has York. Nobody can say in what season the last of the house went or where: it is said the Danes came, and nobody who says it was there. The roofs are off the small churches; sheep graze among the name stones. A few lay families hold on by the river and sell jet and fish to any ship that asks nothing.

867: The great army holds York; Kings Osberht and Aella are killed there on 21 March. It is said, by writers three hundred years later, that Streonaeshalch was laid waste by Ingwar and Ubba in these years and lay empty for more than two hundred. No writer of the time says so; the ground shows only that the house ends in the ninth century.

From 876 to 953: Hvitabyr. Healfdene's men have the land and plough it; the place has a new name in their mouths, and the law is the settlers' custom, reckoned in marks and ores. Boats lie on the sand by the river, not under the church. Up among the ruins a priest or two farm a patch the Danes call Prestebi. York is a kings' town of Danes and Dubliners, and its craftsmen want every lump of jet the shore gives.
876: Healfdene shares out the land of the Northumbrians and his men plough it. The Norse names come after this: Hvitabyr, Whitby, and Prestebi, the priests' farm.
944: King Edmund is said, in one tradition, to have carried Hild's bones south to Glastonbury; another says Gloucester. The year is not given: between 939 and 946.

From 954 to 1032: a harbour under an earl. The last king at York is gone; earls rule for the kings in the south. English and Danish are one speech with two sets of endings here. Jet goes to York to be cut into rings, pins and small crosses; fish, wool and hides go with it. The headland is pasture and a graveyard.

From 1033 to 1066: the earl's manor. Whitby with Sneaton is Earl Siward's, then Tostig's, then Morcar's: a rich holding with a reeve, a hall by the harbour and many boats. In September 1066 the smoke of Scarborough is seen to the south. Three years later King William wastes the north, and in 1086 the book says of Whitby: nearly all waste.
1041: Siward, earl at York from 1033 and of all Northumbria from 1041, holds Whitby with its outlier Sneaton, fifteen carucates. Nothing says he ever came.

1066: In September Harald of Norway and Tostig burn Scarborough, down the coast, on their way to the Humber. Whitby is not named. By now the headland is empty and a substantial town lies down by the harbour; the manor is reckoned at 112 pounds.

pages.title: Dommoc
pages.hint: A town among the East Angles
pages.brief: The East Angles' bishop's see on the coast (?).
pages.game:
A bishop's town on a cliff of sand and gravel, a short day's sail north of the Orwell mouth, with heath behind it and an open river mouth on its north side where boats lie. Felix, the first bishop of the East Angles, was given his seat here about 630, and his successors still keep it. A merchant comes for rope, hemp and salt fish and for whatever the bishop's letters are worth, and brings what a church cannot grow: wine, oil, incense, wax and books.
Hemp is pulled after Lammas and lies rotting in the pond until Michaelmas, and in those same weeks the herring come down the coast and every boat is at sea. In winter the haven is open but empty, and the cliff loses a little to each north-easterly gale.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: eels, wool, Ipswich ware, barley and malt; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Frankish wine, Mayen quernstones and whetstones. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: the last year of an East Anglian king. A small town round a bishop's church on the cliff: priests, boys at their letters (?), ploughmen, herdsmen and the people of the hemp pond. A few boats lie in the river mouth. The news of Lindisfarne is two weeks old and the bishop wants to hear it from someone who has been north.
pages.known:
The East Angles' bishop's see on the coast (?). The place is now Dunwich. In 793 it is under Æthelberht, king of the East Angles.
About 630 Felix, a bishop from Burgundy, was given his see in the city Dommoc by King Sigeberht, and after seventeen years 'ended his days there in peace'. About 631 King Sigeberht 'founded a school wherein boys should be taught letters', with masters whom Felix brought from Kent. Bede does not say where; that it was at Dommoc is a later guess (?). About 654 King Anna of the East Angles was killed by Penda of Mercia and buried at Blythburgh, up the river from Dommoc. In the same year Botolph began his minster at Icanho. About 672 the East Angles' diocese was divided: Dommoc kept the south and a second bishop sat at Elmham for the north. About 675 soil gathered in the bottom of a hollow road that ran down through the town to the shore (between 655 and 770 at the outside). In 793 the bishop of Dommoc was Ælfhun, consecrated between 789 and 793, or if he was not yet consecrated, Heardred before him.

later.text: From 794 to 798: the king is dead by Offa's order and a Mercian king's man sits on the strand asking whose ship that is. The Frankish quarrel reaches this coast too (?): wine for the altar is short. In May people go quietly to pray for the dead king. Offa dies in 796 and for a year or two there are pennies with Eadwald's name; then the Mercians are back. Bishop Ælfhun dies at Sudbury and is carried home.
In 794 'Offa, King of Mercia, commanded that King Ethelbert should be beheaded', and took the East Angles' kingdom. His day is kept on 20 May.
Felix's mass falls in Lent, on the eighth day of March, and King Æthelberht's from 795 in May, when the first ships are out.
In 796 Offa died, and for a year or two the East Angles had a king of their own, Eadwald, known only from some twelve of his pennies.
798: In this year or the year before 'Bishop Alfun died at Sudbury, and was buried at Dunwich. After him Tidfrith was elected to the see.' Tidfrith's written oath to Archbishop Æthelheard survives.

From 799 to 824: bishop Tidfrith's years: a careful man who rides to the Mercian king's councils and comes back with law to read out. The ports are open, Alcuin's letter lies in the church chest, and the boys' bench is full. Rope and hemp go to Gipeswic's shipmasters every autumn.

800: Between 798 and 804 Alcuin wrote from Tours to Tidfrith of Dommoc and Alhheard of Elmham, whom the abbot Lull had praised to him in person: preach to everyone, and have my name remembered in your churches.
In 803 at the council of Clofesho Tidfrith signed as bishop 'of the city of Dummuca', with the abbots Wulfheard and Lull and the priests Ceolhelm, Cynulf, Tilberht and Eadberht.
In 816 on 27 July Tidfrith sat with Sibba of Elmham at the council of Chelsea, King Coenwulf of Mercia being present.

From 825 to 864: the East Angles have kings of their own again, Æthelstan and then Edmund, and pennies with their names. Bishop Wilred, then Æthelwald. From 841 sails off the coast are counted before they are greeted, and the church plate is not left on the altar overnight.

About 825 the East Angles asked King Ecgberht of the West Saxons for 'peace and protection against the terror of the Mercians' and killed Beornwulf, the Mercians' king. In the same year Wilred signed at Clofesho, first as bishop elect of Dommoc and then as bishop.
In 841 'in Lindsey, East-Anglia, and Kent, were many men slain by the army'.

From 865 to 879: the army's years. In 865 it winters among the East Angles and takes their horses; in 869 it comes back and the king is killed. Nobody writes what happens at Dommoc. The bishop's name is not written again. The church stands with a priest or without one; the boys' bench is empty; the hemp is still pulled, because armies need rope as much as anyone.
In 865 a great heathen army took winter quarters among the East Angles, 'where they were soon horsed'. Where it lay is not said.

In 869 on 20 November King Edmund was killed by the army. No bishop of Dommoc is heard of after Æthelwald, whose oath to Archbishop Ceolnoth and whose bronze seal survive. No text says what the army did at Dommoc.

From 880 to 917: a Danish king's land. The plough-lands have new lords with Danish names who were baptised with Guthrum or were not. Silver is weighed as well as counted and fines are reckoned in ores. Pennies with Saint Edmund's name pass on the strand, struck by the people who killed him. A priest says mass in Felix's church; no bishop comes.
In 880 Guthrum's army went from Cirencester into East Anglia, 'settled, and divided the land'. Guthrum, baptised Æthelstan, struck pennies of his own and died in 890.
In 917 'all the army in East-Anglia swore union' with King Edward.

From 918 to 990: under the English kings. The bishop who has the care of this shore sits far off, at London, then Hoxne, then Elmham. The town grows without him, on herring: more boats in the haven every autumn, salt brought in, fish going inland in barrels. Men of the town are called to the hundred court and fined if they stay away.

952: Before 953 Bishop Theodred of London, who had the care of Suffolk, named a bishop's seat at Hoxne in his will; from about 955 one bishop at Elmham had all the East Angles. Dommoc had no bishop again.

From 991 to 1016: the fleets are back. Ipswich is plundered in 991, Norwich burned in 1004, all East Anglia burned for three months in 1010. Ulfcytel leads the East Angles and loses bravely. The haven empties when a fleet is on the coast and the herring are left to swim.
In 1004 Swein's fleet burned Norwich, and Ulfcytel and the East Angles fought it hard. In 1010 the army landed at Ipswich after Easter and burned East Anglia for three months.

From 1017 to 1066: earl Thorkell's land and then the English earls', in King Cnut's peace and after it. A herring town of two hundred households under Edric of Laxfield and the abbot of Ely, with one church of Saint Felix. Nobody alive has seen a bishop here. The old people say the shore was further out when they were children, and they are right.
In 1017 King Cnut gave East Anglia to Earl Thorkell.

1066: In this year Edric of Laxfield held Dommoc, by then called Dunwich: two ploughlands, one church, twelve cottagers and a hundred and twenty burgesses, rendering ten pounds. The abbot of Ely had eighty more burgesses on fourteen acres. There was no exchanger in the town, but one at Blythburgh.
1086: After the game's end the king's clerks wrote of the two ploughlands: 'now 1. The sea carried away the other.' The town then gave sixty thousand herrings a year.

pages.title: Legacæstir
pages.hint: A town among the Mercians
pages.brief: The old legionary town on the Dee, facing Wales and Ireland.
pages.game:
A dead Roman fortress of red stone on a ridge in a bend of the Dee, far bigger than the handful of people who live under its south wall. In 793 it is King Offa's far shore: a church on the cliff, a landing, a few households, and lead that comes down from the hills to lie on the bank for want of a lawful buyer. A merchant comes for the lead, for salt from the wiches, and because nobody else comes; a hundred years on his heirs come for the mint and the Dublin men.
The tide runs up past the town twice a day and a boat comes and goes on it or not at all; the sands in the river mouth shift after every winter gale. Lead and salt come down the tracks when the ground is dry, from Easter to Michaelmas. Saint John's feast at midsummer fills the church on the cliff.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Droitwich salt and lead. Prices are in pennies, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: Offa's far shore. Red walls with nobody on them, a priest and his church on the cliff, a few households under the south gate and an ale-house in the corner of the old baths. Lead lies stacked on the bank because the Frankish ports are shut to English goods. Welsh herdsmen come over the ford with honey and go back with salt, and nobody takes a toll because nobody has been told to.
pages.known:
The old legionary town on the Dee, facing Wales and Ireland. The place is now Chester. In 793 it is under Offa, king of the Mercians.
About 616 Æthelfrith of the Northumbrians beat the Welsh at the City of the Legions. Bede says he first cut down the monks of Bangor who had come to pray against him, about twelve hundred of them, and that only fifty got away. 689: They say King Æthelred of the Mercians founded the church of Saint John outside the walls in this year. It is a late tradition and no charter shows it. 793: Offa is king of the Mercians. Nothing is recorded of the city in this year: no reeve, no market, no mint.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier); ASC (A) 755 (=757), 794 (=796); HR 796 (Design/content/realms/england_south.json); Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.2 (paraphrased from memory (?)); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chester; Late tradition only: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John_the_Baptist's_Church,_Chester; VCH Cheshire 5.1 has 'possibly'; VCH Cheshire 5.1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230'; the silence is the fact

later.text: 796: King Offa died on the 29th of July. His son Ecgfrith reigned a hundred and forty-one days after him, and then Coenwulf took the kingdom.

From 797 to 892: the kings of the Mercians change and grow smaller, and the city does not change at all. A wall stone falls now and then. The priest's successors bury the same few families. From the 860s the talk at the landing is of a heathen army that does not go home, and in 874 it drives the Mercian king over the sea; the lead goes on coming down, a little less each year.

From 893 to 906: a waste city. In 893 a Danish army lies inside the walls and the English burn the corn round it. After 902 Northmen out of Dublin sit on the Wirral shore by the Lady's leave, with Irish among them, and their boats come up on the tide to sell and to look. Nobody is sure who the walls belong to.

893: A Danish army rode day and night to a waste city in Wirral which is called Legaceaster. The English could not overtake them before they were inside; they lay about the place two days, took the cattle, burned the corn or let their horses eat it, and the Danes went on into Wales.
902: The Northmen were driven out of the fort at Dublin. Hingamund, one of their leaders, was beaten off Anglesey and came to the Lady of the Mercians, who gave him land in Wirral.

From 907 to 924: the Lady's burh. The walls are mended, a new length runs down to the river, and there is a gravel road inside the west wall. A minster rises in the north-east corner with a saint brought from the south, there is a market at the old cross-roads and a mint whose pennies carry no king's head. The reeve asks every hull whose leave she came by. In 924 the town rises with the Welsh, and a king dies of putting it down.
Saint John's feast at midsummer fills the church on the cliff, and after 907 Saint Werburgh's day in the dead of winter fills the minster.
In 907 Chester was rebuilt.

910: In 907 or about this year Hingamund and his men came against the town and were beaten off. An Irish saga-history tells it with boiling ale and beehives thrown from the wall; historians call the tale over-dramatised.
918: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, died at Tamworth on the 12th of June, and her brother King Edward took Mercia.
924: The men of Chester rose with the Welsh. King Edward put them down, and died at Farndon up the Dee on the 17th of July.

From 925 to 972: the mint's great years. More moneyers strike here than in London for a while, and their pennies lie thick in Dublin and Man. Dublin skippers bring marten skins and take salt, pots and people. A church of Saint Bridget stands by the river for the Irish and the Northmen, and huts with bowed walls line the street down to the landing. About 965 a man buries his silver by the wall and does not come back.
958: King Edgar gave land to the minster of Saint Werburgh: the first sure word that the minster stands.
About 965 somebody buried a pot of some five hundred pennies with ingots and cut jewellery by the south-west corner of the walls, and never came back for it.

From 973 to 1015: king Edgar comes with his fleet and six kings swear to him; within a lifetime the tale has eight of them rowing his boat. His new coin leaves the town five moneyers where there were twenty. In 980 ships out of the north plunder the shire, and in 1000 the king's fleet goes out from here and comes back with nothing but Manx cattle.
973: King Edgar 'led all his marine force to Chester; and there came to meet him six kings; and they all covenanted with him, that they would be his allies by sea and by land.'
980: 'The county of Chester was plundered by the pirate-army of the North.'
1000: King Æthelred wasted Cumberland. His ships were to come round from Chester to meet him and could not, and harried the Isle of Man instead.

From 1016 to 1066: the earls' town. Leofric and Godgifu give to both minsters; a church of Saint Olaf goes up for the Northmen after 1030; four in ten of the moneyers have Norse or Irish names. Earl Ælfgar pays off his hired Irish fleet at the landing, Harold rides out from here against the Welsh king, and in the last winter of the story Harold's queen is brought here for safety.
1016: Edmund the ætheling and Earl Uhtred of the Northumbrians plundered Staffordshire, Shrewsbury and Chester.
1057: Earl Leofric died. He and his wife Godgifu had enriched both the minsters of the town.
1063: Earl Harold rode from Chester against Gruffudd of the Welsh at Rhuddlan and burned his hall and his ships.
No fair is recorded here before 1066 (?).
1066: The city has 487 houses, seven moneyers, twelve judges, and pays the king forty-five pounds and three timbers of marten skins a year.

pages.title: Hī
pages.hint: A monastery in Dal Riata
pages.brief: Columba's island.
pages.game:
A low green island with one hill, a mile of shallow sound between it and the pink rocks of Mull, and on its east shore the mother house of all Columba's churches: a timber church, cells, a writing house and a guest house inside a great bank and ditch. Nothing is bought or sold here and no coin is struck within three hundred sea miles. A merchant comes as the abbot's guest, with wine for the Mass, calfskin, colours, iron, salt and timber, and leaves with a blessing, sealskin, a letter, the abbot's protection in every land that honours the saint, and news that will be written down. In June 793 nobody here has yet seen a heathen sail.
The year turns on Colum Cille's feast, the ninth of June, when boats come from every house of his family, and on Adomnan's, the twenty-third of September, after the reaping on the western plain. Wednesdays and Fridays are fasts, broken for a guest. The seals pup on their islet at the back of the year, the cranes and geese come over from Ireland on the west wind, and from November to Brigit's day the Sound is often shut by weather for a week at a time.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: oats, salt salmon and otter pelts; wanted here, and so dearer: wine of Aquitaine. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: the quiet end of a long peace. Bresal is very old, the house is full, the writing house is busy and the news from Lindisfarne is a thing that happened to a daughter far away. Guests are washed, fed and asked for news. Nobody keeps a watch.
pages.known:
Columba's island. The place is now Iona. In 793 it is under Conall mac Taidg, king in Dal Riata (earlier a king among the Picts, beaten in 789).
563: Columba comes over from Ireland with twelve companions and founds his house on the island. 597: Columba dies on the ninth of June before the altar, after copying the psalter to the foot of a page and blessing the island from the little hill. His stone pillow is kept by his grave. About 634 Aidan is sent from Hi at King Oswald's asking, and Lindisfarne is founded as a daughter of this house. 697: Abbot Adomnan's law is proclaimed: the fines for killing or carrying off women, clerics and children are owed to the community of Hi. It is renewed in 727. 716: The house gives up its own reckoning of Easter and its old tonsure and takes Rome's. About 740 the record of each year's events, kept on the island since Columba's time, is carried on elsewhere. The annals of Ireland grow from it. 772: Bresal son of Segene becomes abbot, the successor of Colum Cille. He holds the island for thirty-one years. 778: Niall Frossach, who had been king of Tara, dies on the island as a pilgrim. Artgal of Connacht does the same in 791. 792: Donncoirce, king of Dal Riata, dies. After him nobody can say for sure who is king over the island's own people.

later.text: From 794 the brothers count the summer by the days nothing came out of the north.
In 794 all the islands of Britain are wasted by heathens.

From 795 to 806: the years of the sails. Plundered in 795, burned in 802, and in 806 sixty-eight dead. The church is rebuilt each time, in timber and then in stone (?); a brother sits on the hill from Easter to Michaelmas; the best books and vessels are kept packed. The house still receives guests, and wants timber, iron and hulls more than wine.
The northmen come in 795.
795: Hi is plundered for the first time. Skye and Rechru are struck the same summer.
801: Bresal dies in the thirty-first year of his abbacy. Suibne, who gave up the abbacy in 771, dies the same year.
802: Hi is burned by heathens. Abbot Connachtach, a choice scribe, dies. Cellach son of Congal follows him.
804: Kells in Ireland is given to the community of Colum Cille without a battle.
806: Sixty-eight of the community of Hi are killed by heathens. The annal does not say where on the island they died.

From 807 to 825: the house is two houses. The abbot is mostly at Kells in Ireland and the treasures cross the sea in small boats; the island keeps its graves, its crosses, a smaller company of stubborn men and, some summers, the saint's shrine. The strict clients of God set the tone under Diarmait: more fasting, fewer words. In 825 Blathmac dies for the shrine.
807: The building of the new house of Colum Cille at Kells is begun. It is finished in 814; Cellach gives up the abbacy and Diarmait, fosterling of Daigre, takes it. Cellach dies the next year.
818: Diarmait goes to Alba with the relics of Colum Cille; again in 829; and to Ireland with them in 831.

825: Blathmac son of Flann, a king's son turned monk, is killed by heathens on the island. A Frankish abbot far away by the Rhine puts it in verse: he had the shrine buried under turf, said Mass, would not tell, and was cut down.

From 826 to 878: a small company on a famous rock. The Hebrides are full of little fleets until about 840 and a careful master stays away. In 849 the relics are shared between Kells and Dunkeld; in 878 the shrine goes to Ireland. Pilgrims still come to the grave, and kings ask to lie in the graveyard.
849: The relics of Colum Cille are shared. Abbot Indrechtach brings some to Ireland; King Kenneth takes some to Dunkeld. Indrechtach is killed among the English on his way to Rome on 12 March 854.
878: The shrine of Colum Cille and his other relics are taken to Ireland in flight from the foreigners. An abbot and monks remain on the island.

From 879 to 979: quiet, poor and holy. The man who calls himself Columba's successor sits in Ireland; the island has its own head and a dozen or two of brothers (?). The lords of the sea round it are Northmen who have begun to be baptised, and their dead start to come to Oran's ground with crosses on their stones. Silver is weighed in rings and cut pieces.
927: Mael Brigte son of Tornan dies on 22 February, successor of Patrick and of Colum Cille together. He sat at Armagh, not on the island.

From 980 to 989: a hard decade. An old king of Dublin dies here in sackcloth; six years later, on Christmas night, Danes kill the abbot and fifteen elders. The next year the killers are killed. Keep south of the island in 986 and 987 unless you have a strong reason.
980: After his sons are beaten at Tara, Amlaib Cuaran, king of the foreigners of Dublin, comes to Hi in penance and dies here, this year or the next.

In 986, on Christmas night Danes plunder Hi and kill the abbot, Mael Ciarain, and fifteen elders of the house. About this time a bag of some three hundred and fifty pennies, mostly English, is hidden on the island and never fetched.
987: Three hundred and sixty of those who plundered Hi are killed.

From 990 to 1066: an island among the kings of the Isles and the earls of Orkney (?), who honour it. Norse and Irish are both spoken on the beach, a rune stone lies among the cross slabs, and English and Dublin pennies turn up in alms. The stone abbey a later age will know is not built: it is still thatch, turf, a small stone chapel and the old crosses.
1007: At Kells the great Gospel of Colum Cille is stolen by night for the sake of its shrine. It is found months later under a sod, its gold gone.
1025: Abbot Flandabra dies. Abbots are on the island before him and after him, to the end of the century.

pages.title: Duiblinn
pages.hint: A monastery among the Irish
pages.brief: A church by the black pool on the Liffey.
pages.game:
In 793 this is a church in a ring bank beside a dark pool, and a village of farmers and fishermen at a ford of hurdles a short walk up the river. There is no town, no coin, no toll and no market: a stranger from over the sea trades only as the guest of the man who keeps the church's land, who takes a gift and the first choice. A merchant comes with wine and salt for hides and wool cloaks, and comes back because somebody at the ford knows his boat.
The cattle go to the hill pastures at the start of May and come home at the start of November, when the slaughter fills the strand with hides and the food-rents fall due. The fairs are inland at the start of August, and in the heathens' years the captives come in at the leaves' fall, after the raiding. Every winter gale moves the bar in the bay, so the way in is learned again each spring.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: cattle hides, oats, salt salmon, butter and cattle; wanted here, and so dearer: Frankish wine, wine of Aquitaine, bay salt, Droitwich salt and swords. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a church in a ring bank by the pool, perhaps without an abbot since Siadal, and the ford village up the river. No coin, no toll, no market. The steward of the church's land stands for a stranger, takes a gift and first choice, and names sureties for every bargain; worth is said in cows and ounces. Each summer after that the fishermen watch the mouth of the bay.
pages.known:
A church by the black pool on the Liffey. The place is now Dublin.
785: Siadal, abbot of Duiblinn, died (the Four Masters give it under 785; it may be as late as 790). No abbot or bishop of the house is named after him. 792: Máel Ruain of Tallaght, 'bishop and soldier of Christ', died on the seventh of July. Airerán followed him.
