later.text: Rechru burns in 795 and the smoke is seen from the strand.
795: Bran Ardchenn, king of Leinster, was burned in a house with his queen by Fínsnechta, who was king after him. The same year: 'The burning of Rechru by the heathens.'
798: The heathens burned the island off Skerries, took the cattle-tribute and broke the shrine.
804: Áed son of Niall, king of Tara, wasted Leinster twice in one month.
807: Cellach, abbot of Iona, began the new house of Columba at Kells, after sixty-eight of his community were killed in 806. The church there was finished in 814.
811: The community of Tallaght stopped the fair of Tailtiu, so that neither horse nor chariot ran.
821: Howth was raided and many women were carried off.
833: Clondalkin was plundered.
Each summer after that the fishermen watch the mouth of the bay, and in 837 sixty ships come up the river.
837: Sixty ships came on the Liffey and sixty on the Boyne.

From 841 to 852: a turf bank, ships drawn up inside it, and men who mean to stay till spring. The church is theirs or empty. They have captives and church silver and want grain, wine and salt, and they weigh everything. In 849 the king of Tara plunders the fort; in 851 other Foreigners come and wreck it. Nobody here can promise a merchant next year.
The longphort comes in 841.
841: The heathens made a ship-fort at Duiblinn, and stayed the winter.
845: Swords and Finglas were raided. Turgeis was taken by Máel Sechnaill and drowned.
849: Máel Sechnaill plundered the fort. A hundred and forty ships of the king of the Foreigners came to the Liffey.
851: Dark Foreigners came to Duiblinn, beat the Fair Foreigners and wrecked the fort.

From 853 to 902: the fort has kings: Amlaíb, Ímar, and after 873 their quarrelling heirs. A king's man takes his share on the strand. Captives go out by the shipload, above all in 871; silver goes by weight in arm-rings and cut pieces; the dead are laid up the river with swords and scales. Irish kings fight the place, hire it and marry into it. In 893 it splits in two, and in 902 it is taken in a day.
853: Amlaíb, son of the king of Lochlann, came to Ireland. The Foreigners gave him hostages and the Irish gave him tribute.
863: The kings of the Foreigners searched the old tombs on the Boyne, which had never been done before.
867: Amlaíb's fort at Clondalkin was burned and a hundred of his men were killed.
871: Amlaíb and Ímar came back to the Liffey from Dumbarton, taken after four months, with two hundred ships and a great prey of English, Britons and Picts.
873: Ímar, king of the Northmen of all Ireland and Britain, died. A later telling says of a sudden horrible disease.
893: The Foreigners of the fort split into two parties.

902: The men of Leinster under Cerball and the men of Brega under Máel Finnia took the fort. The heathens were driven out, left a good number of their ships, and fled half dead to Wales, the Wirral and beyond.

From 903 to 916: empty of Northmen. Hulls rot where they were left half built, the bank slumps, and cattle graze inside it. The ford village goes on as before, and so does Tallaght. There is nothing to buy but hides and nobody to pay a toll to. Men who know say the people of the fort are on Man, in the Wirral and by the Ribble, and have not forgotten the way back.

From 917 to 979: Dyflin: fenced plots along plank paths, wattle houses with a hearth and two benches, comb-makers, smiths, shoemakers and shipwrights, and a king whose kin also sit at York. An earth bank goes round it about 950. Slaves, hides, cloaks and ships go out; wine, salt, amber, walrus tooth and silk come in. It burns in 944 and is built again on the same fence lines. Old Amlaíb Cuarán is baptised and keeps poets of both tongues.
917: Sitriuc, grandson of Ímar, came back and took the place.
919: Niall Glúndub, king of Tara, was killed fighting the Foreigners at the weir up the river.
937: Amlaíb son of Gothfrith came home from the battle in England with few ships.
944: The town was sacked and burned by the Irish.
951: The Foreigners plundered Kells and took three thousand captives, with gold, silver and cattle.

From 980 to 1013: after Tara the Irish slaves walk out free and the old king goes to Iona to die. The town pays the king of Tara: cattle, and from 989 an ounce of gold from every plot each Christmas night. Sitriuc Silkbeard strikes pennies with his name on them. Brian holds the town at New Year 1000 and burns Thor's wood. No load moves on a Sunday when an Irish king's steward is looking.

980: The Foreigners were beaten at Tara. Máel Sechnaill besieged the town three days and three nights, and every Irish slave in it was set free. Amlaíb Cuarán went to Iona in penitence and died there.
989: Máel Sechnaill besieged the town again. They had no water but the sea's. An ounce of gold from every plot was laid on them, to be paid each Christmas night for ever.
997: About this year, or two years before, King Sitriuc struck the first pennies made in Ireland, copies of King Æthelred's.
999: Brian and Máel Sechnaill beat the Foreigners and the Leinstermen at Glenn Máma in the last days of the year. Brian was in the town at New Year and burned Tomar's wood.

From 1014 to 1051: Clontarf is fought within sight of the bank and the town trades the week after. Sitriuc goes to Rome and builds a wooden church of the Holy Trinity on the height, with a bishop who looks to Canterbury. The pennies grow light and stay at home. Kings change three times in ten years. About 1042 the yard lays the keel of a sixty-oar ship.
In 1014, on Good Friday, the twenty-third of April, Brian's army fought the Foreigners and the Leinstermen at Clontarf. Brian was killed. Sitriuc stayed inside and the town was not taken.
1028: King Sitriuc went to Rome. Soon after he founded the church of the Holy Trinity, with Dúnán as its first bishop.
1029: Sitriuc's son was taken by the king of Brega. His ransom was twelve hundred cows, six score Welsh horses, sixty ounces of gold, sixty of silver and the sword of Carlus.
About 1042 a warship of sixty oars was built here of oak. She ended on the bottom of Roskilde fjord.

From 1052 to 1066: Leinster's town. Diarmait sets his son Murchad over it; the Foreigners keep their plots, their law mound and their ships, and hire both out. Harold son of Godwin wintered here and went home with crews. Man pays tribute from 1061. English exiles and Welsh kings come for fleets, and a skipper is asked whose silver he sails on.
1052: Diarmait, king of Leinster, took the town and set his son Murchad over it. That winter Harold son of Godwin had been here in exile.
1061: Murchad took tribute from the Isle of Man.

pages.title: Ripa
pages.hint: A market among the Danes
pages.brief: The Danes' oldest market town, on the Ribe river behind the Wadden: beads, combs, wine and Frisian cloth.
pages.game:
A row of narrow plots on a sand bank along a winding river, a short way in behind the tidal flats: the oldest market of the Danes, about ninety years old in 793. Bead-makers, comb-makers, bronze-casters and cattle men work the plots in summer, and Frisian boats bring them glass, wine, querns and cloth. A merchant comes for beads, combs, amber, hides and cattle, and for buyers who pay in weighed silver and ask no king's leave that anyone has written down.
The market fills from late May to the middle of August, when the plots are all taken and the bank is lined with boats; in autumn the herds come down from the heath and the cattle ground is loud. In winter only a few households stay, the river skins with ice at the edges, and no stranger's boat crosses the flats.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: rye, barley, cattle, antler combs and glass beads; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Mayen quernstones, Tating-ware jugs, glass vessels and raw glass and tesserae. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: an open market on the north bank: forty or fifty plots, booths and workshops, no ditch, no church, no hall anyone has found. Heathen. Silver goes on the scale; the old small pennies with the bearded face are still seen and are weighed like everything else. The bead-makers complain of thin eastern beads.
pages.known:
The Danes' oldest market town, on the Ribe river behind the Wadden: beads, combs, wine and Frisian cloth. The place is now Ribe. In 793 it is under Sigfred, king of the Danes.
705: The market is laid out in one act on a spread layer of sand: plots side by side at right angles to the river. A well is lined with oak felled between 704 and 710. 720: From about this year small silver pennies with a bearded facing head and a curled beast pass inside the market. Most of those ever found among the Danes are found here; that they were struck here is the common view, not a proven one. 725: A piece from the top of a human skull is cut with runes naming Ulf and Odin and High-Tyr, with a bored hole that no cord ever wore. It lies in the market layers. 790: Cheap beads from the Caliphate begin to reach the north by the eastern rivers. The bead-makers of Ripa start to fade.
