later.text: From 810 to 853: a boundary ditch now runs round the market. The king's wars with the Franks and then among his own kin pass by on the heath road; Sliesthorp grows and takes some of the eastern trade. From about 825 small coins of Sliesthorp turn up on the scale.
810: About now a ditch two or three paces wide is dug round the market and the ground behind it, some twelve hectares: a boundary and not a defence.

From 854 to 899: a boy king, and across the river a plot given to the Christians' god: a timber church, a priest, graves laid east and west. The narrow ditch gives way to a moat six or seven paces wide. Heathen and Christian trade on the same plots and bury on opposite banks.
In 854 King Horik and almost all his kin were killed in a war of kinsmen. A boy of the same name was made king.

About 857 the young King Horik gave Bishop Anskar a plot at Ripa for a church, and leave for a priest to live there: the second church among the Danes, after Sliaswic. Burghard, kinsman of both Horiks, had spoken for the bishop.
864: The pope writes to King Horik. He is not heard of again.
In 865, on the third day of February Bishop Anskar died at Bremen.
888: After Bishop Rimbert's death the church at Ripa is said to have been destroyed in a heathen turn. The claim is late.
From 900 to 947: quieter. Fewer booths, fewer foreign boats, or so it looks; the cattle still come. Whether the church stands is not certain. Gold goes into the ground on the farms round about.

From 948 to 1017: a bishop's seat in name from 948, and after the king's baptism about 965 in more than name. English pennies come home with men from the fleets after 991 and are weighed, then counted.
948: Leofdag sat as bishop of Ripa at the synod of Ingelheim on 7 June, with the bishops of Sliaswic and Aarhus: the first sees among the Danes.
965: The emperor Otto frees the Danish bishops' churches from dues; the privilege is renewed in 988.
About 1000 Odinkar the younger, a Dane of great family and wealth, became bishop of Ripa. He held the see to about 1043.

From 1018 to 1042: king Cnut's peace on both shores of the sea. Pennies are struck with Ripa's name; Bishop Odinkar, rich and well born, builds and gives. Ships go to England and Frisia and come back.
1018: From King Cnut's time pennies are struck with Ripa's name on them.
From 1043 to 1066: the Wends come as far as Ripa and are beaten on the heath. The market is busy again, the see is one of four in Jutland from 1060, and the town looks west as it always has.
In 1043 the Wends harried Jutland as far as Ripa. King Magnus met them on Lyrskov heath on Michaelmas eve and beat them.
1060: Jutland north of the Kongea is divided into four sees. Ripa is one of them.
1075: A writer at Bremen sets down that from Ripa one sails to Frisia, to England and to Saxony. (After the game's end: it shows where the town had been looking all along.)

pages.title: Sliesthorp
pages.hint: A market among the Danes
pages.brief: A market at the head of the Schlei, where the road crosses to the Eider.
pages.game:
In 793 Sliesthorp is a young market on a green field at the head of the Slie, where a ship from the eastern sea can sail a long day inland and lie in a sheltered inner water a short cart road from the rivers of the western sea. There is no wall, no coin, no church and no king's name on it yet: thatched houses along a brook, booths in summer, a dealer's pen, and the old earth wall of the Danes on the ridge behind. A merchant comes for amber, furs, combs, beads and people, sells wine, cloth, querns and (if he dares) Frankish blades, and pays and is paid in silver by weight.
The market is full from late May to the middle of August, when ships from the Svear, the Wends and Vestfold lie in the inner water and the carts go west every day; outside those weeks half the booths are bare poles. In autumn the cart road to the Treene turns to mud and the herring come into the Slie (?); in a hard winter the head of the Slie, which is shallow and half fresh, freezes over (?), and the place lives on fish, smoke and talk until the water opens.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: antler combs, glass beads, amber beads and brooches; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Mayen quernstones, Tating-ware jugs, glass vessels and antler. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a market on a green field. A dozen long thatched houses south of the brook, booths in summer, boats drawn up or lying to stakes in the inner water. No wall, no coin, no king's man with a name: gifts are given to whoever speaks for the place, silver goes on the scales, and a stranger needs a host. Asulf's pen is the biggest roof on the strand.
pages.known:
A market at the head of the Schlei, where the road crosses to the Eider. The place is now Hedeby (Haithabu). In 793 it is under Sigfred, king of the Danes.
737: The Danes fell the oaks for the North Wall of their earthwork, and about now build a barrier of log caissons across the narrows of the Slie. About 770 the first houses stand south of the brook: a trading place on a green field, without a town's fittings.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept); ARF 777, 782, 798 (Design/content/realms/denmark.json); de.wikipedia Danewerk; de.wikipedia Schlei-Seesperrwerk (tree-ring dates 737 to 740), as in the dossier [WDW; WSP]; de.wikipedia Haithabu; da.wikipedia Hedeby (the southern settlement, dug from 1959) [WDE; WDA]

later.text: From 804 to 810: Godfred's years. In 804 the Slie is full of the king's ships and the heath of his horses: fodder, ale and bread are dear. In 808 the merchants of Reric are set down on the strand with what they could carry, plots are paced out with a knotted rope, and a wall is dug and timbered across the neck with one gate and the king's man at it. Every guest owes days on the wall. In 810 the fleet goes west and the king does not grow old.

In 804 Godfred, king of the Danes, came with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom to the place called Sliesthorp, on the border of his kingdom and Saxony. He promised to meet the emperor and did not.
It grows when Godfred moves Reric's merchants here in 808.

In 808 Godfred destroyed the trading place on the shore which the Danes call Reric, which by its tolls brought his kingdom great profit, carried its merchants off, and came by ship to the harbour called Sliesthorp. He stayed some days and ordered the border closed with a wall, with one gate only, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and let in.
In 809 Thrasco, prince of the Obodrites, was killed at Reric by Godfred's men.
In 810 two hundred ships harried Frisia and took a hundred pounds of silver, and Godfred was murdered by one of his own followers. While the emperor waited on the king's threats his elephant died.

From 811 to 824: after the peace on the Eider. The Wends' plots have houses on them and children who speak Danish. Kings change and fight each other; the gate stays, and so does the toll at it. A warden keeps the border. Dirhams from the east are cut up on the scales beside Frankish pennies and arm rings.

In 811 peace was sworn on the Eider, twelve men a side: for the Danes the king's brothers Hancwin and Angandeo, Osfrid called Turdimulo, Warstein, Suomi, Urm, Osfrid son of Heiligen, Osfrid of Sconaowe, Hebbi and Aowin.
In 815 an army of Saxons and Obodrites crossed the Eider for Harald, the king who had been driven out.
817: Gluomi is named as warden of the Northmen's border.

From 825 to 849: the king's own pennies are struck here, copied from Dorestad's, letters and all, and pass by count on the strand. Horik is sole king from about 828. From 834 men in the harbour sell Dorestad cloth with the lead seal still on it, and Dorestad people, and the king says the fleets are not his. A new row of houses stands north of the brook and plank streets run down to the jetties.
About 825 the first coins of the North are struck here: light pennies copied from Dorestad's.
In 826 Harald was baptised among the Franks, and the monk Anskar went north with him.

From 850 to 872: a wooden church by the harbour and a priest's house. Merchants baptised at Dorstadt and Hamburg hear Mass openly; others take the sign of the cross and leave baptism for their deathbed. After Horik's death in 854 the count nails the door shut; then it opens again and a bell is allowed. Anskar comes and goes until he dies in 865.
About 850 King Horik gave leave for a church at the port of Sliaswic, with a house for its priest. After that the merchants of Dorstadt and Hamburg came freely and without fear.

In 854 Horik was killed in a war among his own kin. Hovi, count of the port, had the church shut, saying the gods were angry; soon the young king put him out, the church was opened, and a bell was allowed, which the heathen held unlawful.

From 873 to 899: peace with the Saxons' king: merchants cross the border freely. The town is at its busiest, the middle settlement on the brook: comb-makers, bead-makers, a glass furnace, smiths, weavers. An Englishman and a Northman from the far north meet on the jetties and each says how many days he sailed.
In 873 the kings Sigfred and Halfdan made peace with King Louis, so that merchants of either realm might cross the border and buy and sell in peace.

About 890 Ohthere of Halogaland sailed from Sciringes heal to the port the English call 'at the Heaths' in five days, and Wulfstan sailed from it to Truso in seven days and nights, under sail all the way. Both told King Alfred.

From 900 to 947: kings of a house from the Svear's land (?). Great men are buried with horses and a boat. In 934 the Saxon king beats Chnuba and takes tribute and a baptism from him. After 930 a half-ring of turf and ditch goes up round the houses, running out into the water as a row of piles.

About 900 a house from the Svear's land rules here: Olaf, and after him his sons Chnob and Gyrd (?). A great man is laid in a chamber under a boat south of the houses, with two companions and three horses.
In 934 King Henry beat the Danes' king Chnuba, made him pay tribute and take baptism.

From 948 to 982: a bishop is named for the place, at least on parchment. Harald is king and is baptised about 965. A traveller from Spain finds a great town at the far end of the world sea, eating fish and singing badly. The rampart is joined to the old wall. From 974 the emperor's men hold the border and tribute goes south.
In 948 a bishop, Hored, was named for Sliaswig. Whether he ever came is not known.

965: In the 960s Ibrahim ibn Yaqub of Tortosa walked the town: fish the main food, a few Christians with a church, a sacrifice hung on poles at the yard gate, women free to divorce, both sexes with painted eyes, and singing like the howling of dogs.
About 968 the Connection Wall joins the town's half-ring rampart (begun after 930) to the old Danes' wall.
In 974 the emperor Otto took the border and the wall. In 983 the Danes took them back.

From 983 to 1049: the Danes hold their gate again. Svein and then Cnut are kings; from 991 English pennies are everywhere, and men come home from England with more than they can spend. About 1000 warriors sit round the town and stones are raised for the dead. The rampart stands as high as four men. Big ships no longer like the shallow inner water.

About 985 a king's longship is built here, some thirty-one metres long and under three metres wide. Years later she is burnt to the waterline as a fire ship in the harbour (the year is given two ways).
About 1000 warriors sat round the town. King Svein raised a stone for Skarthi, his retainer, 'who had fared west and now fell at Hedeby'; Thorolf raised one for his partner Erik, a steersman.

From 1050 to 1066: about 1050 Harald of Norway burns the town from end to end. People build again, smaller, inside the black ring. In 1066 the Wends come and it is finished: the last families carry their gear over the Slie to the north shore.
About 1050 Harald of Norway burned the town from end to end with fire ships.
In 1066 West Slavs sacked and burned what was left, and the people moved over the Slie to Sliaswic on the north shore. The empty ring was afterwards called Oldenburg, the old fort.

pages.title: Reric
pages.hint: A market among the Obodrites
pages.brief: The Obodrites' emporium.
pages.game:
Reric is the Obodrites' market on a low reedy shore at the bottom of the Baltic, and in 793 it is near its best years: straight lanes of sunken huts, more wells than any town of its size, and Wends, Danes and Saxons selling side by side. The land is the Obodrite prince's, but the due on every cargo goes over the water to the king of the Danes. A merchant comes for wax, honey, furs, amber, horses and captives, and brings iron, whetstones, querns, glass and anything Frankish; nothing is paid in coin, everything on the scale.
There is no tide to speak of, no church and so no feast days: the year is counted by the ice in the bay, the first boats after it, the hay, the honey taken late in summer and the autumn killing of beasts. The market is a summer thing (?); in winter the Breitling freezes, the boats lie turned over on the shore and only the craftsmen stay at their pits.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: honey, captives, beeswax, rye and mead; wanted here, and so dearer: glass beads, swords and mail byrnies. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: the best years. Witzan is prince and marches with the Frankish king; the lanes are full from the first open water to the autumn killing, the smiths and bead-makers work with their doors open, and the Danish king's man takes his due at the shore without anyone raising a voice.
pages.known:
The Obodrites' emporium. The place is now Groß Strömkendorf, Wismar Bay. In 793 it is under Witzan, king of the Obodrites (rex in the Frankish annals).
735: The first settlement, about three hectares at the north end of the shore, with timber-lined wells set close together; the oldest timber was felled this year or the next. 765: In the 760s and early 770s the town moves south and is laid out afresh in a regular, chequered plan; the old northern ground becomes the grave field. 785: More wells are dug in the 780s than in any other ten years: the town is growing fast. 789: Witzan, prince of the Obodrites, marches with King Charles against the Wilzi.
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.; ARF 789 (he marches with Charles against the Wilzi), ARF 795. First named in 789: the start is a guess (?) (Design/content/realms/wends_baltic.json); Tree-ring dates of the wells, Gross Stromkendorf (Tummuscheit 2013, through de.wikipedia 'Reric'); de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Reric' (after Tummuscheit; Brather 2003); the year is the middle of the range; de.wikipedia 'Reric' (tree-ring dates); Annales regni Francorum 789 (from memory in the dossier (?)); de.wikipedia 'Drasco'

later.text: From 795 to 803: Witzan is dead at the Elbe and Thrasco rules. After the Sventana field in 798 his riders sell Saxon spoil and Saxon captives on the grass above the shore, and every Frank is asked, quietly, about blades.
795: Witzan is killed by Saxons while crossing the Elbe at Hliuni to join the king. Thrasco follows him as prince.
798: Thrasco, with the king's envoy Eburis beside him, beats the Saxons from beyond the Elbe on the Sventana field.

From 804 to 807: the Obodrites have been given the Saxons' land beyond the Elbe and want ploughshares, seed and iron for it. Godfred has shown his fleet at Sliesthorp; boats from the Danish islands are counted as they come into the bay. From 805 the emperor's law shuts the land road to Frankish merchants, so more of them come by sea. New wells go down in 806.
804: The emperor empties the Saxon land beyond the Elbe and gives it to the Obodrites. The same summer Godfred, king of the Danes, comes to Sliesthorp with his fleet and all his horsemen.
805: By the emperor's order merchants going to the Slavs may go only as far as the named border posts on the Elbe road, and may carry no arms or mail for sale.
806: New wells are dug in the town.

From 808: until the hay is in, an uneasy market. Then the king's ships fill the bay, the strongholds inland are stormed, Godelaib hangs and Thrasco is gone. The booths are pulled down, the merchants are put aboard with what they can carry, and the fleet sails for Sliesthorp. Craftsmen with nothing a king wants are left standing among the pits.
Godfred burns it and takes its merchants to Sliesthorp in 808.
As a trading place it ends about 808.

808: Godfred crosses with fleet and army, the Wilzi with him, and storms Obodrite strongholds at the cost of his nephew Reginold and many chief men. Thrasco flees; Duke Godelaib is taken by a trick and hanged; two thirds of the Obodrites pay tribute. Before he goes home the king destroys the emporium 'which in the Danes' tongue was called Reric, and which by the payment of dues brought great profit to his kingdom', carries off its merchants and sails to Sliesthorp.

From 809 to 811: a third of a town. Those who hid or were not worth taking roof a few pits again and dig a well; a boat or two calls. Thrasco comes back in 809 and is killed here before the year is out. The last timber is cut in 811, and then the people go inland.

809: A well is dug: people are living here again. Godfred sends word to the emperor by merchants; the talks at Badenfliot come to nothing. Thrasco, with Saxon help, wastes the Wilzi's land, and is then killed 'by guile, in the emporium of Reric, by Godfred's men'.
810: Godfred is killed by one of his own following. Sclaomir rules the Obodrites.
811: The last dated timber of the town is felled. Nothing is built after it.

From 812 to 928: an empty shore. Reeds, low hummocks where the huts were, well shafts fallen in and dangerous to cattle, the grave field going under grass. Fishers from the villages inland draw their boats up here and do not stay the night.
844: Louis the German kills Goztomuizli, king of the Obodrites, and shares the people among chiefs. The bay has no market that any text names.

From 929 to 1066: the Obodrites' strength is at the great fort inland now, and their markets are elsewhere on the coast. Nobody on the shore can say what stood here or what it was called; the Danes still have the word, and no place to put it.
929: Between this year and 945 the great rampart of the Mecklenburg is built, half a day inland (?); about 965 a traveller from Tortosa calls it Nakon's fort.
983: The Wends rise against the Saxons and their bishops; the churches in their land burn.
1066: The Christian prince Gottschalk is killed at Lenzen on the seventh day of June and the Obodrites go back to their own gods.

pages.title: Skíringssalr
pages.hint: A market in Vestfold
pages.brief: In 793 there is no town here: a chieftain's hall on a height, a thing heath, a holy lake, and below them a sheltered bay behind an island where boats are drawn up and a few tents stand in summer.
pages.game:
In 793 there is no town here: a chieftain's hall on a height, a thing heath, a holy lake, and below them a sheltered bay behind an island where boats are drawn up and a few tents stand in summer. A merchant comes for whetstones, soapstone pots, iron and the far north's furs, tooth and hide rope, and brings wine, glass, pots, grain and blades; silver is weighed here, never counted.
The market is full from the end of May to the end of July; the ships of the far north come after midsummer, a month along the land. Iron and hones come down from the valleys on the last snow. The tide is slight (?), the winter bay may freeze (?), and outside the summer weeks a stranger finds a few households, a forge and an ale bench.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: whetstones, soapstone pots, bar iron, oak timber and pine masts; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, bay salt, glass vessels, swords and wheat. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a landing, not a town. The hall on the height, smoke from four or five farms, boats on the grass, and in the summer weeks a row of tents where men of the Vik, a few Danes and now and then a Frisian lay goods on cloths. The chief takes a gift and gives his protection. Nothing is built to last.
pages.known:
The place is now Kaupang. It has been a trading place since about 780.
760: The oldest graves are laid on the rock by the harbour (Bikjholberget). The hall on the height at Huseby is built about this time.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/skiringssal.md (6 Oct 2026), and through it:; Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal (after Skre 2007); English Wikipedia, Skiringssal

later.text: From 800 to 812: the shore is pegged out in plots with lanes between, posts are driven for a jetty, and the first small houses go up with their doors to the sea. Casters and bead-makers come from the Danish markets. People say the king of the Danes wished it; the chief says he did.
About 800 a market is laid out along the shore in fenced plots, most likely at a Danish king's bidding, and for four generations it is the one town of the North Way.
Vestfold's market town (from about 800, (?) earlier): Ohthere sails here from Hålogaland.

800: A market is founded on the shore below the hall. The first buildings stand between 800 and 810, on plots laid out with fixed lanes. Who ordered it is not recorded; Dagfinn Skre holds that a Danish king did.
803: Posts are felled for the shore works: the oldest tree-ring date in the town.
808: Godfred, king of the Danes, moves the merchants of Reric to Sliesthorp, the next market south, five days' sail away.

From 813: the summer of the Danish host. Two kings and their ships lie in the fjord to make Vestfold's chiefs obey; the market is shut, cattle are driven inland, and a merchant's hull is something an army can use.

In 813 the kings of the Danes, Harald and Reginfrid, went with a host to Westarfolda, the furthest part of their realm to the north-west, because its princes and people would not obey them. It is the first time Vestfold is written down.
813: While the two kings were away in the north, the sons of Godfred came back from the Svear, and before winter drove both kings out of the Danish kingdom.

From 814 to 853: the town at its height: four to six hundred people the year round, six wells, forges, moulds drying, pots from the Rhine in every house. The Danish kings are over the Vik in name. In the 830s a Frisian household settles; in 843 church silver from the Loire is sold between the booths.
834: A great lady is laid in a ship under a mound further up the Vestfold coast (Oseberg), with her household goods about her.
843: Men of Vestfold storm Nantes on Saint John's day. What they bring home is on the market here in the autumn.
850: The latest house floors that survive the plough are of about this time. A Frisian trading household lives in one of the plots.

From 854 to 899: the Danish kingship breaks and Vestfold is its own master. Barter gives way to weighed silver: cut dirhams, pennies, rings, and lead weights in every purse. Men of the far north come each summer with tooth, rope and furs; about 890 one of them is Ohthere.
890: Ohthere of Halogaland tells King Alfred of the port called Sciringes heal: a month's sail south of his home, and five days from there to Hedeby.

From 900 to 930: the hall on the height stands empty and the bay grows shallow. Two houses fewer each summer. The young men are in England, Ireland and the islands. The whetstones still come down, and the mounds on the north road are still added to.
900: The hall at Huseby goes out of use.
930: The town is given up, whether for the shoaling bay or the ebb of Danish power is argued. Some trade goes on for a generation.
From 931 to 960: a summer market on old house floors. Grass in the lanes, the jetties rotting, a few tents and a lawman who still tries the weights. The ships that come are small and come for hones.
As a trading place it ends about 960.
960: The last trade at Skiringssal. After this the shore is a farm's pasture.

From 961 to 1066: pasture. The whetstones go out through other inlets, and in 998 a ship full of them is lost in the next bay. A big house stands at Huseby again in the eleventh century. Nobody on the coast can say for certain where the market was.
998: A cargo ship of oak with pine top strakes, twenty or more metres long, is built; she sinks in the next inlet east with whetstones of Eidsborg aboard, in sight of the dead town.

pages.title: Birka
pages.hint: A market among the Svear
pages.brief: The Svear's market town on an island in the bay (the sea came in further then).
pages.game:
The one market town of the Svear: a few hundred people on a small island of birch and rock in a bay that is an arm of the sea, a generation old in 793, heathen, with no coin, no church and no wall worth the name. A merchant comes for furs in their winter coat, bar iron, antler combs and wax, and brings glass, wine, cloth and blades, which are weighed against silver on a folding scale and never counted. The king's hall is on the next island; here his prefect keeps the jetties, and nothing great is settled without the thing and the lots.
The bay has no tide and freezes from early winter to about Easter: then the iron comes in on sledges from the forest country, the fur dealers do their business on the ice, and men and horses go about on bone skates and crampons. Ships come from the going of the ice to the autumn storms, and the town is fullest between late May and the middle of the harvest moon, when the thing meets if the king is there.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: squirrel pelts, marten, beaver pelts, bar iron and battle axes; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Frisian cloth, silk, silk ribbon and trim and Tating-ware jugs. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a young heathen craft town. Small sheds packed inside a low inner bank, plank-laid lanes, stone-footed jetties, a slight fort on the rock. The far trade runs south and west, to Dorestad. No priest, no coin, no named king.
pages.known:
The Svear's market town on an island in the bay (the sea came in further then). The place is now Björkö, Mälaren. It has been a trading place since about 750.
750: The town is laid out on the west shore of the birch island, about this year or as late as 790. Which king of the Svear founded it is not known. 793: A young craft town under a king whose name no one wrote down: bronze-casters, comb-makers and bead-makers in small sheds by the shore, strangers lodging in summer, no priest and no coin.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.; en.wikipedia and sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (about 750); B. Magnus, Birka (Riksantikvarieämbetet 1999) and de.wikipedia 'Birka und Hovgården' (about 790); dossier 1; Magnus 1999; sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (the radar survey of 2018: the first town packed with small workshops); dossier 1, 2

later.text: The first white silver of the east turns up in traders' bags from about 800.
800: From about this year silver coins of the caliphs come down from the east and are cut and weighed like any silver (?).

From 829 to 844: the years of the first mission. King Björn lets Anskar preach; Herigar the prefect is baptised and has a church on his own land; from about 832 there is a bishop, Gautbert. A handful of Christians, most of them captives and traders baptised at Dorestad, in a town that still asks the lots. Hedeby's new pennies arrive and are weighed like any silver.

829: Envoys of the Svear ask Emperor Louis for priests. The monk Anskar sails with merchants; pirates take the ships and nearly forty books, and he comes to Birka on foot and by boat across the waters between. King Björn receives him.
830: Herigar, prefect of the town and a counsellor of the king, is baptised and builds a church on his own family land. Christian captives in the town are glad of a priest.
831: After a year and a half Anskar goes home with a letter from King Björn to the emperor, written 'in characters fashioned after the Swedish custom'.
About 832 Bishop Gautbert comes to the Svear and begins a church.

From 845 to 851: the bishop is driven out and his kinsman killed. No priest for nearly seven years. Herigar keeps his faith alone and is jeered at for it at the thing. An exiled king comes with Danish ships and is bought off with a hundred pounds of silver. A bad time to be known as a Christian, and a good one to be known as a man with a ship.
About 845 a crowd breaks into the bishop's house, 'not by command of the king', kills his kinsman Nithard, and binds Gautbert and drives him out. For nearly seven years there is no priest.

847: Between 845 and 851 the exiled king Anund comes with twenty-one Danish ships and eleven of his own while the king is away. The town offers a hundred pounds of silver; the Danes say each merchant in the place has more. The lots send the Danes off to a Slav town, and Anund gives the silver back.
About 851 the hermit priest Ardgar comes. Herigar dies; the old widow Frideburg dies, having kept bought wine three years for her last hour; Ardgar goes home.

From 852 to 865: Anskar's second visit: King Olof, the lots and two things allow a priest and a hall of prayer. Herigar and Frideburg are dead; Catla carries her mother's alms south. The host comes home from Courland with ransom. From 863 Dorestad is gone, and the western trade goes by the Danes' town on the Schlei.
852: Anskar comes a second time, nearly twenty days in a ship. King Olof says the matter rests with the whole people; the lots and two things say yes, and the king grants a plot for a hall of prayer.
854: King Olof's Svear burn Seeburg in Courland and take ransom at Apulia, five days inland. After the lots there favoured Christ, some of the host keep a forty days' fast from meat.
About 855 Catla, Frideburg's daughter, carries her mother's wealth to Dorestad for the poor, because 'there are here but few poor'.
856: Before this year the abbot of Fulda is said to send two bells to the mission (?).
865: Anskar dies on the third day of February. The priests Erimbert, Ansfrid and Rimbert have served here in turn; after them the mission lapses.

From 866 to 899: no priest again, and nobody asks for one. The trade has turned east: furs, wax and people out by Aldeigjuborg, silver by the bagful back. Weights made to the eastern standard are in every booth. Larger houses begin to stand among the sheds.

From 900 to 959: the best years. The town's rampart is raised with timber on top and the fort is rebuilt; some fifty armed men, horse and foot, keep a hall on the slope below it, dressed in coats of eastern cut. Silk, carnelian and silver in the graves. In 936 a foreign archbishop dies here and is buried.
910: Early in the 900s the town's rampart is enlarged with timber on top, and more than fifty graves of about 900 are built into it.
936: Archbishop Unni of Hamburg-Bremen dies here on the seventeenth day of September, when Ring is king. His body is buried here and his head is taken to Bremen.

945: About 940 to 950 a woman is buried seated in a timber chamber by the fighting men's hall, with sword, axe, twenty-five arrows, two horses, three weights, three dice and twenty-eight gaming pieces.

From 960 to 975: the eastern silver thins and worsens. The land has risen, the southern sound shoals, and plots stand empty. Household by household the people load their boats and go. No enemy burns the town; the fort burns about the time the last of them leave.
960: The latest coins found in the town are of about this year.
As a trading place it ends about 975.
975: About 970 to 975 the people leave. There is no sign of sack or fire in the town; the fort burns about then. Why they left is not known.

From 976 to 1066: grass over black soil, the grave mounds, and the bank. Ships pass on their way to Sigtuna and do not stop. On the next island the king's estate goes on; about 1070 its steward Tolir has a stone cut by the harbour there. A bishop looks for the archbishop's grave in the 1060s and does not find it.
980: About now a king's town, Sigtuna, is laid out further up the bay.
1065: In the 1060s Bishop Adalvard of Sigtuna visits the place and finds 'hardly a vestige' of the town, and not Unni's grave.

pages.title: Helgö
pages.hint: A market among the Svear
pages.brief: An older craft and trading place, giving way to Birka.
pages.game:
A rocky, wooded island in the bay of the Svear, a short row east of Birka, that was a place of goldsmiths and bronze-casters for three hundred years and is now one farm with a long memory. A merchant comes for a night's shelter on the way in to Birka, for barley, cheese and a little bar iron, and for the last caster's weights. He stays for what hangs in the old hall, which came from further away than anyone on the island can say.
The bay has no tide and freezes every winter: from the first hard frost until the ice goes, nothing floats and everything is drawn by sledge. Ships pass from the going of the ice to the autumn storms, most of them without stopping; midsummer and the autumn slaughter are the two times the hall is full.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: squirrel pelts, marten, beaver pelts, bar iron and battle axes; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Frisian cloth, silk, silk ribbon and trim and Tating-ware jugs. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: one farm and a half. The old man Ingemund still keeps the long hall and feasts in it twice a year; his son's widow runs the fields, the cows and the boat. One hearth is still lit in the casters' terraces, for mending kettles and pouring weights. Ships for Birka pass every day of the summer, and a few put in for the night.
pages.known:
An older craft and trading place, giving way to Birka. The place is now Helgö.
200: People settle on the island; a fort is kept on its height until about 500. 400: Goldsmiths and bronze-casters work here from the 400s. The broken clay moulds for brooches, buttons and pins lie in tens of thousands, the largest such find in the north (the count is from memory (?)). 650: The fine bronze-casting stops in the 600s, and after that the island 'took on the character of an ordinary farm'. 750: A market begins on Björkö, a short row to the west, and takes the trade of the bay. 793: The island is a farm with old workshops gone cold. No ruler is named for it and no text of the time mentions it.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/helgo.md (the research this file is built on; its doubts are kept, marked (?)); sv.wikipedia 'Helgö' (citing Stockholms läns museum); dossier 1, 2; sv.wikipedia and no.wikipedia 'Helgö'; W. Holmqvist, Excavations at Helgö (not opened (?)); dossier 2; en.wikipedia 'Gullgubber'; de.wikipedia 'Helgö (Mälaren)'; dossier 2; sv.wikipedia 'Helgö'; da.wikipedia 'Helgö'; dossier 1; sv.wikipedia 'Helgö'; en.wikipedia 'Birka'; dossier 5; sv.wikipedia 'Helgö'; dossier 1, 3, 5

later.text: From 797 to 800: quieter each year. The hall roof leaks unless someone has paid for bark and turf. The caster talks of Birka; the farm wife has already been to look at a plot there. Fewer boats put in, and those that do are asked to stay for a meal so that the benches are not empty. After the old man's death in 799 the feasts stop unless the merchant has made them his business.
As a trading place it ends about 800.

550: Gold-foil figures, stamped leaves of gold one or two centimetres across, often a man and a woman face to face, are laid down in the north between about 550 and 800, some of them in the hall on this island (26 there is from memory (?)).
800: The game's table ends the landing here: ships no longer call. People go on living on the island into the 800s, and someone still brings treasures home.

From 801 to 900: no landing for a trading ship: the island is a farm seen from the water on the way to Birka, smoke from one roof, cattle on the shore meadow. People still live here and still bring far things home: in these years the crook of an Irish staff lies in one of the houses, and nobody has written down how it came.
829: Anskar comes to Birka by ship and on foot. The island he passes on the way is not mentioned.

From 901 to 975: the terraces are grass and hazel. Birka's ships pass close under the height in the years of the eastern silver; a herdsman may wave. Nobody on the water knows the island was ever anything but pasture, though its name is still the holy island.
975: Birka is given up; in the next years Sigtuna takes its place. The settlement on the holy island has left no traces for a long time.

From 976 to 1066: Birka is empty and the bay's trade goes north to Sigtuna. The land has risen, the old beach is a meadow, the sounds to the sea are narrower. On the island sheep graze over the hall floor, and the gold is under the turf.

pages.title: Uppsalir
pages.hint: A king's seat among the Svear
pages.brief: The Svear kings' seat and temple, up the Fyris river.
pages.game:
Uppsalir is not a town. It is the Svear kings' estate, their holy place and the place of the great thing: a ridge with three huge mounds, a hall on a built-up terrace, a low flat mound where the law is said, and graves as far as a man can see, among farms. No quay, no mint and no toll are recorded: a boat is left where the river gives out in the wet meadows and the goods go up on backs, carts or sledges. A merchant comes to sell wine, glass, cloth, salt and blades to a king's household, to buy iron and furs when the whole people meet in late winter, and because what the thing decides here binds Birka.
The bay is ice from early winter until about April and no ship moves, but in late winter, while the ice still bears, the Svear come by sledge to the thing, the market and the offering to the women who watch over the kin (LATER: Snorri). In spring the river floods the plain; ships go out in May and are home by autumn; Yule is kept at midwinter, and about the spring equinox of every ninth year, Adam of Bremen says, comes the great feast that nobody is excused.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: squirrel pelts, marten, beaver pelts, bar iron and battle axes; wanted here, and so dearer: Rhenish wine, Frisian cloth, silk, silk ribbon and trim and Tating-ware jugs. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: the kings' estate at its oldest: three mounds on the ridge; no year is known, sunk houses of weavers and smiths, farms, and graves in every direction. Whose hall it is no writer says: people here say 'the king'. Heathen, no coin: silver is weighed. The market is at Birka; here there are dues, gifts and, in late winter, the whole people.
pages.known:
The Svear kings' seat and temple, up the Fyris river. The place is now Gamla Uppsala.
575: Between about 550 and 625 three great mounds are raised on the ridge, each over a burning: seven to eleven metres high and fifty-five to seventy across. In 793 they are some two hundred years old and nobody can prove whose they are. 600: About this time a hall fifty to sixty metres long is built on a terrace of piled clay, with doors three metres wide and iron spirals laid in the post holes, and a row of tall posts is set across the plain, a hundred and forty-four of them in a line a kilometre long. 793: Nothing is written of Uppsalir this year or any year near it. The mounds are old. The great hall stands, or has just gone.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/uppsalir.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on. Its warnings are kept: no golden temple drawn, no number of victims given as fact, no king's name for 793, no year fixed for the hall's burning except as the game's switch, Bjorn, Olaf, Anund and Anskar not placed here, and the words Disting, Fyris and Uppsala od not put in any mouth.; sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala (dossier, section 2). The names Aun, Egil and Adils are modern labels.; sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala. The hall's date is from memory of Ljungkvist's digs (?); the posts are dated to the mid 400s or to about 600.; dossier, section 5: no text written between 793 and 1066 by anyone who stood here survives

later.text: The kings' estate at its oldest: three mounds on the ridge, a hall two hundred years old on its clay terrace (the game lets it stand until about 800).
About 800 (?) the great hall on the terrace burns, so hot that the clay of its walls is fired to brick. Those who dug it read the fire as set on purpose.

From 801 to 828: the terrace is burnt clay and the household eats in a lesser house beside it. Why the old hall was fired nobody tells a stranger. The first coins of the caliphs come up from the east and are weighed like any silver. The sons of a dead Danish king live somewhere among the Svear until 813, and then go home to take his kingdom.
813: The sons of Godfred, king of the Danes, come home from exile among the Svear and take the Danish kingdom. Where among the Svear they had lived is not written.

From 829 to 865: the years the Franks write about, though they write of Birka. Word comes up the river of a monk who preaches there by the king's leave, of a bishop driven out about 845 and not by the king's order, of an exiled king with Danish ships and a hundred pounds of silver paid. In 852 the lots and two things say the new god may be preached. At Uppsalir the feasts are kept as before.
829: The monk Anskar comes to Birka and King Bjorn lets him preach. The Svear had sent to the emperor to ask for priests. Uppsalir is not named.

About 847 Anund, a king of the Svear driven out, comes against Birka with Danish ships. The town buys peace with a hundred pounds of silver, and the lots send the Danes away to rob a town of the Slavs.

852: King Olaf puts Anskar's request to the lots and then to the thing at Birka, and to a second thing in another part of his kingdom. Both say yes. A man says the gods have offered to take the dead King Eric among them if the people want more gods.

From 866 to 974: the mission lapses and nobody here misses it. Silver comes from the east in a flood: weights are made to the caliphs' measure and even farmers carry scales. The great are laid unburnt in boats on the hill upriver and by the estate. From 871 the king's skald keeps the first stick of a chain of riddles that ends in the ground on Gotland. About 950 the silver is at its height; after it thins.
871: After this year a Gotland farmer buries sixty-seven kilograms of silver under his floor. From about this time weights made to the measure of the caliphs' coin are common among the Svear.
936: Archbishop Unni of Bremen dies at Birka on the seventeenth day of September. The mission he came to raise up lapses again.

From 975 to 994: Birka is empty and the land goes on rising: the plain is drier each lifetime and boats stop lower down. About 980 the king lays out Sigtuna on the lake, a town of plots, and a merchant now deals there with a host. About 985 a fleet comes up the river and is beaten on the plain; the dead lie where they fell for a season and the ravens are fat.
975: Birka is empty by about this year. About 980 a king's town of measured plots, Sigtuna, is laid out on the water a day's row south of Uppsalir.

About 985 King Eric beats his brother's son Styrbjorn and a fleet of Danes on the wet plain below Uppsalir. A stone in Skane says of a dead Dane that he did not flee at Uppsala. An Icelander, Thorvald Hjaltason, makes verses on the fight and the king pays him.

From 995 to 1021: king Olof strikes pennies at Sigtuna with his own name on them, cut by an Englishman, and for the first time a price here can be counted. He is baptised about 1008, far to the south-west, and may force nobody. Men come home from England with tribute silver, and stones with crosses begin to stand by the roads. The feasts at Uppsalir are kept.
About 995 Olof, Eric's son, is king, and English moneyers strike pennies with his name at Sigtuna: the first coin of the Svear.
About 1008 (?) King Olof is baptised, in the land of the western Gotar and not here. The Svear keep their feasts.
1015: In the early years of this century Sigvid, who had been to England, raises a stone at Uppsalir for his father Vedjarf.

From 1022 to 1066: kings Anund, Emund and Stenkil. The mint stops about 1030 and the scales come out again. A cross and a hammer hang on one neck and nobody mocks either. In the 1060s a bishop sits at Sigtuna and wants fire at Uppsalir; the king forbids it. In a ninth year a Christian still pays to stay away. In 1066 Stenkil dies and the land is at odds with itself.
About 1030 the mint at Sigtuna stops. The Svear go back to the scales.
1041: Ingvar's fleet is lost in the east. Twenty-six stones round the bay remember men who went with him.

About 1062 Adalvard, bishop at Sigtuna, and Egino, bishop in Skane, mean to close or burn the holy place at Uppsalir. King Stenkil forbids it: they would be killed and he driven out. Adalvard has to leave for the western Gotar.
1066: King Stenkil dies. Two men named Eric fight for the kingdom and both are killed, and the bishops stay away.

pages.title: Paviken
pages.hint: A market on Gotland
pages.brief: A Gotland harbour market of shipwrights and smiths.
pages.game:
A beach harbour on the east shore of a still lagoon on the west coast of Gotland, reached from the sea by one narrow strait: boats drawn up on shingle, hearths where beads, bronze and silver are worked, and men mending hulls with iron rivets. The island has no king, no town and no toll man; the farmers behind the beach are its merchants, and a stranger pays nobody but the farmer whose shore he lies on. A merchant comes for beads, combs, cast bronze and silver rings, for a boat mended or a new one laid down, and to learn how silver is weighed, because here no coin has a name.
The lagoon has no tide and freezes in winter, so nothing floats from the hard frosts until the ice goes. Boats go out when the water opens and the east-farers are away all summer; the silver they bring comes home between midsummer and the first frost, and that is when the weighing shore is busiest. No fair or feast of the harbour's own is recorded.
Wanted here, and so dearer: bay salt and carnelian and crystal beads. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a young harbour. Eight or ten boats on the shingle in summer, a walled yard where glass is melted for beads, hearths on a floor of laid stones, and hulls propped on the beach with men under them clenching rivets. Silver is rings, bars and old brooches cut to the weight; nobody here has yet seen a white coin with writing all round it.
pages.known:
A Gotland harbour market of shipwrights and smiths. The place is now Västergarn, Gotland.
750: A harbour and working ground is begun in the 700s on the east shore of the lagoon, where the stream runs in. One posthole of a gravel-floored shelter on the beach is of this century. 793: The harbour is one or two generations old: beads, bronze and boat-mending. No lord, reeve or toll man is named for it in any text, then or later.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below); sv.wikipedia 'Paviken' (after P. Lundström); Länsstyrelsen i Gotlands län, 'Paviken' (archived 2011); Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 1, 2, 5 (the year 750 stands for 'the 700s'); dossier 1, 5; Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'

later.text: From 800 to 869: the east-farers come home each year between midsummer and the first frost with thin white coins, whole and cut in halves and quarters. The smith melts some into bars; most of it goes inland and is not seen again. A stone-walled store stands between the working ground and the southern graves. More boats, more scales, and the same silence about what a farm holds.
800: From about this time the Saracens' silver reaches the Baltic and Gotland. Whole and cut pieces of it lie in Paviken's workshop ground.

From 870 to 899: the best-off farms have more silver than they can use, and it lies under floors. Weights cut to the eastern coin's standard are common on the shore. Men from the Svear's side come to talk of a yearly payment and free passage; the beach speaks of it for years and nobody says who agreed. Strangers say the island belongs to the Svear. No Gotlander says so.
871: After this year sixty-seven kilograms of silver, in two lots, are laid under the floor of a farm building at Spillings in the north-east of the island, and never fetched.
890: Wulfstan tells King Alfred that Blekinge, Möre, Öland and Gotland belong to the Svear. It is the only dated word of the time on who holds the island.

895: Before the end of this century, by a modern guess, Avair Strabain of Alva makes the Gotlanders' agreement with the king of the Svear: sixty marks of silver a year, forty to the king and twenty to the jarl, and the Gotlanders go free of toll in the Svear's lands. He is not known ever to have stood on this beach.

From 900 to 995: the flood of silver, then its thinning. Until about the middle of the century every boat from the east rides low; after it the coins are fewer and worse, and the smith nicks each one. Arm rings are made to a weight, a hand's worth of silver that can be worn. The lagoon is a little shallower every lifetime, and the old men say so.
950: A silver arm ring, a hammer of Thor and a bronze pendant of the 900s or 1000s are lost in the northern working ground.

From 996 to 1007: bad years on the water. A jarl from Norway robs ships off the island two summers running, and a boy king takes tribute of it. Boats are hauled higher and watched at night. No white coin has come from the east in years: what comes now is the emperor's pennies and the English king's, weighed like everything else.
996: Jarl Eirik of Lade robs ships off Gotland this year and the next.

1000: About now, if the usual date holds, a half-ring wall a thousand paces long is raised at Västergarn, on the seaward side of the lagoon's outlet. Its date is not settled, and the houses dug inside it are later.
About 1007 the boy Olaf Haraldsson of Norway takes tribute of the island.

From 1008 to 1049: the harbour is moving. Timber quays stand at the outlet, where laden boats can still lie, and a row of piles shuts the old entrance to all but those who know the gap. Across the outlet, earth is being heaped into a long curved bank. A few men come home baptised and a few bring a priest; the smith casts hammers and crosses from one stone. The old beach is for small boats and mending.
1008: Timber quays and jetties and a stone facing are built at the lagoon's outlet; the trees were felled this year. A spring flood later wrecks them.
1015: In the early 1000s a row of piles is driven across the entrance to the lagoon and closes it.
1029: Olaf Haraldsson lies at Akergarn in the north-east of the island on his way east. It is a long way from this lagoon.
1035: An English penny of the 1030s, pierced and worn as a pendant, is lost at Västergarn.

From 1050 to 1066: the lagoon is nearly a lake: reeds where boats were hauled, the strait a ditch a boy can wade. A few hearths still burn for beads and rivets, and the dead are still carried to the grave fields, but silver from abroad is scarce and the weighing is done on the seaward shore, behind the bank at Västergarn. A skipper who knew the old water would not find his way in.

1050: By about now the lagoon is too shallow for laden boats: the land has risen and the stream has silted it. What trade is left is said to move to the Västergarn shore, though the finds there are thin for these years.

pages.title: Áhús
pages.hint: A market among the Danes
pages.brief: A trading place at the Helge river mouth in Skåne.
pages.game:
In 793 this is a town of craftsmen on the north bank of the Holy River, a short way up from the sea: about a hundred fenced plots on sand, and on nearly every one somebody cuts combs, casts brooches, works amber, forges knives or spins thread finer than you have seen. No king's man meets you and no coin is taken at its face: silver is weighed, nicked and cut. A merchant comes for whole sets of fine dress, combs, locked chests and knives, and brings antler, raw amber, scrap bronze, silver and beads.
The town is fullest in winter: many craftsmen go away with the ships from the first day of summer to the winter nights and work the markets of the coast, and come home to their own hearths when the boats are drawn up. Herring comes to the bay in autumn and is cheap by the winter nights; ice lies along the shore after Yule (a guess), and the river runs brown into the bay all year.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: salt herring. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: the craft town at its fullest. Rows of fenced plots along the river with open lanes between, a low workshop hut dug into the sand on each, smoke from casters' and smiths' hearths, boats drawn up on the bank and traders sleeping aboard them. No king's officer, no toll that anyone can name, no coin taken by count. In winter every hearth is lit; in summer a third of the men are away at other markets.
pages.known:
A trading place at the Helge river mouth in Skåne. The place is now Åhus. In 793 it is under Sigfred, king of the Danes.
About 700 a market begins on the south bank of the river, a few hundred paces upstream: used for short spells, with shelters only. Beads are made there on a great scale, with bronze casting, comb-making and smithing. With Ribe it is the earliest such place in the north. About 750 the town on the north bank begins, in a strip of plots along the river. Within a generation it doubles inland. The bead-makers stop: beads from the west and from the Saracens' lands come in by the thousand, unstrung, cheaper than they can be made. 793: The town is at or near its full size: over twelve hectares, about a hundred plots of about 25 by 20 metres, five hundred to a thousand people, several hundred of them craftsmen who work for the whole coast.
pages.source: J. Callmer, 'North-European trading centres and the Early Medieval craftsman. Craftsmen at Åhus, north-eastern Scania, Sweden ca. AD 750-850+', in Central Places in the Migration and Merovingian Periods, Uppåkrastudier 6 (Lund 2002), 125-157. https://www.uppakra.lu.se/fileadmin/_migrated/content_uploads/6._Central_Places_in_the_Migration_and_Merovingian_Periods.pdf (read in full by the dossier's writer; everything about the town of 793 rests on it); ARF 777, 782, 798 (Design/content/realms/denmark.json); J. Callmer, 'North-European trading centres and the Early Medieval craftsman', Uppåkrastudier 6 (Lund 2002), 125-157 (Åhus I); Callmer 2002 (Åhus II, Transval); Callmer 2002

later.text: 829: Anskar, sailing for Birka, is robbed by pirates at sea of nearly forty books and the emperor's gifts. Where the books went is not recorded; the game lets what is left of them come ashore here or on Gotland.

From 830 to 859: the town thins. Some plots stand empty and their fences are burnt; the casters still pour brooches of the new fashion, and dirhams are common enough to be cut without comment. Families talk of moving. A stranger notices that the lanes are wider than the traffic needs.

850: In the second half of this century the town is given up, probably moved a short way; the ground is ploughed from then on. Brooches of a ninth-century kind were still being cast here before the end.

From 860 to 989: the town is gone and ploughed over. What is left is a landing at the river mouth among farms: herring in autumn, cattle, a boat or two for hire, a ship on the Baltic road putting in for water and news. Skåne answers to the Danish king when there is one strong enough to ask. What the place sells is the game's guess (?): no market is known here in these years.
885: About 880 to 890 Wulfstan sails from Haddeby to Truso with Skåne on his left hand: 'Langland, Laaland, Falster and Sconey, on his left, and all these lands belong to Denmark.'
950: About the middle of this century Skåne comes firmly under the Danish king, Harald Gorm's son.

From 990 to 1044: the king's Skåne. Lund is founded and priests come through; some farms have a cross on the wall and a hammer under the shirt. King's coin is known but is still weighed. In 1025 or 1026 the bay is full of fleets for a summer and no cargo passes.
About 990 King Sven founds Lund, two days' ride to the south-west. The first churches in Skåne are of these years.

1025: 'This year went King Knute to Denmark with a fleet to the holm by the holy river; where against him came Ulf and Eglaf, with a very large force both by land and sea, from Sweden. There were very many men lost on the side of King Knute, both of Danish and English; and the Swedes had possession of the field of battle.' Other accounts put it in 1026, name Olaf of Norway and Anund of the Svear as his enemies, and say Knute won. Whether it was this river or one in Uppland is disputed.

From 1045 to 1066: a house of stone stands by the river mouth, the first anyone here has seen, and whoever sits in it takes a share of what is landed. Herring boats crowd the beach in autumn. The old town is a field where the plough turns up bits of antler and green bronze.
1050: About the middle of this century a house of stone is built by the river mouth, about twenty metres by ten: perhaps the oldest stone castle in the north. Who built it is not known.
1060: Lund is made a bishop's seat.

pages.title: Truso
pages.hint: A market among the Prussians
pages.brief: The Prussians' amber market on Lake Drużno; Wulfstan sails here from Hedeby.
pages.game:
Truso is a market of craftsmen and traders on the reedy shore of a shallow lake behind the Estmere, in the land of the Este, seven days and nights east of Sliesthorp. No king's penny counts here and no toll is known: amber, honey, wax, furs and people are weighed against cut silver on folding scales. A merchant comes for amber at the source, and stays because the Este's customs are worth more to know than their prices.
Ice shuts the lake and the lagoon from about Martinmas to Easter (?). The amber is gathered after the autumn and winter gales and is cheapest when the first boats come in spring; the honey comes in after Lammas; by autumn the sheds are bare and the fast horses are being fed up for the winter's burnings.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: amber, beeswax, mead, honey and amber beads; wanted here, and so dearer: bay salt, glass beads, iron tools and swords. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a summer market growing into a town. Danes and Gutes keep houses on marked plots along the shore, the Este hold the fort on the rise and the country behind, and the first silver with the Saracens' writing is a thing men pass from hand to hand and bite. Amber is cheap in spring and nobody asks whose man you are.
pages.known:
The Prussians' amber market on Lake Drużno; Wulfstan sails here from Hedeby. The place is now Janów Pomorski. It has been a trading place since about 750.
537: A letter of King Theodoric of the Goths, kept in a collection made about this year, thanks the Aesti of this shore for a gift of amber and explains to them what amber is. The king had died in 526. 700: About now, by one reckoning, the market on the lake begins; by another, not until late in the next century. 793: A working market, busiest in the sailing months and not yet at its largest. No event is recorded.
pages.source: The Old English Orosius, Wulfstan's account. The sailing part: texts_793.json 'wulfstan' (J. Bosworth 1859). The Estland part: H. Sweet, King Alfred's Orosius, EETS 79 (1883), pp. 19-21, https://archive.org/stream/kingalfredsorosi79oros/kingalfredsorosi79oros_djvu.txt ; every quotation of the customs here is our own plain rendering of the Old English, not Bosworth's or Thorpe's words; Cassiodorus, Variae V.2, as cited in en.wikipedia 'Old Prussians' (dossier 7); the date of the letter itself is before 526 (?); en.wikipedia 'Truso' and the Elblag museum (end of the 7th century); pl.wikipedia 'Truso' (late 8th century); dossier 1; dossier 5; the picture for 793 is the dossier's safe reading of the disagreeing dates

later.text: From 815 to 849: the silver comes steadily now, whole and cut, up the Vistula and across from Gotland. More houses, more scales, more men who bury a purse under a post before they go inland. The comb-makers and amber-cutters work with their doors open from the thaw to the first ice.

815: In this year or soon after, a purse of eleven whole coins and five pieces is put in the ground at Truso: ten dirhams of the caliphs and one drachm of the Persian king Khosrow, two hundred years old. Nobody comes back for it.
830: In the first half of this century dirhams reach the country round: six more and two pieces lie in woodland to the north.

From 850 to 879: the traders winter here with their wives and children; long houses of three rooms stand where booths stood (?). Children on the shore speak Danish to their fathers and the Este's tongue to everyone else. Grobin is gone quiet and its Gutes have come here or gone home.
As a trading place it ends about 850.
850: About now, by one account, the traders settle the year round with their families and build long houses.

From 880 to 899: the town at its fullest: twenty hectares of plots, workshops and boats. An Englishman from the Heaths walks about asking why the dead do not rot, and writes nothing down because he cannot write; he remembers it instead, in order.

890: Wulfstan sails from the Heaths to Truso in seven days and nights, the ship running under sail all the way, and afterwards tells King Alfred of the Este: their kings, their mead, their cold and the riding for a dead man's goods.

From 900 to 949: still busy, but the silver is of a new kind and comes by other roads, and the best amber goes north to Kaup on the Sambian shore (?). Fewer new houses. The old craftsmen's sons take a share in a ship and do not come back to the bench.
920: The latest amber and antler work that can be dated is of about these years.

From 950 to 999: a ditch and a bank where there was open ground (?). Each spring the channel through the reeds is narrower, and skippers who used to come up to the houses now lie in the Ilfing and send a boat. A new harbour at the Vistula's mouth takes the ships. Men carry bows to the shore.
950: By one account works of defence are raised about now.
970: In the second half of this century the silt of the Nogat begins to cut the lake off from the lagoon and the sea, and a new harbour at the Vistula's mouth takes the trade.

997: Bishop Adalbert of Prague comes by sea to the Vistula's mouth after Easter, enters the country of the Bruzi on 17 April and is killed some days after the 22nd, somewhere in this land; a priest of idols named Sicco is said to have struck first. Duke Boleslaw buys the body for its weight in gold. No Life names Truso.

From 1000 to 1066: ash under the grass, charred posts, a few fishers' huts. Reeds stand where the boats lay. The Este of the country round still gather amber and still burn their dead; they sell at the Vistula's mouth now, and nobody under forty has heard the name Truso said as a place one goes to.
1000: In this century or about this year the place burns: a thick layer of ash, burnt timbers and many arrowheads. Who did it is not known. The people scatter into the country round.

pages.title: Grobiņa
pages.hint: A market among the Curonians
pages.brief: A Scandinavian settlement among the Curonians.
pages.game:
A fort hill on a spit of a small river, a black-earthed settlement beside it and three fields of the dead round both: Gotlanders and Svear have lived here among the Curonians for five generations, and nobody can say any longer whose place it is. A merchant comes for amber after the gales, grey squirrel in spring, seal oil, wax and honey, and brings iron, blades, beads and salt; everything goes by weight, since no coin is struck on this coast. He gets in over a sand bar and across a wide shallow lake, and he gets out again only if the wind and the bar allow.
The sea is shut by ice from the first hard frost to well after the spring thaw, and the ice goes out late here. The Gotlanders come when it opens, wanting furs; the gales of autumn throw amber on the open shore, and the last ship must be over the bar before the lake skins over.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: squirrel pelts, amber and captives; wanted here, and so dearer: glass beads, iron tools and swords. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a mixed place with no one lord. Gotland households trade on the black earth and bury their women in island dress; a few armed men from the Mälar valley keep the fort hill and still speak of a tribute their fathers took; the Curonians, who were here first, sell them amber, pelts and wax and are more of them every year. Three tongues in the market, and every bargain weighed twice.
pages.known:
A Scandinavian settlement among the Curonians. The place is now Grobiņa. It has been a trading place since about 650.
650: People from Gotland and from the Mälar valley settle beside a Curonian fort on the river Ālande, about 11 km in from the open coast. The place is older than Hedeby and Birka both. 675: A flat stone carved with two duck-like birds, of a kind otherwise made only on Gotland, is set in a grave in the mound field. It is 0.70 m high. 793: The settlement stands: a fort plateau up to 80 m by 45 m, about 3 ha of houses on black earth, and grave fields of some thousands of burials. Nothing is recorded for the year, and no ruler is named.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/grobin.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with what could and could not be checked.; en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' ('comparable in many ways to Hedeby and Birka but probably predating them both'); lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; dossier 1, 5; en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis' (found 1987 at Priediens; second half of the 7th century); dossier 2, 7; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'; dossier 1, 5

later.text: 800: By the Latvian accounts the Curonians take the settlement over about now. The Northmen's graves are dated to 800 by one page and to 850 by others: between those years the Gotlanders and Svear stop being buried here.

From 801 to 852: the Curonians hold the hill. Whether the Northmen were bought out, married in or pushed off depends on who tells it, and on what the house did here. The Gotland booths thin to two or three; the mound field is no longer added to. Ships from Gotland still come in spring, and are counted as guests now, by the day.
As a trading place it ends about 850.
850: The Cori, who 'had in former time been in subjection to the Swedes', have 'a long while since rebelled'. Their kingdom holds five towns.

From 853 to 854: war on this shore. About 853 the five towns break a Danish fleet and the market is suddenly full of Danish gold and Danish ships for sale. The next summer the Svear come with their king. A merchant who is here at the wrong moon sees the town burn; one who is here just before it can do something about who is inside.
In 853 a fleet of the Danes came to plunder the Cori and bring them under. The men of the five towns gathered, killed half the Danes, and took half their ships, with gold, silver and spoils.

In 854 Olof, king of the Svear, 'collected an immense army' and came first to a town of the Cori called Seeburg, which they 'ravaged and despoiled and burnt'. Then they marched five days to Apulia and besieged it eight days.

In 854, on the ninth day at Apulia the Cori offered the gold and arms taken from the Danes, 'half-a-pound of silver for each individual man now in this town', the old tribute and thirty hostages. The Svear took it and went home.

From 855 to 1066: no market for strangers. The settlement is ash under new grass and the three fields of the dead are pasture; the Curonians keep the fort and pay the Svear a tribute for as long as the Svear can come and fetch it. A ship that stands in to this coast in these years is taken for a raider or is one. What trade there is goes by a truce counted in days.

855: After the burning the market loses its standing to others, such as Truso. No later graves of Northmen are found. The Curonians keep the fort hill, and its layer of use runs on for four hundred years.
925: A saga written three hundred years later sets a truce of half a month for trading in Kurland, and a raid when it ran out. No place is named.

pages.title: Aldeigjuborg
pages.hint: A market at Ladoga
pages.brief: The gate to the east on the Volkhov: furs going west, dirhams coming north.
pages.game:
A cluster of log houses and workshops on the left bank of a brown river, twelve kilometres up from a lake as wide as a sea, where a small river runs in and makes a harbour. It is the last place a sea ship can lie: above it the river breaks over rock, and everything goes on by river boat and other men's leave. A merchant comes for furs, wax and honey out of the woods and for thin silver with writing on it out of the south, and he brings blades, beads, cloth and a scale.
The river is ice from about the first snows of early winter until some weeks after the spring equinox, and the lake shore a month longer; in that time the furs come in over the snow on sledges. Boats leave when the ice breaks, the sea ships come from midsummer, and the silver comes back down the river before the frost. Nobody who means to sail home stays past the first cold nights.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: squirrel pelts, marten, beaver pelts, beeswax and mead; wanted here, and so dearer: Frisian cloth, glass beads, swords, mail byrnies and helmets. Prices are in dirhams, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a small place with no lord. Log cabins of the Slavs on the bank of the small river, a bead-maker's shop, a smith who also casts bronze, a barn of emmer, and one house bigger than the rest where a Svea dealer weighs silver. Men from the woods bring skins and stand apart. An older Slav fort watches the river two kilometres below. You deal with whoever sits in the biggest house, and nobody takes a toll.
pages.known:
The gate to the east on the Volkhov: furs going west, dirhams coming north. The place is now Staraya Ladoga. It has been a trading place since about 753.
753: The oldest timber of the place is felled. The first settlers are Northmen, perhaps Gotlanders, in three big houses with a hearth in the middle, and one of them is a smith. 765: In the 760s the first Norse colony ends. People from the south who build log cabins take the site, and from about now Slavs are the larger part of those who live here. 785: A bead-maker's shop begins work in the 780s, making glass eye beads by a low-heat method learned from the Arab lands. 786: A small hoard of the caliphs' silver is put in the ground here; its youngest coin is of this year. These are the oldest such coins in the lands of the eastern rivers. 793: A trading place forty years old of two to four hectares and fewer than a hundred people: Slav and Finnic householders, Northmen coming and going with the season. No writer names a ruler, a toll or a law for it.
