later.text: It works until the end of the 830s, and its beads buy furs.

839: Men who call their people Rhos come to the emperor Louis at Ingelheim by way of Constantinople, and prove to be Svear. It is the first time the name is written. Nobody in this town was called that before.

From 840 to 864: the town has been burned and half of it is nettles. Northmen hold what stands and build along the left bank of the small river; they take skins from the people of the woods as tribute and call it peace. The bead shop is gone. Fewer sea ships come, and those that do ask at the river mouth who is master this year before they row up.
About 840 an enemy burns the town, and much of it lies empty for some twenty-five years. Northmen hold it from about now and settle the left bank of the small river. Who burned it is not known.
852: Danes sent east from Birka by the casting of lots sack an unnamed town of the Slavs and come home rich. Some think it was this one (?).
862: The chronicle of Kiev's year for Rurik, called from over the sea to rule. Most copies make this town his first seat; the Laurentian copy says Novgorod. The tale is partly legend (?).

From 865 to 869: ash. The town was burned to the ground and nothing has been raised but a few lean-tos against charred posts. There is nobody to weigh with. Men dig in the black earth for what their fathers hid, and a ship that comes for furs finds trappers who do not know whom to sell to. Stay away, or come with timber and food.
865: Between 863 and 871 the town is burned to the ground. It is rebuilt with more Norse things in it than before, Thor's hammers among them.

From 870 to 899: rebuilt, and more Norse than it ever was. A wooden fort stands on the point between the two rivers; from 881 a big house takes in merchants, and about 894 a larger one goes up. Men wear small iron hammers at the neck. New silver is scarce for a generation, and the trade is in furs, cut silver and trust. The lord's men sit in the fort and are named to you at the landing.
875: In the 870s a wooden fort is raised on the point between the small river and the great one. Only from now does the Norse name with 'fort' in it fit the place.
881: A big house in the Norse manner is built, read by its diggers as an inn for merchants. A stick cut with runes lay by it.
About 894 a very large new building goes up, perhaps of two floors, as the trade grows.

From 900 to 950: the best years. A stone fort of dry-laid flagstone stands on the point with a hatch high in the river wall for hoisting goods. Heavy new silver comes up the rivers by the sackful, and with it glazed pots that shine like metal. The prince sits far away in Kiev and his men at Holmgard take what is his. Mounds stand tall along both banks, and the dead on the far side are burned.
About 900 a stone fort replaces the wooden one: flagstone laid without mortar, walls some eight metres high with a fighting walk, and a loading hatch seven metres up the river wall.
922: The Novgorod chronicle's year for the death of Oleg, and its word that his mound is at Ladoga. Kiev's chronicle says 912 and shows a grave of its own (?).
950: About now the town's best years end. Novgorod grows up two hundred kilometres up the river, and this place becomes its gate to the sea.

From 951 to 996: still a harbour, no longer the market. The furs are bought up the river at Novgorod and the tribute comes in to fixed stations; this town loads what Novgorod has already sold. The silver from the south grows thinner each year. After 988 the prince's men are Christians of the Greek rite, though no church is known here.

From 997 to 1018: jarl Eirik's men burned the stone fort in 997 and harried the coast for some summers. A wooden fort is raised again behind a new ditch. The silver now is pennies of the English and the Germans. In the brothers' wars after 1015 the harbour is full of hired fighting men going up to Novgorod, and any ship that carries them is well paid.
997: Jarl Eirik Hakonarson takes and burns the fort after a long siege. His skald Eyjolf praises the burning about 1010, and the burnt layer was found in the 1980s. The year is the sagas' (?).
1005: In the early 1000s a wooden fort stands again, behind a ditch cut from the small river to the great one.
1016: Yaroslav gives the men of Novgorod a written law: a merchant's life is worth forty grivnas, the same as a retainer's, and a man from over the sea clears himself by his oath alone.

From 1019 to 1045: the town is the bride-gift of the Svea princess Ingigerd and is held for her by a Svea jarl, Ragnvald, and after him his son Eilif (late). Norse is spoken in the fort and Slavic in the houses. Kings out of Norway pass through, in flight or coming home rich. The law of Novgorod runs here for a stranger, and the jarl's word besides.
1019: Ingigerd, daughter of Olof of the Svear, marries Yaroslav and has this town for her bride-gift. Her father's cousin, Jarl Ragnvald Ulfsson, holds it for her from the summer (late).
1029: Olaf Haraldsson of Norway comes through into exile at Yaroslav's court and leaves his son Magnus there; Harald Sigurdsson comes east about 1031 and sails home from here about 1045 (late).

From 1046 to 1066: Novgorod's sea-gate, held by the prince's governor. Christians are laid without mounds on the far bank. Silver is bars and western pennies; the furs go west in Gotland ships. In the winter of 1066 to 1067 Novgorod itself is burned from Polotsk and its bells are hauled away on sledges, and the news comes down the ice.
1050: Ingigerd dies on 10 February. Her jarls are gone from the town by now, and it is held again from Novgorod.

pages.title: Ögvaldsnes
pages.hint: A king's seat on the west coast of the Northmen
pages.brief: A king's seat on the Karmsund, the sheltered way north along the coast.
pages.game:
Ogvaldsnes is a great farm on a ness of the island Kormt, at the narrowest part of the sound that every ship on the coast road must use. It is a hall and a household, not a town: there is no market, no toll house and no coin, and a stranger trades with the lord or his man, by gift and by leave, with silver on the scale. A merchant comes for iron, soapstone pots, whetstones, down, a walrus tusk when the northern men have passed, and whatever the young men brought home from west over the sea; he brings grain, malt, glass, fine cloth and the Frankish blades he is forbidden to sell.
Ships go into the water after the first day of summer and come out before the winter nights; nobody sails the coast in the dark months. The young men are away from sowing to harvest, so high summer is a quiet farm of women, old men and thralls, and autumn is the time of feasts, home-comings and things for sale. The tide hardly moves the sound: a hand's breadth at neaps, a forearm at springs.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: soapstone pots, pine masts, dried fish, whale meat and blubber and butter; wanted here, and so dearer: wheat, barley, Rhenish wine, bay salt and swords. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: the old lord of the ness is alive and failing; nobody will be surprised by a second mound. His sister's son Thorleif has the ship and, more and more, the hall. In the summer of 793 the young men are west over the sea, and from the hay moon they are home with things no farm has a use for: silver cut from a shrine, a box of painted skins, two English boys.
pages.known:
A king's seat on the Karmsund, the sheltered way north along the coast. The place is now Avaldsnes, Karmøy.
250: About this time a great man is laid in the mound by the farm later called Flaghaug, with a neck ring of gold, weapons and Roman vessels of silver and bronze. In the game's years the mound stands whole and nobody knows what is in it. 715: Between about 680 and 750 a ship grave is made on the island, called the oldest in the North. Which mound is meant is not said (?). 779: In the summer a lord is laid in an oak ship some twenty-seven metres long under the Great Mound north of the farm, with a smaller boat, a horse, a sledge, two Frankish swords, a gold arm ring, gaming pieces of amber and glass, a cake of wax marked with a cross and a feather sealed in tin. 789: Three ships of Northmen from Hordaland, the next land north of here, come to Portland. The king's reeve takes them for traders and is killed.

later.text: The game puts the burial in the autumn of 794.

From 795 to 810: the Green Mound is new turf on the ridge beside the old one. Thorleif holds the hall. Every spring the ship goes west and every autumn the benches are full of men with something to sell and a story that leaves most of it out. Thralls of the islands' speech carry the water. A Frank is asked about blades before he is asked his name.
793: Between 790 and 795 a second man is buried in a boat of some fifteen metres under the Green Mound at Bo, with a fine glass beaker, hooped vessels, turned bowls, tapestry and bedding.

From 811 to 871: the lords of the ness in these years have no names that anyone wrote down. The farm is the same: the hall, the forge, the boats on the strand, the lord's man at the water in the morning. From the 840s there is a ship-fort at Dyflin, and Irish silver, Irish wives and Irish thralls come up the coast road with the home-coming ships.

From 872 to 932: the king's farm. After Hafrsfjord the hall is Harald's and a steward keeps it for him; the lord's gift becomes the king's due. Chiefs who will not have a king sell up and go west, and the steward counts heads at five ounces of silver for every man bound for Iceland. In his old age the king himself sits here some winters, heavy and slow, with too many sons.

872: By tradition in this year, by most scholars in the 880s, Harald Fairhair beats the kings of the west in Hafrsfjord, a day's sail south, and the farm becomes his. That he made it his chief seat is a modern claim: his own poet does not name it.
About 932 King Harald dies, having dwelt in old age on his great farms, this one among them, and is laid under a mound at Haugar on the sound.

From 933 to 961: Eric, and then Hakon, who was fostered in England and keeps his Fridays quietly. The west has one law at the Gula thing. Beacons stand ready on the heights. In 953 they burn: Eric's sons land on the island itself, and afterwards the heath among the old mounds has a new name.
953: The sons of Eric land on the island. King Hakon meets them on the heights among the old mounds and Guthorm Ericsson falls. The ground is afterwards called the Blood Heath.

From 962 to 994: hard years first: under Harald Greycloak it snows at midsummer and a sack of rye is worth more than its weight in whetstones. Then Jarl Hakon and good seasons. The old feasts are kept at the stone as they always were, and a Christian guest is wise to praise the ale and say nothing.

From 995 to 1000: king Olaf Tryggvason. A heathen crew is offered the first signing or no sailing. Sacrifice is forbidden, the mounds are looked at with a new eye, and a small wooden church goes up beside the hall (saga) (?). At Easter 998 the king feasts here with a bishop and the sound is full of ships.

998: King Olaf Tryggvason keeps Easter here with three hundred and sixty men and a bishop. The sorcerer Eyvind Kelda and his crew, blinded in their own mist, are taken and left bound on a skerry that the flood tide covers. That spring an old one-eyed guest keeps the king awake with tales of King Ogvald and his cow.
1000: About now the workshop ground south of the farm, where iron was forged, grain dried and salt boiled since about the year 200, goes out of use.

From 1001 to 1015: the jarls rule for the Danish king, and on the spot the great man is Erling Skjalgsson of Sola, a day south. Fifteen easy years: English pennies in every purse, weighed all the same, and nobody asks a skipper his faith twice.

From 1016 to 1028: king Olaf Haraldsson and his bailiffs. Thorir Sel, low-born and well dressed, comes down to the strand each morning to ask who commands and what the errand is. From 1022 no corn may go north; from 1024 no loading on a Sunday or a feast. In 1028 Cnut's silver has done its work and the king is gone.

1022: King Olaf Haraldsson forbids corn, malt and meal to go from the south to the north. Late in the summer his bailiff Thorir Sel seizes the whole cargo of Asbjorn Sigurdsson of Halogaland and takes his good striped sail in swap for an old one.

In 1023, on the Thursday of Easter week Asbjorn strikes off Thorir Sel's head at the king's table. On the Sunday Erling Skjalgsson of Sola comes with nearly fifteen hundred men and frees him. Asbjorn is named bailiff in the dead man's place and never comes back to serve.
1024: The church law for the west is set at Moster, a short sail north: no trade or loading on Sundays and feasts, no meat on Fridays.
1028: Cnut comes with his fleet and is taken as king. On the twenty-first day of December Erling Skjalgsson is killed off Bokn, at the south end of the sound.

From 1029 to 1035: the worst years. Svein and his mother Alfiva rule for Cnut: a room across every outbound ship is the king's, nobody leaves without leave, and in a suit one Dane's oath outweighs ten of the country's. From 1031 the dead King Olaf is a saint, and pilgrims begin to pass north.
1031: King Olaf's body is taken up and he is held a saint. His feast, the twenty-ninth of July, is kept on the sound from now on.

From 1036 to 1066: Magnus, then Harald Sigurdsson. The farm is one of the king's many and the bailiff's word is the king's. After about 1055 the king's own penny is two parts copper: take weighed silver or goods. In the summer of 1066 every farm on the sound sends a man to England, and in the autumn the widows have things to sell.
1066: About three hundred ships sail for England with King Harald Sigurdsson. Twenty-four come home.

pages.title: Hleiðr
pages.hint: A king's seat among the Danes
pages.brief: The Skjöldung kings' hall, up the Roskilde fjord.
pages.game:
Hleidr is a great man's hall on a rise among old mounds, an hour's walk inland from the head of a long shallow fjord on Zealand. It is not a town and has no market, no toll and no quay: a ship lies on the beach under the watch farm and her goods go up the stream valley on backs and carts to the steward's store. A merchant comes because a hall of two hundred mouths wants wine, glass, blades, querns and horses, and pays in weighed silver, hides, barley and captives, and because the men on its benches decide who is a guest in the Danish isles.
The fjord has almost no tide: a hard west wind fills it and an east wind drains the landing, and in a cold winter the inner water freezes (?). The year turns on the hall's feasts, winter's start at the Winter Nights in the tenth month, Yule at midwinter, the offering for victory before the ships go out in spring, and on the autumn herring in the sound to the east.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: barley and salt herring; wanted here, and so dearer: swords, horses, Mayen quernstones and captives. Silver goes by weight here, and no toll is taken on what you sell.
In these years: a hall a hundred years old, patched and smoke-black, with a lord's following on its benches, craftsmen and farm people in the houses round it and old mounds on every skyline. Whose hall it is no writer says; the game lets the king of the Danes keep feasts here (?). Silver is weighed, never counted. Strangers are met at the beach before they are met anywhere else.
pages.known:
The Skjöldung kings' hall, up the Roskilde fjord. The place is now Lejre. In 793 it is under Sigfred, king of the Danes.
About 680 the first great hall is raised on the rise at Hleidr. 700: About this time a lord's man here wears a helmet with gilded bronze brows, of the kind buried at Valsgarde and Sutton Hoo. A piece of one is lost at the landing and another by the hall. 777: The Franks name Sigfred king of the Danes. No writer of his time says where he kept his hall. 793: The hall stands and is lived in. Nothing is written of it this year or any year near it.

later.text: About 800 a stone is cut and raised a half day's walk to the south-east: Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son, reciter at Salhaugar. Three drinking horns are cut over the words.

From 804 to 813: the king's hall when he is not with the fleet (the game's choice, with the spine; unrecorded). In 804 and 808 the benches empty for the muster and fodder, ale and bread are dear. After the killing of 810 Hemming keeps it for two winters; in 812 the hall is half empty of men, and the women know the count before the Franks do.
804: Godfred, king of the Danes, comes with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom to Sliesthorp, on the border of his land and the Saxons'.
810: Godfred is killed by one of his own following. Hemming, his brother's son, is king after him and makes peace with the emperor.
812: Hemming dies. Sigfred and Anulo fight for the kingdom and both are killed; the Franks hear that 10,940 men died in the battle.

From 814 to 879: a quieter house. Kings are made and killed in Jutland and the hall feeds whoever holds Zealand that year. Pieces of the caliphs' coin and, from about 825, the small pennies of Sliesthorp come up the valley in purses, and are weighed like any other silver. The old hall leans; the feasts are kept.

From 880 to 933: a new hall on the old spot, the longest roof a Dane has seen. Men come home from England with silver and English words. Fine smiths work by the hall, the dead are laid in the earth east of the houses and stones are set over some of them in the shape of ships (?).
About 880 the hall is built new on the old spot.
About 900 a smith casts a silver figure the height of a thumbnail: someone on a high seat with two birds on its arms.

About 910 the dead of the hall are laid unburnt in the earth east of the houses, a few are burned, and stones are set over some in the shape of ships. One man is buried with gifts and a beheaded man laid over him.

From 934 to 979: after the Saxon king's victory the great offering is no longer kept (so a German bishop says, long after). A king takes baptism in Jutland about 965 and the hall goes on as before, with a hammer under most shirts and a cross under a few.
934: King Henry of the Saxons beats the Danes and makes their king take baptism. A German bishop writes eighty years later that Henry then forbade the great offering held at Hleidr every ninth year.

From 980 to 999: the king builds a church and a house at Roskilde across the water, and the following goes where the king eats. The hall at Hleidr has a steward, a few old men and too many empty benches. Ships still land at the watch farm, bound now for the new town.
985: In the 980s King Harald, Gorm's son, founds a town with a wooden church of the Trinity and a king's house at Roskilde, across the head of the fjord from the landing.
995: About the end of the 900s somebody at Hleidr puts four silver vessels, a weight, a silver disc and forty-four beads in a clay pot and buries it. Nobody comes back for it.

From 1000 to 1066: the hall is gone: post-holes under grass, a farm, the mounds and the stone ships. The landing serves Roskilde, a bishop's town from 1020, with a stone church building by the middle of the century (?). Knarrs from Norway and small coasters use the fjord. What the place was is a thing for old people's talk.
Four more follow on the same spot until about 1000.
About 1000 the last hall goes out of use. The seat of the Danish kings on Zealand is Roskilde.
1020: King Cnut makes Roskilde a bishop's seat.
1026: At Christmas Earl Ulf is killed in the church of the Trinity at Roskilde at King Cnut's word, after a quarrel over a game of tafl the night before.
1042: A warship thirty paces long, built at Dublin of Irish oak, is new this year. She ends her days sunk across the channel of this fjord at Skuldelev, with four others, after the game's years.

pages.title: Namnetis
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: The Loire city at the Breton march: salt and wine.
pages.game:
Namnetis is an old Roman bishop's city of the Franks on the north bank of the Loire, where the Erdre runs in: a wall of sixteen hectares too big for the people inside it, a cathedral with a tin roof, and a port under the wall that takes the king's toll on everything that comes by ship or any other way. West of it the Bretons begin, and the count who holds the city holds the march against them. A merchant comes for bay salt in autumn and Loire wine after the vintage, for river fish, for the Saint John's gathering when the whole country is in the streets, and because this is the mouth of the road to Tours, where the best books in Gaul are being written.
The river is high and brown with snow water in spring and runs thin over its sandbanks by Lammas; ice comes down it in a hard winter. Saints Donatian and Rogatian are kept on 24 May; on Saint John's day, 24 June, pilgrims come from far cities and the night before is a vigil at his church. Salt comes up from the bay from the Assumption to Saint Luke's day, wine comes down after the vintage, the cathedral keeps its dedication on the last day of September, and by Martinmas the sea trade is over.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Frankish wine and bay salt. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: king Charles's years and Count Wido's. A quiet, half-empty walled city with a working port under it: the king's toll, bay salt and Loire wine, pilgrims at midsummer, old Bishop Odilard and then his successors in Felix's church. No mint yet.
pages.known:
The Loire city at the Breton march: salt and wine. The place is now Nantes. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
276: After this year the city is walled: 1,665 metres round, about eight metres high and four thick, with round towers at the corners, along the Erdre and the Loire. It encloses 16 hectares (18 by another count). 570: About now Bishop Felix dedicates his basilica of Saints Peter and Paul on 30 September: three naves, a tin roof, marble columns. He also cuts a channel to bring the river to the city's port. (The dedication fell between 567 and 573.) 610: About now a ship lies at Nantes that has brought Irish wares; the bishop and the count put the exiled abbot Columban aboard her to be sent home to Ireland. 673: About now Hermeland founds his monastery on the island of Indre, three leagues below the city, in water rich in fish. 776: About now Odilard becomes bishop.

Munro (Fordham sourcebook); fr.wikipedia Hermeland d'Indre; Chronicon Namnetense c. 6 (dossier 2); fr.wikipedia Liste des eveques de Nantes (dossier 3)

later.text: From 796 the monks of Tours send down for calfskins and send books out.
In 799 the count rides through Brittany and comes back with a cart of named weapons.

In 799 Count Wido, who presided in the march of Brittany, went through the whole of that land with his fellow counts and brought King Charles the weapons of the chiefs who had yielded, each marked with its owner's name.
King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
He is bishop still when the game begins and until about 800.
800: About now Alcuin, abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours, writes for Count Wido a short book on the virtues and the vices, for a man busy with war.
811: An army is sent against the Bretons to punish their breach of faith.
814: From the reign of the emperor Louis pennies are struck here reading NAMNETVM, of 1.78 grams. (None is known for King Charles.)
818: Count Wido is dead by now; Lambert holds the county until 831, and Ricuin after him.

From 819 to 842: the emperor Louis's years. Pennies are struck in the city with its name on them. The counts change (Lambert, Ricuin, Renaud) and quarrel; from 835 Gunhard is bishop. The monks of Herio leave their island for good in 836 and the salt men of the bay bring their business and their talk to Nantes. Every summer somebody on the quay has seen sails.
835: Gunhard becomes bishop.
In 841, on 25 June Count Ricuin dies in the battle at Fontenoy. King Charles gives Nantes to Renaud of Herbauges and not to Lambert, who goes over to the Bretons.

From 843 to 850: the year of Saint John's day and after. The cathedral is stripped and for three months unclean; Indre is black posts on its island; half the families have somebody dead or sold. Bishop Actard holds on. Captives come home one at a time, bought back dear, and the market is small and frightened.

In 843, on 24 May Lambert and the Bretons kill Count Renaud at Blain. On Saint John's day, 24 June, Northmen come up the river on a west wind, climb the wall with ladders, break in by an entrance long since blocked, kill Bishop Gunhard and the crowd in the cathedral, and leave at dusk with captives. On 29 June they burn Indre. On 30 September the cathedral is cleansed and Mass is said again.
850: Lambert and Nominoe of the Bretons take Nantes and throw down its walls.

From 851 to 918: a Breton city with its walls thrown down. Danes sit on the river islands from 853 to 856 and come back whenever they like; for ten years about 860 the place is called a desert. The toll belongs half to the bishop from 857. About 900 Bishop Fulcher rebuilds the cathedral and walls a refuge round it, and for a few years ships lie under it again.
851: King Charles grants Erispoe of the Bretons Rennes, Nantes and Retz. The city is Breton from now on.
853: In July Danes from the Seine plunder Nantes; they hold the islands of the Loire until 856.

857: Erispoe gives the bishop back half the toll of all goods that come to the port of the city, by ship or any other way: markets, cart-toll, wheel-toll, all ale-houses and workshops, gathered by the bishop's own men. He makes the gift by a gold-trimmed key of Saint Peter's relics.
867: The king writes that Nantes, once most flourishing, has been a desert for ten years.
873: Northmen beaten on the Loire ask to stay on an island in the river until February and to hold a market there.
886: Northmen again; Bishop Landran flees to Angers until about 889.
897: Bishop Landran dies on 5 February. Fulcher, bishop until about 910, rebuilds and lengthens the cathedral and walls a refuge round it.

From 919 to 936: the Northmen's town. Ragenold and then Incon hold the river; the cathedral is roofless and brambles grow in the nave; a few poor Bretons till the soil. There is no toll but what the chief's men ask and no law but his, yet salt and loot are sold on the strand, and a merchant with nerve and a Norse tongue aboard can trade.
919: Northmen take Nantes. The people hold the castle one day and flee by night; the cathedral burns; Bishop Adalard flees.
921: Robert besieges the Northmen of the Loire five months, then yields them Nantes and Brittany. A second siege of five weeks fails in 927.

From 937 to 989: Alan's city and his heirs'. A great earthwork and a tower by the cathedral, Notre-Dame rebuilt, the canons home, the toll shared in three. After 952 Fulk of Anjou takes sacks of its pennies; in 960 the townsmen themselves drive Northmen off. The port fills again, slowly, with salt, wine and fish.

937: Alan, called Twisted-beard, come back from the English king's court, beats the Northmen in Saint Aignan's meadow and enters a city deserted for many years, cutting his way to the cathedral door through brambles with his sword.
952: Alan dies and is buried, in the end, in Notre-Dame, which he rebuilt. Fulk the Good of Anjou is guardian of his son until 960.
960: Northmen seize Bishop Walter; after eight days the townsmen drive them off, and ransom is paid at Guerande.
981: Count Hoel is murdered; his brother Guerech, count and bishop both, fights Conan of Rennes at Conquereuil and rebuilds the east end of the cathedral before 988.

From 990 to 1066: a count's town between Rennes and Anjou. The Bouffay castle stands at the river corner, the bishops are counts' sons and quarrel with the counts, and the salt of Guerande and the wine of the Loire go out in more hulls each year. A knight's household drinks where the carters used to.
990: Conan of Rennes takes Nantes and builds a castle, the Bouffay, in the western corner by the Loire. On 27 June 992 he dies at Conquereuil against Fulk Nerra of Anjou.
1033: About now Count Budic razes the bishop's palace while Bishop Walter is away at Jerusalem; war, then peace.
1049: Bishop Budic, who had the see from his father, is deposed for simony at the council of Reims.
1066: Hoel, count of Nantes, becomes duke of Brittany.

pages.title: Herio
pages.hint: A monastery among the Franks
pages.brief: Saint Philibert's island monastery and its salt pans.
pages.game:
A low island south of the Loire mouth, two rocky islets joined by a sand bar and a lagoon, with Saint Philibert's monastery on the northern one and the founder's body in a marble coffin under three lamps. In 793 it lies under Louis, the king's son, king of Aquitaine; no toll is taken and no coin is struck, and what is sold is sold on the sand at Conca, where ships anchor to wait for a wind. A merchant comes for grey bay salt, cheapest of anything he will ever load, and brings what an island of monks cannot grow: grain, lamp oil, wine, lead, shoes and cloth.
Salt is raked from midsummer until the autumn rains and is cheapest after the Assumption; the saint's feast is kept through the night before the twentieth day of August. The ebbs rule every day of it: the monastery's channel dries twice a day, and the flats west and south are bare rock and sand at low water.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: Frankish wine and bay salt. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a quiet island house under an abbot whose name nobody wrote down. The monks keep the hours; the cellarer buys oil for the three lamps and bread corn for the house; Breton and Bordeaux ships lie windbound at Conca and are fed for charity. It is a famine year on the mainland and the island counts its sacks.
pages.known:
Saint Philibert's island monastery and its salt pans. The place is now Noirmoutier. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
About 675 Philibert, abbot of Jumieges, driven out of his own house, came to the island of Herio and built a monastery there. 677: This year, on the first day of July, Ansoald, bishop of Poitiers, endowed the house; it was hallowed to the apostles Peter, Andrew and Paul and the martyrs Lawrence and Florent, and given salt works at Ampan on the mainland. About 685 Philibert died and was laid in a marble coffin in the basilica. In his day a ship from Bordeaux brought forty measures of lamp oil, an Irish ship shoes and clothing, and 237 porpoises stranded in a famine year and fed the house.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout; ARF 768, 794, 801, 814; Einhard VK 30 (Design/content/realms/francia.json); Vita Filiberti c. 21, in R. Poupardin, Monuments de l'histoire des abbayes de Saint-Philibert (1905); Poupardin 1905, list of diplomas; I. Cartron, Les peregrinations de saint Philibert (2010) ch. III; Vita Filiberti cc. 27-29 (Poupardin 1905). The year of his death is the common one (?)

later.text: From 799 to 818: the years of the first fear. Heathen ships have been among the islands of Aquitaine and everyone has a cousin who saw them. Bishop Atto of Saintes holds the house and tightens its rule. From 814 a great man lives in the guest house as the emperor's prisoner, and the gate asks strangers more questions.
Raided in 799.
In 799 pagan ships did much harm among the islands off Aquitaine, and about a hundred and five of the raiders were killed on the shore. The letter names no island.
King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
813: By this year Atto, bishop of Saintes, to whom King Charles had given the monastery, had set the rule to rights there.
In 814 the new emperor Louis sent Adalard, abbot of Corbie, his father's cousin and counsellor, to live on the island as an exile. He stayed seven years.

From 819 to 835: the summer house is half empty. From early spring to the end of autumn the monks are at Deas; a few brothers stay for the lamps and the salt. From 830 a rampart stands round the monastery with the abbey's own armed men on it, and the lead is off the church roof and lying at Furca for safety. On the feast of 835 there is a fight on the shore and the island wins it.

The same fair weather that dries the salt brings the heathen ships, so from 819 the monks spend the sailing months at Deas on the mainland and the island is kept by a few brothers, the abbey's armed men and the islanders.

819: This year, on the sixteenth day of March, the emperor gave Abbot Arnulf leave to build a new house at Deas on the mainland as a refuge, because the island house was often laid waste by barbarians.
In 820 thirteen pirate ships, beaten off from Flanders and the Seine, sacked the island of Bouin across the bay and went home with great plunder.
In 821 Adalard was called back from the island and given his abbey again.
About 825 Abbot Arnulf died and Hilbod was abbot after him.
826: This year, on the eighteenth day of May, King Pippin of Aquitaine confirmed his father's grant: six boats of the abbey go free of toll on the Loire, the Allier, the Cher and the Dordogne.

In 830 in June the island was left by the general body of the monks for the summer. On the second day of August the emperor took the abbey under his protection, confirmed the fort Abbot Hilbod had built around the monastery, and set its due at six pounds of silver a year.

835: This year, on Saint Philibert's own feast, nine ships came to the island. Count Rainald and the abbey's men fought them from the ninth hour until evening; the monks wrote that 484 Northmen fell, and one defender, and many horses.

From 836 to 842: the saint is gone and the basilica has an empty pit in its floor. A handful of monks, the islanders and their lord remain. Breton ships still come for salt and bring grain. The fort stands with fewer men each year.

836: This year, on the seventh day of June, the monks dug up Saint Philibert in his marble coffin and took him by ship to Furca, and from there on men's shoulders by Ampan, Varenne and Paulx to Deas, where he came on the eleventh.

About 839 Breton ships with yards, sails and anchors came to the abbey's port of Furca to trade: they had brought grain and carried away only salt. One crew took some of the monastery's lead as well, partly by theft and partly by buying on the quiet.

From 843 to 846: after Nantes. The fleet that took the city shares its loot on this shore and fights over it; some summers long ships lie in Conca and their chiefs take a share of the salt as the abbot once did (?). In July 846 the monastery burns.

843: This year, after the sack of Nantes on Saint John's day, the Northmen came to Herio to share the loot and killed each other over it. Captives slipped away when the sea drew back, one with the great Bible of Nantes hung on his neck.
In 846 in July the monastery of Herio was burned by the Northmen.

From 847 to 936: whoever holds the island holds the salt. The islanders rake the beds for their own lord in a quiet year and for a ship's chief in a bad one, and sell to anyone who lands with grain. Two or three monks keep a roofed corner of the church (Falco). Fleets go up and down the Loire; Nantes is a Northmen's town from 919. No king's man comes here.
847: This year, on the thirtieth day of March, Deas was burned. The saint's body went on to Cunault in 858, to Messay in 862, and came to rest at Tournus on the fourteenth day of May 875.

From 937 to 999: the Loire is the Bretons' and the Franks' again after Alan Barbetorte takes Nantes back. The island belongs to its lords on the mainland shore. The church is patched; the old fort is a grassy bank with sheep on it. Salt goes north in Breton hulls every autumn.

From 1000 to 1066: a priory of Tournus: a prior and a few monks sent from the house on the Saone where the saint now lies, come to keep his empty grave. The lords of La Garnache hold the island and talk of a tower. More salt beds are cut each year, and English and Norman ships are seen in the bay (?).
About 1000 the house on the island was a priory of Tournus. Falco of Tournus wrote that the island had never been wholly without a few monks.

pages.title: Burdigala
pages.hint: A town among the Franks
pages.brief: The Garonne city of Aquitaine: wine.
pages.game:
An old Roman city of Aquitaine, four-square behind a wall of grey stone on the left bank of the Garonne, with marsh on three sides and a hundred kilometres of brown tidal water between it and the sea. In 793 it belongs to the kingdom King Charles made for his son Louis; the Gascons live across the river. A merchant comes for the wine of the country, cheap after the vintage, and for a little salt and dried fish from the river mouth, and he comes with a pilot or not at all.
The year turns on the vintage: grapes are cut from Holy Cross day in September into October, and new wine is cheapest from then to Christmas and dearest before the next harvest. The tide rules every day of it: the flood carries a boat up from the sea and the ebb takes her down, and at the spring tides of late summer, when the river is low, a wave runs up the Garonne ahead of the flood (?). Saint Amand is kept on 18 June and Saint Seurin in October (the day here is not checked (?)); the sea shuts at Martinmas.
Made in its country, and so cheaper here: wine of Aquitaine. Prices are in deniers, and the toll on what you sell is a tenth.
In these years: a quiet walled city of King Louis's Aquitaine: half its Roman ground is garden and ruin, the old harbour inside the wall is mud, and boats lie on the river bank. The bishop's chair has no name on it in the lists. Country wine is the trade, and the Gascons across the water are the worry.
pages.known:
The Garonne city of Aquitaine: wine. The place is now Bordeaux. In 793 it is under Charles, king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774.
778: King Charles sets a count named Seguin over Bordeaux when he orders Aquitaine. Whether the same man still holds it in 793 is not recorded. 793: Louis, the young king of Aquitaine, is away in Italy in the spring. The list of the city's bishops is blank from the seventh century to Sicharius.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.; ARF 768, 794, 801, 814; Einhard VK 30 (Design/content/realms/francia.json); The Astronomer, Vita Hludowici ch. 3 (la.wikisource.org/wiki/Vita_Ludovici); dossier 1; chronicle_793.json; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_des_archevêques_de_Bordeaux; dossier 1

later.text: King of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800.
811: Bordeaux is one of the twenty-one chief cities named in the emperor's will, each to have its share of his treasure.

814: Louis the Pious gives the bishop's church of Saint Andrew its immunity, with Saint Mary's church and Saint Helen's chapel beside it. Sicharius is the first bishop named in two hundred years. Pennies are struck with BVRDIGALA in two lines.

From 816 to 843: Seguin is put out and the Gascons rise, but the city is busier than it has been: a bishop again, the king's pennies struck with the city's name, Pippin's court passing through (?). Wine goes down the river and good silver comes up from Melle.
816: Seguin, called duke of the Gascons, is put out of his office for arrogance and wicked ways, and the Gascons beyond the river rise.

From 844 to 848: the Northmen are on the Garonne. In 844 they pass upriver to Toulouse; in 845 the count is killed on the Saintes road; in 847 they sit round the wall for a long time. Wine lies unsold in every cellar and a boat that can get out to sea names her own price. In 848 the city is taken by night and burned.
In 844 the Northmen went up the Garonne as far as Toulouse, plundering on every side, and nobody stood against them.
845: In the autumn the Northmen broke out between Bordeaux and Saintes. The Christians fought them on foot and were cut down; Count Seguin was taken and killed, and Saintes burned.
In 847 the Danes lay about Bordeaux and besieged it for a long time.

848: In Lent King Charles took nine Danish ships on the Dordogne. After that the Northmen took Bordeaux by night, with William its duke, and wasted and burned it. One annal, written far off, says the Jews betrayed it; others read that as Pippin's party. The Aquitanians, sick of Pippin's sloth, chose Charles at Orléans. Melle, the silver mint to the north, was sacked the same year.

From 849 to 886: the pagans' years. Fleets come and go from the river and winter in the country; the archbishop cannot stay in his city and lives at Bourges. Whether the Northmen hold the town or only use it nobody far away can say (the sources dispute it). No mint, little law, and trade only for those who can deal with both sides.
In 851, on 13 October the fleet of Asgeir, come from Bordeaux, a place most strongly fortified, entered the Seine. The next June it went back to Bordeaux laden.
855: The Northmen are at Bordeaux again, roaming as they please. They winter in the country in 848, 855 and 864.
876: At Ponthion Archbishop Frotar pleads that he could not stay in his city for the pagans. The pope lets him have Bourges for as long as the pagans hold the church of Bordeaux.

From 887 to 976: a count sits here again and the wall is patched with stone from the Arenas; armed men on horses are a thing the town now has. Ships from Spain are spoken of. The churches outside the wall are roofless or poor, and the pennies are thin.
887: Amalvinus, count of Bordeaux, is at the council of Bourges.

906: A letter in the name of Alfonso, king in Spain, says he will buy a crown of gold and gems from the clergy of Tours; it is to wait at Bordeaux with 'our friend' Amalvinus for his ships in May. Some scholars doubt the letter.

From 977 to 1031: the dukes of the Gascons hold the city and it mends: Holy Cross rebuilt in the marsh, canons at Saint Seurin, an archbishop who leads the bishops at Charroux. The duke's pennies say SANCHIVS and want weighing.

977: Before this year Count William the Good, son of Raymond and Entregodis, rebuilds Holy Cross in the marsh for thirteen monks under Abbot Elis, on the counsel of young Trencard, and gives it lands with vines and the oratory of Saint Mary at Soulac with its pine wood and fishery.
In 989, on 1 June Gombaud, archbishop of Bordeaux, presides at Charroux, where the bishops curse any who break into churches, strike unarmed clergy or take a poor man's beasts.

1027: Geoffrey, a Frank by birth and honest in his ways, is chosen archbishop and anointed at Blaye before Duke Sancho's assembly. A charter of the same date gives Holy Cross the road toll of Saint-Macaire and a custom of three measures of salt.

From 1032 to 1066: Poitou's counts and then Guy Geoffrey hold Bordeaux, and in the years between nobody quite does. Stone churches go up at Saint Seurin and Saint Andrew. Pilgrims for Spain cross here in growing numbers (?), and the wine of the abbeys' vines is worth a ship's coming.
In 1039, on 10 March Eudes of Poitou, who held Bordeaux and Gascony, is killed. Bernard of Armagnac disputes the county until Guy Geoffrey wins it, in 1044 or 1052.

pages.title: The bank under the town
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Áhús. A brown river a hundred paces wide between low sandy banks, and open country with hardly a tree.
pages.game: A beach at Áhús. A brown river a hundred paces wide between low sandy banks, and open country with hardly a tree. In front, a dozen clinker boats drawn up or lying to a stone, some with a tent rigged over the hold and a cooking fire beside them: traders live aboard. Behind, fences and thatch in long rows, thin smoke, and the tap of hammers. It smells of tar, wet sand and burning oak. What is done here: load and unload, ask the keeper, wait for wind, hire carriers and lodge ashore.
pages.source: J. Callmer, 'North-European trading centres and the Early Medieval craftsman. Craftsmen at Åhus, north-eastern Scania, Sweden ca. AD 750-850+', in Central Places in the Migration and Merovingian Periods, Uppåkrastudier 6 (Lund 2002), 125-157. https://www.uppakra.lu.se/fileadmin/_migrated/content_uploads/6._Central_Places_in_the_Migration_and_Merovingian_Periods.pdf (read in full by the dossier's writer; everything about the town of 793 rests on it)

later.text: It stands until about 859.

pages.title: The open place
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Áhús. A bare trodden square in the middle of the plots, fifty paces by thirty, with lanes running out of it wide enough for two carts.
pages.game: A market at Áhús. A bare trodden square in the middle of the plots, fifty paces by thirty, with lanes running out of it wide enough for two carts. Goods lie on hides and chest lids: combs in rows, brooches in pairs, knives, strings of beads, bundles of antler, a farmer's amber in a sack. Women string beads as they talk. Every dealer has a small folding scale, and nobody shouts a price. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, call witnesses and ask the news. Found here: Hebbi.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: one open space of at least 50 by 30 m; lanes of 10 to 20 m; beads bought unstrung by the thousand.

pages.title: Toke's plot
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Áhús. A fenced plot on the oldest strip, right above the bank.
pages.game: A workshop at Áhús. A fenced plot on the oldest strip, right above the bank. A small house on the ground, and beside it a hut sunk knee-deep in the sand with its roof at shoulder height: inside, a bench by the door for the light, a heap of sawn antler, a row of comb plates waiting for their teeth, clay moulds drying. A dog gnaws something under the bench. It smells of scorched horn. What is done here: take an order, buy from makers, give a gift and rent store room. Found here: Toke.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: sunken-floored huts as workshops and stores; one plot cast brooches, cut combs and worked amber; 28,136 pieces of antler waste.

pages.title: The fire plots
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Áhús. Three plots downwind where the hearths are: a smith's with a stone anvil and a heap of cauldron sheet waiting for rivets, and two casters' with crucibles no bigger than an egg cup glowing in charcoal.
pages.game: A smithy at Áhús. Three plots downwind where the hearths are: a smith's with a stone anvil and a heap of cauldron sheet waiting for rivets, and two casters' with crucibles no bigger than an egg cup glowing in charcoal. Broken clay moulds crunch underfoot. A man weighs scrap bronze against a row of lead weights; another files a key. Only men work at the fires. What is done here: weigh the silver, test the silver, buy ship's tools, take an order and fit her out. Found here: Alle.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: 3,596 mould pieces, 532 crucible pieces, about 100 kg of slag, chest locks, keys, riveted cauldron sheet; that fire crafts were forbidden to women he calls likely, not proven (?).

pages.title: The spinning huts
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Áhús. A sunken hut with the door-flap tied back and four women in the light of it.
pages.game: A workshop at Áhús. A sunken hut with the door-flap tied back and four women in the light of it. Spindles turn with whorls no bigger than a hazelnut; an upright loom leans on the back wall with its weights swinging. One woman weaves a patterned ribbon on a little antler comb held in her lap. Outside, a sail lies over the fence with a bone needle stuck in the seam. What is done here: trade riddles, buy from makers, take an order and fit her out. Found here: Thjodvi.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: 107 spindle whorls, many for very fine thread; light loom weights; 33 bone needles, perhaps for sailcloth; two antler ribbon-weaving combs, matched only at Birka.

pages.title: The rivet bank
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Áhús. The upstream end of the bank. A boat lies on her side on rollers with three strakes off, and a man drives old rivets out of them into a basket.
pages.game: A boat yard at Áhús. The upstream end of the bank. A boat lies on her side on rollers with three strakes off, and a man drives old rivets out of them into a basket. Beyond him a fire of grey boat planks burns with a green edge where the iron was. New oak lies split, not sawn. It smells of tar, and of the river. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, buy a boat, order a ship and fit her out. Found here: Sote.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: over 2,400 boat rivets, ship repair 'a major activity', old boat timber burnt; the waterfront is the least-dug part.

pages.title: Asbod's house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Áhús. A house on the ground like the others, ten paces long, with the door open and a bench outside it.
pages.game: An ale-house at Áhús. A house on the ground like the others, ten paces long, with the door open and a bench outside it. Inside, a long hearth, a vat, smoke under the roof, and men of four peoples sitting where they can see the door. On a flat stone by the fire somebody is moving amber pieces across scratched squares. It smells of malt and wet wool. An ale-house, though nobody here has a word for it. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, play tafl, throw dice, hire a hand, pay the singer and lodge ashore. Found here: Asbod.
pages.known: Invented; the house size and three amber gaming pieces from Callmer 2002; a guest's needs from Hávamál 2-4 (Bellows 1923).
pages.source: J. Callmer, 'North-European trading centres and the Early Medieval craftsman. Craftsmen at Åhus, north-eastern Scania, Sweden ca. AD 750-850+', in Central Places in the Migration and Merovingian Periods, Uppåkrastudier 6 (Lund 2002), 125-157. https://www.uppakra.lu.se/fileadmin/_migrated/content_uploads/6._Central_Places_in_the_Migration_and_Merovingian_Periods.pdf (read in full by the dossier's writer; everything about the town of 793 rests on it)

pages.title: The old market ground
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Áhús. Across the river and a little upstream: a stretch of grazing where the village of Yngsjö keeps its cattle.
pages.game: A field at Áhús. Across the river and a little upstream: a stretch of grazing where the village of Yngsjö keeps its cattle. Nothing stands on it. Underfoot, wherever a hoof has cut the turf, the sand is full of glass: drops, rods and broken beads in blue, white and yellow. In the bank below it a pale cliff of clay shows where men have dug. What is done here: cross over, have him remembered and bury a man.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: Åhus I, about 700 to 750, over 70,000 pieces of glass waste, grazing land of Yngsjö after; kaolin dug from the bank for crucibles. That the dead are remembered on this ground is the game's choice: no grave field is reported (?).

pages.title: The still water
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Áhús. A slow bend above the town where the brown water stands almost still under an alder.
pages.game: A shrine at Áhús. A slow bend above the town where the brown water stands almost still under an alder. No building, no post, no fence. A flat stone at the edge is worn smooth, and there is a smear of fat on it. People lower their voices here without being told, and nobody waters cattle at this spot. What is done here: make an offering, make a vow, cast the lots and swear an oath.
pages.known: INVENTED (?): no shrine has been found at Åhus. The river's name means the holy or luck-bringing river, and why is not known; offerings in water are known elsewhere among the Danes. The district's holy place may have been Vä, inland, whose name means one.

pages.brief: A beach at Áhús. The river meets the bay over sand, with surf on the bar in an easterly. A few boats are drawn up above the weed line, nets on poles, a farm's cattle standing in the shallows.
pages.game: A beach at Áhús. The river meets the bay over sand, with surf on the bar in an easterly. A few boats are drawn up above the weed line, nets on poles, a farm's cattle standing in the shallows. Upriver, where the town was, there is ploughland. A woman sells from a chest lid; a boy watches your boat as if he means to remember her. What is done here: load and unload, ask the keeper, wait for wind, hire a pilot, buy stores, ask the news and trade riddles. Found here: Tonna and Erik.
pages.known: Callmer 2002: abandoned in the later 9th century and ploughed; the landing and its trade are the game's guess, because the game keeps the port open (?).

pages.title: The herring shore
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Áhús. North of the mouth, in autumn: small boats run up on the sand before noon, silver to the gunwales, and gulls over them like smoke.
pages.game: A fishery at Áhús. North of the mouth, in autumn: small boats run up on the sand before noon, silver to the gunwales, and gulls over them like smoke. Women gut on boards, and the tubs want more salt than anyone has. By the winter nights the beach is empty and smells of it still. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores and hire carriers.
pages.known: The great Skåne herring markets are later, about 1200: this is a beach, not a fair.

pages.title: The stone house
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Áhús. A house of grey stone laid in mortar, twenty paces long and ten wide, standing by the river mouth with no thatch near it.
pages.game: A hall at Áhús. A house of grey stone laid in mortar, twenty paces long and ten wide, standing by the river mouth with no thatch near it. The door is above a man's reach, up a ladder. Lime dust still whitens the grass. Nobody here has built in stone before, and the farmers come to look at it on feast days. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hear the law and show the charter.
pages.known: Wikipedia (sv) 'Åhus borg': about 20 by 10 m, mid 11th century, perhaps Scandinavia's oldest stone castle. Who held it is not known; the door and the ladder are the game's guess (?).

pages.title: The mouth of the small river
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Aldeigjuborg. A narrow side river running into a broad brown one under a low bank of clay.
pages.game: A landing at Aldeigjuborg. A narrow side river running into a broad brown one under a low bank of clay. Sea ships lie nose to the mud with their masts down, and beyond them flat-bottomed river boats and dugouts are drawn up in a row. Log houses stand close behind, grey smoke lying flat over them. Wet clay, tar, wood smoke and the sour smell of raw skins; a hammer somewhere, and a tongue you do not know. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar, mend the boat and hire a pilot. Found here: Budimir.
pages.known: The mouth and channels of the Ladozhka are the harbour, on the left bank of the Volkhov, about 12 km from the lake; the first houses on the Ladozhka's right bank. No toll is known here, so none is taken.

pages.title: The trading bank
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Aldeigjuborg. A strip of trodden ground between the houses and the water. Skins lie in tied bundles of forty, stacked like firewood: squirrel, marten, beaver, a few black fox.
pages.game: A market at Aldeigjuborg. A strip of trodden ground between the houses and the water. Skins lie in tied bundles of forty, stacked like firewood: squirrel, marten, beaver, a few black fox. Cakes of yellow wax the size of a quern, honey in birch-bark tubs, sacks of emmer. Men in fur caps from the woods stand a little apart with a woman who speaks for them. No booths, no stalls: a blanket on the ground and a scale held up to the light. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods, buy from makers, buy stores and listen for talk. Found here: Ihalempi.
pages.known: No market square is recorded: this open ground is the game's guess (?). Furs above all, bought with beads; wax, honey and captives out, silver, beads, blades and amber in. Furs counted by the timber of forty and marten skins reckoned as money are from later usage. Emmer: the burned barn of the 700s, 80 parts emmer to 20 of soft wheat.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/aldeigjuborg.md (the research this file is built on; its doubts are kept, marked (?), and its section 8, what must not be claimed, is followed)

pages.title: The biggest house
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Aldeigjuborg. One long house among the cabins, built the old Northern way with a hearth down the middle and benches at the walls.
pages.game: A hall at Aldeigjuborg. One long house among the cabins, built the old Northern way with a hearth down the middle and benches at the walls. A broad man sits near the door where the light is, a folding scale in front of him and a leather bag of thin white coins at his knee. Bundles of skins hang from the rafters out of reach of the dogs. Behind the house, a pen of split logs roofed at one end, and somebody coughing in it. What is done here: weigh the silver, test the silver, give a gift, ask an audience, swear an oath, call witnesses, ask the news and lodge ashore. Found here: Vigmund and Folkbern.
pages.known: The 'big houses' with a central hearth are those of the first Norse settlers; that one is still a dealer's house in 793 is the game's guess (?). 'Deal with whoever sits in the biggest house'. The dealer Vigmund and the pen are the silver road chain's; captives as a thing sold east.

pages.title: The bead-maker's shop
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Aldeigjuborg. A low cabin with its door propped open for the heat.
pages.game: A workshop at Aldeigjuborg. A low cabin with its door propped open for the heat. Inside, a small clay hearth no bigger than a cooking fire, an iron rod, and a woman turning a blob of dark glass on the rod's end while she lays a thread of yellow round it. Finished beads hang drying on a line of bast like berries: blue, green, black, each with a ring of white and a dot, so that it looks back at you. Hot glass, singed hair. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and haggle the price. Found here: Milava.
pages.known: The beads bought furs. The maker and how she learned are invented.

later.text: The bead-maker's shop of the 780s to the end of the 830s, making glass eye beads by an Arab low-heat method.
It stands until about 839.

pages.title: The old workshop
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Aldeigjuborg. The oldest roof in the place, black with sixty winters of soot. A stone-lined forge, a block with an anvil let into it, tongs and hammers of a dozen sizes hung in order on pegs, and clay moulds stacked by the wall.
pages.game: A smithy at Aldeigjuborg. The oldest roof in the place, black with sixty winters of soot. A stone-lined forge, a block with an anvil let into it, tongs and hammers of a dozen sizes hung in order on pegs, and clay moulds stacked by the wall. On a shelf above the door sits a bronze man the length of a finger, with two curved horns rising from his head and meeting above it. Charcoal, hot iron, and the hiss of the quenching tub. What is done here: mend the boat, buy ship's tools, take an order, fit her out and trade riddles. Found here: Audvald.
pages.known: The Scandinavian workshop of the 750s in the oldest layer, with a smith's tool hoard (some 26 pieces is not checked (?)) and the small bronze finial of a man with a horned head-dress in the Vendel style, called 'the singing Odin'; casting moulds. The horns are a head-dress on a figure: nobody wore such a helmet. That a smith works the same ground through every age is the game's simplification (?).

pages.title: The fort at the Lyubsha mouth
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Aldeigjuborg. The first thing a skipper passes: on the right bank, two kilometres below the town, a rampart of stone and earth with a palisade on top, standing over the mouth of a stream.
pages.game: A wall at Aldeigjuborg. The first thing a skipper passes: on the right bank, two kilometres below the town, a rampart of stone and earth with a palisade on top, standing over the mouth of a stream. Boats lie under it, and men on the wall watch you go by without waving. Smoke from a few roofs inside. Each year the stream's mouth is a little siltier and the boats lie a little further out. What is done here: hire a pilot, ask the keeper, give a gift, ask the news and wait for wind. Found here: Budimir.
pages.known: The Lyubsha fort: built about 700 by Slavs on an older Finnic palisaded site, a stone-and-earth rampart, over 1,000 finds with ship rivets, moulds and both Norse and local arrowheads. That the river pilots live here is invented.

later.text: Given up in the later 800s as the lake fell and the Lyubsha silted.

pages.title: The river-boat bank below the rocks
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Aldeigjuborg. Above the last houses the river narrows between limestone banks, and from the bend comes a steady noise like wind in pines: the first of the rapids.
pages.game: A ferry at Aldeigjuborg. Above the last houses the river narrows between limestone banks, and from the bend comes a steady noise like wind in pines: the first of the rapids. Here the river boats load. Long shallow hulls and dugouts widened with a plank a side, men up to the thigh in brown water passing bales hand to hand, a line of porters going up the bank path with wax on their shoulders. Nothing with a keel goes further. What is done here: hire a pilot, hire carriers, cross over, buy a boat, order a ship and use your store. Found here: Budimir.
pages.known: Sea ships stop here and goods go on by river boat; rapids above the town, hard at low water, drowned by the dam of 1926. River pilots are a fair inference, not a find.

pages.title: The posts on the bank
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Aldeigjuborg. A little way from the houses, where the bank is highest, a tall post stands in the ground with a face cut in it, and smaller posts round it.
pages.game: A shrine at Aldeigjuborg. A little way from the houses, where the bank is highest, a tall post stands in the ground with a face cut in it, and smaller posts round it. Bread, an onion, a strip of dried meat and a bowl lie at its foot, and the dogs have been at them. No roof and no fence. A trader with his cap in his hand is talking to the big post in a low voice, as a man talks to a creditor. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots, make a vow and swear an oath.

later.text: Heathen through the 800s and 900s, Thor's hammers after 865.

No temple or holy place is recorded here: this one is invented (?), after what an envoy of the caliph saw among the Rus traders on the Volga in 922, who laid bread, meat, onions and drink before a tall wooden post and asked it for a buyer with much silver who would not haggle.
After 988 nobody swears by the old gods in the prince's towns.
It stands until about 988.

pages.title: The tall mounds
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Aldeigjuborg. Along the river below the town stand steep round hills too regular to be hills, grass-grown, the tallest as high as five men and seen from the water long before the roofs.
pages.game: A mound at Aldeigjuborg. Along the river below the town stand steep round hills too regular to be hills, grass-grown, the tallest as high as five men and seen from the water long before the roofs. Nobody builds near them. Cattle graze the lower slopes and will not go to the top. From the tallest you can see the river both ways, the far grave-field, and on a clear day a pale line that is the lake. What is done here: make an offering, have him remembered, make a vow, cast the lots and trade riddles.
pages.known: The sopki, the tall mounds along the Volkhov.

later.text: One, about 10 m high, is called Oleg's Grave: a third of it was dug in 1820 and gave burnt bone, a two-barbed spearhead of the 700s or early 800s and iron scraps, so it is older than the prince it is named for.

pages.title: The Northmen's street and the big house
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Aldeigjuborg. A plank-laid lane along the left bank of the small river, houses gable-end to the water, each with its boat below.
pages.game: A lodging at Aldeigjuborg. A plank-laid lane along the left bank of the small river, houses gable-end to the water, each with its boat below. Halfway along stands a house twice the length of the others with a carved door-post and a bench outside worn hollow. Inside, a long fire, sleeping benches with men's sea chests under them, a tafl board scratched on a plank, and a host who knows what ship each chest came off. Fish, wet wool, ale. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer, ask the news and listen for talk, and more.
pages.known: Varangian Street (Varyazhskaya) on the left bank of the Ladozhka.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/aldeigjuborg.md (the research this file is built on; its doubts are kept, marked (?), and its section 8, what must not be claimed, is followed)

later.text: Varangian Street (Varyazhskaya) on the left bank of the Ladozhka, settled by the Northmen who took the town about the 830s-840s.
The 'big house' of 881, read as a merchants' inn, with a rune stick beside a large Norse-style house.
Before 881 the lodging is an ordinary house on the lane (invented).
A very large building about 894.
In its early 900s layers: lustre pottery from Mesopotamia and a birch-bark roll with a ship drawn on it.

pages.title: The grave-field on the far bank
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Aldeigjuborg. Across the great river, on a low terrace opposite the town, a dozen small mounds in rough grass.
pages.game: A graveyard at Aldeigjuborg. Across the great river, on a low terrace opposite the town, a dozen small mounds in rough grass. On some the turf is new and the ground round them is black with a pyre's ash; boat rivets lie rusting where a hull was burned. At the edge one mound is larger and has a timber chamber under it. In later years flat graves without mounds lie beside them, heads to the west. What is done here: cross over, bury a man, have him remembered and make an offering.
pages.known: Plakun: thirteen mounds counted in 1940; the early graves cremations; Mound 11 a chamber grave of a man of 60 to 70 with a horse, perhaps a Christian; at least five incomers from the Mälar country by strontium. Boat rivets in some mounds are not checked (?).

later.text: Plakun: thirteen mounds counted in 1940, in use about 850 to 950 (Mikhailov: only from the 900s).
Unmounded Christian graves of the 1000s-1100s.

later.text: On the tongue of land between the small river and the great one: in the 870s a palisade and a gate; from about 900 a wall of grey flagstone laid dry, eight metres high, with men walking the top and a square hatch far up the river face where a beam swings out to hoist bales from a boat below.
After the burning of 997 it is timber again behind a ditch, and the old stone shows black at its foot.

The wooden fort of the 870s on the point between Ladozhka and Volkhov (Kirpichnikov); the stone fort of about 900, flagstone without mortar, walls about 8 m, a fighting walk 2 m wide and a loading hatch 7 m up the river wall; broken in 997; wood again in the early 1000s behind a ditch.

pages.title: The werf
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Andoverpis. A blunt point of firm sand pushed out into a wide grey-brown river, with three or four boats grounded along it and mud shining on either side where the inlets cut back.
pages.game: A landing at Andoverpis. A blunt point of firm sand pushed out into a wide grey-brown river, with three or four boats grounded along it and mud shining on either side where the inlets cut back. Behind, a low rise with thatch and one thread of smoke; across the water, a flat green line and nothing. The tide sucks at the stakes, a pig squeals somewhere inland, and the air is river mud and peat smoke. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper and scrape and tar. Found here: Adalwin.
pages.known: Bellens 2021: the ragged bank of points and inlets, the chief point the werf; stakes and jetties are his supposition, none were dug. The tide range of 2.5 to 3.5 m is a guess.
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf

pages.title: The toll post
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Andoverpis. A squared oak post at the head of the werf with notches cut down one side, and a bench under a hide awning where a man sits with a tally stick and a small scale.
pages.game: A toll place at Andoverpis. A squared oak post at the head of the werf with notches cut down one side, and a bench under a hide awning where a man sits with a tally stick and a small scale. Every path up from the boats passes his knee. In the later years the bench is a timber toll house inside the bank, with a shuttered window on the landing. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, weigh the silver, hear the law and ask the news. Found here: Adalwin.
pages.known: The toll is in the charter of 726, a third of it the church's (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845). The post and bench are ours. A toll house in the castle: Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Het Steen (date not given).
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf

pages.title: Saint Peter and Saint Paul
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Andoverpis. A small timber church with a shingled roof on the highest of the sand, its west door facing the river and a wooden cross by the path.
pages.game: A church at Andoverpis. A small timber church with a shingled roof on the highest of the sand, its west door facing the river and a wooden cross by the path. Inside it is dark and smells of tallow and a little old incense; two lamps hang before the altar and one is not lit. A chest with an iron hasp stands against the north wall. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, read a book, have it copied, fund a work and ask the news. Found here: Hildulf.
pages.known: The church built by Amandus and given to Willibrord in 726, for incense and lights (Mertens and Torfs I). Its site is unknown: guesses are the later castle, the Koraalberg or under Saint Michael's (Bellens 2021). That it is of timber and stands on the rise is ours.
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf

pages.title: The comb-maker's lean-to
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Andoverpis. A lean-to of hurdles against the big house's south wall, open to the light.
pages.game: A workshop at Andoverpis. A lean-to of hurdles against the big house's south wall, open to the light. Stag skulls with the antlers still on them hang by their eye-holes from a rail; under them a man sits astride a bench with a fine saw, and the ground round his feet is white with chips and dust. Finished combs lie in a row on a board, teeth up, and it smells of scorched bone. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods, haggle the price and buy ship's tools. Found here: Liafgrim.
pages.known: Bellens 2021: 18 combs, 13 pin beaters, 11 whorls, and the whole chain of work from sawn stag skulls to finished comb, beginning before the rampart; the makers perhaps travelling men. The lean-to is ours.

pages.brief: A market at Andoverpis. The trodden ground between the werf and the first fence.
pages.game: A market at Andoverpis. The trodden ground between the werf and the first fence. Crates of grey Rhenish pots packed in straw stand open by a boat's bow; a woman holds two piglets by the hind legs; hides are pegged out, hair down, and somebody is always arguing over a measure of rye. There are no booths. When the tide makes, the boats lift and half the sellers go with them. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and hire carriers.
pages.known: Goods from Bellens 2021: Badorf ware and relief-band amphorae about 793; pork, old plough oxen, sheep, rye, wheat and barley from the back country.

later.text: No market is recorded before 1066: this is where goods change hands, and the name is ours.

pages.title: The house on posts
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Andoverpis. The biggest roof in the place: a long timber house with two great posts at its middle and a door wide enough for a cask.
pages.game: An ale-house at Andoverpis. The biggest roof in the place: a long timber house with two great posts at its middle and a door wide enough for a cask. One wall plank is curved, with a row of old rivet holes along it. Inside, a fire on the floor, benches, a vat under a cloth, and split tally sticks hanging in bunches from a rafter. It smells of malt, smoke and wet wool. This is the ale-house; in later years it is one of a row. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, lodge ashore, throw dice, trade riddles, hire a hand, buy stores and use your store. Found here: Ermentrud.
pages.known: Reused ship's timber in the oldest houses (Van de Walle). That ale is brewed and sold in it is ours.

later.text: Bellens 2021: a post-built house of 770-900 on the south plot, two deep posts and stake rows.

What is done here: cross over, ask the news, listen for talk and hire a pilot.
pages.known: A ferry crossed the mouth of the Schijn at Dambrugge toward Merksem; later it was the abbey of Lobbes's (?). The low peat of the Schijn delta: Bellens 2021.

At the field's edge stands a round pen of thirty pointed stakes, hardly wider than a man is tall twice over, with a sow and her young in it. Open country beyond: meadow, few trees, a boy with a stick. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, haggle the price and give a gift.
pages.known: Bellens 2021: the dark layer of grey sand full of worn Roman sherds, worked from Roman times into the early 9th century; a round pen just under 4 m across of some thirty pointed stakes; pig bones 46 in a hundred.

pages.known: Bellens 2021: two burials of the 9th century on the Koraalberg, probably more, perhaps a chapel (his proposal); outside the later rampart.

A small boat lies on her side on rollers with two strakes off; a man with an adze works at a plank laid over trestles, and old ship's timbers are stacked under a hurdle to be used again. Wood chips, the knock of a mallet, a pot of tar warming. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Bellens 2021: the inlets between the points are the later town ditches (ruien); carpenters, and ship's timber reused in houses. No ship or yard has been found: the yard is ours.

pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen

pages.game: A wall at Andoverpis. A grass bank twice a man's height and as wide as a house is long, curving from the river round the houses and back to the river, with a row of posts along its crest. At its inner foot a path of split logs runs dry over the mud; a smith's hammer rings somewhere behind the wattle and hides hang on the fences. What is done here: fund a work, buy a plot, buy ship's tools, mend the boat, call witnesses and ask the keeper. Found here: Hartbert.
pages.known: Bellens 2021: post rows, then a bank of turves and spoil 13.5 m wide, D-shaped and open to the river, still 4 m high in 1887; corduroy paths 1.5 m and 1 m wide; over 12 kg of smith's slag; leather work after the rampart. Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Burchtzone.

later.text: After the year 1000 grey stone begins to stand along its outer face.

pages.game: A hall at Andoverpis. A long timber hall in the middle of the ground inside the bank, its door posts carved, shields on the wall inside and a high seat at the far end under a hanging. Armed men lounge at the door; a clerk with a wax board sits by the hearth. Close by stands a small chapel of Saint Walburga, whom sailors call on in storms. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, bring a case, swear an oath, hear the law, show the charter and hold a feast.
pages.known: A toll house, a mint house and the margrave's timber hall in the castle, date not given (Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Het Steen); Saint Walburga's chapel mid-castle, probably 11th century (Bellens 2021); Walburga and sailors.

pages.title: The inlet under the rock
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Bebbanburg. A shallow tide inlet runs in behind a bar of sand at the north foot of the rock, and boats lie tilted on the wet sand below a wall of black stone that goes straight up into the light.
pages.game: A beach at Bebbanburg. A shallow tide inlet runs in behind a bar of sand at the north foot of the rock, and boats lie tilted on the wet sand below a wall of black stone that goes straight up into the light. Low grey islands show out to sea, and far up the shore to the north-west the long hump of the holy island. Gulls and terns scream, the surf drags on the bar, and the place smells of weed and tarred rope. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar and hire carriers. Found here: Bacga.
pages.known: A tidal inlet north of the gate, 'now cut off from the sea by the developing sand dunes', a harbour for shallow craft: Bamburgh Research Project, St Oswald's Gate. Nothing of 793 is recorded there (?).

pages.title: The cleft gate
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Bebbanburg. A cleft in the rock at its lowest point, wide enough at the top for two men and at the foot for one, with steps cut up through it and the stone underfoot worn as smooth as a bowl.
pages.game: A gate at Bebbanburg. A cleft in the rock at its lowest point, wide enough at the top for two men and at the foot for one, with steps cut up through it and the stone underfoot worn as smooth as a bowl. Spears lean in the shadow at the head of the stair and a man looks down between them. Behind him is a strip of sky and the gable of a timber hall. What is done here: ask the news, give a gift and call witnesses. Found here: Cuthgar.
pages.known: 'One hollowed entrance ascending in a wonderful manner by steps': Symeon, Historia regum 774 (Stevenson 1855). The cleft 3.4 m wide at the top and 1.6 m at the foot, 'the bedrock was worn smooth': Bamburgh Research Project, St Oswald's Gate. No toll is recorded: a stranger gives a gift, which is custom and not law.
