pages.brief: A storehouse at Bebbanburg. Inside the gate a long timber hall, twelve paces by seven, where the wardens sleep and the food-rents are tallied: sacks, tubs of butter, hides in bundles, a quern nobody has carried further.
pages.game: A storehouse at Bebbanburg. Inside the gate a long timber hall, twelve paces by seven, where the wardens sleep and the food-rents are tallied: sacks, tubs of butter, hides in bundles, a quern nobody has carried further. A trestle stands in the doorway with a balance on it and a bundle of notched sticks. It smells of wet wool and smoke, and somebody is always arguing about a count. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, use your store and buy stores. Found here: Eanwine.
pages.known: A timber hall of 12 m by 7 m by the gate, perhaps the gate wardens': Bamburgh Research Project. No market, toll or merchant is recorded here: the dealing with the household is the game's, as a king's rock lives on food-rents and gifts (?).

pages.title: The hall on the rock
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Bebbanburg. The lord's hall stands in the middle of the rock with its door to the south: a long roof, carved door-posts, benches down both walls and a hearth the length of three men.
pages.game: A hall at Bebbanburg. The lord's hall stands in the middle of the rock with its door to the south: a long roof, carved door-posts, benches down both walls and a hearth the length of three men. Shields hang over the benches and a carved stone seat stands at the upper end. On a feast it is full of noise and dogs; on other days two old men play at tables by the door and the wind hums in the thatch. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, hear the law, play tafl, trade riddles and pay the singer.
pages.known: Bede's 'royal city'; the stone chair.

later.text: Timber halls and a piece of a carved sandstone chair of about 800: Bamburgh Research Project (West Ward).
Which king or lord sat here in a given year is not recorded before 913.

pages.title: Saint Peter's and the hand
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Bebbanburg. A small stone church on the highest ground, sixteen paces long, lime-washed, with narrow windows that let in bars of sea light.
pages.game: A church at Bebbanburg. A small stone church on the highest ground, sixteen paces long, lime-washed, with narrow windows that let in bars of sea light. On the altar's north side stands a silver case under a cloth; when the priest lifts the cloth on a feast there is a hand in it, wrapped, pale and whole. Wax smoke, the cold of stone, and far below the sea working at the rock. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, take sanctuary and swear an oath. Found here: Wilgar.
pages.known: 'A fair and costly shrine. In this, wrapped in a pall, lies the uncorrupted right hand of St. Oswald': Symeon, Historia regum 774 (Stevenson 1855); a silver case: Bede III.6. A building of about 16 m by 8 m under the later chapel: Bamburgh Research Project, Inner Ward.

later.text: The arm was carried off to Peterborough between 1006 and 1055: Victoria County History, Northamptonshire 2.

pages.hint: A well, not yet seen

pages.game: A well at Bebbanburg. At the west end, on the highest point, a square mouth in the bare stone with a windlass over it and a rope worn pale. A bucket takes a long time going down and comes up cold and sweet. Women wait their turn with yokes and talk; from here a man sees the whole shore, the flats, the holy island and every sail between. What is done here: listen for talk, buy stores and ask the news.
pages.known: 'A well, excavated with extraordinary labour, sweet to drink, and very pure to the sight': Symeon, Historia regum 774 (Stevenson 1855). 145 feet through the rock: bamburghcastle.com.

pages.game: A smithy at Bebbanburg. Cobbled paths between low timber sheds along the west side of the rock, a stone-lined runnel of water, charcoal in heaps under a lean-to. One forge burns white and a man twists rods of iron together like a woman plaiting hair; in the next shed somebody small works at a bench with gold wire and a lamp. Hammer-scale crunches underfoot and the air tastes of hot iron. What is done here: take an order, buy ship's tools, buy from makers, test the silver and mend the boat. Found here: Garmund.
pages.known: Cobbled paths, timber halls, a possible smithy, a stone-lined water channel, hammerscale from high-heat welding and scraps of decorated gold: Bamburgh Research Project, West Ward and Trench 3 (2010). Two pattern-welded swords were found on the rock, one welded of six strands.

pages.brief: A lodging at Bebbanburg. A scatter of thatched houses and byres on the green ground south-west of the rock, a pond, geese, a hurdle fold full of sheep come in for the rent.
pages.game: A lodging at Bebbanburg. A scatter of thatched houses and byres on the green ground south-west of the rock, a pond, geese, a hurdle fold full of sheep come in for the rent. One house has a bush tied over the door and a bench outside it. The rock fills the sky behind every roof, and on a still day the forge can be heard down here like a slow bell. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, listen for talk, hire a hand, buy stores, throw dice and buy from makers. Found here: Muirenn.

pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen

pages.game: A shrine at Bebbanburg. A small wooden church at the edge of the vill, twice rebuilt after fire. One post in its west wall is older and darker than the rest, scorched and not burnt, and polished at the height of a hand. People cut slivers from it for the sick and drop them in water. Inside it is dim and smells of old thatch and tallow. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, see the leech, make a vow and have him remembered.
pages.known: The church where Aidan died on 31 August 651 and the post fire could not burn, from which chips were taken to heal the sick: Bede III.17 (paraphrased).

pages.game: A graveyard at Bebbanburg. A hollow in the sand hills three hundred paces south of the rock, out of the wind, with low mounds in rows and here and there a stone set on edge. Marram grass hisses. Nothing is written on anything, but the woman who tends it knows each one and where they came from, and few of them came from here. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered and give alms.
pages.known: The Bowl Hole: 91 skeletons, mostly of the 7th and 8th centuries, few grave goods, few who grew up near by (western Scotland, Ireland, Scandinavia, the Mediterranean): Bamburgh Research Project, Bowl Hole. Whether it was still used in 793 is not settled, and its end is our guess (?).

pages.title: Farne, two miles out
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Bebbanburg. A flat black island with white-streaked cliffs on its seaward side, a round wall of turf and stones, and inside it a cell with no window but the sky.
pages.game: A shrine at Bebbanburg. A flat black island with white-streaked cliffs on its seaward side, a round wall of turf and stones, and inside it a cell with no window but the sky. Eider ducks sit on their eggs by the path and do not move for a man. Seals lie on the skerries beyond, the tide runs between the rocks like a river, and the rock of Bebbanburg stands small and dark on the shore behind. What is done here: make a vow, wait for wind, take sanctuary and have him remembered.
pages.known: Farne 'nearly two miles from the city': Bede III.16. Cuthbert's cell, with a wall so high he saw only the sky: Bede, Life of Cuthbert (from memory (?)).

In front, clinker boats nose to the planks and bales of fur lie stacked under hides; behind, plank roofs climb the slope in rows and smoke stands over them; to the left the bare fort rock drops sheer into the bay. Mallets, gulls, a dog, and the smell of tar, fish and wet birch. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, pay the toll, wait for wind, hire a pilot and buy stores.

pages.game: A market at Birka. Narrow lanes run up from the shore between wattle fences, planks laid over the mud, pigs and dogs at the refuse. In front a spare man sits in his doorway with a folding scale on his knee; behind him small plank and clay houses, eight paces by five, each with smoke seeping from the roof. There is no square: the selling is done in doorways and on the planks, and the soil underfoot is black. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods, listen for talk and buy a plot. Found here: Holmfast and Fastlög.
pages.known: The Black Earth: about 7 hectares of dark soil, houses about 8 by 5 m in rows, wattle-fenced plots, planks over the mud, refuse in the lanes; no market square is known. The plots are the king's ground and holders pay him a due (Magnus).

A Gotlander mends a net, two Wends sit by grey pots of honey, a Frisian airs cloth on a pole. In the evening the cooking fires make one line of smoke and four tongues are spoken at once. What is done here: lodge ashore, rent store room, use your store, ask the news, throw dice and hire a hand. Found here: Holmfast.
pages.known: Merchants and strangers lodging among the craftsmen's households (Magnus 1999); Danes, Northmen, Slavs and Prussians each year; honey in grey Slav pots (Magnus). Booths of turf and sailcloth are the ordinary northern kind and are not dug here (?).

In one a caster breaks a clay mould off a hot brooch; in the next a man saws elk antler into plates and the dust lies white on his knees; a woman winds molten glass on an iron rod and drops beads into ash. Charcoal smoke, burnt horn, the tap of small hammers. What is done here: take an order, buy from makers, try the goods and buy ship's tools. Found here: Ragnvi.
pages.known: Bronze-casters by the shore with moulds for oval and equal-armed brooches, comb-makers in elk antler, bead-makers (Magnus 1999); the first town packed with workshops, nothing over 20 square metres.

Bundles of bar iron from the forest country lean against the fence, still tied with the bast they were sledged in with. A smith draws out rivets one after another and drops them hissing in a trough; a boy works the bellows with his foot. Locks and keys hang on a peg to show what can be had. What is done here: buy ship's tools, fit her out, buy from makers and take an order.
pages.known: Smiths among the town's crafts; iron from the forest country to the north-west, sledged in over winter; many locks and keys. The smith here is the role forge's; no smith of Birka is named.

pages.title: The slip in the hollow

pages.game: A boat yard at Birka. A stone-lined hollow on the shore with a timber slip running into the water, and a half-planked hull on it, pale new oak against black tar. Rivets lie in a wooden bowl, whetstones of grey slate by the adze, shavings ankle deep. Two wrights sight along a strake and say nothing; a third heats tar and the smell reaches the jetties. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat and fit her out.
pages.known: A stone-lined hollow on the old shore with a timber slip, used and unused boat rivets, slate whetstones and woodworking tools, announced in 2022. Its years of use are not given (?): the game keeps it for the whole life of the town.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 975.

pages.title: The brewing-woman's house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Birka. A house like the others but with benches along both walls and the hearth kept high.
pages.game: An ale-house at Birka. A house like the others but with benches along both walls and the hearth kept high. Skippers and craftsmen sit knee to knee with horn cups; a board with glass playing pieces lies between two of them and a third gives advice nobody asked for. By the fire a hoarse man speaks a verse and stops short of its end. Ale, mead that smells of lime flowers, smoke in the eyes. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, trade riddles, play tafl, throw dice, pay the singer and hire a hand. Found here: Grimulf.
pages.known: An ale-house is the game's; glass playing pieces from Birka's graves; lime-flower pollen, so honey from south or east of the Baltic (Magnus 1999).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 975.

pages.title: The open plain
pages.hint: A meeting place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A meeting place at Birka. A level field above the town, grazed short, with a low stage of planks at one side and beside it a shelter of cut branches for the chief men.
pages.game: A meeting place at Birka. A level field above the town, grazed short, with a low stage of planks at one side and beside it a shelter of cut branches for the chief men. When the thing meets the field is full of standing men and the talk is a roar; a white cloth is spread and the lot sticks are thrown on it where all can see. The rest of the year it is sheep and wind. What is done here: hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, swear an oath and cast the lots.
pages.known: 'An open plain' with a stage and a shelter of branches, near enough to Herigar's church for a lame man to be carried there (Rimbert 19); lots cast in the open before any great decision (Rimbert 19, 26, 27); 'the control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king' (Rimbert 26, Robinson 1921). Where the field lay is not known.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 975.

pages.title: The long house on the terrace
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Birka. Above the town to the east, on a levelled terrace, stands a long house twenty paces from gable to gable, older than most of the roofs below it.
pages.game: A hall at Birka. Above the town to the east, on a levelled terrace, stands a long house twenty paces from gable to gable, older than most of the roofs below it. Inside, a long fire, benches, a seat with carved posts for the king's man, shields on the wall. From the door one looks down over every roof and jetty, and north across the water to the next island, where the king's own hall stands above its harbour. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath and show the charter.
pages.known: Longhouses of a better sort on terraces east of the town, one 20 m long and built about when the town began (Magnus 1999). That the prefect kept it is the game's guess (?). The king's hall at Hovgården on Adelsö is the diggers' reading, not Rimbert's; the king's gift-giving at table is Rimbert 26.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 975.

pages.title: Herigar's church
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Birka. A small timber house on the prefect's own ground, set east and west. Inside, an earth floor, a table with a linen cloth, one lamp.
pages.game: A church at Birka. A small timber house on the prefect's own ground, set east and west. Inside, an earth floor, a table with a linen cloth, one lamp. A dozen people stand close: two or three townsmen, a rich old woman on a stool, and thin men and women with cropped hair who weep when the priest speaks Latin. When there is no priest the door is still swept. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, read a book, ask the news and take sanctuary. Found here: Frideburg.
pages.known: Herigar 'built a church on his own ancestral property' (Rimbert 11). None has been found (Arbman looked in 1932-34: Magnus 1999); the game shows one building for all three.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Gautbert's church from about 832 (14).
A small timber house on the prefect's own ground, set east and west, with a plain wooden cross over the door and no bell before the 850s.
A hall for prayer on a plot the king granted in 852 and a house bought for the priest (28).
It stands until about 866.

pages.title: The grave field east of the town
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Birka. On the higher ground behind the town the mounds lie as thick as molehills under birch and pine, hundreds of them, low and green, the newest still raw earth.
pages.game: A mound at Birka. On the higher ground behind the town the mounds lie as thick as molehills under birch and pine, hundreds of them, low and green, the newest still raw earth. A woman sets a small flat loaf on one and speaks to it as to a neighbour. Further up a single great standing stone marks a grave older than the town. It is quiet here; the mallets below sound far off. What is done here: have him remembered, bury a man, make an offering and cast the lots.
pages.known: Hemlanden, over 1,600 mounds; some 3,000 graves in six fields; most burnt and laid in a pot under a mound, with small flat loaves on the pyre (64 found); the dead asked for counsel at the mound (Magnus 1999). The standing stone on a grave of the early 700s stood on the fort rock in sight of the town; the game sets it at the edge of this field's view.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The fort rock
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Birka. The island's highest point: bare grey rock that falls thirty metres sheer into the bay on the west, closed on the land side by a half-ring bank of stone and earth with a timber breastwork.
pages.game: A wall at Birka. The island's highest point: bare grey rock that falls thirty metres sheer into the bay on the west, closed on the land side by a half-ring bank of stone and earth with a timber breastwork. A watchman stands by a heap of dry wood, looking north to the king's island. What is done here: ask the keeper, ask the news, play tafl, throw dice and give a gift.
pages.known: Borg: a bank about 350 m long with a timber breastwork and three gates, one called the King's Gate, the cliff closing the west; built in two stages, the first slight; watchmen could signal to Hovgården. The garrison terrace, about 50 men, horse and foot, with mail, scale armour, locks, comb cases and nothing of women's.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/birka.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: From 900 on, a hall of fighting men stands on the slope below, and horsemen in belted coats of eastern cut come and go by the King's Gate.
The garrison terrace, about 50 men, horse and foot, with mail, scale armour, locks, comb cases and nothing of women's, is tenth century (?): the game opens it from 900.
It stands until about 975.

pages.title: The bank under the wall
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Burdigala. A long bend of brown river, wide as a lake, and a bank of grey mud and gravel under a high stone wall with round towers.
pages.game: A landing at Burdigala. A long bend of brown river, wide as a lake, and a bank of grey mud and gravel under a high stone wall with round towers. Boats sit canted on the mud at low water: flat river barges, small fishing boats, now and then a sea-going hull. Planks are laid from the gravel to the firm ground. Behind the wall, to the north, a row of tall white columns stands against the sky. Gulls, the slap of the tide turning, the smell of mud and pitch. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper and scrape and tar. Found here: Amantius.
pages.known: The Roman basin inside the wall silted from the 6th century and work moved to the river bank; the river about 700 m wide at the crescent bend; no quay of these years is known, so this is a bank and the table's 'quay' is unproven. The planks are assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The water gate and Saint Peter's
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Burdigala. A dark arch in the wall where a stream runs out across the mud, with a small old church of patched stone hard beside it, its door open to the river.
pages.game: A church at Burdigala. A dark arch in the wall where a stream runs out across the mud, with a small old church of patched stone hard beside it, its door open to the river. Through the arch a reedy hollow shows where ships once lay inside the city. A man with a tally stick sits on a block by the gate; women wash at the stream. A cracked bell, wet stone, candle smoke. What is done here: pay the toll, hear Mass, give alms, make a vow and ask the news.
pages.known: Porta Navigera, the water gate by Saint Peter's, at the old harbour mouth; Saint Peter's is the harbour church in Gregory of Tours and is then unnamed until 1173. No toll is recorded for Bordeaux: the man at the gate is the game's (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The wine sellers by the old harbour
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Burdigala. An open space of trodden earth inside the water gate, on the rim of the silted basin, with Roman paving showing through in places.
pages.game: A market at Burdigala. An open space of trodden earth inside the water gate, on the rim of the silted basin, with Roman paving showing through in places. Casks lie on their sides under lean-to roofs against old walls; a woman tips a dipper for a buyer to taste; sacks of grey salt and strings of dried fish hang at one end. Vine smoke, sour must, flies, the knock of a mallet on a hoop. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy from makers and listen for talk. Found here: Felix.
pages.known: No market, market day or fair is recorded for Bordeaux in these years: the place is assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: Saint Andrew's, the bishop's church
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Burdigala. A long low church of small Roman stones and reused marble against the inside of the west wall, with a smaller church and a chapel close by it and a yard between where clerks walk.
pages.game: A minster at Burdigala. A long low church of small Roman stones and reused marble against the inside of the west wall, with a smaller church and a chapel close by it and a yard between where clerks walk. Inside it is dim, with one lamp before the altar and a cupboard of books chained shut. Singing at the hours; cold stone; wax. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, read a book, have it copied, take sanctuary, ask an audience and fund a work.
pages.known: Saint Andrew's by the west wall; rebuilt in the 11th century. The book cupboard is assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Saint Andrew's by the west wall, with Saint Mary's and Saint Helen's chapel in the immunity of 814.
Said to be wrecked in 848 and 864.

pages.title: The count's enclosure
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Burdigala. A walled yard inside the city with a gate you must knock at: a long hall with a tiled roof in poor repair, a chapel, a well with a stone rim, horses tied under a fig tree.
pages.game: A hall at Burdigala. A walled yard inside the city with a gate you must knock at: a long hall with a tiled roof in poor repair, a chapel, a well with a stone rim, horses tied under a fig tree. Men with spears sit in the shade and stand when the count's steward crosses. Dogs, horse dung, a smith's hammer somewhere behind. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, show the charter, hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, swear an oath and hold a feast. Found here: Seguin.
pages.known: The enclosure at Saint-Projet with a hall ('la Salle'), a chapel, the mint, gates and a well is known only from 11th- to 13th-century texts and the street plan and has never been dug: its date is open, and it is placed here in 793 as an assumption (?). Not the Ombrière, whose tower is first named in 1080.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The moneyer's bench, Burdigala
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Burdigala. A low room off the count's yard with a barred window: a block of oak with an iron die set in it, a second die in a man's fist, a hammer, a pan of blank silver discs and a scale hung from a beam.
pages.game: A mint at Burdigala. A low room off the count's yard with a barred window: a block of oak with an iron die set in it, a second die in a man's fist, a hammer, a pan of blank silver discs and a scale hung from a beam. Each blow rings like a small bell. Charcoal, hot metal, a boy sweeping the floor for clippings. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Bertric.
pages.known: No penny of Charles from Bordeaux in Prou; Louis the Pious BVRDIGALA in two lines; Lothar I BVRDICALA round a temple, 1.60 g; King Lothar (954-986) 'Burdegal'; then the counts' poor silver SANCHIVS (0.76 to 1.30 g), BERNARDV, GVILELMO. The mint lay in the Saint-Projet enclosure in later texts.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: No striking is assumed between 848 and 887 (?).

pages.title: The pillars
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Burdigala. Just outside the north wall, on the highest ground, two dozen white columns as tall as five houses stand in a square with no roof, carved figures along the top and sky between them.
pages.game: A shrine at Burdigala. Just outside the north wall, on the highest ground, two dozen white columns as tall as five houses stand in a square with no roof, carved figures along the top and sky between them. Goats graze inside. From the river they are the first thing seen of the city and the last thing lost. Wind in dry grass, jackdaws, warm stone. What is done here: have him remembered, trade riddles and wait for wind.
pages.known: The columns of a roofless Roman temple, 26 m high, 'seen from afar', 24 when whole and 17 still standing in 1669. Nobody worships here: the old gods are only ruins and a gate's name.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The Arenas
pages.hint: A quarry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A quarry at Burdigala. North-west of the wall a great oval of broken arches stands in the vines, taller than the city wall and open to the sky.
pages.game: A quarry at Burdigala. North-west of the wall a great oval of broken arches stands in the vines, taller than the city wall and open to the sky. Men with bars and wedges are prising squared blocks out of its lower tiers and sledging them away behind oxen. Brambles in the arena floor. Stone dust, the creak of a sledge, lizards on the warm blocks. What is done here: buy from makers, hire carriers and take an order.
pages.known: The ruined amphitheatre, 132 by 111 m, used as a stone quarry and called 'the Arenas' in the 10th century; not 'Palais Gallien', a name of 1367.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: Saint Seurin's among the graves
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Burdigala.
pages.game: A graveyard at Burdigala. Outside the west gate, the gate of Jove, a road runs through a field of the dead: stone coffins lying lid to lid in rows, some stacked, grass between them, and in the middle a low old church over the saint's tomb with its door worn hollow. Old women sell candles at the wall. Larks, a spade working, incense when the door opens. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, make a vow, hear Mass, give alms and see the leech.
pages.known: A burial church over Saint Seurin's tomb, first built about 450, in a grave field used from the 4th to the 13th century: 435 burials dug, 265 in stone coffins up to five deep, 70 in amphorae; rebuilt early in the 11th century. Porta Jovia is the west gate. The candle sellers and healing at the tomb are assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Canons about 990.

pages.title: Holy Cross in the marsh
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Burdigala. South of the wall a causeway of logs crosses reed and black water to a rise of dry ground beside a stream.
pages.game: An abbey at Burdigala. South of the wall a causeway of logs crosses reed and black water to a rise of dry ground beside a stream. In 793 there is an old oratory there with a sagging roof and one keeper; after the pagans, bare walls. Frogs, a mill wheel on the stream, new mortar. What is done here: give alms, lodge ashore, hear Mass, fund a work, buy from makers and read a book.
pages.known: Holy Cross south of the wall by the Eau Bourde: a Merovingian house where Mommolin, abbot of Fleury, died about 679; 'destroyed by the pagans'; rebuilt before 977 by Count William the Good for thirteen monks and Abbot Elis, with 'lands with vines'. What stood there in 793 is not known: the oratory with one keeper follows the old men's memory in the charter (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: From the 970s a new stone church, a cloister of thirteen monks, vines on the slope and a press-house.

pages.title: The house by the Broken Tower
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Burdigala. A long room built against the inside of the city wall where a tower has lost its top, the Roman stone for a back wall and a vine over the door.
pages.game: An ale-house at Burdigala. A long room built against the inside of the city wall where a tower has lost its top, the Roman stone for a back wall and a vine over the door. Benches, a cask on trestles, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the thatch. River men at one end, Gascons with their own knives at the other. Sour wine, onions, wet wool. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, pay the singer, hire a hand, lodge ashore and buy stores. Found here: Placidina.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: A 'Broken Tower' stood by a mill given to Saint Seurin between 1027 and 1043: the name is borrowed for 793 (?).

pages.title: The boat bank below the stream
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Burdigala. Downstream of the wall, where a second stream comes out through reeds, a slope of gravel with two hulls on it: a flat barge with new pale planks let into her side and a small boat upside down for pitching.
pages.game: A boat yard at Burdigala. Downstream of the wall, where a second stream comes out through reeds, a slope of gravel with two hulls on it: a flat barge with new pale planks let into her side and a small boat upside down for pitching. Oak logs from upriver lie half floated at the water's edge. An adze, a pitch pot bubbling, smoke blown flat along the bank. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Invented: no yard or shipman is recorded. The streams are the Devèze and the Peugue, at whose mouths the city lies. Oak rafted down the Garonne is assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The strand under the wall, Colonia
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Colonia. A long shelf of gravel and trodden mud between the brown river and a Roman wall eight metres high, its towers patterned in coloured stone.
pages.game: A landing at Colonia. A long shelf of gravel and trodden mud between the brown river and a Roman wall eight metres high, its towers patterned in coloured stone. Flat river boats lie nose-in with planks run ashore; tow ropes dry on stakes. Gulls, hammering from the smiths, and the smell of wet rope, dung and wood smoke. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper and scrape and tar. Found here: Wido.
pages.known: The east wall faces the river across low ground that was the Roman harbour, silted since the 2nd and 3rd centuries. Boats most likely lay along it; no quay is recorded (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

pages.title: The market on the old harbour ground
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Colonia. An open stretch of dark trampled earth between low thatched pit houses.
pages.game: A market at Colonia. An open stretch of dark trampled earth between low thatched pit houses. In front, tall pale jars with bands of clay ribbon stand in straw, casks lie on their sides, and black querns are stacked like loaves. Behind, the wall and the roofs of the bishop's church. Smoke, sour wine lees, pigs. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy from makers and ask the news. Found here: Meginher, Gerhild and Liutwin.
pages.known: Pit houses of the 5th to 7th centuries and a dark layer of dung, bone and craft waste under the later markets (the Heumarkt dig (?)). Badorf jars up to 70 cm for wine and oil.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: 'Mercatus coloniae' is first written in 922, 'forum' in 988.

pages.title: The river gate, Colonia
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Colonia. A Roman gate in the east wall, one of its arches walled up with rubble, the other worn smooth at cart-axle height.
pages.game: A gate at Colonia. A Roman gate in the east wall, one of its arches walled up with rubble, the other worn smooth at cart-axle height. A bench, a balance on a post, and a clerk with a wax tablet in the shade. Beyond the arch a straight paved street runs uphill between gardens and broken walls. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, hear the law and call witnesses. Found here: Hrotbert.
pages.known: Nine Roman gates.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: No toll rate and no toll man is recorded before 1066 (?): the bench is the game's. From 953 the toll is the archbishop's.

pages.title: The king's mint, Colonia
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Colonia. A stone room built into a Roman cellar near the bishop's hall, lit by a charcoal hearth.
pages.game: A mint at Colonia. A stone room built into a Roman cellar near the bishop's hall, lit by a charcoal hearth. A man sets a blank on an iron die fixed in a block, lays the upper die on it and strikes once. On the table: a small balance, a pan of clipped old pennies, a touchstone. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Hrotbert.
pages.known: Pennies of Charles for Colonia; the S COLONIA A type from Louis the Child (900-911) to Henry II (Münze des Monats, Münster, July 2017). Where the mint stood is not known (?). No moneyer is named: the pennies name king and city.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Pennies of Charles for Colonia, 771-794 (seen only in a search summary (?)).

pages.title: Saint Peter's, Colonia
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Colonia. The bishop's church in the north-east corner of the walls: a long plain stone hall with a tiled roof, half of it under scaffolding in most years.
pages.game: A minster at Colonia. The bishop's church in the north-east corner of the walls: a long plain stone hall with a tiled roof, half of it under scaffolding in most years. Inside it is cold and lamp-lit; boys chant at the east end and a scribe sits in the light of a west window with a book chest beside him. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, ask an audience, read a book, have it copied, make a vow, take sanctuary and fund a work. Found here: Hildebold.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: A church of about 800 burned some ten years later; the great church with a choir at each end was dedicated in 870 or 873, its nave 97.5 m. 175 books listed in 833.
From about 970 the Gero Cross hangs mid-nave.

pages.title: The smiths' row
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Colonia. A lane of open-fronted sheds along the foot of the wall, each with a hearth, a stone anvil block and a boy at the bellows.
pages.game: A smithy at Colonia. A lane of open-fronted sheds along the foot of the wall, each with a hearth, a stone anvil block and a boy at the bellows. Scythe blades, knives and boat nails hang in bunches. At the far end a shed is closed with hurdles, and it is the only quiet one. Charcoal, hot iron, scorched horn. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order and weigh the silver. Found here: Bero.
pages.known: Waste of metal, glass and bone working by the river (the Heumarkt dig (?)); swords among the Rhine's exports.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: It stands until about 900.

pages.title: The boat bank below Saint Kunibert's
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Colonia. North of the wall the bank shelves gently under a small stone church.
pages.game: A boat yard at Colonia. North of the wall the bank shelves gently under a small stone church. A flat-bottomed barge sits on rollers with her side planks off; two men split an oak log with wedges, and moss and tar for caulking wait in a trough. Chips underfoot, the sweet smell of green oak, a tar pot smoking. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and hire a hand.
pages.known: Saint Kunibert's on the bank north of the walls. River craft. No yard is recorded (?): placing it here is the game's.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Hired rowers in 1062 and merchants with their own ships in 1074.

pages.title: The Deutz crossing
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Colonia. A broad ferry of planks worked across the stream on sweeps, landing under the square stone fort of Deutz on the far side, eighteen towers against the morning light.
pages.game: A ferry at Colonia. A broad ferry of planks worked across the stream on sweeps, landing under the square stone fort of Deutz on the far side, eighteen towers against the morning light. At low water grey stumps of masonry show in a line across the river where the Romans' bridge stood (?). Wind, horses stamping on the deck. What is done here: cross over, ask the news, call witnesses and hear the law. Found here: Erkanbert and Wido.
pages.known: The fort of Deutz, 142 m square with 18 towers, a royal estate. The bridge of 310: whether any of it still stood is unknown (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Heribert's abbey in it from 1003.

pages.title: The ale-house in the tower
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Colonia. The ground floor of a Roman wall tower on the river side, its doorway knocked through at strand level.
pages.game: An ale-house at Colonia. The ground floor of a Roman wall tower on the river side, its doorway knocked through at strand level. A fire on a stone hearth in the middle, smoke going up into the hollow tower, benches round the curve of the wall, a tub of ale and a row of pale Badorf cups. Boatmen, a dice cup, a dog. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, trade riddles, pay the singer, hire a hand, lodge ashore and buy stores. Found here: Adaltrud.
pages.known: Nineteen towers on the wall. The ale-house is the game's (?); people lived and worked on the river strip from the 5th century.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

pages.title: The Golden Saints
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Colonia. Outside the north-west corner of the wall, among Roman tombs and vegetable plots, an old oval hall of brick and stone with deep round niches.
pages.game: A church at Colonia. Outside the north-west corner of the wall, among Roman tombs and vegetable plots, an old oval hall of brick and stone with deep round niches. Inside, the vault still shows gold glass in patches where the lamp reaches. Graves crowd up to the walls outside. Quiet, crows, cold stone and wax. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, bury a man and have him remembered. Found here: Erkanbert.
pages.known: Saint Gereon: a late Roman oval hall of about 350-365, 'at the Golden Saints' in Gregory of Tours. Burial by the saints outside the walls in the old Roman cemeteries.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Hildebold's grave from 818.

pages.title: Saint Mary's on the temple mound
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Colonia. In the south of the town a church stands on a great squared platform of Roman stone higher than a man, reached by a ramp.
pages.game: A church at Colonia. In the south of the town a church stands on a great squared platform of Roman stone higher than a man, reached by a ramp. From its door you look over the wall to the river and the boats. Inside, a plain stone coffin lies before the altar with a lamp that is never let go out. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, have him remembered, ask the news and see the leech.
pages.known: Plectrude's church and grave (she died after 717) on the podium of the Capitoline temple. Whether women kept the church and tended the sick there in 793 is not known (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Rebuilt 1049-1065, its carved wooden doors survive.

pages.title: Saint Martin's on the island
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Colonia. A new stone church and a cluster of timber buildings on the rise that was once an island in the Roman harbour, right above the market.
pages.game: An abbey at Colonia. A new stone church and a cluster of timber buildings on the rise that was once an island in the Roman harbour, right above the market. Monks with their hair shaved across the front of the head in the old Irish way (?) go between church and guest house, speaking Latin with an accent nobody here can place. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, lodge ashore, read a book, have it copied, ask the news and trade riddles. Found here: Bruno.
pages.known: Irish abbots Minnborinus, Kilian (1003), Helias (1040), Aaron (1052), Molanus (1061). The two articles differ on when the Irish came. The Irish tonsure so late is a guess (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/colonia.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows; its own references are repeated here where used.

later.text: Bruno's chapter of about 960 over Roman warehouses.
Irish abbots Minnborinus (died 986), Kilian (1003), Helias (1040), Aaron (1052), Molanus (1061).
Marianus Scotus there about 1056.

pages.title: The bank below the church
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Daventre. A sloping bank of sand and trodden mud, boats drawn up bow first and two barges moored to stakes; behind them the sand ridge with its row of thatched houses, and to the right the wooden church on its dune.
pages.game: A landing at Daventre. A sloping bank of sand and trodden mud, boats drawn up bow first and two barges moored to stakes; behind them the sand ridge with its row of thatched houses, and to the right the wooden church on its dune. Across the brown river lies the Worp, flat, green and empty. It smells of tar, wet rope and smoked eel; in May there are carts on it from end to end. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, hire a pilot and buy stores. Found here: Brunger.

pages.title: Lebuin's church
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Daventre. A plank church with a thatched roof on a river dune, the third on the spot; the posts of the south wall are newer than the rest and stand a stride further out.
pages.game: A church at Daventre. A plank church with a thatched roof on a river dune, the third on the spot; the posts of the south wall are newer than the rest and stand a stride further out. Inside it is dark, one lamp over a stone slab in the floor on the south side; Franks stand north of the slab and Saxons south. A hand bell, wet thatch and tallow. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, take sanctuary and fund a work. Found here: Liudbod.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: Wooden until 882, stone under Bishop Balderic in the 10th century.
It stands until about 1039.

pages.title: Saint Lebuin's basilica
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Daventre. Grey tuff walls higher than anything else on the river: three aisles on round columns, two transepts, a square westwork toward the bank.
pages.game: A minster at Daventre. Grey tuff walls higher than anything else on the river: three aisles on round columns, two transepts, a square westwork toward the bank. Steps go down into a crypt where lamps burn before the relics of Lebuin and Marchelm. Canons sing the hours; masons are still working on the north side, where the bishop's palace is going up. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, read a book, bury a man and fund a work.
pages.known: The chapter of twenty canons and a provost is mid 11th century.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The churchyard
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Daventre. Open trodden ground between the church and the houses, graves marked with posts along the church side.
pages.game: A market at Daventre. Open trodden ground between the church and the houses, graves marked with posts along the church side. After Mass and on feast days people set out what they have on cloths and cart tails: eels in baskets, honey in crocks, a horse held by its halter, pots from the Rhine. Saxon and Frankish are spoken across the same cloth, slowly. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, listen for talk and ask the news.
pages.known: The square by the church is still the Grote Kerkhof, the great churchyard. An early market is only supposed, so that it was held here is the game's (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The crossing to the Worp
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Daventre. A flat ferry barge on a pole and two oars, nosed into the east bank beside a post with a horn hanging on it.
pages.game: A ferry at Daventre. A flat ferry barge on a pole and two oars, nosed into the east bank beside a post with a horn hanging on it. The far side is low grass with a cart track going west toward the heath, and upstream of it, small against the trees, the roof of Lebuin's chapel at Wilp. In late summer sandbars show and the ferryman wades the horses over. What is done here: cross over, ask the news and hire a pilot. Found here: Thancric.
pages.known: The ferry itself is invented; capitularies allow a toll only where a ferry or bridge gives help.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The host's ground
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Daventre. A sandy field on the ridge north of the houses, grazed bare. From Easter to midsummer it holds horse lines, ox carts wheel to wheel, stacked sacks under hides and a count's man with a wax tablet at a trestle.
pages.game: A field at Daventre. A sandy field on the ridge north of the houses, grazed bare. From Easter to midsummer it holds horse lines, ox carts wheel to wheel, stacked sacks under hides and a count's man with a wax tablet at a trestle. Smoke of cooking fires, dung, and a smith's boy going from cart to cart with a bucket of nails. What is done here: take an order, haggle the price and ask the news.
pages.known: The field is invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: It stands until about 805.

pages.title: The forge on the bank
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Daventre. An open-sided shed at the south end of the bank, its thatch black above the hearth.
pages.game: A smithy at Daventre. An open-sided shed at the south end of the bank, its thatch black above the hearth. Bars of dark iron from the heath lie stacked by the door like firewood; kegs of rivets stand in a row. Hammer, bellows, the hiss of the trough, and charcoal smoke that follows you down the bank. What is done here: buy ship's tools, buy from makers, take an order and fit her out. Found here: Einbert.

pages.title: Hathugard's ale-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Daventre. The last house on the ridge toward the bank, a low door, a bush on a pole above it.
pages.game: An ale-house at Daventre. The last house on the ridge toward the bank, a low door, a bush on a pole above it. Two benches along a hearth in the middle of the floor, a brewing tub in the corner, cattle heard through the wattle at the far end in the Saxon way. The woman at the tub looks at every stranger's hands and boots before she looks at his face. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, lodge ashore, throw dice, trade riddles and hire a hand. Found here: Hathugard and Brunger.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: It stands until about 806.

pages.title: The houses on the ridge
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Daventre. A single row of timber houses along the top of a sand ridge, end on to the river, each with a yard, a pit for storage and a boat path down to the bank.
pages.game: A lodging at Daventre. A single row of timber houses along the top of a sand ridge, end on to the river, each with a yard, a pit for storage and a boat path down to the bank. What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, rent store room and buy a plot.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: From 863 pegs and strings mark new plots between them, and the ground is being raised with sods against the floods.

pages.title: The weirs at the brook mouth
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Daventre. South of the bank a brook comes in under alders, and across its mouth run two fences of stakes and wattle with basket traps in the gaps.
pages.game: A fishery at Daventre. South of the bank a brook comes in under alders, and across its mouth run two fences of stakes and wattle with basket traps in the gaps. A logboat is tied to the last stake. Eels hang smoking on a rack over a slow fire; herons stand in the shallows and wait their turn. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, buy a boat and fund a work.
pages.known: The weirs are invented; Ælfric's fisherman takes eels, pike and salmon.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The Heest
pages.hint: A holy wood, not yet seen
pages.brief: A holy wood at Daventre. A second dune south-east of the church, steep where the river and the brook have cut it, covered in low beech scrub.
pages.game: A holy wood at Daventre. A second dune south-east of the church, steep where the river and the brook have cut it, covered in low beech scrub. Nobody lives on it. A path goes up that nobody admits to using, and at the top, in a hollow, there are things on the ground: a crock, a twist of rags, the ash of a small fire. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots and call witnesses.
pages.known: The offerings are invented, after the vows at trees and groves and the idols of rags forbidden in the Saxon capitulary and the Indiculus superstitionum.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: It stands until about 950.

pages.title: The barge slip
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Daventre. A cut in the bank north of the houses where a flat barge lies on rollers, half planked: oak boards pegged with wood, moss driven into the seams.
pages.game: A boat yard at Daventre. A cut in the bank north of the houses where a flat barge lies on rollers, half planked: oak boards pegged with wood, moss driven into the seams. Beside it an old barge is being broken up plank by plank, and the good timber goes down to the water to hold the bank. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat and fit her out.
pages.known: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1, Deventer 2 (about 1035), Deventer 3, all reused in the quay. A slip here in 793 is assumed (?).

later.text: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1 (spring 990: flat-bottomed, oak, moss caulking, wooden pegs), Deventer 2 (about 1035), Deventer 3 (after about 913), all reused in the quay.

pages.title: The bishop's house
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Daventre. A timber hall with a fenced yard a little way from the church, better roofed than its neighbours and no bigger.
pages.game: A hall at Daventre. A timber hall with a fenced yard a little way from the church, better roofed than its neighbours and no bigger. Clerks sit in the doorway for the light with wax tablets and a chest of charters behind them. A swallow's nest is stuck under the eave over the door, and nobody is allowed to knock it down. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hear the law, show the charter and read a book.
pages.known: The swallow is from Radboud's poem on a swallow; the nest is invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: It stands until about 920.

pages.title: The earth wall
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Daventre. A bank of earth and cut sods as high as a house, a palisade of split oak along the top and a wet ditch at its foot, running in a long curve from the river round the houses and back to the river.
pages.game: A wall at Daventre. A bank of earth and cut sods as high as a house, a palisade of split oak along the top and a wet ditch at its foot, running in a long curve from the river round the houses and back to the river. Where it is being dug you can see a black band a hand deep under the grass: what was here before. What is done here: fund a work, call witnesses and ask the news. Found here: Thiadlef.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The king's toll
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Daventre. A post with a beam across the head of the bank and a lean-to beside it, where a toll man looks into every boat before a sack comes out of her.
pages.game: A toll place at Daventre. A post with a beam across the head of the bank and a lean-to beside it, where a toll man looks into every boat before a sack comes out of her. A church's man shows a token and walks through. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter and ask the keeper.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

later.text: Before 896 a toll here is not recorded, so the site opens then.
From 1046 the toll man is the bishop's and looks the same.

pages.title: The mint, Daventre
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Daventre. A strong house inside the wall with one door and a man at it.
pages.game: A mint at Daventre. A strong house inside the wall with one door and a man at it. Inside, a hearth, a block with an iron die set in it and a second die in the moneyer's fist; silver sheet is cut with shears into rounds and each is struck with one blow. New pennies lie in a wooden bowl, pale, with a cross on them. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Hrotmar.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md (4 Oct 2026), which this file follows throughout and whose keys are given in the entries above

pages.title: The bank under the hill, Diusburg
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Diusburg. A long curve of brown mud and gravel under a steep green hill, eight or ten flat barges and dugouts drawn up bow first, the wide Rhine running hard on the outside of the bend.
pages.game: A landing at Diusburg. A long curve of brown mud and gravel under a steep green hill, eight or ten flat barges and dugouts drawn up bow first, the wide Rhine running hard on the outside of the bend. Wet rope, river weed and wood smoke; men shout from the towpath to the boats. Behind, the thatch of the king's barns shows over the edge of the hill. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, pay the toll and show the charter. Found here: Wolfhelm.
pages.known: The Rhine ran in a bend right under the hill; boats lay on the bank below it and probably round to the Ruhr mouth.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: A harbour is proved only from about 870; a toll is first named in 1065 (Lacomblet I no. 205): a landing due to the steward before that is a guess (?).

pages.title: The king's court on the hill
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Diusburg. On top of the spur, five men's height above the water: a long timber hall with a shingled roof, barns, a byre and a fenced yard with geese in it, and no wall round any of it in the early years.
pages.game: A hall at Diusburg. On top of the spur, five men's height above the water: a long timber hall with a shingled roof, barns, a byre and a fenced yard with geese in it, and no wall round any of it in the early years. After the Northmen's winter it is built again in grey tuff: a ring of stone houses with cellars, a gate, a hall for a king. From the yard you see the Rhine both ways and the Ruhr coming in from the east. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, hold a feast and fund a work. Found here: Raginhard and Hathuswith.
pages.known: A flood-free spur about 8 m above the bank; the court unfortified in the 9th century, rebuilt after 883/84 as a palace with a closed ring of tuff houses, finished in the first third of the 10th century. That a court stood here in 793 is likely, not proved.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

pages.title: The old grave field
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Diusburg. A sandy field south of the hill, rough grass over low rows of graves, the oldest sunk and the newest still mounded.
pages.game: A graveyard at Diusburg. A sandy field south of the hill, rough grass over low rows of graves, the oldest sunk and the newest still mounded. A wooden cross as tall as a man stands at the east end, grey with weather. On feast days a priest from the island monastery upriver says Mass here in the open, and the estate's people stand in the wind with their hoods up. What is done here: hear Mass, have him remembered, bury a man, give alms and make a vow. Found here: Liudger.
pages.known: The Frankish grave field, about 450 into the 8th century.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: The cross and the visiting priest from Saint Suitbert's at Kaiserswerth are invented: no church or priest is attested here before 893.

pages.title: The Saviour's church
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Diusburg. A small wooden chapel inside the court yard, tarred against the rain, one bell under a little roof of its own.
pages.game: A church at Diusburg. A small wooden chapel inside the court yard, tarred against the rain, one bell under a little roof of its own. After the rebuilding it is a hall church of stone beside the king's hall, and in the last years a taller one that the moneyers put on the pennies. Inside it is dark and smells of wax and damp cloaks; one lamp burns before the altar. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, swear an oath, ask the news and fund a work.
pages.known: The church of the Saviour; a wooden chapel at the court proved by digging, a stone palace church in the 11th century.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: The opening year 860 is a guess (?).
The church of the Saviour, first named in 893 and owing Prüm 30 shillings a year (Prüm estate book ch. 97).

pages.title: The head of the Hellweg
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Diusburg. Where the track from the landing climbs past the hill and turns east, a worn hollow road wide enough for two carts, going off between oaks toward the Ruhr ford and Saxony.
pages.game: A gate at Diusburg. Where the track from the landing climbs past the hill and turns east, a worn hollow road wide enough for two carts, going off between oaks toward the Ruhr ford and Saxony. A hurdle across it and two of the steward's men with spears; ox dung, dust in summer, deep mud by Martinmas. Whoever comes down it is tired, and whatever they know is three days old. What is done here: ask the news, listen for talk, hire carriers and call witnesses. Found here: Raginhard.
pages.known: Diusburg lies at the west end of the Hellweg, the road east, which crosses the Ruhr at Broich. The hurdle and the watch are invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: The search of eastbound goods after 805 is the capitulary of Thionville c. 7.

pages.title: The Ruhr mouth
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Diusburg. North of the hill the Ruhr slides into the Rhine, clear brown water into grey, with a line of foam where they meet.
pages.game: A ferry at Diusburg. North of the hill the Ruhr slides into the Rhine, clear brown water into grey, with a line of foam where they meet. A wide flat ferry lies on a gravel spit, a rope and a horn hung on a post. Up the smaller river the banks close in under alder and oak. What is done here: cross over, hire a pilot, ask the news and buy from makers. Found here: Wolfhelm and Liudger.
pages.known: The hill lies between the mouths of the Dickelsbach and the Ruhr.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: Half a day's poling up it is the ford at Broich, and beyond that, after 799, the monks of Werden.
Werden up the Ruhr from 799.

pages.title: The caulkers' strand
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Diusburg. A flat stretch of bank below the hill where a barge lies on rollers with her planks open to the light.
pages.game: A boat yard at Diusburg. A flat stretch of bank below the hill where a barge lies on rollers with her planks open to the light. Two men drive moss into a seam with a mallet and pin it under an iron clamp; a pot of pitch smokes on three stones. Oak chips underfoot, and a stack of long trunks from the king's forest waiting for the adze. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Iron clamps that held moss caulking between planks, 9th to 13th century; the king's forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel; river barges and expanded logboats built here in the project's tables.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

later.text: The king's forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel (Lacomblet I no. 205, of 1065).

pages.title: The smith by the road
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Diusburg. A low shed open on one side where the road leaves the landing, black inside, a boy on the bellows and a ring of light on the anvil.
pages.game: A smithy at Diusburg. A low shed open on one side where the road leaves the landing, black inside, a boy on the bellows and a ring of light on the anvil. Horseshoes, boat nails and hooks hang on the post. In the war years there are spear heads in the quenching trough, and a man who is not a customer sits on the bench by the door and watches who stops. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order and ask the news.
pages.known: Lance heads and a rider's spur lay in the burn layer of 883/84 (Krause, Wikinger I). Nailed horseshoes are not surely attested north of the Alps before the 9th or 10th century, so a smith who shoes horses in 793 is a guess (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

pages.title: Gerlind's ale-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Diusburg. A long low house at the top of the landing with a green bush on a pole over the door.
pages.game: An ale-house at Diusburg. A long low house at the top of the landing with a green bush on a pole over the door. Inside, one fire on the floor and the smoke going out through the thatch, benches along both walls, boatmen at one end and road people at the other. It smells of malt, wet wool and onions, and everything said on the river is said here a second time. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, trade riddles, pay the singer, hire a hand, lodge ashore and buy stores. Found here: Gerlind and Hathuswith.
pages.known: Invented; an ale-house where a road meets a river needs no source. In later eras it is kept by Gerlind's daughters' daughters under the same bush.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

pages.title: The market under the hill
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Diusburg. Wet trodden ground between the bank and the foot of the hill, laid with planks and brushwood, with booths of wattle and a timber-lined well in the middle.
pages.game: A market at Diusburg. Wet trodden ground between the bank and the foot of the hill, laid with planks and brushwood, with booths of wattle and a timber-lined well in the middle. Leather workers, bone workers and potters sell beside wine barges; a pig goes for five pennies and is argued over as if it were a horse. After the palace is built a causeway with a drain beside it runs through to the gate. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy stores, ask the news and fund a work. Found here: Thiadward.
pages.known: The Alter Markt at the foot of the hill, in use from the last third of the 9th century; wet ground kept wood, leather, bone and plants; a pig at 5 d in the Prüm estate book (893); the causeway with its side drain and small stone bridge, early 10th century (Krause, Königpfalz).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md (4 Oct 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its keys.

pages.title: The Frisians' houses
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Diusburg. A short row of long houses a little apart from the rest, built the Frisian way with the byre under the same roof and a boat shed at the water end.
pages.game: A lodging at Diusburg. A short row of long houses a little apart from the rest, built the Frisian way with the byre under the same roof and a boat shed at the water end. Bales under tarred cloth, a scale hanging in a doorway, children who speak two tongues. On Saint Martin's eve a man from the abbey of Prüm sits at the first house with a bag and a wax tablet. What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, rent store room, buy a plot, weigh the silver, listen for talk and take an order. Found here: Thiadward.
pages.known: The Frisians who 'stay' at Dusburhc and pay Prüm 8 ounces at Martinmas and 5 ounces and 12 pence at Easter. Where they lived is unknown: not inside the later old town.

later.text: The opening year 880 is a guess (?).
The Frisians who 'stay' at Dusburhc and pay Prüm 8 ounces at Martinmas and 5 ounces and 12 pence at Easter (Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 97).

pages.title: The old banks on the wooded hill
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Diusburg. North-east of the landing a wooded hill stands over the Ruhr, with two grassed ramparts running through the trees, older than anyone's grandfather.
pages.game: A wall at Diusburg. North-east of the landing a wooded hill stands over the Ruhr, with two grassed ramparts running through the trees, older than anyone's grandfather. Herd boys keep pigs in the ditch. In the winter of the Northmen there is fresh earth on the old banks, a palisade, smoke, and long ships drawn up below; in the spring after, only burnt stakes. What is done here: ask the news, have him remembered and call witnesses.
pages.known: Two old ramparts on the Kaiserberg, which Krause proposes for the Northmen's fort of 883/84; the fort itself has not been found, and the Ruhr mouth is his other guess. Duke Henry's camp lay at Broich, at the Ruhr crossing.

pages.title: The king's moneyers
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Diusburg. A stone cellar under one of the houses of the palace ring, with a barred door and a bench under the one window.
pages.game: A mint at Diusburg. A stone cellar under one of the houses of the palace ring, with a barred door and a bench under the one window. A man sets a blank on the lower die and another strikes it; the pennies come off bright, with a king's head on one side and on the other, in the last years, a church seen from the water above a wall. A third man weighs every twentieth one. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver, pay the toll and show the charter.
pages.known: Duisburg pennies of Conrad II (1024-39), Henry III and Henry IV; Henry IV's show a church twice, once from the water above a wall. That the mint lay in a cellar of the ring is invented.

pages.title: The creek landing
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Doccinga. A grey mud bank below the long mound where several creeks join the sea arm that runs east to the Lauwers.
pages.game: A beach at Doccinga. A grey mud bank below the long mound where several creeks join the sea arm that runs east to the Lauwers. Boats lie tilted on the ooze at the ebb, a line of stakes shows where the hard ground is, and behind them the church stands dark on its own mound against a wide sky. It smells of salt mud and cattle; curlews call, and the tide comes in without a sound. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, hire carriers and scrape and tar. Found here: Radbrand.
pages.known: The creeks and the sea arm: Cultuurhistorische verkenning binnenstad Dokkum 2008; nothing of the landing itself has been found, so the stakes are ours (?).

pages.title: The long mound
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Doccinga. A long low hill of sods and dung with one path along its back, square to the water.
pages.game: A lodging at Doccinga. A long low hill of sods and dung with one path along its back, square to the water. Turf-walled houses with their byres under the same roof stand end-on to the wind, smoke seeping through the thatch. Cheeses dry on a rack, hides are pegged out on the slope, and in front a woman sells butter from a tub to whoever has come off a boat. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, listen for talk, buy stores, hire a hand, buy from makers and trade riddles. Found here: Liafhild, Aldger and Meinbod.
pages.known: The dwelling mound south of the church, its street square to the water; its age is not known and digs found nothing before the late 12th century on its west flank: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008 (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/doccinga.md (the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed)

pages.title: The church of Saint Paul and Saint Boniface
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Doccinga. A plank church with a reed roof on the top of a steep round mound, higher than anything else to the horizon.
pages.game: A church at Doccinga. A plank church with a reed roof on the top of a steep round mound, higher than anything else to the horizon. Inside it is dim and smells of wax, wet wool and salt timber; a single lamp burns before the altar and a wooden board is cut with the names of the dead of 754. From the door the whole marsh lies open, creeks shining, as far as the sea. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, ask the news, have him remembered and fund a work. Found here: Meinward.
pages.known: Willibald ch. 9: the church built on the mound; the dedication from Alcuin's verses (MGH Poetae I 304) as cited in Robinson's note; timber traces found 1950-1978. The board of names is ours; the names are Willibald's (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/doccinga.md (the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed)

pages.title: The clergy house
pages.hint: A meeting place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A meeting place at Doccinga. A long timber house on the lee side of the church mound, with a bench along its south wall where the priests sit to hear cases.
pages.game: A meeting place at Doccinga. A long timber house on the lee side of the church mound, with a bench along its south wall where the priests sit to hear cases. Two twigs wrapped in white wool lie on a shelf inside the door, one cut with a cross. Men stand about in the wind waiting their turn, and a boy is being taught his letters on a wax board. What is done here: hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, swear an oath, read a book, have it copied and see the leech. Found here: Meinward.
pages.known: The clergy's dwelling: Willibald ch. 9; later the seat of church law for the district: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. The lot of two twigs, one marked with a cross, wrapped in clean wool and laid on the altar: Lex Frisionum XIV.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/doccinga.md (the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed)

pages.title: The spring on the mound
pages.hint: A well, not yet seen
pages.brief: A well at Doccinga. A small clear pool beside the church, edged with sods, in a country where every other water is brackish.
pages.game: A well at Doccinga. A small clear pool beside the church, edged with sods, in a country where every other water is brackish. A wooden dipper hangs on a post. Women come up the path with yokes and buckets; a pilgrim kneels, drinks, and fills a little flask to carry home. What is done here: buy stores, make a vow, give alms and have him remembered. Found here: Adelsuit.
pages.known: Willibald ch. 9: Abba rode round the finished mound, a servant's horse sank to its forelegs, and a sweet spring broke out; a 9th-century Utrecht Life puts it beside the church. Perhaps a pond of the fresh water that gathers under a mound: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008.

pages.title: The graves on the mound
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen

pages.game: A graveyard at Doccinga. The east slope of the church mound, set with low wooden markers that lean with the wind, all the graves lying east and west. The grass is cropped short by a tethered ewe. From here the landing is in plain sight, so that the dead, people say, can see who comes home. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered and give alms. Found here: Liafhild.
pages.known: Burial on the mound: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; Rijksmonument 47514.

pages.title: The meadow and the reeds
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Doccinga. Flat salt pasture beyond the creek, bitten close by small dark cattle, with a wide bed of reeds along the water that hisses when the wind gets up.
pages.game: A field at Doccinga. Flat salt pasture beyond the creek, bitten close by small dark cattle, with a wide bed of reeds along the water that hisses when the wind gets up. Nothing marks it. People crossing it lower their voices; this, they say, is where the books lay in the grass. What is done here: have him remembered, buy from makers and ask the news. Found here: Adelsuit.
pages.known: Willibald ch. 8: the books strewn over the meadow and thrown into the reeds, found long after unharmed. That it was this meadow is the people's belief, not the record (?).
