pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Doccinga. The next mound north, bigger and older than the church's, a short walk over the marsh by a plank path.
pages.game: A workshop at Doccinga. The next mound north, bigger and older than the church's, a short walk over the marsh by a plank path. In a sunken hut with its door to the south three women stand at upright looms, beating up the weft with oak swords; the thud carries outside. Finished cloth hangs striped and checked on a pole, and the place smells of wet wool and tallow. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods, haggle the price, take an order and pay the singer. Found here: Meinhild.
pages.known: Aalsum: about 4 ha, 5.3 m above the sea; finds of an oak weaving sword, a bronze cloak pin with inlaid stones and a gold ring with a red stone: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aalsum_(Noardeast-Fryslân). The woman who weaves fresum: Lex Frisionum, judgements of Wlemar.

pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen

pages.game: A hall at Doccinga. A farm on a mound of its own toward the sea, built like the others but with a boat shed beside the byre and a ship's strake for a lintel. An old man sits by the door mending a net with fingers that have held other things. A wooden cross is nailed over the door and a worn hammer of bone hangs inside it. What is done here: give a gift, hold a feast, ask the news, play tafl and swear an oath. Found here: the old Northman.
pages.known: His farm, and that it lay here, are ours (?).

pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Doccinga. The path along the back of the long mound, widened and laid with planks, with booths of hurdle and sailcloth on both sides.
pages.game: A market at Doccinga. The path along the back of the long mound, widened and laid with planks, with booths of hurdle and sailcloth on both sides. Behind the booths rises the new church of grey tuff, half built, with hoists and ropes on it. A man with a tally stick and a small scale stands where the path meets the landing and looks into every basket. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, rent store room, buy ship's tools and listen for talk.
pages.known: Market and toll in the 11th century, the tuff church of Saint Boniface and Saint Paul and the small Saint Martin's: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; H. M. van den Berg, dbnl.

pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen

Each blow leaves a thin bright penny with a crowned head on it. A boy sweeps the floor into a pan, because the sweepings are silver too. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Gerbrand.

pages.title: The shingle in the stream mouth
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Dofras. A grey shingle bank across the mouth of a clear chalk stream, and white cliffs going up on either hand.
pages.game: A beach at Dofras. A grey shingle bank across the mouth of a clear chalk stream, and white cliffs going up on either hand. In front, small clinker boats lie hauled above the weed line on rollers with their oars lashed inboard; a keel sits on the stones at the ebb with planks down to the pebbles. Behind, the stream widens into a tidal pool under the old fort wall. Shingle growls in the backwash, gulls quarrel over fish guts, and on a clear morning the far shore is a pale line. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper, cross over and buy stores. Found here: Wulfric.
pages.known: Where boats lay is not recorded: the Roman harbour was the Dour's estuary, and shingle kept closing its mouth; Hasted (1800) has the haven still 'much further within land' at the Conquest. The far shore seen on a clear day: Wikipedia (en) 'Strait of Dover'.

pages.title: The two tallies, at the old south gate
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Dofras. A gap in a Roman wall of flint and red tile, twice a man's height and furred with ivy, where the path from the shingle comes in.
pages.game: A toll place at Dofras. A gap in a Roman wall of flint and red tile, twice a man's height and furred with ivy, where the path from the shingle comes in. A lean-to of planks stands against a round bastion; under it are a bench, a balance and two bundles of notched sticks hung on separate pegs. The reeve's man sits at one end of the bench and a tonsured clerk at the other, and each watches the other count. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, weigh the silver and call witnesses. Found here: Hereberht and Cynehelm.
pages.known: The canons held 'a moiety of the toll of the port', by their tradition from Wihtred (Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2); Domesday gives them a half share (Hasted's translation, 1800). No rate, toll house or reeve is recorded for 793: the bench, the sticks and the men are invented. The fort wall and its bastions: Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit.

pages.title: The trodden ground before Saint Martin's
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Dofras. An open space of beaten chalk and mud between the church door and the fort wall, with thatched houses close round it.
pages.game: A market at Dofras. An open space of beaten chalk and mud between the church door and the fort wall, with thatched houses close round it. Women sell from cloths on the ground: folded lengths of grey and brown wool, cheeses, eels in a wet basket, a few Frankish pots. A man holds two sheep by the horns. Hearth smoke hangs low, a child drives geese through all of it, and the church's wooden gable stands over the whole. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods and ask the news. Found here: Hildgyth.
pages.known: Goods are Kent's at large: wool, cloth and hides out, wine, querns, pots and glass in.

pages.title: Saint Martin's, the wooden minster
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Dofras. A long narrow church of upright oak planks under a shingled roof, grown eastward by one building after another.
pages.game: A minster at Dofras. A long narrow church of upright oak planks under a shingled roof, grown eastward by one building after another. Inside it is dim and smells of tallow and old wood; the floor is a hard smooth red, like polished stone, and runs up to a stone altar base at the east end. A dozen clerks in dark tunics sing the office from memory. Poor people sit along the outside wall by the south door, waiting for the bread. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, read a book, have it copied, have him remembered and fund a work. Found here: Cynehelm.
pages.known: Rebuilt in wood four times between the 7th and 10th centuries (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit); lengthened eastward in the late 7th century and floored a century later with 'imitation red marble' (The Dover Historian, 'St Martin-le-Grand', reporting the dig: the floor of 793 if the dating holds (?)); twenty-two canons by the house's tradition (Victoria County History).

pages.title: The weaving huts under the west wall
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Dofras. A row of low huts with their floors dug knee-deep into the chalk, thatch coming down almost to the ground.
pages.game: A workshop at Dofras. A row of low huts with their floors dug knee-deep into the chalk, thatch coming down almost to the ground. Through each open door is an upright loom leaning on the wall, its warp threads pulled tight by rings of baked clay as big as a fist. Women beat the weft upward with a bone sword and talk across the lane without looking up. Fleeces soak in a trough; the lane smells of wet wool and stale urine from the dye tub. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order and try the goods. Found here: Hildgyth.
pages.known: Sunken-floored buildings inside the fort; one, burnt in the 7th century, held over 200 loom weights (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit; Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover'). Weaving here in 793 is carried forward from that find (?).

pages.title: Beornflæd's ale-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Dofras. A longer house than its neighbours, built against the inside of the fort wall so that one end of the room is Roman flint.
pages.game: An ale-house at Dofras. A longer house than its neighbours, built against the inside of the fort wall so that one end of the room is Roman flint. A hearth burns down the middle with benches either side; a green bush hangs on a pole over the door when the ale is fresh. Men off the boats sit with their backs to the old wall, pilgrims with their bundles between their feet. It is warm, loud with three kinds of English and one of Frisian, and smells of malt, smoke and drying cloaks. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, trade riddles, pay the singer, hire a hand and lodge ashore. Found here: Beornflæd and Lulla.
pages.known: Invented: an ale-house is the news place every port needs. The host answers for a guest kept three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric of Kent, c. 15 (673-686) (?). The ale-bush as a sign is later custom carried back (?).

pages.title: The boat ground up the Dour
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Dofras. A bend of the stream a bowshot above the shingle, where the tide still comes.
pages.game: A boat yard at Dofras. A bend of the stream a bowshot above the shingle, where the tide still comes. On the bank a small boat stands half planked on blocks, her strakes held with wooden clamps; oak chips lie thick underfoot and a pot of tar smokes over a slow fire. A second boat lies on her side with her bottom being scraped. A man with an adze works and a boy holds the dolly behind each nail. Watercress grows in the shallows. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: No ship or yard has been found at Dover. Clench nails from boats lay in graves here, and the Dour was tidal well inland (The Dover Historian, 'Dour River', no source given (?)). The yard and the wright are invented.

pages.title: The old light on the east height
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Dofras. A steep walk up through thorn and sheep to a grassy bank on the cliff top.
pages.game: A mound at Dofras. A steep walk up through thorn and sheep to a grassy bank on the cliff top. Inside the bank stands a tower of eight sides, grey-green stone banded with red tile, as tall as six houses and open to the sky; jackdaws go in and out of its windows. From its foot the whole strait lies open: the shingle and roofs far below, a second broken tower on the western hill, and across the water the cliffs of the Franks. The wind never stops. What is done here: wait for wind, ask the keeper, trade riddles and fund a work. Found here: Lulla.
pages.known: The eastern Roman lighthouse: eight-sided, of tufa, ragstone and red brick, four Roman stages, about 24 m. The western one's state in 793 is unknown. Earthworks on the hill hint at an older fort, unproven. No source says either was lit after the Romans, and the game keeps Dover dark.

pages.title: The old people's graves on Long Hill
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Dofras. A long chalk hill east of the stream, grazed short, with rows of low grassy humps running across the slope, some no higher than a furrow.
pages.game: A graveyard at Dofras. A long chalk hill east of the stream, grazed short, with rows of low grassy humps running across the slope, some no higher than a furrow. Nobody is buried here now; the dead go to Saint Martin's. Sheep lie on the mounds out of the wind. Where a bank has slipped, a rim of green bronze and a row of rust-red nail heads show in the white chalk. Larks, and the sea far down. What is done here: have him remembered and ask the news.
pages.known: The Buckland grave field: 170 graves found in 1951 and 244 more in 1994, with weapons, jewellery, combs, pots and Frankish goods; older than the game, about 475-750 (?). That the mounds still showed in 793 is assumed (?).

pages.game: A mint at Dofras. A house like the others but for the door, which is oak and barred, and the sound from inside: a hammer on iron, one blow at a time, never two together. Through the hatch a man sits astride a block with a die set in it; a boy lays a blank of silver on, the man sets the upper die and strikes. New pennies lie in a wooden bowl, each with the king's head and, round the back, the moneyer's name and the town's. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver.
pages.known: A mint at Dover by the middle of the 10th century (Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover'); its house has not been found. English pennies name the moneyer and the mint from Æthelstan's time. No moneyer is named here because none has been checked against the coin record.

pages.game: A church at Dofras. On the cliff top a new church of knapped flint with corners and arches of red Roman tile, cross-shaped, a square tower over the middle. Close against its west end stands the old eight-sided light tower, with a fresh stage of flint on top and bells in it where the fire used to be. Graves lie all round with plain wooden markers. When the bells ring the sound goes out over the water, and boatmen say they have steered by it in fog. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, bury a man, have him remembered, wait for wind and fund a work.
pages.known: The lighthouse made its bell tower with a fifth stage; a large late Saxon graveyard round it. Steering by the bells is the game's (?).

Inside is one long room, a raised hearth, shields and oars on the wall and a chest with three locks. The king's reeve has a seat here and so has the earl's man, and the steersmen of the twenty ships sit nearest the fire. What is done here: hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, swear an oath, hold a feast and hire a hand. Found here: Godric and Godwine.
pages.known: Domesday Book names the burgesses' guildhall at Dover (Hasted's translation, 1800); it is on record in 1086 and assumed to stand in King Edward's time (?). The twenty ships, twenty-one men in each, for fifteen days a year, and the king's two parts and the earl's third of the town's dues: the same.

Three or four boats lie on the shingle above the tide line with their oars stacked in them. Behind, upriver, the tower-less roof of Blythburgh's church shows across the reeds on a clear day. Gulls, wind, wet rope and weed. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot and hire carriers. Found here: Hunberht.
pages.known: The Dunwich river and the Blyth reached the sea in one open estuary north of the town; the shingle that choked it came in 1287 and 1328 (Touching the Tide 2015, p. 3). Where boats lay in 793 is not known (?).

What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, fit her out, buy a boat and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: The game's (?): no ship or yard has been found, and the only wreck off the old harbour is later than 1750. New rigging here follows from the hemp pond.

When a boat is in, goods are laid on hides and sailcloth: rope in coils, hemp in bundles, split fish drying on a rack, pots from Gipeswic. A folding scale hangs from an oar stuck in the sand. Above, against the sky, the reed roof of the bishop's church. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and test the silver. Found here: Wigferth.

Inside it is dim and smells of wax and old thatch: a stone altar, one hanging lamp, a carved chair with a cushion that only one man sits in. Boys' voices saying a psalm, and under them the sea. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man, have him remembered and give a gift. Found here: Ælfhun and Tidfrith.
pages.known: Felix's seat and first grave (Bede II.15). The fabric and dedication are unknown: timber and reed are the game's (?). Whether Felix's bones still lay here is not known; later they were at Soham.

On the wall inside someone has scratched a ship. By the end, in King Edward's day, it is called Saint Felix's and the churchyard wall is a good deal nearer the cliff edge than it was. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, bury a man, have him remembered and ask the news.
pages.known: The Victoria History of Suffolk II calls it Saint Felix's. Whether it stood on the old site is not known (?).

pages.known: King Sigeberht's school, 'wherein boys should be taught letters' (Bede III.18): that it stood at Dommoc is a later guess (?).

pages.game: A workshop at Dommoc. A black pond in the marsh below the town, full of hemp stalks held under water with stones and hurdles. Beside it women strip the grey fibre from rotted stems and beat it on a block; along the bank a man walks backward, paying out yarn, while a child turns a crank at the far post. The stink can be smelt from the haven. Frogs, flies, the creak of the crank. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and haggle the price. Found here: Wulfgyth.
pages.known: A pond by St James Street whose mud is up to nine-tenths hemp pollen, with hemp seeds, used from about the 5th century to the 11th; only the third such pit known in Britain (Touching the Tide 2015, pp. 24-28). The rope walk and its crank are the game's (?).

Inside: a hearth, a trestle, a cask on a cradle, wooden cups, a board scratched for a game with pebbles for men. Fishermen with their backs to the wall. Malt, peat smoke and wet wool. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, hire a hand and lodge ashore. Found here: Tidswith.
pages.known: Invented; an ale-wife's house is the ordinary place for news in an English town (Ine's and later laws on ale-houses) (?).

pages.game: A field at Dommoc. Plough strips and rough pasture running to the very edge, where the turf hangs over like a lip. In the cliff face below, a dark band shows where older people threw their rubbish: ash, oyster and whelk shells, broken red pots. Sheep graze to the brink and do not fall. Far out, a line of white where the sea breaks on a bank. What is done here: buy stores, buy from makers and cast the lots.
pages.known: Plough, pasture, oak and hazel by the marsh pollen (Touching the Tide 2015, p. 28). Roman and 'perhaps Saxon' sherds, a pit of ash with oyster, cockle and whelk shells and bronze keys were seen in the cliff top in 1858 (Victoria History of Suffolk I, Romano-British list). The medieval town's east edge is now seabed.

pages.game: A shrine at Dommoc. Less than a morning's walk up the river, or one tide in a small boat: a church on a rise above the reed beds, and inside it a king's grave under a worn cloth, with a lamp. A priest keeps it and writes on a tablet of whalebone. In the later years there is a man here with a bench and a scale who gives new pennies for old. What is done here: make a vow, give alms, have him remembered, make an offering, change coin and cross over.
pages.known: King Anna, killed in 653 or 654, lay at Blythburgh and his tomb was still honoured in the 12th century (?). A whalebone writing tablet with runes was found there (British Museum).

later.text: Domesday Book: no exchanger at Dunwich in 1066 but one at Blythburgh; the game allows coin to be changed there from about 1000 only (?).

On court days men stand in a half circle with their cloaks pinned back, one speaks and the rest answer together. A thief's goods lie in a heap by the tree; the thief himself has been sent up the river. Larks, and a cold wind off the heath. What is done here: hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses and swear an oath.
pages.known: Domesday Book: two or three men of Dunwich must go to the Hundred when warned or forfeit two ores; a thief taken at Dunwich is judged there, punished in body at Blythburgh, and his goods go to Dunwich's lord. The law is written in 1086; the date it began and the mound are the game's (?).

The whole beach north of the cliff path in autumn: twenty boats drawn up, nets spread to dry over oars, women gutting at trestles with their sleeves tied back, barrels and grey heaps of salt. The sand shines with scales. Every gull on the coast is here and every one is screaming. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, hire a hand, load and unload and haggle the price.
pages.known: By 1086 the town gave 60,000 herrings a year and Gilbert Blund's eighty men 8,000 more (Domesday Book; Victoria History of Suffolk I). For 793 a fishery is likely.

pages.known: The tenth (decima) and the bank due (ripaticum): charters of 777 and 815, the precept of 828. Where the toll was taken is not known: this place for it is ours (?).

pages.game: A lodging at Dorestat. A house on the bank road with its door open and a bush of green leaves tied over it. Inside one long room, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the roof, benches along both walls, a gaming board cut into the table. Shipmen of four tongues drink ale out of Badorf pots and a dog cracks a bone under the bench. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer and hire a hand, and more. Found here: Aldswith and Ravn.
pages.known: A lodging (hospitium) at Dorestad: Rimbert c. 20. Gaming pieces, a swan-bone flute, amber lyre bridges and dog-gnawed kitchen bones from the digs (H9.html). The green bush as an ale-sign is later custom (?).

pages.game: A graveyard at Dorestat. Fenced plots of low mounds lying east and west under old alders, and among them a small timber building with three coffins of white stone beside it. Near the gate is the only stone well in Dorestad, built of the Romans' grey tuff. It is quiet; rooks, wind in the alders, and somebody's mother sweeping leaves off a grave. What is done here: have him remembered, bury a man, give alms and make a vow.
pages.known: De Heul, late 7th to early 9th century: fenced plots, a building 14 by 8 m with three limestone sarcophagi, the one stone well, of Roman tuff (H10.html).

pages.game: A beach at Duiblinn. A small river widens into a still pool, dark as peat water, before it meets the brown tidal Liffey; boats lie on the mud at its lip with their sterns to the reeds. Behind is a low ridge with smoke on it, and far off to the north the long head of Benn Étair. It smells of bog water, weed and wet hide, and the only sound at low water is curlews. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar and hire carriers.

pages.game: A ford at Duiblinn. Woven hurdles pegged across the river bed, showing at low water as a pale crooked line from bank to bank, with a punt and a hide boat drawn up beside a round wattle house. Four roads come down to it out of the hills. Cattle are driven over at the ebb with a great deal of shouting, and it smells of dung, turf smoke and the river. What is done here: cross over, hire a pilot, ask the news and listen for talk. Found here: Suibne.

pages.game: A church at Duiblinn. A wooden church with a steep shingled roof inside a wide pear-shaped bank, with a few round cells, a stone cross slab and a graveyard of small plain markers all facing east. A hand-bell stands on the sill. The light comes in at the west door and falls on an altar with one good cloth. It is very quiet: there are more cells than monks. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, take sanctuary, make a vow, bury a man and fund a work.
pages.known: The enclosure of about five hectares: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795. Whether the house was still alive in 793 is doubtful: the game makes it half empty and names no abbot.

Monks in undyed wool stand in a stream to the knees saying psalms. In the writing hut a man rules lines on calfskin by the light of the door. No ale is brewed here and it can be smelt that none is. What is done here: read a book, have it copied, hear Mass, give alms and have him remembered. Found here: Óengus.

Combs, shoes, amber beads and turned bowls are sold from the doorways; antler chips and leather offcuts lie ankle deep. Children sail toy boats in the gutter. It smells of tanning, smoke and pigs. pages.known: The hall itself has not been found; houses with four roof posts and side benches are those of Fishamble Street. A poet of each tongue: Cináed ua hArtacáin praised Amlaíb Cuarán (?).

On a law day the free men of the town stand round its foot and the speakers on its side, and a case is said aloud twice so that none can claim not to have heard. Wind, and gulls from the strand. What is done here: bring a case, hear the law, call witnesses and swear an oath.

pages.game: A mint at Duiblinn. A plot like any other, but with a barred door and a man at it. Inside, a block with a die set in it, a hammer, shears, and a pan of blanks; the moneyer lays a blank, strikes once, and drops a penny with the king's head on it into a bowl. Each coin is weighed. The sound carries down the street like a slow smith. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver.
pages.known: No mint building is known. The moneyer's name Færemin is on the coins (?).

pages.game: A beach at Emuthon. A muddy creek running into the brown river, boats lying on their bilges on the ebb with a plank laid to the bank. Behind them a strip of empty wet ground and then the mound, low and green, with smoke lying flat over it. Curlews, the suck of mud under feet, and the smell of salt, sheep and peat smoke. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, mend the boat and buy a boat. Found here: Folcger.

In front, bolts of grey and blue cloth over a rail, cheeses on a board, a ewe tied by one leg; behind, a hundred miles of flat marsh and sky. After the middle of the ninth century a street runs along the crown. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy from makers, listen for talk, rent store room and buy a plot. Found here: Tetta and Gerlint.

pages.title: The sand the tide covers
pages.hint: A meeting place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A meeting place at Emuthon. A hard grey sand at the river's edge, bare at the ebb and under a man's height of water at the flood.
pages.game: A meeting place at Emuthon. A hard grey sand at the river's edge, bare at the ebb and under a man's height of water at the flood. The free men stand here in a ring when there is law to speak, with the judge on a turf seat and the watch pole behind him, where the men who owe the coast-watch look seaward. Gulls, wind, and voices that carry too far. What is done here: hear the law, swear an oath, call witnesses, bring a case and ask the news.

pages.game: A landing at Eoforwic. Boats lie tilted on brown mud where a small river runs into the great one, with posts driven in to tie to and planks laid over the worst of it. Upstream, above the left bank, stands the grey wall of the old fortress with its ten-sided corner tower catching the light. The tide sucks at the bank, men shout the count of bales, and the place smells of river mud, wet wool and tar. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, hire carriers, pay the toll, show the charter and scrape and tar, and more. Found here: Ecgwulf.
pages.known: The wic at Fishergate where the Foss meets the Ouse (dug 1985-86): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishergate. No quay is proven; that boats took the ground on the bank is a guess (?). No toll rate for 793 is known.

pages.game: A market at Eoforwic. Timber houses stand in rows on the low ground between the two rivers, each with its yard, and goods are sold from the house doors and from boards set on trestles in the lane. In front a woman pours Rhenish wine from a grey jug to be tasted; behind, smoke rises from the bone-workers' and the smiths' sheds. Hammers, a handmill grinding, pigs; the smell of hot horn. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, call witnesses, weigh the silver, buy from makers and take an order. Found here: Wulfheard.
pages.known: Fishergate: eighth and ninth century timber buildings, metal, bone and leather waste; 'the city's principal manufacturing and trading centre', given up in the mid ninth century. Rhenish and north French pots and lava querns (?).

What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, rent store room, drink with them, listen for talk, hire a hand, call witnesses and buy a plot. Found here: Wulfheard.

pages.title: Saint Peter's minster
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Eoforwic. A stone church with a roof of dull lead and small windows of real glass that throw coloured light on the floor, somewhere inside the old fortress wall.
pages.game: A minster at Eoforwic. A stone church with a roof of dull lead and small windows of real glass that throw coloured light on the floor, somewhere inside the old fortress wall. Edwin's font is here and Saint Paul's altar, where kings are hallowed. Not far off stands a second, taller church, Holy Wisdom, with thirty altars and more columns than a man can count at a glance. Chanting at the hours, a hand-bell, cold stone and beeswax. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man, have him remembered, ask the news and give a gift, and more. Found here: Eanbald and Alcuin.
pages.known: Digging in 1967-73 found neither: their places are unknown, and the game does not put them on the present minster.

pages.title: The school and the book room
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Eoforwic.
pages.game: A workshop at Eoforwic. A room with a slanted desk under each small window, a scribe at each with a quill and a knife, and along the back wall the chests: more books than a merchant has seen in his life, each chest with a list nailed inside the lid. Boys recite on a bench by the door. Scratching pens, a master's dry voice; the smell of calfskin, oak-gall ink and cold. What is done here: read a book, have it copied, trade riddles, take an order and ask the news. Found here: Torhthelm and Sigewine.
pages.known: The school and library, 'probably the largest contemporary collection of books... outside of Rome' in Wikipedia's words; Alcuin's verses list its authors. Where it stood is unknown.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/eoforwic.md (the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed)

A boy lays a blank, the hammer falls once, and the coin goes into a bowl. In front, a scale no bigger than a hand; behind, a charcoal hearth and a locked chest. It rings like a small bell all day. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver and ask the news.

Inside, a hearth the length of three men, benches along both walls and a high seat with a red cloth on it. Dogs under the boards, a harp on a peg; smoke, roast meat and wet wool. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, bring a case, hear the law, pay the singer and trade riddles. Found here: Ecgwulf.
pages.known: A king's seat at York is certain; where his hall stood in 793 is not known, perhaps inside the fortress (?). The hall itself is drawn from the common form.

A king sits here; a skald stands by the hearth and men throw dice by the door. In the last years the earl keeps his own house instead at Galmanho beyond the west wall, beside Saint Olaf's church. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, bring a case, hear the law, call witnesses and pay the singer, and more.

pages.brief: A well at Eoforwic. Between the fortress and the Foss lies ground nobody has built on since the Romans: nettles, broken tile, elder bushes, and one well, square, lined with oak planks gone black.
pages.game: A well at Eoforwic. Between the fortress and the Foss lies ground nobody has built on since the Romans: nettles, broken tile, elder bushes, and one well, square, lined with oak planks gone black. The water is good and a rope has worn a groove in the kerb. Women come with buckets at dawn and dusk and talk; a heron stands in the wet by the river. What is done here: buy stores, listen for talk, ask the news and make an offering.
pages.known: From about 900 houses stand round it. Offerings at wells are what the later priests' law fines (?).

pages.title: The hythe at the tide's end
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Fordwic. A low bank of trodden gravel on the south side of a brown river no wider than a long bowshot is far.
pages.game: A landing at Fordwic. A low bank of trodden gravel on the south side of a brown river no wider than a long bowshot is far. Five or six boats lie stem to the bank, masts down, on a falling tide; beyond them reeds, alders and flat wet marsh to the edge of the sky. Behind, a line of hurdle fences and thatch. A heron stands where the last boat ends. Mud, cut reed, woodsmoke, and no sea smell at all. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, mend the boat, scrape and tar, buy a boat and hire a pilot. Found here: Tilred.
pages.known: The river is tidal to Fordwich, its tidal limit (Tatton-Brown 1992); ships 'were moored' at the quay 'where all goods were laded and unladed' (Hasted 1800, of the later port). Where boats lay in 793 is not known: the hythe is ours.

pages.title: The king's toll place, Fordwic
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Fordwic. A bench under a lean-to of hurdles at the head of the hythe, with a peg-board behind it hung with tally sticks, one for each ship that has standing here.
pages.game: A toll place at Fordwic. A bench under a lean-to of hurdles at the head of the hythe, with a peg-board behind it hung with tally sticks, one for each ship that has standing here. A heavy man with a white wand sits on the bench; beside him a clerk's boy holds a wax tablet he cannot read. Three ships have small wooden crosses painted on the board instead of sticks. Everything that lands walks between the bench and the river. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, call witnesses, hear the law, bring a case and give a gift. Found here: Tilred.
pages.known: The king's toll-gatherers (thelonearii) in the public place Fordwic: Sawyer 29 (763 or 764). The toll place has not been found; the bench, the board and the wand are ours. After Edward's writ the toll was the abbot's (Hasted vol. 9).

pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Fordwic. Between the fences and the water, a strip of gravel where goods stand as they come off the boats: querns in straw, jars with their mouths tied, bales under hides.
pages.game: A market at Fordwic. Between the fences and the water, a strip of gravel where goods stand as they come off the boats: querns in straw, jars with their mouths tied, bales under hides. Women from the marsh farms sit with eggs, cheeses and live hens in withy cages; a monk's cart from the city waits with its ox unyoked. A buyer lifts a cloth to the light. Hens, wet straw, hot bread from somebody's oven. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy stores and take an order. Found here: Cwengyth.
pages.known: No cargo of Fordwic is listed; the Thanet nuns' crew deal in 'goods of various kinds'. Wine from the south (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1012), salt from Chislet marsh, querns and hops in the Graveney boat are the region's record, not this strand's. No market day is known.

pages.game: An ale-house at Fordwic. A long low house with its door to the track and its back to the river, a bush on a pole over the lintel. Inside, one hearth in the middle of the floor, smoke in the thatch, benches along the walls and a carter asleep with his whip across his knees. Boatmen sit on the river side and men from the city on the other. The ale is brown and thick, and the trout on the board is as long as a forearm. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, hire a hand and lodge ashore. Found here: Wicga.
pages.known: Invented: an ale-house at the foot of the track to the city. The host answers for a guest of three nights (Hlothhere and Eadric 15). The Stour's big trout were famous by 1653.

pages.brief: A ford at Fordwic. Upstream of the last boat the river spreads thin over gravel, and a line of stakes marks where a cart can cross at low water.
pages.game: A ford at Fordwic. Upstream of the last boat the river spreads thin over gravel, and a line of stakes marks where a cart can cross at low water. On the far bank a few roofs, a smith's lean-to with a bed of charcoal glowing under it, and the road that runs on east to the Thanet ferry. A boy drives geese through the shallows. At high water the stakes stand in the stream to their middles and nobody crosses. What is done here: cross over, buy ship's tools, mend the boat, ask the news and hire carriers.
pages.known: The ford, later a bridge, to Sturry, and the Thanet road through Sturry to Sarre. Hearths and slag at Sturry are of the sixth and seventh centuries (Kent HER, TR 16 SE 91): the smith of 793 is ours.

pages.game: A storehouse at Fordwic. A row of narrow plots running back from the river, each inside its own fence of wattle and thorn: a house, a pit, a store raised on posts against the damp, a boat's ribs leaning on a wall. A gate stands open on one where a man is stacking hides under a thatch. A ditch runs straight down between two plots to the water. Dogs on ropes, a child with a stick counting bales aloud and getting it wrong. What is done here: rent store room, use your store, buy a plot, lodge ashore and fund a work.
pages.known: A reeve's two hagas (fenced plots) and a meadow at Fordwic (Sawyer 1654); a boundary or track running to the river, seen near the church in 2006 (Kent HER, TR 15 NE 1797). How many plots there were in 793 is not known.

A man with a long rake turns hay on the only dry ridge; behind him a farm on a low rise, a midden, a hen-run and a woman calling ten names. Plovers get up as you walk. Under a wide grey sky it smells of mint, dung and standing water. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, trade riddles and ask the news. Found here: Wicga and Cwengyth.

pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Fordwic. Two miles from the river the track climbs a little hill and stops at a small old church of red Roman tile and flint, older than anyone's grandfather can count.
pages.game: A church at Fordwic. Two miles from the river the track climbs a little hill and stops at a small old church of red Roman tile and flint, older than anyone's grandfather can count. Its door stands open; inside it is narrow, dark and cool, with one lamp. From the churchyard the city lies below: a grey wall, thatch and smoke inside it, and outside it, nearer, the long roofs of the abbey. A boatman kneels with his cap in his hand. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, bury a man and take sanctuary.
pages.known: The track from Fordwich runs south-west to Saint Martin's church and the city, two miles (Hasted) or three (Tatton-Brown). A church of Saint Martin on the east side of the city, built while the Romans were in the island, where Queen Bertha prayed: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.26 (Jane 1903), from memory (?).

pages.title: The abbey of the kings' graves
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Fordwic. Outside the east wall, inside a bank and a gate of its own, two stone churches stand in a line with a paved yard between them.
pages.game: An abbey at Fordwic. Outside the east wall, inside a bank and a gate of its own, two stone churches stand in a line with a paved yard between them. In the north side-chamber of the older one the first archbishops lie in a row; in the south, the kings of Kent. A porter with a bunch of keys looks at your shoes. Beyond the churches, a long room with shuttered windows where the books are kept and nobody raises his voice. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, have him remembered, read a book, lodge ashore, see the leech, give a gift and fund a work.
pages.known: The abbey outside the walls: two churches (613, about 624), a library and writing room, the graves of Kent's kings. The side-chambers from Bede II.3 and II.5, from memory (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/fordwic.md (4 Oct 2026, checked again 6 Oct): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known and what must not be claimed

later.text: Abbot Guthheard by its own tradition 787-803.
Renamed for Augustine in 978.
Saint Mildred's body here from 1030.

pages.title: The wall and the east gate
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Fordwic. A Roman wall of flint with courses of red tile, patched with timber where it has fallen, and in it an arch wide enough for one cart.
pages.game: A gate at Fordwic. A Roman wall of flint with courses of red tile, patched with timber where it has fallen, and in it an arch wide enough for one cart. A man with a spear leans in its shade and asks nobody anything. Through the arch, a lane of fenced plots and thatch, pigs, a woman selling onions from a cloth. Carters shout for room. Whatever is news in Kent is said here first and loudest. What is done here: ask the news, listen for talk, hire carriers, call witnesses and ask an audience.
pages.known: The Roman wall and gates of Canterbury; 'the city wall' in the grant of the Lyminge refuge (Sawyer 160, 804); chapels over the gates and the cattle market outside the wall are later. The spearman and the onion seller are ours.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/fordwic.md (4 Oct 2026, checked again 6 Oct): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known and what must not be claimed

pages.title: Christ Church and the writing room
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Fordwic. Inside the wall, the archbishop's church: stone, long and plain, with a porch on its south side where men wait with their caps off.
pages.game: A minster at Fordwic. Inside the wall, the archbishop's church: stone, long and plain, with a porch on its south side where men wait with their caps off. Beside it a hall, and off the hall a room with a north light where four men sit at sloped boards with quills, and a fifth rules lines with a point. A calfskin is stretched on a frame by the door. Nobody looks up. It smells of gall ink, chalk and cold feet. What is done here: hear Mass, ask an audience, read a book, have it copied, trade riddles, take an order, give a gift and give alms, and more. Found here: Æthelheard and Eadhun.
pages.known: The Saxon cathedral found under the nave in 1993, rebuilt larger in the ninth or tenth century and burnt in 1067; the scribes of Christ Church. The room and its light are ours.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/fordwic.md (4 Oct 2026, checked again 6 Oct): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known and what must not be claimed

pages.title: The moneyers' benches, Fordwic
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Fordwic. A lane off the market inside the wall, and in it three open-fronted sheds, each with a stump of oak set in the floor and a die standing in the stump.
pages.game: A mint at Fordwic. A lane off the market inside the wall, and in it three open-fronted sheds, each with a stump of oak set in the floor and a die standing in the stump. A man holds a second die over a blank of silver; another swings the hammer; a boy sweeps the floor with a hare's foot and tips the dust into a dish. Scales no bigger than a hand hang in a wooden case. Each blow rings like a small bell. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver and ask the news. Found here: Eoba.
pages.known: Coin is struck in Canterbury for kings and archbishops; none is known at Fordwic. Offa's heavy penny from 792/3; seven moneyers by Æthelstan's law. The sheds are ours.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/fordwic.md (4 Oct 2026, checked again 6 Oct): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known and what must not be claimed

later.text: Pennies of about 822-824 naming only the moneyer and 'Dorobernia civitas'.

Downstream the thatch and one wooden tower of Saint Bavo's stand where a second river comes in; upstream, smoke from the village; behind everything, a sand hill with a church on it. Wet rope, river mud, sheep somewhere, a bell. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper and buy stores.

Split oak is stacked under a lean-to; a pitch pot smokes on three stones; chips lie ankle deep. The sound is adzes, never saws, and a man swearing mildly at a plank. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools. Found here: Hildgis.

pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Ganda. A cluster of timber and wattle buildings on the point of land between two rivers, with one larger church, limewashed, and a wooden gate where a porter sits.
pages.game: An abbey at Ganda. A cluster of timber and wattle buildings on the point of land between two rivers, with one larger church, limewashed, and a wooden gate where a porter sits. Inside the church a low tomb under a lamp, crutches leaning on the wall beside it. Candle smoke, wet thatch, and in a side room a chest of books with its lid propped open to air. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, see the leech, have him remembered, read a book and have it copied, and more. Found here: Einold.
pages.known: Einhard, Translation I: 'the monastery of Saint Bavon, which is situated near the Scheldt in the place called Ghent, where that stream is joined with the river Lys' (Wendell 1926). The first stone church is probably Einhard's; a fort ('Gandavum castrum') is unproven.

pages.title: Saint Peter's on the hill of Blandinium
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen

pages.game: An abbey at Ganda. A sand hill standing twenty metres over the flats, the only height in sight, with a church and a few houses on its top and a path worn up from the Scheldt. From the door the whole meeting of the rivers lies below: boats, both arms of the Leie, the meadows shining. At the cellar door a man is counting cheeses onto a board. What is done here: take an order, use your store, lodge ashore, give a gift, ask an audience, hear Mass, give alms and bury a man. Found here: Ansold.

pages.title: The village on the bank
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Ganda. Twenty or thirty thatched houses on a dry ridge along the river, each with a fenced yard, a few with a loom shed.
pages.game: A market at Ganda. Twenty or thirty thatched houses on a dry ridge along the river, each with a fenced yard, a few with a loom shed. There is no market cross and no booth: goods are shown at a house door or on an upturned boat, and the abbey's man is usually within hearing. Wool grease, peat smoke, a dog on every plot. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and listen for talk.
pages.known: Verhulst: a lay village on the Scheldt's left bank by the present cathedral from the early 9th century; no market, toll or fair is recorded in 793. Trade here is what the abbeys and their tenants have over.

Bargemen, an abbey carter, a canon who should be elsewhere. A woman with her sleeves tied back watches the bank while she pours. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, trade riddles, hire a hand, lodge ashore and ask the news. Found here: Hildrada.
pages.known: Invented; say 'ale-house'. After Hildrada's time the house is kept by her kin (the role re-forges).

Graves crowd its south side. A grey pot with a spout, the Rhine kind, stands by the door for the holy water. What is done here: hear Mass, bury a man, call witnesses, swear an oath, give alms and ask the news.
pages.known: Verhulst: a church beside the abbey, probably the parish church of the Holy Christ, dug at the old Beestenmarkt, the first phase perhaps timber; Carolingian layers with sherds of Rhenish Badorf ware.

In winter it is one sheet of water with fence tops showing. Larks, a sour smell of fleece, and far off the hill with its church. What is done here: buy from makers, fund a work and ask the news.

pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen

pages.game: A wall at Ganda. The burned abbey with a bank and stakes thrown round it, long ships drawn up in a row below, horses picketed on the meadows as far as the eye goes. In the roofless church men sit among bales and chests and weigh silver on a folding scale. Wood smoke, horse dung, and a dozen tongues, most of them northern. What is done here: weigh the silver, test the silver, haggle the price, give a gift, ask the news and play tafl. Found here: Ketil.
pages.known: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 880. No dig has found the camp and nobody says who led it: the bank, the stakes and the market are ours.

Bales of wool on the bank, cloth on rails, a man with a balance at a door. Fulling tubs stink behind the houses. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, change coin, test the silver, rent store room, buy a plot and listen for talk, and more.
pages.known: Usuard, 858/65: 'in portu Ganda'; the ditch found in 1987 at the Borreputsteeg, 9th-10th century, about 6 ha inside, filled in during the 10th.

later.text: Pennies reading GANDAVVM were struck 864-75 only: changing coin here in other years is done at a merchant's door by weight.
Plots ('mansiones') named in 941, all owned by the abbeys for a yearly rent.
From 942 a new church of Saint John stands in the middle of it.
Saint John's consecrated 942.

pages.game: An abbey at Ganda. Old burned walls patched with new stone, monks in black where there were canons. Masons' chips, lime, a hoist creaking. In the old church the saints lie in a row of new shrines, more of them each generation. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, see the leech, have him remembered, read a book and have it copied, and more.
pages.known: Tournai stone is our guess (?).

pages.title: The count's new castle on the Leie
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Ganda. A raised platform of earth and braced timber on the left bank of the Leie, with a long wooden hall, grain stores on posts and a small chapel of Saint Veerle.
pages.game: A hall at Ganda. A raised platform of earth and braced timber on the left bank of the Leie, with a long wooden hall, grain stores on posts and a small chapel of Saint Veerle. Below it, hides soak in pits and leather-workers scrape at beams. A keeper's man at the gate asks what is in the boat. What is done here: ask an audience, pay the toll, show the charter, bring a case, hear the law, give a gift and hold a feast.
pages.known: The 'new castle' of the Miracles of Bavo (later 10th century); a timber-braced platform with a hall and grain stores, leather-workers beside it (disputed), a chapel of Saint Pharaildis. It is timber: the stone hall is after the game's end. That a toll was taken at it is ours (?).

later.text: First timbers tree-ring dated no earlier than about 950.

pages.title: The hurdle bank
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Gipeswic. A long low bank of gravel faced with oak posts and wattle hurdles, grey with dried mud, and beyond it the brown river going out.
pages.game: A beach at Gipeswic. A long low bank of gravel faced with oak posts and wattle hurdles, grey with dried mud, and beyond it the brown river going out. Three or four boats lie on the ground with their sterns to the town, a Frisian keel among them; behind, thatch and the smoke of the kilns. Gulls, the suck of mud at the posts, and the smell of weed and wet leather. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar and hire a pilot. Found here: Wigmund.
pages.known: Bridge Street waterfront, dug 1981: post-and-wattle revetments from the 7th century on, each further out over the mud, 'little more than a bank protection'; leather survives only here (Suffolk Heritage Explorer; Excavation Archive).

pages.game: A ford at Gipeswic. A hard of gravel going down into the river and coming out on the Stoke bank, passable to a cart at low water. A hurdle shelter stands at the town end where the reeve's man sits with his tally sticks, watching what is carried up from the boats. pages.known: The ford just east of Stoke Bridge. A reeve at the crossing is inference from London (?): no toll is recorded here before 1086.

'The bridge' and the hythe in the bounds of 970 (Sawyer 781).

An open space of trodden earth where the streets from the west and north meet, set with trestles, sacks of wool, crates of grey pots in straw and a man selling honey from a crock. A small timber chapel stands at one side. Voices from four kingdoms, a pig loose, the smell of new bread and old fleece. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, call witnesses and listen for talk.
pages.known: The Cornhill 'perhaps an unsurfaced market'; St Mildred's there 'may have been a royal chapel' (Suffolk Heritage Explorer; Alsford, Medieval Ipswich). Carbonised bread and bronze balance fragments from the digs.

pages.game: A workshop at Gipeswic. Low round kilns of clay under turf at the edge of the town, two of them alight and leaking a thin grey smoke, with stacks of cut wood and rows of unfired jars drying on boards in the wind. Women coil the walls of a pot by hand and a man finishes the rim on a slow turntable. Heaps of broken sherds lie everywhere underfoot, sharp and ringing. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and fund a work. Found here: Tilbeorht.
pages.known: Kilns at Cox Lane (dug 1958), sherds along 160 m of Carr Street; single kilns at the Buttermarket (c. 800-850) and Stoke Quay.

pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen

pages.game: A workshop at Gipeswic. A gravelled street with a row of timber houses hard on its edge, each with a fenced yard behind: a loom under a lean-to, a bench strewn with antler offcuts, a horn-worker boiling horn in a stinking pot. In one yard a well is lined with the staves of a great wine cask, dark with age. Shuttles, a rasp on bone, children. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order, buy stores, buy a plot and trade riddles.
pages.known: St Stephen's Lane, dug 1987-88: two metalled roads, houses on the street, weaving, bone, antler and metal work, antler brooch moulds, basketry. 87 shallow wells are known, many lined with old wine casks; one cask's oak matches the Mainz area (Suffolk Heritage Explorer; Excavation Archive).

A timber church with a shingled roof on the rise above the ford, a wooden cross before its door and a fenced graveyard where the dead lie east and west with nothing beside them. Inside it is dark and smells of beeswax; one small window faces the river. A bell of beaten iron is struck by hand for the hours. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man, have him remembered and read a book. Found here: Hereberht.
pages.known: St Peter's by the ford 'has been suggested as the Minster'; nothing has been found by digging before the 11th century (?). Christian graveyards of the 8th-9th century at Elm Street and Philip Road, without grave goods (Suffolk Heritage Explorer).

pages.known: Thingstead, the green by the north gate, a meeting place by its name (Alsford, Medieval Ipswich); the name is Norse in form and may be of the Danish years (?).

pages.game: A mint at Gipeswic. A small strong house with a barred shutter, near the Cornhill. A man sits astride a block with a die set in it, lays a blank, sets the upper die and strikes once; a boy sweeps the floor for clippings every evening. A folding balance hangs from a peg. The sound carries down the street: one blow, a pause, one blow. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver and ask an audience. Found here: Lul.
pages.known: The mint's site is unknown. Before that, that East Anglian pennies were struck at Ipswich is only 'possible' (?): the game puts the bench here. Fragments of bronze balances, Foundation Street.

Oak logs lie split into wedges; a man trims a plank with a broad axe while a boy heats tar. Chips, the knock of a mallet on a rove, the sweet smell of oak. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: The yard is the game's (?): the waterfront digs are unpublished and no slip is known.

pages.known: The Orwell: some 18 km (?) of estuary, wooded sides, salt marsh, flats that dry at low water, springs of about 3.6 m. Herring August to October.

A bank of gravel and turf taller than a man, with a ditch before it five paces wide, running round the whole town; a timber gate with a walk over it lets the north road through to the Thingstead. Streets that once ran straight on now stop dead at the bank's foot. A watchman, carts waiting, and the smell of the ditch in summer. What is done here: pay the toll, ask the news, call witnesses and fund a work.

pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Grobiņa. A long low coast of pale sand with surf standing on it and no haven anywhere: dunes, bent grass, a line of dark pine behind.
pages.game: A beach at Grobiņa. A long low coast of pale sand with surf standing on it and no haven anywhere: dunes, bent grass, a line of dark pine behind. In one place the surf is broken and brown water runs out through it over a bar. A flat-bottomed boat lies there with a man standing in it, holding a sounding pole. Wind, gulls, and in autumn people walking the tide line with baskets, heads down. What is done here: hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire carriers, buy from makers and try the goods. Found here: Tulegaud.
pages.known: A harbourless surf coast, a sand bar, and an outlet from the lake that kept silting shut until a canal was dug in 1697-1703. Where the outlet lay in 793 and how deep it was are not known, so nothing here is named or measured (?). Amber gathered after the autumn gales is the region's pattern, not this place's evidence. The pilot and the porters who drag a boat over are invented.

pages.brief: A beach at Grobiņa.
pages.game: A beach at Grobiņa. Above them the fort hill rises steep on its spit with a timber fence along the top. Wood smoke, tar, wet dogs, and three tongues being shouted at once. pages.known: The fort stands on a spit on the right bank of the Ālande, which guarded it on three sides. How far a laden boat could come up the river is not known (?). No toll is recorded and none is taken here.

pages.game: A market at Grobiņa. Low timber houses and open-fronted booths on ground so dark with old hearths that it stains the shoes. In front, a plank on two trestles with a folding balance on it, a heap of rough amber the colour of honey and dirty wax, bundles of grey pelts tied by the forty. Behind, the hill. A woman in island dress, two brooches and a string of beads, is counting something a second time. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods, ask the news and listen for talk. Found here: Botgair, Kantegede and Wissegerde.
pages.known: The settlement of about 3 ha beside the fort, culture layer up to 0.6 m: Nerman's 'black earth'. Goods as the region's pattern: amber, squirrel, seal oil, wax, honey, captives out; swords, iron tools, glass beads, salt in. Silver by weight, no coin (?).

pages.game: A storehouse at Grobiņa. A squat log house with a turf roof and the only door in the settlement that has an iron lock. Inside it is dark and dry: sacks of amber sorted by size, pelts hung from the rafters out of reach of mice, a stack of bar iron with a hide over it, a tub of seal oil that can be smelt from the door. A tally of notched sticks hangs on a peg by the post. What is done here: use your store, rent store room, load and unload and weigh the silver. Found here: Botgair.
pages.known: Invented in the period's manner: no storehouse has been reported. Goods kept over a winter for the spring ships are what a settlement of traders 'comparable to Staraya Ladoga' would need (?).

pages.title: The gate of the fort, Grobiņa
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Grobiņa. A steep path up the spit to a gap in a fence of upright logs, with an earth bank as high as a man across the one side the river does not guard.
pages.game: A gate at Grobiņa. A steep path up the spit to a gap in a fence of upright logs, with an earth bank as high as a man across the one side the river does not guard. Two men sit in the gap with spears across their knees and a board game between them. From up here the whole place shows: the bend of the river, the booths, and in a half circle beyond them the low humps of the dead. What is done here: swear an oath, call witnesses, give a gift, ask the news, hire a hand and play tafl. Found here: Arnvald and Wissegerde.
pages.known: The fort plateau up to 80 by 40-45 m with a rampart at the east end about 30 m wide and 2 m high, in use from the 5th to the 13th century. No hall and no ruler are named, so there is no audience here.

later.text: Which people held it in 793 is not settled: the game puts a few Svear at the gate until 800 and Curonians after (?).

pages.title: The field of the armed men
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Grobiņa. A wide heath of low round mounds, each a few paces across and no higher than a man's knee, hundreds of them, running off among birch and pine.
pages.game: A mound at Grobiņa. A wide heath of low round mounds, each a few paces across and no higher than a man's knee, hundreds of them, running off among birch and pine. The oldest are furred with heather; the newest is bare sand with a burnt patch beside it. In the grass between two old ones stands a thin flat stone, grey, with two birds cut on it. Wind in the pines, and nobody about. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering, bury a man, make a vow and fund a work. Found here: Arnvald.
pages.known: The Priediens field: low mounds mostly 7 to 10 m across and 0.5 m high, cremations, men with Scandinavian weapons; about 2,000 by one count and about 1,000 by another. The picture stone was found in a grave here in 1987; that it once stood in the open is the game's guess (?). That this is the field of the Mälar men is from memory of Nerman (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/grobin.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with what could and could not be checked.

pages.title: The women's ground
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Grobiņa. A level stretch of sandy turf by a stand of old hornbeams, with nothing on it but small ringed patches where the grass grows greener.
pages.game: A graveyard at Grobiņa. A level stretch of sandy turf by a stand of old hornbeams, with nothing on it but small ringed patches where the grass grows greener. No mounds, no stones. A woman kneels at one of the patches, pouring something from a cup, and the brooches on her dress are the kind worn on one island in the whole sea. A lark, and the settlement's smoke beyond the trees. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering, bury a man and give a gift. Found here: Rodlikn.
pages.known: The Smukumi flat-grave field: more than 100 graves dug, women with Scandinavian brooches, pendants, rings and glass beads, men with swords and shield bosses; cremations. Women in the flat graves wear Gotland's belt buckles and brooches. The hornbeams are from the Latvian derivation of the name (gruobīns, a hornbeam wood) (?). The offering poured is invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/grobin.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with what could and could not be checked.

pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen

pages.game: A lodging at Grobiņa. The longest house on the black earth: a hearth down the middle, sleeping benches along both walls with sheepskins on them, a loom by the door where the light is, and a brewing vat under the eaves. A board for the table game hangs on a peg with its pieces in a bag. It smells of malt, smoke and drying fish. Every bench has a name, and one of them is kept for your crew after the first night. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, buy stores, listen for talk, play tafl, throw dice, trade riddles and pay the singer, and more. Found here: Rodlikn, Botgair and Tulegaud.
pages.known: The Gotland women of the flat graves are the nearest thing to named households the place has; that one of them lodged strangers and brewed is the game's guess (?).

pages.title: The house of the woman who is asked
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Grobiņa. A small round-cornered house at the edge of the hornbeams, apart from the rest, with bunches of dry plants hanging under the eaves and a fire that is never let out.
pages.game: A shrine at Grobiņa. A small round-cornered house at the edge of the hornbeams, apart from the rest, with bunches of dry plants hanging under the eaves and a fire that is never let out. An old woman sits on the threshold with her hands in her lap. People come to the fence, wait to be looked at, and say what they want to know. She does not get up for Northmen, and does not send them away either. What is done here: cast the lots, make an offering, see the leech and make a vow. Found here: Buite.
pages.known: Adam of Bremen, about 1075, says the Curonians' houses are 'full of pagan soothsayers, diviners and necromancers': late for these years, and used lightly. What she does, whom she calls on and in what words is not recorded and is not written here: the player sees a question asked and an answer given, no more (?).

pages.title: The Slake
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Gyrwe. A broad brown mudflat on the south side of the Tyne where the Don comes in, bare at the ebb and shining, with a firmer strip of shingle under the monastery's bank where boats take the ground.
pages.game: A beach at Gyrwe. A broad brown mudflat on the south side of the Tyne where the Don comes in, bare at the ebb and shining, with a firmer strip of shingle under the monastery's bank where boats take the ground. In front, two tarred fishing boats and the house's own broad coaster leaning on her bilge; behind, a low green rise with two stone churches in a line, their small windows catching the light. Curlews, the suck of the tide in the creeks, and a smell of mud, wrack and wood smoke. What is done here: load and unload, scrape and tar, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot and hire carriers. Found here: Dudda and Beornwine.
pages.known: Jarrow Slake as a natural beaching ground. Symeon's 'port of King Ecgfrith' is the only text that puts ships here. No quay has been found: none is drawn.

What is done here: hire a pilot, wait for wind and have him remembered. Found here: Dudda.

pages.title: Saint Paul's
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Gyrwe. A tall narrow church of squared Roman stone with a porch at the west end and small side chambers along both walls.
pages.game: A church at Gyrwe. A tall narrow church of squared Roman stone with a porch at the west end and small side chambers along both walls. Inside, lamplight on painted boards hung in pairs: a boy carrying wood beside a man carrying a cross, a bronze serpent on a pole beside a crucifixion. Over the inner arch a cut stone names a king and an abbot. East of it, in a line, stands a second, smaller church whose three little windows burn with coloured glass. Chant in two choirs, cold stone, incense. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, read a book and take sanctuary. Found here: Friduin.
pages.known: The great church hallowed 23 April 685 and the east church in line with it, which stands yet with first-build glass (English Heritage, description; Tyne and Wear HER 1229). The paired pictures: Bede, Lives of the Abbots 9. The tower that now joins the churches is later and is not drawn before the 11th century.

pages.game: A graveyard at Gyrwe. Rows of plain grassed graves, all with their heads to the west, between the church wall and the long halls. No stones for most; here and there a small carved slab, one cut with a cross and a line of Latin. Many of the graves are short. A woman from the fishers' houses is setting a pot of flowers on one. Wind in the grass, the scribes' shutter banging. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, give alms and read a book.
pages.known: About 132 burials, west to east, unfurnished; of 111 sure ones, 39 were infants, children or youths, so lay families were buried here. The cross slab whose Latin says that in this sign life is given back to the world: HER 1224, 1225.

In the second, a large room with painted walls and a stone seat for the abbot, and against the far wall the iron-bound chests. Quiet, the scrape of spoons, one voice reading. pages.known: Two long stone halls, one with bench settings and fish bones, one with a finely decorated room and a stone seat. Reading at table is the Rule's.

pages.title: The book chests
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Gyrwe. Six oak chests with iron bands at the end of the abbot's room, each with its key on the schoolmaster's belt, and a bench under the window where four boys sit with wax tablets on their knees.
pages.game: A storehouse at Gyrwe. Six oak chests with iron bands at the end of the abbot's room, each with its key on the schoolmaster's belt, and a bench under the window where four boys sit with wax tablets on their knees. A chest stands open: books lying flat in their boards, a strip of parchment hanging from each with its name. An old monk counts on his finger joints and the boys count after him. Dust, old leather, beeswax. What is done here: read a book, have it copied, trade riddles and give a gift. Found here: Ceolmund and Beornwine.
pages.known: Benedict's library, to be 'kept entire' (Bede, Lives of the Abbots 11, tr. Giles), doubled by Ceolfrith (15). No library room has been found: chests in the abbot's hall are the game's. Books were kept in chests. The number of books in 793 is not known.

pages.game: A workshop at Gyrwe. A lean-to against the south wall of the hall, built for the light: four sloped desks under an open shutter, a rack of quills, horns of black and red ink, a stretched calfskin drying on a frame by the door. A monk writes with his tongue between his teeth and a boy rules lines with a lead point. In winter a pan of coals sits under each desk and does no good. Scratching, coughing, the smell of gall ink and lime. What is done here: have it copied, read a book, take an order, trade riddles and try the goods. Found here: Torhtred.
pages.known: The house wrote three whole Bibles before 716 and Bede's books after; no writing room has been found, and this one is invented. Numbed hands in winter: Abbot Cuthbert to Lul, 764 (?).

pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Hamwic. A long shelving beach of gravel and grey mud on the Itchen, with a dozen clinker hulls drawn up stern to the water and props under their bilges.
pages.game: A beach at Hamwic. A long shelving beach of gravel and grey mud on the Itchen, with a dozen clinker hulls drawn up stern to the water and props under their bilges. In front, porters wade with casks on their shoulders; behind, three gravel streets run straight up between thatched houses to the graveyard of St Mary's. No quay, no post, no tower. It smells of weed, tar and wet wool, and the light is flat and wide off the water. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, wait for wind, hire a pilot and pay the toll. Found here: Eadhun and Hildulf.
pages.known: Morton 1992: boats drawn up on a shelving beach east of St Mary's; no quay or jetty known. The name wic-hythe is from Sawyer 1012 (1045). The toll is the table's 5%: no toll charter survives (?).

What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and call witnesses. Found here: Leofstan and Herewald.
pages.known: Morton 1992: a strand street along the shore; houses 10-12 m by 4-5 m with the long side to the street and an open shed; no market place found. Seine-valley black and grey wares are 18% of the pottery (Hodges 1981).

pages.game: A minster at Hamwic. Where the three river streets meet the main street there is a wide fenced graveyard on the highest ground the town has, which is not high. A timber church stands in it among rows of grass mounds with wooden markers. From its gate the whole beach can be seen, every hull and who is loading her. Rooks, wind, and the bell for the hours, struck by hand. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, have him remembered, bury a man, take sanctuary, ask the news and fund a work. Found here: Ceolhelm.
pages.known: Morton 1992: St Mary's was probably the main graveyard from about 750. Nothing early has been seen in the ground, so the timber church is a guess (?). The founding by Birinus in 634 is not claimed.

pages.game: A workshop at Hamwic. Three open sheds on the street down to the hythe. In the nearest a woman saws cattle bone into plates on a block that is the grey backbone of a whale, and the floor is white with offcuts. Next door a man pours bronze into a stone mould for pins, and a boy draws wire. Sawdust of bone, hot metal, a glue pot. Finished combs hang on a string like fish. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, haggle the price and buy ship's tools. Found here: Catte.
pages.known: Morton 1992; Ellis and Andrews 2006: by Chapel Road 1,668 bone offcuts, mostly cattle, and a whale's vertebra used as a chopping block; ingot moulds, crucibles and pin wire nearby. Workshops stood house by house, not by quarter.

Benches along both walls, a hearth in the middle, a pottery lamp on a post, and a Frankish black jug that is only brought out for those who pay first. On the lintel sits a smooth grey stone axe nobody can explain. Ale, peat-brown smoke, eel broth, four tongues at once. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, trade riddles, pay the singer, hire a hand and lodge ashore. Found here: Beorngyth.
pages.known: Invented: no ale-house has been dug. The house is the town's common house (Morton 1992); lamps of pot and stone, and a Stone Age flint axe kept as a curio, are finds (Addyman and Hill 1969; Morton 1992).

pages.game: A storehouse at Hamwic. A row of house-ends toward the hythe with plank doors and no windows. One stands open: sacks of wool to the rafters, a loom leaning in the door with its clay weights swinging, bolts of cloth laid on a trestle with the makers' knots in the selvedge. Two old casks from the Seine hold the well-lining nobody has got round to. Lanolin, dust, a dog asleep on the best cloth. What is done here: use your store, rent store room, buy a plot, buy from makers, try the goods and load and unload. Found here: Leofstan.
pages.known: Morton 1992; Bourdillon and Coy 1980: sheep were kept old for the fleece, loom weights, pin-beaters and wool combs in every house; wells lined with old casks. That wool and cloth were the export is likely, not proven.

pages.game: A boat yard at Hamwic. South of the houses the gravel gives way to salt marsh, a shingle spit and a small still lagoon. On the last firm ground a hull lies on her side with three strakes off, new oak pale against the old, and a pitch pot smokes over a fire of offcuts. Beyond her the wide grey water runs down toward Wight. Curlews, adzes, the smell of tar and hot moss. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and hire a pilot. Found here: Eadhun.
pages.known: Morton 1992: salt marsh, a shingle spit and a small lagoon south of the town. No yard has been dug: the waterfront is unexcavated (?). Clinker ships and clench nails: Addyman and Hill 1969; oak felled near Hamwic in 769 for an English ship (Ufkes 2012).

Upriver, in the bend of the Itchen on the far bank, grey walls of flint and red tile stand higher than a house, with elder growing from the top and no roof anywhere inside. A ferryman keeps a flat boat on the mud below them. It is the only stone in sight, and people cross themselves or do not, according to who built it in their grandmother's telling. What is done here: cross over, ask the news, have him remembered and take sanctuary.
pages.known: Morton 1992: the Roman walls of Clausentum on the east bank, 1.4 km upstream. Perhaps the fort with 188 m of wall of the Burghal Hidage's 150 hides (?). The ferry is invented.

At each a man sets a blank on a die fixed in a block and strikes once. A reeve's man counts the pennies into a bag and a balance stands between them. Outside, a street of new houses runs down to a second beach on the wider river. Charcoal, hot silver, the stroke of the hammer. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver, call witnesses, pay the toll and hear the law.
pages.known: II Aethelstan (c. 928): two moneyers at Hamtun, and no buying above 20 pence outside a port.

pages.game: A beach at Helgö. A short curve of grey shingle and brown-green water with no tide mark on it, two farm boats drawn up on birch rollers, a net on poles. Behind, a steep slope cut into grassed steps with low turf-roofed houses on them and pine and birch above; one long roof stands higher than the rest. Still water, a cow bell, wood smoke and the smell of tar and wet stone. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar, mend the boat, buy stores and hire a pilot. Found here: Holmfrid and Gillög.
pages.known: Boats drawn up on the beach below the houses, no jetty reported; the houses on terraces cut into the slope (Holmqvist (?)); the bay without tide, brown-green, about 5 m higher than now. The market here is a farm's: barley, cheese, butter, a few hides, bar iron (the iron is likely, not shown (?)).

pages.game: A hall at Helgö. A long, dim timber hall on the highest terrace: a hearth down the middle, benches along both walls, smoke going up to a hole in a roof of birch bark and turf. On a peg by the high seat hangs a small dark bronze man on a leather strap, sitting with his legs folded; beside it a long-handled bronze dipper of foreign make. Shelves hold pale green glass beakers, most of them chipped. It smells of smoke, old ale and dogs. What is done here: hold a feast, give a gift, lodge ashore, drink with them, pay the singer, trade riddles, play tafl and ask the news, and more. Found here: Ingemund.
pages.known: The feasting hall of House Group 2, where the imported things lay; the Buddha, 8.4 cm, with a leather strap round neck and arm, already battered; the bronze ladle from Egypt; sherds of Frankish funnel beakers (?). That these hung on show in 793, and who kept them, is the game's guess (?): when the Buddha came north is not known.
