The ground between them is red and crunches: it is made of broken clay moulds, each with the hollow of half a brooch or a pin in it. One shed has a roof, a stone-lined hearth, a pair of goatskin bellows and a man. Charcoal, hot metal, and a hammer that stops when you come near. What is done here: take an order, buy ship's tools, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods and buy from makers. Found here: Fastulf.
pages.known: The workshops of goldsmiths and bronze-casters from the 400s, cold by 793; mould pieces by the tens of thousands (Holmqvist (?)). A broken rune stick lies in the rubbish here; the smith gives a riddle of fire and flint (text.t-gest-29).

pages.title: The holy rock
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Helgö. A grey hump of bare rock among the houses, as high as a man's chest, split by one long crack.
pages.game: A shrine at Helgö. A grey hump of bare rock among the houses, as high as a man's chest, split by one long crack. In the crack and round its foot lie small things: an iron ring, arrowheads gone to rust, a crust, a bowl with the milk skinned over. No carved post, no roof, no fence. An old woman sits on a stone beside it with a bag of cut twigs in her lap. Flies, and the sun on warm stone. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots, make a vow and swear an oath. Found here: Gudlög.
pages.known: Offerings of rings, arrowheads and food at a rock by the houses, lasting into the Viking Age, are argued by T. Zachrisson, 'The holiness of Helgö', Excavations at Helgö XVI (2004), not opened (?). The island's name is read as 'hallowed island'. The Svear ask the gods by lots (Rimbert c. 18, 19, 27). Hall and rock, not 'temple'.

pages.brief: A graveyard at Helgö. A birch wood on the back of the island where the ground is all small swellings: low round mounds under moss, rings and three-cornered settings of stones, hundreds of them, some sunk almost flat.
pages.game: A graveyard at Helgö. A birch wood on the back of the island where the ground is all small swellings: low round mounds under moss, rings and three-cornered settings of stones, hundreds of them, some sunk almost flat. At the near edge there is a patch of burnt black earth with a new mound beside it no bigger than a cartwheel. On it lies a small round loaf. Wind in the birch leaves, and no other sound. What is done here: have him remembered, bury a man and make an offering. Found here: Gudlög.
pages.known: Five grave fields; cremations under low mounds and stone settings, some of the Viking Age, and loaves of bread laid in some graves: all three from memory of the literature (?). The Svear burn their dead.

From the highest stone the bay lies open on every side, islands behind islands, and to the west a line of smoke that is Birka. A man with a pole across his knees sits here most days, watching sails. Resin, wind, an eagle over the water. What is done here: ask the keeper, wait for wind, hire a pilot and ask the news. Found here: Torbjörn.
pages.known: The hillfort, used about 200 to 500 and a ruin in 793. The ways in from the sea by the sounds at Stockholm and Södertälje; the pilot and his watch are invented.

pages.title: Conca, the shell bay
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Herio. A half-moon of pale sand on the island's north side, low grey rocks at either horn, the open bay beyond and the Loire shore a blue line far off.
pages.game: A beach at Herio. A half-moon of pale sand on the island's north side, low grey rocks at either horn, the open bay beyond and the Loire shore a blue line far off. Two or three ships ride to stone anchors waiting for a wind; boats lie on the sand with their yards lowered. Behind the beach a path climbs through tamarisk to the monastery's west gate. Wind in the rigging, oystercatchers, the smell of weed drying on the tide line. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, mend the boat, hire carriers and buy a boat. Found here: Ursus.
pages.known: Ermentarius, Miracula I.81 and II.9: 'our island's port called Conca', where ships anchor and wait for a wind; II.11: the west gate leads to it. La Conche, on the north side (Poupardin 1905).

pages.hint: A market, not yet seen

pages.game: A market at Herio. Above the tide line at Conca, on trodden sand: grey salt in heaps the height of a man's knee, each under a mat of rushes weighted with stones, and a row of rush baskets for carrying it. A wooden measure stands on a plank; beside it whatever the last ship brought, grain in sacks, a few jars. Women with rakes, a monk with a tally stick, gulls walking between the heaps. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and buy from makers. Found here: Maura.
pages.known: No market is recorded on the island: selling on the beach is the game's (?). The trade itself is Ermentarius, Miracula I.81: grain in, 'only salt' out. Pennies and halfpennies pass at the abbey's market at Deas (I.71).

pages.known: Ermentarius, Miracula II.11: monastery and fort share a west gate, towards Conca. The porter is the Rule of St Benedict c. 66. The cross marking how near women may come is recorded for Deas (I.71); here it is supposed (?).

pages.title: Saint Philibert's basilica
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Herio. A long low church of small squared stone with a roof of grey lead that shines after rain.
pages.game: An abbey at Herio. A long low church of small squared stone with a roof of grey lead that shines after rain. Inside it is dark and cool: at the east end a white marble coffin on a step, three lamps burning at its head by day and by night, a staff laid along it, and a wooden frame with carrying poles leaning against the wall. Sick people sit on the floor with a hand on the stone. What is done here: hear Mass, make a vow, give alms, see the leech, have him remembered, take sanctuary and fund a work.
pages.known: Ermentarius, Miracula I.2 (the marble coffin, the carrying frame, wine in which the staff was washed) and II.8 (three lamps always lit; 'the other church' near by). The look of the building is not known (?); the lead is I.81.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

later.text: After June 836 the step is bare and there is a pit beside it; after 846 the roof is open to the sky.

pages.title: The cellarer's store
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Herio. A stone room half sunk in the ground beside the kitchen, with one door and a slit of light.
pages.game: A storehouse at Herio. A stone room half sunk in the ground beside the kitchen, with one door and a slit of light. Oil jars stand shoulder to shoulder in sand along one wall; sacks of corn hang from the beams out of reach of rats; lumps of lead are stacked like loaves in the corner. A monk with a wax tablet stands in the doorway and looks at what you carry before he looks at you. What is done here: use your store, rent store room, buy stores, take an order and give a gift. Found here: Vitalis.
pages.known: Vita Filiberti cc. 26-27: the kitchen, the cellarer's store, the lamp oil from Bordeaux, the fat of a stranded sea beast for the lamps. The lead in lumps is Ermentarius, Miracula I.81.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

later.text: It stands until about 846.

pages.title: The guest house, Herio
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Herio. A thatched house outside the cloister wall with a hearth in the middle and straw-filled bed frames along both sides.
pages.game: A lodging at Herio. A thatched house outside the cloister wall with a hearth in the middle and straw-filled bed frames along both sides. A basin and a towel wait by the door. Windbound seamen sleep at one end; at the other a table under a small window holds an ink horn, a knife and a few leaves weighted with a stone. What is done here: lodge ashore, listen for talk, read a book, have it copied and trade riddles.
pages.known: Vita Filiberti cc. 27, 29: guests at the abbot's table; windbound Breton ships given two beasts, flour and bread. The Rule of St Benedict c. 53. Adalard's exile: Cartron 2010 ch. II.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

later.text: From 814 to 821 a tall old monk writes there every morning and a king's man sits by the door.
It stands until about 846.

pages.title: The abbot's table
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Herio. A plain room off the cloister with one long table, a bench on each side and a chair at the end with arms.
pages.game: A hall at Herio. A plain room off the cloister with one long table, a bench on each side and a chair at the end with arms. A book lies open on a stand for the reading at meals. Fish, beans, bread and a jug of thin wine; nobody speaks while the reader reads. Through the door the cloister garth is green and a brother is drawing water. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, show the charter and fund a work.
pages.known: Vita Filiberti cc. 26-27 (the abbot's table, guests, a cloister). The abbot of 793 is not known.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

later.text: From 819 the abbot is on the island only before Easter and after the autumn (diploma of 830).
It stands until about 846.

pages.title: The clay beds
pages.hint: A salt works, not yet seen
pages.brief: A salt works at Herio.
pages.game: A salt works at Herio. On the lagoon side, where the sand bar joins the two islets: shallow square beds cut in grey clay, each a hand deep in still water with a white skin forming at the edges, low banks between them and a sluice of planks to the tide. Rakes with long handles, small cones of wet salt draining on the banks, a hut of turf. Flat light, flies, the sour smell of mud in the sun. What is done here: buy from makers, hire carriers, trade riddles and fund a work. Found here: Natalis.
pages.known: Salt beds on the island itself are supposed, not attested (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

pages.title: Abbot Hilbod's fort
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Herio. An earth bank faced with stone and topped with stakes, drawn in a ring round the monastery, with a ditch outside that fills at spring tides.
pages.game: A wall at Herio. An earth bank faced with stone and topped with stakes, drawn in a ring round the monastery, with a ditch outside that fills at spring tides. Men of the abbey's household walk the top with spears and round shields; horses are tied inside the gate. What is done here: take sanctuary, use your store, ask the news, call witnesses and hire a hand.
pages.known: Falco c. 18: a strong citadel with a rampart. Its plan is not known (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

later.text: Diploma of 2 August 830: a castrum built by Hilbod around the monastery, guarded by the abbey's own men.
Horsemen in 835: Ermentarius II.11.
By 950 it is a grassed bank with a gap where the gate stood, and children run along it.

pages.title: The old graves
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Herio. On the north shore, a short walk east of Conca: broken walls of thin red brick standing knee high in the grass, and among them stone coffins, some with their lids askew and sand drifted in.
pages.game: A graveyard at Herio. On the north shore, a short walk east of Conca: broken walls of thin red brick standing knee high in the grass, and among them stone coffins, some with their lids askew and sand drifted in. A small chapel of Saint Hilary stands over the newest graves. Sea pinks, a view straight out to the open water, and no sound but the wind. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered and give alms.
pages.known: Le Vieil: a large Gallo-Roman site reused as a Merovingian burial ground, with a chapel of St Hilary over the graves, undated (Cartron 2010 ch. III); stone coffins from it are shown in the castle keep.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

pages.title: The wood on the east head
pages.hint: A holy wood, not yet seen
pages.brief: A holy wood at Herio. A head of rock some three men's height above the bay, covered with wind-bent oaks and holly, the only trees on the island.
pages.game: A holy wood at Herio. A head of rock some three men's height above the bay, covered with wind-bent oaks and holly, the only trees on the island. Below it a cleft in the rock where the founder is said to have prayed. From the top the whole bay lies open: Bouin low on the water to the east, the Loire shore north of it, and any sail a half day before it arrives. What is done here: make a vow, have him remembered and ask the keeper.
pages.known: The wooded head of La Chaize, about 15 m high; Saint Philibert's cave there is tradition only (the parish's page). Holm oaks are today's wood; what grew there in 793 is not known (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

pages.title: The western flats
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Herio. At low water the sea goes out of sight to the west and leaves a plain of ribbed sand, black reefs and pools.
pages.game: A fishery at Herio. At low water the sea goes out of sight to the west and leaves a plain of ribbed sand, black reefs and pools. Islanders walk it with baskets and forks for cockles and set stake nets in the gullies. The shore is white with gulls and waders, so many that when they rise the light changes. Far out a small steep islet stands off the north-west point. What is done here: buy stores, buy from makers and hire a hand.
pages.known: Flats and reefs west and south that dry at low water; the islet of Le Pilier. The birds: Ermentarius, Miracula II.10. Stranded porpoises and a sea beast: Vita Filiberti cc.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/herio.md (4 October 2026), which this file follows throughout

pages.title: The port of the island
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Hī. A curve of white shell sand on the east shore, the water over it green as glass and so clear the keel's shadow runs ahead of the boat.
pages.game: A beach at Hī. A curve of white shell sand on the east shore, the water over it green as glass and so clear the keel's shadow runs ahead of the boat. Hide boats lie bottom up above the weed line with stones on their gunwales; one wooden boat sits on rollers. Behind, a turf bank as high as a house, thatch above it, and the tops of tall stone crosses. Across the Sound the rocks of Mull are pink in the evening. It smells of weed, peat smoke and wet hide. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, mend the boat and buy a boat. Found here: Domnall.
pages.known: Boats lie on the sand of the east shore below the monastery, no quay known; the Sound: white sand, pink granite on the Mull side.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The shouting place
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Hī. The narrowest water, a mile of it, with low islets in the stream and the tide running a slow walking pace.
pages.game: A ferry at Hī. The narrowest water, a mile of it, with low islets in the stream and the tide running a slow walking pace. On the far rocks a figure cups his hands and shouts; long after, the sound arrives. A brother pushes a hide boat down the sand without hurry. Terns work the tide line and a seal watches from the slack. What is done here: cross over, ask the news, hire carriers and ask the keeper. Found here: Domnall.
pages.known: People on the Mull shore shout across the Sound and a boat is sent: Adomnan, Life of Columba I.20 and elsewhere (Reeves 1874, numbers not re-checked (?)); en.wikipedia Sound of Iona.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The guest house inside the bank
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Hī. A long low house of wattle and thatch just inside the gap in the great bank, its door to the south.
pages.game: A lodging at Hī. A long low house of wattle and thatch just inside the gap in the great bank, its door to the south. In front, a wooden tub and a brother with his sleeves rolled, waiting to wash a stranger's feet whether the stranger likes it or not. Inside: a peat fire on a flat stone, benches, a pot of barley and milk, a pilgrim asleep with his boots on. Wednesday and Friday there is no meat, until a guest comes; then there is. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, see the leech and give alms. Found here: Óengus.
pages.known: The guest house made ready and water drawn to wash the strangers' feet: Adomnan I.4; the fast broken for a guest: I.20. The vallum: Historic Environment Scotland, Iona Abbey.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The kiln and the barn
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Hī. A round drying kiln with a wisp of smoke and a long barn beside it, the door wide enough for two men with a cask on a pole.
pages.game: A storehouse at Hī. A round drying kiln with a wisp of smoke and a long barn beside it, the door wide enough for two men with a cask on a pole. Here is where a cargo is looked at: wine tasted from a horn spoon, iron rung against a stone, salt rubbed between finger and thumb. Nothing is priced. The guest-master says what the house needs, and afterwards what the house gives, and a boy cuts both on a stick. A white horse stands at the door with empty milk pails. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, use your store, buy stores and give a gift. Found here: Óengus.
pages.known: Adomnan names a kiln, a barn, the grinding of corn and a white horse that carried the milk pails. No market, toll or sale is recorded: a house that receives.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The church of Colum Cille
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Hī. A timber church, steep-roofed, its planks grey with a hundred winters and its door facing the crosses.
pages.game: A church at Hī. A timber church, steep-roofed, its planks grey with a hundred winters and its door facing the crosses. Inside it is dark and warm: one lamp, a stone altar, a book on it under a cloth, and to one side the saint's shrine when it is on the island. The psalms go on at all hours in voices that do not hurry. Wax, damp wool and the sea. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, give a gift, ask an audience, take sanctuary and fund a work. Found here: Bresal and Cellach.
pages.known: Timber, wattle and thatch.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

later.text: About 800 the wooden church replaced in stone: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey (no dig cited (?)).
After the burning of 802 a smaller one, and then walls of stone (?).
Whether the church burned in 825 is not known.

pages.title: The high crosses
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Hī. Four great crosses of stone before the church door, taller than two men, cut all over with bosses and snakes and, on one, the Virgin and Child among angels.
pages.game: A shrine at Hī. Four great crosses of stone before the church door, taller than two men, cut all over with bosses and snakes and, on one, the Virgin and Child among angels. One has arms so wide that they have cracked, and the masons have set a ring of stone round the crossing to hold them. Lichen is already at work on the oldest. Brothers bow to them going in; gulls sit on them going nowhere. What is done here: make a vow, swear an oath, make an offering, have him remembered, fund a work and call witnesses.
pages.known: Saint Martin's cross, 8th century, still stands where it was set; Saint John's broke for the width of its arms and the stone ring may have been made here to hold such arms; Saint Oran's and Saint Matthew's in pieces: Historic Environment Scotland; en.wikipedia Iona Abbey, High cross (the ring, from memory (?)). Some stone came by boat from Loch Sween.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The knoll of the writing hut
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Hī. A hump of bare rock facing the church, with a small hut of planks on its top, the door looking east over the Sound.
pages.game: A mound at Hī. A hump of bare rock facing the church, with a small hut of planks on its top, the door looking east over the Sound. This is where Columba sat writing with the door open, and where the abbot sits when he wants to be found. From the top you can see every boat on the sand and count the brothers in the fields. After the burning there is charred wood here and, in time, a socket cut for a cross. What is done here: ask an audience, read a book, make a vow and cast the lots. Found here: Bresal.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The writing house, Hī
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Hī. A long hut with the best light on the island: a row of sloped boards, each with a calfskin leaf pinned on it, horns of ink, shells of colour, a goose wing for dust.
pages.game: A workshop at Hī. A long hut with the best light on the island: a row of sloped boards, each with a calfskin leaf pinned on it, horns of ink, shells of colour, a goose wing for dust. On the widest board lies a page with one great letter on it and nothing else, the letter full of beasts biting each other, done so fine that it tires the eye to follow one line. A scribe breathes on his fingers. Skins stretched on frames outside, and a smell of lime and oak gall. What is done here: read a book, have it copied, trade riddles, take an order and try the goods. Found here: Muiredach.
pages.known: A writing house and library: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey. Ochres, copper green, lichen purple, woad; no lapis: en.wikipedia Book of Kells.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

later.text: The great Gospel most scholars hold was begun here about 800 and finished at Kells, not proved: 340 calfskin leaves.
The site closes when the shrine and the last treasures go to Ireland in 878 (the game's choice (?)).
It stands until about 878.

pages.title: The sheds by the ditch
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Hī. Three open-sided sheds against the inner face of the bank, out of the wind.
pages.game: A workshop at Hī. Three open-sided sheds against the inner face of the bank, out of the wind. A man works a pole lathe with his foot and a bowl grows out of an alder block; another draws a thread of blue glass from a pot no bigger than a fist; a third files a bronze pin. Leather offcuts and wood shavings go into the wet ditch, where they will lie a thousand years. Hammering, the creak of the lathe, charcoal. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order, mend the boat, fit her out, buy from makers and try the goods.
pages.known: Wood-turning, metal-working and glass for windows and beads, perhaps from the 7th century: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey. The house-shaped shrine of about 750: en.wikipedia Monymusk Reliquary (that it was made here is not claimed).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: Oran's ground and the street of the dead
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Hī. A paved way of worn red stones runs from the shore between the fields to a walled plot of small crosses and flat slabs, each slab with a cross and a line asking a prayer for a man.
pages.game: A graveyard at Hī. A paved way of worn red stones runs from the shore between the fields to a walled plot of small crosses and flat slabs, each slab with a cross and a line asking a prayer for a man. Kings who came to die as pilgrims lie here among brothers nobody remembers. The grass is cropped by sheep. From the south bay, some years, a body comes up the paved way on six shoulders with a psalm going before it. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, give alms, make a vow and fund a work.
pages.known: Reilig Odhrain, with a timber building of Columba's age found under it; the Street of the Dead: Historic Environment Scotland. The south bay as the landing of the dead and of the martyrs is tradition; the annal of 806 names no place. Over a hundred early carved stones, some asking a prayer for a named man: from memory (?). Saint Oran's Chapel is 12th century and not here. No king's grave can be shown.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

later.text: After 806 there are sixty-eight new graves in a row.

pages.title: The western plain
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Hī.
pages.game: A field at Hī. Over the low middle of the island, twenty minutes on foot, the land opens to the west: a flat green plain of shell-sand turf, barley in strips, black cattle, and beyond it white beaches and nothing at all until the world's end. Brothers reap in a line with their habits hitched up. A brother stands apart watching the western sky, because a crane is expected from Ireland and the house has orders about cranes. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, try the goods, listen for talk and wait for wind.
pages.known: The crane to be fed three days as a guest: Adomnan I.48 in Reeves (number not checked (?)).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The seals' islet
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Hī. A skerry of wet black rock off the island's end with a hundred seals on it, grey and spotted, the pups white.
pages.game: A fishery at Hī. A skerry of wet black rock off the island's end with a hundred seals on it, grey and spotted, the pups white. They are the house's own herd and are taken by count, as a farmer takes lambs. A lay brother with a club and a hide boat keeps the place; skins dry on a frame, and oil is run down in a stone trough. The noise is like a hall at a feast heard through a wall. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods, ask the keeper and listen for talk. Found here: Domnall.
pages.known: 'The little island where our young seals are brought forth and nurtured', and the thief from Colonsay who hid under his boat to kill them: Adomnan I.33.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hi.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on; what it marks (?) or (memory) is marked (?) here.

pages.title: The strand at the fjord's end
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Hleiðr. A low shore of shingle and black weed at the head of a narrow bay, reeds to either side and alders behind.
pages.game: A beach at Hleiðr. A low shore of shingle and black weed at the head of a narrow bay, reeds to either side and alders behind. Three or four boats lie drawn up on rollers with their masts down; a ship's length off the water is knee deep. There is no tide to speak of: the wrack line shows where the last west wind left the water. It smells of mud, tar and wet rope, and geese go over all day. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, wait for wind, scrape and tar and hire a pilot. Found here: Skardi.
pages.known: Lejre Vig, the southern end of Roskilde Fjord; Gevninge as 'the port of Lejre'; wind and not tide sets the level.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The watch farm
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Hleiðr. A long farmhouse and a byre on the first dry ground above the strand, with a turf bench against the south wall where a man can see the whole bay.
pages.game: A gate at Hleiðr. A long farmhouse and a byre on the first dry ground above the strand, with a turf bench against the south wall where a man can see the whole bay. A saddled horse stands tied by the door at any hour. There is no wall and no gate: only the path, which runs between the house and the midden, and the dogs. Peat smoke and horse. What is done here: give a gift, ask the news, lodge ashore, buy stores and listen for talk. Found here: Skardi.
pages.known: The farmstead at Gevninge, dug in 2000 and read as an outpost that anyone bound for the hall had to pass; the mounted watchman is our reading of it.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The slip under the alders, Hleiðr
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Hleiðr. A cleared patch east of the strand with a keel on blocks, split oak planks stacked and weighted to season, and a tar pot on three stones.
pages.game: A boat yard at Hleiðr. A cleared patch east of the strand with a keel on blocks, split oak planks stacked and weighted to season, and a tar pot on three stones. A man and two boys work with axes; nothing here is sawn. Chips lie ankle deep and the smell of tar carries to the boats. What is done here: mend the boat, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Inferred (?): no yard has been dug at Gevninge. Boats of this water are known from the fjord itself and from the Gislinge boat on the Lammefjord to the west.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Boats of this water are known from the fjord itself (Skuldelev 3, a small Danish coaster of about 1040) and from the Gislinge boat on the Lammefjord to the west.

pages.title: The stream valley
pages.hint: A ford, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ford at Hleiðr. A cart track going south beside a small clear stream, wet meadow on one hand and oak wood on the other, crossing the water twice on flat stones.
pages.game: A ford at Hleiðr. A cart track going south beside a small clear stream, wet meadow on one hand and oak wood on the other, crossing the water twice on flat stones. Pigs root under the oaks with a boy and a man watching them. On the rise ahead the hall roof shows over the trees long before the houses do, with round mounds to left and right of it. What is done here: cross over, hire carriers and buy from makers. Found here: Toki.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The great hall
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Hleiðr. A house as long as six ships laid end to end, its walls bowed like a hull, its roof carried on two rows of posts thicker than a man.
pages.game: A hall at Hleiðr. A house as long as six ships laid end to end, its walls bowed like a hull, its roof carried on two rows of posts thicker than a man. Inside it is dark after the daylight: a long fire down the middle, benches along both walls, shields and hangings behind them, and the high seat halfway down the north side. It smells of smoke, wet wool, dogs and roast pork. A stranger is shown the low bench by the door. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, pay the singer, trade riddles, play tafl and drink with them. Found here: Asgaut and Thorulf.
pages.known: The halls at Mysselhojgard; the length is given as 50 m by one account and 61 m by another, so no figure is used.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: The halls at Mysselhojgard, mid 600s to about 1000.
It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The steward's store
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Hleiðr. A sunken-floored house by the hall's east door with a plank roof and the only lock in the place.
pages.game: A storehouse at Hleiðr. A sunken-floored house by the hall's east door with a plank roof and the only lock in the place. Inside are casks, sacks, bundled hides and a chest; outside, a trestle with a folding scale on it and a whetstone for trying silver. There is no market here. What the hall wants the steward buys at this door, and what it has too much of he sells. What is done here: weigh the silver, test the silver, haggle the price, try the goods, use your store and take an order. Found here: Asgaut.
pages.known: Inferred from the kind of place: goods came to such a seat as gifts, dues and plunder as much as by sale, and no market is recorded.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: A weight lay in the hoard of the late 900s.
It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The brew-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Hleiðr. A low house behind the hall with steam coming out under the eaves: a great kettle on stones, vats, a trough of sprouting barley, bunches of bog myrtle hung to dry.
pages.game: An ale-house at Hleiðr. A low house behind the hall with steam coming out under the eaves: a great kettle on stones, vats, a trough of sprouting barley, bunches of bog myrtle hung to dry. Women come and go with buckets. There is a bench outside where the hall's people sit when they want to talk without the lord hearing. It smells of malt, sweet and sour together. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice and see the leech. Found here: Tola.
pages.known: Inferred (?): a hall of this size brewed daily. Ale flavoured with bog myrtle, not hops, is the northern custom of these centuries.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The cooking stones
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Hleiðr. A grey heap as high as a man's chest beside the hall: stones cracked by fire and thrown out, generations of them, with split bone among them, cattle, pig and horse.
pages.game: A shrine at Hleiðr. A grey heap as high as a man's chest beside the hall: stones cracked by fire and thrown out, generations of them, with split bone among them, cattle, pig and horse. A fenced yard lies behind it with one old post in the middle, dark and greasy at the top. On a feast morning pits are dug here and the meat goes in on hot stones. Crows wait on the fence. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots, make a vow and hold a feast.
pages.known: The heap of fire-cracked stones and bone beside the hall, read by the excavator as feast cooking or a place of offering; Lejre among the halls with a holy yard. The post is ours (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Closed from 934 on Thietmar's word only.
It stands until about 934.

pages.title: The smith's house
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Hleiðr. A small house set apart downwind, with a clay hearth at knee height, a bellows of two goatskins and a stump for an anvil.
pages.game: A smithy at Hleiðr. A small house set apart downwind, with a clay hearth at knee height, a bellows of two goatskins and a stump for an anvil. Moulds of baked clay lie broken by the door. The smith works bronze, silver and iron as they come: a sword's hilt one day, a kettle's patch the next. Charcoal smoke, hot metal and the hiss of a quenching trough. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order, fit her out and test the silver.
pages.known: Smiths and workers in fine metal by the hall.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: The silver figure of about 900.
It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The great mound
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Hleiðr. A round grass mound west of the hall, steep enough that sheep graze it sideways.
pages.game: A mound at Hleiðr. A round grass mound west of the hall, steep enough that sheep graze it sideways. It is the youngest of the big mounds and the only one whose dead the hall still names. A flat stone lies at its foot, stained by ale. From the top the fjord can be seen as a line of light to the north. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering and cast the lots.
pages.known: Grydehoj, a cremation mound of the 600s with a thick layer of ash and gold thread among the remains.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: The old rise
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Hleiðr. A grassed swell of ground a little north of the hall where the horses are turned out.
pages.game: A field at Hleiðr. A grassed swell of ground a little north of the hall where the horses are turned out. Old people say the first hall stood here, and in a dry summer the grass shows two rows of darker rings where its posts were. The young men of the following wrestle, race horses and throw dice here, out of the steward's sight. What is done here: throw dice, hire a hand, have him remembered and wait for wind.
pages.known: Fredshoj, the halls of the 500s and 600s, gone by 793. The marks in the grass are ours (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

pages.title: Salhaugar
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Hleiðr. Half a day's walk south-east: two low mounds by a farm, and against the nearer one a seat of flat stones facing the yard.
pages.game: A mound at Hleiðr. Half a day's walk south-east: two low mounds by a farm, and against the nearer one a seat of flat stones facing the yard. An old man sits there with a horn in his lap and a boy to lead him. Three horns interlocked are cut on the door post. Larks, wind in barley, and far off the sound of someone splitting wood. What is done here: trade riddles, pay the singer, read a book and have him remembered. Found here: Hroald.
pages.known: The Snoldelev stone, DR 248: 'Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son, reciter at Salhaugar'; Salhaugar is taken to be Sallov by Snoldelev, about twelve kilometres from Lejre (?). The seat is invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: It stands until about 830.

pages.title: The stone ships
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Hleiðr. A sloping field east of the houses with low stones set in the outlines of ships, bows to the south, the largest longer than the hall.
pages.game: A graveyard at Hleiðr. A sloping field east of the houses with low stones set in the outlines of ships, bows to the south, the largest longer than the hall. Between them the turf is broken by newer graves. On a clear evening the shadows of the stones make the ships look as if they are under way. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, make an offering and fund a work.
pages.known: Their date within the Viking Age is not known.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: The grave field of the 900s and the ship settings, the largest 70 to 80 m long.
Their date within the Viking Age is not known, so they are shown from 900 only (?).

pages.title: The king's new town across the water
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Hleiðr. An hour's row east from the strand, on a slope above a spring-fed cove: a wooden church with a shingled roof and a bell that carries over the water, a king's house beside it, and booths going up along the shore.
pages.game: A church at Hleiðr. An hour's row east from the strand, on a slope above a spring-fed cove: a wooden church with a shingled roof and a bell that carries over the water, a king's house beside it, and booths going up along the shore. It smells of new-cut oak. This is not Hleidr and the people of the hall say so often. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, ask the news, take sanctuary and ask an audience. Found here: Marcward.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md (6 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed.

later.text: Roskilde, founded by Harald Bluetooth in the 980s with a wooden church of the Trinity; a bishop's seat from 1020.

pages.title: The landing under the south wall
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Legacæstir. A shelf of red mud and shingle on the north bank of the Dee, with a few tarred boats drawn up and a hide boat upside down on stakes like a black bowl.
pages.game: A landing at Legacæstir. A shelf of red mud and shingle on the north bank of the Dee, with a few tarred boats drawn up and a hide boat upside down on stakes like a black bowl. Behind it the ground climbs to a wall of red squared stone with a gap where a gate was, and the light comes down the river from the west. It smells of tide mud and wet rope, and the only sounds are curlews and the water turning. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, mend the boat and hire carriers. Found here: Osfrith.
pages.known: The 'early harbour' on the river bank south of the fortress, below the later Lower Bridge Street, where the clearest pre-Conquest finds come from: VCH Cheshire 5.1. The weir is Norman, so the tide ran past the town (inference).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

pages.title: The bank where things are bartered
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Legacæstir. A trodden patch above the tide line where a plank lies across two Roman column drums.
pages.game: A market at Legacæstir. A trodden patch above the tide line where a plank lies across two Roman column drums. On it, on a good day: a crock of honey, a sack of salt, two cheeses, a bundle of hides. A Welshman and an Englishwoman bargain with their fingers because neither has the other's tongue. Smoke from three hearths drifts across it. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods and ask the news.
pages.known: Invented for play: whether any market was held here in 793 is not known (?). The only sign of goods from oversea is a few Carolingian jar sherds on the river bank: VCH Cheshire 5.1.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: It stands until about 906.

pages.title: The lead stack
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Legacæstir. A lean-to of turf and old roof tiles against the foot of the wall, and under it grey pigs of lead stacked like loaves, each as long as a forearm and as heavy as a calf.
pages.game: A storehouse at Legacæstir. A lean-to of turf and old roof tiles against the foot of the wall, and under it grey pigs of lead stacked like loaves, each as long as a forearm and as heavy as a calf. A two-wheeled cart with a broken felloe stands beside it. Everything near is dusted grey, the grass grows thin, and the man who sits there has grey in the creases of his hands. What is done here: buy from makers, haggle the price, load and unload, use your store and rent store room. Found here: Beornoth.
pages.known: Roman lead was mined in the hills west of the estuary and pigs of it have been found at Chester (memory (?)); working there in 793 is not attested (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

pages.title: The red walls and the south gate
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Legacæstir. A wall of great red blocks without mortar, three men high where it stands whole, with ash trees rooted in the top and one arch of a gateway still up.
pages.game: A wall at Legacæstir. A wall of great red blocks without mortar, three men high where it stands whole, with ash trees rooted in the top and one arch of a gateway still up. Through the arch a straight street runs north between humps of bramble that were barracks. What is done here: ask the news, call witnesses and fund a work.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: After 907 the gaps are filled with new work, a timber gate hangs in the arch, and men walk the top.

pages.title: Saint John's on the red cliff
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Legacæstir.
pages.game: A church at Legacæstir. A small stone church on the cliff above the river, east of the walls, built of blocks carried from the ruin next to it: a great oval hollow in the ground, grassed over, with one curve of stone seats showing like ribs. Jackdaws live in the hollow. From the church door the river shines below, and inside it smells of tallow and damp stone. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, ask the news, read a book, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man and have him remembered, and more. Found here: Eadhelm.
pages.known: The size of the church in 793 is not known (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: After 907 a masons' yard beside it cuts round-headed crosses out of the red rock.

pages.title: The ale-house in the old baths
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Legacæstir. Inside the south gate a Roman wall stands higher than any tree, with a round arch in it and a roof of thatch slung across one corner.
pages.game: An ale-house at Legacæstir. Inside the south gate a Roman wall stands higher than any tree, with a round arch in it and a roof of thatch slung across one corner. Under the thatch are a hearth, three benches, casks on a stone floor patterned in small coloured squares, and a woman who looks at every face twice. It is warm, it smells of malt and woodsmoke, and swallows go in and out over the drinkers' heads. What is done here: drink with them, lodge ashore, listen for talk, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer and hire a hand, and more. Found here: Wigburh.
pages.known: How much stood in 793 is not known, and the ale-house is invented (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: Ale-wives and the bad-ale fine are in the customs of the city before 1066: Domesday Book via VCH Cheshire 5.1.

pages.title: The crossing to the south bank
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Legacæstir. A flat boat on a rope of twisted hide, and at low water a line of stones a careful man can walk.
pages.game: A ferry at Legacæstir. A flat boat on a rope of twisted hide, and at low water a line of stones a careful man can walk. On the far bank a cliff of red rock has been cut back in steps by old quarrymen, and on one face, small and worn, is a carved woman with a spear and a bird at her shoulder. Cattle stand in the shallows. The track beyond goes to Wales. What is done here: cross over, ask the news and listen for talk.
pages.known: None is attested for 793, so the game has a ferry and a low-water ford (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: A bridge stood before 1066 (Domesday).

pages.title: Henwald's Lowe
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Legacæstir. A round green mound in the rough pasture north-east of the walls, twice a man's height, with a thorn tree on it bent away from the sea wind.
pages.game: A mound at Legacæstir. A round green mound in the rough pasture north-east of the walls, twice a man's height, with a thorn tree on it bent away from the sea wind. Sheep lie on its lee side. From the top the whole red square of the fortress shows, and the river, and the hills of the Welsh blue behind. What is done here: have him remembered and listen for talk.
pages.known: Henwald's Lowe, 'Henwald's barrow', a mound north-east of the walls, perhaps an early lord's grave: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Who Henwald was is not known.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

pages.title: Saint Bridget's by the river
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Legacæstir.
pages.game: A church at Legacæstir. A timber church with a shingle roof, south of the walls on the street that goes down to the landing, and round it long huts whose side walls bow outward like a boat's. Men with Norse names and Irish mothers stand at the door after Mass and talk of Dublin prices. A rush cross hangs over the lintel, and the street smells of peat smoke and stockfish. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, ask the news, swear an oath and hire a hand. Found here: Hingamund.
pages.known: St Bridget's, the Irish and Norse settlers' church south of the fortress, probably from their arrival; bow-sided huts of Scandinavian kind on Lower Bridge Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Its first year is not known (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

pages.title: The Lady's hall
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Legacæstir. A long timber hall with a new thatch, set among the bramble humps inside the walls, with a yard of raked gravel and a line of spears in a rack by the door.
pages.game: A hall at Legacæstir. A long timber hall with a new thatch, set among the bramble humps inside the walls, with a yard of raked gravel and a line of spears in a rack by the door. Carts of stone and lime go past it all day to the wall. Inside, a high seat with an empty chair beside it, a board with tally sticks, and a woman's voice asking short questions. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath and hear the law. Found here: Æthelflæd.
pages.known: Timber halls and sunken huts of the 10th century inside the fortress at Hamilton Place, Crook Street and Hunter Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. That one of them was the Lady's is the game's (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: After 918 it is the reeve's, then the ealdorman's and the earl's.

pages.title: The reeve's board at the water gate
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Legacæstir. A trestle under a penthouse roof where the new wall comes down to the river, with a balance, a measure for ale and a peg rail hung with lead tags on cords.
pages.game: A toll place at Legacæstir. A trestle under a penthouse roof where the new wall comes down to the river, with a balance, a measure for ale and a peg rail hung with lead tags on cords. Two reeves' men sit there, the king's and the earl's, and do not much like each other. Every bale that comes up from the landing passes the board, and so does every skin. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, hear the law, call witnesses and bring a case.
pages.known: A lead customs tag from Chester dies of Eadwig's reign was found at Coppergate, York: VCH.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: They describe 1066; the game lets them begin with the burh in 907 (?).

pages.title: The market at the cross
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Legacæstir.
pages.game: A market at Legacæstir. Where the two straight streets of the old fortress meet there is a small church of Saint Peter, and before its door the market: grey-black pots stacked in straw, salt in sacks, cloth, combs of antler, disc brooches on a board, and on some days a rope of people for sale. Dublin men in fur-edged cloaks walk through it, pricing everything. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, hire carriers, buy ship's tools and ask the news.
pages.known: St Peter's at the cross of the Roman streets; Chester-ware pots, salt, cloth, brooches and slaves out, marten skins in; bone and antler working at Abbey Green: VCH Cheshire 5.1.
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: St Peter's at the cross of the Roman streets, by tradition dedicated in 907.

pages.title: The moneyers' benches, Legacæstir
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Legacæstir. A row of low lock-up sheds near the market, each with a block of oak set in the floor and an iron die standing in it.
pages.game: A mint at Legacæstir. A row of low lock-up sheds near the market, each with a block of oak set in the floor and an iron die standing in it. A man sets a blank on the die, a boy holds the upper iron, and the hammer comes down once. It rings like a small bell, twenty times in the space of a prayer. Charcoal smoke, hot metal, and a pot of clippings nobody takes his eyes off. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Irfara.
pages.known: An ingot mould from Lower Bridge Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. The mint's house has not been found, so its place is the game's (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: A mint in north-west Mercia from about 890, most likely here.
About 16 moneyers by 916-918 and at least 25 under Æthelstan.

pages.title: Saint Werburgh's minster
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Legacæstir. In the north-east corner of the walls, a stone church with a timber porch and a row of canons' houses, all new and all built of old red blocks.
pages.game: A minster at Legacæstir. In the north-east corner of the walls, a stone church with a timber porch and a row of canons' houses, all new and all built of old red blocks. Inside, a shrine with a cloth over it and a lamp that is never let go out. On the saint's day in the dead of winter geese are driven up the street to be blessed, complaining the whole way. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man, read a book and fund a work.
pages.known: Werburgh's feast 3 February and her goose: Goscelin, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werburgh. The blessing of geese is invented (?).
pages.source: A History of the County of Chester, vol. 5 part 1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230' (Victoria County History, 2003): https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/ches/vol5/pt1/pp16-33 (through the dossier)

later.text: The minster certainly there by 958, probably founded or refounded by Æthelflæd after 907 with Werburgh's body brought from Hanbury (the date 875 is late and unreliable); a warden and twelve canons in 1066: VCH Cheshire 5.1.

pages.title: The Ouse
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Lindisfarena. A pool of quiet water inside the sands, with a shelving beach of shingle and black weed.
pages.game: A beach at Lindisfarena. A pool of quiet water inside the sands, with a shelving beach of shingle and black weed. In front, two small tarred boats drawn up and the marks of many keels, some of them long; behind, the ridge of the Heugh and the lead roof of the church catching the light. Terns, the slap of the tide coming in over the flats, a smell of weed and wet wool. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar and mend the boat. Found here: Eadstan.
pages.known: The harbour pool is calm in westerlies; where boats lay is not recorded. In 687 Cuthbert's body came from Farne by ship (Bede, Life of Cuthbert 40). The keel marks of June 793 are the game's.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/lindisfarena.md (researched 4 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed

pages.title: The pilgrims' sand
pages.hint: A ford, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ford at Lindisfarena. Three quarters of a mile of wet sand between the island and the mainland, shining like a shield at the ebb and gone altogether at the flood.
pages.game: A ford at Lindisfarena. Three quarters of a mile of wet sand between the island and the mainland, shining like a shield at the ebb and gone altogether at the flood. A line of footprints and cart ruts runs across it, already filling. Far out a man leads an ox cart, small as a beetle; behind him the hills of the mainland, and the sea coming round both ends at once without any noise. What is done here: cross over, hire carriers and ask the news. Found here: Eadstan.
pages.known: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3: twice a day enclosed by the sea like an island, twice joined to the land. No causeway before modern times; crossed on foot or by cart at low water.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/lindisfarena.md (researched 4 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed

pages.title: Saint Peter's church
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Lindisfarena. A long low church of hewn oak, sheathed roof and walls in grey lead so that it looks cast in one piece.
pages.game: A minster at Lindisfarena. A long low church of hewn oak, sheathed roof and walls in grey lead so that it looks cast in one piece. In 793 the doorway stands open with the hinges torn out and daylight falls on a swept floor; inside, to the right of the altar, the carved oak coffin of Saint Cuthbert stands above the ground, untouched. Few lamps. The brethren sing the hours with gaps where voices used to be. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, give a gift, ask an audience and fund a work. Found here: Higbald.
pages.known: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 (oak, then lead plates); Life of Cuthbert 42-43 (the coffin above the floor). Sanctuary at the body: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/lindisfarena.md (researched 4 Oct 2026): the base for every fact here; its section 8 lists what must not be claimed

pages.title: The graveyard and Bishop Æthelwold's cross
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Lindisfarena. Low mounds in rows, feet to the sea, each with a scatter of white pebbles from the shore laid on it, and here and there a small carved stone, painted, with a name and a cross.
pages.game: A graveyard at Lindisfarena. Low mounds in rows, feet to the sea, each with a scatter of white pebbles from the shore laid on it, and here and there a small carved stone, painted, with a name and a cross. In the middle a tall stone cross with the bishop's name cut on it: in 793 its head lies in the grass beside it in pieces. New graves at the near end, the turf still cut square. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, give alms and fund a work. Found here: Æthelgyth.
pages.known: DigVentures and Durham University, burials of the 7th to 11th centuries: shrouded, feet to the sea, white quartz pebbles on the graves; the name stones (English Heritage collection). Æthelwold's cross, broken by the heathen in 793 and run together with lead: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xii. King Oswald's head lay in this graveyard (Bede III.12).

pages.brief: A church at Lindisfarena. A bare ridge of black rock along the island's south edge. On its top a small stone chapel and beside it the footing of something taller.
pages.game: A church at Lindisfarena. A bare ridge of black rock along the island's south edge. On its top a small stone chapel and beside it the footing of something taller. From here everything shows: the Ouse below, the crag of Beblowe to the east with nothing on it, the Farne rocks, the kings' fort on its rock to the south, and to the north only sea. A brother sits with his back to the wall and his face to the north. What is done here: ask the keeper, wait for wind, ask the news, make a vow and fund a work.
pages.known: In 687 a brother waited on a height for two candles shown from Farne (Bede, Life of Cuthbert 40). Footings of a small stone church and a tower-like building on the Heugh, dug 2016-17 (?). No beacon or daymark before 1810; no castle on Beblowe before 1550.

pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Lindisfarena. A hump of black stone a bowshot off the shore, with turf on top and a low wall of piled stones.
pages.game: A shrine at Lindisfarena. A hump of black stone a bowshot off the shore, with turf on top and a low wall of piled stones. At the ebb a man can walk to it over weed and pools; at the flood it is its own island. Eider ducks sit on the water round it. In Lent there is one brother on it and a thread of smoke. What is done here: make a vow, make an offering, give alms and cross over.
pages.known: Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.30: Cuthbert and after him Eadberht kept Lent alone on a place surrounded by the sea at the flood. Wall footings show in the turf today (English Heritage). The eiders are there; the story that Cuthbert protected them has no early evidence.

pages.title: The hard below the Strand
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Lundenwic. A long shelving beach of gravel and cobbles on the outside of the river's bend, grey-brown at low water, with hulls sitting dry on it in a row and bigger ships riding off.
pages.game: A beach at Lundenwic. A long shelving beach of gravel and cobbles on the outside of the river's bend, grey-brown at low water, with hulls sitting dry on it in a row and bigger ships riding off. Along the top runs a timber front a metre high, stakes and wattle and oak planks, with mooring posts; behind it the bank climbs to thatched roofs on the skyline. Downstream the old city wall and the church on its hill stand against the morning light. Gulls, the suck of the ebb, wet rope, river mud, wool grease. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper, pay the toll and buy stores.
pages.known: Killock 2019 and Cowie 1988: the gravel and cobble beach, timber fronts 1 m high with mooring posts at York Buildings (oak felled 670-690), ships run onto the hard at high water. No quay or jetty.

pages.game: A hall at Lundenwic. A long timber hall with a porch, set back from the road on the bluff with a fenced yard and a horse line. Two spearmen sit on the bench by the door. Inside it is dim and smells of rushes and smoke; the reeve stands at a table with tally sticks laid out by length, and a clerk scratches wax. Everybody who has bought anything worth swearing to is waiting his turn. What is done here: call witnesses, show the charter, hear the law, bring a case, swear an oath, ask an audience and give a gift. Found here: Wighelm.
pages.known: The hall is certain from the law, its site unknown: Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16, warranty vouched 'at the king's hall in the wic'. Coenwulf's council of 811: S 168.

pages.game: A mint at Lundenwic. A shed with a locked door and a smoke hole, open on one side to a counter. A man sits astride a block with a die set in it; another feeds him blanks from a bowl. Each blow is one penny, and the sound carries down the road like a slow woodpecker. On the counter a balance, a touchstone and a pan of clippings nobody is allowed to lean over. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Ibba.
pages.known: The mint is certain from the coin, its site unknown. Offa's moneyers very probably of London: Naismith 2010. King Aethelstan gives London eight (II Aethelstan 14, Thatcher 1907). The bench and die are the game's picture (?).

pages.title: The road up from the shore
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Lundenwic. A metalled road five paces wide running north from the Strand between close-set houses of wattle and daub under thatch, end-on to the street.
pages.game: A market at Lundenwic. A metalled road five paces wide running north from the Strand between close-set houses of wattle and daub under thatch, end-on to the street. Doors stand open; a loom thumps in nearly every one. Goods are sold from thresholds and from the tails of carts: Rhenish pots in straw, grey querns stacked like loaves, a cask with a fir-wood head, figs in a jar for somebody's lord. Pigs, woodsmoke, wet dye, hot horn. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, listen for talk, hire carriers and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: The 5 m metalled road with over 60 buildings at the Royal Opera House; parallel roads under James Street and Bow Street; imports of Mayen lava querns, Badorf and Tating ware, glass, Norwegian hones, figs and grapes, a silver-fir cask head. No market place is known: trade is on the shore and in the street.

Finished cloaks lie folded on a chest, brown and grey and one dyed with madder. A woman measures a length along her arm and a girl counts the rings aloud. Lanolin, lye and the sour smell of a dye vat in the yard. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and haggle the price. Found here: Leofrun.
pages.known: Loomweights in almost every house of the wic; cloth and cloaks as the chief export, and the cloaks 'at the old length' of the letter of 796. This house and its weaver are invented.

pages.game: A lodging at Lundenwic. A fenced plot at the east end of the town, on the road that runs on to the old city's west gate. A long house with a loft, a store with a bar on the door, a well lined with an old wine cask, and a cart shed where three Frisians are arguing about freight. A dog that knows who has paid. From the gate the broken wall and the church on its hill are in plain sight over the Fleet's wide mouth. What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, rent store room, ask the news, buy a plot and fund a work. Found here: Tatberht.
pages.known: The plot 'Ceolmundingchaga, not far from the west gate', with measure and weights as is the custom in the port: S 208, 857. Barrel-lined wells and the silver-fir cask head. The host answers for a guest of three nights: Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15. That this plot was a lodging for Frisians, and the family, are invented; Frisians here are inferred from Bede IV.22 and the wine casks.

pages.game: A boat yard at Lundenwic. The upstream end of the hard, where a big clinker ship lies on her side half stripped, her strakes coming off one by one and the iron clench bolts dropping into a basket. Beside her a new keel is set on blocks and a wright sights along it with one eye shut. Heaps of Roman tile and ragstone carted from the old city wait to make somebody a hearth. Tar smoke, adzes, oak chips underfoot. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, buy a boat, order a ship, fit her out, buy ship's tools and hire a hand.

Red cattle, a few sheep, pigs under an oak. A herdsman leans on a pen with two long-legged hounds lying at his feet, not for sale until the price is right. pages.game: A graveyard at Lundenwic. A rise at the west edge of the town above the gravel pits, with graves among thorn trees. Two of them are stone coffins older than anybody's grandfather, carved by the Romans and used again. There is a standing cross of wood and, some say, a small church (?). A priest walks out from Saint Paul's for burials. Wind in the thorns, the river bright below, quarrymen shouting. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, give alms, make a vow and hear Mass.
pages.known: Saint Martin-in-the-Fields: Roman sarcophagi, one of about 410, reused for Saxon graves with glass palm cups, perhaps the site of a church; no church is known inside the wic; gravel quarries to the west at the National Gallery, 2.75 m deep. The cross is invented (?).

pages.title: Saint Paul's in the old city
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Lundenwic. Twenty minutes' walk east, over the Fleet and in by a gate with no doors, among brambles and fallen walls two miles round.
pages.game: A minster at Lundenwic. Twenty minutes' walk east, over the Fleet and in by a gate with no doors, among brambles and fallen walls two miles round. On the western hill stands the bishop's church with a few houses for his clergy about it; men with carts are pulling down a ruin nearby for its stone. Inside, candle wax and cold, and the shrine of Bishop Earconwald with a small wheeled chair kept beside it. Rooks in the broken towers. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, read a book, have it copied, have him remembered and fund a work, and more. Found here: Eanwulf.
pages.known: Saint Paul's, founded 604, its early form unknown; the walled city in ruins and robbed for rubble in 793. Earconwald, bishop 675-693, feast 30 April, lame with gout, went about in a small wheeled chair, and lies here.

pages.game: A landing at Lundenwic. An inlet cut into the river bank below the old south wall, with a timber front and gravel hard, and ships lying stem-in before fenced plots that run back to a street. Each plot has its own posts: that is the bishop of Worcester's, that the archbishop's. An old stone building, roofless at one end, serves as a store. Porters, a clerk with tablets, the tide slapping under the planks, pitch and fish. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper, pay the toll, use your store and rent store room, and more. Found here: Wynsige.

Ships bound upstream lie below it waiting for slack water; small boats shoot the gaps and are sworn at. From the middle the whole town shows: the wall, the hithes, the bishop's church, smoke going up straight on a still morning. What is done here: cross over, wait for wind, ask the news, give alms and listen for talk.

From about 1050 the east end is all scaffolding: masons from over the sea are raising a stone church longer than anything in the kingdom.
King Edward's church, hallowed 28 December 1065.

pages.title: The south bank
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Medemelacha. A peat-brown stream thirty paces wide and a low bank faced with stakes and wattle, a different man's work every few yards.
pages.game: A landing at Medemelacha. A peat-brown stream thirty paces wide and a low bank faced with stakes and wattle, a different man's work every few yards. Flat-bottomed Rhine boats lie nose-in among the reeds with planks run ashore; behind them the thatch of the row and grey sky to every edge. It smells of wet peat, tar and cattle. What is done here: load and unload, ask the keeper, wait for wind, hire carriers and mend the boat. Found here: Eilbern.
pages.known: WAR 61 3.1.6, 6.2, 6.3: boats against the soft bank, each plot-holder his own revetment, the river about 30 m wide; no jetty has been found.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/medemelacha.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own source keys

pages.title: The king's ground
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Medemelacha.
pages.game: A toll place at Medemelacha. An open piece of the bank where no house stands, with a row of oak posts driven in to mark the tenth part that is Saint Martin's. A bench, a balance hung from a pole, a heap of pots and a tethered cow taken in kind. The king's man sits with his back to the wind and counts hulls aloud. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, hear the law, weigh the silver and call witnesses. Found here: Radward.
pages.known: WAR 61 2.2.2.1 and 6.3: the toll and the tenth are sure; the open ground called Koningshof is a guess for where; the posts are as at Dorestad (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/medemelacha.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own source keys

pages.title: The house row
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Medemelacha. Long timber houses with daubed walls and reed thatch, ends to the water, a boat's length of working ground between each.
pages.game: A market at Medemelacha. Long timber houses with daubed walls and reed thatch, ends to the water, a boat's length of working ground between each. Goods are sold from the plots: crates of Rhenish pots in straw, querns leaning on a wall, bolts of grey cloth over a rail, a cheese cut open to be tasted. Smoke comes out under the eaves and hangs. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy a plot and rent store room.
pages.known: WAR 61 6.3: houses at least 10 by 5 m, some 10 m apart, plots square to the water; the wares are those of the finds (WAR 61 4.7, 4.8).

pages.title: Meinburg's house
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Medemelacha. The third house from the stream mouth, the one with a boat's worth of strangers' shoes by the door.
pages.game: A lodging at Medemelacha. The third house from the stream mouth, the one with a boat's worth of strangers' shoes by the door. Inside a long hearth, benches, a vat of ale under a cloth and a green glass beaker nobody but the house's own may touch. The door post is cut with small marks, one house's sign under another, and a row of notches by each. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, trade riddles and hire a hand. Found here: Meinburg.

pages.title: Saint Martin's, Medemelacha
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Medemelacha. A small church of upright oak planks on the highest bit of the ridge, thatched, with a wooden cross on the gable and no bell until someone gives one.
pages.game: A church at Medemelacha. A small church of upright oak planks on the highest bit of the ridge, thatched, with a wooden cross on the gable and no bell until someone gives one. Inside it is dim and smells of tallow; one candle of real wax stands by the altar for feast days. Beyond the door the moss runs flat to the edge of the world. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, ask the news and fund a work. Found here: Liudbrand.
pages.known: None has been found (?). The name Boniface belongs to the later building.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/medemelacha.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own source keys

later.text: WAR 61 2.3.2 and 6.3: a wooden church of Saint Martin is thought possible by 750-800 and likely by 850.

pages.title: The stone ground
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Medemelacha. The working ground between two houses, grey with lava dust.
pages.game: A workshop at Medemelacha. The working ground between two houses, grey with lava dust. Rough black quern stones off the Rhine boats are stacked like loaves; a man sits astride one with a pick, dressing the grinding face, and the chips fly into the nettles. One half-made stone has lain by the wall so long it has moss on it. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order and buy ship's tools. Found here: Tado.
pages.known: WAR 61 6.3: a half-made lava quern, found 1982, suggests rough stones were finished here; the man is invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/medemelacha.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own source keys

later.text: It stands until about 900.

pages.title: The barrel wells
pages.hint: A well, not yet seen
pages.brief: A well at Medemelacha. Behind each house a square frame of planks over a hooped stave barrel sunk in the sand, a bucket on a hide rope beside it.
pages.game: A well at Medemelacha. Behind each house a square frame of planks over a hooped stave barrel sunk in the sand, a bucket on a hide rope beside it. Women meet here at first light, and what the row knows it knows from the wells. The water is brown and sweet; after the great flood it is salt for a year. What is done here: buy stores, listen for talk and ask the news.

pages.title: The lake hamlet
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Medemelacha. A short walk south along the ridge, where it runs out into the reeds of the lake: one long house, ditches, two clay ovens in the open and rye on the dry strip.
pages.game: A field at Medemelacha. A short walk south along the ridge, where it runs out into the reeds of the lake: one long house, ditches, two clay ovens in the open and rye on the dry strip. Cattle stand to the hock in wet grass. At Martinmas the beasts are driven from here to the bank, and the ground by the ovens is black with old fires. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores and give a gift.
pages.known: WAR 61 3.1.4 and 5.5: the hamlet at Schuitevoerderslaan, late 8th and early 9th century, a house of 6 by 20 m, perhaps two field ovens; cattle brought alive to be killed and salted for ships. The burnt patches were once read as salt-making, then doubted.
