pages.title: The count's house, Parisius
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Parisius. The old Roman citadel at the island's west end: high patched walls of small stone and red tile, a gate with spearmen, a yard where the count's court sits on benches in the open on its days.
pages.game: A hall at Parisius. The old Roman citadel at the island's west end: high patched walls of small stone and red tile, a gate with spearmen, a yard where the count's court sits on benches in the open on its days. Facing the gate, the plain house of the nuns of Saint Martial. What is done here: ask an audience, bring a case, hear the law, call witnesses, swear an oath and give a gift. Found here: Stephen.
pages.known: The Roman citadel, about one hectare, house of the counts; rebuilt by Robert II (996-1031) with a King's Hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas; Saint Martial's nuns, founded 635, facing it. The public court and its law-finders: MGH Capitularia I.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: The public court and its law-finders: MGH Capitularia I, 803.
After the year 1000 the king's new hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas stand here and the walls are whole again.

pages.title: The moneyers' bench, Parisius
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Parisius. A low stone room by the count's gate, shuttered on the street side: a charcoal hearth, an anvil set in an oak stump, two men striking in turn, a third weighing blanks on a small balance by the one window.
pages.game: A mint at Parisius. A low stone room by the count's gate, shuttered on the street side: a charcoal hearth, an anvil set in an oak stump, two men striking in turn, a third weighing blanks on a small balance by the one window. The pennies name the king and the city and nobody else. The ring of the hammer carries over the market. What is done here: change coin, test the silver, weigh the silver and ask the news.
pages.known: Pennies of Pippin; of Charles before 793 (CARO/LVS, PRI/SVS, about 1.1 g); of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald (PARISII): M. Prou, Les monnaies carolingiennes (1896); Numista. Where the mint stood is not known: beside the count's house is a guess (?). No moneyer is named.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: One of ten mints allowed in 864 (Edict of Pîtres c. 12).

pages.title: Saint Stephen's, the bishop's church
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Parisius. A very long, low church of five aisles on rows of marble columns taken from older buildings, its floor and walls bright with old mosaic where the damp has spared it.
pages.game: A church at Parisius. A very long, low church of five aisles on rows of marble columns taken from older buildings, its floor and walls bright with old mosaic where the damp has spared it. Behind it a smaller church of Saint Mary, beside it the round baptistery of Saint John. Candle smoke, cold stone, and the bishop's clerks talking in the porch. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, ask the news and have him remembered.
pages.known: Saint Stephen's, 70 m by 36 m, five aisles on marble columns, mosaics; Saint Mary's behind, the baptistery of Saint John beside; the council of 829 sat here. The church that stands today was begun in 1163.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Spared in 856-857 for a payment.

pages.title: The house by the Little Bridge
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Parisius.
pages.game: An ale-house at Parisius. A timber house on stone footings where the southern bridge comes onto the island: one long room, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the thatch, benches, a loft with straw for lodgers, casks on trestles at the back. In October it is full of Frisian and English voices and wet cloaks. It smells of leeks, new wine and eels. What is done here: drink with them, lodge ashore, listen for talk, throw dice, trade riddles, hire a hand and buy stores. Found here: Ermentrud.
pages.known: Invented: an ale-house and lodging; Frisian and Saxon (English) merchants at the fair (Tardif nos. 44, 55); the Little Bridge of timber.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: The Little Bridge of timber, with a timber tower only from the 870s (Abbo).

pages.title: Saint Vincent's and Saint Germain's in the meadows
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Parisius. Across the Little Bridge and west through wet meadows: a church whose roof of gilded copper shows from the river like a second sun, a wide graveyard about it, barns, a walled yard with carts of casks.
pages.game: An abbey at Parisius. Across the Little Bridge and west through wet meadows: a church whose roof of gilded copper shows from the river like a second sun, a wide graveyard about it, barns, a walled yard with carts of casks. Inside, marble columns, a mosaic floor, and lamps before the saint's tomb behind the high altar. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, take an order, show the charter, read a book, have it copied, bury a man and use your store. Found here: Frotbald.
pages.known: Hallowed about 558; gilded copper roof, mosaic floor, marble columns; Germain's body behind the high altar since 754 (or 756); a large graveyard; rebuilt by Abbot Morard (990-1014), whose tower stands. Abbot Irminon's book of estates.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Abbot Irminon's book of estates, about 823-828.
After 861 the roof is black timber for a generation; from about the year 1000 a new stone tower stands at the west door.
Burned in 861.

pages.title: The saint's landing
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Parisius.
pages.game: A toll place at Parisius. A low bank on the outside of a great bend, a day's rowing below the city by water and two hours from it by road: posts, a plank stage, a toll man's table under a hide awning, carts waiting to go up to the abbey, whose roof stands over the fields to the east. A long wooded island lies in the stream opposite. In the fair's weeks boats lie three deep and the mud is ankle deep. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, load and unload, hire carriers and ask the keeper. Found here: Dominicus.
pages.known: Coming up from Rouen a skipper reaches Saint-Denis first, for the river loops north below the city; an island lies in the river beside the abbey. The tolls on ships and harbours are the abbey's (Tardif nos. 55, 77). The stage and table are invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: An island lies in the river beside the abbey, the Northmen's in 865-866.

pages.title: Saint Denis's church
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Parisius. A tall stone church of three aisles, new in the old king's day, with a bronze-bound west door and a king's grave slab set in the ground before it.
pages.game: An abbey at Parisius. A tall stone church of three aisles, new in the old king's day, with a bronze-bound west door and a king's grave slab set in the ground before it. Inside, many small windows, a raised choir, and steps down to a ring passage where the three martyrs lie. North of it a two-storey stone hall for great guests, and beyond that a graveyard as wide as a field. What is done here: hear Mass, make a vow, give alms, ask an audience, give a gift, read a book, have it copied and take an order, and more. Found here: Fardulf and Waldric.
pages.known: Fulrad's church, hallowed 24 February 775: three aisles, a ring crypt, Pippin's grave before the west door; a stone hall north of the church, two storeys, at least 30 m by 14 m; the great graveyard, over 8,000 square metres. The kings buried here: Dagobert, Charles Martel (741), Pippin (768).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Hilduin's chapel of 832.
From 869 all of it stands inside a bank, a timber wall and two wet ditches.
The stronghold of 869.

pages.title: The hospice at the abbey gate
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Parisius. A long low house against the abbey's outer gate, with a porch where a monk stands at a half-door handing out loaves and bowls.
pages.game: A lodging at Parisius. A long low house against the abbey's outer gate, with a porch where a monk stands at a half-door handing out loaves and bowls. In front, people sitting on the ground in rows: old men, women with children, a pilgrim with a staff. Behind, the smoke of the bakehouse and the sound of water running in a stone channel. It smells of barley bread and too many people. What is done here: give alms, lodge ashore, see the leech, ask the news and fund a work. Found here: Waldric.
pages.known: The monastery's bakery, kitchen and baths, and a hospice at the gate; an aqueduct that fed three stone tanks.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

pages.title: The fair of Saint Denis
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Parisius.
pages.game: A market at Parisius. Rows of booths of poles, hides and wattle on open ground by the abbey: bolts of grey and blue cloth on trestles, sacks of wool, crocks of honey, baskets of red root and blue dye balls, and everywhere casks, with a monk chalking them. Englishmen and Frisians shouting prices in their own tongues, a Greek word from a spice seller, the abbey's bell over all. In later years the booths stand among the graves, at two pennies a pitch. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy from makers, pay the toll, listen for talk, trade riddles and take an order. Found here: Dominicus and Waldric.
pages.known: The fair from Saint Denis's day, 9 October; wine out, wool and woollen cloth in, the abbey's grain, spare wine and honey sold. Later the stalls stood in the graveyard at two pennies a pitch. Where the fair stood in 793 is not known: the judgment of 710 has it moved to Paris, the charters of 753 and 775 speak of the market and the city both. Madder at the fair is from a forged charter (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: In later years the booths stand among the graves, at two pennies a pitch, and from 869 inside the wall.

pages.title: The dragging beach
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Paviken. A long curve of pale shingle on still brown water, with a hollow worn into it where boats have been dragged up for longer than anyone remembers.
pages.game: A beach at Paviken. A long curve of pale shingle on still brown water, with a hollow worn into it where boats have been dragged up for longer than anyone remembers. Eight or ten clinker boats lie on rollers, their square sails spread to dry in chequers of two colours. Behind them stand low sheds, and behind those thin blue smoke from a dozen hearths; far across the lagoon a single gap of bright sea. Hammering, gulls, tar, and cattle lowing inland. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire carriers, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, buy stores and give a gift. Found here: Rodiaud and Botbjorn.
pages.known: A hollow worn by dragging boats at the waterfront; a sheltered lagoon joined to the sea by one narrow strait. Chequered sails from Gotland's picture stones. The number of boats is the game's.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The weighing shore
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Paviken. The strip of trodden ground where the stream meets the lagoon. No booths and no benches: hides spread on the stones, and on them strings of beads, combs, bronze pins, coils of rope, a heap of rivets.
pages.game: A market at Paviken. The strip of trodden ground where the stream meets the lagoon. No booths and no benches: hides spread on the stones, and on them strings of beads, combs, bronze pins, coils of rope, a heap of rivets. Every second man has a small folding balance and holds it up against the light off the water before he speaks. Behind, the stone wall of the fine-craft yard and its smoke. It is quiet for a market; the loudest thing is the stream. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods, ask the news, listen for talk and trade riddles. Found here: Botbjorn and Rodiaud.
pages.known: The western, waterfront part of the northern ground ('Area 1'), with the most silver and the most weights, read as the place of exchange. Scale fragments, lead weights and cubo-octahedral weights. No coin is struck; silver is weighed. A Gotland farmer at the market gives a rune stick here.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The walled yard
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Paviken. A yard inside a dry-stone wall as high as a man's chest, open on the side toward the stream.
pages.game: A workshop at Paviken. A yard inside a dry-stone wall as high as a man's chest, open on the side toward the stream. In the middle a hearth as long as a man, and beside it a low platform of baked clay with an iron rod, tongs and a row of small bright cubes laid out on it: red, yellow, a blue like deep water, a few with gold inside the glass. A man turns a rod in the flame and a bead grows on it. Lumps of dark red stone and raw amber lie in a trough. Charcoal smoke, and the hiss of hot glass in water. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods, weigh the silver, test the silver and buy ship's tools. Found here: Hegvisl.
pages.known: The fine-craft yard ('Area 2') inside a stone wall, opening toward the stream Idån: raw glass, raw garnet, amber, ingots; a hearth of 2 by 1 m and a clay platform perhaps used in bead-making, found 2013. Opaque glass cubes read as Italian mosaic stones. The height of the wall is the game's guess (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The paved ground
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Paviken. South of the yard the earth is laid with flat stones to make a working floor, black with soot between them.
pages.game: A smithy at Paviken. South of the yard the earth is laid with flat stones to make a working floor, black with soot between them. Three hearths, one roofed with turf on posts; a pit of slag and burnt bone; a stump with an iron block set in it. Two men draw rivets by the hundred and throw them hissing into a trough. Scraps of bronze and bent iron lie where they fell. It smells of hot iron and singed horn, and the hammers never keep the same time. What is done here: buy from makers, buy ship's tools, take an order, mend the boat and hire a hand. Found here: Hegvisl.
pages.known: The rough-work ground ('Area 3'): stone paving laid as a working floor, hearths, rubbish pits, postholes, bronze and iron scrap, much burnt bone. Boat rivets and nails are found all over the site from the first test pits of 1961. Comb and dice makers in bone and antler.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The slip and the boat sheds
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Paviken. A hull lies on the shingle with half her planks on, pale new wood over dark, each plank lapped on the one below and held by a row of rivet heads.
pages.game: A boat yard at Paviken. A hull lies on the shingle with half her planks on, pale new wood over dark, each plank lapped on the one below and held by a row of rivet heads. A broad man in a leather apron sights along her with one eye shut. Beside her an old boat is propped on her side with a plank cut out. Sheds with turf roofs hold oars, moss, tar pots and a pile of roves. Adze chips underfoot, the smell of tar and split pine, the dull knock of a mallet. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out, buy ship's tools and trade riddles. Found here: Rodbjorn.
pages.known: Boats were mended here: rivets and nails over the whole ground and a slipway hollow. A Gotland shipwright sells and gives rune sticks here.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The stone-walled house
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Paviken. A small house with walls of piled limestone and a roof of turf, standing by itself between the working ground and the southern graves.
pages.game: A storehouse at Paviken. A small house with walls of piled limestone and a roof of turf, standing by itself between the working ground and the southern graves. There is no hearth in it and no smoke hole: it is cold inside on the hottest day. Bales, casks and bundled skins along the walls; on a ledge a folded balance, a row of lead weights and a block of yellow sandstone with a shape cut into it. A heavy plank door with a wooden bar, and a dog asleep against it. What is done here: use your store, rent store room, weigh the silver and take an order. Found here: Rodiaud.
pages.known: The stone-walled house between the northern and southern grounds, dug 1995, of the Viking Age: no hearth; rivets, scale fragments, lead weights, glass, two pieces of Arabic silver coin, and a sandstone mould for crosses or Thor's hammers; a workshop or store, not a dwelling.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: Its year of building is not known: 800 is the game's (?).

pages.title: The gravel-floored shelter
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Paviken. A long low shelter above the tide line: posts, a roof of turf and reed, a floor of beaten gravel, three sides walled with wattle and the fourth open to the water.
pages.game: A lodging at Paviken. A long low shelter above the tide line: posts, a roof of turf and reed, a floor of beaten gravel, three sides walled with wattle and the fourth open to the water. Sea chests and rolled sleeping skins along the back; a fire in a ring of stones at the open end with a pot over it. In the evening men sit on their chests with a board of pegged pieces between them, and somebody is always mending a net. Fish broth, wet wool, peat smoke. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer, listen for talk and ask the news, and more. Found here: Rodiaud and Ottar.
pages.known: The beach house dug in 2014: a thin gravel floor and one posthole dated to the 8th century, a store or shelter. Whether anyone lived at the harbour all year is not settled: strangers sleeping here under a farm's protection is the game's guess (?). Dice in bone and antler were made on the site; dice and tafl are played here.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: From 871 a skald of the Gotlanders sits here.

pages.title: The ring of stones
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Paviken. In the middle of the working ground, with hearths on every side of it, a ring of grey stones as wide as a boat is long, the grass inside it uncut.
pages.game: A shrine at Paviken. In the middle of the working ground, with hearths on every side of it, a ring of grey stones as wide as a boat is long, the grass inside it uncut. Nobody walks across it; the path bends round. On the nearest stone lie an amber bead, a lump of slag and a crust. Beside the ring a pit of ash and split cattle bone, and an iron cauldron upside down on three stones. At dusk the light comes low across the lagoon and the stones throw shadows as far as the yard wall. What is done here: make an offering, make a vow, swear an oath, cast the lots, hold a feast and call witnesses. Found here: Likbjorn and Hailgair.
pages.known: A round stone setting at the centre of the northern ground: one man buried unburnt with a ring brooch, and cremations beside him. The harbour is heathen through its main life: hammers of Thor in amber and metal. That offerings and a shared boiled meal were made beside it is the game's guess (?): the meal and its 'boiling-fellows' are from the Guta saga (late), and the burnt bone is the rough ground's. No shrine building is known and none is shown.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The southern graves
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Paviken. A slope of short grass and juniper south of the hearths, set with low rings and heaps of stone, some sunk almost level, some new and pale.
pages.game: A graveyard at Paviken. A slope of short grass and juniper south of the hearths, set with low rings and heaps of stone, some sunk almost level, some new and pale. One low heap is twice as long as the rest. At the upper edge stands a slab of limestone taller than a man, narrow at the neck and wide at the head, with a ship under sail cut on it and painted red and black. A man with a mallet and a pointed iron kneels at a second slab lying flat. Wind, sheep, and the tap of iron on stone. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, make an offering, make a vow, take an order and read a book. Found here: Likbjorn.
pages.known: The south grave field: stone settings, cremations and burials, one grave holding a dog and a horse; a further field to the south, ploughed out, perhaps hundreds of graves once. Picture stones of 700 to 1100 are tall, with ships under chequered sails; none is recorded from Paviken itself, so the standing stone and the carver are invented (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Aikgard, half a morning inland
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Paviken. Up the stream past two fords, with a low ridge on the left hand: a long house of timber and turf, a storehouse on a stone footing, a well, and sheep on thin grass over white limestone.
pages.game: A field at Paviken. Up the stream past two fords, with a low ridge on the left hand: a long house of timber and turf, a storehouse on a stone footing, a well, and sheep on thin grass over white limestone. By the gate a tall stone with a ship cut on it. A heavy man sets bread and ale on a table by the open door and asks nothing until it is eaten. Beyond the pasture fence a row of old standing stones shows against the sky. Wind in ash trees, a dog on a rope, and a long quiet. What is done here: give a gift, hold a feast, weigh the silver, call witnesses, bring a case, hear the law and buy from makers. Found here: Vivil and Ailikn.
pages.known: True to the island: farmers who are also the merchants, and silver hoards on farms, many inside the footings of houses. The thing that meets on the slope above the farms is the chain's and is not a place at the harbour. The years are the chain's window.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: It stands until about 949.

pages.title: The ship of stones in the east pasture
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Paviken. In the pasture east of the farm, grey standing stones set in the shape of a ship, bow to the sea: the tallest at stem and stern, the rest lower amidships, all leaning and patched with yellow lichen.
pages.game: A mound at Paviken. In the pasture east of the farm, grey standing stones set in the shape of a ship, bow to the sea: the tallest at stem and stern, the rest lower amidships, all leaning and patched with yellow lichen. Sheep lie in the lee of them. The turf at the stern stone is whole. Nobody at the farm knows who raised it or for whom, only that it was old in their grandfathers' time. In the evening the stones are black against a yellow sky. What is done here: make an offering, make a vow and have him remembered.
pages.known: Ship settings of standing stones are common on Gotland and were already ancient in these years (the Bronze Age settings at Gannarve and 'Tjelvar's grave'), as the chain page says (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: The timber quays at the outlet
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Paviken. Where the lagoon drains to the sea, new oak piles stand in two rows with planking on them, and the bank is faced with fitted stone.
pages.game: A landing at Paviken. Where the lagoon drains to the sea, new oak piles stand in two rows with planking on them, and the bank is faced with fitted stone. A laden boat can lie afloat here, which she no longer can at the old beach. Out in the old entrance a line of pile heads breaks the water, with one gap a boat's width across. On the seaward side men are heaping earth and stone into a long curved bank. Fresh-cut oak, wet rope, and the stream running fast under the planks. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, hire carriers, weigh the silver and fund a work.
pages.known: A row of piles closing the entrance. More coins and weights near the outlet than on the northern ground: perhaps a second trading spot. The skipper met here is the heir of the one of 793.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: A row of piles closing the entrance, early 1000s.
The bank is the Västergarn wall, about 1000 if the usual date holds, and is Västergarn's, not this harbour's. The gap in the piles is the game's guess (?).
Timber quays and jetties and a stone facing at the outlet Västergarnsån, tree-ring dated to 1008, wrecked by a spring flood.

pages.title: The bank below the street
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Quentovic. A long reach of the Canche between reed marsh and a low rise of roofs.
pages.game: A landing at Quentovic. A long reach of the Canche between reed marsh and a low rise of roofs. At the ebb the hulls sit on brown mud in a row, stems to the bank: broad Frisian ships, a tall-stemmed English one roped to a post with a guard asleep beside her, river barges from upstream. Planks run from deck to turf. Smoke lies along the roofs behind; curlews, the slap of rope on a mast, the smell of mud, tar and wet wool. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper and buy stores. Found here: Leofstan.
pages.known: Anchors and ship timbers came out of the peat at Visemarest about 1789. The bar that dries and the wait for the flood are the game's; the tide's range is large (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

later.text: It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The procurator's toll house
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Quentovic. A timber hall at the head of the bank with its doors open to the water, so that nothing is carried up unseen.
pages.game: A toll place at Quentovic. A timber hall at the head of the bank with its doors open to the water, so that nothing is carried up unseen. Inside, a long table, a balance hung from a beam, tally sticks in bundles, and a clerk with wax tablets who does not look up at once. Bales stand opened along the wall. When the abbot is here there is a boy with his staff at the door and the place is quiet. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, hear the law, ask an audience, give a gift and bring a case. Found here: Gervold and Hildric.
pages.known: The toll and its procurator: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16. Where the toll was taken is not known: the hall is assumed (?). The rate in 793 is assumed to be the tenth.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

later.text: The tenth: Praeceptum negotiatorum 828.
It stands until about 900.

pages.title: The mint, Quentovic
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Quentovic. A low house with a guarded door and no window on the street side. A charcoal hearth, a row of crucibles, a block with a die set in it and a man who strikes without looking, another who weighs each blank.
pages.game: A mint at Quentovic. A low house with a guarded door and no window on the street side. A charcoal hearth, a row of crucibles, a block with a die set in it and a man who strikes without looking, another who weighs each blank. Foreign silver goes into the pot in handfuls: broad English pennies, cut rings, a spoon. The ring of the hammer carries the length of the street. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Gerwin.
pages.known: Deniers of Pippin; few of Charlemagne and Louis. No Carolingian coin names its moneyer and the building is not found: both assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

later.text: Ship deniers 812-814.
Few of Charlemagne and Louis, many of Charles the Bald after 864.
Coins struck here from the sixth century to about 980.
It stands until about 980.

pages.title: The long street, Quentovic
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Quentovic.
pages.game: A market at Quentovic. A gravelled way running with the river, house ends and fenced yards on both sides, goods set out on boards and hides: wine casks on their sides, grey quernstones stacked like loaves, pottery bottles in straw, bolts of cloth, a tray of amber. Franks, Frisians and men the Franks call Saxons argue in three ways of speaking. Pigs underfoot, a smell of new bread and of the tanner. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, hire carriers, buy ship's tools, ask the news and call witnesses.
pages.known: More than 35 ha occupied; goods: wine, quernstones, cloth, pottery bottles and glass out, English wool, tin, lead and Baltic amber in, slaves. The street's line is assumed (?). No fair is recorded here.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

pages.title: The abbeys' houses
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Quentovic. A row of stout storehouses with locked doors and a cross cut in each lintel: Saint-Vaast, Saint-Riquier, Saint-Bertin, Saint-Germain, Saint-Wandrille, and later Ferrieres.
pages.game: A storehouse at Quentovic. A row of stout storehouses with locked doors and a cross cut in each lintel: Saint-Vaast, Saint-Riquier, Saint-Bertin, Saint-Germain, Saint-Wandrille, and later Ferrieres. Carts stand loading under the eaves. A monk in a travel-stained cowl counts casks against a tablet, and his goods go down to the bank past the toll house without stopping. What is done here: use your store, rent store room, take an order, show the charter, buy a plot and trade riddles. Found here: Meginbert.
pages.known: Abbey houses or stores at Quentovic: Saint-Vaast, Saint-Riquier, Saint-Bertin, Saint-Germain-des-Pres, Saint-Wandrille, Ferrieres; Saint-Germain's freedom from toll, 779 (D.122). That they stood in a row is assumed (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

pages.title: Saint Peter's, Quentovic
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Quentovic. A timber church with a shingled roof a little apart from the houses, Saint-Wandrille's own.
pages.game: A church at Quentovic. A timber church with a shingled roof a little apart from the houses, Saint-Wandrille's own. A plain altar under a small east window, a lamp, a gospel book chained in its box, a warden with a bunch of keys. Seamen's gifts hang by the door: a wax candle as long as a man, a silver penny nailed to a beam. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, bury a man, take sanctuary and fund a work.
pages.known: The church of Saint Peter 'near the emporium of Quentovic', Saint-Wandrille's property. That it stood in 793, and what it was built of, are assumed (?). Vows paid after a storm: Grippo (c. 15).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

later.text: The church of Saint Peter 'near the emporium of Quentovic', Saint-Wandrille's property, with wardens (custodes) and countless clergy and lay folk in 858 (Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 2).
It stands until about 950.

pages.title: The cell of Saint Josse
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Quentovic. A league down the same bank, a small church and a guest hall inside a fence, with the hill and the dunes behind and the river mouth shining beyond.
pages.game: An abbey at Quentovic. A league down the same bank, a small church and a guest hall inside a fence, with the hill and the dunes behind and the river mouth shining beyond. Pilgrims sit along the south wall with their staffs and bundles, waiting for a ship or a horse. A monk brings round a pot of pulses. In the church the saint lies whole, and his keepers cut his hair when it grows. What is done here: lodge ashore, give alms, see the leech, hear Mass, ask the news, read a book, have it copied and trade riddles, and more. Found here: Osmund.
pages.known: The cella sancti Iudoci, 'at Wicus, at Saint Josse' (Alcuin, letter 25); given to Alcuin 'to give alms to pilgrims' (Lupus, letter 11); care of those from over the sea and other poor, and its fish, cheese, pulses and wax (Lupus, letters 43, 71); a league from the port; the uncorrupt body and the hair.

pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Quentovic. A long house near the bank with a bush tied over the door and benches down both walls: the ale-house where the men from over the sea lodge.
pages.game: An ale-house at Quentovic. A long house near the bank with a bush tied over the door and benches down both walls: the ale-house where the men from over the sea lodge. A fire in the middle of the floor, a cask on trestles, a woman who is told everything. English is spoken at one end and Frankish at the other, and in the middle a Frisian is selling something to both. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, lodge ashore, hire a hand, throw dice, pay the singer, trade riddles and hold a feast. Found here: Wulfgifu.
pages.known: Invented: a host among the English ('Saxon') and Frisian merchants of the wic.

later.text: The host who answers for a guest is the Kentish law's. The house is one of those that could buy off the raiders of 842 or not (Annales Bertiniani).

pages.title: The craftsmen's yards
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Quentovic. Behind the street, a scatter of sheds and pits in their own smoke.
pages.game: A workshop at Quentovic. Behind the street, a scatter of sheds and pits in their own smoke. A potter's kiln with bottles drying on a plank; a woman at an upright loom in a doorway; a comb-maker sawing antler into plates; a man winding a green glass bead on an iron. Bone and horn cores lie in heaps. Everything here is for sale before it is finished. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, buy ship's tools, try the goods and haggle the price.
pages.known: The dig on the Chemin de Visemarais, 2009: over a thousand early medieval features, waste from pottery-making, cloth-working, glass, metal, bone and antler; pottery into the tenth century.

pages.game: A field at Quentovic. Hurdled pens on the wet meadow behind the houses, full of small dark cattle and sheep brought down from the chalk. Herdsmen lean on the rails; a butcher works under a lean-to with his sleeves rolled. Hides are pegged out to dry. It smells of dung and blood, and the wind blows it towards the church. What is done here: buy stores, buy from makers, haggle the price and hire carriers.
pages.known: 30,000 animal bones from the 2009 dig, mostly cattle and sheep or goat, with no sea fishing on any scale: the wic ate meat brought in on the hoof.

pages.game: A beach at Quentovic. On the north shore near the river's mouth, a firm strand below a farmstead and a storehouse, with the wide sands and the sea opening beyond. A ship lies aground at the ebb with grey pigs of lead being swung out of her onto a sledge. A monk with a tablet waits beside two ox carts. Wind, gulls, and sand in everything. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, hire a pilot, hire carriers, use your store and take an order.

pages.title: The boat shore, Reric
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Reric. A long low shore of grey sand and reeds, boats drawn up stern to the water in a row, the island of Poel a dark line across the bay behind them.
pages.game: A beach at Reric. A long low shore of grey sand and reeds, boats drawn up stern to the water in a row, the island of Poel a dark line across the bay behind them. In front, men wade with wax cakes on their shoulders; gulls, the knock of a caulking mallet, the smell of tar, wet reed and smoked fish. The water hardly moves: there is no tide here. What is done here: load and unload, scrape and tar, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind and ask the keeper.
pages.known: ARF 808 ('on the shore of the ocean'); de.wikipedia 'Wismarbucht', 'Blowatz' (Poel, the Breitling); no jetty has been reported, the harbour inlet is thought silted and partly lost to the sea (?).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.title: The king's awning
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Reric. A sail stretched over four posts at the top of the shore, a Dane on a chest beneath it with a folding scale hung from a spear shaft, two men with shields asleep against a boat.
pages.game: A toll place at Reric. A sail stretched over four posts at the top of the shore, a Dane on a chest beneath it with a folding scale hung from a spear shaft, two men with shields asleep against a boat. A heap of things taken in due lies behind him: a quern, three wax cakes, a bundle of marten. Wends pass it without looking at it. What is done here: pay the toll, weigh the silver, test the silver and ask the keeper. Found here: Skardi.
pages.known: ARF 808: the dues of Reric profited Godfred's kingdom. The manner, the rate and the place of taking are not recorded: the awning and the scale are the game's (?). No toll house was found in the dig.
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.title: The straight lanes
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Reric. Lanes laid out by line, so straight that a man at one end sees the bay at the other, with low reed roofs to either side hardly higher than his belt and goods set out on the roof edges.
pages.game: A market at Reric. Lanes laid out by line, so straight that a man at one end sees the bay at the other, with low reed roofs to either side hardly higher than his belt and goods set out on the roof edges. Honey in tubs, wax in grey cakes, furs on poles, a line of roped people sitting in the shade with a stout Dane walking up and down it. Three tongues at once, and the interpreter's fourth. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and listen for talk. Found here: Dragomir.
pages.known: The regular, chequered plan of the 760s and the sunken huts; the goods of the Slav coast in general, not shown by this dig; Slav boys bought by Anskar (Rimbert c. 15).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.title: The craft pits
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Reric. A row of pit huts with their doors propped open for the light.
pages.game: A workshop at Reric. A row of pit huts with their doors propped open for the light. In one a man turns an amber bead on a bow drill; in the next a woman winds hot glass round an iron rod; outside, antler shavings lie like snow and a bronze-caster's clay moulds dry on a plank. Burnt horn, charcoal and the sweet resin smell of cut amber. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and buy ship's tools. Found here: Folcbern.
pages.known: Weaving, bronze-casting, glass beads, amber, antler and horn worked on the spot at a modest scale; huts that were dwelling and workshop in one.

pages.game: A well at Reric. Square mouths of split oak let into the ground every few houses, each with a pole and a wooden bucket, the newest still yellow. Women wait their turn with yokes; a man waist-deep in a fresh shaft passes up buckets of grey clay. This is where the town talks: who has come in, what the Danes took at the shore, whose child is sick. What is done here: buy stores, ask the news, listen for talk and fund a work. Found here: Stoimir.
pages.known: Timber-lined wells, 127 samples and 70 dated to the year; the most in the 780s.

A steam trough smokes, oak chips lie ankle-deep, and a grey-bearded Dane and a young Wend argue across a strake with one word in three understood. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat and fit her out. Found here: Toki.
pages.known: Boat graves with rivets at the grave field; Slav boats pegged with treenails and caulked with moss. That boats were built here is likely and not shown (?).

pages.title: Dragomir's table
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Reric. A house above ground, the largest in its lane, with a table that is never cleared: bread, millet, smoked fish, a bowl of honey, mead in a wooden cup that goes round.
pages.game: A lodging at Reric. A house above ground, the largest in its lane, with a table that is never cleared: bread, millet, smoked fish, a bowl of honey, mead in a wooden cup that goes round. No chest in the room has a lock. A woman with silver rings at her temples serves; another, sharper, sits at the end and turns every guest's words into the next guest's tongue. What is done here: lodge ashore, hold a feast, drink with them, trade riddles, use your store, hire a hand and give a gift. Found here: Liuba, Radmila and Dragomir.
pages.known: A table stands laid in every house, and a host is shamed who turns a stranger away (Herbord II.41; Helmold I.82: both witnesses of the 12th century, used here as custom (?)); no wine among them (Herbord II.1).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.game: A field at Reric. Trampled grass above the town where horses are picketed in lines and sold. When the prince comes down from the forts inland his men pitch here: round shields against a wagon, spears stacked, a fire, and one man with a Frankish sword sitting where everyone can see him. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, swear an oath, buy from makers and call witnesses. Found here: Thrasco and Ratimir.
pages.known: Thrasco is put at Reric once by the annals, at his death (ARF 809); that he came to his own market at other times is likely and not recorded (?). No hall is known here. Horses as the Wends' wealth: Herbord II.23 (later).

pages.title: The fenced oaks
pages.hint: A holy wood, not yet seen
pages.brief: A holy wood at Reric. Three old oaks on a rise behind the town with a fence of split stakes round them and a gate nobody has shut.
pages.game: A holy wood at Reric. Three old oaks on a rise behind the town with a fence of split stakes round them and a gate nobody has shut. Inside the ground is swept. A strip of linen hangs from a branch, a honeycomb lies on a stone, a horse skull whitens in the grass. Nobody will tell a stranger the god's name, only that this land is his. What is done here: make an offering, make a vow, swear an oath, cast the lots and take sanctuary.
pages.known: The game's (?): no cult place was found at Gross Stromkendorf and no god is recorded for Reric. Modelled on the fenced oaks of the Wagrians, where anyone in danger of death was safe (Helmold I.83, 12th century).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen

pages.game: A graveyard at Reric. The north end, where the first town stood: low mounds and flat graves in the grass, the dark ring of an old pyre, and here and there the long shape of a boat showing through the turf with a post at its stem. A horse lies buried beside one man, a dog beside another. Wend and Dane are a few paces apart, each in his own fashion. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered and make an offering.
pages.known: The grave field on the ground of the first settlement; boat graves listed for Gross Stromkendorf. Burnt and unburnt burial side by side, horses and dogs, and the numbers are from memory of Gerds 2015 (?).

pages.title: The market bank
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Ripa. A low bank of pale sand along a brown river that bends twice before it reaches you; boats lie nose-in on the sand, a dozen in spring, forty at midsummer, with no jetty and no post to tie to but your own.
pages.game: A landing at Ripa. A low bank of pale sand along a brown river that bends twice before it reaches you; boats lie nose-in on the sand, a dozen in spring, forty at midsummer, with no jetty and no post to tie to but your own. Behind them the booths stand in a row with their backs to the wind. Curlews call on the marsh, mallets knock, and the air smells of mud, peat smoke and cattle. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, wait for wind and ask the news. Found here: Hroald and Roulf.
pages.known: The booths in a strip some 400 m long on the north side of the river; no jetty or quay reported. The count of boats is ours (?).

pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Ripa. Narrow plots run back from the water side by side, each six or eight paces wide with a shallow ditch between, the ground a trodden layer of sand over older floors.
pages.game: A market at Ripa. Narrow plots run back from the water side by side, each six or eight paces wide with a shallow ditch between, the ground a trodden layer of sand over older floors. Awnings of wadmal, tables of planks on casks, a Frisian holding up a bolt of cloth to the light, a woman biting a bead. Scales swing everywhere; nobody calls a price in pennies. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, buy a plot, rent store room and listen for talk.

pages.brief: A workshop at Ripa. Two open-sided booths share a clay hearth no bigger than a shield.
pages.game: A workshop at Ripa. Two open-sided booths share a clay hearth no bigger than a shield. On one side a man turns a blob of blue glass on an iron rod over the coals and the floor glitters with failed beads; on the other a comb-maker saws antler into plates, ankle deep in pale splinters. A Northman's bundle of whetstones leans against the post. It smells of hot glass and scorched bone. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and play tafl. Found here: Toki.
pages.known: Glass waste, rods, failed beads and mosaic cubes; antler splinters by the thousand, some reindeer; 117 whetstones, 17 of Eidsborg stone. That the two crafts shared a hearth is ours (?).

pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen

pages.game: A workshop at Ripa. A booth with a turf wall on the weather side. Clay moulds for buckles and brooches lie broken in a heap like eggshell, a crucible the size of a cup sits in the charcoal, and on a block by the door are a folding scale in a bronze case and a row of small lead weights. pages.hint: A well, not yet seen
pages.brief: A well at Ripa. A square shaft lined with black oak older than anyone living, a pole and a bucket of staves, the ground round it trodden to paste.
pages.game: A well at Ripa. A square shaft lined with black oak older than anyone living, a pole and a bucket of staves, the ground round it trodden to paste. Beside it an ale-wife keeps a bench under an awning and a second, newer well lined with a Frankish wine cask. Everyone who needs water comes here, so everyone who has news leaves some. What is done here: ask the news, listen for talk, drink with them, throw dice, pay the singer, hire a hand and buy stores. Found here: Tola and Gudmund.
pages.known: The first well, oak felled 704 to 710; other wells lined with wine casks from the Mainz country. The ale bench is ours.

pages.game: A lodging at Ripa. A long low house behind the plots, one of the few with smoke in it all winter: turf at the walls, a hearth down the middle, benches along both sides and a loom by the door where the light is. Dried fish hang in the roof. The host's seat has a carved post; a guest's place is the bench end nearest the fire, and you are shown it without a word. What is done here: lodge ashore, hold a feast, give a gift, swear an oath, call witnesses, hear the law, trade riddles and use your store. Found here: Hroald.
pages.known: Houses lived in the year round on part of the market from its first decades. The house itself is invented.

pages.game: A church at Ripa. On the south bank, facing the market across the river, a plot staked out by the king's men: at first four corner posts and a sea chest for an altar, then walls of upright oak and a roof of reed. Graves lie in rows beside it, heads to the west. From the market you can hear the priest sing, and the market has opinions. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man, read a book and fund a work. Found here: Liudlef.
pages.known: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 32 (tr. Robinson 1921): a plot and leave for a priest. Its site is not known, perhaps under the later cathedral on the other bank; graves from the 9th century by the cathedral (?).

Inside, one man holds the die and another swings the hammer; the new pennies are swept into a wooden bowl like peas. The king's name runs round one side and the town's round the other. pages.title: The strand under the south wall
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Rotomagus. A long grey wall of mismatched stone, bits of column and carved block built into it, with the river running brown at its foot.
pages.game: A landing at Rotomagus. A long grey wall of mismatched stone, bits of column and carved block built into it, with the river running brown at its foot. Sea ships lie aground on the mud in a row, leaning a little, and flat barges are poled in between them. Behind the wall, two church roofs. At the top of a spring tide the water slaps the gate; at the ebb men walk out to the keels. Gulls, wet rope, river mud and spilt wine. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, hire a pilot, wait for wind, ask the keeper, cross over and buy stores.
pages.known: Boats under the south wall and the tide on the gates: Dudo ii and iv (LATER); the tide carrying merchant ships to the city: Nithard II.6. No dug quay of this age is known (?). The ferry is the project's.

pages.game: A toll place at Rotomagus. A low arch in the wall with a small church built hard against it, its door opening almost onto the mud. A bench and a table stand under the arch out of the rain; a man with tally sticks sits there, and casks are rolled past him one at a time. A boy chalks each cask. Through the arch, a paved Roman street running uphill in shadow. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, ask the keeper and hear the law. Found here: Angilwin.

pages.title: The market place inside the wall
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Rotomagus. An open square of trodden earth over old paving, with the stumps of a colonnade along one side used as stalls.
pages.game: A market at Rotomagus. An open square of trodden earth over old paving, with the stumps of a colonnade along one side used as stalls. Sacks of wheat and rye, cheeses, baskets of salmon and of small silver fish on wet leaves, pots, a cooper's stack of new casks. Farm carts and oxen, a priest walking through with a boy. No vine grows near: the wine here has come down the river. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, listen for talk and call witnesses. Found here: Ursio.
pages.known: A market place where Rollo had two of the king's knights killed: Dudo ii (LATER); where it stood is not known. Wheat and rye, no vines, salmon and the small fish: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub (960s), retold. The colonnade is invented from the reused Roman stone he saw.

pages.title: Adalsind's house inside the river gate
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Rotomagus. A long low house built into the back of the wall just inside the gate, its end wall Roman brick and its roof thatch.
pages.game: An ale-house at Rotomagus. A long low house built into the back of the wall just inside the gate, its end wall Roman brick and its roof thatch. A bush hangs over the door. Inside, one hearth in the middle of the floor, smoke in the rafters, benches, a row of tally sticks on pegs, each with a mark burned in its end. Shipmen of three tongues, a tollman off his bench, a canon who should be elsewhere. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, hire a hand and lodge ashore. Found here: Adalsind.
pages.known: Invented; an ale-house by a town gate is the commonest thing there is. The house goes on under Adalsind's daughters and theirs.

pages.title: The moneyers' house
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Rotomagus. A stone room with a barred window and a door a man must stoop through.
pages.game: A mint at Rotomagus. A stone room with a barred window and a door a man must stoop through. A small furnace, a pot of melted silver, a block with an iron die set in it, and two men who do not look up: one lays a blank on the die, the other strikes. English pennies and cut silver go into the pot and come out with the king's name on them. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver. Found here: Gerold.
pages.known: Pennies of Charles with the city's name are older than that (?): no coin catalogue was reached. Richard I's and Archbishop Hugh's pennies: the Fecamp hoard. Where the mint stood is not known; no moneyer is named.

later.text: Rotomagus is one of the ten mints of the Edict of Pitres, 864, its right said there to be Quentovic's of old (MGH Capit. II no. 273 c. 12).
From 864 the king's new penny; after 940 the count's and the archbishop's.

pages.title: The broken round house
pages.hint: A quarry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A quarry at Rotomagus. North of the wall, a great curve of ruined arches higher than the city gate, grown over with ivy and thorn, with goats on the upper tiers.
pages.game: A quarry at Rotomagus. North of the wall, a great curve of ruined arches higher than the city gate, grown over with ivy and thorn, with goats on the upper tiers. Men with wedges and an ox sledge are taking squared blocks out of it for somebody's wall. In the middle, a flat floor of grass where boys play. The old say a saint threw down a temple here and that the stones remember. What is done here: buy from makers, hire carriers, cast the lots and have him remembered.
pages.known: The amphitheatre north of the wall, part standing until 1204: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotomagus. The city built of reused stone: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub.

pages.title: The stone coffins at Saint Gervase's
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Rotomagus.
pages.game: A graveyard at Rotomagus. A slope north-west of the city where the Roman road leaves it, crowded with graves older than anyone can name: stone coffins lying half out of the turf, some with their lids slid off, and a small church over a crypt. Two bishops lie in another church to the east. Strangers who die in the city are buried at the edge here, by the road they came on. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, hear Mass, give alms and make a vow.

later.text: After 911 the stream runs red from the dyers above and has a Norse name, and the wrights build in the Norse way too.
The stream's later name Robec, Rodobech about 1020, Norse for red brook: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robec.

pages.title: The count's tower and hall
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Rotomagus. Armed men at the door, horses, hounds, a clerk with tablets. On feast days smoke and noise and benches out in the yard.
pages.game: A hall at Rotomagus. Armed men at the door, horses, hounds, a clerk with tablets. On feast days smoke and noise and benches out in the yard. High in the tower is one narrow window, and the town says who is behind it this year. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, bring a case, hear the law, show the charter and take an order. Found here: Rollo.
pages.known: Rollo died before it was built: where his hall stood is not known, and until the tower stands he is met here on the same ground, in a timber hall (?).

later.text: From about 950 a square stone tower at the south-east corner of the wall (before that, a long timber hall on the same ground), where the red brook meets the Seine, taller than either church, with a timber hall and a yard beside it.

pages.title: Saint-Wandrille's landing, a tide below
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Rotomagus.
pages.game: An abbey at Rotomagus. Half a day down on the ebb, past the white cliffs and the first great loop: a stream coming out of a wooded valley on the north bank, a jetty of stakes, and a path going up to roofs that shine dull grey, because they are lead. A boy monk sits on the jetty with a line. Beyond the bend the river narrows, and on the big tides the flood comes up it as one wave. What is done here: lodge ashore, read a book, have it copied, ask the news, hear Mass, give alms, take an order and wait for wind. Found here: Harduin and Rotgar.
pages.known: Offa's letters to him lay in its chest (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12). The single wave at Caudebec is known only from later centuries (?).

later.text: Saint-Wandrille (Fontenelle), Gervold's house 787-806: he roofed Saint Peter's and Saint Michael's there with lead, set up a school and gave it books.
It ransomed itself in 841 and its monks left with their relics about 858 (?); the house was restored in the 960s.

pages.title: The lying-ground under the chalk
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Serræ. A low white bank of chalk facing west and south, and under it a shelf of shingle and grey mud where a dozen hulls lie on their bilges with their masts down.
pages.game: A beach at Serræ. A low white bank of chalk facing west and south, and under it a shelf of shingle and grey mud where a dozen hulls lie on their bilges with their masts down. Beyond them the strait: brown water a few bowshots wide, saltings on the far side, the Kent shore a low green line. At the meeting of the tides the water stands still and the boats all swing at once. Tar, weed, wet chalk, a mallet on a trenail. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar, mend the boat, order a ship and buy a boat, and more.
pages.known: Boats lay 'under the chalk cliffs facing the west and south' (Brent 1863); 'a place where the shipping often lay at anchor' (Hasted 1800); the tides flow in at both mouths and meet at Sarre (Hasted). The wright and his slip are ours.

pages.title: The king's toll place, Serræ
pages.hint: A toll place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A toll place at Serræ. Where the track comes down through the bank, a hurdle fence, a bench, and a post with notches cut in it for every ship of the season.
pages.game: A toll place at Serræ. Where the track comes down through the bank, a hurdle fence, a bench, and a post with notches cut in it for every ship of the season. A grey-haired man sits with a bundle of tally sticks and a small balance in a wooden case; a boy holds a horse. Whoever lands walks past him, and he has already counted their strakes. On some days a second man stands behind him in a green cloak, saying little. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, weigh the silver, hear the law, call witnesses, ask the news and bring a case. Found here: Dunwalh.
pages.known: The king's toll-collectors (thelonearii) at 'the place called ad Serrae', a public place (Sawyer 29). No building is known; the fence, bench and post are ours.

pages.title: The crossing
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Serræ. A line of stakes runs out across the mud to the low-water channel, and at the end of it a broad flat boat with two oars lies waiting.
pages.game: A ferry at Serræ. A line of stakes runs out across the mud to the low-water channel, and at the end of it a broad flat boat with two oars lies waiting. On the far side the Canterbury road comes down between saltings. At the ebb the ferryman wades out with a passenger on his shoulders and tips him in over the gunwale; at the flood the boat comes to the bank and nobody is carried. Curlews, and a horn blown from the Kent shore. What is done here: cross over, hire a pilot, ask the keeper, ask the news and listen for talk. Found here: Dudda.
pages.known: The road from Canterbury crosses into Thanet here. A boat crossing in 793 is likely, not recorded (?): the ferry is first drawn about 1414, a boatman carrying a passenger on his shoulders to the boat (Perkins 2007; Brent 1863). Bede's two fording places (I.25).

pages.title: The strand market, Serræ
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Serræ. On the dry shingle above the weed line, sacks of corn stood open, a heap of grey salt on a hide, cheeses, fleeces tied in bundles, baskets of oysters under wet weed.
pages.game: A market at Serræ. On the dry shingle above the weed line, sacks of corn stood open, a heap of grey salt on a hide, cheeses, fleeces tied in bundles, baskets of oysters under wet weed. A ship's people sell off the gunwale: a cask, a pair of dark quernstones, a crate of spouted pots in straw. Two men stand by every bargain and do nothing but watch it. Brine, sheep, a broached cask. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, call witnesses and hire carriers. Found here: Dunwalh and Tidburh.
pages.known: Invented: no cargo, price or market day is recorded at Sarre. The goods are the region's and the island's: corn (Bede's fruitful Thanet), salt and fish (Domesday for Minster and Monkton), wool, cloth and hides out, wine, querns, pots and glass in. The two watchers are the witnesses a Kentish buyer needs (Law of Hlothhere and Eadric 16).

pages.title: Tidburh's ale-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Serræ. A long thatched house end-on to the wind, halfway up the bank, with a pole and a bunch of green leaves over the door.
pages.game: An ale-house at Serræ. A long thatched house end-on to the wind, halfway up the bank, with a pole and a bunch of green leaves over the door. Inside, a hearth on the floor, benches, a tub of ale, a board marked in squares with little bone counters on it, yellow with handling. A heap of oyster shells by the door is higher than a child. Skippers waiting for the other tide sit here and say what things cost in Lundenwic three days ago. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer, lodge ashore and buy stores, and more. Found here: Tidburh and Dudda.
pages.known: The counters and dice are the kind found in the graves on the down (about fifty bone gaming counters in grave 6, forty more and two dice in grave 198: Brent 1866, 1868). The oyster riddle is given here.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sarre.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known

pages.title: The abbess's ship-house
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Serræ. A long shed of split oak at the north end of the strand, its doors wide enough for a hull, a wooden cross nailed over them.
pages.game: A storehouse at Serræ. A long shed of split oak at the north end of the strand, its doors wide enough for a hull, a wooden cross nailed over them. Inside, a ship's gear laid out by kind: oars in a rack, a rolled sail, a stack of sealed jars, corn in bins. A nun in an undyed gown stands at a slanted board with a wax tablet. A small ship lies on rollers before the doors, old and much mended, with a newer one afloat beyond her. What is done here: take an order, use your store, rent store room, show the charter, read a book, give a gift and ask an audience. Found here: Cwenburh.
pages.known: The minster's three toll-free ships, one bought from Leubucus and one 'lately built in the minster' (Sawyer 91, 29). That they kept a shed at Sarre is ours; Minster itself lies an hour's walk east.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sarre.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known

later.text: After 1030 the house's lands are Saint Augustine's.
It stands until about 1030.

pages.title: The cross above the landing
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Serræ. On the lip of the bank, where the track tops the chalk, a wooden cross taller than a man with a flat stone at its foot.
pages.game: A shrine at Serræ. On the lip of the bank, where the track tops the chalk, a wooden cross taller than a man with a flat stone at its foot. From here both ends of the strait can be seen: north, far off, the grey Roman wall at Reculver with the minster's roof inside it; south, the broken walls of Richborough. A priest walks over from Reculver on feast days and says Mass in the open; on other days there is a bowl for alms and somebody's candle stub. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, have him remembered, ask the news and fund a work.
pages.known: Sarre has no church in the game's years (Saint Giles is 11th century at the earliest (?) and is not in Domesday). Western Thanet looked to Saint Mary's minster at Reculver, about an hour and a half on foot. Reculver's later twin towers are not to be drawn.

pages.title: The old graves on the down
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Serræ. Above the landing the chalk rises to a bare green shoulder, cropped by sheep, with shallow dips in the turf in rows.
pages.game: A graveyard at Serræ. Above the landing the chalk rises to a bare green shoulder, cropped by sheep, with shallow dips in the turf in rows. Nothing stands on it. From the top the whole country lies open for miles: the strait from mouth to mouth, the island's cornfields, sails off the North Foreland. Larks, wind, and now and then something green and metal in a molehill. What is done here: have him remembered, cast the lots, ask the keeper, wait for wind and fund a work. Found here: Bynna.
pages.known: The grave field on Sarre Down, 'commanding the country for miles around' (Brent 1863): 6th and 7th centuries, already old in 793. No mounds are recorded, and none are drawn. That its people were still remembered is ours.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sarre.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known

pages.title: The ploughland under the down
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Serræ. Long strips of brown and green running up from the marsh edge to the foot of the down.
pages.game: A field at Serræ. Long strips of brown and green running up from the marsh edge to the foot of the down. Eight oxen in pairs drag a heavy plough; a man leans on the tail and a boy walks backwards before the leaders with a goad, singing to them. Gulls follow the furrow. At the marsh end a lord's man sometimes stands with a hawk on his fist, looking at the herons. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, trade riddles and give a gift. Found here: Bynna.
pages.known: Thanet's 'fruitful fields'; the eight-ox plough is the English one of the laws and of Domesday (?). The plough riddle is given here by a ploughman of Thanet.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sarre.md (4 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on, with its own list of what is not known

pages.title: The saltings
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Serræ. South of the landing the shore breaks into creeks and grey-green marsh.
pages.game: A fishery at Serræ. South of the landing the shore breaks into creeks and grey-green marsh. At low water women with baskets walk the mud bent double, and a row of stakes with wattle between them shows where a fish weir stands. Further off a thread of brown smoke rises from a salt pan. Everything shines; the smell is weed, mud and smoke. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods, buy stores and haggle the price. Found here: Tidburh.
pages.known: A salt-pit and two fisheries at Minster, a fishery and a salt work at Monkton, in 1086 (Hasted, from Domesday); Roman pits at Sarre full of oyster shells (Brent 1863). That salt and oysters were worked off Sarre itself in 793 is our guess (?).

pages.title: The strand under the rock
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Skíringssalr. In 793 this is all there is: boats on the grass, a tar pit, and tents in summer.
pages.game: A beach at Skíringssalr. In 793 this is all there is: boats on the grass, a tar pit, and tents in summer. What is done here: load and unload, scrape and tar, mend the boat, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, order a ship and buy a boat, and more. Found here: Bard.
pages.known: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal (Kaupangkilen behind Lamoya; the shore 3.5 m higher than today). That small craft were drawn up, and that ships were built here, is likely and not shown (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/skiringssal.md (6 Oct 2026), and through it:

later.text: A curve of grey shingle and mud in a sheltered arm of the fjord, the long island closing the bay to seaward so the water lies flat. A dozen clinker boats are drawn up on rollers, one on her side with a man caulking her; on a slip of logs a new hull stands in her ribs. Behind, the bare rock of the graves, and high over everything the long roof of the hall. Tar smoke, weed, wood shavings, an adze knocking.
It stands until about 960.

pages.title: The two jetties
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Skíringssalr. Two timber jetties run out over the mud on oak posts still pale from the axe, with stone-laid paths leading down to them between the plots.
pages.game: A landing at Skíringssalr. Two timber jetties run out over the mud on oak posts still pale from the axe, with stone-laid paths leading down to them between the plots. A broad cargo ship from the north lies at the outer one, her yard lowered, coils of dark rope and bundled furs on the planks beside her. Porters go by bent under soapstone pots packed in moss. Gulls, the knock of hulls on posts, a smell of wet hide. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper, wait for wind and give a gift.
pages.known: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal: two timber jetties with paths; the 'stone jetties' are now read as stone-laid paths over the mud. No toll is recorded: the landing gift is ours (?).

later.text: It stands until about 960.

pages.title: The booths
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Skíringssalr. Before 800 there are no fences or houses: tents on the grass above the strand for the summer weeks, and the same goods on the same cloths.
pages.game: A market at Skíringssalr. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods, listen for talk, buy a plot and buy stores.
pages.known: Snl.no/Kaupang (regular plots and lanes, lived in the year round; scales, weights, dirhams and deniers; pottery from the Rhineland, Frisia and the Slav shore); Norwegian Wikipedia (houses with the gable door to the sea; six wells).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/skiringssal.md (6 Oct 2026), and through it:

later.text: A lane of trodden earth along the shore between wattle fences, each plot with a small house whose gable door faces the water and a booth of poles and sailcloth in front. On the cloths: bundles of grey hones tied in twenties, soapstone bowls, iron bars, strings of beads, a Rhineland jug with tin foil on it. A man kneels with a folding scale no bigger than his hand. Many tongues, a dog fight, fish smoke, the sweet reek of a tanning pit.
Before 800 there are no fences or houses: tents on the grass above the strand for the summer weeks, and the same goods on the same cloths.
It stands until about 960.

pages.title: Thordis's bench
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Skíringssalr. A low house with an earth floor and a long hearth down the middle, benches along both walls, a soapstone pot the size of a shield hanging over the fire.
pages.game: An ale-house at Skíringssalr. A low house with an earth floor and a long hearth down the middle, benches along both walls, a soapstone pot the size of a shield hanging over the fire. A broad woman fills horn cups from a tub without looking at them and looks at everybody else. Through the gable door, the bay and the boats. Smoke in the roof, malt, wet wool, dice rattling in a cup, somebody halfway through a story. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer and hire a hand, and more. Found here: Thordis.
pages.known: Invented; the house is the dig's kind.

A thick-armed man holds a sword blade to the light by its bare tang; on the wall hang hilts without blades, of bronze and of walrus tooth. Charcoal, hot iron, the hiss of the quenching trough. What is done here: buy ship's tools, take an order, fit her out and mend the boat. Found here: Vemund.

pages.brief: A workshop at Skíringssalr. Three plots side by side where the ground is black with charcoal.
pages.game: A workshop at Skíringssalr. Three plots side by side where the ground is black with charcoal. A woman turns a rod of blue glass in a small clay furnace and winds a bead off it with an iron pin; next door a man breaks a clay mould from a brooch still too hot to hold. Crucibles the size of an egg, bars of brass and lead, a child sorting broken glass by colour. A pedlar has lumps of amber and a small knife. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods, haggle the price and weigh the silver.
pages.known: Norwegian Wikipedia and snl.no/Kaupang: bronze casting (crucibles, brass and lead bars, clay moulds), a jeweller's work, lead casting, glass-bead making, bone and antler work.

pages.title: The shining hall at Huseby

pages.brief: A hall at Skíringssalr. A hall as long as three ships on a raised platform on the height, its walls bowed like a hull, its ends narrowed, the shingles catching the low sun.
pages.game: A hall at Skíringssalr. A hall as long as three ships on a raised platform on the height, its walls bowed like a hull, its ends narrowed, the shingles catching the low sun. From its door a man sees every boat in the bay and the whole market under him. Inside, a fire the length of the floor, carved posts, benches for sixty, the high seat on the north wall. Roast pork, pine smoke, hounds, a voice saying a poem. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, pay the singer and trade riddles. Found here: Asgrim.
pages.known: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal; snl.no/Skiringssal. 'The shining hall' is Kare Hoel's reading of the name (1986). The furnishing is ours.

later.text: Norwegian Wikipedia: dug 2000-01, 32 to 35 m by 9 to 11.5 m, on a platform over a levelled mound of the 3rd or 4th century, built mid or late 8th century, out of use about 900, looking down on the harbour.
It stands until about 900.

pages.title: Thjodalyng, the people's heath
pages.hint: A meeting place, not yet seen
pages.brief: A meeting place at Skíringssalr. A wide heath of ling and juniper a short walk north of the hall, with a ring of low stones and one standing stone grey with lichen.
pages.game: A meeting place at Skíringssalr. A wide heath of ling and juniper a short walk north of the hall, with a ring of low stones and one standing stone grey with lichen. On a thing day a hundred men sit on the ground in their cloaks, spears stuck upright behind them, and one man stands and says the law from memory. No building at all. Wind, larks, a horse stamping, long silences between the speeches. What is done here: hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses, swear an oath and test the silver.
pages.known: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal: Thjodalyng, 'the people's heath', now Tjolling; things were still held there in 1557. No church stands on it before about 1150. The stones and the trying of weights are ours; nothing of the law's content survives (?).

pages.title: The holy lake
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Skíringssalr. A long still lake among alders, north of the heath, dark as a whetstone and without a boat on it.
pages.game: A shrine at Skíringssalr. A long still lake among alders, north of the heath, dark as a whetstone and without a boat on it. On a flat rock at the water's edge lie small things: a bead, a bent knife, a clipping of silver, a bowl of butter gone to the flies. An old woman with a staff sits a little way off and watches who comes. Reed warblers, midges, the smell of bog. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots, make a vow and see the leech. Found here: Jorunn.
pages.known: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal (Brink): a lake north of Tjolling, about 1.1 km by 500 m then, ringed by place-names of worship. Which gods were honoured, and how, no source says: the offerings are ours (?).
