pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Skíringssalr. A hump of bare rock and thin turf at the harbour's edge with nothing on it to mark a grave, so a stranger walks over the dead without knowing.
pages.game: A graveyard at Skíringssalr. A hump of bare rock and thin turf at the harbour's edge with nothing on it to mark a grave, so a stranger walks over the dead without knowing. Here and there the turf has sunk in the long shape of a boat. A woman is laying a new one out: a small boat in a cut trench, a shield, a pair of bronze brooches on a folded cloak. Below, the market goes on. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered and make an offering.

later.text: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal: Bikjholberget, 74 graves dug 1950-57, about 760 to 940, unmarked, many in boats, with weapon sets, swords and bronze brooches, three of them rich women.
It stands until about 960.

pages.game: A mound at Skíringssalr. The road from the shore to the hall runs between barrows, more than a hundred, green and round, the newest still raw earth with ash in it. Sheep graze over them. A man walking up to the hall with a gift walks the whole length of the chief's dead first, and is meant to. Evening light makes them cast long shadows across the track. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering and make a vow.
pages.known: Norwegian and English Wikipedia: Nordre Kaupang, 115 mounds recorded by Nicolaysen in 1867, mostly cremations, many of the 10th century. Ynglingatal lays King Halfdan Whiteleg in a mound at Skiringssal: a poem, not a fact.

A short man in a cloak too short for the weather counts cloth bolts against a tally stick while his wife salts butter. A small wooden cross hangs inside, where it cannot be seen from the lane. Wine, wax, and somebody singing a psalm badly. What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, rent store room, ask the news, weigh the silver and drink with them. Found here: Folkmar.
pages.known: One house at Kaupang is read as a Frisian trading household of the 9th century (?). The people and the cross are ours: no church, priest or mission is recorded here.

pages.title: The brook-mouth landing
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Sliesthorp. A still, brown inner water ringed with reeds, a brook running out over a strand of sand and mussel shell.
pages.game: A landing at Sliesthorp. A still, brown inner water ringed with reeds, a brook running out over a strand of sand and mussel shell. In front, small clinker boats drawn up on rollers and bigger ships lying to stakes in the shallows; a short timber jetty where the brook has cut a channel. Behind, thatch and smoke on a green slope. Wet rope, tar, fish guts, a hammer on rivets somewhere, gulls arguing over the gutting place. In later years the jetties run sixty paces out and a row of piles closes the harbour. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, give a gift and hire a pilot. Found here: Gunulf.
pages.known: The harbour in the Noor before the brook mouth, 11 ha, later with a pile barrier and jetties up to 60 m. The jetty of 793 is the game's assumption (?). The gift to the place's spokesman stands for a toll no source records.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Sliesthorp. Two rows of booths of poles and sailcloth along the brook, the ground between them trodden to black mud and laid with split planks.
pages.game: A market at Sliesthorp. Two rows of booths of poles and sailcloth along the brook, the ground between them trodden to black mud and laid with split planks. On the boards: furs in bundles of forty, lumps of yellow amber, combs, glass beads on strings, whetstones, soapstone pots, a Frankish cup nobody can afford. Every seller has a folding scale and a bag of weights. Buyers nick silver with a knife before it goes in the pan. Five tongues at once, and the smell of wet fur, ale and smoke. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, try the goods and ask the news.
pages.known: Goods of Norway, Sweden, Ireland, the east Baltic and Francia; Arab silver.

pages.title: The dealer's pen
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Sliesthorp. A fenced yard above the strand with a roof along one side and a water trough.
pages.game: A storehouse at Sliesthorp. A fenced yard above the strand with a roof along one side and a water trough. People sit under the roof in rows, some in iron fetters, most only tired. A row of notched sticks hangs on a peg by the gate, one for each ship that sold here this year. On a bench outside lie the odd things that came with the lots: a sealskin, two cups, a bell without a tongue. It is quiet. The dealer's hazel switch taps his boot while he talks. What is done here: haggle the price and weigh the silver. Found here: Asulf.
pages.known: Slaves and iron fetters at Hedeby; Anskar bought Danish and Slav boys (Rimbert 15). The pen and its keeper are invented.

pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Sliesthorp. A tarred four-oared boat at a stake on the north side of the houses, where the inner water opens into the Slie.
pages.game: A ferry at Sliesthorp. A tarred four-oared boat at a stake on the north side of the houses, where the inner water opens into the Slie. Across the grey water, a low shore of reeds and oak wood, and smoke from farms. The ferryman sits in the stern with a small bag tied under his seat. Further out, where the Slie narrows, a dark line of logs shows at low water, and a ship is feeling for the gap in it. Curlews, the knock of oars, cold air off the water. What is done here: cross over, trade riddles, hire a pilot and ask the news. Found here: Hallbjorn.
pages.known: The Slie, its broads and narrows; the timber sea barrier of about 737-740 off Reesholm, how ships passed it unknown.

pages.game: An ale-house at Sliesthorp. A long house of wattle and reed thatch, the door on the lee side, a fire down the middle and benches along both walls. Sea chests under the benches, a gaming board scratched on a plank, notched sticks stuck in the wall above the ale vat: one for each guest who has not paid. A back room behind a hanging. Smoke in the roof, sour mash, wet wool drying, somebody singing low in his throat and nobody asking him to stop. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, lodge ashore, throw dice, play tafl, pay the singer, hire a hand and buy stores. Found here: Gunnhild.
pages.known: The singing: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub. The house and its keeper are invented.

pages.brief: A boat yard at Sliesthorp. A strip of shore north of the brook, black with old tar. A hull stands on blocks, half planked, her ribs not yet in: the planks are split oak, thin as a hand, and overlap like the scales of a fish.
pages.game: A boat yard at Sliesthorp. A strip of shore north of the brook, black with old tar. A hull stands on blocks, half planked, her ribs not yet in: the planks are split oak, thin as a hand, and overlap like the scales of a fish. A boy heats rivets. Wood chips float along the water's edge, and a pile of oak logs lies under wet hides to keep it green. The wright walks round her with an axe and does not seem to measure anything. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools. Found here: Thormund.
pages.known: The slip and its wright are invented.

pages.title: The pit-houses
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Sliesthorp. Small sunken huts on the north-west edge, each a roof on the ground with a doorway and a man working in the light of it.
pages.game: A workshop at Sliesthorp. Small sunken huts on the north-west edge, each a roof on the ground with a doorway and a man working in the light of it. A comb-maker saws antler into plates, ankle-deep in white shavings; next door a bead-maker turns a rod of glass in a clay oven no bigger than a beehive. Amber chips, bone dust, charcoal smoke, the whine of a small saw. At one yard gate two poles stand with a ram's hide hanging between them. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, buy ship's tools and try the goods. Found here: Tofi.
pages.known: Pit-houses as workshops; over 340,000 pieces of comb-makers' waste; 7,700 beads of carnelian, crystal, amber, jet and glass; a domed oven on a burnt pit-house; goldsmiths' mercury.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

later.text: A glass furnace of 850-900.
The sacrifice poles at a yard gate are Ibrahim's, 960s, carried back to 793 (?).

pages.title: The cart road and the one gate
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Sliesthorp. A rutted road leaving the houses westward along the foot of a long grassy bank: the Danes' old wall, taller than a rider, its oak front grey with age.
pages.game: A gate at Sliesthorp. A rutted road leaving the houses westward along the foot of a long grassy bank: the Danes' old wall, taller than a rider, its oak front grey with age. Ox-carts wait in a line, loaded with bales and casks for the landing on the Treene, a long day west. Dust, dung, axle grease, an ox lowing. What is done here: pay the toll, show the charter, hire carriers, ask the news and call witnesses. Found here: Gunulf.
pages.known: The Main Wall, North Wall and East Wall stand in 793. 'One gate only, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and let in'. Hollingstedt on the Treene, 16 to 18 km west by ox-cart. No toll rate is recorded.

later.text: From 808 there is new earth and raw timber on the bank, and a single gate wide enough for one wagon, with the king's man beside it and a tally stick in his hand.
'One gate only, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and let in' (Annales regni Francorum 808).

pages.title: The king's field
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Sliesthorp. A wide heath south of the houses, purple in late summer.
pages.game: A field at Sliesthorp. A wide heath south of the houses, purple in late summer. When a king is here it is covered: tents of striped wool, horse lines out to the edge of sight, shields hung on spear racks, and in the middle an open space with a high seat carried out of a ship. A spokesman stands in front of it and repeats what is said behind him. Horse sweat, trampled heather, roasting meat, a horn now and then. When no king is here, sheep. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, swear an oath, hear the law and hold a feast. Found here: Godfred and Horik.
pages.known: No hall or thing-place has been found: the field and the high seat are the game's own. The English name 'at the Heaths' (Ohthere) gives the heath.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

later.text: Godfred came 'with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom' (Annales regni Francorum 804) and stayed some days in 808.

pages.title: The grave field, Sliesthorp
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Sliesthorp. Low ground south of the brook, pocked with small mounds and burnt patches, each with a stone or a post.
pages.game: A mound at Sliesthorp. Low ground south of the brook, pocked with small mounds and burnt patches, each with a stone or a post. A woman pours ale on one. Further on, two green barrows stand side by side where the old road passes. In later years there is a great mound here with a boat's stem showing through the turf, and by the ford a tall stone cut with runes, painted red in the grooves. Wind in dry grass, a lark, an old smell of fire. What is done here: have him remembered, bury a man, make an offering, cast the lots, make a vow and read a book.
pages.known: Nearly 1,350 burials: Danish cremation pits, chamber graves, Saxon and Slav urns, later Christian graves. The mound pair Twebargen; the four rune stones of about 940 to 1000. The ale offering is invented in the period's manner.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

later.text: The boat chamber grave of about 900.

pages.title: The moneyer's bench, Sliesthorp
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Sliesthorp. A lean-to against a goldsmith's house, open at the front. A man sits astride a block with an iron die set in it, lays a thin round of silver on the die, sets a second die on top and strikes once.
pages.game: A mint at Sliesthorp. A lean-to against a goldsmith's house, open at the front. A man sits astride a block with an iron die set in it, lays a thin round of silver on the die, sets a second die on top and strikes once. The pennies are small and light and say Dorestad in letters that have begun to turn into a ship. A boy counts them into a wooden bowl. The moneyer cannot read them and says so. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver.
pages.known: No moneyer is named; the bench is invented.

later.text: The first coins of the North, from about 825, copying Dorestad's Frankish pennies.

pages.title: The church by the harbour
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Sliesthorp. A small church of upright oak planks under a shingle roof, a stone's throw from the jetties, with a priest's house beside it.
pages.game: A church at Sliesthorp. A small church of upright oak planks under a shingle roof, a stone's throw from the jetties, with a priest's house beside it. By the door stands a frame of two posts and a beam: empty at first, then with a bronze bell in it the height of a man's forearm. Inside, a board altar, a cross, one lamp, a row of boys reading from wax tablets. Frisians and Saxons go in. The Danes mending nets outside do not look round. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, take sanctuary, make a vow, read a book, have it copied and fund a work. Found here: Anskar.
pages.known: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24, 31-32 (tr. Robinson 1921): the church at the port, the priest's house, the door shut by Count Hovi, the bell. The church has never been found in the ground and its saint is not recorded: none is named.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

later.text: A bronze bell of about 950 was found in the harbour in 1978.

pages.game: A beach at Streonæshalch. A narrow gap between two cliffs with a brown river running out of it, and inside, on the left hand, a shelf of hard sand where a boat sits upright when the tide leaves her. In front, two small tarred boats and a drift of black weed; behind and far above, the roofs of the house against the sky. Gulls, the river talking over stones, a smell of peat water, weed and wet rope. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar, mend the boat and hire carriers. Found here: Cudda.
pages.known: The harbour dries; spring tides rise near 5.8 m; flat rock scars either side of the mouth cover at half tide.

pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Streonæshalch. A wide floor of flat grey rock running out from the foot of the cliff, bare at low water and gone at half tide.
pages.game: A beach at Streonæshalch. A wide floor of flat grey rock running out from the foot of the cliff, bare at low water and gone at half tide. In front, a fresh fall of shale and clay with women and children turning it over; in the stone underfoot, coiled shapes like sleeping snakes. Behind, the cliff, wet and leaning. The pick of a knife on stone, kittiwakes, and when someone tries a lump at a small fire, a smell of coal. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods and haggle the price. Found here: Cudda.
pages.known: Jet was gathered by beachcombing, not quarrying, and burns with a coal smell; Bede I.1 on its virtues. The coiled stones are the ammonites of this shore; the tale that Hild turned snakes to stone is later, of unknown date, and nobody tells it here in 793.

In front, a board scored in squares with pieces of bone and one of black jet; a harp in a bag on a peg. Behind, a shuttered window that looks straight down on the sea. What is done here: lodge ashore, ask the news, listen for talk, play tafl, trade riddles, pay the singer, drink with them and hold a feast, and more. Found here: Hunwine.
pages.known: A jet gaming piece of the Anglian period was found on the headland (English Heritage research page). The harp passed round at a feast here: Bede IV.24, Caedmon. Abbess Aelfflaed was known for care of the sick. Guests kept apart under one brother: the common rule of such houses; this building is not identified (?).

Inside, lamps over two long slabs side by side and a third apart, and the altar beyond with a cloth of the house's own weaving. pages.known: The church of Saint Peter with the graves of Edwin (his body), Oswiu, Eanflaed, Aelfflaed and Bishop Trumwine. The church has not been found and may lie under the later abbey church (?). A double house: whether it still was in 793 is not known.

pages.title: The graveyard south of the church, Streonæshalch
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Streonæshalch. Rows on rows of low graves on the south side, more than a visitor can count at a walk, with plain stone crosses the height of a child and small slabs cut with a name.
pages.game: A graveyard at Streonæshalch. Rows on rows of low graves on the south side, more than a visitor can count at a walk, with plain stone crosses the height of a child and small slabs cut with a name. In front, a stone with a cross and one word; behind, the church wall. Wind in the grass. Later, sheep. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, give alms and fund a work.
pages.known: Part of a large Anglian cemetery found in 2000 south of the church (English Heritage research page); the count of graves is not checked (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/streonaeshalch.md (researched 6 Oct 2026): the base of this file, with its marks of (memory) and (?) carried over

later.text: Behind, the church wall, and after 867 no roof on it.

pages.title: Prestebi: the roofless cells
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Streonæshalch. The headland as the Danes found it: a scatter of small stone churches and cells without roofs, nettles in the doorways, the walls still shoulder high.
pages.game: A church at Streonæshalch. The headland as the Danes found it: a scatter of small stone churches and cells without roofs, nettles in the doorways, the walls still shoulder high. In front, one cell thatched again with a smoke hole and a patch of beans beside it; behind, the old church open to the sky. Larks, wind, and from the one roofed cell a man's voice singing an office alone. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, have him remembered, make a vow, fund a work and ask the news.
pages.known: About 1078 Reinfrid found some forty roofless 'monasteria vel oratoria' here (Victoria County History, Yorkshire vol. 3, Whitby Abbey). Prestebi, 'the priests' farm', is an 11th-century name and suggests priests living here in Danish times (Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2). The one thatched cell is the game's (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/streonaeshalch.md (researched 6 Oct 2026): the base of this file, with its marks of (memory) and (?) carried over

pages.title: Hvitabyr: the booths by the river
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Streonæshalch. Low houses and boat sheds on the flat ground inside the river mouth, on both banks, with boats drawn up between them bow to the land.
pages.game: A market at Streonæshalch. Low houses and boat sheds on the flat ground inside the river mouth, on both banks, with boats drawn up between them bow to the land. In front, fish on racks, a trestle of jet lumps and half-cut rings, a set of folding scales; behind, the cliff and the empty headland. Two tongues at once, hammering, tar and drying fish. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, test the silver, ask the news, listen for talk, drink with them, hire a hand and buy a boat, and more. Found here: Ketil.
pages.known: Hvitabyr is the settlers' name. Northmen made rings and small beasts of jet; York's jet workers flourish in the 10th century. The hall and the booths are the game's: nothing has been dug.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/streonaeshalch.md (researched 6 Oct 2026): the base of this file, with its marks of (memory) and (?) carried over

later.text: From 1033 a long hall with carved door posts stands above the booths.
By 1066 'there was a substantial town called Whitby down by the harbour' (English Heritage).
Earl Siward's manor before 1066 (Victoria County History).

pages.title: The salmon reach
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Streonæshalch. The river a little way above the landing, brown as ale, sliding between alder banks with the tide pushing up under it.
pages.game: A fishery at Streonæshalch. The river a little way above the landing, brown as ale, sliding between alder banks with the tide pushing up under it. In front, a wattle fence run out from the bank and a man standing in the water to his thighs with a long net; behind, oak woods climbing toward the moor. Water over stones, a heron, and the clean cold smell of the river. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, cross over and wait for wind.
pages.known: Salmon and sea trout run the Esk, a moorland river quick to flood, tidal about 3 km up to Ruswarp. The fish fence is the game's (?).

pages.title: The strand under the wall, Traiectum
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Traiectum. In front, a sloping bank of trodden clay with a dozen boats drawn up on rollers and a tow-rope drying over a rail.
pages.game: A beach at Traiectum. In front, a sloping bank of trodden clay with a dozen boats drawn up on rollers and a tow-rope drying over a rail. Behind, the pale tuff wall of the fort with two low church roofs showing over it. Smoke from eel fires, wet hemp, and a bell counting the hours of prayer. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, ask the keeper and wait for wind. Found here: Aldlef.
pages.known: No jetty: boats drawn up the bank.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: De Bruijn, 'De vicus Stathe': Carolingian pottery of 750-1000 on the strand, flood clay and no houses from about 850 to after 900.
It stands until about 919.

pages.title: The crossing at the Vecht mouth
pages.hint: A ferry, not yet seen
pages.brief: A ferry at Traiectum. The river bends round the north of the fort and splits: the Vecht goes north through reeds toward the Almere, the old Rhine west toward the sea.
pages.game: A ferry at Traiectum. The river bends round the north of the fort and splits: the Vecht goes north through reeds toward the Almere, the old Rhine west toward the sea. In front a flat ferry on a pole and a half-hollowed oak on trestles, chips all round it. Behind, the dark line of the peat bog. Adze strokes, curlews, tar. What is done here: cross over, hire a pilot, mend the boat, scrape and tar, order a ship, buy a boat, fit her out and buy ship's tools. Found here: Aldlef.
pages.known: Traiectum means a crossing; the widened logboat built here: Vleuten 1, felled after about 734. Where the Vecht left the Rhine is not sure (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: Hildeburg's ale-house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Traiectum. A low reed-roofed house on the levee above the strand, its door open to the river.
pages.game: An ale-house at Traiectum. A low reed-roofed house on the levee above the strand, its door open to the river. In front a bench, a tub of ale under a wet cloth and eels hanging split in the smoke. Behind, the wall of the fort gone gold in the evening. Boatmen talk Frisian; a clerk from the school pretends he is not there. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, hire a hand, throw dice and buy stores. Found here: Hildeburg.
pages.known: Invented; boatmen, fishers and levee farmers lived below the fort.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: It stands until about 857.

pages.title: The gate of the fort, Traiectum
pages.hint: A gate, not yet seen
pages.brief: A gate at Traiectum. A Roman gateway of grey tuff with newer, rougher stone let into it and an oak door hung where an arch once was.
pages.game: A gate at Traiectum. A Roman gateway of grey tuff with newer, rougher stone let into it and an oak door hung where an arch once was. In front, a porter's bench and a begging bowl. Through the gate a yard of trodden earth and the west end of Saint Martin's. Cold in the shadow even at midsummer. What is done here: give alms, ask the news, take sanctuary and call witnesses. Found here: Hadda.
pages.known: De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht': a fort of 126 by 152 m, tuff walls of about AD 210 patched in the 7th century, gates north, east and south found by digging.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: Saint Martin's, Traiectum
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Traiectum. A small stone church, the bishop's own, with a wooden bell frame beside the door.
pages.game: A minster at Traiectum. A small stone church, the bishop's own, with a wooden bell frame beside the door. Inside, one lamp before the altar, wax candles on feast days only, a painted cloth on the east wall. Behind it the roof of Saint Salvator's, a stone's throw away. Incense when there is any; damp stone always. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, give a gift, have him remembered and fund a work. Found here: Hamacar.
pages.known: The bell: Willibald's Life of Boniface, 754.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: Nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht': Dagobert's chapel of about 630, rebuilt by Willibrord, the cathedral from about 750, destroyed 857, rebuilt after about 920, burned 1017.
It stands until about 1017.

pages.title: Saint Salvator's, the old minster
pages.hint: A church, not yet seen
pages.brief: A church at Traiectum. Willibrord's church: a plain hall of tuff eighteen paces long with a smaller room on its east end, where the dead of the house lie in limestone coffins under the floor.
pages.game: A church at Traiectum. Willibrord's church: a plain hall of tuff eighteen paces long with a smaller room on its east end, where the dead of the house lie in limestone coffins under the floor. In front the clergy file in two by two. Morning light through three small windows. Psalms, sung slowly. What is done here: hear Mass, bury a man, have him remembered, swear an oath and give alms.
pages.known: Nl.wikipedia 'Sint-Salvatorkerk (Utrecht)': a hall of 12 by 18 m with an east annex of 9 by 12 m where limestone sarcophagi were found; Bishops Ricfried, Frederik and Odilbald lie here; Odulf's relics brought here by Balderik.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: The school house
pages.hint: An abbey, not yet seen
pages.brief: An abbey at Traiectum. A long timber house against the inner face of the wall. In front, boys on benches with wax tablets on their knees; a master walking behind them with a switch he does not use.
pages.game: An abbey at Traiectum. A long timber house against the inner face of the wall. In front, boys on benches with wax tablets on their knees; a master walking behind them with a switch he does not use. Behind, an iron-bound chest under the one glazed window, and a sloped desk with a book open on it. Tallow, ink of oak gall, chalk. What is done here: read a book, have it copied, trade riddles and take an order. Found here: Radger.
pages.known: The school of Gregory, where Liudger learned 756-767; timber buildings inside the walls (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: The prior's store
pages.hint: A storehouse, not yet seen
pages.brief: A storehouse at Traiectum. A half-sunk store room of old Roman footings roofed with thatch.
pages.game: A storehouse at Traiectum. A half-sunk store room of old Roman footings roofed with thatch. In front, a scale hung from a beam and a tally board; cakes of wax stacked like loaves, two casks, one jar of oil kept under lock. Behind, sacks counted and counted again. It smells of honey and of mice. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, use your store and take an order. Found here: Hadda.
pages.known: The church buys wax, wine, oil, incense, books and Lenten fish; there is no market here in 793: this is a buyer's store, not a market.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: The guest house, Traiectum
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Traiectum. A timber hall by the gate with a hearth in the middle of the floor and straw along the walls.
pages.game: A lodging at Traiectum. A timber hall by the gate with a hearth in the middle of the floor and straw along the walls. In front a table with a bowl of porridge, a crock of butter and a comb of honey; no wine. Behind, a monk asleep sitting up with a letter case under his arm. Wood smoke and wet wool. What is done here: lodge ashore, see the leech, ask the news, listen for talk and play tafl. Found here: Hadda.
pages.known: Alcuin, carmen 4: Hadda serves honey, porridge and butter, 'utpute non oleum nec vinum Fresia fundit'. Guests kept apart under one monk's care: Rule of Benedict 53.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

pages.title: The bishop's hall, Traiectum
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Traiectum. A timber hall on stone footings beside Saint Martin's. In front, a high seat with a carved back, a deacon at a writing desk and a chest of charters with three locks.
pages.game: A hall at Traiectum. A timber hall on stone footings beside Saint Martin's. In front, a high seat with a carved back, a deacon at a writing desk and a chest of charters with three locks. Behind, a hanging of red wool gone brown. Light from the door only. The talk is low and in two tongues. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, show the charter, hear the law, bring a case, swear an oath and hold a feast. Found here: Hamacar.
pages.known: The fort is the bishop's by the gift of 723; the see's charters (Oorkondenboek van het Sticht Utrecht).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: The bishop's house burned with the cathedral in 1017.

pages.title: The Stathe
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Traiectum. The old strand built over: a street of timber houses with their gables to the river and their back doors to the fort's west bridge.
pages.game: A market at Traiectum. The old strand built over: a street of timber houses with their gables to the river and their back doors to the fort's west bridge. In front, trestles of pots, glass, cloth and salt fish; a merchants' church of wood, later of stone. Behind, Balderik's new wall. Hammering, haggling, a pig loose. What is done here: haggle the price, weigh the silver, try the goods, listen for talk, drink with them, hire a hand, hire carriers and buy a plot, and more.
pages.known: De Bruijn, 'De vicus Stathe'; nl.wikipedia 'Stathe', 'Buurkerk': the merchants' quarter of the 10th century, their church of the 10th or early 11th.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: Burned by its own people in 1007 (Alpertus).

pages.title: The Vecht side
pages.hint: A landing, not yet seen
pages.brief: A landing at Traiectum. A long bank faced with oak posts and wattle, planks of old boats nailed in among them.
pages.game: A landing at Traiectum. A long bank faced with oak posts and wattle, planks of old boats nailed in among them. In front, three long barges nose to tail and a hollowed oak ship with a short towing mast. Behind, storehouses with their doors to the water. Tar, herring brine, wet oak. What is done here: load and unload, mend the boat, scrape and tar, hire carriers, hire a pilot, pay the toll, show the charter and use your store, and more.
pages.known: The Waterstraat dig, 1974-81: 420 m of revetments, timber houses and ships of the 10th to 12th century; planks of a Norse-built keel ship reused in the quay.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: The bishop's toll: Muiden 953, moved here 975 (?).

pages.title: The bishop's mint
pages.hint: A mint, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mint at Traiectum. A small stone room inside the gate with a barred window. In front, a moneyer at a block with a die in one fist and a hammer in the other; a boy cutting blanks with shears.
pages.game: A mint at Traiectum. A small stone room inside the gate with a barred window. In front, a moneyer at a block with a die in one fist and a hammer in the other; a boy cutting blanks with shears. Behind, a scale no bigger than a hand. The ring of the hammer carries to the Stathe. What is done here: change coin, test the silver and weigh the silver.
pages.known: Pennies in the bishop's own name only from Bernold on (?) (numista 373398). No moneyer is named.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: Otto I gives the mint to the bishop in 953, or 936.

pages.title: Adelbold's cathedral
pages.hint: A minster, not yet seen
pages.brief: A minster at Traiectum. A great new church of tuff on the place of the old Saint Martin's, with round arches and a high west end.
pages.game: A minster at Traiectum. A great new church of tuff on the place of the old Saint Martin's, with round arches and a high west end. In the choir floor a stone marked for an emperor. Candles by the score, and a choir of canons. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, give a gift, have him remembered and take sanctuary.
pages.known: Bernold's churches: nl.wikipedia 'Pieterskerk (Utrecht)', 'Janskerk (Utrecht)', 'Paulusabdij (Utrecht)'.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md (the research this file is built on, with its 46 references)

later.text: Nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht': consecrated 1023 before Henry II and twelve bishops.
Conrad II's entrails ('exta' on the choir stone) from 1039.
After 1050 three more churches stand round it.

pages.title: The boat shore, Truso
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Truso. A low shore of grey shingle and trodden reed with boats drawn up side by side, their sterns in brown still water.
pages.game: A beach at Truso. A low shore of grey shingle and trodden reed with boats drawn up side by side, their sterns in brown still water. Behind them the plots and thatched houses, and behind those a rise with a timber fort and smoke. In front, women kneel at cloths spread with wet yellow lumps. Frogs, a caulking mallet, the smell of tar, lake mud and smoked bream. What is done here: load and unload, scrape and tar, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, try the goods and buy from makers. Found here: Nameda.
pages.known: Boat wreckage and ship rivets on the shore; Lake Druzno shallow and reed-ringed. A dug harbour basin is reported by the excavator (?). The sellers on cloths are the game's.
pages.source: The Old English Orosius, Wulfstan's account. The sailing part: texts_793.json 'wulfstan' (J. Bosworth 1859). The Estland part: H. later.text: It stands until about 1000.

pages.title: The mouth of the Ilfing
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Truso. Where the river leaves the lake: a gap in the reeds marked by nothing at all, fish traps of withy on either side, three log boats with men standing in them.
pages.game: A fishery at Truso. Where the river leaves the lake: a gap in the reeds marked by nothing at all, fish traps of withy on either side, three log boats with men standing in them. Northward the water widens to the pale Estmere and a line of sand beyond it. Herons, the slap of a net, the smell of mud and fish scale. The fishers look at every boat and say nothing. What is done here: hire a pilot, ask the keeper, wait for wind, buy from makers and buy stores. Found here: Santirme.
pages.known: Wulfstan: the Ilfing comes into the Estmere 'out of the lake on whose shore Truso stands', and there is 'very much fishing' (Old English Orosius). The fishers who count boats are the chain's. Where the lagoon opened to the sea is not known (?).

pages.title: The weighing ground
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Truso. A trodden space between the shore and the first plots, with no stalls: men stand in pairs, one holding a little folding scale up to the light, the other watching the pans.
pages.game: A market at Truso. A trodden space between the shore and the first plots, with no stalls: men stand in pairs, one holding a little folding scale up to the light, the other watching the pans. On the ground, sacks of amber, tubs of honey, wax in cakes, marten skins tied in forties, and a row of people sitting with their ankles roped. The talk is quiet. Silver clicks on bronze. What is done here: weigh the silver, test the silver, haggle the price, try the goods and listen for talk. Found here: Ketil.
pages.known: Scales, weights and cut dirhams from the dig; amber, furs and slaves; honey (Wulfstan). No market place has been identified as such, and no toll or law is known: there is no toll site in this file on purpose.

pages.title: The Dane's long house
pages.hint: A lodging, not yet seen
pages.brief: A lodging at Truso. A post-built house of three rooms on a marked plot, twenty paces long, its thatch nearly to the ground.
pages.game: A lodging at Truso. A post-built house of three rooms on a marked plot, twenty paces long, its thatch nearly to the ground. Inside, a long hearth, benches with strangers' sea chests under them, a gaming board on a barrel, a scale case hanging from a peg. Smoke, wet wool, mead. Through the end door the lake shows grey between two boats. What is done here: lodge ashore, use your store, drink with them, play tafl, throw dice, ask the news, listen for talk and hire a hand, and more. Found here: Ketil and Wigmar.
pages.known: Three-room post-built houses of 50 to 120 square metres on regular plots; gaming pieces and boards. That one house took guests is the game's. The drink is mead: no ale is brewed among the Este (Wulfstan).

pages.title: The amber-cutters' row
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Truso. Small houses with their doors propped open to the south for the light.
pages.game: A workshop at Truso. Small houses with their doors propped open to the south for the light. On each threshold a board, a knife, a bow-drill and a heap of honey-coloured chips; finished beads hang in strings from the door post and turn in the wind. Raw lumps soak in a bowl of brine to show which float. It smells of warm resin, like a pine wood in the sun. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, try the goods and haggle the price. Found here: Nameda.
pages.known: Amber-working at Truso, dated late 8th to early 10th century. The tests (rub, brine, lip) are the chain's and are true of amber.

pages.title: The comb-makers and the glass fire
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Truso. A plot heaped with antler: tines in one pile, sawn plates in another, a drift of white dust underfoot.
pages.game: A workshop at Truso. A plot heaped with antler: tines in one pile, sawn plates in another, a drift of white dust underfoot. A man rivets tooth-plates between two bars; next door a woman winds a thread of green glass round an iron rod over a clay hearth, and a bead grows on it. The rasp of a saw, the hiss of the bellows, burnt horn. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order, buy ship's tools, ask the news and try the goods.

pages.title: The smith and the goldsmith
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Truso. Two hearths under one roof at the edge of the plots, away from the thatch.
pages.game: A smithy at Truso. Two hearths under one roof at the edge of the plots, away from the thatch. At one a smith draws out rivets by the handful; at the other a small man with a blowpipe bends over a crucible no bigger than an egg. On a plank between them lie brooches, weights of lead and bronze, a sword without its hilt. Charcoal smoke and the ring of the hammer. What is done here: buy ship's tools, test the silver, take an order, fit her out and change coin.
pages.known: Smithing and goldsmithing, weights, swords and Scandinavian jewellery from the dig.

pages.title: The menders' strand
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Truso. The north end of the shore, where a boat lies on her side with three strakes off.
pages.game: A boat yard at Truso. The north end of the shore, where a boat lies on her side with three strakes off. Barrels of tar stand in the shade, a keg of new rivets beside them, moss drying on a hurdle. Two men split an oak log with wedges and do not hurry. Beyond them, in the reeds, the black ribs of a boat nobody mended. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, fit her out, buy a boat, order a ship and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Boat wreckage and Scandinavian ship rivets; riveted boats of 9 to 11 m by 2.5 to 3 m, tar barrels and unused rivets.

pages.game: A hall at Truso. Higher ground behind the town, palings of split oak, a gate with a horse skull over it. Inside, log houses close together and one larger than the rest, its door shut and a store beside it with a bar across. Men sit on the bank with bowls of mares' milk. From the gate the whole lake lies below, and a straight road runs inland over the rise. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, hear the law and call witnesses. Found here: Gedune and Drua.
pages.known: Wulfstan: the Este have many strongholds, 'and in each stronghold there is a king'; the king and the richest men drink mares' milk. He does not say Truso had a king, and no fort has been dug here: this one is the game's and the chain's (?). Whether the traders' shore had an Este lord over it is not known.

pages.game: A field at Truso. A straight track from the fort gate over open grass to a rise about a mile off, worn hollow by hooves. On most days there is nothing on it but a boy leading a lean horse at a walk, and another, and another: more horses than a place this size should feed. On one day in a season there are heaps of goods along it and the whole country at the palings. What is done here: call witnesses, have him remembered and buy from makers.
pages.known: Wulfstan: a dead man's goods are laid in five or six heaps, the largest about a mile from the town, and ridden for from five or six miles off; 'fast horses are very dear there' (Old English Orosius, Sweet 1883; our rendering).

pages.game: A graveyard at Truso. A strip of blackened turf between the houses and the Ilfing, with low mounds along the bank, some old and green, some raw. Women go over a cold pyre with wooden rakes, slowly, looking for bone. A pot stands ready. Nobody speaks loudly. The wind brings the smell of wet ash and, from the mounds, nothing. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering, call witnesses and give a gift.
pages.known: Wulfstan: every man, of whatever people, must be burnt, and if one bone is found unburnt a great atonement is owed. 'Merchant graves along the river'; a large cemetery dug in the 1920s. No 'bury' here: nobody may lie unburnt in this ground.

pages.game: A holy wood at Truso. South of the houses the alders stand in black water, old and uncut, though the town burns wood all year and fetches it from farther off. A path of laid branches goes in a little way and stops at a spring. Rags of cloth hang there, and a bowl. Fish rise in the pools and no trap is set. It is cool, and quieter than it should be. What is done here: make an offering, cast the lots and make a vow. Found here: Drua.
pages.known: Woods, fields and waters so holy that none cut, tilled or fished there, and Christians kept from the groves: Adam of Bremen IV.18, of the 1070s, so later than most of the game and placed here by the game (?). No temple or idol is known at Truso. No high priest and no 'Romove': those are of 1326.

Behind, flat wet meadow to the skyline, and on the skyline three round hills that are not hills. Curlews, the suck of mud, a smell of tar and wet hay. pages.game: A hall at Uppsalir. A bank of piled clay as high as two men, and on it one roof sixty paces long, its shingles silver-grey, its two side doors wide enough for a cart and bound with iron curled like fern heads. Inside, dark and warm: a long fire, benches, shields on the wall, a high seat seen through smoke. Roast pork, wet wool, wood smoke two hundred years deep. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, trade riddles, play tafl, drink with them and pay the singer. Found here: Vifast and Gillaug.
pages.known: The hall on Kungsgardsplatan: 50-60 m by 12 m, doors 3 m wide, iron spirals. Shown standing until 800 by the game's choice; no year is known.

pages.game: A hall at Uppsalir. The clay bank is still there, and on it nothing: a floor fired red and hard as a pot, black stumps, nettles. Children are told not to play there and do. Below its north end stands the house the king eats in now, half the length of the old one, new thatch already going grey. A horn sounds for meat. Ash still blows off the terrace in a dry wind. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hold a feast, swear an oath, trade riddles, play tafl, drink with them and pay the singer, and more. Found here: Vifast and Gillaug.

Barley porridge, herring that has come a long way, wet dog. What is done here: lodge ashore, drink with them, buy stores, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, play tafl and hire a hand, and more. Found here: Gillaug.
pages.known: Invented; cod and herring were carried up from the coast and eaten here. That a traveller may not be refused a roof among the Svear is Adam of Bremen IV.21 (?), about 1075.

Goods lie on hides in front of doors: grey Rhine pots, querns, cheeses, fleeces, a tray of glass beads. Dung heaps and stock pens stand between the houses; pigs root for acorns. It smells of sheep and peat smoke. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver, listen for talk, buy a plot and rent store room. Found here: Wilbraht.

pages.game: A field at Walichrum. Flat green salt marsh cut by silver creeks as far as can be seen, dotted with sheep. A woman sits milking a ewe at a hurdle pen; cheeses dry on a rack under a net against the gulls. Larks, wind, the bleat of lambs, and the sea heard but not seen. What is done here: buy from makers, fund a work and buy stores. Found here: Bernhild.

pages.title: Wiltrud's house
pages.hint: An ale-house, not yet seen
pages.brief: An ale-house at Walichrum. A house like the others, ten paces by fourteen, with one middle room and a fire on the earth floor.
pages.game: An ale-house at Walichrum. A house like the others, ten paces by fourteen, with one middle room and a fire on the earth floor. Benches along the plank walls, a cask on trestles, cups of green glass on a shelf beside wooden ones. Skippers of three tongues sit apart and listen to each other. Smoke, wet wool and sour ale. What is done here: drink with them, listen for talk, ask the news, throw dice, trade riddles, lodge ashore and hire a hand. Found here: Wiltrud.
pages.known: De Man 1899 (houses of 5-10 by 14 m, a central room with side rooms, earth floors; glass cups, one of them green and footless). The ale-house itself is invented.

later.text: It stands until about 850.

pages.title: The king's house, Walichrum
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Walichrum. The longest house on the street, squared oak trunks at its corners, with a fenced yard, a tally shed and a pen of the king's sheep.
pages.game: A hall at Walichrum. The longest house on the street, squared oak trunks at its corners, with a fenced yard, a tally shed and a pen of the king's sheep. A spear leans by the door. Inside, a high seat with a carved back and a bench for those who wait. What is done here: ask an audience, give a gift, hear the law, bring a case, call witnesses and swear an oath. Found here: Reginbert.
pages.known: A royal estate from the late sixth century is Erfgoed Zeeland's reading, not a charter (?); the first named count is Eggihard. No reeve, toll or court is recorded here: the house and its uses are the game's.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md (6 Oct 2026 reading): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what is not known and is kept to here.

later.text: The first named count is Eggihard, killed 837 (Annales Fuldenses).
From 841 a Danish shield hangs over the door.
Harald from 841 (Annales Bertiniani).
It stands until about 850.

pages.title: Where the idol stood
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Walichrum. A bare place at the west end of the street where nothing is built: a pit grown over with grass and a plain oak cross, grey with weather, taller than a man.
pages.game: A shrine at Walichrum. A bare place at the west end of the street where nothing is built: a pit grown over with grass and a plain oak cross, grey with weather, taller than a man. Mussel shells and a twist of wool lie at its foot. Sheep graze up to it and no closer. Wind in the marram grass. What is done here: make a vow, give alms, make an offering, have him remembered, hear Mass and cast the lots.
pages.known: Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi: an idol stood at Walichrum and Willibrord broke it. The cross, the place in the street and the things left at its foot are invented (?). No church or priest is recorded here in 793; a priest out of Traiectum saying Mass in the open at the great feasts is the game's. Churchmen thought the islanders half heathen (Thiofrid, about 1103; the Passio Friderici).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md (6 Oct 2026 reading): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what is not known and is kept to here.

later.text: It stands until about 950.

pages.title: The fenced graves
pages.hint: A graveyard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A graveyard at Walichrum. A long grave field between the houses and the dune, fenced with oak pales, three hundred paces by seventy.
pages.game: A graveyard at Walichrum. A long grave field between the houses and the dune, fenced with oak pales, three hundred paces by seventy. On the west a gate of two great tree trunks. Inside, low mounds in rows, all lying the same way, heads to the west. A new coffin waits on trestles: a hollowed trunk with a thin lid. What is done here: bury a man, have him remembered, make a vow, give alms and fund a work. Found here: Bernhild.
pages.known: De Man 1899 (Westhove: about 50 graves, 7th to 9th century, fenced with oak pales, 325 paces by 70, a gate of two great trunks on the west; trunk coffins pegged with wood, a small board under the head, heads to the west); ten Harkel and others 2023 (four grave fields; churchyard burial on this coast only from the tenth century).

later.text: It stands until about 950.

pages.title: The menders' bank
pages.hint: A boat yard, not yet seen
pages.brief: A boat yard at Walichrum. The firm bank at the head of the creek, where a barge lies on rollers with three strakes off.
pages.game: A boat yard at Walichrum. The firm bank at the head of the creek, where a barge lies on rollers with three strakes off. Old planks are stacked by length under a hide; a man splits an oak log with wedges, another boils tar in a pot. Nothing here is thrown away. Axe strokes, and the smell of pitch. What is done here: mend the boat, scrape and tar, buy a boat, order a ship, fit her out and buy ship's tools.
pages.known: Ten Harkel and others 2023 and Ufkes 2012 (planks of an English clinker ship and of Rhine barges reused on the island, some as coffins; oak hewn with the axe). The yard is invented: the island has no timber, which is why oak is wanted.

pages.title: The high dune
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Walichrum. The tallest dune, with a path worn up its landward side. From the top: the whole long street below, the marsh and its creeks behind, and to seaward white water on the shoals off the north-west corner.
pages.game: A mound at Walichrum. The tallest dune, with a path worn up its landward side. From the top: the whole long street below, the marsh and its creeks behind, and to seaward white water on the shoals off the north-west corner. A boy lies in the grass watching for sails. No tower, no stone, no mark but the dune itself. What is done here: wait for wind, ask the keeper, cast the lots and fund a work.
pages.known: The watch is invented; the place lay behind the dunes.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md (6 Oct 2026 reading): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what is not known and is kept to here.

pages.title: The ring wall
pages.hint: A wall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A wall at Walichrum. A round bank of stacked sods as high as two men, a wet ditch outside it, two roads crossing in the middle and four gaps for gates.
pages.game: A wall at Walichrum. A round bank of stacked sods as high as two men, a wet ditch outside it, two roads crossing in the middle and four gaps for gates. Inside there is room for every beast on the island. Long byre-houses stand in the quarters, and cattle look out of the doors. What is done here: take sanctuary, use your store, rent store room, fund a work and buy stores. Found here: Unno.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md (6 Oct 2026 reading): the research this file is built on; its section 8 lists what is not known and is kept to here.

later.text: Ufkes 2012 (sod rampart and moat, 4.5 ha, two crossing roads, five byre-houses of about 875-950, begun 835-838 on his dating); others date it after 851 or about 890, and its builders are unknown (?).

pages.title: The Ried bank
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Winaldum. A grey creek between banks of shining mud, sea lavender and glasswort on either side, the row of green mounds behind under a very large sky.
pages.game: A beach at Winaldum. A grey creek between banks of shining mud, sea lavender and glasswort on either side, the row of green mounds behind under a very large sky. Two small clinker boats lie on their bilges on a bed of hurdles. Curlews, wind, and the smell of mud and drying nets. What is done here: load and unload, wait for wind, ask the keeper, hire a pilot, scrape and tar and hire carriers. Found here: Sicco.
pages.known: The Ried may have kept an opening to the sea (Aalders et al., Paleo-aktueel 2004, after Vos 1999); boats grounding on its bank is a guess (?): the waterside was never dug.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md (4 October 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its source keys.

pages.title: The foot of the mound
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Winaldum. Trodden turf at the foot of the terp where the cattle path comes down.
pages.game: A market at Winaldum. Trodden turf at the foot of the terp where the cattle path comes down. When a boat is in, cloth is laid over a rail, cheeses stacked on a hide, and a folding scale hung from a spear shaft stuck in the ground. Children and dogs in front, the sod houses above against the light. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, weigh the silver and test the silver. Found here: Folcward.
pages.known: No market is recorded (?). The goods are from the finds: Rhineland pottery in an unusually high share, Rhenish glass, iron bars, antler, amber, Carolingian pennies (Paleo-aktueel 1992-2004; JALC 2011).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md (4 October 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its source keys.

pages.title: The head house
pages.hint: A hall, not yet seen
pages.brief: A hall at Winaldum. A long low house with walls of stacked sods as thick as a man is tall and a reed roof smoking through the thatch.
pages.game: A hall at Winaldum. A long low house with walls of stacked sods as thick as a man is tall and a reed roof smoking through the thatch. Inside it is dark and warm: cattle breathing at one end, a peat fire at the other, a bench along the wall, dice on a board. It smells of peat, wet wool and cows. What is done here: give a gift, hold a feast, lodge ashore, ask the news, listen for talk, hear the law, swear an oath and call witnesses, and more. Found here: Folcward.
pages.known: One farmstead with a main house, outbuildings and sunken huts in every period; sod walls throughout (Paleo-aktueel 3-4; Gerrets et al. 1996). Dice and an antler tuning pin are in the finds (JALC 2011).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md (4 October 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its source keys.

pages.title: The weaving huts
pages.hint: A workshop, not yet seen
pages.brief: A workshop at Winaldum. Three small sheds dug knee-deep into the mound, their roofs hardly higher than a standing man.
pages.game: A workshop at Winaldum. Three small sheds dug knee-deep into the mound, their roofs hardly higher than a standing man. Through a door: an upright loom against the back wall, a row of clay weights swinging, two women passing the shuttle without looking. Damp, lanolin, and the knock of the sword beater. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods, take an order and haggle the price. Found here: Liafburg.
pages.known: Paleo-aktueel 4. The law's screona, the weaving hut it is death to break into (Lex Frisionum, Additio I 3).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md (4 October 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its source keys.

later.text: Sunken huts until about 850 with loom weights and spindle whorls gathered in them (JALC 2011).
It stands until about 850.

pages.title: The smith's floor
pages.hint: A smithy, not yet seen
pages.brief: A smithy at Winaldum. An open-sided shed on the lee of the mound, its floor black and glittering with scale.
pages.game: A smithy at Winaldum. An open-sided shed on the lee of the mound, its floor black and glittering with scale. A stone anvil block, a clay hearth, a boy at the bellows, bundles of iron bars from the north under the eave. Charcoal smoke, hot iron, and a keg of rivets by the door. What is done here: mend the boat, buy ship's tools, take an order and fit her out. Found here: Bernrad.
pages.known: A smithy floor of hammer-scale (Nijboer and Tulp 1997, an earlier period); iron forged from bars and scrap into the 10th century; 81 clench nails and roves from the 5th to the 9th century (Aalders et al. 2004).

pages.game: A workshop at Winaldum. A plank on two posts in the sun by the house wall. A thumb-sized clay cup of yellow glass over a little fire, an iron rod, a heap of raw amber and the flakes knapped off it, beads cooling in a bowl of ash. A man working with his tongue between his teeth. What is done here: buy from makers, take an order and try the goods. Found here: Gerbrand.
pages.known: A crucible with yellow glass, a yellow mosaic cube and many yellow beads (Sablerolles 1994); raw amber knapped into beads on the terp (Paleo-aktueel 4); craftsmen who came and went (JALC 2011).

pages.title: The bare mound
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Winaldum. The second mound in the row, lower than the rest and grazed bare. At the top a square of darker grass where posts once stood, and a single thorn bush bent east by the wind.
pages.game: A mound at Winaldum. The second mound in the row, lower than the rest and grazed bare. At the top a square of darker grass where posts once stood, and a single thorn bush bent east by the wind. Sheep keep off the square. From here the whole marsh and the line of the sea can be seen. What is done here: have him remembered, make an offering, cast the lots and make a vow. Found here: Aldward.
pages.known: The Franks burned the shrines in 734; Liudger broke more about 780 and the king took two thirds of the treasure (Altfrid I.16). The other six terps have never been dug.

pages.title: The cross on the terp
pages.hint: A shrine, not yet seen
pages.brief: A shrine at Winaldum. An oak post a little taller than a man with a crosspiece pegged to it, set in the turf at the top of the head terp, grey already from the salt wind.
pages.game: A shrine at Winaldum. An oak post a little taller than a man with a crosspiece pegged to it, set in the turf at the top of the head terp, grey already from the salt wind. A flat stone before it. When the priest is here he says Mass in the open with his back to the weather and his box on the stone. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, take sanctuary, bury a man and ask the news.
pages.known: The game's (?): no church, saint or churchyard is recorded before the late-medieval St Andrew's. Christian by law: Sunday work costs 4 solidi, and a man in feud has peace in church (Lex Frisionum XVIII; Additio I 1).

pages.title: The folds on the marsh
pages.hint: A field, not yet seen
pages.brief: A field at Winaldum. Low sod walls on the salt grass below the mounds, hundreds of sheep moving like one thing, red cattle beyond them, a few small thick-necked horses.
pages.game: A field at Winaldum. Low sod walls on the salt grass below the mounds, hundreds of sheep moving like one thing, red cattle beyond them, a few small thick-necked horses. A herd boy with a long pole for jumping the creeks. Bleating, larks, and dung drying in stacks for the fire. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores and haggle the price. Found here: Aldward.
pages.known: The bone counts: sheep 2,881, cattle 1,601, horse 86 (Prummel et al., JALC 2011, table 3). A marsh without dikes, flooded at times (JALC; Frisia Coast Trail).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/wijnaldum.md (4 October 2026): every dated fact here is from it, with its source keys.

pages.title: The flats at low water
pages.hint: A fishery, not yet seen
pages.brief: A fishery at Winaldum. Where the creek runs out the land simply stops being land: brown sand and mud to the edge of sight, stake nets standing dry, a man and a child small in the distance with a basket.
pages.game: A fishery at Winaldum. Where the creek runs out the land simply stops being land: brown sand and mud to the edge of sight, stake nets standing dry, a man and a child small in the distance with a basket. Seals on a far bank. When the tide turns it comes in faster than a walk. What is done here: buy from makers, buy stores, hire a pilot and have him remembered. Found here: Sicco.
pages.known: Net-menders and fishers in the finds; a porpoise's skull and jaw (JALC 2011; Prummel et al. 2012). The tide at Harlingen is about 2 m today and the flats dry. 'The sand the tide covers' is where the law puts the robber of a shrine (Lex Frisionum, Additio XI).

pages.title: The creek strand, Witla
pages.hint: A beach, not yet seen
pages.brief: A beach at Witla. A wide tidal creek at low water: grey mud, a dozen round-hulled boats sitting upright on it, ropes run to posts on the bank.
pages.game: A beach at Witla. A wide tidal creek at low water: grey mud, a dozen round-hulled boats sitting upright on it, ropes run to posts on the bank. Behind, the low ridge with its thatched roofs and smoke; ahead, the open mouth and a white line where the bar breaks. Gulls, wet rope, the slap of mud under a porter's feet, a smell of weed and tar. What is done here: load and unload, hire carriers, wait for wind, ask the keeper, scrape and tar and mend the boat. Found here: Radward.

An old man sits in the doorway looking at the water, not at you. It smells of tallow, tarred net and wet wool. What is done here: hire a pilot, ask the keeper, listen for talk and buy ship's tools. pages.title: The strand market, Witla
pages.hint: A market, not yet seen
pages.brief: A market at Witla.
pages.game: A market at Witla. Above the tide line, hurdles laid on the sand and goods on them: bolts of cloth in white, grey, red and blue, stacked grey pots with spouts, quernstones in pairs with straw between, a row of wine casks chocked with driftwood. Women sell from the hurdles; men stand about and say what things cost last year. Wet wool, smoke, a broached cask. What is done here: haggle the price, try the goods, buy from makers and use your store. Found here: Thiadlint.
pages.known: Invented; the goods are those of this coast: Rhenish wine, Badorf and Mayen pots, lava querns, Frisian cloth (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315); the four colours are Notker II.9.

Graves without markers lie in rows to the east. From here you see both shores: the dune spit to the north, and beyond it, on a clear day, the roof of the church across the water. What is done here: hear Mass, give alms, make a vow, bury a man, have him remembered, ask the news and fund a work. Found here: Bernrad.
pages.known: No church of Witla is known; the mother church is the one 'where the Maas goes into the sea', Echternach's from 726/727 (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 281-285). A preaching cross served from it is our guess (?).

pages.known: The farm at Witle given to Saint Peter's at Ghent: a house, pasture for five cows, four serfs (Dijkstra 2011, p. 175). The loom and the people are ours.

pages.title: The salt burners
pages.hint: A salt works, not yet seen
pages.brief: A salt works at Witla. Out on the marsh, a black scar where peat has been cut below the turf, and beside it mounds of grey ash and a clay pan steaming over a low fire.
pages.game: A salt works at Witla. Out on the marsh, a black scar where peat has been cut below the turf, and beside it mounds of grey ash and a clay pan steaming over a low fire. A man and a boy rake the ash and pour sea water through it. The smoke is thick and brown and lies flat along the ground. Everything here is the colour of ash, and so are they. What is done here: buy from makers, try the goods and haggle the price.
pages.known: Salt was burned from salt-soaked peat in Zeeland; in South Holland only the islands in the Maas mouth were fit for it (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315). That it was made at Witla is our guess (?).

pages.title: The mark on the dune
pages.hint: A mound, not yet seen
pages.brief: A mound at Witla. At the seaward end of the ridge a mound of turf with a tall post on it, a cross-piece near the top and a basket of dry furze at its foot.
pages.game: A mound at Witla. At the seaward end of the ridge a mound of turf with a tall post on it, a cross-piece near the top and a basket of dry furze at its foot. From the mound the whole mouth lies open: brown water, the bar breaking white, the far shore a thin line. A ship coming in puts the post over the end of the ridge and holds it there, in the years when that still works. What is done here: wait for wind, cast the lots, fund a work and ask the keeper. Found here: Gerlef.

pages.game: Vigmund is the chief at Aldeigjuborg, one of the Svear and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the biggest house. The man in the biggest house. No lord and no king's man: he is simply the one with the scale, the silver and the pen behind the wall, and everyone in the place owes him something. To look at: about fifty, broad and heavy, a grey-fair beard combed and a fur-lined cap he wears indoors, a belted coat with silver-wire trim, a folding scale on a cord at his neck and three rings on a hand missing its smallest finger.

pages.title: Milava
pages.hint: A craftsman, not yet met
pages.brief: Milava, the craftsman at Aldeigjuborg. The bead-maker. Makes eye beads on a small fire by a way no one north of here knows, and understands exactly what that is worth: a marten skin a bead in a good winter.
pages.game: Milava is the craftsman at Aldeigjuborg, a Slav and one who keeps the gods of the Wends. Found at: the bead-maker's shop. The bead-maker. Makes eye beads on a small fire by a way no one north of here knows, and understands exactly what that is worth: a marten skin a bead in a good winter. To look at: a little over thirty, thin, strong-wristed, fair hair bound under a linen cloth, eyebrows half singed away, a grey shift with the sleeves tied back and a string of her own worst beads round her neck.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The shop is real: glass eye beads by an Arab low-heat method; the beads bought furs. 'A bead for a slave' is a 10th-century Arab traveller's word, cited by the Russian page, and Ibn Fadlan's dirham a bead on the Volga is not checked (?): both later than her, so she has it only as hearsay. The name is Mil- with a short woman's ending, after later Slavic names (?).

pages.title: Audvald
pages.hint: A smith, not yet met
pages.brief: Audvald, the smith at Aldeigjuborg. Smith and bronze-caster in the oldest workshop, grandson of the Gotlander who first lit its forge.
pages.game: Audvald is the smith at Aldeigjuborg, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the old workshop. Smith and bronze-caster in the oldest workshop, grandson of the Gotlander who first lit its forge. Fits northern hilts to bare Frankish blades and keeps his grandfather's tools in the order he found them. To look at: past forty, lean and stooped from the anvil, a long plaited fair beard tucked into his belt away from the fire, a leather apron, burn scars to the elbow, and a small iron ring on a thong that he turns when he is thinking.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The workshop and its tool hoard are real, in the oldest layer of the 750s; the first settlers were perhaps Gotlanders (Ryabinin), and their colony ended in the 760s. The bronze finial with the horned head-dress, 'the singing Odin', is real; that it sang is his own tale (?). His riddle is r-gest-24. The name is Aud- + -vald, both common on Gotland's later stones (?).

pages.title: Budimir
pages.hint: A pilot, not yet met
pages.brief: Budimir, the pilot at Aldeigjuborg. River pilot, of the fort at the stream mouth below the town.
pages.game: Budimir is the pilot at Aldeigjuborg, a Slav and one who keeps the gods of the Wends. Found at: the mouth of the small river, the fort at the Lyubsha mouth and the river-boat bank below the rocks. River pilot, of the fort at the stream mouth below the town. Knows the lake's south shore by the colour of the water and the rapids by their sound, and has never lost a boat he was paid for. To look at: forty or so, short and very wide in the shoulder, brown beard, a belted shirt of undyed linen to the knee, bast shoes, a sounding pole taller than himself and a wooden charm on a cord.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. River pilots for the rapids are a fair inference, not a find. The Lyubsha fort, Slav on an older Finnic site; the lake's shoals and waves; the upper Volkhov can reverse; ice from late November to early April. The name is Bud- + -mir, after later Slavic names (?): no ordinary Slav of the Volkhov is named in the period.

pages.title: Ihalempi
pages.hint: An interpreter, not yet met
pages.brief: Ihalempi, the interpreter at Aldeigjuborg. She speaks for the trappers.
pages.game: Ihalempi is the interpreter at Aldeigjuborg, one of the Finnic peoples and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the trading bank. She speaks for the trappers. Finnic by her mother, raised at the stream-mouth fort, with Slavic and Norse enough to count in both: no skin from the woods is sold on the bank without her blanket under it. To look at: under thirty, small and straight-backed, black hair in one plait, a dark woollen dress with bronze spirals sewn along the apron hem, a knife and a bag of tally sticks at her belt, and a string of Milava's best beads.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Finnic people lived on this river before Slav or Northman, and the Lyubsha fort stands on a Finnic site; furs are bought with beads. Bronze spirals on the apron: Luistari, not checked (?). No Finnic woman of the period is named: the name is built from the old stems Iha (joy) and Lempi (love). No woman go-between is recorded (?).

pages.title: Folkbern
pages.hint: A factor, not yet met
pages.brief: Folkbern, the factor at Aldeigjuborg. A Frisian ship's boy of Wijnaldum, taken off the Danish coast and sold east for his tallying.
pages.game: Folkbern is the factor at Aldeigjuborg, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the biggest house. A Frisian ship's boy of Wijnaldum, taken off the Danish coast and sold east for his tallying. If the house bought him out, he is its own man on the Volkhov: free, baptised, fluent in three tongues, and the only person here who remembers the tide. To look at: as a man: thirty, slight, fair hair cut short, a clean grey tunic of Frisian cloth kept for the day your boat comes, a tally stick behind his ear, a small wooden cross under his shirt and a rope scar on his neck.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The boy of the silver road chain. No Frisian is known this far east in 793: he is here because he was sold, not because Frisians came. The ransom of captives as a good work: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 15, 35 (not re-read (?)). The name is Folk- + -bern.

pages.title: Ragnvald Ulfsson
pages.hint: A chief, not yet met
pages.brief: Ragnvald Ulfsson, the chief at Aldeigjuborg. A jarl of the Gauts and a cousin of King Olof of the Svear, who came east with the king's daughter Ingigerd and holds the town as her bride-gift (late).
pages.game: Ragnvald Ulfsson is the chief at Aldeigjuborg, one of the Svear and a Christian. Found at: the fort on the point. A jarl of the Gauts and a cousin of King Olof of the Svear, who came east with the king's daughter Ingigerd and holds the town as her bride-gift (late). His son Eilif is jarl after him. An old hand at standing between two kings without being crushed. To look at: sixty or near it, tall, grey hair cut to the collar and a trimmed beard, a red cloak pinned at the shoulder with a gold ring-pin, a silver cross on a chain over a coat of eastern cut, and a sword he does not take off indoors.
pages.known: A real person. Historical, but told only in Heimskringla (about 1230: late): Ragnvald Ulfsson, jarl in Västergötland, cousin of Olof of the Svear; his sons Eilif, jarl after him, and Uleb. His birth and death are not recorded, so both are 0. That he was a Christian is the saga's picture (?). Novgorod's law of 1016. No toll is known here. His lines are invented.

pages.game: Hildulf is the priest at Andoverpis, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: Saint Peter and Saint Paul. A priest alone in a small church who was schooled in a great abbey and has not forgiven the difference. To look at: thin, about forty, tonsured, a patched black-brown tunic to the ankle, ink on two fingers, a small iron key on a thong round his neck.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The church, its third of the toll, the incense and lights and the curse from the charter of 726 (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845); Alcuin's Life of Willibrord; whether Echternach still held the church in 793 is unchecked (?); 'jugi instantia Andoverpis decertavit' (Life of Eligius, Latin, our rendering); the false grain of 793.
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf

later.text: Beornrad, abbot of Echternach 775-797 and Alcuin's cousin.
Alcuin's Life of Willibrord, written for Beornrad before 797 (?).

pages.title: Liafgrim
pages.hint: A craftsman, not yet met
pages.brief: Liafgrim, the craftsman at Andoverpis. A travelling comb-maker who comes with the swallows and goes at Martinmas, and judges every man by his hair.
pages.game: Liafgrim is the craftsman at Andoverpis, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the comb-maker's lean-to. A travelling comb-maker who comes with the swallows and goes at Martinmas, and judges every man by his hair. To look at: lean, in his thirties in 793, fair hair combed flat and tied, a Frisian short cloak pinned on the right shoulder, white bone dust to the elbows, a fine saw in his fist.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The comb work and its waste from Bellens 2021 (antler workers 'perhaps travelling men'); Frisians living here are not attested after the 7th century, so he is a visitor; the short cloak from Notker I.34.
pages.source: T. Bellens, Het DNA van stadswording. De vroeg-stedelijke nederzetting van Antwerpen, late 9de-11de eeuw (2021), chapters 2.2-2.8: https://oar.onroerenderfgoed.be/publicaties/SYNT/5/SYNT005-001.pdf

pages.title: Ermentrud of Andoverpis
pages.hint: An alewife, not yet met
pages.brief: Ermentrud, an alewife at Andoverpis. Keeps the house on posts and a split stick for every man who ever drank in it.
pages.game: Ermentrud is an alewife at Andoverpis, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the house on posts. Keeps the house on posts and a split stick for every man who ever drank in it. Forgets nothing and says so kindly. To look at: a big woman past forty, grey-brown hair under a linen cloth, sleeves rolled, a wooden ladle in her belt and a bunch of tally sticks on a cord at her hip.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place.

pages.title: Ansgard
pages.hint: An alewife, not yet met
pages.brief: Ansgard, an alewife at Andoverpis. Ermentrud's granddaughter: counted the sails in the year of the fire and has counted every sail since.
pages.game: Ansgard is an alewife at Andoverpis, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the house on posts. Ermentrud's granddaughter: counted the sails in the year of the fire and has counted every sail since.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. That Rorik or Harald ruled the Scheldt is unsourced, and she does not say they do.
