pages.title: Fardulf
pages.hint: An abbot, not yet met
pages.brief: Fardulf, the abbot at Parisius. A Lombard priest who came north in a beaten king's following and rose by telling King Charles of his own son's plot: learned, watchful, grateful, and never quite at home.
pages.game: Fardulf is the abbot at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: Saint Denis's church. A Lombard priest who came north in a beaten king's following and rose by telling King Charles of his own son's plot: learned, watchful, grateful, and never quite at home. To look at: about fifty-five, lean, dark-eyed, olive-skinned, a grey tonsure, a black wool habit of good cloth, a plain abbot's staff and a small wax tablet in his sleeve.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 740. His birth year, his verses in conversation and his temper are invented (?). 'Romance' stands for a Lombard: the game has no Lombard people.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Died in 806.
Fardulf, a Lombard, abbot of Saint-Denis 793-806, given the abbey for uncovering the plot of Pippin the Hunchback; envoy with Count Stephen in 802 (MGH Capit. I no. 34).

pages.title: Stephen
pages.hint: A count, not yet met
pages.brief: Stephen, the count at Parisius. Count of Paris since before most of his men were grown: a soldier turned judge, who knows the Salic law by its fines and grudges every penny that goes north to the monks.
pages.game: Stephen is the count at Parisius, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the count's house. Count of Paris since before most of his men were grown: a soldier turned judge, who knows the Salic law by its fines and grudges every penny that goes north to the monks. To look at: near sixty, thick-necked, a long grey moustache and a shaved chin, a blue cloak pinned at the right shoulder, a sword with a worn grip, a heavy ring.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 750. The head-penny: Tardif no. 55. His birth year, looks and grudge are invented (?); the year of his death is not sure.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Stephen, count of Paris 779 to 811 or 815; envoy in 802; had the additions to Salic law read in the public court in 803 (MGH Capit. I).

pages.title: Dominicus
pages.hint: A toll man, not yet met
pages.brief: Dominicus, the toll man at Parisius. The abbey's lay toll man at the landing and the fair: a vine-dresser's son who reckons faster than the monks who check him, and enjoys it.
pages.game: Dominicus is the toll man at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: the saint's landing and the fair of Saint Denis. The abbey's lay toll man at the landing and the fair: a vine-dresser's son who reckons faster than the monks who check him, and enjoys it. To look at: about forty, small and wiry, sunburnt, black hair cut round, a short brown tunic belted high, a notched tally stick as long as his arm and a lead token of the abbey on a thong.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The abbey's toll men and the count's agents are in the charters (Tardif nos. 55, 77), none by name. The name is a Romance one of the time; the monk Natalis at Herio is another man. The cloaks' length: Charles's letter to Offa.

later.text: The cloaks' length: Charles's letter to Offa, 796.

pages.title: Waldric
pages.hint: A cellarer, not yet met
pages.brief: Waldric, a cellarer at Parisius. Cellarer of Saint Denis's: holds that every cask on the Seine is the saint's until proved otherwise, and writes everything down on strips of parchment that he then cannot find.
pages.game: Waldric is a cellarer at Parisius, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: Saint Denis's church, the hospice at the abbey gate and the fair of Saint Denis. Cellarer of Saint Denis's: holds that every cask on the Seine is the saint's until proved otherwise, and writes everything down on strips of parchment that he then cannot find. To look at: about forty-five, round-shouldered and quick, tonsured, chalk on both sleeves of his habit, a lump of chalk, a tasting cup and strips of parchment stuck in his belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The abbey sold its grain and spare wine; the saying turns Ecclesiasticus 9:10, 'a new friend is as new wine'.

pages.title: Ermentrud of Parisius
pages.hint: A host, not yet met
pages.brief: Ermentrud, the host at Parisius. A boatman's widow who has lodged the Frisians every October since she could see over the table: forgets no face, no debt and no kindness.

A boatman's widow who has lodged the Frisians every October since she could see over the table: forgets no face, no debt and no kindness. To look at: about fifty, broad, red-handed, a linen head-cloth tied behind, a dark wool gown kilted up for work, a ring of keys and a wooden cup on a cord at her waist.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Frisian and English merchants at the fair (Tardif nos. 44, 55); tenants who owe wine to Saint-Germain are the matter of Irminon's book of estates. The name is built from attested Frankish parts (Ermen- + -trud), as borne by tenants in Romance-speaking Neustria.

pages.game: Frotbald is a cellarer at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: Saint Vincent's and Saint Germain's in the meadows. Cellarer of Saint Germain's: keeper of the abbey's wine, its traders and its toll letter, who thinks the monks of Saint Denis are stallholders in habits. To look at: mid-forties, tall and stooped, tonsured, a habit patched at the elbows and in winter a sheepskin pelisse to the heels and mittens, a ring of keys and a small tasting cup.

pages.title: Hilduin
pages.hint: An abbot, not yet met
pages.brief: Hilduin, the abbot at Parisius. Abbot of Saint-Denis and a great man at the emperor's court: restless, splendid, and sure that his saint is the Athenian who heard the apostle Paul.
pages.game: Hilduin is the abbot at Parisius, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: Saint Denis's church. Abbot of Saint-Denis and a great man at the emperor's court: restless, splendid, and sure that his saint is the Athenian who heard the apostle Paul. To look at: about forty, tall, well fed, a fine dark habit under a fur-lined cloak, a gold ring, a jewelled book held shut under one arm.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 785. His birth year and death year are not sure; his words are invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: That he was the emperor's archchaplain after Hildebold of Cologne, and sided against the emperor in 830, is from memory (?).
Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis 814-841: the Greek book of 827 put into Latin; the chapel of 832; his Passion of Saint Denis, 835-840, the first to say the saint carried his head.

pages.title: Hildegaud
pages.hint: A merchant, not yet met
pages.brief: Hildegaud, the merchant at Parisius. A wine merchant of the island with his own boat, who was chased up the river by the Danes as a young man and has reckoned every year since as profit.
pages.game: Hildegaud is the merchant at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: the strand under the island wall and the house by the Little Bridge. A wine merchant of the island with his own boat, who was chased up the river by the Danes as a young man and has reckoned every year since as profit. To look at: bald early, lean, a burn scar down the left forearm, a patched green cloak, a boat-hook for a walking stick and a purse worn inside his shirt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The city's merchants with their own boats; the two hundred who found no wine (865); the penny and the ten mints of the edict of Pîtres. The name is built from attested Frankish parts (Hild- + -gaud), as borne in Romance-speaking Neustria.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: The city's merchants with their own boats, chased up the river and caught in January 861 (Annales Bertiniani 861).
The penny and the ten mints of the edict of Pîtres, 864.
The tenth of 866.

pages.title: Abbo
pages.hint: A monk, not yet met
pages.brief: Abbo, a monk at Parisius. A young monk of Saint Germain's who watched the great siege from the wall and is putting it into hard Latin verse that nobody asked him for.
pages.game: Abbo is a monk at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: the Great Bridge and Saint Vincent's and Saint Germain's in the meadows. A young monk of Saint Germain's who watched the great siege from the wall and is putting it into hard Latin verse that nobody asked him for. To look at: late twenties in the siege year, thin, tonsured, ink to the knuckles, a patched black habit with soot on one sleeve, a wax tablet always in his hand.
pages.known: A real person. His words here are invented. That Rollo was at the siege is Dudo's story.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Died in 923.

Abbo of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, about 850 to after 923, author of the Bella Parisiacae urbis: the twelve of the tower, the hawks, the flask, Sigfred's sixty pounds, the rebuke of the Franks' fine dress.
That Rollo was at the siege is Dudo's story, written about 1015 (LATER) (?).

pages.title: Robert of Parisius
pages.hint: A count, not yet met
pages.brief: Robert, the count at Parisius. Count of Paris and lay abbot of Saint Denis's, brother of the count who was made king: he fought on the wall as a young man and has been making terms ever since.
pages.game: Robert is the count at Parisius, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the count's house. Count of Paris and lay abbot of Saint Denis's, brother of the count who was made king: he fought on the wall as a young man and has been making terms ever since. To look at: in his forties, broad, a cropped greying beard, a mail shirt worn as other men wear a tunic, a red cloak, an abbot's ring on a soldier's hand.
pages.known: A real person. The Robertian counts held the abbey of Saint-Denis after Ebles. His birth year is a guess (?). The godfather story is Dudo's (LATER). His words are invented.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Robert, count of Paris 888-922, brother of Odo, in the siege of 885-886.
Died in 923.
He was made king in June 922 and killed in battle at Soissons on 15 June 923 (Flodoard, Annales 922-923).

pages.title: Aimoin
pages.hint: A monk, not yet met
pages.brief: Aimoin, a monk at Parisius. A monk of Saint Germain's who writes down what the Northmen did to his house and what the saint did to them: orderly, sharp about dates, and still angry about one Easter.
pages.game: Aimoin is a monk at Parisius, a Romance speaker and a Christian. Found at: Saint Vincent's and Saint Germain's in the meadows. A monk of Saint Germain's who writes down what the Northmen did to his house and what the saint did to them: orderly, sharp about dates, and still angry about one Easter. To look at: a grey, upright monk with a clean habit and a ruled wax tablet, a penknife on a cord, and a way of looking at a man as at a doubtful reading.
pages.known: A real person. Abbo of Saint-Germain names him as his master. His birth year is not known. The Rotomagus file's Einold names him: this is that man.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md (the research this file rests on; its section 8 lists what is not known and must not be claimed)

later.text: Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Pres, who wrote the Miracles of Saint Germain (the fleet of 845 and the flights of the saint's body) and the bringing of the martyrs George, Aurelius and Nathalia from Cordoba in 858.
Died in 889.

pages.title: Rodbjorn
pages.hint: A shipwright, not yet met
pages.brief: Rodbjorn, the shipwright at Paviken. The man the beach sends for when a plank is sprung.
pages.game: Rodbjorn is the shipwright at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the slip and the boat sheds. The man the beach sends for when a plank is sprung. Slow to answer, exact, and unable to pass a hull without knocking on it. To look at: about forty-five, broad and short-legged, a brown beard with wood chips in it, a leather apron black with tar over a grey wool shirt, an adze in his hand and a bag of rivets at his belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Name: Rod- (Rodvisl, G 134) + -björn (Hegbjörn, G 280), both on Gotland stones of a later century. His son and grandson keep the slip after him.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Hegvisl
pages.hint: A smith, not yet met
pages.brief: Hegvisl, the smith at Paviken. Bead-maker, bronze-caster and pourer of silver bars, in that order of pride.
pages.game: Hegvisl is the smith at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the walled yard and the paved ground. Bead-maker, bronze-caster and pourer of silver bars, in that order of pride. Patient with fire and short with people who hurry him. To look at: about forty, lean and stooped, a singed fair beard, burn scars on both forearms, a wool cap, a leather apron, an iron rod with a blob of red glass on its end.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Bead-makers, bronze-casters and silversmiths casting bars are shown by the finds: raw glass cubes, raw garnet, amber, ingots, a mould for silver bars. Name: Heg- (Hegbjörn, G 280) + -visl (Rodvisl, G 134). His heirs keep the hearth.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Botbjorn
pages.hint: A skipper, not yet met
pages.brief: Botbjorn, the skipper at Paviken. A farmer with forty sheep who is at sea from the going of the ice to the first frost.
pages.game: Botbjorn is the skipper at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the dragging beach, the weighing shore and the timber quays at the outlet. A farmer with forty sheep who is at sea from the going of the ice to the first frost. Easy, lucky, and closed like a chest about what he owns. To look at: about thirty-five, long and loose-limbed, sun-bleached hair tied back, a short fair beard, a sea-stained blue cloak with a ring pin, a silver arm ring pushed high under the sleeve, a round bronze scale case at his belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Name: Bot- (Botair, Guta saga) + -björn. His son keeps the boat after him.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: His son keeps the boat after him, and his son's sons are met at the outlet quays after 1008.

pages.title: Rodiaud
pages.hint: A host, not yet met
pages.brief: Rodiaud, the host at Paviken. The widow whose farm owns the beach. She takes the landing gift, says where a stranger sleeps, and answers for him while he sleeps there.
pages.game: Rodiaud is the host at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the dragging beach, the weighing shore and the stone-walled house. The widow whose farm owns the beach. She takes the landing gift, says where a stranger sleeps, and answers for him while he sleeps there. To look at: about fifty, straight-backed, grey hair under a linen cloth, a brown strap dress held by two round box brooches with strings of glass and amber beads between them, keys and a small knife at her belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. No ruler, reeve or toll is recorded for the harbour; on Gotland a stranger pays 'the farmer whose beach it is, and nobody else' and needs a host who answers for him. Wergild of ten and twenty-four marks from the Guta Lag (about 1220, late). The sinking island from the Guta saga (late). Women run farms and hold silver. Name: Rodiaud, on a Gotland stone, G 111 (?). Her farm's daughters keep the shore after her.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Likbjorn
pages.hint: A rune carver, not yet met
pages.brief: Likbjorn, the rune carver at Paviken. Cuts and paints the tall stones for the dead.
pages.game: Likbjorn is the rune carver at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the ring of stones and the southern graves. Cuts and paints the tall stones for the dead. Has thought about death longer than most men and finds it mainly a matter of measurement. To look at: about fifty-five, thin and grey, stone dust in his beard and brows, a patched undyed tunic, knees wrapped in sheepskin, a wooden mallet and a pointed iron, red ochre under his nails.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. No picture stone is recorded from Paviken itself; stones stand in neighbouring parishes (?). Name: Lik- (Liknat, G 113) + -björn. A carver works this slope in every generation.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Hailgair
pages.hint: A lawman, not yet met
pages.brief: Hailgair, the lawman at Paviken. A farmer of the west shore who says the law at the ring of stones when the farms meet: he has it by heart, and says it at one speed whoever is listening.
pages.game: Hailgair is the lawman at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the ring of stones. A farmer of the west shore who says the law at the ring of stones when the farms meet: he has it by heart, and says it at one speed whoever is listening. To look at: near fifty in 793, broad and weathered, a grey beard cut square, a brown wool cloak pinned at the shoulder with a plain bronze ring-pin, a farmer's hands, and a staff he does not lean on.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. No ruler, reeve or toll is recorded for the harbour; the Gotlanders' own law and thing, a stranger's lower price and the host who answers for a guest are from the Guta law as written down about 1220, here as custom. That the island paid the Svear king a yearly tax for peace is the Guta saga's tale of a later agreement (?): in 793 he can still say 'nothing yet'. Name: Hail- + -gair, both on Gotland rune stones (?). A farmer says the law at the ring in every generation.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

pages.title: Vivil
pages.hint: A farmer, not yet met
pages.brief: Vivil, the farmer at Paviken. The elder brother who holds the farm Aikgard.
pages.game: Vivil is the farmer at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: Aikgard, half a morning inland. The elder brother who holds the farm Aikgard. Careful to the point of pain: he has not sold a sheep he could keep in twenty years. To look at: about fifty, heavy, a grey-brown beard, a farmer's undyed tunic and a good belt, earth on both knees, a spade never far from the door post.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. He is alive in whatever year the chain is played, so no birth year is given. Name: Vivil, on the Pilgårds stone, G 280 (later). Inheritance custom from the Guta Lag (about 1220, late), used for colour only (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: He is alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949), so no birth year is given.

pages.title: Ailikn
pages.hint: A widow, not yet met
pages.brief: Ailikn, the widow at Paviken. The dead east-farer's only child: widowed two winters, one small boy, living with her mother's people under three ash trees near the shore.
pages.game: Ailikn is the widow at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: Aikgard, half a morning inland. The dead east-farer's only child: widowed two winters, one small boy, living with her mother's people under three ash trees near the shore. She asks her uncle for nothing. To look at: about twenty-six, spare and upright, fair hair under a widow's cloth, a grey strap dress with plain bronze brooches, a tally stick and a small knife at her belt, a boy of four holding her skirt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. She is alive in whatever year the chain is played. A woman with silver of her own is true to the time: Frideburg and Catla of Birka (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20, tr. Robinson 1921); women who raise stones and hold farms. Name: Ailikn, on a Gotland stone, G 114 (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: She is alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949).

pages.title: Ottar
pages.hint: A steersman, not yet met
pages.brief: Ottar, the steersman at Paviken. A young man of the Aikgard kin who has steered other men's boats east four summers and wants one of his own.
pages.game: Ottar is the steersman at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the gravel-floored shelter. A young man of the Aikgard kin who has steered other men's boats east four summers and wants one of his own. Open-faced, for a Gotlander. To look at: about twenty-four, tall, wind-reddened, a short fair beard, a salt-stained wool tunic and sealskin shoes, a steering thong wound round one wrist, hands harder than his years.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. That he is of the Aikgard kin and nephew to the dead Hegbjorn follows the chain's words; how near he stands to Vivil the chain does not say (?). Alive in whatever year the chain is played. Name: Ottar, on a Gotland stone, G 113 (later). Partnership in one purse, the félag, is on rune stones of the 11th century and is used earlier here as the chain does (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: Alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949).

pages.title: Liknat
pages.hint: A skald, not yet met
pages.brief: Liknat, the skald at Paviken. The Gotlanders' skald, such as a people of farmers keeps: he works his own land by day, and each evening asks one question of whoever sits in the shelter above the beach.
pages.game: Liknat is the skald at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the gravel-floored shelter. The Gotlanders' skald, such as a people of farmers keeps: he works his own land by day, and each evening asks one question of whoever sits in the shelter above the beach.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The Spillings silver (youngest coin 870/871) is the hoard every Gotlander 'knows' of; nobody on the beach says whose farm. Name: Liknat, on the Gotland rune stone G 113. A skald asks his evening question in the shelter in every later generation.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: An old man by 890, lean and brown, white hair tied back, a farmer's undyed tunic with a good blue cloak over it, a rune-cut stick dark with tar on one side laid across his knees.

pages.title: Gairvid
pages.hint: A shipwright, not yet met
pages.brief: Gairvid, the shipwright at Paviken. The wright at the old slip two lifetimes after Rodbjorn, and of his line: he builds the broad Gotland boat as it was always built, and distrusts whatever was not under a keel when he was a boy.
pages.game: Gairvid is the shipwright at Paviken, a Gotlander and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the slip and the boat sheds. The wright at the old slip two lifetimes after Rodbjorn, and of his line: he builds the broad Gotland boat as it was always built, and distrusts whatever was not under a keel when he was a boy. To look at: broad and stooped, forearms scarred with old pitch burns, a leather apron, wood shavings in a grey beard, an adze with a haft worn to the shape of his hand.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Boat-menders are shown by the rivets and nails all over the working ground. Name: Gair- + -vid, both on Gotland rune stones (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md (the research this file is built on; its keys are given in full below)

later.text: Boat-menders are shown by the rivets and nails all over the working ground, and the working of the shore went on into the 900s.

pages.title: Gervold
pages.hint: An abbot, not yet met
pages.brief: Gervold, the abbot at Quentovic. A king's officer more than a monk: the procurator who takes the tolls of the Channel ports, King Offa's friend, by his own monks' account no great scholar, a fine singer and a builder.
pages.game: Gervold is the abbot at Quentovic, a Frank and a Christian. Gervold is abbot of Saint-Wandrille; the king's procurator, who takes the tolls at Quentovic. Found at: the procurator's toll house. A king's officer more than a monk: the procurator who takes the tolls of the Channel ports, King Offa's friend, by his own monks' account no great scholar, a fine singer and a builder. To look at: about fifty-five, portly, tonsured, a fine dark cowl with a silver cross, an abbot's staff carried by a boy, a seal on a cord and a clerk with tablets at his elbow. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 738. Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16 (c. 12 in later editions). His seat is the abbey, not the port: he is here on his rounds. His birth year is a guess (?). Abbot from 787 or 788.
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md (the sourced research this file is built on; its keys are given in full there)

later.text: 29 July 796: Offa dies. The temper turns to grieving.
797: the tolls go on. The temper turns to steady.
Died in 806.

Ed. Loewenfeld 1886: chaplain to Queen Bertrada, bishop of Evreux, abbot 787-806, procurator 'chiefly in Quentawich', envoy to Offa, 'not much learned in other letters' but a fine singer, roofed two churches with lead.
Died 806 or 807.

pages.title: Hildric
pages.hint: A clerk, not yet met
pages.brief: Hildric, the clerk at Quentovic. Keeps two tallies, one on wax for the king and one in his head for the abbot, and has never yet confused them.
pages.game: Hildric is the clerk at Quentovic, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the procurator's toll house. pages.game: Wulfgifu is the host at Quentovic, one of the English and a Christian. Found at: Wulfgifu's house. A Kentish woman, widow of a Frankish wine man, who answers to the toll for every guest under her roof and so makes it her business to know them. To look at: near forty, tall, a linen head-cloth, a blue wool gown pinned at the throat with one small round silver brooch, a bunch of keys and a little knife on her girdle, a ladle in her hand.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. English merchants lived at the wic. Wulf- and -gifu are English name parts. The host who answers for a guest kept three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric (wording to check (?)). Women trading in their own names are not attested among the Franks: she keeps a house, not a ship.

pages.title: Osmund

pages.brief: Osmund, the guest master at Quentovic. A Northumbrian monk who keeps Alcuin's hospice: patient with the poor, short with the proud, and homesick for a library he last saw at York.
pages.game: Osmund is the guest master at Quentovic, one of the English and a Christian. Found at: the cell of Saint Josse. A Northumbrian monk who keeps Alcuin's hospice: patient with the poor, short with the proud, and homesick for a library he last saw at York. To look at: nearing fifty, broad and stooped, tonsured, a patched black habit kilted up for work, a wooden ladle and a ring of two keys at his cord, bare red feet in sandals.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The monk in charge of guests at the cella sancti Iudoci, which the king gave Alcuin 'to give alms to pilgrims' (Lupus, letter 11) and which cared for 'those from over the sea and other poor' (letter 71). Os- and -mund are English name parts. The porter's 'Thanks be to God' is the Rule of St Benedict c. 66.

pages.title: Grippo
pages.hint: A harbour master, not yet met
pages.brief: Grippo, the harbour master at Quentovic. The prefect of the emporium under King Charles the Bald, an illustrious man and the king's envoy to the kings of the English: a hard officer who made a vow in a storm and kept it.
pages.game: Grippo is the harbour master at Quentovic, a Frank and a Christian. Found at: the procurator's toll house. The prefect of the emporium under King Charles the Bald, an illustrious man and the king's envoy to the kings of the English: a hard officer who made a vow in a storm and kept it. To look at: about fifty, grey and weathered, a long moustache, a red cloak with a gilt brooch over a mail-less leather coat, a sword in a tooled sheath and a small silver cross worn outside his shirt.
pages.known: A real person. Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 15 (MGH SS XV.1): Grippo, 'prefect of the emporium of Quentovic', illuster vir, Charles the Bald's envoy 'to the kings of the English'; the storm near dawn, the lighthouse on the shore 'built of old by the skill of the ancients' (Boulogne's, by inference), his prayer and the gifts paid on Christmas Eve. The arms law is the edict of Pitres. His looks and his temper are invented.

later.text: Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 15 (MGH SS XV.1): Grippo, 'prefect of the emporium of Quentovic', illuster vir, Charles the Bald's envoy 'to the kings of the English', 858 or soon after.
His years in office beyond 858 are a guess (?).

pages.title: Liuba
pages.hint: An interpreter, not yet met
pages.brief: Liuba, the interpreter at Reric. Dragomir's sister, taken by Danes as a girl and bought back at fifteen with four tongues in her head: quick, unsentimental, and the one person in the town who hears everything twice.
pages.game: Liuba is the interpreter at Reric, a Wend and one who keeps the gods of the Wends. Found at: Dragomir's table. Dragomir's sister, taken by Danes as a girl and bought back at fifteen with four tongues in her head: quick, unsentimental, and the one person in the town who hears everything twice. To look at: about thirty, thin, dark brows, a linen headcloth with two bronze rings at each temple, a grey wool dress girdled high, a small knife and a bunch of tally sticks at her belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Slav captives among the Danes: Rimbert c. 15. No source shows a Wendish woman merchant, so she is an interpreter in her brother's house. Temple rings are from later Slavic graves (?). The Slavic words are plain common Slavic, not attested for the Obodrites (?). Name: Liub-, a short name.
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.game: Skardi is the toll man at Reric, a Dane and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the king's awning. The Danish king's man at the shore: patient, exact, alone among people who wish him elsewhere, and too proud to show that he minds. To look at: past forty, lean, a notch out of his upper lip, fair hair tied back, a blue cloak with a ring pin worn thin, a folding bronze scale in a leather bag round his neck.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The toll-taker implied by the dues of ARF 808. Who was king of the Danes in 793 is Sigfred (?). Name: Skardi, 'notched', a Danish byname used as a name.
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

later.text: Who was king of the Danes in 793 is Sigfred (?) (named 777 to 798).
Godfred first in 804.

pages.title: Thrasco
pages.hint: A chief, not yet met
pages.brief: Thrasco, the chief at Reric. The emperor's friend among the heathen, and proud of it: a fighter who keeps his word to the Franks and his own gods at home.
pages.game: Thrasco is the chief at Reric, a Wend and one who keeps the gods of the Wends. Thrasco is prince of the Abodrites. Found at: the riders' field. The emperor's friend among the heathen, and proud of it: a fighter who keeps his word to the Franks and his own gods at home. To look at: about forty, broad, dark hair cut round and a long moustache, a fur-lined cloak, a Frankish sword on a belt set with silver, guards with round shields and spears behind him. Temper at the start: vengeful. That is: acts against one person or people beyond reason; resists Nerve one step less (a firm word turns them), and remembers.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 760. The annals put him at Reric only at his death; his other visits, his birth year, the sister's son and the sword from the emperor are the game's (?). The saying on horses after Herbord II.23 (later).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

later.text: His predecessor Witzan was killed by Saxons in 795.
798: he beats the Saxons beyond the Elbe at Bornhoved. The temper turns to exalted.
Died in 809.
About 795 to 809.

pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The Scandinavians who lived and died here, shown by boat graves with rivets at the grave field. The bone hammer is a small amulet of the later kind (?).
pages.source: Annales regni Francorum 789, 795, 798, 804, 808, 809, 810 (Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/annalesregnifrancorum.html); renderings ours.

pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. He is the 'ploughman of Thanet' who gives Exeter riddle 21; his riddle is ours, on that riddle's lines, not a quotation. The finds are the kinds Brent dug from graves nobody had ploughed: a bronze balance with weights made of Roman coins ground down (grave 26), gaming counters, a fossil sea-urchin (grave 4). The 'thunder stone' name for the urchin is later English folk speech (?).

To look at: in his forties, tall, long fair hair combed back, a red cloak with a great gilt pin, gold arm rings, a sword with a silvered hilt; always among armed men, horses and ships. Temper at the start: exalted. That is: over-reaches; resists Lore one step less (flattered by learning) and Nerve one step more.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 762. His birth year is a guess (?). The boast about Frisia, Saxony and the emperor's own hall is Einhard, Life of Charles 14 (tr. Grant 1907), not opened tonight (?). The spokesman and all the words are invented. Why that temper: Einhard's reading of him

pages.game: Horik the younger is a king at Sliesthorp, a Dane and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the king's field. pages.known: A real person. Real: Horik the younger. Hovi, count of the port, shut the church; the king put him out, asked the priest back, allowed a bell, and gave a plot for a church at Ripa, Burghard speaking for the bishop (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 31-32, tr. Robinson 1921). His age, his looks and every word are invented (?).
pages.source: Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md (the research this file is built on; its (?) marks are kept)

later.text: A boy made king after the kinsmen's war of 854: first led by the men who shut the church, then his own master, who put the count out, opened the door and allowed a bell.
Real: Horik the younger, made king in 854 after Horik and almost all the royal kin were killed.
Pope Nicholas I wrote to him in 864, after which he is not heard of.

A king's distant kinswoman who rules monks and nuns alike without raising her voice; practical, a good hand with a wound, and slow to be frightened. To look at: about fifty, tall, spare, a weathered face; a dark wool gown and a white linen veil pinned with two plain bronze pins; a ring of keys at her girdle and a small knife for lancing.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. No abbess is named after Aelfflaed's death in 714. Aelfflaed's surgery: en.wikipedia. Hild's rule 'that no one there was rich and none poor': Bede IV.23 (memory). Edwin's body here and head at York: Victoria County History. Name: Ead- + -swith.

Jet 'being warmed with rubbing holds fast whatever is applied to it, like amber', and smells of coal on the fire: Bede I.1; en.wikipedia Jet. The house 'abandoned at some point in the 9th century; we do not know exactly when or how': English Heritage. His line about nobody burning it is one reading, not a fact. Name: Here- + -mod.

His saying turns Havamal 36 ('better a house, though a hut it be', Bellows 1923) into our own words. Name: Ketil, a common Norse name.

pages.title: Hamacar
pages.hint: A bishop, not yet met
pages.brief: Hamacar, the bishop at Traiectum. Keeper of Willibrord's house and its school: careful, formal, more a steward of lands than a preacher.
pages.game: Hamacar is the bishop at Traiectum, a Frank and a Christian. Hamacar is bishop of Traiectum. Found at: Saint Martin's and the bishop's hall. Keeper of Willibrord's house and its school: careful, formal, more a steward of lands than a preacher. To look at: about fifty, tonsured, a white linen alb under a dark wool cloak, a bishop's ring and a plain staff with a curled head, a deacon with a book beside him. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 743. Nl.wikipedia 'Lijst van bisschoppen van Utrecht': Hamacarus. The man is real; nothing else is known of him, and his character, his age and his words are invented. The temper is the game's own reading.

pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The crossing gives the place its name, and the widened logboat is built on this river from about 734. Alcuin has a boat towed up 'prelongo remulco'.

En.wikipedia 'Balderic of Utrecht': bishop 918-975, brought the see home about 920, rebuilt churches, school and walls, taught Bruno, received the mint and Muiden's toll in 953, brought the relics of Agnes, Pontian and Odulf.

pages.title: Hunger
pages.hint: A bishop, not yet met
pages.brief: Hunger, the bishop at Traiectum. The last bishop to sit at Traiectum before the Northmen: plain, stubborn, not made for courts, and unlucky in his years.

pages.known: A real person. Called a Frisian and described as ill-favoured by later tradition (?). His words, his dealings with Rorik's toll man and the list are invented.

later.text: Died in 866.

Historical: Hunger, bishop of Utrecht 854-866, fled in 857 when Northmen wasted Utrecht while Rorik was in Denmark; Lothar II gave him the monastery of Berg (Sint Odiliënberg) in 858; he died at Prüm on 22 December 866.

pages.title: Ketil of Truso
pages.hint: A host, not yet met
pages.brief: Ketil, the host at Truso. A Dane who has kept a house and a pair of scales on this shore for half his life: he weighs for both sides and never says what is in the pan.
pages.game: Ketil is the host at Truso, a Dane and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the weighing ground and the Dane's long house. A Dane who has kept a house and a pair of scales on this shore for half his life: he weighs for both sides and never says what is in the pan. To look at: about forty-five in 793, broad, grey in a plaited beard, a blue cloak pinned at the shoulder, folding scales in a round bronze case at his belt and a bag of weights that clinks when he sits.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Scandinavians are plain in the finds and are credited with founding the place. Name: Ketil, common on Danish rune stones.

pages.title: Gedune
pages.hint: A chief, not yet met
pages.brief: Gedune, the chief at Truso. The dead king's brother and then king of the fort: a horseman who has never been in a boat and judges men by what they do with a bowl.
pages.game: Gedune is the chief at Truso, a Prussian or a Curonian and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the fort on the rise. The dead king's brother and then king of the fort: a horseman who has never been in a boat and judges men by what they do with a bowl. To look at: about thirty-five in 793, lean, long fair hair, clean chin and a heavy moustache, a neck ring of twisted bronze, a belted wool tunic, riding whip in his hand even on foot.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. A king in each stronghold, much fighting among them, mares' milk for the king and the richest, fast horses dear (Wulfstan, Old English Orosius). The name is built in the manner of Old Prussian names recorded centuries later (?); no person of Truso is named in any source.

pages.title: Drua
pages.hint: A wise woman, not yet met
pages.brief: Drua, the wise woman at Truso. An old woman of the kin that can make cold: sent for when a great man dies, feared a little, and bored by being asked how.
pages.game: Drua is the wise woman at Truso, a Prussian or a Curonian and one who keeps the old gods. Found at: the fort on the rise and the wood nobody cuts. An old woman of the kin that can make cold: sent for when a great man dies, feared a little, and bored by being asked how. To look at: past sixty, small and upright, a grey wool shawl over her head pinned with a bronze spiral, hands red and cracked from cold water, a covered clay pot always within reach.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Wulfstan: one kin among the Este can make cold, so that the dead lie long and do not rot; set down two vessels of ale or water and they freeze one over, summer or winter (Old English Orosius, Sweet 1883; our rendering). How is not known; winter ice kept in a pit is the modern guess (?).

To look at: thirty-three, broad and short, burned forearms, singed brown beard, a leather apron black with scale; tongs in one hand and a rove threaded on his little finger like a ring.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. A resident smith (Paleo-aktueel 4), the clench nails and roves and the reading that old ship timber was burnt (Aalders et al. 2004), iron bars of Scandinavian kinds, the 7th-century gold foil die (Bos and Nijboer 1997). Name: Bern- + -rad.

pages.game: Gerbrand is the craftsman at Winaldum, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the bead bench. pages.title: Wilsuit
pages.hint: An alewife, not yet met
pages.brief: Wilsuit, the alewife at Witla. Gerlef's daughter: brews, lodges skippers waiting on a wind, and keeps in her head what each of them owes and what each of them said when he had drunk.
pages.game: Wilsuit is the alewife at Witla, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: Wilsuit's ale-house. Gerlef's daughter: brews, lodges skippers waiting on a wind, and keeps in her head what each of them owes and what each of them said when he had drunk. To look at: about thirty in 793, strong forearms, a linen head-cloth pinned with one bronze pin, a grey gown kilted up out of the wet, a dipper in her hand and a ring of tally sticks on a cord.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. Wil- as in Willibraht, -suit as in Meinsuit (Altfrid I.25). Her saying turns the Exeter gnomic verse on the Frisian wife (Thorpe 1842). Sunday work is fined four shillings in the Frisians' law (Lex Frisionum XVIII).

pages.title: Folcrad
pages.hint: A toll man, not yet met
pages.brief: Folcrad, the toll man at Witla. The king's toll man at the post: slow, exact, impossible to hurry and hard to dislike; takes the tenth and not a penny more, and expects to be thanked for it.
pages.game: Folcrad is the toll man at Witla, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the king's post. The king's toll man at the post: slow, exact, impossible to hurry and hard to dislike; takes the tenth and not a penny more, and expects to be thanked for it. To look at: about forty-five, broad and slow, a grey short cloak with a plain iron pin, a bundle of notched tally sticks at his belt and a small pair of scales he polishes when he thinks.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. A toll-taker at the Maas mouth is likely and not proven (Dijkstra 2011, p. 324) (?). Folc- and -rad are both attested Frisian name parts. The cloak joke is Notker I.34 (Grant 1907); 4:2:1 is Dijkstra 2011, p. 359; the blocked public way is Lex Frisionum, Additio VI.

pages.brief: Bernrad, the priest at Witla. The priest of the church across the water, Saint Willibrord's gift to his abbey: rows over on feast days to say Mass at the cross, bury the dead and count who came.
pages.game: Bernrad is the priest at Witla, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the cross on the ridge. The priest of the church across the water, Saint Willibrord's gift to his abbey: rows over on feast days to say Mass at the cross, bury the dead and count who came. To look at: nearly forty, thin, tonsured, a brown wool tunic patched at the elbows, bare muddy legs, a small book in a sealskin bag hung round his neck and an oar over his shoulder.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. No priest of the Maas-mouth church is named. The church and its gift to Echternach, Saint Martin's tithe, and Harg ('heathen shrine') in the fen behind Vlaardingen are Dijkstra 2011, pp. 281-288, 301. Alcuin's poem down the Rhine (Carmina IV) is paraphrased, not quoted. The Sunday fine is Lex Frisionum XVIII.

pages.hint: A weaver, not yet met
pages.brief: Thiadlint, the weaver at Witla. One of the four serfs of Saint Peter's farm: keeps the five cows and weaves the best cloth on the strand, a bolt of which goes to Ghent each year whether there is bread or not.
pages.game: Thiadlint is the weaver at Witla, a Frisian and a Christian. Found at: the strand market and Saint Peter's farm. One of the four serfs of Saint Peter's farm: keeps the five cows and weaves the best cloth on the strand, a bolt of which goes to Ghent each year whether there is bread or not. To look at: a little over thirty, small and straight-backed, hair under a plain grey cloth, a gown of her own good weave with no brooch to it, fingers dyed blue to the first joint, a weaving sword of whalebone in her belt.
pages.known: Not in the record: the game's own person, set in a real place. The farm with grazing for five cows and four serfs is real (Dijkstra 2011, p. 175); its people are not named. Thiad- and -lint (as in Folclint) are attested.

pages.title: Charles
pages.hint: King of the Franks and Lombards
pages.brief: Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards. Tall, loud and cheerful; talks more than a king should; plain Frankish dress; loves strangers, swimming, roast meat and learning; cannot bear a fast or a doctor.
pages.game: Charles is king of the Franks and Lombards. Tall, loud and cheerful; talks more than a king should; plain Frankish dress; loves strangers, swimming, roast meat and learning; cannot bear a fast or a doctor. The seat nearest you is Noviomagus: no fixed seat; the palace above the Waal at Noviomagus is the nearest to the twelve. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: hardened. That is: acts sooner and harsher than the record; resists Tongue and Name one step more.
pages.known: A real person. Born 748 (?); king 768. Why that temper: 792 and 793 are his worst years: his eldest son's plot, famine, the Saxons and Frisians risen, a count's host wiped out by the Weser, the canal lost to rain.
pages.source: Einhard, Vita Karoli c. 18-25; ARF 792-814; chronicle_793.json

later.text: 10 August 794: queen Fastrada dies. The temper turns to grieving.
Winters at Aachen from 794.
795: the Avars beaten and their treasure brought home. The temper turns to steady.
4 June 800: queen Liutgard dies; he does not marry again. The temper turns to grieving.
Emperor from 25 December 800.
25 December 800: crowned emperor. The temper turns to exalted.
19 May 804: Alcuin dies. The temper turns to grieving.
Died 28 January 814.

pages.title: Charles the Younger
pages.hint: The king's eldest son by Hildegard

pages.game: Charles the Younger is the king's eldest son by Hildegard; leads the hosts in Saxony and against the Slavs. His father's right hand in war. It was for him that a daughter of Offa was asked, about 789, and from Offa's answer that the ports were shut. You know this person only by word. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person. Born about 772.
pages.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12; ARF 794, 799, 805, 806, 811

later.text: Anointed king on Christmas Day 800.
Died 4 December 811.

pages.title: Angilbert

pages.game: Angilbert is abbot of Saint-Riquier (Centula). The court's 'Homer': a poet, a builder with three hundred monks under new roofs, and father of two sons by the king's daughter Bertha. The seat nearest you is Quentovic: Saint-Riquier is a day's ride south of Quentovic, which is its port. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: exalted. That is: over-reaches; resists Lore one step less (flattered by learning) and Nerve one step more.
pages.known: A real person. Abbot from about 790. Why that temper: he is rebuilding his abbey on a scale no one north of the Alps has seen.
pages.source: Nithard, Historiae IV.5; ARF 792, 796, 800; Hariulf, Chronicon Centulense (11th century: LATER) (?)

pages.title: Offa
pages.hint: King of the Mercians, and lord of every kingdom south of the Humber
pages.brief: Offa, king of the Mercians, and lord of every kingdom south of the Humber.
pages.game: Offa is king of the Mercians, and lord of every kingdom south of the Humber. Forty years a king. A reformer of coin and a giver to churches, who answers a slight from the greatest king in the west by shutting his ports. The seat nearest you is Lundenwic: his hall is at Tamworth; Lundenwic is his port, and his councils sit at Chelsea, two miles up the river. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: hardened. That is: acts sooner and harsher than the record; resists Tongue and Name one step more.
pages.known: A real person. King 757. Why that temper: he is old and has one son. Alcuin wrote afterwards of the blood the father shed to make the kingdom safe for him.
pages.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A) 755, 792, 794; Alcuin, letters 100, 122; Design/content/realms/england_south.json

later.text: Died 29 July 796.

pages.title: Cynethryth
pages.hint: Queen of the Mercians
pages.brief: Cynethryth, queen of the Mercians. The only English queen with her face on a penny.
pages.game: Cynethryth is queen of the Mercians. The only English queen with her face on a penny. Alcuin calls her the steward of the king's house and tells her son to learn mercy from her. The tale that she plotted king Aethelberht's death is of the 12th century. The seat nearest you is Lundenwic: with the court; pennies were struck in her name at Canterbury by the moneyer Eoba. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person. Queen by 770.
pages.source: her pennies; Alcuin, letters 61, 62 (?); the record of the synod of Clofesho, 798 (S 1258)

later.text: 29 July 796: Offa dies. The temper turns to grieving.
17 December 796: her son dies after 141 days. The temper turns to broken.
After 796 abbess of Cookham on the Thames.
798: she keeps Cookham by a bargain with the archbishop. The temper turns to steady.
Alive in 798.

In 804 she asks for, and gets, a plot inside the walls of Canterbury as a refuge for her women: she can see what is coming by sea.

pages.title: Beorhtric

pages.brief: Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, Offa's son-in-law. A king by Offa's leave.
pages.game: Beorhtric is king of the West Saxons, Offa's son-in-law. A king by Offa's leave. It was to his reeve that the first three ships of Northmen came, and killed him. The seat nearest you is Hamwic: Winchester. This person sits in a port beyond the twelve. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person.
pages.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A) 784, 787, 800; Asser c. 14

later.text: 29 July 796: his protector dies and the exile over the sea is still alive. The temper turns to hardened.

pages.title: Eadburh
pages.hint: Daughter of Offa
pages.brief: Eadburh, daughter of Offa. As her enemies told it ninety years on: her father's daughter, used to ruling, quick to hate.
pages.game: Eadburh is daughter of Offa; queen of the West Saxons from 789. As her enemies told it ninety years on: her father's daughter, used to ruling, quick to hate. The seat nearest you is Hamwic: Winchester. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person.
pages.source: Asser c. 13-15 (893: LATER); Historia regum 802

later.text: 29 July 796: her father dies. The temper turns to hardened.
802: her husband dies and she runs. The temper turns to broken.
At Quentovic once, in 802, by the game's guess.
Fled 802.

pages.title: Ecgberht
pages.hint: An exile of the West Saxon royal kin
pages.brief: Ecgberht, an exile of the West Saxon royal kin. Years on another king's bread.
pages.game: Ecgberht is an exile of the West Saxon royal kin. Years on another king's bread. Patient, unforgiving, exact about debts. The seat nearest you is Quentovic: in Francia, by the king's leave; where is not recorded (?). You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: vengeful. That is: acts against one person or people beyond reason; resists Nerve one step less (a firm word turns them), and remembers.
pages.known: A real person. Why that temper: driven out by Offa and Beorhtric
pages.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A) 800, 836

later.text: 802: he has his kingdom. The temper turns to steady.
King of the West Saxons from 802.
King 802.
Died 839.

pages.title: Heathoberht
pages.hint: Bishop of London
pages.brief: Heathoberht, bishop of London. Only the name and the death are real. Here: a tired man with a burned town.
pages.game: Heathoberht is bishop of London. Only the name and the death are real. Here: a tired man with a burned town. The seat nearest you is Lundenwic: Saint Paul's in the old walled city. You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person. The temper is the game's own reading.
pages.source: Historia regum 801. His predecessor Eadbald 'left the land' in 796 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (D, E) 794).

later.text: 798: the fire. The temper turns to grieving.
Bishop by about 798 (?).
Died 801.

pages.title: Sigfred
pages.hint: King of the Danes
pages.brief: Sigfred, king of the Danes. Sheltered the Saxon leader Widukind, and sent envoys to Charles all the same.
pages.game: Sigfred is king of the Danes. Sheltered the Saxon leader Widukind, and sent envoys to Charles all the same. A king who keeps both doors open. The seat nearest you is Ripa: where he sat is not known; his men are at Ripa in the market weeks, by the game's guess (?). You may meet this person in one of the twelve ports. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person.
pages.source: ARF 777, 782, 798; Design/content/realms/denmark.json

later.text: Named in 777, 782 and 798.

pages.title: Leo III
pages.hint: Pope
pages.brief: Leo III, pope.
pages.game: Leo III is pope. You know this person only by word. Temper at the start: steady. That is: acts as the record says.
pages.known: A real person.
pages.source: ARF 799, 800, 801; Liber pontificalis

later.text: 25 April 799: attacked in the Greater Litany procession. The temper turns to broken.
Set upon in the street by his predecessor's kin in 799, and carried back to Rome by Frankish spears.
25 December 800: he crowns an emperor. The temper turns to exalted.
December 795 to 816.

pages.title: Wheat
pages.hint: A good not yet seen: food
pages.brief: Wheat is counted among food. One unit is a sack (about a modius and a half), of 60 kg. Bread corn of the Frankish heartland.
pages.game: Wheat is counted among food. One unit is a sack (about a modius and a half), of 60 kg. Where it is neither made nor wanted, a unit is worth about 6 pennies. This good keeps about a year. Where it is made: Neustria, the Rhineland, Southern England and Flanders and the Scheldt; ports there: Quentovic, Lundenwic, Serræ and Fordwic. Where it is wanted: Frisia, Western Norway, Vestfold and the Vik and the Svear; ports there: Medemelacha, Doccinga, Winaldum and Emuthon. Cheapest after the harvest (Aug-Oct); dear before it, dearest in a hungry spring. This is one of the foods the crew eat aboard.

pages.source: Capitulary of Frankfurt (794), c. 4: the public prices of oats, barley, rye and wheat, and of bread.; Verhulst, A. (2002). The Carolingian Economy. Cambridge UP.

later.text: In 794 the king fixed the public price of a modius at 4 pennies.

pages.title: Gislinge boat
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A small open clinker boat with six oars and one square sail, worked by four men.
pages.game: A small open clinker boat with six oars and one square sail, worked by four men. She carries about two thirds of a ton: wine by the cask, querns by the pair. She is the start: the one hull that goes everywhere a little, up a creek, over the flats and along the coast. She can go on the rivers, the tidal flats and the coast; on the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 600 pennies and takes 45 days to build, at Dorestat, Traiectum, Medemelacha, Daventre, Ripa or Winaldum. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 4.
pages.known: What she was called then: batr; a six-oar boat, ON sexaeringr (?) (the Norse names are attested only later, LATER). Viking Ship Museum, the Gislinge boat: built about 1130, 7.7 m; the replica Langoe 7.7 x 1.64 x 0.25 m, sail 10 m2, six oars, two to four men, put at 6 kn under sail. For 793 the same kind of boat is vouched for by the Kvalsund boat (9.5 m, 780-800) and by iron rivets in the Frisian terps, 400-800. Not certain: LATER: built about 1130, a stand-in for the working boats of 793; Mast and sail reconstructed: none survived (?); Cargo: the museum tonne is four men and ten sheep, so it counts the men; 660 kg beside four men is the project figure.
pages.source: ships.md 4.3, 5.1, 7.2, 8.2; ship_classes_793.json gislinge; price as CHAINS.md (bare boat 300 to 450 d (D), 600 d with her gear)

pages.title: Small working boat
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A four-oar boat of the creeks and harbours, for two men. On her own she fishes and ferries; towed behind a ship she is the boat that lands the goods.
pages.game: A four-oar boat of the creeks and harbours, for two men. On her own she fishes and ferries; towed behind a ship she is the boat that lands the goods. As a fitting she lets a deep ship unload where there is no jetty, which a knarr or the great ship cannot do without her. She can go on the rivers and the tidal flats; on the coast only with care; never on the open sea. New, with her gear, she costs 150 pennies and takes 30 days to build, at Dorestat, Traiectum, Medemelacha, Witla, Walichrum or Lundenwic. She needs 1 man at the least and is meant for 2.
pages.known: What she was called then: OE bat; Latin navicula (?). Clench nails and boat timbers from Dover-Buckland, Caister-on-Sea and Barton-upon-Humber, 7th-9th c. The London toll of about 1000: a small boat a halfpenny, a larger one with a sail a penny. LATER stand-in for size: the smallest Gokstad boat, about 895, 6.5 x 1.38 x 0.20 m, four oars, two or three men. Not certain: No complete 8th-c hull (?); Frisian ones may be logboat-based (?).

She is the cheap second hull: a partner's stake, a towed boat, or a new start after a wreck in the north. She can go on the rivers, the tidal flats and the coast; on the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 250 pennies and takes 30 days to build, at Ripa, Sliesthorp, Skíringssalr, Ögvaldsnes, Hleiðr or Áhús. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 4.
pages.known: What she was called then: batr; ON faeringr / sexaeringr (?) (names attested later, LATER). Kvalsund boat (Sunnmore), 9.5 m, tree-ring date 780-800. Reric boat graves, Staraya Ladoga rivets, Valsgarde and Vendel boats of 6-15 m. LATER: the Gokstad small boats, about 895: 6.5 m, and two of about 8 and 9.75 m (?). Not certain: How many small boats carried a sail in 793 (?).
