pages.title: River freighter of the Utrecht kind, small
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: One great oak hollowed thin, spread, and raised with a plank on wooden pegs: long, narrow and flat.
pages.game: One great oak hollowed thin, spread, and raised with a plank on wooden pegs: long, narrow and flat. Three men and two to three tons, hauled up the river on a line and drifting down. Four times the house boat's cargo on the Rhine for half her price: the river road to Cologne opens as a trade and not a visit. She can go on the rivers and the tidal flats; on the coast only with care; never on the open sea. New, with her gear, she costs 300 pennies and takes 40 days to build, at Dorestat, Traiectum, Daventre, Noviomagus or Colonia. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 3.
pages.known: What she was called then: none known (?). Vleuten 1: felled after about 734, about 15 x 1.10 m, Rhineland oak, by 8th-century quay remains on the old Rhine: the earliest of the Utrecht type. Eke (Weser), 8th c: a double logboat widened with frames, 10.25 x 1.4-1.5 m. Zeewolde PZ 49, about 900; Velsen and Utrecht 2 (12.8 x 3 m), 11th c. Not certain: Sail or towing mast (?).
pages.source: ships.md 4.6, 6, 8.2, 10, 11.2; ship_classes_793.json logboat_expanded

pages.title: Flat-bottomed plank river barge, 15 m, towed upstream
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A flat box of oak planks caulked with moss, with no iron in her, hauled upstream by men on the bank.
pages.game: A flat box of oak planks caulked with moss, with no iron in her, hauled upstream by men on the bank. Seven tons of stone, grain or wine with three men aboard. Bulk: she carries what ten boats carry, at the lowest price for each ton of any hull, but only where the river goes. She can go on the rivers; never on the tidal flats, the coast and the open sea. New, with her gear, she costs 600 pennies and takes 60 days to build, at Dorestat, Traiectum, Daventre, Colonia, Mogontia or Diusburg. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 3.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navis (?); German Prahm (modern term). Krefeld-Gellep III (Rhine), 8th c: 15.2 m; load 6,961 kg; mast step read as a towing mast. Kalkar-Niedermormter, about 802: sank with a cargo of tuff stone, at least 4.5 t. Karl (Bremen, Weser), after 808: 16-20 x 2.5-3 m. Not certain: Drift speed is an estimate (?); Seine and Loire hulls (?): no find.
pages.source: ships.md 4.7, 7.2, 8.2; ship_classes_793.json river_barge

pages.title: Large river barge
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The Rhine barge at the size it reaches after Charlemagne: twenty metres of flat oak, hauled by a gang.
pages.game: The Rhine barge at the size it reaches after Charlemagne: twenty metres of flat oak, hauled by a gang. She carries fifteen to twenty-five tons with three men aboard. More than twice the old barge in one hull: whole cargoes of wine in tuns, building stone and grain, which is how a river fleet feeds a sea ship. She can go on the rivers; never on the tidal flats, the coast and the open sea. New, with her gear, she costs 800 pennies and takes 75 days to build, at Dorestat, Traiectum, Daventre, Colonia, Diusburg or Noviomagus. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 4.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navis (?); the name is lost: call her a flat boat or a river ship. Cothen: after about 826, about 20 x 2.5-4 x 1.25 m, in the bed of the old Rhine a few km below Dorestad. Vleuten 2: about 959, about 20 x 3.5 m, side 1.15 m high; no iron in her at all; Ardennes oak; a wooden peg in the side as a thole. Utrecht 3: after about 1004, 23 x 3.3-4 m, nearly complete.
pages.source: ships.md 2.1, 4.7, 7.2, 8.2, 11.1 (river_barge_large)

pages.title: Utrecht ship
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A single huge oak hollowed, spread and built up into a seventeen-metre freighter with no iron in her hull.
pages.game: A single huge oak hollowed, spread and built up into a seventeen-metre freighter with no iron in her hull. Four men take thirteen tons from Cologne to the Almere, hauled up and drifting down. The river and the sheltered sea in one hull: wine goes from Cologne to the Frisian coast without being moved from a barge to a ship. She can go on the rivers and the tidal flats; on the coast and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 1,200 pennies and takes 100 days to build, at Traiectum, Daventre, Noviomagus or Colonia. She needs 3 men at the least and is meant for 4.
pages.known: What she was called then: none known; perhaps the hulc of the London toll of about 1000 (?), not proved [MASS-Utr]. Utrecht 1: after about 1019 or 997-1027; 17.45 x 3.84 m; about 13 t on 0.7 m of draught; the bottom one oak trunk at least 14 m long, hollowed to 4-6 cm and spread to 2 m; raised with clinker planks on wooden pegs; a small mast step a third of the way from the bow. Utrecht 2, 11th c, 12.8 x 3 m; Zeewolde PZ 49, about 900. Queenhithe, London: fragments of a large Utrecht type, the wood perhaps from the lower Rhine: if so she crossed the sea. Not certain: Sail or tow line only (?); Whether she is the hulk is not known.

pages.title: Coaster, minster and estate ship
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A ten-metre sailing and rowing boat that lands on a beach, the kind the minsters and abbeys kept toll-free.
pages.game: A ten-metre sailing and rowing boat that lands on a beach, the kind the minsters and abbeys kept toll-free. Four to six men and two and a half tons. The first hull that makes the crossing to Lundenwic an ordinary summer voyage, with nearly four times the cargo, and still lands on any beach. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 1,200 pennies and takes 100 days to build, at Dorestat, Medemelacha, Witla, Walichrum, Lundenwic or Serræ. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 3 men at the least and is meant for 6.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navis (the ships of the toll charters); OE scip. S 86 (about 733): Aethelbald of Mercia remits to Minster-in-Thanet the toll on one ship at London; S 29 (763/4): two ships at Fordwich and a third at Fordwich and Sarre. Cormery (800): two toll-free boats for salt, wine and grain. Boats of 9 to 15 m at Truso, Reric and Kvalsund. Not certain: Hull inferred between the Gislinge (under 1 t) and Graveney (6-7 t) scales (?).
pages.source: ships.md 4.9, 6, 8.2, 10; ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship

pages.title: Small Norse carrier
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The Norse answer to the coaster: a slim eleven-metre boat with a raised side and few oars.
pages.game: The Norse answer to the coaster: a slim eleven-metre boat with a raised side and few oars. Five men and under two tons, fast for her size and at home on a beach. The step up for a house that has gone north: the Danish islands and the Baltic in summer, where the house boat can only creep along the shore. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 1,100 pennies and takes 100 days to build, at Ripa, Sliesthorp, Hleiðr, Skíringssalr, Ögvaldsnes or Áhús. She needs 4 men at the least and is meant for 6.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON byrdingr (later word) (?). LATER: Skuldelev 6, about 1030, Sognefjord pine, birch and oak: 11.2 x 2.5 x 0.5 m, displaces 3 t, sail 26.5 m2; built with 14 oars for fishing, rebuilt for carrying with the rowlocks taken off and fewer oars. The replica Kraka Fyr: 4 to 5 kn on average, put at 10 kn at the most; 2.5 kn with four oars, 5 kn with fourteen; she came through a stiff gale to Anholt. For 793: Kvalsund boat 9.5 m (780-800); boats of 9 to 15 m in the Reric graves and at Truso. Not certain: LATER by two centuries for 793: the size is vouched for then, the carrier rebuild is not.
pages.source: ships.md 2.3, 4.9, 5.3, 6, 7.2, 8.2, 11.1 (norse_cargo_boat)

pages.title: Southern Baltic coastal boat
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A beamy ten-metre clinker boat of the Wendish and Prussian coast, pegged with wood and caulked with moss.
pages.game: A beamy ten-metre clinker boat of the Wendish and Prussian coast, pegged with wood and caulked with moss. Six men and two and a half tons. The cheapest two and a half tons afloat, for a house that speaks a Baltic tongue: the lagoons and river mouths of the amber coast. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 500 pennies and takes 80 days to build, at Reric, Truso or Grobiņa. She needs 4 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: none known (?). Truso (Janow Pomorski), about 750-850: riveted clinker boats 9-11 m long, 2.5-3 m wide; tar barrels, unused rivets (?). LATER: Szczecin boat 8 m (early 9th c) (?); Ralswiek 2, 9.5-9.8 x 2.5-2.8 m, treenails and moss (?). A Slav shipbuilding tradition closely related to the Scandinavian. Not certain: No 8th-c Slav hull found (?); Slav rig in 793 (?).
pages.source: ships.md 2.5, 4.17; ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat; price as unlocks_793.json (500 d)

pages.title: Norse all-purpose sailing and rowing ship
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The ship of the north before 900: fifteen metres, sixteen oars and a sail, built to be rowed by many.
pages.game: The ship of the north before 900: fifteen metres, sixteen oars and a sail, built to be rowed by many. She carries four tons and twelve men, and every man eats. She crosses open sea in almost any summer weather and can row out of trouble, which no western trader of her day can: the road to Skiringssal and Birka. She can go on the tidal flats, the coast and the open sea; on the rivers only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 3,000 pennies and takes 150 days to build, at Ripa, Sliesthorp, Skíringssalr, Hleiðr or Birka. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 8 men at the least and is meant for 20.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON skip (ship) (?). Salme II (Saaremaa), about 750: 17-17.5 x 3 m, a sail indicated; 34 dead. Kvalsund ship, 780-800: 18 m; a side rudder that could be removed in shallow water. The Dorestad keel ship (after about 739) is built this way: riveted clinker, wool caulking. Not certain: Cargo with a full crew (?).
pages.source: ships.md 4.13, 5.3, 6, 10; ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship; price as unlocks_793.json (3,000 d; sold only to a man the Dane has eaten with)

pages.title: Frisian, Frankish and English sea-going merchant ship
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The Dorestad merchant's ship: a broad keeled clinker hull of fourteen metres under one square sail.
pages.game: The Dorestad merchant's ship: a broad keeled clinker hull of fourteen metres under one square sail. Five or six men carry six to seven tons to Lundenwic, Quentovic, Hamwic and Ripa. The first real ship: ten times the house boat's cargo across the sea with one more man, so a whole cargo of wine or querns goes in one crossing. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 3,000 pennies and takes 150 days to build, at Dorestat, Medemelacha, Witla, Traiectum, Lundenwic or Quentovic. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 4 men at the least and is meant for 6.
pages.known: What she was called then: OE ceol (keel) and scip; Latin navis negotiatorum; Frisian cog from the 9th c [BJM]. The Dorestad keel ship: wood felled after about 739, riveted clinker with wool caulking, found 1973-74 in the northern harbour. The Graveney boat (Kent), built about 895: about 13.6 x 4 x 1 m amidships; a flat plank keel; 6 to 7 t of cargo; low freeboard; Mayen lava querns and hops aboard. The ship on the deniers of Dorestad and Quentovic, to 840 (?); the Tiel keel ship, 995-1008. Not certain: Sizes for 793 are bracketed by the Graveney boat of 895 (?); Nothing of mast, sail or oars survived at Graveney.
pages.source: ships.md 2.1, 2.2, 4.10, 5.3, 6, 8.2, 10, 11.2; ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship

pages.title: Early cog
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The Frisians' own ship as far as words and coins show it: flat-bottomed, straight-ended, clinker-sided, and able to be rowed in the king's service.
pages.game: The Frisians' own ship as far as words and coins show it: flat-bottomed, straight-ended, clinker-sided, and able to be rowed in the king's service. Six men and eight to fifteen tons, loaded on the bare sand between tides. Ten tons over the flats: she works the Wadden, the Almere and the Limfjord at any state of tide, where a keel ship must wait for water or a jetty. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 3,500 pennies and takes 150 days to build, at Medemelacha, Doccinga, Witla, Winaldum or Emuthon. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 5 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: cog; Frisians are Cokingi in a 9th-century annal; the due cogsculd on the Almere, 10th c [BJM]. The words: Frisians called Cokingi (the Annals of St Bertin for 867 (?)); a royal tithe on the Almere called cogsculd, 10th c; Frisian districts owe rowed ships called kogge or heerkogge. The angular, straight-ended ship on the Hedeby coins from about 825, which some call the forerunner of the cog. Iron caulking clamps of the later cog's kind, traced to the Frisian area. Not certain: From 870 follows the word, not a find.

pages.title: Small sailing trader with an open hold
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A fourteen-metre ship built only to carry under sail, with decks at the ends and a hold between.
pages.game: A fourteen-metre ship built only to carry under sail, with decks at the ends and a hold between. Five men take four and a half tons, and they hardly row at all. A trader's cargo with half the crew of the old Norse ship: the Baltic run pays, because five men eat and not twelve. She can go on the coast; on the rivers, the tidal flats and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 2,400 pennies and takes 150 days to build, at Ripa, Sliesthorp, Hleiðr, Áhús, Birka or Paviken. She needs 5 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON byrdingr (?), skuta (?) (later words). Skuldelev 3, about 1040, Danish oak: 14 x 3.3 x 0.9 m, displaces 9.6 t, carries 4.6 t, sail 45 m2, five oar ports, 5 to 8 men; a deck fore and aft and an open hold amidships. Roar Ege trials, 1984-85: about 4 kn over long distances, 8 to 10 kn at the most; six oars give 3.2 kn at the top and 2.0 kept up; 1.7 kn made good to windward in light air; in the open Kattegat water comes in across the gunwale. Roar Ege took 54 m3 of green timber, 1,204 rivets and about 20,000 hours, 5,000 of them for sail and rope.

pages.title: Large Slav trading boat
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The largest of the Wendish boats: fourteen metres, pegged with wood and caulked with moss, with no iron to buy.
pages.game: The largest of the Wendish boats: fourteen metres, pegged with wood and caulked with moss, with no iron to buy. Seven men and about six tons. A sea trader's cargo for half a sea trader's price, for a house with a friend or a factor on the Wendish coast. She can go on the tidal flats and the coast; on the rivers and the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 1,500 pennies and takes 120 days to build, at Truso or Grobiņa. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 5 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: none known (?). Ralswiek (Rugen), four boats found 1967-1980 at the trading place, 9th-10th c (?): up to 14 metres long and 3.40 metres wide. Ralswiek 2: planks pegged with treenails, moss caulking (?); a replica made a trial voyage in 1998 (?). The Slav boat is clinker, double-ended, with a keel, a mast step and a side rudder: a tradition closely related to the Scandinavian.
pages.source: ships.md 2.5, 4.17

pages.title: Knarr
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The first ship built for nothing but cargo on the open sea: sixteen metres, broad and deep, under ninety square metres of wool.
pages.game: The first ship built for nothing but cargo on the open sea: sixteen metres, broad and deep, under ninety square metres of wool. Six to eight men carry twenty tons, and she rides out a gale. Three times the keel's cargo with the same crew, and the whole North Sea in any sailing weather: York, Norway and Dublin stop being ventures and become routes. She can go on the coast and the open sea; never on the rivers and the tidal flats. New, with her gear, she costs 6,000 pennies and takes 180 days to build, at Ripa, Sliesthorp, Skíringssalr, Ögvaldsnes or Hleiðr. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 5 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON knorr; OE cnear by 937 (?); kaupskip (?). Askekarr (Gota alv), built about 900-920, repaired about 1010: about 16 x 4.6 m, about 20 t, sail about 90 m2, in use at least a hundred years. Skuldelev 1, about 1030, Sognefjord pine: 15.84 x 4.8 x 1.0 m; 24 t at a 40 per cent freeboard, the replica about 20 t; sail 90 m2; 2 to 4 oars; 6 to 8 men, 5 at the least. Klastad (Vestfold), tree rings 998: 20 to 22 m, lost with whetstone blanks aboard; the Tiel keel ship, 995-1008. Not certain: The name in a Frisian's mouth (?).
pages.source: ships.md 2.3, 4.15, 5.1, 5.3, 6, 7.2, 8.2, 10, 11.1 (knarr); the id is the one unlocks_793.json already waits for

pages.title: The great cargo ship of Hedeby
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The largest trader known from the age, built at Hedeby about 1025: twenty-two metres long, over six broad, carrying forty to sixty tons with about ten men.
pages.game: The largest trader known from the age, built at Hedeby about 1025: twenty-two metres long, over six broad, carrying forty to sixty tons with about ten men. No single house fills her alone. A whole season's trade in one voyage: fifty tons at the lowest sea price for each ton, for a house with partners, a factor and a jetty at both ends. She can go on the coast and the open sea; never on the rivers and the tidal flats. New, with her gear, she costs 15,000 pennies and takes 360 days to build, at Sliesthorp. She can be bought, and she can come as a reward. She needs 8 men at the least and is meant for 12.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON knorr (?); in an Englishman's mouth about 1000 a keel or a hulk. Hedeby 3, built at Hedeby about 1025: a sturdily built cargo ship of a type similar to Skuldelev 1 but with a cargo capacity of as much as about 60 tons by the hypothetical reconstruction, about 22 m long and 6.25 m wide; another summary gives 40 to 50 t. LATER: Lynaes, mid 12th c, at least 60 t; Bergen in the 1240s, over 150 t. Not certain: Cargo 50 t stands between the two readings (40 to 50 and up to 60).
pages.source: ships.md 2.3, 4.16, 5.3, 6, 7.2, 8.2, 10, 11.1 (great_cargo_ship); the id is the one unlocks_793.json already waits for

pages.title: Gaelic currach
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A boat of ox hides stretched on a lashed wooden frame, greased against the sea.
pages.game: A boat of ox hides stretched on a lashed wooden frame, greased against the sea. Five men and under a ton, so light that her crew carry her. She goes where nothing else in the west can land: the island monasteries and surf beaches of the Irish Sea and the Hebrides, and over a portage on her crew's shoulders. She can go on the rivers, the tidal flats and the coast; on the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 120 pennies and takes 20 days to build, at Hī or Duiblinn. She is not sold: a house comes by her only as a reward. She needs 2 men at the least and is meant for 5.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin curuca / curucus; Old Irish curach. Texts only, no hull: Adomnan, Life of Columba (about 700): hide boats beside wooden boats on Iona. Dicuil (825), of voyages about 795: to the northern islands in two days and two nights under full sail. The Voyage of St Brendan (9th-10th c (?)): a mast amidships, a sail, hides tanned with oak bark. Not certain: Sizes and rig (?).
pages.source: ships.md 4.5, 5.3, 6; ship_classes_793.json currach; price and makers as unlocks_793.json (120 d, for a man who has served the house of Hi)

pages.title: River ship of a king, bishop or abbey
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A lord's river ship with cabins, rowed by eight and hauled upstream.
pages.game: A lord's river ship with cabins, rowed by eight and hauled upstream. She is lent with her lord's letter for a season, never sold; her lord keeps her up. She carries people of rank dry and under a lord's freedom from toll: a bishop aboard is worth more than her three tons. She can go on the rivers; never on the tidal flats, the coast and the open sea. New, with her gear, she costs 700 pennies and takes 75 days to build, at Traiectum, Colonia, Mogontia, Rotomagus, Parisius or Ganda. She is not sold: a house comes by her only as a reward. She needs 4 men at the least and is meant for 8.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navis; naves of the toll charters. Rimbert, Life of Anskar ch. 7 (of 826): the bishop of Cologne gives a good boat with two cabins for the voyage down the Rhine past Dorestad. Charlemagne's charter of 779 for Saint-Germain-des-Pres: its ships on the rivers are free of toll. Annales regni Francorum 793: Charles goes by boat from Regensburg to the Fossa Carolina. Not certain: No hull: the type is assumed from the barges (?); Crew and oars (?).
pages.source: ships.md 4.8; ship_classes_793.json river_estate_ship; how she is had as unlocks_793.json

pages.title: Small warship of 26 oars
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: The smallest ship fit for war: seventeen metres, twenty-six oars, thirty men and almost no cargo.
pages.game: The smallest ship fit for war: seventeen metres, twenty-six oars, thirty men and almost no cargo. A house holds one only as a duty or an honour, when a king or a shire lays a ship on it. She is rank and safety, not trade: an escort that catches any raider in light air and carries the house's name to a king's muster. She can go on the rivers, the tidal flats and the coast; on the open sea only with care. New, with her gear, she costs 2,400 pennies and takes 150 days to build, at Ripa, Lundenwic, Sliesthorp, Hleiðr or Eoforwic. She is not sold: a house comes by her only as a reward. She needs 14 men at the least and is meant for 30.
pages.known: What she was called then: ON snekkja; OE snacc (?). Skuldelev 5, about 1030, Denmark: 17.3 x 2.5 x 0.6 m, displaces 7.8 t, 26 oars, about 30 men, sail 46 m2; built partly of reused timber: a levy ship kept going cheaply. Ladby (Funen), 900-950: about 22 x 3 x 0.5 m, 16 pairs of oars. With 13 benches, that is, 26 oarsmen, a snekke was regarded as the smallest ship usable for warfare. Not certain: Whether a merchant ever held one: the levy fell on districts and great men (?); The max of 15 kn is the museum's estimate.

pages.title: Logboat
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: One hollowed trunk: a long narrow trough, flat sheer, blunt ends; paddled or poled.
pages.game: One hollowed trunk: a long narrow trough, flat sheer, blunt ends; paddled or poled. She is 5 metres long, with 2 men and about 0.3 tonnes of cargo. Used for: fishing, ferry, estate and river haul. She is other people's craft: you meet her on the water, and a house does not own her.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin monoxylus / linter (?); OE aesc or bat (?). Welham Bridge (E. Yorkshire): a logboat built into a landing revetment, trackway dated AD 530-690. Langstone (Hampshire) c. AD 500; Callow (Ireland) 9th c (radiocarbon). Catalogues: McGrail 1978 (England and Wales); Mowat 1996 (154 Scottish logboats, all periods); Lanting 2000. Not certain: Sizes are from all-period catalogues, not a 793 series (?); Speed is an estimate (no period figure).
pages.source: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/ship_classes_793.json

pages.title: Small plank skiff or punt
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: Short, low and wide; square or raked ends (punt) or a pointed bow (skiff); one pair of oars, a sculling oar or a pole.
pages.game: Short, low and wide; square or raked ends (punt) or a pointed bow (skiff); one pair of oars, a sculling oar or a pole. She is 5.5 metres long, with 2 oars, 2 men and about 0.5 tonnes of cargo. Used for: ferry, fishing and estate. She is other people's craft: you meet her on the water, and a house does not own her.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navicula; OE bat (?). Pactus legis Salicae tit. XXI 'De navibus furatis' (c. 507-511): fines for taking or stealing another man's boat. LATER: IV Aethelred 2 (c. 1000), Billingsgate: a small boat (navicula) 1/2d, a larger one with a sail 1d, a keel or hulk 4d. Not certain: Almost no 8th-c archaeology (?); Size and speed are estimates (?).
pages.source: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/ship_classes_793.json

pages.title: Horse and cart ferry
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A wide flat punt, square ends, low sides; a cart, horses or cattle standing in it; poled, rowed or pulled along a rope (?).
pages.game: A wide flat punt, square ends, low sides; a cart, horses or cattle standing in it; poled, rowed or pulled along a rope (?). She is 10 metres long, with 4 oars, 2 men and about 1.5 tonnes of cargo. Used for: ferry. She is other people's craft: you meet her on the water, and a house does not own her.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin navigium (the ferry of the capitularies) (?). Size from the load: a cart and its oxen weigh about 1-1.5 t; or 2-3 horses; or 15-20 people (estimate). Capitularies on tolls (Thionville 805 c. 13 and repeats, LATER but codifying custom): toll only where a bridge or ferry (navigium) is provided (?). Einhard, Vita Karoli 17: the Mainz Rhine bridge (500 paces, ten years building) burned in 813, so before c. 803 the crossing there was by boat (?). Not certain: No 8th-c ferry find (?); Rope ferries in 793 (?).
pages.source: Assets/Kapman/Game/Data/ship_classes_793.json

pages.title: Timber raft
pages.hint: A kind of craft
pages.brief: A platform of lashed logs just above the water; men with poles and steering sweeps; it drifts with the current.
pages.game: A platform of lashed logs just above the water; men with poles and steering sweeps; it drifts with the current. She is 12 metres long, with 2 oars, 4 men and about 10 tonnes of cargo. Used for: river haul. She is other people's craft: you meet her on the water, and a house does not own her.
pages.known: What she was called then: Latin ratis. Bede, Prose Life of Cuthbert ch. 3 (c. 721): monks of the monastery at the Tyne mouth bring timber down the Tyne on rafts; a west wind carries them out to sea. Not certain: Rhine and Moselle rafting in 793 (?).

pages.title: The Franks
pages.hint: The Franks
pages.brief: These are the Franks of the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt, speaking Frankish.
pages.game: These are the Franks of the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt, speaking Frankish. You may begin as a Frank: your home is then Quentovic. Their tongue is Frankish; one of them half follows Romance, Frisian and English. The faiths usual among them: Christian, of Rome; a Jew, a merchant of the palace. What is hard about beginning as one of them: the tenth is taken at your own quay, by the man you owe. Your crews are English and Frisian and talk past you.
pages.known: One kingdom under "the lord king Charles". No capital: the court moves. In 793 the king is at Regensburg digging a canal from the Rezat to the Altmühl; Saxons have destroyed a Frankish force at Rüstringen in Frisia; Saracens have beaten the counts near Narbonne. A Frank swears by Saint Martin and Saint Denis, pays his tithe because the king's law now makes him, and holds that the king's wars on the heathen are God's work. His priest still has to forbid him the old things: charms tied on, auguries from birds and horses, feasts at graves and vows at springs, trees and stones. Was their tongue written then? The Low Frankish behind Dorestad: almost nothing. The Rhine Frankish of Mainz and Worms: yes, from c. 800 (catechism, oaths, the Ludwigslied). What the Franks of the lower Rhine and Meuse spoke in 793 was never written down as connected speech. The Franks called it theodisca lingua, 'the tongue of the people' (Royal Frankish Annals 788) (?), the word that became both Deutsch and Dutch. Frankish lords in Neustria also spoke Romance: that is learning, not kinship.
pages.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12 (Gervold procurator 'for many years', chiefly at Quentovic; the ban on English merchants); Alcuin, letter 100 (Charles to Offa, 796: each king's merchants protected in the other's realm); Council of Tours 813 c. 17 (sermons to be put into the Roman country speech or the German: two tongues in one realm); Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md; Design/content/peoples/frankish.md; Design/content/peoples/frankish.md; Capitulary of Herstal 779 c. 7 (tithes); Admonitio generalis 789 c. 65 (against enchanters, weather-makers and vows at trees, stones and springs) (?); Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum (a list of about 743 in a manuscript of about 800, Vatican Pal. lat. 577)

pages.title: The Frisians
pages.hint: The Frisians
pages.brief: These are the Frisians from the Scheldt to the Weser.
pages.game: These are the Frisians from the Scheldt to the Weser. You may begin as a Frisian: your home is then Dorestat. Their tongue is Frisian; one of them half follows English, Frankish and Saxon. The faiths usual among them: Christian, of Rome; the old gods; prime-signed. What is hard about beginning as one of them: nothing more than the count's day: this is the plain start, and the others are measured against it. The year itself is hard: the harvest of 792 failed, grain is dear on every quay.
pages.known: No king since Radbod (d. 719): counts rule for King Charles. West and Middle are two generations Christian. The East, conquered in 785, rose about 793 under Unno and Eilrat and burned its churches; Liudger was back within the year. That summer Saxons wiped out Count Theoderic's force in Rüstringen. A Frisian west of the Lauwers is two generations baptised, keeps Boniface's day at Doccinga, and tells how King Radbod drew his foot back from the font rather than be parted from his fathers; east of the Lauwers the churches burned as lately as 793. He remembers that Fosite's spring was drawn in silence, and that the old law gave a man who robbed a shrine to the sea, at the tide line, to the gods he had wronged. Was their tongue written then? No. About two dozen short rune inscriptions (5th to 10th century); the first connected Frisian is a psalm gloss of c. 1100 and the law books of 1276-1300. Nothing a Frisian of 793 said was written down. The name Kapman is itself Frisian: kapmon, the merchant (?).

pages.title: The Old Saxons
pages.hint: The Old Saxons
pages.brief: These are the Old Saxons between Rhine and Elbe, baptised by force since 785.
pages.game: These are the Old Saxons between Rhine and Elbe, baptised by force since 785. Their tongue is Saxon. You cannot begin as one of them in this game.
pages.known: A Saxon has said the vow, 'I forsake all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot', because since about 785 the law is baptism or death, and it is death too to eat meat in Lent or to burn the dead. He pays the tithe and keeps quiet, and some still go to the springs and groves that the same law names. Was their tongue written then? A little: the baptismal vow (8th century), the Heliand and Genesis (c. 830-850), a few blessings and lists. The tongue of the Saxons between Rhine and Elbe. The Heliand tells the Gospel as the story of a lord and his men, with ships, storms and sea words: the best store of period sea-speech on the Continent. Scholars dispute whether the baptismal vow is Saxon, Low Frankish (Old Dutch) or coloured by English; it may have been used at Utrecht.
pages.source: The Old Saxon baptismal vow (texts_793.json saxon_vow; Vatican Pal. lat. 577); Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4, 7, 8, 21 (about 782-785), softened by the Capitulare Saxonicum of 797

later.text: The tongue of the Saxons between Rhine and Elbe, who were being conquered and baptised by Charles from 772 to 804: in the first life (793-805) it is a tongue under the sword.

pages.title: The English
pages.hint: The English
pages.brief: These are the Mercians, West Saxons, Kentishmen, East Angles, Northumbrians.
pages.game: These are the Mercians, West Saxons, Kentishmen, East Angles, Northumbrians. You may begin as one of the English: your home is then Lundenwic. Their tongue is English; one of them half follows Frisian, Saxon and Frankish. The faiths usual among them: Christian, of Rome. What is hard about beginning as one of them: your king's new heavy penny is not yet trusted abroad.
pages.known: Kingdoms, not one people. Offa of Mercia is overlord south of the Humber: Kent and Lundenwic are his, he beheads the East Angles' king, Beorhtric of Wessex is his son-in-law. Northumbria kills its own kings. A man is a Mercian or a Kentishman first. An Englishman's people have been Christian five or six generations: he counts time by saints' days, gives to his minster, and has kings who went to Rome to die. Yet monks still listen at table to stories of the old heathen kings, so that Alcuin asks what Ingeld has to do with Christ, and in 786 the pope's legates had to forbid the English to cast lots, eat horse and mark their bodies as the heathen do. Was their tongue written then? Yes: laws, charters, verse, glosses; the Chronicle from the 890s. Four dialects in 793 (Northumbrian, Mercian, Kentish, West Saxon); most of what survives is later West Saxon. Frisian is its nearest kin, and the English missionaries of the 8th century went to the Frisians and the Old Saxons because they could preach to them without an interpreter (Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.9-10) (?). They called their speech Englisc and themselves Angelcynn.
pages.source: Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16 (buying in Lundenwic before the king's wic-reeve); Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12; Alcuin, letter 100 (796); Historia regum 798, 801 (the fires of London); chronicle_793.json 793-offa-heavy-penny; the mancus of thirty pence (?); Design/content/dossiers/lundenwic.md; Design/content/peoples/english.md; Design/content/peoples/english.md; Alcuin's letter of 797 to a bishop he calls Speratus, once taken to be Higbald (MGH Epistolae IV no. 124: 'Quid Hinieldus cum Christo?'); the legates' report of 786, c. 19 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 3) (?); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15, for the old English months and Mothers' Night

pages.title: The Danes
pages.hint: The Danes
pages.brief: These are the Danes of Jutland, the islands and Skane.
pages.game: These are the Danes of Jutland, the islands and Skane. You may begin as a Dane: your home is then Ripa. Their tongue is Norse; one of them half follows Frisian and Saxon. The faiths usual among them: the old gods; prime-signed. What is hard about beginning as one of them: in every other port your oath is worth nothing in court, no abbey is your host, and you cannot be buried as you would wish. After 8 June 793 your speech frightens people.
pages.known: Often two kings at once. A Dane gives the gods their due at the turns of the year and asks them by lot before a voyage or a war; an oath on the holy ring binds him as nothing else does, and what he wants to leave behind is a good name. If his king allows it he will hear a Christian priest out, and take the sign of the cross as a guest's courtesy, without leaving his own gods. Was their tongue written then? Runes on stone, wood and metal; the verse and sagas were written down from the 12th century on. One tongue from Jutland to the Lofoten in 793; its own speakers later called it the Danish tongue (dönsk tunga) whoever spoke it. A Northman and an Englishman could trade and quarrel each in his own speech, slowly, with the endings lost: a workable half-understanding.

pages.title: The Irish
pages.hint: The Irish
pages.brief: These are the Irish of Ireland.
pages.game: These are the Irish of Ireland. You may begin as one of the Irish: your home is then Hī. Their tongue is Irish; one of them half follows English. The faiths usual among them: Christian, of the Irish houses. What is hard about beginning as one of them: the boat is the monastery's and so is what she earns.
pages.known: They are Goídil, Gaels; in Latin, and to every neighbour, Scotti; "Scotia" is Ireland. One tongue, one law and one learned class from Kerry to Mull, but some 150 small kingdoms (túatha); "king of Tara" is a claim, not a state. The great monasteries (Armagh, Clonmacnoise, Kildare, Hí) are the only towns. Dál Riata is the Gaels of Argyll and the Isles, under Pictish over-kings (?). An Irish monk fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays, sings the psalms through, and counts leaving his own land for God the best road there is: brothers of his have sailed to islands in the northern ocean where the midsummer night is light enough to pick the lice from a shirt. At home the stricter sort, the clients of God, want fewer wanderers and tighter houses, and can stop a king's fair. Was their tongue written then? Yes, richly: glosses, verse, law, annals (from the 7th century). No kin among the other tongues of the game: to a Frank or a Northman it is closed until learned. Its bridge to everyone is the Latin of its monks. The annals of the first life are written half in Latin and half in Irish, and their word for the raiders is geinti, 'heathens'.
pages.source: Annals of Ulster 801.4, 802.9, 806.8; Annals of Inisfallen 795.2; Bede, Historia ecclesiastica III.3 (Irish and English at one board, with a king to interpret); Design/content/dossiers/hi.md; Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md; Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md; Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae VII (825), on clerics who stayed in Thule from February to August thirty years before (texts_793.json dicuil); Annals of Ulster 811, the fair of Tailtiu prevented by the community of Tallaght (chronicle_793.json 811-08-tailtiu-fair); the Rule of Tallaght (9th century) for the fasts (?)

pages.title: Christian, of Rome
pages.hint: Christian, of Rome
pages.brief: This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep.
pages.game:
This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep.
By the day it asks: no loading, selling or carting on a Sunday; no court sits; keep the feasts: no work or market on them; no meat in Lent, on Fridays, on the eves of great feasts or on the Rogation days; a tenth of what you gain to the church; be shriven at the start of Lent. A blessing before a long crossing is custom, not law.
Of your cargo it asks: sell no Christian to heathens or out of the realm; carry no byrnies or swords out of the realm; lend without gain; do not buy a harvest cheap to sell it dear; do not eat horse, and do not sit down to an offering; do not buy church treasure from a needy priest.
It opens: abbeys as hosts and as keepers of silver: a guest is to be received as Christ; sanctuary: a man who reaches a church has his life; an oath on relics that a court will take, with oath-helpers; toll-free passage as a true pilgrim; a grave in hallowed ground.
Troth rises for one who keeps a Sunday in port when a sale was to be had; keeps Lent aboard; gives alms at a feast; pays the tenth unasked; keeps a vow made in a storm.
Troth falls for one who sells on a Sunday or a feast; eats meat in Lent before the crew; sits down to horse at a heathen board; sells a Christian to heathens; leaves a vow unpaid past its day.
pages.known:
How its people swear: on relics, the altar or the Gospel book, with free men of your rank swearing after you that your oath is clean. In Kent a stranger clears himself at the altar; in Lundenwic a purchase is good if the king's wic-reeve saw it.
How its dead are laid: unburned, in the churchyard, with nothing in the grave, as near the saint as silver allows. A man dead at sea is brought to the next churchyard if he will keep, and given to the sea with a prayer if he will not.

pages.title: Christian, of the Irish houses
pages.hint: Christian, of the Irish houses
pages.brief: This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep; it cannot be chosen in the first game.
pages.game:
This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep; it cannot be chosen in the first game.
By the day it asks: the same feasts and the same Easter as Rome: Iona took the Roman reckoning in 716; fast every Wednesday and Friday, and keep three Lents in the year; from Saturday evening to Monday morning no journey, no buying, no selling.
Of your cargo it asks: carry no women, children or clerics as plunder, and harm none; a tenth of every cargo to the house you sail for.
It opens: every Irish house as a friend, from Iona to Bobbio, and the hermits on the far rocks; exile for God's sake as an honoured road: a boat put to sea without oars, to land where God wills.
Troth rises for one who keeps the Wednesday fast; carries a brother or a book for nothing; lies to over the Sunday.
Troth falls for one who sails or sells between Saturday evening and Monday; takes a fare from a pilgrim.
pages.known:
How its people swear: on the relics, bell or staff of the house's saint (?).
How its dead are laid: in the saint's own graveyard if the body can be brought there; otherwise where a cross can be set.

pages.title: The old gods
pages.hint: The old gods
pages.brief: This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep. By the day it asks: offer at the turns of the year: the start of winter, midwinter, the start of summer; cast the lots before a voyage, and go by them; honour your dead at their graves.
pages.game:
This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep.
By the day it asks: offer at the turns of the year: the start of winter, midwinter, the start of summer; cast the lots before a voyage, and go by them; honour your dead at their graves.
Of your cargo it asks: never turn a guest from your fire or your board; nothing is forbidden to carry. Horse is eaten at the feasts.
It opens: halls and markets in the north, where a Christian is a guest and you are a neighbour; a crew that trusts your luck, because the lots fell well.
Troth rises for one who makes the offering at the turn of the year; goes by the lots when they fall ill; feeds a guest in a lean week; sets a stone or a mound for a dead crewman.
Troth falls for one who lets a priest sign him to please a buyer; sails against the lots; turns a guest away; leaves a dead man to the Christians' ground against his wish.
pages.known:
How its people swear: on a ring reddened or held, before witnesses.
How its dead are laid: burned on a pyre or laid in a mound with goods for the road; a great one in a ship. No priest is needed, only kin.

pages.title: Prime-signed
pages.hint: Prime-signed
pages.brief: This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep. By the day it asks: you have taken the sign of the cross as a learner, not baptism.
pages.game:
This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep.
By the day it asks: you have taken the sign of the cross as a learner, not baptism. In a Christian port you keep Sunday and stand in the church porch; you leave before the mystery; at home you still pour at the turns of the year.
Of your cargo it asks: eat with either. Each side notices what you leave on the board.
It opens: the porch, the market and the table of Christians, and the halls of the north: both worlds, half trusted by each; baptism at the last, which washes everything: a card that comes once.
Troth rises for one who keeps both calendars in one month; stands in the porch on a feast and pours at home that winter.
Troth falls for one who every winter that passes without choosing, by a little; is seen at an offering by a Christian partner; is seen at mass by the hall.
pages.known:
How its people swear: neither oath is whole. A Christian court takes your oath only with baptised men to swear after you; a hall takes the ring from you and remembers the cross.
How its dead are laid: not in the churchyard unless you were baptised dying. Kin in the north will mound you if the body reaches them.

pages.title: A Jew, a merchant of the palace
pages.hint: A Jew, a merchant of the palace
pages.brief: This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep. By the day it asks: from Friday dusk to Saturday dusk no buying, selling, loading or fire.
pages.game:
This is one of the faiths a merchant may keep.
By the day it asks: from Friday dusk to Saturday dusk no buying, selling, loading or fire. Do not put to sea in the three days before the Sabbath; once at sea you may sail on.
Of your cargo it asks: your own food and your own wine: no pork, no eel, no shellfish, no meat you did not see killed. So your own stores, and a longer lading; whether you may deal in other men's wine is argued; the masters of the Rhine allow taking it for a debt, two centuries on; you may buy heathen slaves and sell them in the realm. A slave of yours who is baptised is not thereby free; a Christian may not be sold out of the realm by anyone; take no church plate in pledge.
It opens: a chain of kin and letters from the Rhine to Spain and beyond, who lend on your name alone; six tongues in one family: Arabic, Persian, Greek, Frankish, Spanish, Slavic.
Troth rises for one who lies to over a Sabbath when a tide was to be had; keeps Passover aboard; ransoms a captive of your own people.
Troth falls for one who sells on the Sabbath; eats at a Christian's table to close a bargain; sails on the Day of Atonement by choice.
pages.known:
How its people swear: by the Law of Moses, in your own form. A Christian court may take it or not as the count pleases; no rule is written yet.
How its dead are laid: among your own, at once, unburned, in ground that is yours. None is known at any of the twelve ports: a dead man of your house must be carried up the Rhine (?).
pages.source: Codex Theodosianus 16.8.3 (Cologne, 321); ARF 801, 802; MGH Capit. I no. 46 c. 4; Formulae imperiales 30, 31, 52; Agobard of Lyon, De insolentia Iudaeorum (about 826-827); Design/content/lore/law_tolls.md (lines on the Jewish merchants); Exodus 20:8-11; 35:3; Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 19a (?); Leviticus 23; Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14; Talmud, Avodah Zarah; the rulings of Gershom of Mainz and Rashi (about 1000 to 1100): LATER (?); Louis the Pious's letters of protection, about 825 (Formulae imperiales 30, 31, 52): a generation after this life (?); Capitulary of Nijmegen 806 c. 4 (church treasure is not to be sold off to Jewish and other merchants, who boast they can buy what they like); Ibn Khordadbeh, Book of Roads and Kingdoms (about 847, revised about 885), on the merchants called Radhanites: a lifetime after this one; ARF 801, 802; Ibn Khordadbeh; the 'Capitula de Iudaeis' that go under Charles's name are of doubtful date (?); custom; no Jewish graveyard is recorded in the north in the 790s (?)

later.text: The king's word. In 797 Charles sends Isaac the Jew to the caliph with two Franks; Isaac alone comes home, in 801 and 802, with the elephant.

pages.title: The Lord's day
pages.hint: The Lord's day
pages.brief: The Lord's day comes every week, on Sunday. It runs from: Saturday dusk in Kent, by Wihtred's law; Sunday dawn elsewhere.
pages.game: The Lord's day comes every week, on Sunday. It runs from: Saturday dusk in Kent, by Wihtred's law; Sunday dawn elsewhere. Kept by: Christians of Rome, Christians of the Irish houses and the prime-signed. A keeper may not: load or unload; cart goods, except food, a body for burial, or for the host; bring a suit: no court sits. Bread, ale and fish sell on Saturday; no hands can be hired till Monday.
pages.known: What it cost to break it: Frisia: a fine in solidi, heavier beyond the Lauwers (Lex Frisionum XVIII: 12 and 4 solidi (?)). Kent: a free man who works in the forbidden time pays his healsfang; a servant set to work by his lord costs the lord 80 sceattas (Wihtred 9-11). Wessex: a slave made to work on Sunday goes free (Ine 3). A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Admonitio generalis 789 c. 81 (no servile work, with the three cartings allowed); Lex Frisionum XVIII (about 802); Wihtred 9-11 (695); Ine 3 (about 690); markets: capitulary of 809, MGH Capit. I nos. 61-62 (?) and chronicle_793.json 809-sunday-markets

later.text: Sell on the open market (a sin everywhere; forbidden by the king in Francia only from 809).

pages.title: The Sabbath
pages.hint: The Sabbath
pages.brief: The Sabbath comes every week, on Saturday. It runs from: Friday dusk to Saturday dusk.
pages.game: The Sabbath comes every week, on Saturday. It runs from: Friday dusk to Saturday dusk. Kept by: Jews. A keeper may not: buy, sell, weigh or count silver; load, unload or carry a burden ashore; kindle a fire; put to sea in the three days before it, unless the voyage is a duty; walk beyond the town's edge. A port whose market day is Saturday is closed to a Jewish merchant.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.

pages.game: Washing day comes every week, on Saturday. Kept by: those who keep the old gods and the prime-signed. The Northmen's name for Saturday is 'washing day' (Old Norse laugardagr). A wash, a comb and a clean shirt before a hall is worth a pip of Name for that day (the game's rule). The English complaint that the Danes combed daily, bathed every Saturday and changed their clothes often, and so won English women, is in the chronicle that goes under John of Wallingford's name.
pages.known: It rests on a source written long after: say 'it is said'.
pages.source: Old Norse laugardagr (written 12th century and after); the chronicle attributed to John of Wallingford (13th century)

pages.game: The moon and the tide comes every week. Kept by: Christians of Rome, Christians of the Irish houses, those who keep the old gods, the prime-signed and Jews. Springs at full and new moon; high water at a different hour in each port. Every faith counts by the moon: Easter and Passover hang on the same spring moon, and the heathen north counts its feasts by it.

pages.hint: Saint Mildrith of Thanet

pages.game: Saint Mildrith of Thanet is a feast, kept on 13 July every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. A keeper may not: work on the abbess's land. Dearer for it: ale and beeswax. The day of the minster on Thanet, whose abbess has the toll on her own ships at Sarre and Fordwic by the kings' charters.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: the Kentish toll charters for the abbesses of Thanet (S 29 of 763 or 764 (?); S 86 and others (?)); the Mildrith legend is written down later

pages.title: Lammas
pages.hint: Lammas
pages.brief: Lammas is a feast, kept on 1 August every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome.
pages.game: Lammas is a feast, kept on 1 August every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. Cheaper: wheat, barley and rye. A loaf of the new corn is blessed. Harvest has begun: grain is about to fall and no hands can be hired. The English name is written from the 9th century, so likely in 793 (?).
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom.
pages.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 917, 921 (hlafmaesse); Alfred 43

pages.title: The Assumption of Saint Mary
pages.hint: The Assumption of Saint Mary
pages.brief: The Assumption of Saint Mary is a feast, kept on 15 August every year.
pages.game: The Assumption of Saint Mary is a feast, kept on 15 August every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade. Cheaper: honey. Harvest in full swing; honey is taken.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: Michaelmas
pages.hint: Michaelmas
pages.brief: Michaelmas is a feast, kept on 29 September every year.
pages.game: Michaelmas is a feast, kept on 29 September every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade. Cheaper: wheat, rye, barley and oats. The day the house's debt falls due (the game's rule: that Dorestat reckoned debts on it in 793 is not recorded). The harvest is sold; the autumn gales begin. A count who is owed sits to be paid on a feast, and may not hear a suit that day.
pages.known: This is the game's own rule, not the record's.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (the feast); Design/DECISIONS.md no. 10 (the debt); saints_calendar.md section 10

pages.title: Saint Remigius
pages.hint: Saint Remigius
pages.brief: Saint Remigius is a feast, kept on 1 October every year.
pages.game: Saint Remigius is a feast, kept on 1 October every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. A keeper may not: work. Cheaper: Rhenish wine. A Frankish feast of the first rank and a rent day on many estates (?). The vintage begins on the Rhine.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: All Saints
pages.hint: All Saints
pages.brief: All Saints is a feast, kept on 1 November every year.
pages.game: All Saints is a feast, kept on 1 November every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work. English and Irish in 793.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Alcuin's letter to Arn of Salzburg, 800 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 193 (?)); Design/content/spine.json calendar

later.text: Do not put it in a Frankish mouth before 800.
Alcuin urges it on his Frankish friends about 800; it is ordered for the whole realm only in 835.

pages.title: Saint Willibrord
pages.hint: Saint Willibrord
pages.brief: Saint Willibrord is a feast, kept on 7 November every year.
pages.game: Saint Willibrord is a feast, kept on 7 November every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. Dearer for it: beeswax. He died in 739. At Walichrum he broke an idol and its keeper struck him on the head with a sword: the place where it stood is still shown.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi c. 14, 24

pages.title: Martinmas
pages.hint: Martinmas
pages.brief: Martinmas is a feast, kept on 11 November every year.
pages.game: Martinmas is a feast, kept on 11 November every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade. Dearer for it: bay salt and Droitwich salt; cheaper: cattle hides, cattle, pigs and Rhenish wine. The sea shuts: the end of the game's sailing year, by the old rule every clerk could read. The slaughter month: salt is dearest, hides and beasts cheap, the new wine comes down the Rhine. Martinmas week, 7 to 11 November, is Traiectum's high time; servants are hired and let go.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris IV.39 (the seas shut from 11 November to 10 March); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (Blotmonath); Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: Saint Lebuin
pages.hint: Saint Lebuin
pages.brief: Saint Lebuin is a feast, kept on 12 November every year.
pages.game: Saint Lebuin is a feast, kept on 12 November every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. Dearer for it: ale. He died about 775; the Saxons burned his church and Liudger built it again. One day after Martinmas: the two feasts make one gathering on the IJssel.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.14-15

pages.title: Saint Andrew
pages.hint: Saint Andrew
pages.brief: Saint Andrew is a feast, kept on 30 November every year.
pages.game: Saint Andrew is a feast, kept on 30 November every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. A keeper may not: work or trade. The fast before Christmas begins about now in most churches.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: Saint Josse
pages.hint: Saint Josse
pages.brief: Saint Josse is a feast, kept on 13 December every year.
pages.game: Saint Josse is a feast, kept on 13 December every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome. The cell of Saint Josse by Quentovic, a hospice for travellers from over the sea, said to have been given to Alcuin about 792 (?).
pages.known: It rests on a source written long after: say 'it is said'.
pages.source: Lupus of Ferrieres, letters (about 840), on the cell given to Alcuin for the reception of strangers (?); dossier quentovic.md

pages.title: Christmas
pages.hint: Christmas
pages.brief: Christmas is a feast, kept on 25 December and the 3 days after every year.
pages.game: Christmas is a feast, kept on 25 December and the 3 days after every year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade for four days; bring a suit. For 20 days before, dearer for it: Rhenish wine, beeswax, pepper and frankincense. Four days kept whole, twelve of feasting.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36; ARF 801

later.text: The Frankish annals turn the year here: the 'year 801' of the royal annals begins on Christmas Day 800, the day Charles was crowned emperor.

pages.title: Septuagesima
pages.hint: Septuagesima
pages.brief: Septuagesima is a season. It moves with Easter: 63 days before it.
pages.game: Septuagesima is a season. It moves with Easter: 63 days before it. Kept by: Christians of Rome. The Alleluia is laid aside. In later English law no oaths or ordeals from now until two weeks after Easter: a merchant who needs an oath to clear himself may wait two months for it. Its day, year by year: 3 February in 793; 19 January in 794; 8 February in 795; 31 January in 796; 19 February in 797; 4 February in 798; 27 January in 799; 16 February in 800; 31 January in 801; 23 January in 802; 12 February in 803; 28 January in 804; 16 February in 805; 8 February in 806.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: I Cnut 17 (about 1020)

pages.title: Ash Wednesday
pages.hint: Ash Wednesday
pages.brief: Ash Wednesday is a fast. It moves with Easter: 46 days before it.
pages.game: Ash Wednesday is a fast. It moves with Easter: 46 days before it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: eat meat until Easter; wed or feast; hunt. Dearer for it: salt herring, stockfish, dried fish, eels and salt salmon; cheaper: salt pork and bacon, cheese, butter, cattle and pigs. Forty fast days: one meal, late, and no flesh. Fish is wanted before and through it; meat, cheese, butter and eggs do not sell. In Saxony, by the first law for the conquered, a man who ate meat in Lent 'in contempt of the Christian faith' was to die unless a priest judged it need; Daventre lies on that border. Its day, year by year: 20 February in 793; 5 February in 794; 25 February in 795; 17 February in 796; 8 March in 797; 21 February in 798; 13 February in 799; 4 March in 800; 17 February in 801; 9 February in 802; 1 March in 803; 14 February in 804; 5 March in 805; 25 February in 806.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4 (about 782-785); Wihtred 14-15 (695); Theodulf of Orleans, Capitula I (about 800) (?)

pages.title: Palm Sunday
pages.hint: Palm Sunday
pages.brief: Palm Sunday is a feast. It moves with Easter: 7 days before it.
pages.game: Palm Sunday is a feast. It moves with Easter: 7 days before it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade. Processions with branches: willow and yew in the north. Its day, year by year: 31 March in 793; 16 March in 794; 5 April in 795; 27 March in 796; 16 April in 797; 1 April in 798; 24 March in 799; 12 April in 800; 28 March in 801; 20 March in 802; 9 April in 803; 24 March in 804; 13 April in 805; 5 April in 806.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: saints_calendar.md section 3

pages.title: Good Friday
pages.hint: Good Friday
pages.brief: Good Friday is a fast. It moves with Easter: 2 days before it.
pages.game: Good Friday is a fast. It moves with Easter: 2 days before it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: eat before evening, and then only bread and water; trade; ring a bell. The black fast. No mass, no bell, no market. Its day, year by year: 5 April in 793; 21 March in 794; 10 April in 795; 1 April in 796; 21 April in 797; 6 April in 798; 29 March in 799; 17 April in 800; 2 April in 801; 25 March in 802; 14 April in 803; 29 March in 804; 18 April in 805; 10 April in 806.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: saints_calendar.md section 3

pages.title: Holy Saturday
pages.hint: Holy Saturday
pages.brief: Holy Saturday is a feast. It moves with Easter: the day before it.
pages.game: Holy Saturday is a feast. It moves with Easter: the day before it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. For 14 days before, dearer for it: fine linen, beeswax and olive oil. The vigil and the great day for baptisms: the new Christians wear white, and fine linen sells before it (?). A prime-signed player who is baptised this night leaves that faith for good. Its day, year by year: 6 April in 793; 22 March in 794; 11 April in 795; 2 April in 796; 22 April in 797; 7 April in 798; 30 March in 799; 18 April in 800; 3 April in 801; 26 March in 802; 15 April in 803; 30 March in 804; 19 April in 805; 11 April in 806.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Notker, Gesta Karoli II.19 (about 885: Northmen baptised more than once for the white clothes); Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 19 (infants to be baptised within the year)

pages.title: Easter
pages.hint: Easter
pages.brief: Easter is a feast. It moves from year to year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses.
pages.game: Easter is a feast. It moves from year to year. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade through Easter week. Dearer for it: Rhenish wine, Frankish wine, cattle and sheep; cheaper: salt herring and dried fish. The year's first feast and the end of the fast: wine for every altar, new clothes, meat again, and the sea opens. The crew is hired and sworn about now. After it come the hungry weeks: grain is dearest in April and May. Its day, year by year: 7 April in 793; 23 March in 794; 12 April in 795; 3 April in 796; 23 April in 797; 8 April in 798; 31 March in 799; 19 April in 800; 4 April in 801; 27 March in 802; 16 April in 803; 31 March in 804; 20 April in 805; 12 April in 806.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (Easter week kept whole); seasons_793.json

pages.title: The Rogation days
pages.hint: The Rogation days
pages.brief: The Rogation days is a fast. It moves with Easter: 36 days after it.
pages.game: The Rogation days is a fast. It moves with Easter: 36 days after it. Kept by: Christians of Rome. A keeper may not: eat meat; work until the procession is home. Monday to Wednesday before the Ascension: the fields are walked with the cross and the relics. Its day, year by year: 13 May in 793; 28 April in 794; 18 May in 795; 9 May in 796; 29 May in 797; 14 May in 798; 6 May in 799; 25 May in 800; 10 May in 801; 2 May in 802; 22 May in 803; 6 May in 804; 26 May in 805; 18 May in 806.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Council of Orleans 511 c. 27; Council of Clofesho 747 c. 16

pages.title: The Ascension
pages.hint: The Ascension
pages.brief: The Ascension is a feast. It moves with Easter: 39 days after it.
pages.game: The Ascension is a feast. It moves with Easter: 39 days after it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade. The first crossings to England are made about now. Its day, year by year: 16 May in 793; 1 May in 794; 21 May in 795; 12 May in 796; 1 June in 797; 17 May in 798; 9 May in 799; 28 May in 800; 13 May in 801; 5 May in 802; 25 May in 803; 9 May in 804; 29 May in 805; 21 May in 806.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: Pentecost
pages.hint: Pentecost
pages.brief: Pentecost is a feast. It moves with Easter: 49 days after it.
pages.game: Pentecost is a feast. It moves with Easter: 49 days after it. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. A keeper may not: work or trade through the week. Dearer for it: fine linen; cheaper: wool and fleeces. Kept like Easter; the second day for baptisms. Wool is shorn about now and the long voyages start. Its day, year by year: 26 May in 793; 11 May in 794; 31 May in 795; 22 May in 796; 11 June in 797; 27 May in 798; 19 May in 799; 7 June in 800; 23 May in 801; 15 May in 802; 4 June in 803; 19 May in 804; 8 June in 805; 31 May in 806.
pages.known: It was written down after 805, but describes older custom. The days are reckoned by the rule of Easter as Bede taught it; no record gives them one by one.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

pages.title: Lent
pages.hint: Lent
pages.brief: This is a fast, kept from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday.
pages.game: This is a fast, kept from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. No flesh of beast or bird; by the strict rule no milk, butter, cheese or eggs. One meal, after vespers or, by now, in mid-afternoon. Ale and wine are drink, not food. Whale and porpoise count as fish. Excused: children, the old, the sick, women with child, and those at heavy work or on a hard journey, by a priest's leave (?): a crew at sea in Lent is a fair case, and the fish is to hand anyway.
pages.source: saints_calendar.md section 4; Theodulf, Capitula I.40 (?)

pages.title: The fasts of the four seasons
pages.hint: The fasts of the four seasons
pages.brief: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of Rome.
pages.game: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of Rome. A Wednesday, Friday and Saturday in each season.
pages.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 34

later.text: The weeks were not the same everywhere: the council of Mainz of 813 fixed them for the Frankish realm as the first week of March, the second of June, the third of September and the full week before Christmas eve.

pages.title: The fast before Christmas
pages.hint: The fast before Christmas
pages.brief: This is a fast, kept from 11 November or 30 November to 24 December.
pages.game: This is a fast, kept from 11 November or 30 November to 24 December. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. Lighter than Lent and not the same in any two dioceses: in Gaul by old rule three days a week; monks keep it whole.
pages.source: Council of Macon 581 c. 9 (?); saints_calendar.md section 4

pages.title: The three Lents of the Irish
pages.hint: The three Lents of the Irish
pages.brief: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of the Irish houses.
pages.game: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of the Irish houses. A winter Lent before Christmas, the spring Lent, and a summer Lent after Pentecost, kept by the stricter Irish houses.
pages.source: the Tallaght documents (9th century) (?)

pages.title: Horse flesh
pages.hint: Horse flesh
pages.brief: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses.
pages.game: This is one of the rules of fasting. Kept by: Christians of Rome and Christians of the Irish houses. Never eaten. It is on the table at every heathen feast: what is on the board tells a guest where he is.
pages.source: pope Gregory III to Boniface, about 732 (Boniface, letter 28); the legates' report of 786 c. 19

pages.title: The feast at the start of winter
pages.hint: The feast at the start of winter
pages.brief: The feast at the start of winter is a day of those who keep the old gods.
pages.game: The feast at the start of winter is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: mid October; the game's day for Ripa: 14 October (?). Kept by: those who keep the old gods and the prime-signed. A keeper may not: turn a guest from the board. Dearer for it: malt and bay salt; cheaper: cattle hides. A beast killed, the meat shared, ale brewed for it. Raiders are home; hire and fostering run from now to summer.
pages.known: What is sure: that the heathen north feasted at the start of winter: a Christian poet riding east in autumn about 1019 was turned from farm after farm because the households were 'keeping the elves' sacrifice'. The name 'winter nights' and the three feasts a year are Snorri's, about 1230. It rests on a source written long after: say 'it is said'.
pages.source: Sigvat, Austrfararvisur (about 1019); Snorri, Ynglinga saga c. 8 (about 1230); saints_calendar.md section 8

pages.title: Yule
pages.hint: Yule
pages.brief: Yule is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: midwinter; the night is not known for 793 (later accounts put it after Christmas, in January).
pages.game: Yule is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: midwinter; the night is not known for 793 (later accounts put it after Christmas, in January). Kept by: those who keep the old gods and the prime-signed. Dearer for it: malt, mead and pigs. Ale drunk, pork eaten, oaths sworn. Yule is 'drunk': that much is sure.
pages.known: What is sure: a king means 'to drink Yule at sea' in a poem of about 900. Bede says the heathen English began their year on 25 December with 'mothers' night'. Thietmar, writing 1012 to 1018 at second hand, puts a great feast at Lejre every ninth year in January, after the Epiphany. A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Haraldskvaedi (about 900); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (725); Thietmar of Merseburg I.17

pages.title: The February doings
pages.hint: The February doings
pages.brief: The February doings is a day of those who keep the old gods.
pages.game: The February doings is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: February. Kept by: those who keep the old gods. A keeper may not: be seen at it in a Frankish port: it is the count's business in Saxony and the priest's in Frisia. Among the lately baptised Frisians and Saxons the priests' list of forbidden things names 'the filthy doings in February', feasts at graves and offerings at springs and trees. Bede's February is 'the month of cakes' offered to the gods. No day is given.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum, heads 1-3, 11 (about 743, in a manuscript of about 800); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15

pages.title: The feast at the start of summer
pages.hint: The feast at the start of summer
pages.brief: The feast at the start of summer is a day of those who keep the old gods.
pages.game: The feast at the start of summer is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: mid April; the game's day for Ripa: 14 April (?). Kept by: those who keep the old gods and the prime-signed. The ships are launched and an offering made for the season. Lots are cast before a voyage to learn whether the gods will help.
pages.known: What is sure: lots before a voyage are in Rimbert (of the 850s). Adam of Bremen, about 1075, puts the great nine-yearly feast of the Svear at Uppsala about the spring equinox. A spring 'sacrifice for victory' is Snorri's. It rests on a source written long after: say 'it is said'.
pages.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 18-19, 27, 30; Adam of Bremen IV.27 and its note; Snorri, Ynglinga saga c. 8

pages.title: The darkened moon
pages.hint: The darkened moon
pages.brief: The darkened moon is a day of those who keep the old gods.
pages.game: The darkened moon is a day of those who keep the old gods. Kept by: those who keep the old gods and the prime-signed. People shout to help the moon: 'Win, moon!' A Christian crew is forbidden to join in; a heathen one will not stop.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Indiculus superstitionum, head 21 ('de lunae defectione, quod dicunt Vince luna'); the eclipses are in rare_793.json

later.text: At an eclipse of the moon seen from the port: 28 March 796 before dawn; 21 September 796 in the evening; 5 February 798 in the evening; 15 January 800 in the evening; 21 May 802 before dawn; the night of 2 to 3 November 803; 12 September 805 at moonrise.

pages.title: The town's feast for its god
pages.hint: The town's feast for its god
pages.brief: The town's feast for its god is a day of those who keep the old gods.
pages.game: The town's feast for its god is a day of those who keep the old gods. When: not known. Kept by: those who keep the old gods. The town eats and drinks to honour its god, and a man who has killed a beast hangs it on a pole before his door so that all know he has made his offering.
pages.known: What is sure: seen at Hedeby about 965 by a traveller from Tortosa. Shown at Ripa in the 790s it is a guess (?). It rests on a source written long after: say 'it is said'.
pages.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub al-Turtushi (about 965), in al-Qazwini

pages.title: The summer market at Ripa
pages.hint: The summer market at Ripa
pages.brief: This is a fair at Ripa, from 25 May to 12 August every year.
pages.game: This is a fair at Ripa, from 25 May to 12 August every year. Dearer for it: Rhenish wine, Frisian cloth and Mayen quernstones; cheaper: amber, antler combs, glass beads and cattle. The plots on the bank are let and worked by season: beads, combs, bronze casting, amber, cattle, Frisian cloth and Rhenish pots. Outside these weeks the landing is half empty.
pages.known: The day is reckoned by rule; no record gives it.
pages.source: the digs at Ribe (plots laid out about 705 and used by season); the days are the game's (fairs_793.json: day 145, eighty days)

pages.title: The fair of Saint-Denis
pages.hint: The fair of Saint-Denis
pages.brief: This is a fair at Parisius, for 28 days from 9 October every year.
pages.game: This is a fair at Parisius, for 28 days from 9 October every year. Dearer for it: Frisian cloth and woollen cloth; cheaper: Frankish wine, honey and madder. English ('Saxon') and Frisian merchants sell cloth and buy wine, honey and madder; the abbey takes the tolls. It is talked of at Quentovic, Lundenwic and Dorestat.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: the judgement of 710 and the charters of Pippin (753) and Charles (775) on the fair's tolls; dossier parisius.md

pages.title: The gathering at Boniface's church
pages.hint: The gathering at Boniface's church
pages.brief: This is a market held at a feast at Doccinga, from 3 June to 6 June every year.
pages.game: This is a market held at a feast at Doccinga, from 3 June to 6 June every year. Pilgrims by boat, pedlars and the lord's men in one yard.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii c. 8-9

pages.title: Martinmas week at Traiectum
pages.hint: Martinmas week at Traiectum
pages.brief: This is a market held at a feast at Traiectum, from 7 November to 12 November every year.
pages.game: This is a market held at a feast at Traiectum, from 7 November to 12 November every year. Willibrord's day to Lebuin's: the see's high time, and the last market before the sea shuts.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: saints_calendar.md section 5

pages.title: The count's court
pages.hint: The count's court
pages.brief: This is a matter of the court at Dorestat, and at Walichrum, Witla, Medemelacha, Daventre and Quentovic.
pages.game: This is a matter of the court at Dorestat, and at Walichrum, Witla, Medemelacha, Daventre and Quentovic. When: the general sittings: one about summer and one about autumn in the capitulary of 769, three a year later (?). The game's days: the Monday after Low Sunday, the Monday after Saint John, the Monday after Saint Remigius. Debts and thefts are heard, oaths sworn with oath-helpers, fines set. Not on a Sunday or a feast.
pages.known: A law or a text of the time says so.
pages.source: Capitulare primum 769 c. 12 (?); Lex Frisionum (about 802); the days are the game's

pages.title: The king's assembly and the host
pages.hint: The king's assembly and the host
pages.brief: This is an assembly. When: between May and August, where the king is, before the summer's campaign.

A keeper may not: eat or keep leavened bread or beer aboard for the eight days: the ship's bread and the ale go ashore or are sold to a stranger first; trade on the first two and last two days. Dearer for it: wheat, flour and Frankish wine; cheaper: ship's bread and ale. pages.title: Great famine in Burgundy, Francia, Italy, Gothia and Provence; many die
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 793: Great famine in Burgundy, Francia, Italy, Gothia and Provence; many die.
pages.game: In the game: famine across the Frankish lands: grain very dear, deaths, people sell what they have. It is felt in: Italy, the Rhine delta, the Scheldt and Maas mouths, Frisia, the Rhineland and the Meuse valley, and 6 more lands. In the chronicle it stands under “famine”: famine or hunger.
pages.known: In 793: Great famine in Burgundy, Francia, Italy, Gothia and Provence; many die. Ann. Mosell. (a year behind) date its start to the harvest of 792 and tell of cannibalism; Moissac adds Italy, Gothia and Provence. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Lauresh. 793; Chron. Moiss. 793; Ann. Mosell. 792 (=793); MGH Capit. I no. 28 c. 25. Ann. Lauresh.: Annales Laureshamenses (Lorsch), to 803. Chron. Moiss.: Chronicon Moissiacense (MGH SS 1-2). Ann. Mosell.: Annales Mosellani; their years run one behind (their 792 = 793). MGH Capit. I: Capitularia regum Francorum I (ed. Boretius, 1883), by number and chapter (c.)

later.text: It lasted until August 794.
Eased by the harvest of 794.

pages.known: On 22 February 793: Ealdorman Sicga, slayer of King Aelfwald, dies. viii kal. Mar. HR: he died by his own hand (?); his body was taken to Lindisfarne on 23 April. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D/E) 793; HR 793. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year.
