pages.game: In the game: famine in southern Italy: grain very dear; Frankish army foraging. It is felt in: Italy. In the chronicle it stands under “famine”: famine or hunger.
pages.known: In the spring of 793: Famine in Benevento: the Frankish army under Pippin and Louis must eat meat in Lent. Sent in winter 792/793; Lent 793 ran 20 Feb-6 Apr (Easter 7 Apr). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Lauresh. 793; Chron. Moiss. 793. Ann. Lauresh.: Annales Laureshamenses (Lorsch), to 803. Chron. Moiss.: Chronicon Moissiacense (MGH SS 1-2).

pages.game: In the game: omen at Eoforwic: unease. It happens at or near Eoforwic. It is felt in: Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “portent”: a sign in the sky or a marvel: comets, auroras, rains of blood.
pages.known: In the spring of 793: Blood-red rain falls from the roof of St Peter's church at York in Lent. Lent 793 ran 20 Feb-6 Apr. Told by Alcuin to King Aethelred after the Lindisfarne raid: it fell from the north side in clear weather. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Alcuin ep. 16. Alcuin ep.: Alcuin's letters (MGH Epp. IV, ed. Duemmler), by number.

In the chronicle it stands under “portent”: a sign in the sky or a marvel: comets, auroras, rains of blood.
pages.known: In the spring of 793: False grain seen in fields, woods and marshes that could be touched but not eaten. Frankfurt (794) c. 25 recalls the empty ears 'eaten by demons' in the year of the famine. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Ann. Mosell. 792 (=793); MGH Capit. I no. 28 c. 25. Ann. Mosell.: Annales Mosellani; their years run one behind (their 792 = 793). MGH Capit. I: Capitularia regum Francorum I (ed. Boretius, 1883), by number and chapter (c.)

pages.known: In the spring of 793: Portents over Northumbria: flashes of light, whirlwinds and fiery dragons in the sky. No day given; the ASC orders them: portents, then famine, then the raid. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D/E) 793; HR 793; Symeon, Libellus de exordio ii.5. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year. Symeon, Libellus de exordio: Symeon of Durham's history of the church of Durham, by book and chapter.

pages.source: ASC (D/E) 793; HR 793. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year.

It is felt in: Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: On 8 June 793: Heathen seamen sack the monastery of Lindisfarne, killing and carrying off monks. ASC D/E read vi id. Ian. (8 January), usually emended to vi id. Iun. (8 June); Symeon gives vii id. Iun. (7 June). The raid is certain; the day is 7 or 8 June. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D/E) 793; HR 793; Symeon, Libellus de exordio ii.5; Alcuin epp. 16, 19-21. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year. Symeon, Libellus de exordio: Symeon of Durham's history of the church of Durham, by book and chapter.

pages.known: In the summer of 793: News: Count Theoderic's force wiped out by Saxons in Rüstringen by the Weser. The revised ARF gives the news in 793, reaching Charles at Regensburg. Ann. S. Amandi put a slaughter of Franks by the sea in 792, Ann. Mosell. troops coming by ship through Frisia betrayed in 792: the defeat itself was probably 792 (?). It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: ARF rev. 793; Ann. S. Amandi 792; Ann. Mosell. 791 (=792). ARF rev.: the revised version of the ARF (formerly 'Einhard's annals'). Ann. S. Amandi: Annales Sancti Amandi. Ann. Mosell.: Annales Mosellani; their years run one behind (their 792 = 793).

pages.known: In 793: Offa's heavier, broader penny replaces the lighter Mercian coinage (c. 792/3). Dated by coin study only, not by an annal; often linked with the Frankish coin reform of 793/794. It is uncertain.
pages.source: numismatic: Offa's heavy coinage (Blackburn & Grierson, MEC 1; Chick, The Coinage of Offa). numismatic: dated by coin study, not by any annal.

Moissac names the stream Oliveius: Orbieu or Orbiel (?). Heavy Frankish losses; the raiders went home with booty. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ARF rev. 793; Chron. Moiss. 793; Ibn al-Athir AH 177. ARF rev.: the revised version of the ARF (formerly 'Einhard's annals'). Chron. Moiss.: Chronicon Moissiacense (MGH SS 1-2). Ibn al-Athir AH: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-ta'rikh, by hijri year.

pages.known: On 18 May 839: Byzantine envoys reach Louis at Ingelheim with men who call themselves 'Rhos'; they prove to be Swedes, and are held. The first record of the Rus. xv kal. Iun. (18 May). Louis suspected them of being spies. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 839. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

pages.known: On 20 June 840: Emperor Louis the Pious dies on an island in the Rhine near Ingelheim. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 840; Astronomer 64; Ann. Fuld. 840. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). pages.known: On 25 June 841: Battle of Fontenoy: Charles the Bald and Louis the German defeat Lothar in a great slaughter. The place: Fontenoy-en-Puisaye. The sources are sure of it.

Nithard: Nithard, Histories of the sons of Louis the Pious, by book and chapter. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901.

pages.known: In 841: Northmen build a ship-fort (longphort) at Dublin and winter there. The same year a longphort was made at Linn Duachaill (Annagassan). The sources are sure of it.

pages.known: In 841: Lothar grants Walcheren and the neighbouring places to the Danish exile Harald, to keep other raiders out. The AB call it a deed 'to be detested'. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 841; Nithard iv.2. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Nithard: Nithard, Histories of the sons of Louis the Pious, by book and chapter.

pages.known: On 14 February 842: Oaths of Strasbourg: Louis the German and Charles the Bald swear alliance, each in the other's tongue. Nithard gives the oaths' texts in early French and German. The sources are sure of it.

pages.known: In 842: A Northman fleet sacks Quentovic at dawn, killing and carrying off its people and sparing only the houses that paid. The AB tell of the dawn attack; Nithard adds that they crossed the sea and plundered Hamwic (Hamwig) and Nordhunnwig, perhaps Norwich (?), in the same way. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 842; Nithard iv.3. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Nithard: Nithard, Histories of the sons of Louis the Pious, by book and chapter.

pages.known: On 24 June 843: Northmen, led by the rebel count Lambert, storm Nantes on St John's day and kill Bishop Gunhard in his cathedral. The AB seem to call the fleet Westfaldingi, men of Vestfold (?). They wintered on the island and brought their households, 'as if to stay for ever'. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 843; Chronicle of Nantes. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Chronicle of Nantes: Chronicon Namnetense (11th century, from older notes).

pages.known: In 843: Kenneth son of Alpin, king of Dal Riata, becomes king of the Picts as well (c. 843). It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Chronicle of the Kings of Alba; AU 858. Chronicle of the Kings of Alba: short Scottish king-list chronicle (10th century). AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry.

later.text: The year is reckoned back from his death in 858, said to be in the sixteenth year of his reign over the Picts.

pages.game: In the game: three kingdoms: Frisia, the Rhine delta, the Meuse, Cologne and Italy to Lothar; Flanders, Neustria, the Loire and Aquitaine to Charles; Saxony, Mainz and the east to Louis. It is felt in: the Rhine delta, the Scheldt and Maas mouths, Frisia, the Rhineland, the Meuse valley and Flanders and the Scheldt, and 6 more lands. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: In August 843: Treaty of Verdun: the Frankish empire divided into west (Charles), middle (Lothar, with Frisia and Italy) and east (Louis). The day is not recorded; early August 843. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 843; Ann. Fuld. 843. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901.

pages.title: A Viking fleet comes up the Guadalquivir and takes Seville; the emir's army defeats them at Tablada in November

pages.game: In the game: raid in al-Andalus: Seville plundered for weeks; afterwards Cordoba builds a fleet and an arsenal at Seville. It is felt in: Al-Andalus. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In the autumn of 844: A Viking fleet comes up the Guadalquivir and takes Seville; the emir's army defeats them at Tablada in November. They had raided Lisbon and Cadiz on the way. The Arab writers call them al-majus. The days vary between the sources; the defeat is usually put on 11 November 844. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ibn al-Qutiyya; Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH 230; AB 844. Ibn al-Qutiyya: Ibn al-Qutiyya, Ta'rikh iftitah al-Andalus. Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH: Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan al-mughrib, by hijri year. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

later.text: It lasted until November 844.

It is felt in: Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: On 28 March 845: Ragnar's fleet of 120 ships comes up the Seine and sacks Paris on Easter Sunday; Charles the Bald pays 7,000 pounds of silver for them to go. The first tribute paid to Vikings by a Frankish king. On the way home many of them died of sickness (the AB and the Translatio see God's punishment). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 845; Ann. Xant. 845; Translatio S. Germani. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Xant.: Annales Xantenses. Translatio S. Germani: the account of St Germain's relics moved during the siege of Paris in 845.

pages.known: In 845: A Danish fleet takes Hamburg by surprise and burns it, church, books and all; Ansgar flees with the relics. The AB say King Horik sent 600 ships up the Elbe that year and the Saxons beat them; whether this was the same fleet is not certain. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 16; AB 845. Rimbert, Vita Anskarii: Rimbert's life of Ansgar, archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, by chapter. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

pages.known: In 845: The Viking leader Turgéis captured by Máel Sechnaill and drowned in Loch Uair. The place: Lough Owel. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AU 845. AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry.

pages.known: In 846: Danish pirates burn Dorestad and two other villages while Lothar watches from Nijmegen and cannot stop them. The Xanten annals have the burning in sight of Lothar at Nijmegen. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Ann. Xant. 846; AB 846. Ann. Xant.: Annales Xantenses. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

later.text: The AB of 846-847 tell of Danes taking tribute from Frisia and holding Dorestad and the Betuwe.

pages.known: In August 846: Arab raiders from Africa land at Ostia, plunder St Peter's and St Paul's outside the walls of Rome. The day is usually given as 23 August (?). The sources are sure of it.

pages.known: In 850: Lothar grants Dorestad and other counties to the Danish chief Rorik, who had taken them with his fleet, in return for his fealty. He was to defend the coast against other Danes. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 850; Ann. Fuld. 850. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901.

pages.known: In 850: King Horik lets Ansgar build a church at Sliesthorp, the port where merchants from Dorestad and Hamburg come. The place: Hedeby. Rimbert: before it, Christian traders from Dorestad and Hamburg were afraid to come. The year is about 850 (?). It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 24. Rimbert, Vita Anskarii: Rimbert's life of Ansgar, archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, by chapter.

pages.known: In 851: Heathens winter on Thanet for the first time; 350 ships storm Canterbury and London; King Æthelwulf beats them at Aclea. The place: London and Canterbury. Some manuscripts have Sheppey for Thanet. The wintering may be that of 850/851. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 851; Asser 3-5. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: In 854: Horik I and most of the Danish royal house fall in a civil war with his nephew Guthorm. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 854; Ann. Fuld. 854; Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 31. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901. Rimbert, Vita Anskarii: Rimbert's life of Ansgar, archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, by chapter.

pages.known: In 854: The Svear under King Olof take Seeburg in Courland and besiege Apulia until the Curonians pay and submit. Rimbert says the Curonians had thrown off Swedish rule, and that the Danes had tried and failed before. Seeburg is usually taken to be Grobina; the year is c. 854 (?). It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 30. Rimbert, Vita Anskarii: Rimbert's life of Ansgar, archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, by chapter.

pages.title: Danish pirates sail through the Straits of Gibraltar, raid Spain and Morocco, winter in the Camargue and go on to Italy (859-861)

pages.known: In 859: Danish pirates sail through the Straits of Gibraltar, raid Spain and Morocco, winter in the Camargue and go on to Italy (859-861). The two leaders are named by later writers (Dudo, the Irish Fragmentary Annals); the story that they took Luna for Rome is Dudo's. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 859; AB 860; Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH 245; Chronicle of Alfonso III. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH: Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan al-mughrib, by hijri year. Chronicle of Alfonso III: Asturian chronicle (late 9th century).

later.text: It lasted until July 861.

The Fulda annals say merchants went to Venice over the ice with horses and carts. The AB put the winter's end in April. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: AB 860; Ann. Fuld. 860. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901.

pages.known: On 18 June 860: A Rus fleet of 200 ships attacks Constantinople while the emperor is away, plundering the suburbs and the islands. The Brussels chronicle gives 18 June; the Rus left in early August. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Photios, Homilies 3-4; Brussels Chronicle 860. Photios, Homilies: Patriarch Photios' sermons on the Rus attack of 860. Brussels Chronicle: the short Byzantine chronicle in a Brussels manuscript (Cumont's Anecdota Bruxellensia).

pages.known: In 862: The Primary Chronicle's year for Rurik and his brothers being called from over the sea to rule the Slavs and Finns; Rurik settles at Ladoga, later Novgorod. Written down about 250 years later; the date is the chronicle's own (AM 6370), and the story is partly legend. The Hypatian copy has Rurik first at Ladoga. It is uncertain.
pages.source: PVL 6370. PVL: Povest' vremennykh let, the Russian Primary Chronicle (about 1113), by annus mundi (subtract 5508).

pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 863: The Danes sack Dorestad once more and sail up the Rhine towards Cologne.
pages.game: In the game: raid on Dorestat: the last time it is named as a trading place; trade moves to Tiel and Deventer. It happens at or near Dorestat and Colonia. It is felt in: the Rhine delta, Frisia and the Rhineland. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In 863: The Danes sack Dorestad once more and sail up the Rhine towards Cologne. Among the first events of 863 in the AB. Dorestad's river was silting up and the Rhine's main stream moving south to the Lek and Waal. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 863. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

pages.title: Edict of Pîtres: a new coinage from ten mints only, fortified bridges on the rivers, and no arms or horses to be sold to the Northmen
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 25 June 864: Edict of Pîtres: a new coinage from ten mints only, fortified bridges on the rivers, and no arms or horses to be sold to the Northmen.
pages.game: In the game: coin: old pennies exchanged for the new by 11 November; law: selling arms or horses to Northmen punished by death; a fortified bridge built at Pont-de-l'Arche to close the Seine. It happens at or near Rotomagus, Parisius and Quentovic. It is felt in: Neustria, Flanders and the Scheldt, the Loire and the Bay and Aquitaine. In the chronicle it stands under “law”: a law, capitulary or cain taking effect: prices, tolls, arms, markets, measures.
pages.known: On 25 June 864: Edict of Pîtres: a new coinage from ten mints only, fortified bridges on the rivers, and no arms or horses to be sold to the Northmen. The ten named mints include Quentovic, Rouen and the palace. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: MGH Capit. II no. 273. MGH Capit. II: Capitularia regum Francorum II (ed. Boretius and Krause, 1897), by number.

pages.title: A great heathen army comes to England and winters in East Anglia, where the people make peace and give them horses
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In the autumn of 865: A great heathen army comes to England and winters in East Anglia, where the people make peace and give them horses.
pages.game: In the game: a great army in England: East Anglia buys peace with horses; war for years to come. It is felt in: East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: In the autumn of 865: A great heathen army comes to England and winters in East Anglia, where the people make peace and give them horses. The ASC's year began in the autumn. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 866 (=865); Asser 21. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

later.text: The ASC's year began in the autumn, so its 866 entry tells of autumn 865.

pages.title: The great army crosses the Humber and takes York on All Saints' Day
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 1 November 866: The great army crosses the Humber and takes York on All Saints' Day.
pages.game: In the game: Eoforwic held by the Danes: its trade and mint theirs. It happens at or near Eoforwic. It is felt in: Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: On 1 November 866: The great army crosses the Humber and takes York on All Saints' Day. Northumbria was split between the rival kings Osberht and Ælla. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 867; HR 867; Symeon, Libellus de exordio ii.6. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year. Symeon, Libellus de exordio: Symeon of Durham's history of the church of Durham, by book and chapter.

pages.title: The Northumbrian kings Osberht and Ælla storm York together and both are killed
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 21 March 867: The Northumbrian kings Osberht and Ælla storm York together and both are killed.
pages.game: In the game: Northumbria under the Danes, with an English puppet king (Ecgberht) north of the Tyne. It happens at or near Eoforwic. It is felt in: Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 21 March 867: The Northumbrian kings Osberht and Ælla storm York together and both are killed. HR: xii kal. Apr. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 867; HR 867. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. HR: Historia regum (Symeon of Durham), by year.

pages.title: The great army winters at Thetford; King Edmund of East Anglia fights them and is killed, and they take the kingdom
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 20 November 869: The great army winters at Thetford; King Edmund of East Anglia fights them and is killed, and they take the kingdom.
pages.game: In the game: East Anglia under the Danes: Gipeswic's trade in their hands. It happens at or near Gipeswic and Dommoc. It is felt in: East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: On 20 November 869: The great army winters at Thetford; King Edmund of East Anglia fights them and is killed, and they take the kingdom. Abbo's later Passio has Edmund martyred, shot with arrows; the cult made him St Edmund. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 870 (=869); Abbo of Fleury, Passio S. Eadmundi. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Abbo of Fleury: Abbo of Fleury, Passio S. Eadmundi (about 985).

pages.title: Amlaíb and Ímar besiege Dumbarton Rock for four months and destroy it; next year 200 ships bring Britons, Picts and Angles to Dublin as slaves
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 870: Amlaíb and Ímar besiege Dumbarton Rock for four months and destroy it; next year 200 ships bring Britons, Picts and Angles to Dublin as slaves.
pages.game: In the game: a great haul of slaves at Duiblinn: slaves cheap there next year. It happens at or near Duiblinn. It is felt in: Ireland and Dal Riata and the Isles. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: In 870: Amlaíb and Ímar besiege Dumbarton Rock for four months and destroy it; next year 200 ships bring Britons, Picts and Angles to Dublin as slaves. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AU 870; AU 871. AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry.

pages.title: Treaty of Meerssen: Charles the Bald and Louis the German divide Lotharingia, Frisia and the Meuse between them
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 8 August 870: Treaty of Meerssen: Charles the Bald and Louis the German divide Lotharingia, Frisia and the Meuse between them.
pages.game: In the game: the middle kingdom gone: the Meuse and Frisia split between west and east; tolls and lords change. It is felt in: Frisia, the Rhine delta, the Scheldt and Maas mouths, the Meuse valley and the Rhineland. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: On 8 August 870: Treaty of Meerssen: Charles the Bald and Louis the German divide Lotharingia, Frisia and the Meuse between them. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 870. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims).

pages.title: Battle of Ashdown: King Æthelred and his brother Alfred defeat the Danish army
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 8 January 871: Battle of Ashdown: King Æthelred and his brother Alfred defeat the Danish army.
pages.game: In the game: Wessex holds; nine battles that year. It is felt in: Southern England. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 8 January 871: Battle of Ashdown: King Æthelred and his brother Alfred defeat the Danish army. The day is from Asser's account and the ASC's reckoning; the year of battles went on with Basing and Meretun. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 871; Asser 37-39. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

pages.title: King Æthelred of Wessex dies after Easter; his brother Alfred becomes king
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In April 871: King Æthelred of Wessex dies after Easter; his brother Alfred becomes king.
pages.game: In the game: new king of Wessex: Alfred buys peace with the army that autumn. It is felt in: Southern England and Cornwall. In the chronicle it stands under “accession”: a ruler or prelate takes power or is crowned.
pages.known: In April 871: King Æthelred of Wessex dies after Easter; his brother Alfred becomes king. Æthelred's death is traditionally put on 23 April 871. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 871; Asser 40-42. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

pages.title: Battle of Hafrsfjord: Harald Fairhair defeats the kings of the west and rules most of the Norwegian coast (traditional date)
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 872: Battle of Hafrsfjord: Harald Fairhair defeats the kings of the west and rules most of the Norwegian coast (traditional date).
pages.game: In the game: one king over the western coast: chiefs leave for Iceland and the isles (the sagas' story). It happens at or near Ögvaldsnes. It is felt in: Western Norway and Vestfold and the Vik. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: In 872: Battle of Hafrsfjord: Harald Fairhair defeats the kings of the west and rules most of the Norwegian coast (traditional date). The date 872 comes from Icelandic reckoning of the 12th-13th centuries. It is uncertain.
pages.source: Haraldskvæði (Hornklofi); Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga hárfagra. Haraldskvæði (Hornklofi): skaldic poem on Harald Fairhair and Hafrsfjord, said to be by his court poet. Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

later.text: Many historians put the battle about 885-900.

pages.title: The great army winters at Repton and drives King Burgred out of Mercia; he goes to Rome and the Danes set up Ceolwulf
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 874: The great army winters at Repton and drives King Burgred out of Mercia; he goes to Rome and the Danes set up Ceolwulf.
pages.game: In the game: Mercia under a Danish-made king; London's mint and trade disturbed. It happens at or near Lundenwic and Legacæstir. It is felt in: Western Mercia and Southern England. In the chronicle it stands under “deposition”: a ruler or abbot driven out or stepping down.
pages.known: In 874: The great army winters at Repton and drives King Burgred out of Mercia; he goes to Rome and the Danes set up Ceolwulf. The army had wintered at London in 871-872, where the Mercians bought peace. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 874. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: Ingólfr Arnarson settles at Reykjavík: the beginning of the settlement of Iceland (traditional date)
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 874: Ingólfr Arnarson settles at Reykjavík: the beginning of the settlement of Iceland (traditional date).
pages.game: In the game: Iceland settled from Norway and the isles: a new land wanting iron, timber, grain and malt, and selling wool and walrus. It is felt in: Iceland and Western Norway. In the chronicle it stands under “founding”: a town, monastery, fort or church founded.
pages.known: In 874: Ingólfr Arnarson settles at Reykjavík: the beginning of the settlement of Iceland (traditional date). Ari puts the beginning of the settlement about 870, Landnámabók has Ingólfr settle in 874; the 'settlement layer' of volcanic ash under the first farms is dated by Greenland ice cores to the 870s. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Íslendingabók 1; Landnámabók. Íslendingabók: Ari Þorgilsson's Book of the Icelanders (about 1125), by chapter. Landnámabók: the Book of Settlements (13th-century versions of an older work).

pages.title: Halfdan shares out the land of Northumbria and his men begin to plough and live there
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 876: Halfdan shares out the land of Northumbria and his men begin to plough and live there.
pages.game: In the game: Danish settlers in Yorkshire: a Danish kingdom at Eoforwic, trading with Dublin and the Danes. It is felt in: Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “politics”: a submission, change of allegiance, trial, exile or will.
pages.known: In 876: Halfdan shares out the land of Northumbria and his men begin to plough and live there. The first record of a Viking army settling down in England. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 876. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: The Danish army takes Chippenham by stealth after Twelfth Night; Alfred escapes into the Somerset marshes at Athelney
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In January 878: The Danish army takes Chippenham by stealth after Twelfth Night; Alfred escapes into the Somerset marshes at Athelney.
pages.game: In the game: Wessex overrun: many flee overseas; the south cut off from its king. It is felt in: Southern England. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: In January 878: The Danish army takes Chippenham by stealth after Twelfth Night; Alfred escapes into the Somerset marshes at Athelney. 'At midwinter after Twelfth Night'. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 878; Asser 52-53. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

pages.title: Battle of Edington: Alfred defeats Guthrum, who gives hostages and is baptised three weeks later
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In May 878: Battle of Edington: Alfred defeats Guthrum, who gives hostages and is baptised three weeks later.
pages.game: In the game: Wessex saved; Guthrum's army leaves and settles East Anglia (880); the boundary later set by treaty. It is felt in: Southern England and East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: In May 878: Battle of Edington: Alfred defeats Guthrum, who gives hostages and is baptised three weeks later. In the seventh week after Easter (Easter was 23 March). Guthrum was baptised at Aller as Æthelstan, and his chrism loosed at Wedmore. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 878; Asser 55-56. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

pages.title: The great army crosses from England to Francia and winters at Ghent, raiding Flanders and the Scheldt
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In November 879: The great army crosses from England to Francia and winters at Ghent, raiding Flanders and the Scheldt.
pages.game: In the game: raid on Ganda: the abbey and the town held as a winter camp; the lands round plundered for a year. It happens at or near Ganda and Andoverpis. It is felt in: Flanders and the Scheldt, the Scheldt and Maas mouths and Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In November 879: The great army crosses from England to Francia and winters at Ghent, raiding Flanders and the Scheldt. The ASC says they stayed at Ghent for a year. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Vedastini 879; ASC (A) 880. Ann. Vedastini: Annales Vedastini, the annals of Saint-Vaast at Arras, 874-900. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

later.text: It lasted until October 880.

pages.title: A Viking army crushes the Saxons in a winter battle; Duke Brun, two bishops and twelve counts fall
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 2 February 880: A Viking army crushes the Saxons in a winter battle; Duke Brun, two bishops and twelve counts fall.
pages.game: In the game: Saxony's leaders killed: the Elbe lands unguarded. It is felt in: Saxony. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 2 February 880: A Viking army crushes the Saxons in a winter battle; Duke Brun, two bishops and twelve counts fall. The place: near Ebstorf (Lüneburg Heath). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Fuld. 880. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901.

pages.title: Battle of Saucourt: King Louis III defeats a Viking army in Vimeu
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 3 August 881: Battle of Saucourt: King Louis III defeats a Viking army in Vimeu.
pages.game: In the game: the raiders turn east, to the Meuse and Rhine. It happens at or near Quentovic. It is felt in: Neustria and Flanders and the Scheldt. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 3 August 881: Battle of Saucourt: King Louis III defeats a Viking army in Vimeu. The place: Saucourt-en-Vimeu. The Old High German Ludwigslied sings of the victory. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AB 881; Ann. Vedastini 881; Ludwigslied. AB: Annales Bertiniani, the West Frankish royal annals of Saint-Bertin, 830-882 (Prudentius, then Hincmar of Reims). Ann. Vedastini: Annales Vedastini, the annals of Saint-Vaast at Arras, 874-900. Ludwigslied: Old High German poem on the victory at Saucourt (881).

pages.title: From their camp at Elsloo on the Meuse the Northmen burn Liège, Maastricht, Cologne and Bonn, and stable horses in the palace chapel at Aachen
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In the winter 881/882 of 881: From their camp at Elsloo on the Meuse the Northmen burn Liège, Maastricht, Cologne and Bonn, and stable horses in the palace chapel at Aachen.
pages.game: In the game: raids on Colonia and the Meuse towns: the whole valley plundered for the winter; Trier sacked on 5 April 882. It happens at or near Colonia. It is felt in: the Meuse valley and the Rhineland. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In the winter 881/882 of 881: From their camp at Elsloo on the Meuse the Northmen burn Liège, Maastricht, Cologne and Bonn, and stable horses in the palace chapel at Aachen. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Fuld. 881; Ann. Fuld. 882; Regino 881. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901. Regino: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, to 906.

later.text: It lasted until May 882.

pages.title: The Primary Chronicle's year for Oleg taking Kiev and making it the Rus capital, 'the mother of Rus cities'
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 882: The Primary Chronicle's year for Oleg taking Kiev and making it the Rus capital, 'the mother of Rus cities'.
pages.game: In the game: the way from the Varangians to the Greeks under one Rus prince: furs and slaves down the Dnieper. It is felt in: Ladoga. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: In 882: The Primary Chronicle's year for Oleg taking Kiev and making it the Rus capital, 'the mother of Rus cities'. A chronicle date written down much later. It is uncertain.
pages.source: PVL 6390. PVL: Povest' vremennykh let, the Russian Primary Chronicle (about 1113), by annus mundi (subtract 5508).

pages.title: At Asselt, Charles the Fat buys peace: Godfrid is baptised and given Frisia as a fief, Sigfrid takes thousands of pounds of silver
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In July 882: At Asselt, Charles the Fat buys peace: Godfrid is baptised and given Frisia as a fief, Sigfrid takes thousands of pounds of silver.
pages.game: In the game: Frisia held by a Danish duke: raiders kept off, but his men lord it. It happens at or near Dorestat. It is felt in: Frisia, the Rhine delta and the Meuse valley. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: In July 882: At Asselt, Charles the Fat buys peace: Godfrid is baptised and given Frisia as a fief, Sigfrid takes thousands of pounds of silver. The Fulda annals put the payment at about 2,080 pounds of gold and silver (?). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Fuld. 882; Regino 882. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901. Regino: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, to 906.

pages.title: Duke Godfrid of Frisia killed at Herispich in the Betuwe by the emperor's men
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In June 885: Duke Godfrid of Frisia killed at Herispich in the Betuwe by the emperor's men.
pages.game: In the game: the Danish rule of Frisia ends; Frisia back under the East Frankish king. It happens at or near Dorestat. It is felt in: Frisia and the Rhine delta. In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: In June 885: Duke Godfrid of Frisia killed at Herispich in the Betuwe by the emperor's men. The place: Spijk (Herispich). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Fuld. 885; Regino 885. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901. Regino: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, to 906.

pages.title: Siege of Paris: a huge Viking fleet under Sigfrid besieges the city for eleven months; Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin hold it
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 24 November 885: Siege of Paris: a huge Viking fleet under Sigfrid besieges the city for eleven months; Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin hold it.
pages.game: In the game: the Seine closed above Rouen for a year; in November 886 Charles the Fat pays 700 pounds and lets them winter in Burgundy. It happens at or near Parisius and Rotomagus. It is felt in: Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: On 24 November 885: Siege of Paris: a huge Viking fleet under Sigfrid besieges the city for eleven months; Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin hold it. Abbo, an eyewitness, speaks of 700 ships, perhaps too many (?). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Abbo, Bella Parisiacae urbis; Ann. Vedastini 885; Ann. Vedastini 886. Abbo, Bella Parisiacae urbis: Abbo of Saint-Germain's verse account of the siege of Paris, 885-886 (an eyewitness). Ann. Vedastini: Annales Vedastini, the annals of Saint-Vaast at Arras, 874-900.

later.text: It lasted until November 886.

pages.title: Alfred occupies London and gives it to Ealdorman Æthelred of Mercia; all the English not under the Danes accept him
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 886: Alfred occupies London and gives it to Ealdorman Æthelred of Mercia; all the English not under the Danes accept him.
pages.game: In the game: Lundenwic moves inside the old Roman walls (Lundenburh); the treaty with Guthrum fixes the Danelaw border along the Lea and Watling Street. It happens at or near Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England and Western Mercia. In the chronicle it stands under “politics”: a submission, change of allegiance, trial, exile or will.
pages.known: In 886: Alfred occupies London and gives it to Ealdorman Æthelred of Mercia; all the English not under the Danes accept him. The treaty of Alfred and Guthrum is undated. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (A) 886; Asser 83. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred, by chapter.

later.text: It belongs between 878 and 890.

pages.title: Charles the Fat deposed at Tribur; Arnulf of Carinthia is made king in the east and the empire breaks up for good
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In November 887: Charles the Fat deposed at Tribur; Arnulf of Carinthia is made king in the east and the empire breaks up for good.
pages.game: In the game: new kings everywhere: Odo in the west (888), Arnulf in the east; each kingdom fights the raiders alone. It is felt in: the Rhineland, Saxony, Neustria, Provence and the Rhone and Italy. In the chronicle it stands under “deposition”: a ruler or abbot driven out or stepping down.
pages.known: In November 887: Charles the Fat deposed at Tribur; Arnulf of Carinthia is made king in the east and the empire breaks up for good. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ann. Fuld. 887; Regino 887. Ann. Fuld.: Annales Fuldenses, the East Frankish annals of Fulda, to 901. Regino: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, to 906.

later.text: Charles died on 13 January 888.

pages.title: Ohthere of Hålogaland and Wulfstan tell King Alfred of their voyages: north to the White Sea, south to Skiringssal and Hedeby, and from Hedeby to Truso
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 890: Ohthere of Hålogaland and Wulfstan tell King Alfred of their voyages: north to the White Sea, south to Skiringssal and Hedeby, and from Hedeby to Truso.
pages.game: In the game: news of the northern sea-roads: the days' sailing from Hålogaland to Skiringssal (a month) and on to Hedeby (five days), and from Hedeby to Truso (seven days and nights). It happens at or near Skíringssalr, Sliesthorp and Truso. It is felt in: Halogaland and the Sami, Vestfold and the Vik, Schleswig, the Prussians and Southern England. In the chronicle it stands under “embassy”: envoys sent or received, gifts, news carried.
pages.known: In 890: Ohthere of Hålogaland and Wulfstan tell King Alfred of their voyages: north to the White Sea, south to Skiringssal and Hedeby, and from Hedeby to Truso. Added to the Old English Orosius made at Alfred's court; the visit is undated, about 890 (?). Ohthere brought the king walrus tusks and told of the Sami's tribute in furs, feathers, whalebone and ship-ropes. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Old English Orosius (Ohthere and Wulfstan). Old English Orosius: the Old English Orosius made at Alfred's court, with the voyages of Ohthere and Wulfstan.

pages.title: King Arnulf storms the Viking camp on the Dyle near Leuven and destroys the army
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In the autumn of 891: King Arnulf storms the Viking camp on the Dyle near Leuven and destroys the army.

pages.known: In the autumn of 891: King Arnulf storms the Viking camp on the Dyle near Leuven and destroys the army. The day is usually given as 1 September (?). The sources are sure of it.

pages.game: In the game: law: tolls at Lundenwic by size of ship; the men of Rouen pay on wine and blubber-fish; the emperor's men pay at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar. It happens at or near Lundenwic and Rotomagus. It is felt in: Southern England, Neustria, Flanders and the Scheldt, the Meuse valley and the Rhineland. In the chronicle it stands under “law”: a law, capitulary or cain taking effect: prices, tolls, arms, markets, measures.
pages.known: In 1000: London's toll rules: at Billingsgate a small boat pays a halfpenny, a sailing ship a penny, a keel or hulk fourpence; men of Rouen, Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and France show their goods; the emperor's men trade like Londoners. Undated; usually put about 1000 (?). Men of Huy, Liège and Nivelles pay toll as they pass through. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: IV Æthelred 2

pages.title: Sea battle of Svolder: Olaf Tryggvason is beaten by the kings of the Danes and Svear and Jarl Eiríkr, and leaps from his ship
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 9 September 1000: Sea battle of Svolder: Olaf Tryggvason is beaten by the kings of the Danes and Svear and Jarl Eiríkr, and leaps from his ship.
pages.game: In the game: Norway shared out under the Danish king and the jarls of Lade. It is felt in: Western Norway, Vestfold and the Vik, the Danish isles and the Svear. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 9 September 1000: Sea battle of Svolder: Olaf Tryggvason is beaten by the kings of the Danes and Svear and Jarl Eiríkr, and leaps from his ship. The year is Ari's; 9 September is the later Icelandic tradition. Adam puts the battle in the Øresund. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Íslendingabók 7; Adam of Bremen ii.40; Snorri, Heimskringla: Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar. Íslendingabók: Ari Þorgilsson's Book of the Icelanders (about 1125), by chapter. Adam of Bremen: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter. Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

pages.title: St Brice's Day: King Æthelred orders all the Danish men in England killed; at Oxford they are burned in St Frideswide's church
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 13 November 1002: St Brice's Day: King Æthelred orders all the Danish men in England killed; at Oxford they are burned in St Frideswide's church.
pages.game: In the game: Danish traders in England killed or fled; Sweyn Forkbeard's revenge raids follow (1003). It is felt in: Southern England, Western Mercia and East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “politics”: a submission, change of allegiance, trial, exile or will.
pages.known: On 13 November 1002: St Brice's Day: King Æthelred orders all the Danish men in England killed; at Oxford they are burned in St Frideswide's church. The charter S 909 (1004) tells of the burning at Oxford. That year the army had been paid 24,000 pounds. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1002; S 909. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. S: Sawyer's list of Anglo-Saxon charters.

pages.title: Northmen sail up the Waal and burn Tiel; at Utrecht the people burn their own trading quarter rather than leave it to them
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 1006: Northmen sail up the Waal and burn Tiel; at Utrecht the people burn their own trading quarter rather than leave it to them.
pages.game: In the game: Tiel, the new port of the Rhine delta, burned; Traiectum's trading quarter burned. It happens at or near Traiectum. It is felt in: the Rhine delta. In the chronicle it stands under “burning”: a town, port or fort burned (by raiders, accident or lightning).
pages.known: In 1006: Northmen sail up the Waal and burn Tiel; at Utrecht the people burn their own trading quarter rather than leave it to them. Tiel took over much of Dorestad's trade in the 10th century (?). It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum i. Alpert of Metz: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum (about 1021-1024).

pages.title: Æthelred pays the Danish army 36,000 pounds to leave

pages.game: In the game: a great tribute in silver: English pennies go north in huge numbers. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens and Western Mercia. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: In 1007: Æthelred pays the Danish army 36,000 pounds to leave. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1007. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: 'Thorkell's army' lands at Sandwich; East Kent pays 3,000 pounds; the army winters on the Thames and raids all the south
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In August 1009: 'Thorkell's army' lands at Sandwich; East Kent pays 3,000 pounds; the army winters on the Thames and raids all the south.
pages.game: In the game: raids across southern England for three years; the new English fleet of 1009 has come to nothing. It happens at or near Serræ, Fordwic and Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England and East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In August 1009: 'Thorkell's army' lands at Sandwich; East Kent pays 3,000 pounds; the army winters on the Thames and raids all the south. 'Soon after Lammas'. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1009. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: The Danish army kills Archbishop Ælfheah at Greenwich; 48,000 pounds of tribute is paid
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 19 April 1012: The Danish army kills Archbishop Ælfheah at Greenwich; 48,000 pounds of tribute is paid.
pages.game: In the game: a great tribute: the army breaks up; Thorkell and 45 ships take service with Æthelred. It happens at or near Lundenwic and Fordwic. It is felt in: Southern England. In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: On 19 April 1012: The Danish army kills Archbishop Ælfheah at Greenwich; 48,000 pounds of tribute is paid. Canterbury had been taken in September 1011. He refused to be ransomed and was pelted with bones at a feast. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1012; Thietmar vii.42-43. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Thietmar: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon (1012-1018), by book and chapter.

pages.game: In the game: a Danish king of England: the English and Danish markets under one ruler. It happens at or near Lundenwic, Eoforwic and Hamwic. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens, Northumbria and Western Mercia. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: In 1013: Sweyn Forkbeard conquers England: the north submits at Gainsborough, then Oxford, Winchester and London; Æthelred flees to Normandy. Æthelred went to Normandy at Christmas. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1013. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.game: In the game: England at war again; Harald, Sweyn's other son, king of the Danes. It is felt in: East Anglia and the Fens, Northumbria, Jutland and the Danish isles. In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: On 3 February 1014: Sweyn Forkbeard dies at Gainsborough; the fleet chooses his son Cnut as king, but the English send for Æthelred. Candlemas. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1014. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: Battle of Clontarf: Brian Boru's army defeats the Leinstermen, the Dublin Norse and their allies from the isles; Brian and Sigurd of Orkney are killed

pages.game: In the game: many Norse of the isles and Dublin killed; Dublin stays a Norse town under Sihtric, trading for the Irish kings. It happens at or near Duiblinn. It is felt in: Ireland, Shetland and Orkney and Dal Riata and the Isles. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 23 April 1014: Battle of Clontarf: Brian Boru's army defeats the Leinstermen, the Dublin Norse and their allies from the isles; Brian and Sigurd of Orkney are killed. Good Friday. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: AU 1014; Cogadh Gáedhel re Gallaibh; Njáls saga 157. AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry. Cogadh Gáedhel re Gallaibh: The War of the Irish with the Foreigners (12th century, praising Brian Boru). Njáls saga: 13th-century saga, with an account of Clontarf.

pages.title: The great sea-flood: on Michaelmas eve the sea runs further inland than ever before, drowning many villages and countless people
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 28 September 1014: The great sea-flood: on Michaelmas eve the sea runs further inland than ever before, drowning many villages and countless people.
pages.game: In the game: storm surge on the English coast: low ports, salt-pans and marsh pastures drowned. It is felt in: Southern England and East Anglia and the Fens. In the chronicle it stands under “storm”: a storm, gale or storm surge.
pages.known: On 28 September 1014: The great sea-flood: on Michaelmas eve the sea runs further inland than ever before, drowning many villages and countless people. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1014. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

pages.title: Yaroslav gives the men of Novgorod a written law, the oldest part of the Russkaya Pravda (traditional date)
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 1016: Yaroslav gives the men of Novgorod a written law, the oldest part of the Russkaya Pravda (traditional date).
pages.game: In the game: law: fixed fines (in marten skins and silver) in Novgorod and its lands, Varangians and townsmen alike. It happens at or near Aldeigjuborg. It is felt in: Ladoga. In the chronicle it stands under “law”: a law, capitulary or cain taking effect: prices, tolls, arms, markets, measures.
pages.known: In 1016: Yaroslav gives the men of Novgorod a written law, the oldest part of the Russkaya Pravda (traditional date). The Novgorod chronicle ties the law to 1016; its date is debated. It is uncertain.
pages.source: Novgorod First Chronicle 6524; Russkaya Pravda (Short version). Novgorod First Chronicle: by annus mundi (subtract 5508). Russkaya Pravda: the law of the Rus; its Short version begins with Yaroslav's law.

pages.title: Battle of Assandun: Cnut defeats Edmund Ironside; they share England, and on Edmund's death (30 November) Cnut becomes king of all England
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 18 October 1016: Battle of Assandun: Cnut defeats Edmund Ironside; they share England, and on Edmund's death (30 November) Cnut becomes king of all England.
pages.game: In the game: a Danish king of England: London and the North Sea ports under Cnut. It happens at or near Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens, Western Mercia and Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 18 October 1016: Battle of Assandun: Cnut defeats Edmund Ironside; they share England, and on Edmund's death (30 November) Cnut becomes king of all England. Æthelred had died in London on 23 April 1016. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1016; Encomium Emmae ii. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Encomium Emmae: Encomium Emmae reginae (about 1041).

pages.title: Cnut takes a tribute of 72,000 pounds from England and 10,500 from London, pays off his army and sends most of the fleet home, keeping forty ships

pages.brief: In 1018: Cnut takes a tribute of 72,000 pounds from England and 10,500 from London, pays off his army and sends most of the fleet home, keeping forty ships.
pages.game: In the game: the greatest tribute of all: English silver floods into Denmark; a standing tax (heregeld) for the king's ships. It happens at or near Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens, Western Mercia, Northumbria, Jutland and the Danish isles. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: In 1018: Cnut takes a tribute of 72,000 pounds from England and 10,500 from London, pays off his army and sends most of the fleet home, keeping forty ships. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1018. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796.

later.text: Cnut became king of the Danes too in 1018-1019.

pages.title: Battle of Vlaardingen: Count Dirk III of West Frisia beats the emperor's army sent to stop his toll on the Merwede, where the Tiel merchants pass
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 29 July 1018: Battle of Vlaardingen: Count Dirk III of West Frisia beats the emperor's army sent to stop his toll on the Merwede, where the Tiel merchants pass.
pages.game: In the game: a count's toll at the river mouth: ships to and from Tiel and Utrecht pay at Vlaardingen; the county of Holland grows from it. It is felt in: the Rhine delta, the Scheldt and Maas mouths and Frisia. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 29 July 1018: Battle of Vlaardingen: Count Dirk III of West Frisia beats the emperor's army sent to stop his toll on the Merwede, where the Tiel merchants pass. The merchants of Tiel had complained to the emperor. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum ii.20-21; Thietmar viii.23. Alpert of Metz: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum (about 1021-1024). Thietmar: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon (1012-1018), by book and chapter.

pages.title: The merchants of Tiel live by their own law: they claim an imperial charter to judge their own cases, and swear and drink together
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 1020: The merchants of Tiel live by their own law: they claim an imperial charter to judge their own cases, and swear and drink together.
pages.game: In the game: a merchants' guild on the Waal: Tiel the chief port of the Rhine delta, trading with England. It is felt in: the Rhine delta. In the chronicle it stands under “trade”: treasure or goods flowing into a market.
pages.known: In 1020: The merchants of Tiel live by their own law: they claim an imperial charter to judge their own cases, and swear and drink together. London's laws of about 1000 (IV Æthelred) already name the emperor's men. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum ii.20. Alpert of Metz: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum (about 1021-1024).

later.text: Alpert wrote about 1021-1024 and disapproved of them.

pages.title: Norsemen cut wood with iron tools at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland (dated to the year)
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 1021: Norsemen cut wood with iron tools at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland (dated to the year).
pages.game: In the game: evidence of the Norse in America: the camp is used only a few years. It is felt in: Greenland. In the chronicle it stands under “evidence”: a date from archaeology or coins, not a recorded event.
pages.known: In 1021: Norsemen cut wood with iron tools at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland (dated to the year). The first exact year for Europeans in the Americas. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: dendrochronology and the cosmic-ray event of 993 (Kuitems et al. 2021). dendrochronology: dated by tree rings.

pages.title: Cnut at Rome for Conrad II's crowning wins lower tolls and safe passage for English and Danish merchants and pilgrims on the roads to Rome

It is felt in: Italy, Southern England, Jutland, the Danish isles, the Rhineland and Provence and the Rhone. In the chronicle it stands under “treaty”: a peace, truce, pact or tribute agreed.
pages.known: On 26 March 1027: Cnut at Rome for Conrad II's crowning wins lower tolls and safe passage for English and Danish merchants and pilgrims on the roads to Rome. Easter Day. The letter says the emperor, the pope, King Rudolf and the princes agreed to it. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Cnut's letter to the English (1027); ASC (D/E) 1031 (=1027); Wipo, Gesta Chuonradi 16. Cnut's letter: Cnut's letter to the English of 1027 (in John of Worcester and William of Malmesbury). ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Wipo: Wipo, Gesta Chuonradi imperatoris (about 1046).

pages.known: In 1028: Cnut sails to Norway with fifty ships, drives out King Olaf Haraldsson and is taken as king. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (E) 1028; Snorri, Heimskringla: Óláfs saga helga. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

pages.title: Battle of Stiklestad: Olaf Haraldsson, back from Russia, is killed by the farmers' army; soon he is held a saint
pages.hint: A day that has not come

pages.known: On 29 July 1030: Battle of Stiklestad: Olaf Haraldsson, back from Russia, is killed by the farmers' army; soon he is held a saint. Sighvatr's poem tells of the sun darkening, usually taken as the eclipse of 31 August 1030. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D) 1030; Sighvatr Þórðarson, Erfidrápa; Snorri, Heimskringla: Óláfs saga helga. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Sighvatr Þórðarson, Erfidrápa: Sighvatr's memorial poem for St Olaf (skaldic verse, 1030s-1040s). Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

pages.known: On 30 November 1031: The caliphate of Cordoba is abolished; al-Andalus breaks up into the taifa kingdoms. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH 422. Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan AH: Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan al-mughrib, by hijri year.

pages.known: On 12 November 1035: Cnut dies at Shaftesbury; his empire breaks up among his sons. The sources are sure of it.

pages.known: On 8 June 1042: Harthacnut dies at a wedding feast at Lambeth; Edward, son of Æthelred, is chosen king. 'As he stood at his drink.' The sources are sure of it.

pages.title: The last Rus attack on Constantinople, under Vladimir son of Yaroslav, is beaten with Greek fire and storms

pages.known: In the summer of 1043: The last Rus attack on Constantinople, under Vladimir son of Yaroslav, is beaten with Greek fire and storms. It began with a quarrel in which a Rus merchant was killed. The sources are sure of it.

pages.title: Battle of Lyrskov Heath near Hedeby: King Magnus of Norway and Denmark crushes a great army of Wends

pages.known: On 28 September 1043: Battle of Lyrskov Heath near Hedeby: King Magnus of Norway and Denmark crushes a great army of Wends. Michaelmas eve. The site is usually put at Lürschau, north of Schleswig (?). The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Adam of Bremen ii.79; Snorri, Heimskringla: Magnúss saga góða. Adam of Bremen: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter. pages.source: Adam of Bremen iii; Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar. Adam of Bremen: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter. pages.brief: In 1050: Harald Hardrada burns Hedeby from end to end.
pages.game: In the game: Sliesthorp burned: its trade shifts across the Schlei to Schleswig. It happens at or near Sliesthorp. It is felt in: Schleswig. In the chronicle it stands under “burning”: a town, port or fort burned (by raiders, accident or lightning).
pages.known: In 1050: Harald Hardrada burns Hedeby from end to end. Dated 1049 or 1050 from the skalds' verses; the archaeology agrees that Hedeby declined in the 11th century. It is likely, not certain.
pages.source: Þorleikr fagri, flokkr on Sweyn; Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar. Þorleikr fagri: skaldic verse on Sweyn Estridsen (11th century), quoted by Snorri. Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

pages.title: Cardinal Humbert lays a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the churches of Rome and Constantinople split
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 16 July 1054: Cardinal Humbert lays a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the churches of Rome and Constantinople split.
pages.game: In the game: news only: the Latin and Greek churches estranged; Latin merchants' churches at Constantinople closed. It is felt in: Byzantium and Italy. In the chronicle it stands under “church”: a church privilege, pallium or refuge.
pages.known: On 16 July 1054: Cardinal Humbert lays a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the churches of Rome and Constantinople split. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Commemoratio brevis (Humbert); Edictum synodale (Keroularios)

pages.title: Edward the Confessor dies; Harold Godwinson is crowned king the next day
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 5 January 1066: Edward the Confessor dies; Harold Godwinson is crowned king the next day.
pages.game: In the game: a new king: Duke William of Normandy and Harald Hardrada both claim England; ships and men gathered all summer. It happens at or near Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens, Western Mercia and Northumbria. In the chronicle it stands under “death”: the death of a ruler, lord or prelate (who rules a port may change).
pages.known: On 5 January 1066: Edward the Confessor dies; Harold Godwinson is crowned king the next day. The place: Westminster. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; Vita Ædwardi regis. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Vita Ædwardi regis: the life of Edward the Confessor (about 1067).

pages.title: A great comet (Halley's comet) seen for a week from 24 April
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 24 April 1066: A great comet (Halley's comet) seen for a week from 24 April.
pages.game: In the game: news only: an omen everywhere; men wonder what it foretells. It is news only: it moves no price and shuts no port. In the chronicle it stands under “portent”: a sign in the sky or a marvel: comets, auroras, rains of blood.
pages.known: On 24 April 1066: A great comet (Halley's comet) seen for a week from 24 April. 'On the eve of the Greater Litany'. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; Bayeux Tapestry. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. Bayeux Tapestry: the embroidered account of 1066 (about 1070).

pages.title: After the Obodrite prince Gottschalk is killed, the Slavs rise, burn Hamburg and sack Schleswig
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: In 1066: After the Obodrite prince Gottschalk is killed, the Slavs rise, burn Hamburg and sack Schleswig.
pages.game: In the game: raid on Sliesthorp: the old town finished; Schleswig on the north shore carries on its trade. It happens at or near Sliesthorp and Reric. It is felt in: Schleswig, the Wends and Saxony. In the chronicle it stands under “raid”: a raid or piracy from the sea or by land: plunder, captives, burning.
pages.known: In 1066: After the Obodrite prince Gottschalk is killed, the Slavs rise, burn Hamburg and sack Schleswig. Gottschalk was killed on 7 June 1066. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: Adam of Bremen iii.50-51. Adam of Bremen: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter.

pages.title: Harald Hardrada and Tostig beat the northern earls at Fulford, then are killed by King Harold at Stamford Bridge; 24 ships of 300 take the survivors home
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 25 September 1066: Harald Hardrada and Tostig beat the northern earls at Fulford, then are killed by King Harold at Stamford Bridge; 24 ships of 300 take the survivors home.
pages.game: In the game: Eoforwic gave hostages to the Norwegians after Fulford; no Norse king tries to conquer England again. It happens at or near Eoforwic. It is felt in: Northumbria, Western Norway and Shetland and Orkney. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 25 September 1066: Harald Hardrada and Tostig beat the northern earls at Fulford, then are killed by King Harold at Stamford Bridge; 24 ships of 300 take the survivors home. Fulford was on 20 September. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; John of Worcester 1066; Snorri, Heimskringla: Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. John of Worcester: John of Worcester's Chronicle (12th century, from older sources). Snorri, Heimskringla: Snorri Sturluson's lives of the kings of Norway (about 1230), by saga; late, drawing on skaldic verse.

pages.title: Duke William of Normandy lands at Pevensey and builds a castle at Hastings
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 28 September 1066: Duke William of Normandy lands at Pevensey and builds a castle at Hastings.
pages.game: In the game: the Sussex coast ravaged by the Norman army. It happens at or near Dofras. It is felt in: Southern England and Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “war”: a war, siege or conquest that closes or changes routes and borders.
pages.known: On 28 September 1066: Duke William of Normandy lands at Pevensey and builds a castle at Hastings. Michaelmas eve. The fleet had waited at Saint-Valery-sur-Somme for a wind. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D) 1066; William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi ii; Bayeux Tapestry. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. William of Poitiers: William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi (about 1071-1077). Bayeux Tapestry: the embroidered account of 1066 (about 1070).

pages.title: Battle of Hastings: King Harold is killed and the English army destroyed by Duke William
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 14 October 1066: Battle of Hastings: King Harold is killed and the English army destroyed by Duke William.
pages.game: In the game: England open to the Normans: Dover and Canterbury submit; London holds out until December. It happens at or near Dofras and Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England and Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “battle”: a battle or fight on a named day or place.
pages.known: On 14 October 1066: Battle of Hastings: King Harold is killed and the English army destroyed by Duke William. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D) 1066; William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi ii; Bayeux Tapestry. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. William of Poitiers: William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi (about 1071-1077). Bayeux Tapestry: the embroidered account of 1066 (about 1070).

pages.title: William of Normandy crowned king of England at Westminster on Christmas Day
pages.hint: A day that has not come
pages.brief: On 25 December 1066: William of Normandy crowned king of England at Westminster on Christmas Day.
pages.game: In the game: England joined to Normandy: its trade turns towards Rouen and France; the end of the Viking Age in England. It happens at or near Lundenwic. It is felt in: Southern England, East Anglia and the Fens, Western Mercia, Northumbria and Neustria. In the chronicle it stands under “accession”: a ruler or prelate takes power or is crowned.
pages.known: On 25 December 1066: William of Normandy crowned king of England at Westminster on Christmas Day. The sources are sure of it.
pages.source: ASC (D) 1066; William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi ii. ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, manuscript letters in brackets; '794 (=796)' = filed under 794, really 796. William of Poitiers: William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi (about 1071-1077).

pages.source: Latin: Alcuin, ep. 16, MGH Epp. IV p. 42 (check). English: the game's own draft.

pages.known: Written down: the E text c. 1121 copying older annals; the D and E texts carry this entry. Where it stands: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, MS E (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 636), annal 793; English: J. A. Giles (London: Bohn, 1847). The English is by J. A. Giles, 1847.
